pages.title: Ravenclaw
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Ravenclaw Tower, on the west side of the castle
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Ravenclaw is one of the four houses of Hogwarts, founded by Rowena Ravenclaw for 'the quick of wit'. Its colours are blue and bronze; its emblem is the eagle. Through the early 1990s it was the strongest of the houses standing between Slytherin and Gryffindor. In 1992 it finished second for the House Cup, and it beat Gryffindor at Quidditch that year.

Founder and history

The house is named after Rowena Ravenclaw, the tall, proud girl from the glens of Scotland who thought nothing worth knowing that could not be written down in a book. She was one of the four founders whom Gandalf brought together in the mud on the crag above the lake in 990. She once argued with him all night and lost. It was the only time, she said, that any man had won an argument with her.

When Ambrose Greyhame came up to the castle in December 1992, he saw the jewelled hourglasses that keep the house points in the Entrance Hall and laughed out loud. That, he said at once, would have been Rowena's idea: 'Make a competition of it, and then make sure everybody wins something.'

Her daughter Helena, the Grey Lady, haunts the castle as the Ravenclaw ghost. Rowena owned a diadem that was said to enhance the wisdom of its wearer. It passed out of the knowledge of the wizarding world after Helena stole it and fled to Albania. Moaning Myrtle, who died in the second-floor bathroom in 1943 when the Chamber of Secrets was opened, was a Ravenclaw.

In 1971 John Constantine, a Slytherin, was going out with a Ravenclaw girl whose laugh carried right across the Great Hall. Lucius Malfoy had wanted her for a year. The quarrel ended the two boys' friendship, with a duel and then a fistfight in a fourth-floor corridor.

Traits

The Sorting Hat's song promises that 'in Ravenclaw the quick of wit will find their kindred kind'. The house prizes intelligence, learning, wisdom and wit. Its pupils are known for their love of books, and for their originality of mind. The words carved in its common room are 'Wit beyond measure is man's greatest treasure'. In 1992 the Hat warned that Ravenclaw's cleverness, like every house's virtue, can be turned to evil in the wrong hands.

John Constantine, at eleven, took Ravenclaw to be the house for the clever ones, and fully expected to be sorted into it. Hermione Granger, before her own Sorting, thought Ravenclaw would be all right too.

Colours and emblem

Ravenclaw's colours are blue and bronze. Its emblem is an eagle, and its element is air. Its hourglass in the Entrance Hall is filled with sapphires. At the March 1994 match against Gryffindor, the Ravenclaw team stood in the middle of the pitch, a block of blue against the grass.

Head of house

Filius Flitwick, the tiny Charms master, is Head of Ravenclaw. In 1991 he knew of the special circumstances behind Harry's broomstick. In 1994, after Sirius Black's second break-in, he spent a morning on a stool in the Entrance Hall, holding up a poster of Black until the oak front doors had learnt the face. He kept the captured Black in his office, and Black escaped from it through a D'ni linking book.

He secretly paid a pupil's nine-Galleon debt in 1994, then shamed the boy, Hobday, over two Sickles. He remembers the long feud between Bellatrix and Narcissa Black in his Charms classes in the 1970s.

House ghost

The Ravenclaw ghost is the Grey Lady: tall, pale and beautiful, in a high-collared gown. She rarely speaks to anyone. Her favourite window is on a landing near the top of a tower. There, in December 1992, she recognised Ambrose Greyhame as the man who had come to her mother when she was very small.

Common room

The Ravenclaw common room is at the top of Ravenclaw Tower, on the west side of the castle, up a spiral staircase. Its door has no handle and no keyhole. There is only a bronze knocker in the shape of an eagle, which asks a riddle of anyone who wants to come in. A sensible answer opens the door, so that nobody gets in without thinking.

The room is wide and circular. Silks of blue and bronze hang on its walls. Arched windows look out over the grounds to the mountains. The domed ceiling is painted with stars, and the carpet matches it. In a niche opposite the door stands a tall statue of Rowena Ravenclaw in white marble, wearing her diadem.

Notable members in the saga

Penelope Clearwater is the curly-haired prefect whom Harry and Ron met by mistake in the Entrance Hall at Christmas 1992. She was Petrified near the library in 1993, and she was secretly going out with Percy Weasley. In 1994 she bet him ten Galleons on the Ravenclaw against Gryffindor match, and lost.

Cho Chang, the house's small, quick Seeker, stuck to Harry like glue in 1994. Roger Davies, the captain in 1993 to 1994, was a big fifth-year built like a rower. Terry Boot, Mandy Brocklehurst and Lisa Turpin were sorted into Ravenclaw in Harry's year, in 1991, along with Padma Patil. Among earlier generations the house counts Moaning Myrtle and the Grey Lady herself.

House Cup and Quidditch Cup by year

1991 to 1992: Ravenclaw finished second for the House Cup with 426 points. Gryffindor won with 472; Slytherin had 372, and Hufflepuff 352. At Quidditch, Ravenclaw ended the season by steamrollering Gryffindor, whose Seeker was in the hospital wing.

1992 to 1993: Ravenclaw cheered against Slytherin at the November match and joined in Dean Thomas's chant from the Gryffindor stand. Quidditch was suspended in the spring, and no Cup was played for. Gryffindor won the House Cup.

1993 to 1994: Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff at the end of November, Cho Chang taking the Snitch from Cedric Diggory like a thrown dart. In January it lost narrowly to Slytherin, having led for an hour; Dracina Malfoy took the Snitch at the Ravenclaw end with about four inches to spare. In March it led Gryffindor 30 to 10, and later it closed the gap to 80 to 70. Then Harry caught the Snitch, and Gryffindor won 230 to 70. Gryffindor took both cups.

In the saga

At the House Cup feast in 1992 the Ravenclaws enjoyed Slytherin's defeat as much as everybody else. Earlier that year, like the rest of the school, they had turned on Harry when he lost Gryffindor a hundred and fifty points, since everyone had wanted to see Slytherin lose the Cup for once.

In 1992 a big Ravenclaw sixth-year leaned over the barrier to tell Dean Thomas that football was a game in which nobody scored, and nearly came to blows with him. During the scare of spring 1993, a Ravenclaw first-year burst into tears in the Charms corridor because somebody had dropped a book behind her.

On Hallowe'en night 1993, when the school slept in the Great Hall after Black's first break-in, the Ravenclaws came down clutching books they had no intention of reading. Early in 1994 Harry found a Ravenclaw sixth-year lying flat on the gravel with a lantern, testing a fleece twice over. The Ravenclaws applauded good play even against their own side. At the 1994 final the house, which usually stayed out of things, stood up to shout at the Slytherins.

pages.html:
Slytherin is one of the four houses of Hogwarts. Salazar Slytherin founded it for the ambitious and for the cunning, 'who leave no means behind'. Its colours are green and silver. Its emblem is a serpent, after its founder's gift for talking to snakes. It is the house of Dracina Malfoy, of every Malfoy before her, of its head, Severus Snape, and of Tom Riddle. It held the House Cup six years running until 1991, then lost it to Gryffindor in each of the three years that followed.

Founder and history

The house is named for Salazar Slytherin, the dark, clever, watchful young man from the fens who spoke to the adders in the reed-beds and trusted nobody, with good reason. He was one of the four founders whom Gandalf brought together on the crag above the lake to build the school, which opened in 990. He mistrusted the Muggle-born, and wished the school to be more particular about whom it took. He kept a Basilisk, which he set on the Muggles when they came against the castle. Godric Gryffindor would not abide it. Over that the two friends fell out past mending, and Slytherin left the school. Before he went, he built the Chamber of Secrets deep beneath the castle and left the Basilisk sleeping in it, sealed so that only his true heir could open it. Legend says he meant his heir to purge the school of the unworthy.

The Sorting Hat, which knew him, insists that he was never evil. He was difficult, proud and suspicious, with good reason, given what had been done to people like him before the four founders came together. He would never have stood for evil in his house. Dumbledore told Harry Potter in 1993 that there is no inherent evil in Slytherin. All the same, a great many dark witches and wizards have come out of it. Chief among them is Tom Riddle, Slytherin's last living descendant. Riddle opened the Chamber in his fifth year, in 1943, and a Muggle-born girl died.

In the 1960s the house was ruled by the old pure-blood families. A Muggle-born in Slytherin was almost unheard of when the Hat sent John Constantine there in 1964 for his cunning, almost before it had touched his hair. Minutes later it sorted his new friend Lucius Malfoy, then a stammering boy, into the same house. For seven years the house persecuted Constantine for his birth. They locked him out of the common room and hung his robes from the Astronomy Tower. Meanwhile Lucius drifted towards the circle that became the Death Eaters. The two of them ended their schooldays with a duel and a fistfight over a Ravenclaw girl.

The Black sisters, Bellatrix and Narcissa, were in the house from 1971 to 1978. James Potter and Lily Evans were in their year, as was Severus Snape, a Slytherin like them.

From 1986 to 1991 Slytherin won the House Cup six years running. In 1991 Nearly Headless Nick complained that the Bloody Baron was becoming insufferable.

Traits

The Sorting Hat's song of 1991 promised that 'in Slytherin the cunning thrive, who leave no means behind'. In 1992 the Hat told Harry that Slytherin takes the ambitious and the cunning. There is nothing wicked in either quality in itself, it said, though both are common enough in wicked men, as common as Gryffindor's courage or Ravenclaw's cleverness. Dumbledore listed the qualities Salazar Slytherin prized in his students as Parseltongue, resourcefulness, determination and a certain disregard for rules. The Hat found in Harry pain, a need to prove himself, drive and resolve, all of them traits that Slytherin prized. Of all the minds it had sat on, it said, his reminded it most of Slytherin's.

The house has long been bound up with blood and lineage. Every Malfoy has been sorted into it. As a boy, John Constantine took it for the house of 'the posh ones with the long family trees'.

Colours and emblem

Slytherin's colours are green and silver. Its emblem is a serpent, chosen for Salazar Slytherin's gift for talking to snakes. Its element is water, and its hourglass in the Entrance Hall holds emeralds. At the end-of-year feast in June 1992 the Great Hall was hung in green and silver, with an enormous serpent banner behind the High Table. Slytherin expected its seventh House Cup in a row, until Dumbledore changed the decorations to Gryffindor's. Dracina Malfoy wears an heirloom serpent brooch of silver and green.

Head of house

Severus Snape, the Potions master, is Head of Slytherin. He has never once pretended to be fair about it. Dracina Malfoy can get away with anything in his dungeon, and Harry has claimed that the Slytherins only put up with Snape because he fixes their marks. Still, he is more than a partisan. He took five points from his own house after the troll in 1991. In 1993 he rebuked Dracina for speaking of Professor McGonagall without respect. He warned Harry and Dracina that friendships had ended over a single word. When Dracina came to him in tears in 1994, he told her she still had a chance to do something rather than merely say something. By then he had been her Head of House for nearly three years.

House ghost

The Slytherin ghost is the Bloody Baron, a gaunt figure with blank, staring eyes and robes stained with silver blood. He is the only one at Hogwarts who can control Peeves. At the start-of-term feast in 1991 he sat beside Dracina Malfoy. She edged away from him an inch at a time as his ghostly blood dripped on to the bench.

Common room

The Slytherin common room lies deep in the dungeons, at the end of a maze of passages that branch and wind back on themselves. Its entrance is a stretch of bare, damp stone wall, in which a door slides open to the password. At Christmas 1992 the password was 'Pureblood'. The room was dug out of the bedrock beneath the castle and lies under the black lake. Its walls are rough stone beaded with damp, and the ceiling hangs low. Lamps of thick green glass swing on long iron links and give a light the colour of pondweed, so that the room seems to be under water.

A fire burns in a vast stone hearth, beneath a mantelpiece carved into a row of grinning skulls with serpents winding through their eye sockets. A woven hanging on the far wall shows a long-dead witch in green doing something extremely unpleasant. There are high-backed chairs by the fire and chains on the walls. Stairs lead up to the dormitories, where the four-posters are hung with green silk.

Harry thought the place seemed designed to prove every unkind thing ever said about the house. Snape called it a warren in 1993. Some forty students were in it when Dracina walked through it dripping mud in March 1994.

Notable members in the saga

Dracina Malfoy, sorted in 1991, has been the house's Seeker since 1992. Vincent Crabbe and Gregory Goyle are her minders. Pansy Parkinson is her friend and her shadow; in 1994 she confessed to posting Dracina's letter about Buckbeak to Lucius Malfoy. Millicent Bulstrode, Blaise Zabini, Theodore Nott and Daphne Greengrass are of the same year. Marcus Flint captained the 1994 side and played Chaser alongside Montague. The Beaters were Bole and Derrick.

Of earlier generations there was Tom Riddle, who was Head Boy and opened the Chamber in 1943. Lucius Malfoy and John Constantine were both sorted in 1964. The Black sisters, Bellatrix and Narcissa, came after them, with Severus Snape in the same year.

House Cup and Quidditch Cup by year

1986 to 1991: Slytherin won the House Cup six years running.

1991 to 1992: Slytherin lost to Gryffindor 170 to 60 in November, when Marcus Flint's foul and a jinxed broom nearly threw Harry off. At the end-of-year feast it led the House Cup with 472 points. Dumbledore's last-minute awards brought Gryffindor level with it. Then he took a hundred points from Slytherin for Dracina Malfoy's trespass in the Gryffindor common room. Slytherin finished third with 372, ahead of Hufflepuff (352) but behind Ravenclaw (426) and Gryffindor (472).

1992 to 1993: Dracina became Seeker. Lucius Malfoy gave the team seven Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones. Slytherin lost to Gryffindor in November, when Harry caught the Snitch from just above Dracina's head with a broken arm. Quidditch was suspended in the spring, and Gryffindor won the House Cup again.

1993 to 1994: Slytherin withdrew from the opening match against Gryffindor, citing Dracina's injured arm. Flint had engineered it so that Gryffindor would have to face Hufflepuff in a storm. In January Slytherin beat Ravenclaw by a whisker, Dracina taking the Snitch with about four inches to spare. In March the house lost fifty points when Dracina, Crabbe, Goyle and Flint dressed as dementors at the Ravenclaw match. It went into the final at the top of the Quidditch table, two hundred points clear. It lost the final 230 to 20, and the Cup with it. Gryffindor won the House Championship.

In the saga

In 1991 Harry, who had feared above everything that the Hat would put him in Slytherin, thought the Slytherin table looked well fed and pleased with itself, like Dudley. Dracina went there the moment the Hat touched her. In 1992 to 1993 every Slytherin escaped the Basilisk's attacks, which Lee Jordan took as proof of the house's guilt. In fact the Heir's work was done through a possessed Slytherin girl, Dracina herself. At Christmas 1992 Harry and Ron got into the common room by Polyjuice Potion, Harry disguised as Goyle, Ron as Crabbe.

In 1993 to 1994 the Slytherins gloated after Gryffindor's defeat in November. They drummed their goblets at the news of Buckbeak's sentence, and they hissed at the Gryffindor team in the Great Hall before the final. During the final Dracina followed Harry's feint although she had already seen the Snitch. She let a Bludger meant for him hit her. Once Gryffindor were sixty points clear, she dived where he could not miss her. She had let him win. After Sirius Black's escape the Slytherin table was bitter, sulky and defeated. The wildest theories about the escape came from there.

pages.title: House Cup
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Four great hourglasses of jewels in the Entrance Hall
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The House Cup is given every year to whichever Hogwarts house has the most points when the school year ends. Points are won for good work and lost for broken rules. The running totals are kept in four great hourglasses of jewels in the Entrance Hall, where everybody can see them. Slytherin won the Cup six years running up to 1991. Gryffindor took it off them in 1992, then kept it through 1993 and 1994.

How it works

Professor McGonagall explains the Cup to every new intake before the Sorting. Successes win points for a house, she tells them, while broken rules lose them. Whichever house has the most points at the end of the year receives the House Cup, which is a considerable honour. Teachers can give points or take them away, and so can prefects. The Headmaster may make last-minute awards at the end-of-year feast, and a house's Quidditch results count towards its total as well. For the feast the Great Hall is hung with the winning house's colours.

Each house's points are shown in a giant hourglass in the Entrance Hall: rubies for Gryffindor, emeralds for Slytherin, sapphires for Ravenclaw and yellow diamonds for Hufflepuff. When Ambrose Greyhame saw them in 1992, he took them at once for Rowena Ravenclaw's idea: make a competition of it, and then make sure everybody wins something.

Winners

1986 to 1991: Slytherin, six years in a row. For nearly seven years Gryffindor could not get ahead of Slytherin in the house championship at all. It managed it at last early in 1992, by beating Hufflepuff at Quidditch.

1991 to 1992: Gryffindor. Before Dumbledore's last-minute awards the totals stood at Slytherin 472, Ravenclaw 426, Hufflepuff 352 and Gryffindor 312. Dumbledore then gave fifty points to Ron Weasley for the best-played game of chess in many years. Hermione Granger had fifty for cool logic in the face of fire. Harry Potter had sixty, for pure nerve, outstanding courage and the will to destroy evil. That brought Gryffindor level with Slytherin at 472. After that he took a hundred points from Slytherin, because Dracina Malfoy had entered the Gryffindor common room, which is an expellable offence, though he said he sympathised with her wish to make amends. The final order was Gryffindor 472, Ravenclaw 426, Slytherin 372 and Hufflepuff 352. It was Gryffindor's first Cup in seven years.

1992 to 1993: Gryffindor, for the second year running. Harry's catch against Slytherin in November put the house on top. It was settled by the Special Awards for Services to the School that Harry and Ron received after the Chamber of Secrets, worth two hundred points each.

1993 to 1994: Gryffindor, for the third year running, chiefly on the strength of its win over Slytherin in the Quidditch final.

1994 to 1995: not yet begun in late August 1994.

Points won and lost

In September 1991 Snape took two points from Gryffindor in Harry's very first Potions lesson. In December he took five more, when Ron grabbed Dracina's robes. After the troll at Hallowe'en 1991, Hermione and Dracina each lost their house five points. Both of them had lied to protect Harry and Ron. In the spring of 1992 Professor McGonagall took fifty points each from Harry, Hermione and Neville Longbottom for being out of bed on the night of Norbert the dragon. It dropped Gryffindor from first place to last and made Harry the most hated boy in the school.

In 1992 to 1993 Professor McGonagall took no points for the flying car, because term had not yet begun. Gryffindor lost twenty points when Harry mocked Filch's parentage. It lost ten in Potions, five to Percy Weasley and twenty more for Dean Thomas's second chant at the Slytherin match. It gained fifty for Harry's catch.

In 1993 to 1994 Harry's cauldron boiled over in Potions, and so did Dracina's. Snape docked each of their houses ten points. Gryffindor lost sixty points in a single Potions lesson after Ron threw a crocodile heart into Dracina's face. Slytherin lost fifty for the fake dementors at the Ravenclaw match.

Snape has seen Dracina Malfoy weep over house points.

pages.title: Quidditch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Seven a side: three Chasers, two Beaters, a Keeper, a Seeker
10 points a goal; 150 for the Snitch
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Quidditch is the great sport of the wizarding world, played on broomsticks by two teams of seven. At Hogwarts each house fields a team, and the four of them compete every year for the Quidditch Cup. Harry Potter has played Seeker for Gryffindor since 1991, and Dracina Malfoy for Slytherin since 1992.

Rules

The game is played over an oval pitch, with three hoops on fifty-foot poles at each end. Each side has three Chasers, who pass the red Quaffle among themselves and score ten points for every goal they put through the other side's hoops. A Keeper defends the hoops. Two black Bludgers fly about of their own accord, trying to knock players off their brooms. Each side's two Beaters fend them off with bats, driving them at the enemy instead.

The Seeker hunts the Golden Snitch, a winged golden ball no bigger than a walnut. Catching it ends the match. It is worth a hundred and fifty points, which nearly always decides the result. A match ends only when the Snitch is caught. The longest is said to have lasted three months, with substitutes brought on so that the players could sleep.

Seekers are usually the smallest and fastest players on a team. Most of the game's serious accidents happen to them, and they are fouled more than anybody else. There are seven hundred ways of committing a foul, every one of which was committed in a single World Cup match in 1473. Players cannot be sent off. Attacking the Keeper is illegal unless the Quaffle is within the scoring area.

People very rarely die playing. Referees, however, have been known to vanish in the middle of a match and turn up months later in the Sahara Desert. Every one of them, a footnote in Quidditch Through the Ages records, had been having trouble at home with his wife. At Hogwarts the Bludgers have never killed anyone.

History

The game takes its name from Queerditch Marsh, where it was first played, and it is very old. For more than a thousand years the English argued with the French over its rules, now and then settling the matter with wands. The Snitch descends from the Golden Snidget, a bird that was once released for the Seeker to catch, until hunting it was banned. The ball that replaced it was invented by Bowman Wright, a metal-charmer of Godric's Hollow. The Quidditch World Cup has been played since the fifteenth century.

In 1877 a dispute over the proper weight of a Quaffle, between the England manager, Francis Grail, and the French manager, Juste Valmond, ended in a duel. The duel left two hundred witches and wizards dead in the crossfire; the casualty list in Quidditch Through the Ages runs to three pages. The matter was finally settled when every national team agreed to play by the Austrian rules from 1901 onwards.

At Hogwarts

Each house team is picked by its captain at trials early in the autumn term. First-years are not normally allowed brooms of their own, or places on a team. When Professor McGonagall put Harry Potter on the Gryffindor side in 1991, he became the youngest house player in about a century. McGonagall herself played for Gryffindor in her schooldays.

Madam Hooch referees. In the early 1990s Lee Jordan commentated, under McGonagall's close supervision. The season builds through the winter to a final in the summer term, and the Headmaster presents the Quidditch Cup on the pitch. A house's results also count towards the House Cup.

From 1991 the Gryffindor stand, led by Dean Thomas, a West Ham supporter, took up football-style chanting. The other houses learnt to join in, and Hufflepuff learnt to answer back. In 1992 a Ravenclaw sixth-year told Dean that football was the game in which they kicked a ball about for ninety minutes and nobody scored.

Brooms matter a great deal. McGonagall gave Harry a Nimbus Two Thousand in 1991. In 1992 Lucius Malfoy bought the Slytherin team seven Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones. In 1994 the Ravenclaws flew Cleansweep Sevens. Harry's Nimbus was smashed by the Whomping Willow in November 1993. At Christmas it was replaced by an anonymous Firebolt, the best broom in the world, which Sirius Black later admitted he had sent. While the Firebolt was being checked for jinxes, Dracina lent Harry her spare Nimbus Two Thousand and One.

The Hogwarts Cup, 1991 to 1994

1991 to 1992: Gryffindor beat Slytherin 170 to 60 in November. Quirrell jinxed Harry's broom during the match, and Harry caught the Snitch in his mouth. Under Snape's refereeing, Gryffindor then beat Hufflepuff in about five minutes. With Harry in the hospital wing after the Philosopher's Stone, it was steamrollered by Ravenclaw in its last match.

1992 to 1993: Gryffindor beat Slytherin in November, in the rain. A rogue Bludger, bewitched by Dobby, broke Harry's right elbow, and Harry caught the Snitch above Dracina's head with his arm broken. Dracina had thrown her own broom in front of the Bludger to shield him. The tournament was cancelled in the spring, on the morning of Gryffindor's match against Hufflepuff, when Hermione Granger and Penelope Clearwater were Petrified.

1993 to 1994: Slytherin withdrew from the opening match. In a November hurricane Hufflepuff beat Gryffindor by a hundred points, after more than a hundred dementors flooded the pitch and Harry fell fifty feet. Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff. Slytherin beat Ravenclaw narrowly. In March Gryffindor beat Ravenclaw 230 to 70, with Harry driving off false dementors with his first solid Patronus.

Gryffindor needed to beat Slytherin by more than two hundred points in the final. It was leading 80 to 20 when Harry knocked Dracina's arm aside at the bottom of her dive and caught the Snitch. Gryffindor won 230 to 20, taking the Cup for the first time in seven years, its first since Charlie Weasley's time as Seeker. Dracina had let him win.

Beyond Hogwarts

Ron Weasley supports the Chudley Cannons, and his bedroom at the Burrow is covered in their orange posters. The Quidditch World Cup final of 1994, Ireland against Bulgaria, is to be played on a Monday night in August. Arthur Weasley got tickets, and in August 1994 Molly Weasley invited Harry to come with them. Ron was a bit miffed that England had not brought the Cup home this time.

pages.title: Chocolate Frog
infobox: Chocolate Frogs; Famous Witches and Wizards cards
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A Famous Witches and Wizards card
On the Hogwarts Express; at Honeydukes; at Gringotts
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Chocolate Frogs are wizarding sweets: frogs of chocolate, sold in packets on the Hogwarts Express, at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade and from the trolley at Gringotts. They are not real frogs. Each one comes with a collectable Famous Witches and Wizards card, whose moving portrait can wander out of its frame.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the train, Harry asked whether they were real frogs. They were not. His first card was Albus Dumbledore, who strolled off and left the picture empty. In Chapter Eight Hermione gave Harry a big box for Christmas 1991. In Chapter Nine he gave the last of them to Neville Longbottom, who had just been hit with a Leg-Locker Curse by Dracina Malfoy. ‘You’re worth twelve of Malfoy,’ said Harry.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry bought Mrs Weasley a box from the trolley at Gringotts to thank her for everything. For some reason it very nearly made her cry. She told him not to be so silly, then put it in her bag very carefully, as if it might break.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, a box of Chocolate Frogs stood by Dracina Malfoy’s bed in the hospital wing on 2 September 1993. Harry suspected that it had come from Daphne Greengrass. In Chapter Nine Ron bit the head off one after hearing how Angelus had been cursed. In Chapter Twelve Professor Lupin gave Harry a Chocolate Frog after he had fainted in front of the boggart. In Chapter Sixteen Percy confiscated three of Seamus Finnigan’s, and was later seen eating the last of them.

pages.title: Buttercup, custard, morning sun
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Buttercup, custard, morning sun, make this lazy rat a yellow one
pages.html:
'Buttercup, custard, morning sun, make this lazy rat a yellow one' is a rhyme that George Weasley gave his younger brother Ron, passing it off as a spell for turning a rat yellow. It is not a spell at all.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1991, Ron told Harry Potter that he had tried to turn Scabbers yellow the day before, to liven him up. It had not worked. He was about to show Harry when Hermione Granger came in, looking for Neville's toad, and asked to see. Ron cleared his throat, recited the rhyme and flourished his wand. Scabbers stayed grey. He went on sleeping. Hermione asked whether Ron was certain it was a proper spell.

When she had gone, Ron flung his wand back into his trunk. 'I don't care which house I get, as long as she's not in it,' he said. 'Rubbish spell. George gave it to me. I bet he knew it was a dud.'

pages.title: Modern Magical History
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Hermione Granger, before her first term
pages.html:
Modern Magical History is a history of the wizarding world in recent times. Harry Potter is in it, as the baby who survived Lord Voldemort's curse in 1981 and brought about his downfall. Harry himself had no idea of it until Hermione Granger told him.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1991, Hermione introduced herself to Harry and Ron Weasley in a single breath. When she heard Harry's name, she told him that she knew all about him. She had bought some extra books for background, which was how she knew that he was in Modern Magical History, The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts and Great Wizarding Events of the Twentieth Century. 'Am I?' said Harry faintly. Hermione was astonished that he did not know. She would have looked up every word, she said, if it had been her.

pages.title: The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts is a history of Dark magic and those who have practised it. Harry Potter is in it, for the night in 1981 when Lord Voldemort's curse failed to kill him and Voldemort fell.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express in September 1991, Hermione Granger told Harry that she knew all about him, because she had bought some extra books for background. He was in Modern Magical History, The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts and Great Wizarding Events of the Twentieth Century. 'Am I?' said Harry faintly. Hermione could hardly believe he did not know: she would have looked up every word, she said, if it had been her.

pages.title: Great Wizarding Events of the Twentieth Century
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The great events of the wizarding world since 1900
pages.html:
Great Wizarding Events of the Twentieth Century is a history of the great events of the wizarding world since 1900. Harry Potter is in it, because of what happened at Godric's Hollow on 31 October 1981, when Lord Voldemort's curse failed to kill him. Hermione Granger had read about him there before she ever met him.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1991, Hermione introduced herself to Harry and Ron Weasley. When she learnt who Harry was, she said she knew all about him. She had bought some extra books for background, and he was in three of them, this one among them. 'Am I?' said Harry faintly. 'Gracious, didn't you know?' said Hermione. 'I'd have looked up every word if it were me.'

pages.title: Hogwarts: A History
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
All out, with a two-week waiting list, after the first attack of 1992
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Hogwarts: A History is the standard history of Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Hermione Granger had read it before she ever set foot in the castle, and has been quoting it ever since. Almost nobody else reads it, except in emergencies.

Contents

The book covers the castle, its founders and its enchantments. It records that the ceiling of the Great Hall is bewitched to look like the sky outside. It describes the castle's defences, which forbid Apparition inside the grounds and make any stealthy entry very hard indeed. It tells the legend of the Chamber of Secrets. It also records that the Fat Friar, the Hufflepuff ghost, was a real friar before he died.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, on 1 September 1991, Harry Potter looked up from among the first years in the Great Hall and saw a ceiling of velvety black, scattered with stars. 'It's enchanted to look like the sky outside,' he heard Hermione whisper. 'I read about it in Hogwarts: A History.'

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after the first attack at Halloween 1992, every copy in the library was out, with a two-week waiting list, as the whole school looked up the legend of the Chamber.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, in September 1993, Hermione told Ron that the Fat Friar had been a real friar before he died: it was in Hogwarts: A History. In Chapter Nine, on the night Sirius Black broke in, the whole school slept in the Great Hall. When the others wondered how he had got in, Hermione lost patience. 'Honestly, am I the only person who's ever bothered to read Hogwarts: A History?' The castle had all sorts of enchantments on it to stop people entering by stealth, she explained. 'You can't just Apparate in here.'

pages.title: The Sorting Hat's song (1991)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Sorting of the new first years, 1 September 1991
That it had never yet been wrong
pages.html:
The Sorting Hat's song of 1991 was sung in the Great Hall at Hogwarts on 1 September 1991, just before the Hat sorted that year's first years, Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy among them. The Hat makes up a new song every year.

The song

The Hat began by owning that it was patched and plain, with a brim past its best. Show it a cleverer hat, it said, and it would eat its crest. Nothing in any head it had ever worn was hidden from it. Then it named the houses. Gryffindor was for the bold, the daring and the true. Hufflepuff took the fair of heart, who see a hard task through. The quick of wit belonged in Ravenclaw, while the cunning, who leave no means behind, thrived in Slytherin. It ended with a boast: ‘I've not been wrong to date.’

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, a tear near the Hat's brim opened like a mouth, and it burst into song. The Hall applauded, the Hat bowed to each table in turn, and Ron Weasley whispered that all they had to do was put on a hat. He was going to murder his brother Fred, who had kept on about wrestling a troll.

pages.title: The Hogwarts school song
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Conjured from Dumbledore's wand as a golden ribbon
pages.html:
The Hogwarts school song is the song of Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Every pupil sings it to his or her own favourite tune, reading the words off a long golden ribbon that Albus Dumbledore conjures from his wand, so that no two people finish at the same moment.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, at the start-of-term feast of 1991, Dumbledore called for the song before bed, and the other teachers' smiles went rather stiff. At a flick of Dumbledore's wand the ribbon rose above the tables and curled itself into words. Seamus Finnigan bawled it to something like a football chant, while Hermione Granger sang every word very precisely to a tune of her own. Fred and George Weasley finished last, to a very slow funeral march. Dumbledore conducted their final lines with his wand, then dabbed at his eyes and declared music a magic beyond anything taught at Hogwarts.

pages.title: Caput Draconis
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Caput Draconis was the password to the Gryffindor common room at the start of the school year in 1991. It is Latin for ‘dragon's head’.

The password

The common room lies behind the portrait of the Fat Lady, who swings forward only for those who give the right password. It is changed from time to time, and the prefects pass each new one on to the house.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, on the first night of term, Percy Weasley led the new Gryffindors up to the portrait and gave the password. It swung forward to show a round hole in the wall. They clambered through, Neville Longbottom with a leg-up.

pages.title: Blackpool pier
pages.html:
Blackpool pier stands out over the Irish Sea from the front at Blackpool, the Muggle seaside town on the Lancashire coast. Neville Longbottom's Great-uncle Algie once pushed him off the end of it, and he nearly drowned.

Great-uncle Algie

For years Neville's family were afraid that there was no magic in him at all. Great-uncle Algie kept trying to startle some out of him, and the pier was one of his attempts. It did not work.

Neville's magic showed itself at last when he was eight. Algie was dangling him out of an upstairs window by his ankles when Great-auntie Enid offered him a meringue, and he let go by accident. Neville bounced all the way down the garden and out into the road. When his Hogwarts letter came, Algie was so pleased that he bought Neville his toad, Trevor.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, at the start-of-term feast in 1991, Ron Weasley asked Neville about his family. Neville told him: 'He pushed me off the end of Blackpool pier once, and I nearly drowned.'

pages.title: Aurora Sinistra
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The top of the tallest tower
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Aurora Sinistra teaches Astronomy at Hogwarts. She holds her lessons at midnight, on top of the tallest tower. She is tall and severe, a witch of very few words.

Teaching

Astronomy is a core subject for the first five years. Every Wednesday at midnight Professor Sinistra's pupils climb the tallest tower with their telescopes. There they learn the names of the stars and the movements of the planets. She teaches that the phase of the moon affects almost all magic.

Her first lesson with Harry Potter's year, in 1991, covered twenty-two stars, the moons of Jupiter and the Plough. She made Harry draw the Plough three times. In June 1994 she supervised the midnight Astronomy exam, and told Dracina Malfoy that Jupiter lay in the opposite direction from Hagrid's cabin.

In the saga

In 1992 Sinistra had to sit through Gilderoy Lockhart's stories at the staff table. She helped Professor Flitwick carry the Petrified Justin Finch-Fletchley up to the hospital wing. After Dumbledore was suspended in 1993 she patrolled the corridors at night with the rest of the staff. At dinner on 2 September 1993 Snape sat talking with her, two seats away from the new Defence teacher, Remus Lupin.

pages.title: Cuthbert Binns
infobox: Hogwarts staff, Ghost, History of Magic, ghost, History of Magic teacher
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
In his sleep, in front of the staff-room fire
Many decades, in life and after death
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Cuthbert Binns is the ghost who teaches History of Magic at Hogwarts, and the only ghost on the staff. He was already very old, and very dull, when he fell asleep in front of the staff-room fire one evening. The next morning he got up to teach, leaving his body behind him in the armchair. In Ron Weasley's opinion he has not noticed yet.

His lessons

History of Magic is the dullest lesson on the timetable. Binns drifts into the classroom through the blackboard, opens his notes and reads from them in a thin, dry, wheezing voice, like a bath draining or a distant vacuum cleaner left running in an empty house. Inside a quarter of an hour the whole class has usually gone glassy. The most exciting thing that ever happens in his lessons is his arrival through the blackboard. He has the gift of making a war sound like a bus timetable.

He gives out the lists of who married whom among the old pure-blood houses, going back nine hundred years, in exactly the voice he uses for goblin rebellions, which is to say no voice at all. He sets compositions such as three feet on the Medieval Assembly of European Wizards, and lectures at length on the International Warlock Convention of 1289. He gets his pupils' names wrong: Hermione Granger has been Miss Grange to him, Seamus Finnigan O'Halloran and Parvati Patil Miss Pettigrew. Nobody has ever told him that he is dead. Harry Potter suspects that nobody dares get close enough, for fear of being bored to death.

He teaches history as though wizards and Muggles had always been enemies. He has no time for legend either: 'I deal in facts, Miss Granger. Not in myths and legends.'

His examinations are as dry as his lessons. The first-years' paper in the summer of 1992 was an hour on the war between the Norse völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London, which ended when the Anglo-Saxons took Jorvik in 954. Harry was rather proud of having got the date to stay in his head.

In the saga

In the autumn of 1992, in the middle of a remarkably dull account of the International Warlock Convention, Hermione Granger put up her hand. It seemed to be the first raised hand Binns had noticed in a century and a half. She asked him about the Chamber of Secrets. He told her he dealt in facts, not legends, but she asked again. The whole class was suddenly listening, which threw him completely, because he had never had an audience before.

So he told them, while insisting that it was nonsense. The four founders had raised the castle together, far from the eyes of the common people, in an age when magic was feared. Slytherin had wanted the school to be more particular in whom it took. In the end he fell out bitterly with Gryffindor, and left. That much, Binns said, the reliable sources would bear. His notes say nothing of the Basilisk, though Slytherin's use of it to defend the castle from Muggles was what the two founders had really quarrelled over. The rest was the legend of a hidden chamber that only Slytherin's true heir could open, with a horror inside it to cleanse the school of the unworthy. When Dean Thomas suggested that you might have to be related to Slytherin to open it, Binns had had enough: 'There is not one scrap of evidence that Slytherin ever built so much as a secret broom cupboard!' Within five minutes the class had sunk back into its usual stupor.

In 1994 his empty classroom, which smelt of a hundred years of chalk dust, was where Remus Lupin taught Harry the Patronus Charm on Thursday evenings. At the end of that school year Harry wrote his examination essay on the witch-burnings. He put in everything Florean Fortescue had taught him, together with the Fat Friar's belief that magic had been given to wizards for a reason. By the time Binns told them to put down their quills, Harry had covered both sides of four rolls of parchment and was starting on a fifth.

In the autumn of 1993, when Ron wanted him to do Hermione's voice, Harry made a joke of how Binns had died: 'I can't do the voice, nobody can do the voice. Binns tried once. It's why he died.'

In their own words

I deal in facts, Miss Granger. Not in myths and legends.Professor Binns · B2 Ch10

pages.title: Filius Flitwick
infobox: Hogwarts staff, Charms, Charms teacher, Ravenclaw
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Teaching by 1971; still on the staff
Top of the West Tower, seventh floor
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Filius Flitwick is the Charms master at Hogwarts and Head of Ravenclaw House. He is a tiny wizard with a shock of white hair, who has to stand on a pile of books to see over his desk. Once a champion duellist, he is a cheerful, squeaky and unexpectedly shrewd teacher, who has now taught Charms to two generations of Potters.

Background

Flitwick is so small that Harry wondered, on first sight of him, whether he had goblin blood. He does have goblin ancestry. As a younger man he duelled for his living, and was a champion at it.

He was teaching Charms by the 1970s. In those years the dark Bellatrix Black and her fair-haired sister Narcissa feuded across his classroom over a boy with untidy black hair. Their hexes sent him to hide behind his desk. It went on until Lily Evans came along, and neither sister ever quite forgave anybody. He still shudders to remember it.

His office is a small study at the top of the West Tower, crammed with books from floor to ceiling. It has a set of library steps, and a very low desk with a cushion on the chair.

Teaching

Flitwick taught Harry's year the Levitation Charm on Hallowe'en 1991. He warned them about Wizard Baruffio, who said 's' instead of 'f' and found a buffalo on his chest. Hermione Granger was the first to make her feather fly, and he praised her for it.

His exams are cheerful affairs. In 1992 the first-years had to make a pineapple tap-dance across a desk. There was a secret bonus question that only Hermione answered. He privately gave her a hundred and twelve per cent. In 1994 the third-years did Cheering Charms. He praised the most effective charm he had seen all year, which was the one Ron Weasley had received from Harry.

His contribution to the defences of the Philosopher's Stone was a chamber of winged keys. At Christmas he hangs the trees with golden bubbles, and decorates his classroom with real fairies, who sulk.

In the saga

At Harry's first lesson, reading the register, Flitwick came to Harry's name, gave a squeak and toppled off his books. In September 1992 Ron's broken wand struck him between the eyes, and raised a large green boil. Hermione had read about his duelling days and hoped he would run the Duelling Club. Lockhart ran it instead. He later called Flitwick an expert on Entrancing Enchantments, at which Flitwick put his face in his hands. Flitwick helped Professor Sinistra carry the Petrified Justin Finch-Fletchley to the hospital wing. When Ginny Weasley's abduction was announced he burst into tears, before reminding Lockhart of his boasts.

After Sirius Black's first break-in he escorted Harry to Charms. He measured Harry's fall at the Hufflepuff match at fifty feet. In the Three Broomsticks he explained the Fidelius Charm to Madam Rosmerta. He helped Madam Hooch strip down the anonymous Firebolt, over some eight weeks, in case it carried a Hurling Hex. He also stood on a stool in the Entrance Hall, holding up a poster of Black so that the oak doors could learn his face.

On 11 December 1993 he quietly paid, out of his own pocket, the nine Galleons of his father's money that Hobday, a fifth-year Slytherin, had lost at cards. When he later found Hobday pinning a first-year to the wall over two Sickles, he did the arithmetic aloud: nine Galleons come to a hundred and fifty-three Sickles.

In June 1994 Black was locked in Flitwick's office to await the Dementor's Kiss. He escaped from it through a linking book that had been left open on the desk. The next day Flitwick squeaked with delight that not a single dementor had got into the castle: 'The old protections held, you see.'

In their own words

There are a hundred and fifty-three.Filius Flitwick · B3 Ch12
Not one of them got in! Not a single one! The old protections held, you see.Professor Flitwick · B3 Ch22

pages.title: Dean Thomas
infobox: Gryffindor, Hogwarts student, West Ham supporter, West Ham United, Muggle-born, football fan
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Dean Thomas is a Muggle-born wizard of Gryffindor House, in Harry Potter's year and dormitory. A tall Black boy from South London, he is the best artist in Gryffindor. He is also a devoted supporter of West Ham United, and it was he who brought terrace chanting to Hogwarts Quidditch.

Background

Dean is Muggle-born on both sides: 'Both of them. Mum and Dad,' as he put it. His family are Muggles, though not English ones, and he grew up on the terraces at Upton Park. He keeps a West Ham poster in the dormitory. He and Ron Weasley have argued about football since their first week, with Ron prodding the poster to try to make the players move.

Ron's remarks about footballers, and about 'Dean's people', have strained their friendship. Dean is touchy about any talk of crime statistics. He can draw anything, and he once offered to forge Uncle Vernon's signature on Harry's Hogsmeade form.

Quidditch chants

For Harry's first match, in 1991, Dean painted the Gryffindor lion on the Potter for President banner. He wore his West Ham scarf to the match, and shouted for a red card when Marcus Flint fouled Harry.

He thought it a disgrace that Hogwarts had no decent chants, so he spent three evenings writing some, and led the Gryffindor stand with them against Hufflepuff in 1992. After Harry's five-minute catch he started up 'Can we play you every week?' When Professor McGonagall said that would do, he agreed with her, then sang one more verse.

In the autumn of 1992 he taught the house a mocking terrace chant against Slytherin. At the match he conducted it with a rolled-up programme, standing on his seat at the front of the stand. He held up a red card at Dracina Malfoy, and nearly came to blows with a Ravenclaw who sneered at football. In the end his singing cost Gryffindor twenty points. At the final in 1994 he brought the song back against Slytherin.

In the saga

Dean thought the flying-car arrival of September 1992 was cool. He drew Lockhart being eaten by a vampire in the margin of his book, rather well. In History of Magic he asked Professor Binns whether you had to be related to Slytherin to open the Chamber of Secrets. After the double attack of 1993 he sat up at night with a lit wand, watching the dormitory door. He helped Harry restrain Ron in Potions, and challenged Lockhart's claim that the danger had passed. He chose his third-year subjects by waving his wand over the list with his eyes shut.

In 1993 his boggart was a crawling severed hand, which he caught in a mousetrap. He shouted 'Midget wolf!' at Lupin's shrunken boggart. He said that Dracina had asked for Buckbeak's attack, and after watching her cow the Slytherin team he asked what she was. He lit the lamp on the night of Sirius Black's break-in. At the end of the year he suggested a vampire as the next Defence teacher, and was crushed when Hermione told him that vampires had more important things to do.

In their own words

You want to come down Upton Park on a Saturday and say that to the Chicken Run, mate.Dean Thomas · B2 Ch11
I'm Muggle-born, aren't I. Both of them. Mum and Dad.Dean Thomas · B2 Ch17
Midget wolf!Dean Thomas · B3 Ch7
Maybe a vampire.Dean Thomas · B3 Ch22

pages.title: Bathilda Bagshot
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Godric's Hollow, in the West Country
pages.html:
Bathilda Bagshot is the most celebrated historian of the wizarding world. Her A History of Magic is a set book at Hogwarts. Her Blood and Bone, on the blood traditions of the old families, is not, though Hermione Granger read it anyway. She lives in Godric's Hollow, and she is the great-aunt of Greta Grindelwald.

Her books

A History of Magic is the standard history of wizardkind. It has a great deal to say about the Muggles who burnt witches, and it lays most of the blame on the Church. As far as Bathilda is concerned, Christianity was the main reason wizards and Muggles should never have mixed in the first place. It was also the main reason they stopped. Older wizarding books, according to Hermione, are a good deal less polite about it.

Blood and Bone is not on the Hogwarts list. Hermione drew on it, with A History of Magic, for her account of blood in wizarding history. That account runs from the blood rites of the Celts, the Norse and the Druids to the dark magic with which the great Norman families won William the Conquest.

Godric's Hollow

Bathilda has lived for most of her long life in Godric's Hollow, in the West Country. The Dumbledores were her neighbours there when Albus was a boy. In the summer of 1899 her great-niece, Greta Grindelwald, came to stay with her, and that was how Greta met the young Albus Dumbledore.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Hermione explained to Harry Potter and Ron Weasley why blood still matters to wizards. It was all, she said, in A History of Magic and in Blood and Bone, 'which isn't on the list but you really ought to...'

In Book Three, Chapter One, in July 1993, Harry wrote his History of Magic essay on witch-burning at Privet Drive, with A History of Magic propped open against his lamp. The book was full of frightened Muggles setting fire to anybody who looked at them sideways. It blamed the Church every few chapters, in the tone Aunt Petunia kept for the neighbours' bins.

In Chapter Six Hermione told Harry that wizards do not simply ignore Christianity. They hate it, and they have their reasons: 'Bathilda Bagshot's polite about it, compared to what's in the older books.'

In Chapter Fifteen Harry told the Fat Friar that A History of Magic said the Church had called magic heresy. The Friar laughed until he had to wipe his eyes, though nothing came out of them. 'She's never set foot in a monastery in her life, more's the pity; it might have done her prose some good.'

pages.title: Armand Malfoy
infobox: Land in Wiltshire, by William himself
pages.html:
Armand Malfoy was the first of the Malfoys in England. He came over from Normandy with William the Conqueror, and William himself rewarded him with land in Wiltshire. Malfoy Manor stands on it still.

The Conquest

The great Norman wizarding families, as A History of Magic and Bathilda Bagshot's Blood and Bone both tell it, won William his conquest largely by dark magic. The old Anglo-Saxon families were light wizards, much more pagan, and they lost. The Normans have looked down on everybody else ever since. The Malfoys themselves prefer another story. They say they were in Britain before there was a Britain.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, after a History of Magic lesson in 1991, Dracina Malfoy told Harry Potter that the Malfoys had been in Britain before there was a Britain. Her father had the family tree in the drawing room, she said, and it took up a whole wall. Hermione Granger corrected her at once. The Malfoys had come over from Normandy with William the Conqueror, she said, and Armand Malfoy had been given his land in Wiltshire by William himself. Two spots of pink appeared on Dracina's cheeks.

pages.title: William the Conqueror
pages.html:
William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy, took England in 1066 and ruled it until his death in 1087. By the wizards' account he won it mostly with dark magic, for the great Norman wizarding families fought on his side. He rewarded one of them, Armand Malfoy, with land in Wiltshire.

The Conquest

William claimed that the English throne had been promised to him. When Harold Godwinson was crowned instead, in January 1066, William crossed the Channel. He landed at Pevensey in September and met Harold near Hastings on 14 October. Harold was killed. On Christmas Day William was crowned in Westminster Abbey.

Over the next twenty years the Normans put down every rising, built castles across the country and handed the lands of the English lords to their own men. In 1086 William had the whole kingdom surveyed for the Domesday Book. He died at Rouen the following year.

The wizards' Conquest

Behind the Norman knights came the Norman wizarding families, and it was their dark magic, more than anything, that won William his kingdom. The Anglo-Saxon families they beat were light wizards of an older, more pagan kind. Among the newcomers were the Malfoys. William himself gave Armand Malfoy his land in Wiltshire, and Malfoy Manor stands on it still.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, in the autumn of 1991, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley that the big Norman wizarding families had won William the Conquest with dark magic, mostly. The old Anglo-Saxon families were light wizards, much more pagan, and they lost. It was all, she said, in A History of Magic, and in Blood and Bone by Bathilda Bagshot.

Dracina Malfoy, who had stopped a few feet away, said that her family went back further than that: the Malfoys had been in Britain before there was a Britain. Hermione corrected her before anybody could stop her. 'The Malfoys came over from Normandy. With William the Conqueror. Armand Malfoy was given his land in Wiltshire by William himself.'

pages.title: Uncle Vernon's boss
pages.html:
Uncle Vernon's boss is the man Vernon Dursley answers to at work, at Grunnings, the drill-making firm. He has a big nose and curly hair.

Harry's memory of him

Aunt Petunia once warned Dudley and Harry Potter about him. The goblins of Gringotts reminded Harry of him, which put Harry on edge around them.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Dracina Malfoy told Hermione Granger that her father had warned her about people like Hermione, with her bushy hair and her big nose. Harry wondered what she was talking about. He remembered Aunt Petunia's warning about Uncle Vernon's boss, and he began to ask, but Dracina got in first. 'Mudbloods,' she said.

pages.title: Goblins
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Goblins are a clever, proud people who run Gringotts, the wizarding bank in Diagon Alley, and guard its vaults deep beneath London. They are the finest metalworkers in Britain. Their long and bloody quarrels with wizards, the goblin rebellions, take up a great deal of the History of Magic syllabus.

Gringotts

The vaults are reached by small goblin-driven carts that hurtle along miniature railway tracks through the tunnels under the bank. The goblins bow their customers in, count out their gold and keep their own counsel.

The goblins and the sword

Goblin hands once worked on the most famous sword in Britain. Gandalf gave Andúril, the sword of Aragorn, to Godric Gryffindor, and Godric took it to the goblins to be repaired after millennia of wear. The goblin smith Ragnuk the First did the work. After Godric died, the goblins named it the Sword of Gryffindor and claimed to have forged it, as a pretext for stealing it. Gandalf stole it back, and kept it for Aragorn's heirs. The histories say only that it vanished.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, the goblins of Gringotts put Harry Potter on edge, because they reminded him of a man Aunt Petunia had once warned him about, Uncle Vernon's boss. In History of Magic, Professor Binns gave out the goblin rebellions in the same voice as everything else, which was no voice at all. Harry, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger learnt their dates for the exams all the same. In Chapter Six Professor Flitwick was so small that Harry privately wondered whether there was a goblin somewhere in his family.

In Book Two, Chapter One, while the Dursleys grovelled to the Masons, Harry privately suspected the Masons of being closely related to goblins. In Chapter Five a bowing goblin showed the Weasleys into Gringotts, and another led them down to their vault by cart. In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry sat on a wall by Gringotts watching the goblins come and go. It was there, on about his third day, that he worked out that there were two of him.

pages.title: The lady with the lute
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter 4
pages.html:
The lady with the lute is one of the portraits at Hogwarts. Like the other people in the castle's paintings, she goes visiting, so nobody can be sure of finding her where they left her.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, in his first weeks at Hogwarts, Harry found that the castle would not stay still. The staircases moved, some doors were only pretending to be doors, and the people in the portraits went visiting. He could never rely on the lady with the lute being where he had left her.

pages.title: Oliver Wood
infobox:
Oliver Wood's father father
Marcus Flint rival captain
Harry Potter Seeker, teammate
Gryffindor, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Gryffindor Quidditch team, Quidditch captain, Keeper
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Oliver Wood is a Scottish wizard who was Keeper and captain of the Gryffindor Quidditch team until he left Hogwarts in 1994. A burly, obsessive and fiercely loyal leader, he recruited Harry Potter as Seeker in 1991. In his last season he won the Quidditch Cup.

Background

Wood's father served in the RAF. Oliver collects magazines about Muggle jet planes, and he once explained their payloads to Harry with great enthusiasm. He swears constantly. He believes in Quidditch above almost everything else, and he spent the summer of 1992 devising a new training programme. On leaving school in 1994 he signed for the reserve team of Puddlemere United.

Harry's captain

In September 1991 Professor McGonagall took Wood, then a fifth-year, out of Charms to meet his new Seeker. He judged Harry's light, quick build perfect, and kept him hidden as Gryffindor's secret weapon. He taught Harry the rules on the pitch at seven in the evening, with the ball crate and a bag of golf balls. Harry caught every one of them.

After training one night Wood chased Dracina Malfoy off the pitch. She mumbled something as she went, which Wood took for an apology for coming on to the pitch. It was in fact her first apology to Harry, who never caught it, so Wood was the only person to hear it. When the house turned on Harry over the lost points in 1992, Wood refused to let him resign.

In 1992 he woke the team at dawn for practice, then lectured until the twins fell asleep. He found the Slytherins on his booked pitch with Snape's permission, every one of them mounted on a new Nimbus Two Thousand and One. Before the Slytherin match he told Harry that Dracina's father had bought her place, so Harry must beat her to the Snitch or die trying. When Harry insisted on facing the rogue Bludger alone, Wood looked frightened of him. Then he ordered the twins to leave Harry be. Afterwards he called it the best catch Harry had ever made.

Last season (1993 to 1994)

In his seventh year Wood was seventeen. When Slytherin withdrew from their fixture, he was devastated to have to play Hufflepuff in a storm instead. After the defeat he refused Cedric Diggory's offer of a rematch. He trained the team brutally with a Beater's bat, though he never once turned on Harry. He told Harry that Angelina Johnson would probably succeed him, but that Harry would be captain one day. When the Firebolt was confiscated he told Harry not to apologise. He asked who had taught him to apologise for things that got done to him, then lobbied McGonagall for the broom's return.

Against Ravenclaw he backed Harry's reorganisation of the team in the air, in front of everyone. Then he made the save of his life, and shouted 'That's my boy!' At the party afterwards he worked out on a slate that Gryffindor had to beat Slytherin by more than two hundred points. He wept, blaming the smoke. One of the songs had nine verses about him.

In the final both Slytherin Bludgers hit him in the stomach. When Gryffindor won the Cup he sobbed on Harry's shoulder, then handed him the trophy. It was a memory Harry later tried to use for a Patronus.

In their own words

This year, we batter the competition, or I batter you lot.Oliver Wood · B2 Ch8
You beat Malfoy to that Snitch, or you die trying.Oliver Wood · B2 Ch11
Perfect conditions! Couldn't ask for better!Oliver Wood · B2 Ch16
Natural, that's what. You're a natural.Oliver Wood · B3 Ch10

pages.title: Poppy Pomfrey
infobox: Hogwarts staff, Matron, hospital wing, matron, Healer, healer
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
From 1971 or earlier to the present
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Poppy Pomfrey is the matron of Hogwarts. She runs the hospital wing like a fortress and can mend a broken bone with one flick of her wand. Brisk, protective and discreet, she has patched up Harry Potter more often than any other pupil of his generation. She also keeps a great many secrets without being asked.

The hospital wing

Madam Pomfrey enforces strict visiting hours, though she once allowed Harry's visitors five minutes and then let them stay nearly fifteen. In a cold October her Pepperup Potion goes out by the gallon. After dementors her standard remedy is chocolate, broken up with a small silver hammer. She once grew Charlie Weasley a new ear after a Welsh Green attacked him.

She asks no questions that she does not need answered. She recognised Hermione Granger's condition at once as Polyjuice gone wrong with an animal hair, and she had plainly seen it before, probably more than once.

Her discretion is old. When Remus Lupin was a boy at the school, she led him across the grounds to the Whomping Willow every month so that he could transform.

In the saga

In 1991 to 1992 she mended Neville Longbottom's broken wrist in about a minute. Later that year she patched him up again after his fight with Crabbe and Goyle. She treated Ron's poisoned dragon bite while plainly doubting his story about a dog. After the Stone she gave Harry a medicine that tasted of pepper.

In the autumn of 1992 Gilderoy Lockhart removed all thirty-three bones from Harry's arm, and she regrew them overnight with Skele-Gro. A broken bone, she observed, was one thing to mend; growing bones back from nothing was quite another. Privately she told Harry that she agreed with every word of his opinion of Lockhart, but that it was not a thing to say about a member of staff in front of witnesses. She kept her promise not to tell him the name of the crying girl who left him sugared violets.

That Christmas, with a single look, she warned Harry not to tell Hermione that Dracina Malfoy was in the next bed. On Boxing Day she refused Hermione all visitors. She overheard the two girls fighting over Harry through the curtains, and afterwards she gave him a deeply sympathetic look every time he visited. She told Filch, whom she called Argus, that the Mandrakes would soon restore Mrs Norris. After Dumbledore's suspension she banned all visitors from the hospital wing, for fear that the attacker would come back. On the night of the Chamber she handed out the Mandrake juice.

In September 1993 she examined Harry in Professor McGonagall's office after the dementor on the train. She sniggered at his jokes, telling him that his humour would be the death of her ('Cause of death: Harry Potter being clever at me'). She approved of Lupin's chocolate. Harry would not be the last to collapse, she said, with dementors set round a school.

After the hippogriff she bandaged Dracina's arm from wrist to shoulder. At half past ten that night she ran in, in her dressing gown with her hair in a net, and threw Harry out of her ward. After his fall at the Hufflepuff match she kept him in until the Monday. She wanted to burn the splinters of his broom, and in the end she let Ron sleep in the next bed. In January 1994 she healed a first-year Hufflepuff's cut forearm in about four seconds. After the Ravenclaw match she treated Alicia Spinnet's injured arm and forbade her to fly for a week.

On the night of the escape she treated Harry, Hermione and Ron, breaking up chocolate with her silver hammer. When Harry raged at the Minister, she silenced him by pushing chocolate into his mouth and demanded to know whether this was a hospital wing or not. Later, in a foul temper after the Headmaster's visit, she made Harry and Hermione eat their chocolate in front of her. She mended Ron's broken leg overnight and let all three of them go at noon the next day. She did her best with the wounds the Garou had left on Harry's arm, which had to heal without magic.

In their own words

A broken bone I can put right in a second. One flick! But growing them back from nothing...Poppy Pomfrey · B2 Ch11
Cause of death: Harry Potter being clever at me.Poppy Pomfrey · B3 Ch5
Is this a hospital wing or not?Poppy Pomfrey · B3 Ch20
Did I hear the headmaster leaving? Am I allowed to look after my patients now?Madam Pomfrey · B3 Ch21

pages.title: Mrs Norris
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Skeletal and grey, with lamp-like yellow eyes
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Mrs Norris is the cat of Argus Filch, the Hogwarts caretaker, and his deputy in the corridors. In 1992 she became the first victim of the reopened Chamber of Secrets.

Filch's deputy

Mrs Norris is a skeletal grey cat with lamp-like yellow eyes, whom Filch calls 'my sweet'. She patrols the corridors alone. She sits on the stairs waiting for pupils to put a foot wrong, and fetches Filch the moment they do. Most of the school would dearly like to give her a good kick.

She seems to have a nose for Harry Potter. His Invisibility Cloak appears to work on her all the same. In December 1991 she nearly caught Harry and Ron at the Mirror of Erised. In June 1992 Harry, Ron and Hermione climbed round her on the stairs under the Cloak. Ron whispered that they should kick her, just this once, but Harry shook his head. She turned her lamp-like eyes on them as they passed, and did nothing.

Petrification

On Hallowe'en 1992 she was found hanging by her tail from a torch bracket on the second floor, stiff and staring, beneath a message announcing that the Chamber of Secrets had been opened. Filch screeched at Harry that he had murdered her. Dumbledore declared her Petrified rather than dead. She had seen the Basilisk's reflection in the water from Moaning Myrtle's flooded bathroom. Gilderoy Lockhart blamed the Transmogrifian Torture.

Filch kept watch on the spot for months. Madam Pomfrey promised him that she would be restored once the Mandrakes were ready. She was revived at the end of the year. In 1994 she trotted after Filch as he boarded up the castle against Sirius Black.

pages.title: Gregory the Smarmy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Fred and George Weasley, in their first week
pages.html:
Gregory the Smarmy is a statue at Hogwarts of the wizard of that name, who invented Gregory's Unctuous Unction, a potion that convinces whoever drinks it that the giver is their very best friend. There is a secret passage behind it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Fred and George told Harry that Lee Jordan reckoned he had found a new secret passage out of the school. They bet it was the one behind Gregory the Smarmy, which they had found in their first week.

pages.title: Fluffy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Guarding the trapdoor to the Philosopher's Stone, 1991 to 1992
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Fluffy is Rubeus Hagrid's monstrous three-headed dog. From 1991 to 1992 he guarded the trapdoor to the Philosopher's Stone in the forbidden third-floor corridor at Hogwarts, and the only safe way past him was to play him a tune.

Hagrid's dog

Hagrid bought Fluffy in 1990 off a man he met in a pub. He took the man for a Greek, because he had a caravan and what Hagrid called the funny voice the Greeks have. The man was in fact a Traveller. Hagrid named the dog himself, and he lent him to Albus Dumbledore to guard something Dumbledore was keeping for Nicolas Flamel.

Fluffy fills a corridor from floor to ceiling. He has three heads, with three pairs of rolling, mad eyes, three twitching noses and three slavering mouths, from whose yellow fangs hang ropes of drool. He also has one weakness. Music sends him straight to sleep, although he wakes the moment it stops. Only Hagrid and Dumbledore knew it. Then Hagrid let it slip to a hooded stranger in the Hog's Head, who kept buying him drinks and had a dragon's egg to offer him at cards.

In the saga

At the start-of-term feast in September 1991 Dumbledore warned the school that 'this year the third-floor corridor on the right-hand side is out of bounds to all who do not wish to die a most painful death.' Later that month Harry, Ron, Hermione and Neville Longbottom blundered into the corridor at night while they were running from Filch. Fluffy was looking at them with all six eyes. The only reason they lived was that he was as surprised as they were. Back in the common room Hermione, who had got her breath back, pointed out that he had been standing on a trapdoor.

On Hallowe'en Fluffy savaged Severus Snape's leg when Snape went to cut off Quirrell. It left Snape limping, his leg torn and bloody, wondering how anybody was supposed to watch all three heads at once.

In June 1992, on the night Harry, Ron and Hermione went after the Stone, the door to the corridor already stood open a crack. A harp lay silent at Fluffy's feet, left there by Quirrell. The dog was awake and growling. Harry played him to sleep on the wooden flute Hagrid had carved him for Christmas, which sounded a bit like an owl. When Harry went down through the trapdoor, Hermione took the flute and kept Fluffy asleep.

Hagrid loves him, and used to bend over him cooing that he was a lovely little feller. In June 1994, when a Garou circled Harry on the dark lawns above the lake, he thought of Fluffy, who had been bigger still. Fluffy, though, had never looked at him like that.

pages.title: The vampire in Romania
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The vampire in Romania is the creature that Professor Quirrell was rumoured to have fought on his travels, before he took up the Defence Against the Dark Arts post at Hogwarts. The story went that the garlic in his turban was there to keep it away.

The turban

Whether he ever met a vampire at all, nobody knows. What the turban really hid was worse. Under it, the face of Lord Voldemort grew out of the back of Quirrell's head.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, in September 1991, Quirrell's classroom stank of garlic. When Seamus Finnigan asked whether it was true that he had fought a vampire in Romania, Quirrell went white and knocked over his inkwell. Afterwards Ron Weasley said the turban was stuffed with garlic too, so that the vampire could not come for him in the night. Harry Potter thought it a very good story, and a great deal more interesting than the man who was supposed to be in it.

In Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, beside the Mirror of Erised, Quirrell unwound the turban in front of Harry. On the back of his head, pushing out of the skull, was the face of Lord Voldemort.

pages.title: Remembrall
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A glass ball the size of a large marble, full of white smoke
The smoke turns scarlet when its holder has forgotten something
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
A Remembrall is a glass ball about the size of a large marble, filled with white smoke. When the person holding it has forgotten something, the smoke turns scarlet. It does not say what has been forgotten. Neville Longbottom's grandmother sent him one in September 1991, and it led to Harry Potter's first flight.

Neville's Remembrall

A barn owl brought it to Neville at breakfast. It went scarlet as soon as he held it. He was still trying to work out what he had forgotten when Dracina Malfoy plucked it out of his hand. Professor McGonagall came over at once, and Dracina dropped it back on the table. 'Only looking,' she said.

Later that day, at the first-years' flying lesson, Dracina snatched it up out of the grass. She flew fifty feet up with it. Harry Potter, who had never been on a broom in his life, went up after her to get it back. She threw it, and he caught it a foot from the ground. Dracina was beside herself.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Neville's gran sent him the Remembrall, a glass ball the size of a large marble full of white smoke. 'Gran knows I forget things,' Neville explained. 'It tells you if you've forgotten something.'

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Dracina looked angrier than Harry had ever seen her, angrier even than when he had caught the Remembrall.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry reached for the memory of that first flight when he tried to make a Patronus: the lawn, the lift, the glass ball coming down out of the sky with his fingers closing round it.

pages.title: Nimbus Two Thousand
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Smashed by the Whomping Willow, November 1993
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Nimbus Two Thousand is a racing broom, top of the range in 1991. Harry Potter's was his first broom, sent to him by Professor McGonagall in September 1991 after he was made Seeker for Gryffindor. He never lost a Quidditch match on it until the last one, in November 1993, when he fell from it and the wind carried it into the Whomping Willow, which smashed it to splinters.

The broom

It is a sleek, glossy broom with a handle of polished mahogany and a tail of neat, straight twigs. Its name is written in gold near the tip. First-years are not usually allowed brooms of their own; Harry had his by Dumbledore's special permission.

It went wherever Harry thought of going, at the lightest touch. Only after he had flown a Firebolt did he admit to himself that the Nimbus had always needed a little pushing. Dracina Malfoy's Nimbus Two Thousand and One was faster.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Oliver Wood walked round Harry, sizing him up, and said that he would need a proper broom: a Nimbus Two Thousand, or a Cleansweep Seven. In Chapter Six it arrived at breakfast in a long parcel carried by six large screech owls, with a note from Professor McGonagall telling him not to open it at the table. Dracina Malfoy felt the parcel through the paper and warned Harry that first-years were not allowed brooms. When Professor Flitwick turned up and asked which model it was, Harry gave Malfoy his best imitation of her own smug look. 'And I've really got Malfoy to thank for it. So, thanks, love.'
