In Book Two, Chapter Five, it spent the summer of 1992 padlocked in the cupboard under the stairs at Privet Drive. At the Burrow it was easily the best broom the boys had to practise on. In Chapter Eleven Dracina came up from below Harry in the Slytherin match at a speed his Nimbus could never have matched. In Chapter Fifteen Harry flew it with Ron on the snowy, empty pitch on Boxing Day 1992. In Chapter Sixteen he fetched it for the Hufflepuff match, which was called off.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry stood day after day before a Firebolt in a Diagon Alley shop window. But he had never lost a match on his Nimbus, so he saw no point in emptying his Gringotts vault. In Chapter Nine, during the Hufflepuff match in November 1993, the Dementors came onto the pitch and Harry fell fifty feet. The wind took his broom up over the stands like a crisp packet and dropped it on the Whomping Willow, which took it personally. Hermione asked Professor Flitwick to bring back what was left. In the hospital wing Ron put a small drawstring bag into Harry's hands. Inside were a dozen splinters, a strip of the handle with half the serial number on it and a fistful of twigs.

In Chapter Thirteen, after the Firebolt had come, Cedric Diggory sought Harry out to apologise. 'Sorry about your Nimbus. That tree's a menace.'

pages.title: Cleansweep Seven
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Cleansweep Seven is a racing broom made by the Cleansweep Broom Company. It is a sound, cheap broom, but it is no match for a Nimbus, let alone a Firebolt.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Oliver Wood looked Harry over and told Professor McGonagall that he would need a proper broom, a Nimbus Two Thousand or a Cleansweep Seven. McGonagall chose the Nimbus.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, after the Whomping Willow had smashed that Nimbus, Harry read through Which Broomstick and found the Cleansweep Seven listed as the cheap one. In Chapter Twelve, when the Firebolt came back to him, somebody in the crowded common room shouted that Ravenclaw would have no chance, since they were all on Cleansweep Sevens.

pages.title: Shooting Star
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Charlie, then Ron Weasley; Hogwarts School
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Shooting Star is an old, cheap broomstick, first made in 1955. It was never fast, and it grows slower as it ages. The Weasleys have one, handed down from Charlie to Ron. Hogwarts keeps a number of them for lessons, all of them ancient.

The Weasley broom

Charlie Weasley's old Shooting Star passed to Ron. On it Ron once nearly hit a hang-glider. These days it is regularly overtaken by passing butterflies.

The school brooms

The school's Shooting Stars are slow, pull to the left and take about three seconds to think over a turn. In a strong enough gust they have been known to stop altogether.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Ron's story was that he had once nearly hit a hang-glider on Charlie's old Shooting Star.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer holidays at the Burrow, Ron's old Shooting Star was regularly overtaken by passing butterflies.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, after losing his Nimbus, Harry Potter had to practise on an ancient school Shooting Star. It pulled to the left. Once, in a gust, it simply stopped.

In Chapter Twelve, Dracina Malfoy stepped into his path in the Entrance Hall. 'You'll be on that school thing again, I suppose, the one with the bent handle.' She thought it an insult to everybody who had to watch him fly it, and offered him her spare Nimbus Two Thousand and One instead.

pages.title: Chudley Cannons
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Two black Cs and a speeding cannonball
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Chudley Cannons are a Quidditch team of the Prime League who play in bright orange robes. They are Ron Weasley's favourite team, and they are not very good.

The team

Every Cannons player is English, as Ron is proud to point out. The club has won the League twenty-one times, but not once since 1892, and its supporters have learnt to live in hope.

Ron has supported them all his life. His bedroom at the Burrow is a violent orange, walls, ceiling and all, covered with posters of the seven players, who wave at visitors like mad. His bedspread has two enormous black Cs on it, with a speeding cannonball.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Ron poked at Dean Thomas's poster of West Ham, trying to make the players move. He told Dean: 'A Chudley Cannons Beater would batter that bloke with the ball.' In Chapter Nine he and Harry Potter argued about what they would do with a Philosopher's Stone of their own. Ron would buy the Cannons and sort them right out. 'I'd have them top of the Prime league inside a year.'

In Book Two, Chapter Four, Harry saw Ron's bedroom for the first time, in August 1992. The Cannons were ninth in the league that year. In Chapter Fourteen Ron gave Harry Flying with the Cannons, a book of interesting facts about the team, for Christmas 1992.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, after Gryffindor lost to Hufflepuff by a hundred points, Fred Weasley worked out how they might still win the Cup. 'Dad saw Chudley come back from worse, and Chudley are Chudley.'

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Dracina Malfoy wrote to Harry in the summer of 1994 that Pansy Parkinson, who used to take a novel to the Slytherin matches, had suddenly taken up the Chudley Cannons. 'They came bottom, Harry. Bottom.' Pansy now had an orange poster of them over her bed, which clashed with everything she owned. She had written to Dracina four times that fortnight about their Keeper. Harry knew only too well who else supported the Cannons.

pages.title: West Ham United
infobox: Football club, Muggle, football, football club
The Boleyn Ground (Upton Park), East London
pages.html:
West Ham United is a Muggle football club from the East End of London. They play in claret and blue at the Boleyn Ground, which everybody calls Upton Park. Dean Thomas has supported them all his life.

The club

The club began in 1895 as Thames Ironworks, the works team of a shipyard, and took its present name in 1900. It is still nicknamed the Irons, or the Hammers, after the riveting hammers on its crest. Its supporters sing 'I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles'. Three West Ham men, Bobby Moore, Geoff Hurst and Martin Peters, won the World Cup for England in 1966.

Dean grew up on the terraces at Upton Park. He talks of scarves, red cards and the Chicken Run, the part of the ground where the loudest supporters stand.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Ron tried to make the players on Dean's West Ham poster move. In Chapter Seven Dean wore his West Ham scarf to Harry's first match, until Hagrid wound a Gryffindor one round his neck over the top of it. In Chapter Nine Dean, who had grown up on the terraces at Upton Park, gave the Gryffindor stand its first proper chant.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, he led the Gryffindor stand in another, to a tune he had learnt on the terraces at West Ham. When a big Ravenclaw sixth-year called football boring, Dean invited him to come down Upton Park on a Saturday and say so to the Chicken Run.

pages.title: Quidditch Through the Ages
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The history and rules of Quidditch
pages.html:
Quidditch Through the Ages is a history of Quidditch, and a far more interesting book than its cover suggests. Hermione Granger borrowed the Hogwarts library copy in her first year, read it out at breakfast and lent it to Harry Potter. Then Professor Snape confiscated it.

Contents

The book records seven hundred ways of committing a foul in Quidditch, every one of which was committed in a single World Cup match in 1473. It explains that Seekers are generally the smallest, fastest players on a team, and that most of the game's serious accidents happen to them. Players very rarely die, it says, but referees have been known to vanish in the middle of a match and turn up months later in the Sahara Desert. A footnote adds that every one of those referees had been having trouble at home with his wife, and then says no more about it.

It also covers more than a thousand years of argument between the English and the French over the rules, settled from time to time with wands. In 1877 the England manager, Francis Grail, and the French manager, Juste Valmond, fell out over the proper weight of a Quaffle. The quarrel ended in a duel. The duel left two hundred people dead in the crossfire; the book's casualty list runs to three pages. The matter was settled at last when every national team agreed to play by the Austrian rules from 1901 onwards.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Hermione bored the Gryffindor table rigid at breakfast with flying tips from it, before the first flying lesson. In Chapter Seven she lent it to Harry. 'Wizards are mad, sometimes,' he told her and Ron, reading about the duel of 1877. He thought privately that the Austrians would have had rather more on their plate about thirteen years later. He wondered whether the wizarding world had even noticed the First World War going on around it.

The day before his first match, Snape caught him with it in the frosty courtyard. Library books, said Snape, were not to be taken out of the school, and he took it away with five points from Gryffindor. When Harry went to the staff room that evening to ask for it back, he found Filch bandaging a bloody wound on Snape's leg. 'How is anyone supposed to watch all three heads at once?' Snape was saying.

pages.title: A History of Magic
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The history of the wizarding world
pages.html:
A History of Magic, by Bathilda Bagshot, is the standard history of the wizarding world and a set book for History of Magic at Hogwarts. Among a great deal else, it covers the Norman wizarding families and the Conquest. It is also very firm about the witch-burnings of the Middle Ages, which it blames on the Church.

Contents

According to Hermione Granger, the book tells how the great Norman wizarding families came over with William and won him the Conquest, mostly with dark magic. The old Anglo-Saxon families, who were light wizards, lost, and the Normans have looked down on everybody else ever since. The book also deals with the blood magic of the old wizarding world, and Hermione has cited it on the subject.

Bagshot is scornful about the burnings of the fourteenth century. The Muggles of medieval Europe, she writes, lived in terror of witchcraft yet were almost wholly unable to detect it, so that nearly all of the thousands put to the stake between 1300 and 1400 had no magic at all. On the rare occasions when a real witch or wizard was caught, a simple Flame-Freezing Charm turned the fire into a mild, rather agreeable warmth, and the condemned had only to shriek convincingly. Wendelin the Weird enjoyed it so much that she contrived to be burnt forty-seven times, under a variety of names and hats. She lays the blame squarely on the Church. As far as she is concerned, Christianity is the main reason wizards should never have mixed with Muggles in the first place, and the main reason they stopped. It comes up every few chapters.

A disputed account

The Fat Friar, who was a real friar before he died, disputes it. The Church he knew never called magic heresy: its old rule, the Canon Episcopi, said that the sin lay in believing in such things. Magic became an organised heresy only later, after the Formicarius of Johannes Nider and the Malleus Maleficarum of 1486.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, after a History of Magic lesson early in their first year, Hermione explained the Norman families to Harry Potter. It was all in A History of Magic, she said, 'and in Blood and Bone by Bathilda Bagshot, which isn't on the list but you really ought to...' Ron Weasley told her she was as boring as Binns.

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, Harry had the book propped open against the lamp in his bedroom at Privet Drive while he wrote his holiday essay for History of Magic. The essay was called Witch Burning in the Fourteenth Century Was Completely Pointless. Discuss. The book had a good deal to say on the subject.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry told the Fat Friar that the book said the Church had called magic heresy. The Friar threw back his head and roared with laughter. 'Bathilda Bagshot!' he said. 'Oh, dear Bathilda. She's never set foot in a monastery in her life, more's the pity; it might have done her prose some good.' Then he asked Harry whether he had ever heard of the Canon Episcopi.

pages.title: Blood and Bone
infobox: Blood magic; the old wizarding families
Not on the Hogwarts set list
pages.html:
Blood and Bone is a book by Bathilda Bagshot on blood magic and the old wizarding families. It is not on the Hogwarts set list. Hermione Granger has read it all the same, and recommends it to anybody who will listen.

Contents

The book is a history of blood in British magic. The Celts used blood in their rites, as did the Norse, while druidic magic was practically all blood: oaths, bindings and the like. Hermione drew on it, with A History of Magic, for her account of the Norman Conquest. As she tells it, the Norman wizarding families won England for William with dark magic, while the old Anglo-Saxon families, who were light wizards, lost.

No wizarding history knows where those rites came from. They are fragments of a far older craft, thinned by distance: the dark magic of Morgoth, which Stygia kept before the Flood. A scholar who follows the trail back finds Egypt, then Stygia, then nothing, because that is where the written record drowns. Wizards have dug up half of their own history, in other words, and it is the wrong half.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, after a History of Magic lesson early in their first year, Hermione told Harry Potter how the Normans had won the Conquest. It was all in A History of Magic, she said, 'and in Blood and Bone by Bathilda Bagshot, which isn't on the list but you really ought to...' Ron Weasley told her she was as boring as Binns, then told her to shut up.

pages.title: One Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
One Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi is one of the set books for first-years at Hogwarts, a thick guide to the magical plants used in Herbology or brewed in Potions. It is the sort of book Professor Snape expects his pupils to have by heart before they arrive.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, at Harry Potter's first Potions lesson in September 1991, Snape singled him out with question after question he could not answer. Harry had looked through his books at the Dursleys' in the small hours with a torch. Nobody could have expected him to have the whole of One Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi by heart, when he could still hardly believe he was a wizard at all. In Chapter Ten he was looking up dittany in it in the library when Hagrid shuffled into view with something hidden behind his back.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, on a stormy night in November 1993, Ron Weasley lay sideways in an armchair in the Gryffindor common room with the book unopened on his chest. Hermione Granger was in a temper over Dracina Malfoy. Ron asked her to tell them the story of Angelus, the famous vampire, which she did, from the start.

pages.title: The Lord of the Rings
aliases: the book of the three parts
infobox: Dudley's Lord of the Rings; Dudley's doorstop; Lord of The Rings; Lord of the Rings books; Lord of the Rings

Aragorn character in it
J. R. R. Tolkien author
The Fellowship of the Ring (29 July 1954), The Two Towers (11 November 1954), The Return of the King (20 October 1955)
The War of the Ring at the end of the Third Age
Dudley Dursley's one-volume paperback, a present from Aunt Marge
Harry Potter, July 1993 to July 1994; Hermione Granger, twice
A green ribbon from Narcissa Malfoy
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Lord of the Rings is J. R. R. Tolkien's account of the War of the Ring, at the end of the Third Age of Middle-earth. Nearly everyone takes it for a novel. It is in fact a history, for the Flood left the great ages only as story. Harry Potter read Dudley Dursley's copy all through his third year, hunting for the drowned kingdom, the sword and the king.

Contents

The book tells how the hobbit Frodo Baggins inherited the One Ring from Bilbo, whom he called his uncle. Gandalf told him what it was, and Frodo carried it out of the Shire with the Black Riders behind him. The Fellowship of the Ring set out from Rivendell. Frodo and Sam Gamgee went into Mordor to destroy the Ring in the fire where it was made. Meanwhile Aragorn, the ranger called Strider, claimed his inheritance and took the Paths of the Dead. Gandalf crowned him king before Minas Tirith.

Along the way the book speaks of Elves, Ents and Uruk-hai. It tells of the drowned kingdom of Númenor, as well as of the sword that was broken and made again.

Dudley's copy

Dudley's copy is a fat paperback with all three parts in one volume. It has a cracked spine, a tea stain and a great-aunt's name on the flyleaf. Aunt Marge gave it to him, and he used it to prop up a wobbly table. Dudley reads nothing.

Harry had read parts of it in the school library while hiding from Dudley. In his first year at Hogwarts he thought that Crabbe and Goyle would make great, terrible Uruk-hai. In 1992 he teased Dudley with the Ents.

In July 1993, after Dumbledore told him that his mother's protection was the magic of Elves and of Númenor, Harry dug the book out from among Dudley's unwanted presents. He read it hunting for those words, for the sword and for the king. In August 1993, at the Leaky Cauldron, he found it lying on top of his trunk in a ray of sunlight, with no memory of having packed it, and began it properly from the first page. Of everything in it, a hooded shape on a black horse sniffing at the edge of a field frightened him most, until he met a dementor. At Rivendell he stopped for a day or two and read that part twice. He felt a light come off the Elves like pages left in the sun. Hermione Granger had read the whole book twice.

He read it all through his third year, keeping his place with a thin green ribbon that smelt faintly of cold flowers. It had come with Dracina's birthday letter, by Narcissa Malfoy's owl. In the winter he reached the reforging of the sword at Rivendell, and understood that the sword he had drawn from the Sorting Hat was Andúril. In early 1994 he compared himself to the ranger with a broken sword and no kingdom. On the night of the lake in June 1994 he badly wanted to know whether Aragorn came out of the Paths of the Dead. He finished it in July 1994, by streetlight, on the night before his first Evensong.

A history hardly anybody knows is one

The ages of Middle-earth were real history, older than the Hyborian Age and the Flood. Nearly all knowledge of them went under the water, and what reached the present reached it as Tolkien's book. Harry Potter, who descends from Aragorn and Arwen, has held Andúril in his own hands. He has no idea that he was reading his own family's history.

pages.title: Uruk-hai
infobox: They could march and fight under the sun
pages.html:
The Uruk-hai were the great orcs of the Third Age of Middle-earth, as tall as Men and much stronger than the lesser orcs. Unlike most of their kind, they could march under the sun without flinching.

History

They first came out of Mordor in about the year 2475 of the Third Age, and sacked Osgiliath. In the War of the Ring Saruman bred his own in Isengard. In 3019 they stormed the Hornburg at Helm's Deep, and were beaten there.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in his first weeks at Hogwarts in 1991, Harry Potter, who had read The Lord of the Rings once or twice, sized up Crabbe and Goyle. If he had not known better, he thought, the pair of them would have made great and terrible Urak'ai. He would not have put it past the wizarding world to keep some real ones in a dismal hole somewhere.

pages.title: Daily Prophet
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Every morning, with an evening edition
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Daily Prophet is the wizarding newspaper of Britain, delivered by owl. Most of wizarding Britain reads it, and a good many of its readers believe it. The Ministry of Magic finds this convenient, since the Prophet prints a great deal of what the Minister tells it.

The paper

The Prophet comes out every morning, with an evening edition as well. Subscribers pay the owl that brings it, dropping Knuts into a little leather pouch on its leg.

It follows the Ministry closely. Cornelius Fudge tells it a great deal, not all of it true, and keeps out of it anything he would rather the public did not hear.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in the autumn of 1991, Harry Potter asked Hagrid about a cutting from the Prophet reporting the break-in at Gringotts. In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, a Prophet photographer took pictures of Gilderoy Lockhart with Harry at Flourish and Blotts, and Lockhart asked him afterwards to work the fight there into his report. In Chapter Six, on the evening of 1 September 1992, the paper reported Muggle sightings of the flying Ford Anglia. In Chapter Fourteen it ran MINISTRY OFFICIAL FINED OVER FLYING CAR: Arthur Weasley had been fined fifty Galleons, and Lucius Malfoy was demanding that he resign. By Christmas 1992 it had still printed nothing about the attacks at Hogwarts, which Dracina Malfoy took as proof that Dumbledore was hushing them up. In Chapter Nineteen Dumbledore planned to advertise in it for a new Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher for 1993.

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, the Prophet reported that Arthur Weasley had won its Grand Prize Galleon Draw, seven hundred Galleons, which the family spent on a month in Egypt. It also ran the headline BLACK STILL AT LARGE. In Chapter Four Arthur Weasley said that Fudge had kept out of the paper what Sirius Black had been saying in his sleep, and that much of what Fudge told the Prophet was untrue. In Chapter Seven it reported a Muggle sighting of Black, in September 1993.

In Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, it reported that the dementors had been given permission to perform the Kiss on Black. In the same chapter Professor Trelawney told Harry, over his palm, that she had never seen so short a life line. 'Right,' said Harry. 'Could you write that down for the Prophet? Only they've been running out of things to say about me.' In Chapter Eighteen it came out that Fudge had given his copy to Black on a visit to Azkaban. On the front was a photograph of the Weasleys in Egypt, with Scabbers on Ron's shoulder, and a line saying that Ron would be going back to Hogwarts.

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, Stan, the conductor of the Knight Bus, unfolded a newspaper with Sirius Black on the front. John Constantine, riding the bus, kept his eyes on his shoes. He had not read the Prophet for twenty years. As far as he could tell it was written by idiots for idiots, and the only thing it had ever been good for was wrapping chips.

pages.title: Mudblood
infobox: Slur, Blood purity, slur, blood status
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Mudblood is a filthy name for a witch or wizard with Muggle parents. It means dirty blood, or common blood, and it is about the most offensive thing one witch can call another.

The word

It belongs to the pure-blood families who believe that magic should stay among the old names. To them Muggle-borns are thieves of magic, who have somehow taken what was never theirs. Decent people do not use it at all. To Lucius Malfoy blood is not a prejudice but a fact, ‘like the colour of your eyes’, and he uses the word as plainly as that.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, in September 1991, Dracina Malfoy began calling Hermione Granger a Mudblood. By Book One, Chapter Seven, she was calling the two of them ‘wee Pottyhead and his little Mudblood friend’ to Pansy Parkinson as they passed in the corridors. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, she called Hermione a disgusting thieving Mudblood, and chaos followed. In Hagrid's hut afterwards Hagrid called it a horrible thing to call another witch. Ron Weasley, between slugs, explained what it meant: dirty blood, common blood. In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, Dracina called Muggle-borns thieves of magic.

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, in the hospital wing in June 1993, after the Chamber, Dracina stopped herself using the word of Hermione and said Granger instead. Harry Potter saw what it cost her, and remembered it in Book Three, Chapter Five.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in Diagon Alley that summer, Lucius Malfoy told Harry to his face that his mother had been a Mudblood, while insisting that she had been a witch all the same: ‘She was one of us.’ In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express, Dracina sneered to the Slytherins about Potty, the Weasel and the Mudblood, all in a heap at the back of the train. By Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Harry had heard her use the word more often than he could count, as casually as if she were remarking on the weather. In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Hermione put it plainly. ‘She’s called me a Mudblood since our first week,’ she said. ‘Every week, Harry.’

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine remembered his own schooldays as a Muggle-born Slytherin. The Slytherins painted MUDBLOOD across the lid of his trunk in letters a foot high, and when he scrubbed it off it came back the next morning in a different colour. In their seventh year, one night in March, in an empty corridor on the fourth floor, Lucius called him one for the first time, over a Ravenclaw girl who was going out with John. It began as a duel and ended with the two of them punching each other on the flagstones.

pages.title: Blood purity
aliases: the most ancient and noble houses
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Pure marriages, nine hundred years back
pages.html:
Blood purity is the old wizarding belief that a witch or wizard's worth lies in their ancestry, and that the purest blood is the best. Wizards set great store by it. The old families keep records of who married whom going back nine hundred years, with a note of whether each match was pure on both sides.

Where it comes from

The belief is older than any of the families that hold it. Celtic magic used blood in its rites, as Norse magic did. Druidic magic was practically all blood, oaths and bindings. When the Normans came over with William, the great Norman wizarding families won him the Conquest, mostly with dark magic. The old Anglo-Saxon families, who were light wizards and much more pagan, lost. The Normans have looked down on everybody else ever since. The prejudice against Muggle-borns is traced to Salazar Slytherin, who mistrusted children whose parents were not magical.

Losing ground

In practice it is a matter of degree, and most wizards these days are half-blood. Without marrying Muggles, wizards would have died out long ago, and the families who have kept themselves pure have done it by marrying their cousins. Even its believers admit that it counts for less than it did.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Professor Binns's notes on the most ancient and noble houses got Ron Weasley talking about blood. His mum held that blood is power, he said, though he had no idea what she meant by it. Hermione Granger traced the idea back through the Norman Conquest to Celtic, Norse and druidic blood rites. It was all, she said, in A History of Magic. It was in Bathilda Bagshot's Blood and Bone as well.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Lucius Malfoy and Mr Borgin agreed that wizard blood was counting for less everywhere, to Lucius's disgust. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, after Dracina Malfoy had called Hermione a Mudblood, Ron said that most wizards were half-blood anyway. Harry Potter passed on Dumbledore's idea that Muggle-borns carry recessive magic from old magical ancestors. Hermione called it the magical equivalent of pseudoscience, since nobody had ever tested it.

pages.title: The Norman Conquest
infobox: The dark magic of the great Norman wizarding families, mostly
The old Anglo-Saxon families, light wizards
pages.html:
The Norman Conquest was the conquest of England by William, Duke of Normandy, in 1066. In the wizarding world it was a victory for dark magic. The great Norman wizarding families won William the Conquest, mostly with dark magic, over the old Anglo-Saxon families, who were light wizards and much more pagan. The Normans have looked down on everybody else ever since. The Malfoys came over with them.

The Conquest

Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, and Harold Godwinson was crowned in his place. William, who claimed that the throne had been promised to him, landed at Pevensey that September. On 14 October he met Harold near Hastings. Harold was killed, and on Christmas Day William was crowned in Westminster Abbey. Over the next twenty years the Normans put down every rising, built castles across the country and gave the lands of the English lords to their own men.

The wizards' Conquest

Behind the Norman knights came the Norman wizarding families. By the account of the wizarding histories, A History of Magic and Bathilda Bagshot's Blood and Bone among them, it was their dark magic, more than anything, that won William his kingdom. The Anglo-Saxon families they beat were light wizards of an older, more pagan kind.

Among the newcomers were the Malfoys. Armand Malfoy was given his land in Wiltshire by William himself, and the family has been Dark ever since.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, after a History of Magic lesson in the autumn of 1991, Hermione Granger explained the Conquest to Harry Potter and Ron. Dracina Malfoy, overhearing, said that her family went back further than that. 'The Malfoys were in Britain before there was a Britain,' she said. Hermione told her that the Malfoys had come over from Normandy with William the Conqueror. Armand Malfoy, she said, had been given his land in Wiltshire by William himself.

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Fred Weasley told Harry that the Malfoys had always been Dark wizards, all the way back to the Norman conquest, when they first came over. In Chapter Five, hearing Lucius Malfoy call Arthur Weasley a flea-bitten, Muggle-loving fool, Harry thought Arthur worth more than every piece of Norman plunder the Malfoys had ever got their hands on.

pages.title: Alohomora
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Alohomora is the Unlocking Charm. A wand tapped on a lock with the incantation springs the lock, and the door can be opened.

Use

It is one of the most useful charms a young witch or wizard can know, and one of the best known. Not every door gives way to it. Wards built by wizards to keep out wizards can be made to notice it the moment it is cast.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in 1991, Harry, Ron, Hermione and Neville were out of bed at night when Peeves gave them away, bellowing that there were students out of bed in the Charms corridor. They ran for their lives to the end of the corridor and slammed into a locked door. Ron moaned that they were finished. 'Oh, get out of the way,' Hermione snarled. She snatched Harry's wand, tapped the lock and whispered 'Alohomora!' The lock clicked. They tumbled through the door into the forbidden third-floor corridor.

In Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, on the way to the Philosopher's Stone, Hermione tried her Alohomora on the locked door on the far side of the chamber of winged keys. It would not give.

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine weighed up the wards on Shacklewell House in New Mexico. He reckoned they would know an Unlocking Charm the moment one was cast.

pages.title: Shield Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Raises a wall of light that blocks spells and throws back attackers
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Shield Charm, Protego, throws up a shimmering, faintly humming wall of silvery-blue light between the caster and whatever is coming. It blocks spells and turns back attackers. It is the first real defence a young witch or wizard learns, if the teacher is any good. A great many never quite master it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, in September 1991, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter what his brother had said about Defence Against the Dark Arts. 'Charlie says you learn a Shield Charm in the first year, if the teacher's any good.'

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, in 1993, with the school about to be closed, Angelina Johnson pointed out that half of Gryffindor could not do a Shield Charm. In Chapter Nineteen, in the hospital wing, Dracina Malfoy offered to be Harry's friend if he would admit that she was the superior witch. 'Superior? You can't do a Shield Charm,' said Harry. Dracina insisted that she could. 'You can't. I've seen you try. You go Protego and then you duck.'

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, Hermione Granger had drilled the charm into Harry in the common room every night for a fortnight before the Quidditch final. 'I'm not losing you to a man with a knife,' she had said. On the night of the full moon in June 1994, when the Garou sprang at him in the grounds, Harry cast it: a shimmering, humming wall of silvery blue. It threw the creature back. Then the Garou raised one hand and began to claw at the shield, tearing it away piece by piece, until the last of it began to give.

In Chapter Twenty, in the Forbidden Forest, he cast it again, kneeling in a stream with Dracina crouched behind him. This time it hit back, with a sound like a great bell, and hurled the werewolf across the clearing. When the creature came back to tear at it, Lupin's cross grew warm against Harry's chest, the cloud slid off the moon, and the shield turned white. It blazed like starlight on snow, and the holes in it ran together until it stood whole. Then it moved. It swept out from his wand in a single silent wave, went straight through the werewolf and forced it back into Remus Lupin's human form.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, before he left Hogwarts, Lupin told Harry that he remembered it. 'I'm sorry to be leaving such a bright young student. But I think you'll turn out well in the end. Whatever you did to that Protego spell showed me that.' In Book Four, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1994, Harry thought back to that moment in the Forest. The Shield Charm had turned white in his hand, with something in it far bigger than he was, and it had burnt Lupin's war form away like frost off a window.

pages.title: Switching Spells
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Exchanges one thing, or part of a thing, for another
pages.html:
Switching Spells are a branch of Transfiguration. They exchange one thing for another, or swap a part of one object for a part of another. They are taught properly in the middle years at Hogwarts, though a keen first-year can read about them well before then.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in the autumn of 1991, Hermione Granger earned Gryffindor points from Professor McGonagall for knowing about Switching Spells. When Harry Potter and Ron Weasley set off at midnight to duel Dracina Malfoy, Hermione was furious with them. 'I don't want Slytherin winning the House Cup, and you'll lose every point I earned off Professor McGonagall for knowing about Switching Spells.'

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, Harry's class was studying Switching Spells in Transfiguration. Harry arrived eight minutes late, after a strange encounter with a cracked painting of Cain and Abel on the fourth floor. He could not stop thinking about the brother whose face he had not been able to see. It itched at him all through Switching Spells.

pages.title: Curse of the Bogies
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Curse of the Bogies is a curse that Professor Quirrell told his first-years about in 1991. Nobody has ever explained exactly what it does, though the name gives a fair idea.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Harry and Ron crept out of Gryffindor Tower to meet Dracina Malfoy in the trophy room at midnight, for a wizard's duel. Hermione followed them through the portrait hole to stop them, then found herself locked out. A little way on they came upon Neville, who had forgotten the password. Ron looked at his watch, then glared at Hermione and Neville.

'If either of you gets us caught, I'll never rest till I've learned that Curse of the Bogies Quirrell told us about, and I'll use it on you.'

Hermione opened her mouth, very possibly to explain to Ron exactly how the Curse of the Bogies was done. Harry hissed at her to be quiet.

pages.title: Draught of Living Death
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Powdered root of asphodel, added to an infusion of wormwood
pages.html:
The Draught of Living Death is a sleeping draught so strong that whoever drinks it sleeps as though dead. It is made by adding powdered root of asphodel to an infusion of wormwood.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, in Harry's very first Potions lesson, Snape asked him what he would get if he added powdered root of asphodel to an infusion of wormwood. Harry did not know. Hermione's hand was in the air, and Snape snapped at her to sit down. Then he told Harry: 'For your information, Potter, asphodel and wormwood together produce a sleeping draught so strong that it is called the Draught of Living Death.'

pages.title: Boil-curing potion
aliases: a simple potion for curing boils
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Dried nettles, crushed snake fangs, stewed horned slugs, porcupine quills
Add the quills only off the fire
pages.html:
The boil-curing potion is a simple potion for curing boils, and often the first that a Hogwarts class brews. It is made from dried nettles, crushed snake fangs, stewed horned slugs and porcupine quills. The quills must go in only after the cauldron has been taken off the fire; added too soon, they ruin it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Snape paired his first-years off to brew it, finding fault with nearly everyone except Dracina Malfoy, whom he seemed to like. Neville Longbottom somehow melted Seamus Finnigan's cauldron into a twisted lump. The potion spread across the flagstones, eating holes in people's shoes. Neville had been soaked when the cauldron gave way, so angry red boils bloomed up his arms and legs. 'You added the porcupine quills before you took the cauldron off the fire, I suppose?' said Snape.

pages.title: Bezoar
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
A bezoar is a stone taken from the stomach of a goat. It will counter most poisons, which makes it well worth knowing where to find one in a hurry.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, at Harry’s first Potions lesson, Professor Snape asked him where he would look if he were sent to fetch a bezoar. Harry had no idea what a bezoar was. Hermione’s arm stretched as high as it would go. On the Slytherin side of the room Dracina Malfoy was making a rude gesture at him behind her hand, while she, Crabbe and Goyle shook with laughter. In the end Snape answered the question himself: ‘A bezoar is a stone from the stomach of a goat, and it will counter most poisons.’

pages.title: Aconite
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Potions, the Wolfsbane Potion among them
pages.html:
Aconite is a poisonous plant used in potions. Monkshood and wolfsbane are not two plants but one, which also goes by the name of aconite. It is exactly the sort of thing Professor Snape likes to ask first-years in their very first lesson.

Uses

The Wolfsbane Potion takes its name from the plant. Snape brews the potion every month for Remus Lupin. It holds Lupin’s war form down, though never entirely.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, at Harry’s first Potions lesson, Snape asked him what the difference was between monkshood and wolfsbane. Harry had no idea. There was no difference at all, Snape told the class. They were the same plant, which is also called aconite.

pages.title: The trophy room
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
About a hundred cups, with shields, plates, medals and statues
pages.html:
The trophy room at Hogwarts, on the third floor, keeps the school's cups, shields, plates, medals and statues in crystal cases. It is never locked. Ron Weasley, who once had to polish its contents by hand, reckoned there must be about a hundred cups in it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Dracina Malfoy challenged Harry to a wizard's duel at midnight and chose Crabbe as her second. Ron, who was Harry's second, named the place: 'The trophy room. It's never locked.' Harry, Ron, Hermione and Neville crept in by moonlight while the crystal cases glimmered, but Dracina never came. Filch came instead, and the four of them ran. Hermione was certain Dracina had tipped him off.

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, after the flying car, Ron served his detention there with Filch, polishing the silver without magic. Filch made him buff up one Quidditch Cup fourteen times before he was satisfied. Then Ron had another attack of slugs all over a Special Award for Services to the School, which took ages to shift.

In Chapter Fifteen Harry came back with Hermione and an unwilling Ron to look at the same award. It was Tom Riddle's: a gold shield, very well polished, tucked away at the back of a corner cabinet, with nothing on it to say why it had been given. Riddle's name was also on an old Medal for Magical Merit, and on a list of former Head Boys. Ron said he had seen enough of the trophy room to last him the rest of his life, and probably the one after.

pages.title: The Owlery
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The school owls, with students' owls such as Hedwig
Arrow slits, open to the wind off the lake
pages.html:
The Owlery is the owl house at Hogwarts, where the school owls roost alongside the students' own. It is a cold, draughty room, its floor littered with feathers and pellets. The wind comes in off the lake through its arrow slits.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Hedwig took to sleeping in the Owlery with the school owls. Sometimes she came down at breakfast to nibble Harry's ear and take a corner of his toast.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, on the night Sirius Black broke into the castle at Halloween 1993, the Owlery was searched along with everywhere else. Chapter Ten tells how, earlier that autumn, Pansy Parkinson had carried up there the four pages Dracina Malfoy had written to her father about Buckbeak. Dracina had never meant to send them. Pansy thought she was doing what a friend would want.

In Chapter Twelve Dracina left her spare Nimbus there for Harry, roped in brown paper, with a note in small spiky handwriting: Mind the left-hand foot-rest, it goes if you kick it. D. Harry sat down on the Owlery floor among the feathers and read it about nine times. When he had his own broom back from McGonagall, he sent the Nimbus back to her from the same place with a school owl. Standing in the doorway afterwards, with the wind coming off the lake through the arrow slits, he admitted to himself that it was decent of you had been the easiest line in his note to write.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, hearing Pansy sob out her apology on the front steps, Harry understood at last that it was she, not Hermione, who had sent the Buckbeak letter. Soon afterwards two girls arrived at the top of the Owlery steps within a few seconds of each other, both slightly out of breath: Hermione and Dracina, each with a letter for Molly Weasley. They stopped dead and looked at each other.

pages.title: The Potions dungeon
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Pickled things in jars along every wall; a stone sink fed from a gargoyle's mouth
pages.html:
The Potions dungeon is the classroom in the dungeons of Hogwarts where Professor Snape teaches Potions. It is colder than the castle above, and pickled things float in jars along every wall. In one corner is a stone sink, where water runs in a freezing stream from a gargoyle's open mouth.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Harry's first Potions lesson was held there. Snape asked him what he would get if he added powdered root of asphodel to an infusion of wormwood, then set the class to brew a simple potion for curing boils. Neville Longbottom melted Seamus Finnigan's cauldron into a twisted lump, and the potion spread across the flagstones, eating holes in people's shoes.

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Harry lobbed a firework into Goyle's cauldron, and the Swelling Solution came down over half the class while Hermione slipped out to steal what she needed from Snape's office. In Book Three, Chapter Seven, Harry and Ron went to wash their ladles at the stone sink in the corner, in the lesson in which Neville's Shrinking Solution was tried out on his toad, Trevor. In Chapter Sixteen the third-years sat their Potions exam in the dungeon, at benches Snape had set out himself.

pages.title: Hospital wing
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The hospital wing is the infirmary of Hogwarts, on the first floor, where Madam Pomfrey mends whatever the castle breaks. It is a dim ward of beds with curtains that can be drawn round them, and it smells of Dittany.

The ward

Madam Pomfrey can mend a broken bone in a night. Her patients stay in bed until she is satisfied with them, whatever they think about it; arguing with her is like arguing with a door. When the Petrified were brought in during the school year of 1992 to 1993, they lay at the far end behind screens until the Mandrakes were ready. The bed under the window at the far end, the one with curtains, was Dracina Malfoy's in September 1993.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Snape sent Neville Longbottom to the hospital wing with boils coming up on his nose. In Chapter Five Madam Hooch took him there with a broken wrist. Harry Potter lay in the ward himself at the end of his first year, with what looked like the entire stock of Honeydukes on the table beside his bed. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, he remembered how Dumbledore had talked to him there about Muggle-born ancestry.

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, the Petrified Colin Creevey and Justin Finch-Fletchley lay behind drawn curtains. Hermione Granger was hidden in the far corner after her Polyjuice mishap. In Chapter Fifteen, over Christmas 1992, Dracina lay in the next bed to Hermione's. In Chapter Nineteen, after the Chamber, Ginny Weasley and Dracina were sent there for bed rest with hot chocolate, while the Petrified were given Mandrake juice.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, Harry remembered talking with Dracina there in June 1993. On 2 September 1993 he went in at night and found the lamp lit by her bed at the far end, with its curtains half drawn. They argued. In Chapter Seven he kept slowing down at the doors on his way to Charms, then walking on.

In Chapter Ten, in November 1993, Harry was a patient there again after the Hufflepuff match. Pansy Parkinson stood looking at the bed under the window, which had been Dracina's in September, and at the bare table beside it. In Chapter Fourteen Dracina said that she had left an unsent letter on that table in September: four pages to her father, in her own handwriting. Somebody had taken it while she slept, she told Pansy.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Harry, Hermione and Ron were brought to the hospital wing after the dementor attack. At five minutes to midnight Dumbledore locked them in. In Chapter Twenty-One, on the night of Sirius Black's escape, Harry and Hermione ran back along the corridor to the same door, with Dracina Malfoy behind them. As far as Slytherin House knew, she had been in the hospital wing since lunch with a sprained wrist. From outside the door they heard him say the same words all over again. 'It is five minutes to midnight,' Dumbledore was saying. 'Miss Granger, three turns should do it. Good luck.' He stepped back out of the ward, closed the door and turned his wand on the lock. Harry and Hermione dashed towards him, while Dracina hung back a little.

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine remembered his fifth year at Hogwarts. Somebody had put something in his pumpkin juice, and he spent nine days in the hospital wing with his skin going slowly green. Lucius Malfoy came and sat at the end of his bed, reading aloud.

pages.title: Hagrid's hut
aliases: the little wooden house on the edge of the forest
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The edge of the Forbidden Forest, in the Hogwarts grounds
Rubeus Hagrid, with his boarhound Fang
A pumpkin patch; a paddock five minutes along the trees
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Hagrid's hut is the little wooden house at the edge of the Forbidden Forest where Rubeus Hagrid, the Hogwarts gamekeeper, lives with his boarhound, Fang. It has only one room. Lucius Malfoy, by his daughter's account, calls it a shack. More than one unhappy student has found it the friendliest place in the grounds.

Inside and out

Hams hang from the ceiling, and a kettle boils on the open fire. There is an enormous bed, a basket for Fang and, on the mantelpiece, a tin of treacle fudge. The hut has a front door and a back door. Behind it lies the pumpkin patch where Hagrid grows his giant pumpkins, with a big tree near the edge of the Forest. His paddock lies five minutes along the trees.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter One, Dracina Malfoy told Harry Potter in Madam Malkin's that, according to her father, Hagrid was practically wild and lived in a shack in the grounds. In Chapter Four Harry and Ron Weasley went down to the little wooden house on the edge of the forest for tea on the Friday of their first week. In Chapter Ten an enormous black egg sat in the heart of Hagrid's fire, under the kettle. 'Hagrid,' Hermione said. 'You live in a wooden house.' Soon afterwards Norbert the dragon hatched there, on the table.

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1992, Harry and Hermione got Ron, who was belching slugs, into the one-roomed cabin. It had an enormous bed in one corner and a fire crackling in another. In the vegetable patch behind it grew a dozen of Hagrid's pumpkins, each the size of a boulder. In Chapter Sixteen Harry and Ron hid there under the Invisibility Cloak while Cornelius Fudge arrested Hagrid. Lucius Malfoy came to the hut to suspend Dumbledore. He looked slowly round at the hams hanging from the ceiling, the enormous bed and Fang drooling in his basket. 'Forgive me. What do you call this? A house?' Before he was taken away, Hagrid told the empty air that anyone wanting to find something out need only follow the spiders. In Chapter Seventeen Harry and Ron came back to the empty hut at night. They fed Fang treacle fudge from the tin on the mantelpiece to keep him quiet. When they got back from following the spiders, Ron was violently sick in the pumpkin patch.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, Hagrid led his first Care of Magical Creatures class from the hut along the edge of the trees to his paddock, five minutes' walk away. In Chapter Eleven Buckbeak spent Christmas 1993 inside the cabin, lying in front of the fire like an enormous hearthrug. In Chapter Sixteen, on the day of his execution, he was tethered to the big tree behind the cabin, at the edge of the pumpkin patch. In Chapter Twenty, as he broke free, his hind legs smashed straight through Hagrid's fence.

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, Hagrid came running from the hut to greet John Constantine, whom he had not seen for twenty-two years. John remembered how he had gone down to the hut in the 1960s, when he was eleven, twelve or thirteen and the Slytherins had locked him out of their common room again. Hagrid, then a great shaggy gamekeeper in his thirties, never once asked what was wrong. He simply put the kettle on.

pages.title: Vault seven hundred and thirteen
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A grubby little package: the Philosopher's Stone
pages.html:
Vault seven hundred and thirteen is a high-security vault deep under Gringotts, the wizarding bank in Diagon Alley. Until the summer of 1991 it held a single grubby little package: the Philosopher's Stone of Nicolas Flamel. Hagrid took it out on Dumbledore's business on the day he brought Harry Potter to Diagon Alley. That same day somebody broke into Gringotts to search the vault, only to find it empty.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, after meeting the three-headed dog on its trapdoor, Harry remembered what Hagrid had told him about the break-in: there was nowhere safer than Gringotts for something you wanted to hide, except perhaps Hogwarts. It looked as though he had just found out where the grubby little package had gone.

pages.title: Malfoy Manor
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
William the Conqueror, to Armand Malfoy
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Malfoy Manor is the ancestral house of the Malfoy family, in Wiltshire, on land that William the Conqueror granted to Armand Malfoy. It is the home of Lucius Malfoy, his wife Narcissa and their daughter Dracina. Beneath its elegant rooms lies one of the finest private collections of Dark artefacts in Britain.

History

The Malfoys came over from Normandy with William the Conqueror. Armand Malfoy was given his land in Wiltshire by the King himself, in return for services the family has never cared to describe. The land had been taken from its Anglo-Saxon owners to make room for him. The Malfoys have lived on it ever since. Their crest, embossed on the family's cream writing paper, is a letter M with a serpent through it.

The house and grounds

The Manor has forty bedrooms, with ancestral portraits on every wall. The Malfoy family tree covers the whole of one wall of the drawing room. In the east drawing room Narcissa Malfoy keeps a woven hanging of Saint George. The library is so large that Dracina describes it as a whole wing. She took lessons there for years from a man from Paris. Dracina has a wing of her own as well, with a bedroom the size of the Gryffindor common room.

The grounds hold rose gardens, an orangery and a lake. When Dracina was eight, Lucius had the lake frozen so that she could skate on it. White peacocks walk the lawns. When Dracina was frightened of them as a little girl, her father had them moved.

The house keeps a gamekeeper, from whom Dracina learnt to whistle, and servants who are afraid of her. Until 1993 it also kept a house-elf, Dobby. It lies at the far end of the Hogwarts Express line, beyond London.

Hidden rooms

Beneath the drawing-room floor is a secret room, where Lucius keeps his oldest and most valuable Dark artefacts. When the Ministry of Magic raided the Manor in December 1992, its officers walked over the room twice without finding it. The cellar holds an armoury, with a further collection of objects that have not been used in anger for a hundred years.

In August 1992, expecting the raids, Lucius arranged for Mr Borgin of Borgin and Burkes to collect a selection of poisons from the house, with a few other items besides. Borgin was quite sure he had not been offered half of what was hidden there.

Harry and the Manor

Harry has never been to Malfoy Manor. Narcissa invited him for Christmas in 1991, and he laughed the invitation off as a prank. Dracina wrote to him from the Manor in July 1993, then again in July 1994. The portraits in the house took to leaving their frames whenever Dracina came in talking about him.

pages.title: Dracina Malfoy's eagle owl
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's eagle owl is the great eagle owl that brings Dracina parcels of sweets from home at breakfast. Strictly the bird is not hers. He is Ganymede, and he belongs to her mother, Narcissa.

Description

He is a huge, dark, barred eagle owl, with ear tufts like horns and eyes the colour of marmalade. He has nothing in common with Dracina's own owl, Juniper, a small, dull brown bird who carries her secret letters to Harry Potter.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Harry, who had not had a single letter since Hagrid's note, watched the eagle owl bring Dracina her parcels of sweets. She unwrapped them at the Slytherin table with a great deal of noise, looking over at Gryffindor as she did it. The owl has gone on bringing them every week ever since.

In Book Three, Chapter One, Dracina's birthday letter to Harry gave the bird his name. It was Mother who sent Ganymede, she wrote, 'who is hers really'.

pages.title: Leprechauns
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Gold that vanishes after a few hours
pages.html:
Leprechauns are small, green, mischievous creatures found only in Ireland. They are cleverer than fairies, and they can talk. They make a kind of gold that looks perfectly real, though it vanishes after a few hours, which comes as a disappointment to anybody who has stolen it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in his first weeks at Hogwarts in 1991, Seamus Finnigan was full of boastful stories about flying. To hear him tell it, he had spent his whole childhood zooming over the Irish countryside on a broomstick, chased by leprechauns whose gold he had stolen.

pages.title: Astronomy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The top of the tallest tower
pages.html:
Astronomy is the study of the night sky, and one of the core subjects at Hogwarts. Professor Sinistra teaches it at midnight, on top of the tallest tower in the castle.

Lessons

Professor Sinistra is a tall, severe witch who says very little and expects her classes to say less. First-years lie on their backs on the cold stone of the tower top while she points at the sky with a long thin finger, and they draw what she points at. They learn the names of the stars, the constellations and the moons of Jupiter. Astronomy is not astrology, though the two are closely linked. The old Greek and Roman sorcerers believed that the planets governed magic itself. Professor Sinistra holds that the phase of the moon affects almost everything.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, on the Wednesday of his first week in 1991, Harry Potter climbed to the top of the tallest tower at midnight with his telescope. On the way up Hermione Granger explained that Astronomy and Astrology were different, though very closely linked. Harry drew the Plough three times before Professor Sinistra accepted it. By the end of the lesson he knew the names of twenty-two stars, and he had a chart of the moons of Jupiter. He had also learnt that Hermione could whisper the Latin name of a constellation faster than he could find it.

pages.title: History of Magic
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Goblin rebellions, pure-blood families, wizards' conventions
The dullest lesson on the timetable
pages.html:
History of Magic is the Hogwarts subject that covers the wizarding past. It is taught by Professor Binns, the only ghost on the staff, and it is generally held to be the dullest lesson on the timetable.

Professor Binns

Binns was already very old, and very dull, when he fell asleep in front of the staffroom fire one evening. He got up next morning to teach, leaving his body behind him in the armchair, and in Ron Weasley's opinion he has not noticed yet. He drifts in through the blackboard to read from his notes in a voice like a bath draining, and within five minutes a whole class has the glazed look of a congregation on a hot Sunday. He has the gift of making a war sound like a bus timetable.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Binns gave out pure-blood family histories in exactly the voice he used for goblin rebellions. By Book One, Chapter Five, Harry Potter had found that Gryffindor shared only two lessons with Slytherin, Potions and History of Magic. In History of Magic everybody was asleep. In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Hermione Granger prevailed upon Binns, for once, to tell a story: the legend of the Chamber of Secrets. He told it, then insisted that there was no such thing.

pages.title: Potions
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Potions is the art of brewing magical draughts, and one of the core subjects at Hogwarts. It is taught by Professor Snape, the Head of Slytherin House, in a dungeon colder than the castle above, with pickled things floating in jars along every wall.

The subject

It is an exact art, and a dangerous one. Snape calls it ‘a precise art and a subtle thing’, with very little foolish wand-waving about it. A potion that goes wrong can melt a cauldron, or do worse to the person standing over it. Snape has no patience with mistakes, and very little with Gryffindors.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, the Gryffindor first-years took double Potions with Slytherin. Snape stopped at Harry Potter's name in the register, as Flitwick had done. ‘Ah,’ he said softly. ‘Harry Potter. How very... famous.’ Later in the lesson Neville Longbottom melted Seamus Finnigan's cauldron into a twisted lump. The potion ate holes in people's shoes, and Neville came out in angry red boils.

pages.title: Transfiguration
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Branch of magic; a core subject at Hogwarts
Turning a match into a needle
pages.html:
Transfiguration is the branch of magic that turns one thing into another: a match into a needle, say, or a desk into a pig. At Hogwarts it is taught by Professor Minerva McGonagall, Head of Gryffindor House. It is some of the most complex magic taught at the school, and some of the most dangerous.

Its limits

Transfiguration has limits, and Gamp's Law sets out a good many of them. Food cannot be transfigured out of nothing. A living creature cannot be turned into a person, nor a person permanently into a creature against their will, without the most serious consequences. Nor will any Transfiguration separate a person from a creature that has taken up residence inside him.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, at the start-of-term feast, Hermione Granger told Percy Weasley that she was particularly looking forward to Transfiguration. Percy said she would begin with small things, matches into needles and so forth. In Chapter Four, in September 1991, McGonagall turned her desk into a pig and back again before her first years had even sat down. She warned them that anybody messing about in her class would leave it and not come back. Then she set them to turning a matchstick into a needle. By the end of the lesson Hermione's match had gone silver and pointed at one end. McGonagall showed it to the class. Harry Potter's was still a match, though he thought it looked slightly more tired than it had.

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Hermione showed off a handful of perfect coat buttons she had made in Transfiguration. Ron Weasley's broken wand swallowed him in grey smoke that smelt of rotten eggs every time he tried to transfigure his beetle. In Chapter Eighteen McGonagall told the second years that their exams would begin on the first of June, Chamber or no Chamber.

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in October 1993, McGonagall taught the third years the limits of Transfiguration. There are creatures, she told them, that go in through the back of the neck, wrap themselves round the spine and speak with the host's mouth. 'No Transfiguration will separate the two,' she said. 'I know, because I once tried.' In the end only a knife had answered, with a steady hand and a good deal of help from a man she would not name. The host had died, and so had the creature. She had kept it, as a reminder that some problems cannot be solved with a wand.

pages.title: Charms
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Charms is the Hogwarts subject that teaches the spells which make things do what they would not do on their own: fly, shine, unlock or grow. It is taught by Professor Flitwick, a tiny wizard who stands on a pile of books to see over his desk.

Lessons

Early lessons are all theory. The theory is all wand movements: the swish, the flick and the difference between them. Only when a class has those right does Flitwick let it try a real spell. The words matter as much as the wand, as Wizard Baruffio found out.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Flitwick gave a squeak and toppled off his books when he reached Harry Potter's name in the register. The lesson after that was all theory, and Harry's wand would not swish in the least. In Book One, Chapter Six, on Hallowe'en, Flitwick judged the class ready to make things fly, which they had all been longing to do since the day he sent Neville Longbottom's toad whizzing round the classroom. They tried the Levitation Charm at last.

pages.title: Defence Against the Dark Arts
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Hexes, jinxes and how to block them
Quirrell (1991 to 1992); Lockhart (1992 to 1993); Lupin (1993 to 1994)
pages.html:
Defence Against the Dark Arts is the Hogwarts subject that teaches hexes, jinxes and how to block them. It also covers the dark creatures, from vampires to werewolves. For some years nobody has lasted long in the post, and by 1992 it was widely believed to be jinxed.

A jinxed post

The school does seem to get through its teachers. Professor Quirrell, a stammering man in a purple turban, taught the subject from 1991 to 1992 with Lord Voldemort living on the back of his head. Gilderoy Lockhart, who had made his name with other people's deeds, took it in 1992 because nobody else would, and left it a year later with no memory of who he was. Remus Lupin, the best teacher the subject had had in years, took it in 1993. He resigned in June 1994, after the night when, without his potion, he very nearly tore Harry Potter to pieces.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, the first-years' first lesson with Quirrell, in a classroom that stank of garlic, taught them nothing at all in an hour and a half. When Seamus Finnigan asked whether it was true that he had fought a vampire in Romania, Quirrell went white and knocked over his inkwell. In Book Two, Chapter Six, Harry and Ron Weasley supposed that Snape had missed out on the post again. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Hagrid told them the post was thought to be jinxed, and that Lockhart had been the only candidate.

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, with Lockhart gone, lessons were cancelled for the rest of the summer term of 1993. Dumbledore remarked that the school did seem to get through its teachers. In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry counted up the three he had had so far. One had had Voldemort living on the back of his head. One had tried to wipe his memory. One had very nearly torn him to pieces, though that had not been Lupin's fault. Whoever came next, Harry worked out, was very likely to try to kill him as well, and this time he meant to be ready.

pages.title: Wizard's duel
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Takes over if the duellist dies
pages.html:
A wizard's duel is a formal fight between two witches or wizards, fought with wands only and no touching. Each duellist has a second, who takes over if the duellist dies.

History

Duels have settled a good many wizarding quarrels, not always tidily. The English and the French argued over the rules of Quidditch for more than a thousand years, settling the matter with wands from time to time. In 1877 a dispute over the proper weight of a Quaffle, between the England manager, Francis Grail, and the French manager, Juste Valmond, ended in a duel. Two hundred witches and wizards died in the crossfire. The casualty list ran to three pages.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in September 1991, Dracina Malfoy challenged Harry Potter in the Great Hall. 'A wizard's duel. Wands only, no touching. What's the matter? Never heard of a wizard's duel, I suppose?' Ron Weasley named himself Harry's second. Dracina looked her two friends over as though choosing a pudding. 'Crabbe,' she said. Ron fixed the time and place: midnight, in the trophy room. A second, he explained afterwards, is the one who takes over if you die. Seeing Harry's face, he added quickly that the only people who die in proper duels are real wizards. The most Harry and Dracina could manage, he said, was a few sparks at each other.

That night Harry and Ron crept down to the trophy room. Hermione Granger, who had tried to stop them, came too, with Neville Longbottom. Dracina and Crabbe never came. Filch did. Hermione was sure that Dracina had tipped him off, and had never meant to turn up at all.

pages.title: Wizard Baruffio
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Wizard Baruffio is the wizard Professor Flitwick holds up to his pupils as a warning. He said ‘s’ when he meant ‘f’ in the middle of a spell, and found himself flat on the floor with a buffalo on his chest.

A cautionary tale

In spell-work the words matter quite as much as the wand movement, and a single wrong letter can turn a charm into something else entirely. When and where Baruffio made his mistake is not recorded. Nor is what became of the buffalo.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, on Hallowe'en morning in 1991, Professor Flitwick put his first-years into pairs to try the Levitation Charm. From his pile of books he squeaked a reminder about the wrist movement, swish and flick. Then he told them to pronounce the words properly and to remember Wizard Baruffio.

pages.title: The Hallowe'en troll
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Granite-grey skin, a small bald head, a huge wooden club
Ron Weasley, with its own club (31 October 1991)
pages.html:
The Hallowe'en troll was a twelve-foot mountain troll that got into Hogwarts on Hallowe'en 1991. Professor Quirrell had let it in. It cornered Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy in the girls' toilets. Ron Weasley knocked it out with its own club. From that night on, Hermione was Harry's friend, and Ron's.

Description

It was horrible to look at. It had skin the dull grey of granite, a great lumpy body like a boulder and a small bald head perched on top like a coconut. Its legs were short, as thick as tree trunks, with flat, horny feet. Its arms were so long that the vast wooden club it carried dragged along the floor. The smell was beyond belief, like old socks crossed with a public lavatory nobody ever cleans.

It was not the biggest troll in the castle that year. An even bigger one was later found out cold among the defences round the Philosopher's Stone.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, Professor Quirrell came sprinting into the Hallowe'en feast with his turban askew. 'Troll. In the dungeons. Thought you ought to know.' The prefects led everyone to their dormitories. Harry Potter and Ron Weasley, knowing that Hermione had not heard, slipped away. They saw the troll go into a room and locked it in. Then they heard two screams from inside: it was the girls' toilets.

Hermione was shrinking against one wall. Dracina was flattened against the other, and the troll was lumbering towards her, knocking the sinks off the wall as it went. Harry threw a tap to draw it away from Dracina. Ron yelled at it and threw a length of pipe. Then Harry jumped on to the troll's back with his wand still in his hand, and the wand went straight up one of its nostrils. As it flailed its club with Harry clinging on, Ron raised his wand. 'Wingardium Leviosa!' he cried. The club rose high into the air and came down on its owner's head with a sickening crack.

Professor McGonagall arrived with Snape. Quirrell came behind them, took one look at the troll and sat down quickly on a toilet. Hermione lied to save the boys, saying she had gone looking for the troll herself. Dracina lied too: she had come with Granger, she said, to fight it and impress her father. McGonagall took five points from Gryffindor for Hermione, and Snape five from Slytherin for Dracina. Harry and Ron won five points each.

In Chapter Thirteen, deep beneath the school in June 1992, Harry asked Quirrell whether he had let the troll in. 'Naturally. Trolls and I have an understanding.'

pages.title: Troll
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Great strength, very little sense, a terrible smell
pages.html:
Trolls are huge, stupid, foul-smelling creatures of great strength. A mountain troll, the largest and most dangerous kind, can stand twelve feet tall. It has a small bald head on a body like a boulder, and it carries a club.

Trolls and wizards

Trolls are no good at thinking, but they can be trained to do simple work, such as guarding a door. They can hardly feel an ordinary blow. Even a troll notices, though, when something goes up its nose.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, at Hallowe'en 1991, a twelve-foot mountain troll was let into the castle. It wandered into the girls' toilets, where Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy were. It went for Dracina first. Harry Potter jumped on to its back and stuck his wand up its nose. Ron Weasley brought its own club down on its head with a Levitation Charm.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, in 1994, the Fat Lady refused to go back to work unless somebody stood guard over her, so the castle hired a gang of security trolls. They paced the corridor outside her portrait at all hours, grunting at one another and holding up their clubs side by side like boys comparing conkers.

In Chapter Twenty, on the night of 6 June 1994, Hermione told Harry what she still remembered of that first Hallowe'en. ‘It smelt like a sewer,’ she said. She still dreamt about it. It had gone straight for Dracina, and for about one second, Hermione confessed, she had been glad.

pages.title: Centaurs
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Beings, half man and half horse
A herd in the Forbidden Forest
Reading the future in the planets
pages.html:
Centaurs are half man and half horse. A herd of them lives in the Forbidden Forest at Hogwarts. They read the future in the movements of the planets, and they have sworn not to set themselves against the heavens.

Nature

Centaurs are proud and keep to themselves. They concern themselves with what has been foretold, and most of them hold that it is no business of theirs to help humans. Wizards tend to think them violent. Their readings are not always right. As Firenze has said, the planets have been read wrongly before now, even by centaurs.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, after the troll, Harry Potter pulled his wand out of its nose and wiped it on its trousers. 'You barbarian!' Dracina Malfoy cried. 'I've met centaurs with better manners than you, Potter!'

In Chapter Eleven, during a detention in the Forest, the centaur Firenze saved Harry from the black shape that had been feeding on a dead unicorn, and let him ride on his back. Bane, black-haired and black-bodied, was furious. 'Have you no shame? Are you some common mule?' He reminded Firenze that they had sworn not to set themselves against the heavens. Centaurs, he said, concern themselves with what has been foretold. Firenze reared up. 'I set myself against what is lurking in this Forest, Bane. Yes. With humans beside me if I must.' When he left Harry with Hagrid, he wished him luck. 'The planets have been read wrongly before now. Even by centaurs. I hope this is one of those times.'

In Chapter Twelve Professor Quirrell was found at the edge of the Forest, covered in cuts and howling in tongues. The whole school decided that centaurs had attacked him. Centaurs were violent; everyone knew that. Harry did not believe it.

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, when Ron Weasley asked whether there were werewolves in the Forest, Harry told him that there were good things in there too. 'The centaurs are all right. And the unicorns.'

pages.title: Comet Two Sixty
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Comet Two Sixty is a racing broom made by the Comet Trading Company. It is flashy and expensive. In its day it was a very good broom, but it has never been in the same class as a Nimbus.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, after Harry’s Nimbus Two Thousand arrived, Ron asked Dracina Malfoy whether it was a Comet Two Sixty she had at home. Then he grinned at Harry. ‘Comets look flashy, but they’re nowhere near a Nimbus. Only poor people have a Comet Two Sixty.’

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Which Broomstick listed it among the expensive brooms. In Chapter Thirteen Cho Chang rode one as Ravenclaw’s Seeker against Gryffindor. Oliver Wood had predicted that it would look like a joke next to the Firebolt. When Harry pulled out of a feint dive, Cho went hurtling on past him, wrestling with her Comet, and finished eighty feet below the match. Harry and Ron were still arguing about it on the way up to bed: could a Comet Two Sixty ever have pulled out of that dive?

pages.title: Quaffle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Quaffle is the bright red ball used to score goals in Quidditch. It is about the size of a football. The three Chasers on each side pass it from hand to hand, trying to throw it through one of the other team's hoops for ten points. The Keeper's job is to stop them.

In play

There are three hoops at each end of the pitch, on golden poles fifty feet high. Of the four balls in the game, the Quaffle is the only one that does nothing of its own accord. It goes where it is thrown.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, Oliver Wood showed Harry the Quaffle: a bright red ball about the size of a football, though a good deal harder, which the Chasers use to score ten points a goal.

In Chapter Seven Harry read in Quidditch Through the Ages that a dispute over the proper weight of a Quaffle, in 1877, had ended in a duel between the England manager, Francis Grail, and the French manager, Juste Valmond. Two hundred witches and wizards died in the crossfire.

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Harry explained the game to Colin Creevey. 'Well, the Quaffle, that's the biggish red one, is the one that scores goals.'

pages.title: Bludger
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Bludgers are the two jet-black balls in Quidditch that rocket about the pitch trying to knock players off their brooms. Each side has two Beaters, who carry short clubs to beat them away from their own team.

The balls

A Bludger is a heavy iron ball, about ten inches across, quite hard enough to break a bone. It has no favourites. It goes for whichever player is nearest, which is why a good Beater is worth a great deal to a Seeker.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, Oliver Wood showed Harry the two Bludgers straining against their straps in the crate.
