They fly about trying to knock players off their brooms, he said, which is why each side has two Beaters to hit them away. Harry asked whether they had ever killed anyone. ‘Never at Hogwarts. A couple of broken jaws, nothing worse.’

By the summer of 1992 Fred and George had spent a whole term belting Bludgers at Harry’s head in practice. In Book Two, Chapter One, when Aunt Petunia swung a soapy frying pan at him, he ducked it with a foot to spare. Next to a Bludger, he decided, a frying pan was nothing at all.

In Chapter Eleven, at the Slytherin match of November 1992, one Bludger ignored every other player on the pitch and came after Harry alone, time after time. Fred and George flew so close on either side of him, batting it away, that he could hardly look for the Snitch. Late in the match Dracina Malfoy threw her own broom across its path in front of him, and it clipped the tail of her Nimbus. A moment later it came up from below and broke Harry’s right elbow. He caught the Snitch all the same.

That night, in the hospital wing, Dobby the house-elf owned up. It had been his Bludger. He had never meant to kill Harry, only to hurt him badly enough to be packed off home.

pages.title: Golden Snitch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
About as big as a walnut
pages.html:
The Golden Snitch is the smallest ball in Quidditch, a gold ball about the size of a walnut, with fluttering silver wings. Each team's Seeker hunts for it. Catching it ends the match and wins the Seeker's team 150 points.

The ball

The Snitch is so small and so fast that it is very hard to see. A match is not over until somebody catches it. Oliver Wood believes the record is three months, with substitutes brought on so that the players could sleep. The Snitch was made in the fourteenth century by Bowman Wright, a metal-charmer of Godric’s Hollow, to take the place of the Golden Snidget, a little bird that wizards had hunted almost to nothing for the game.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, Oliver Wood took the Snitch out of the crate for Harry, tiny and bright gold, with small silver wings that fluttered. Catching it, he said, was the Seeker’s whole job. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Harry explained it all over again to Colin Creevey.

In Chapter Eleven, at the match against Slytherin in November 1992, Harry saw the Snitch hovering just above Dracina Malfoy’s head, so close that it almost touched her hair. She had not seen it. She was looking at Harry. He waited a second too long, afraid she would look up, and the rogue Bludger broke his right arm. Then he dived at her, steering with his knees, and snatched the Snitch out of the air above her head with his left hand. He hit the mud hard. His fingers were still locked round it.

pages.title: Hogwarts Quidditch pitch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Hundreds of tiered seats; a wooden stand for each house
Three at each end, golden, fifty feet high, with hoops
The wind at the corner by the south stands
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Hogwarts Quidditch pitch is the stadium in the school grounds where the four house teams train and play their matches. Hundreds of seats rise in tiers round the field, high enough for the spectators to see what is going on. At either end stand three golden goalposts, fifty feet high, with hoops on the top.

The stadium

Each house has its own wooden stand, hung with its colours on match days. When a crowd gets going the whole structure shakes. Madam Hooch, who referees the matches, has an office beside the pitch.

The worst of the weather comes at the corner by the south stands, where the wind comes round the tower.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, on 5 September 1992, Gryffindor and Slytherin both claimed the pitch for practice. It led to the fight between Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, at the match against Slytherin in November 1992, the stamping of feet during Dean Thomas's chant made the whole stadium shake.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, on the eve of the Hufflepuff match in November 1993, the Fat Friar gave Harry Potter a warning: 'do mind the weather on that corner by the south stands, the wind comes round the tower there like a bailiff.' The next day it came round exactly as he had promised, like a bailiff, and tried to repossess Harry's broom. On the next circuit Harry took it on purpose.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, at the final of 1994, nearly every seat in the stadium was scarlet. The exception was a block of two hundred Slytherins in green, behind their own goalposts.

pages.title: The girls' toilets
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A mountain troll cornered Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy there
pages.html:
The girls' toilets were where Hermione Granger shut herself away to cry on Hallowe'en 1991, after hearing what Ron Weasley thought of her. That night a mountain troll got loose in the castle and found its way in. Hermione was trapped there with Dracina Malfoy, until Harry Potter and Ron came back to fight it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, on the way down to the Hallowe'en feast, Parvati Patil told Lavender Brown that Hermione was crying in the girls' toilets and wanted to be left alone. At the feast Harry noticed that Dracina was missing from the Slytherin table as well. When word came that a troll was loose, Harry remembered that Hermione did not know. He and Ron went to find her.

They found the troll instead, watched it go into a room and locked it in, only to hear two screams from behind the door. It was the girls' toilets. Inside, Hermione was shrinking against the far wall, with Dracina flattened against the wall opposite, and the troll was lumbering towards Dracina. Between them, Harry and Ron knocked it out.

pages.title: Wingardium Leviosa
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Wingardium Leviosa, the Levitation Charm, makes objects rise and fly. It is the first proper charm most Hogwarts students learn. It needs a swish and flick of the wand. The words have to be said properly too, with the 'gar' nice and long.

Pronunciation

Professor Flitwick warns his first-years to pronounce their spells properly by telling them about Wizard Baruffio, who said 's' when he meant 'f' and found himself flat on the floor with a buffalo on his chest.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, on Hallowe'en 1991, Flitwick's first-years tried to make feathers fly. Ron Weasley bellowed the words, waving his long arms like a windmill, and got nowhere. 'You're saying it wrong,' Hermione Granger snapped. 'It's Win-gar-dium Levi-o-sa. Make the "gar" nice and long.' Then she did it herself. Her feather rose four feet into the air. Flitwick was delighted. Ron was not. What he said about her in the corridor afterwards sent her off in tears to the girls' toilets, which is where the troll found her that evening.

That night Ron used the same charm to save her. With Harry clinging to the troll's neck, Ron pulled out his wand. 'Wingardium Leviosa!' he cried. It was the first spell that came into his head. The club leapt out of the troll's fist, rose high into the air, turned over slowly and came down on its owner's head with a sickening crack.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, in September 1993, Harry tried to tell Professor Trelawney that Muggles believed somebody was watching over them and could send them a sign. She told him that the signs studied in her classroom were real signs. They were 'not the muddled wishful thinking of people who cannot perform so much as a Levitation Charm and so must comfort themselves with angels.' Half the room laughed with her.

pages.title: The IRA
infobox: A united Ireland, free of British rule
pages.html:
The IRA, the Irish Republican Army, is the paramilitary force that has fought since 1969 to drive Britain out of Northern Ireland. Its bombs in English cities make it a regular item on the Muggle news, to Vernon Dursley's fury.

The campaign in England

Its bombs have reached far into England. In 1984 it bombed the Grand Hotel at Brighton during the Conservative conference. In 1991 it fired mortars at Downing Street. In 1993 it bombed Warrington and the City of London. On 31 August 1994 it announced a complete ceasefire.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, when Harry finally lost his temper with Dracina Malfoy, he was right in her face, redder than Uncle Vernon when he saw an IRA attack on the news.

pages.title: Apache helicopter
pages.html:
The Apache is an American attack helicopter, a heavy, well-armed Muggle machine that the United States Army has flown since 1986. Dracina Malfoy, for one, had never heard of it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, Dracina Malfoy told long, boastful stories about flying. They always ended with her narrowly outflying a Muggle in a helicopter, while adoring Muggles with enormous cameras begged her for interviews.

In Chapter Six she came down to Gryffindor’s Quidditch practice to sneer at Harry. He told her that she could not even hold a broom properly, yet she reckoned she had dodged one of those enormous American Apache helicopters. Dracina did not let it go. ‘I don’t know what an Apache is, Potter, but I was dodging those big black Muggle helicopters while you were still in nappies.’ Her laugh would not quite come, and she knew she was losing ground.

pages.title: Angelina Johnson
infobox: Gryffindor, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Gryffindor Quidditch team, Chaser
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Angelina Johnson is a Gryffindor witch in the same year as Fred and George Weasley. She is one of the Chasers on the Gryffindor Quidditch team. She is tall, quick to lose her temper and very reliable in front of goal. Oliver Wood expected her to follow him as captain.

Quidditch

Angelina scored the first goal of Harry Potter's first match, against Slytherin in November 1991, while Harry did loop-the-loops over her head. She once had to remind Oliver Wood that his team had women in it. In September 1992, when the Slytherin team insulted Hermione, she and Katie Bell held the twins back. In the Slytherin match that November Marcus Flint barged into her so hard that she went twice round the goalposts. Later a Bludger knocked her off a scoring run.

In 1993 she swore back at Wood at practice. Wood told Harry afterwards that he expected McGonagall to make her captain when he left. Against Ravenclaw in 1994 Harry told her to wait on the outside, and she scored the goals that mattered from there. After the win she kissed Harry. At the party that night Wood propped a slate on the mantelpiece to walk them all through the sums. When he gazed at it for slightly too long, Angelina said gently, 'Oliver, you're crying on the mantelpiece.' In the final Flint barged her almost off her broom, but she scored several goals all the same, among them the one that put Gryffindor eighty points to twenty ahead.

In the saga

Angelina is Black. She was once upset by a strange Ravenclaw girl, a year below Harry, who started going on to her about crime statistics. In the spring of 1993 Lee Jordan proposed duelling the Slytherins. Angelina dismissed the plan, pointing out that half of Gryffindor could not do a Shield Charm.

pages.title: Alicia Spinnet
infobox: Gryffindor, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Gryffindor Quidditch team, Chaser
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Alicia Spinnet is a Gryffindor witch in the same year as Fred and George Weasley. She is one of the three Chasers on the Gryffindor Quidditch team, though she spent the season before Harry Potter joined it as a reserve.

Gryffindor

Alicia came to Hogwarts in 1989 and was sorted into Gryffindor. She spent the 1990 to 1991 season as a reserve. From the following autumn she flew as a Chaser beside Angelina Johnson and Katie Bell, under Oliver Wood's captaincy, with Harry as their Seeker.

On the pitch

In Harry's first match, in November 1991, Marcus Flint fouled him, and Alicia scored from the penalty. At Wood's dawn practice on 5 September 1992, early in her fourth year, she dozed off against the changing-room wall, and Fred fell asleep on her shoulder in the middle of the tactics talk. In the Slytherin match that autumn Pucey and Warrington sandwiched her between them. When the rogue Bludger went for Harry, she argued for an inquiry rather than leaving him to face it alone.

Against Ravenclaw in the spring of 1994 a Bludger broke her left forearm. She played on one-handed, and scored. She came back from the hospital wing with the arm strapped up, under orders not to fly for a week. In the final the Slytherin Beater Bole clubbed her. She was so furious that she sent the penalty yards wide, though she scored again afterwards. George paid Bole back with an elbow across the nose.

In the saga

Alicia once described Cedric Diggory, the Hufflepuff captain, as strong and quiet.

pages.title: Katie Bell
infobox: Gryffindor, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Gryffindor Quidditch team, Chaser
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Katie Bell is a Gryffindor witch, a year above Harry Potter. She has played Chaser for the Gryffindor Quidditch team since 1991.

Life

Katie grew up with four brothers, yet she still went pink when Oliver Wood swore at practice. She joined the Gryffindor team as a Chaser in her second year. She has played alongside Angelina Johnson and Alicia Spinnet ever since.

In the saga

In Harry's first match, in November 1991, a Bludger hit Katie on the back of the head. On 5 September 1992, when Dracina Malfoy insulted Hermione, Katie and Angelina held back the Weasley twins. Before the Slytherin match that autumn she shredded her toast with nerves. In the match itself she dropped the Quaffle when Dracina's elbow caught her.

During a practice in a storm in 1993, the Snitch blundered, half drowned, into her hood. She scored Gryffindor's opening goal against Ravenclaw in 1994. After the win she kissed Harry so enthusiastically that his glasses went askew. In the final the Slytherin Chaser Montague grabbed her head instead of the ball, and she scored the penalty that followed.

pages.title: Marcus Flint
infobox: Slytherin, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Slytherin Quidditch team, Quidditch captain, Chaser
Chaser; captain of the Slytherin Quidditch team
A fifth-year in 1991 to 1992; left in 1994
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Marcus Flint was the captain of the Slytherin Quidditch team, as well as one of its Chasers, through Harry Potter's first three years at Hogwarts: a big, cunning and thoroughly dirty player. He was also one of the instigators of the fake-dementor prank of March 1994.

Captain of Slytherin

Flint was already a fifth-year and captain in 1991. He was a large boy with a look of trollish cunning about him, and a single black eyebrow ran across his face. In Harry's first match, in November 1991, he blocked Harry on purpose as Harry went for the Snitch. While Harry's broom was jinxed, Flint scored five times without anybody noticing. Afterwards he complained that Harry had nearly swallowed the Snitch rather than caught it.

On 5 September 1992 he arrived at the pitch with a note from Professor Snape, at the head of a team on new Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones. The brooms were the gift of Lucius Malfoy, on the day Dracina became Seeker. At the match that November he led his side out like the prow of a ship. He shook hands with Oliver Wood with his teeth bared, until both sets of knuckles went white. He barged Angelina Johnson, then shouted at Dracina for missing the Snitch while it hovered just over her head.

In November 1993 he withdrew Slytherin from their fixture against Gryffindor, pleading Dracina's injured arm. Wood called it a ploy. It left Gryffindor to face Hufflepuff in a storm. For the final in 1994 Flint picked his side for size. He barged Angelina again, was hit on the head by Fred Weasley's bat and bled from the nose. After the defeat he spat on the grass. Later he mocked Wood by impersonating him sobbing on Harry's shoulder.

The fake dementors

From November 1993 Flint, Montague and half the Slytherin team kept telling Dracina that she had gone soft on Potter. Flint threatened to write to Lucius Malfoy himself if she would not help with a prank at the Ravenclaw match. In March 1994 he dressed as one of the three rigged dementors below Harry's broom, with Dracina, Crabbe and Goyle.

Harry answered with a corporeal Patronus. Professor McGonagall gave the four of them detention, then took fifty points from Slytherin. Dracina later admitted to Snape that she had only said yes to make them stop, before her father heard about it.

pages.title: Adrian Pucey
infobox: Slytherin, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Slytherin Quidditch team
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Adrian Pucey is a Chaser on the Slytherin Quidditch team. He played for his house in 1991 to 1992 under Marcus Flint's captaincy. He played again the following season, when he scored for Slytherin over and over in the rain.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, at Harry Potter's first match in November 1991, Pucey went tearing towards the Gryffindor hoops early on, until a Bludger from one of the Weasley twins cut him off. Later he ducked two Bludgers, both Weasleys and Katie Bell. Then the Snitch shot past his ear. Pucey dropped the Quaffle, too busy staring over his shoulder at the streak of gold, while Harry dived after it.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the match of November 1992, Pucey and Warrington sandwiched Alicia Spinnet between them. Madam Hooch blew her whistle at the pair of them. Pucey scored again and again for Slytherin. By the time Lee Jordan was miserably announcing his latest goal, Slytherin had sixty points and Gryffindor had none.

pages.title: Bletchley
infobox: Slytherin, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Slytherin Quidditch team
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Bletchley was the Keeper of the Slytherin Quidditch team in 1991 to 1992. In Harry Potter's first match, in November 1991, he let in the opening goal.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, Slytherin played Gryffindor in November 1991, with Marcus Flint as their captain. Early on, Angelina Johnson got the Quaffle with open pitch ahead of her. She swerved a Bludger and made for the hoops. Bletchley dived for it, but he missed. Gryffindor had scored. The cheers rang out across the frozen air, with groans and howls from the Slytherin end.

pages.title: Terence Higgs
infobox: Slytherin, Hogwarts student, Quidditch, Slytherin Quidditch team
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Terence Higgs was the Slytherin Seeker in 1991 to 1992. In Harry Potter's first match, in November 1991, Harry outflew him in the dive for the Snitch. The next season the position went to Dracina Malfoy.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, the Snitch flashed past Adrian Pucey's ear and away past the Slytherin stand. Harry saw it and dived. Higgs had seen it too. The two Seekers hurtled after it neck and neck, until Harry began to pull ahead. Then Marcus Flint blocked Harry on purpose, and the Snitch was lost again.

pages.title: The Greek man in the pub
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Greek man in the pub is the man from whom Rubeus Hagrid bought the three-headed dog Fluffy in 1990. Hagrid took him for a Greek, because he had a caravan and what Hagrid called the funny voice the Greeks have. Harry Potter doubted it from the first, and later decided that the man had been a Traveller.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1991, Hagrid told Harry, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger where Fluffy had come from: 'Bought him off a Greek chappie I met down the pub las' year. Well, I think he was Greek. He had the caravan and funny voice the greeks have.' Harry rather doubted that Hagrid was describing a Greek at all.

In Chapter Twelve, working out how a stranger could have got the secret of Fluffy out of Hagrid, Harry reflected that a man who could mistake a Traveller for a Greek could be fooled in a great many ways.

pages.title: Francis Grail
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter 7
Manager of the England Quidditch team
pages.html:
Francis Grail was the manager of the England Quidditch team in 1877. His dispute with the French manager, Juste Valmond, over the proper weight of a Quaffle ended in a duel. Two hundred witches and wizards were killed in the crossfire.

The duel

The English and the French had argued over the rules of Quidditch for more than a thousand years, settling the matter with wands from time to time. The duel between Grail and Valmond was one such settlement. Quidditch Through the Ages gives a casualty list that runs to three pages. The question was only put to rest in 1901, when every national team agreed to play by the Austrian rules.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1991, Harry Potter read about the duel in Quidditch Through the Ages, which Hermione Granger had lent him. 'Wizards are mad, sometimes,' he told Ron and Hermione.

pages.title: Juste Valmond
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter 7
Manager of the French Quidditch team
pages.html:
Juste Valmond was the manager of the French Quidditch team in 1877. He fought a duel with the England manager, Francis Grail, over the proper weight of a Quaffle. Two hundred witches and wizards died in the crossfire.

The duel

The French and the English had argued over the rules for more than a thousand years, settling the matter with wands from time to time. Valmond's duel with Grail was one such settlement. Quidditch Through the Ages prints a casualty list three pages long. In 1901 every national team agreed to play by the Austrian rules, which ended the argument at last.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1991, Harry Potter read about Valmond's duel in Quidditch Through the Ages, which Hermione Granger had lent him, and decided that wizards were mad, sometimes.

pages.title: Gryffindor Quidditch team
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Angelina Johnson, Alicia Spinnet, Katie Bell
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Gryffindor Quidditch team plays for Gryffindor House in scarlet robes. For three seasons, from 1991 to 1994, it was the same seven players under Oliver Wood, with Harry Potter as Seeker. In 1994 they won the Quidditch Cup, which Gryffindor had not won in seven years.

The players

Oliver Wood was captain and Keeper. Fred and George Weasley were the Beaters, flying Cleansweep Fives, which the Slytherins mocked as museum pieces. The Chasers were Angelina Johnson, Alicia Spinnet and Katie Bell. Harry Potter was the Seeker, with no reserve. Rallied by Wood's pep talks, the team trained through wind, rain, hail and sleet.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in 1991, Professor McGonagall took Harry, a first-year, to Oliver Wood and told him: 'Wood, I have found you a Seeker.' In Chapter Seven Harry played his first match, against Slytherin. Gryffindor won by a hundred and seventy points to sixty. In Chapter Nine, early in 1992, they beat Hufflepuff in barely five minutes, while Dean Thomas led the Gryffindor stand in songs. In Chapter Thirteen, without Harry, who was in the hospital wing, they were steamrollered by Ravenclaw in the last match of the season.

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, the Slytherin team turned up on new brooms, the gift of Lucius Malfoy. Dracina Malfoy mocked the twins' Cleansweeps as museum pieces. In Chapter Eleven, that autumn, Gryffindor trailed Slytherin by sixty points to nil while a rogue Bludger hunted Harry round the pitch. He caught the Snitch all the same. The next day, in Chapter Twelve, Percy Weasley told him that Gryffindor had gone top for the House Cup: 'Fifty points, all down to you!' In Chapter Sixteen, in 1993, the Hufflepuff match was cancelled during the warm-up, and Quidditch was suspended for the rest of the year.

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Wood opened his last season by reminding the team that Gryffindor had not won the Cup in seven years. In Chapter Nine, in November 1993, they lost to Hufflepuff by a hundred points after the dementors brought Harry down. In Chapter Ten Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff, which put Gryffindor back in the running, and in Chapter Thirteen Gryffindor beat Ravenclaw.

In Chapter Fifteen, in 1994, it all came down to the final against Slytherin, who were two hundred points clear. Gryffindor had to beat them by more than two hundred to win the Cup. Lee Jordan introduced the team as widely acknowledged to be the best Hogwarts had seen in a good few years. Dracina, the Slytherin Seeker, waited until Gryffindor were sixty points ahead, then dived where Harry could not possibly miss her. He caught the Snitch on his Firebolt. Wood, still weeping, put the Cup into his hands.

pages.title: Slytherin Quidditch team
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Slytherin Quidditch team plays in green for Slytherin house at Hogwarts. Through the early 1990s it was captained by Marcus Flint. Since September 1992 it has flown Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones bought by Lucius Malfoy, whose daughter Dracina became its Seeker the same month.

The side

In 1991 to 1992 Flint played as a Chaser beside Adrian Pucey. Bletchley kept goal, and Terence Higgs was the Seeker. When Dracina joined in 1992 she was the only girl on the side.

For the final of 1994 Flint went for size rather than skill, so that Dracina looked tiny among them. Montague, Warrington, Derrick and Bole were all in the team.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, Slytherin lost to Gryffindor by 170 points to 60 in November 1991. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in September 1992, Dracina became Seeker after her father bought the team seven Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones. In Chapter Nine Fred Weasley described them at practice as seven green blurs. In Chapter Eleven the team, with Dracina as Seeker, went about the school in a knot.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, they were still riding the brooms Lucius had paid for. In Chapter Fifteen Slytherin came to the final of 1994 two hundred points clear at the top of the table, so that Gryffindor had to beat them by more than two hundred to win the Cup. Lee Jordan announced that Flint seemed to be going for size rather than skill. Gryffindor beat them by enough to take the Quidditch Cup.

pages.title: Potter for President banner
infobox: POTTER FOR PRESIDENT; POTTER FOR PRESIDENT banner
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Ron Weasley, Hermione Granger, Neville Longbottom, Seamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas
pages.html:
The Potter for President banner was made by Harry Potter's friends for his first Quidditch match, in the autumn of 1991. Ron Weasley, Hermione Granger, Neville Longbottom, Seamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas painted it on an old sheet that Scabbers had chewed through.

The banner

Dean, who is good at drawing, painted a large Gryffindor lion under the words. Hermione put a tricky little charm on the paint, so that it flashed one colour after another.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, the five of them painted the banner on the chewed sheet as a surprise for Harry's first match, against Slytherin. During the match Harry caught sight of it out of the corner of his eye, high above the crowd, rippling and flashing. His heart jumped, and he felt braver.

pages.title: Bluebell flames
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Bluebell flames are a bright blue fire that Hermione Granger can conjure from her wand. They give out a good deal of warmth, they can be carried about in a jam jar, and they will set things alight when she wants them to.

Uses

Hermione has used her bluebell flames to keep her friends warm in a frosty courtyard, to set a teacher's robes on fire and to drive off Devil's Snare, which cannot bear light or heat.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, on the day before Harry's first Quidditch match in November 1991, Hermione conjured a bright blue fire into a jam jar in the courtyard at break. She, Harry and Ron stood with their backs to it to keep warm. When Professor Snape limped across the courtyard, they shuffled together to hide it, since they were fairly sure it was not allowed.

At the match the next day Harry's broom began to buck as if it were jinxed. Hermione was sure Snape was doing it. She hurried along the stands, knocked Professor Quirrell head first into the row in front, crouched down behind Snape and sent bright blue flames from her wand to the hem of his robes. As soon as he yelped, she scooped the flames off him into a little jar in her pocket. Snape never knew what had happened.

In Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, Devil's Snare caught Harry and Ron below the trapdoor. Hermione sent a jet of the same bluebell flames at the plant. It cringed away from the light and warmth. The two boys pulled free.

pages.title: The staff room
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Dark wooden chairs; a wardrobe of teachers' cloaks
pages.html:
The staff room at Hogwarts is a big panelled room full of dark wooden chairs, where the teachers gather. Against one wall stands an ugly great wardrobe stuffed with their cloaks.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, Harry went down to the staff room to ask Snape for his copy of Quidditch Through the Ages, thinking Snape would not refuse him with other teachers listening. Nobody answered his knock, so he pushed the door open a crack. Inside, Filch was handing Snape bandages for a leg that was torn and bloody. 'How is anyone supposed to watch all three heads at once?' Snape was saying.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, on 29 May 1993, Harry and Ron went there to wait for Professor McGonagall. Then Professor McGonagall's voice, magically magnified, ordered every student back to the dormitories and every teacher to the staff room, so the boys hid in the wardrobe among the cloaks. From there they heard McGonagall tell the staff that the monster had taken a student into the Chamber itself. It was Ginny Weasley. Ron slid silently down the inside of the wardrobe until he was sitting among the shoes. Snape added that one of his own Slytherins had not answered the register, and that her bed had not been slept in.

pages.title: First World War
infobox: France, Russia, the British Empire; later Italy and the United States
Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria
pages.html:
The First World War was the great war of 1914 to 1918. On one side were the Allies, chiefly France, Russia and the British Empire; Italy joined them in 1915, the United States in 1917. On the other were the Central Powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. It began about thirteen years after every national Quidditch team agreed to play by the Austrian rules, which struck Harry Potter in 1991 as rather bad timing for the Austrians.

The war

On 28 June 1914 a Bosnian Serb student shot the heir to the Austrian throne, the Archduke Franz Ferdinand, at Sarajevo. A month later Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. Within a week the alliances had drawn in Russia, Germany, France and Britain. In the west the armies dug in along a line of trenches from the Channel to Switzerland. They stayed there for four years. Millions died at Verdun, on the Somme and at Passchendaele.

The fighting stopped with the Armistice, at eleven o'clock on the morning of 11 November 1918. Among the men who had served were the young Canadian Lester Pearson and the soldier later known as Wolverine, who went on to fight in the Second World War as well.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, reading Quidditch Through the Ages in the autumn of 1991, Harry learnt that the long quarrel over the rules of the game had been settled at last when every national team agreed, from 1901 onwards, to play by the Austrian rules. He thought privately that the Austrians would have had rather more on their plate about thirteen years after that. He had no idea whether the wizarding world had even noticed the First World War going on around it, and he made a mental note to ask Hermione, who would know.

pages.title: Hermione's parents
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Hermione's parents, the Grangers, are both Muggle dentists. Their only child, Hermione Granger, is a witch.

Dentists

Mr and Mrs Granger run a dentist's surgery together. Like their daughter, they are atheists. Neither has a drop of magic, and their daughter's Hogwarts letter in 1991 came as a great surprise to them.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, before the Christmas holidays of 1991, Ron Weasley suggested that Hermione ask her parents who Nicolas Flamel was, since that would be safe enough. 'Very safe,' said Hermione dryly. 'They're both dentists.'

In Chapter Nine, back from Christmas at home, she told Harry all about it, her grandmother's house and a dentistry conference in Harrogate included, most of it twice.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, angry with Muggles after Aunt Marge's visit in 1993, Harry made an exception of Hermione's mum and dad, the dentists.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, when Dudley's diet threatened to leave Harry living on carrot sticks in the summer of 1994, Hedwig came back from Hermione's with a box crammed with sugar-free snacks, because Hermione's parents were dentists.

pages.title: Madam Pince
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The school library, including the Restricted Section
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Irma Pince is the librarian of Hogwarts: a thin, irritable woman who looks like an underfed vulture, and who guards her books as though they were her own children.

The library

Madam Pince keeps the library silent, and hisses at any pupil who makes a noise in it. A book from the Restricted Section leaves her shelves only against a note signed by a teacher, and she examines every signature for forgery. Certain volumes, Blood Nobility among them, she keeps behind her own desk, to be signed for.

She is said to put unusual jinxes on the books in her care, to punish anybody who mistreats them. Nobody at Hogwarts has ever been keen to find out whether the story is true.

In the saga

In 1991 Harry, Ron and Hermione dared not ask her about Nicolas Flamel, in case word of it reached Snape. In 1992 she held Gilderoy Lockhart's signature up to the light before handing over Moste Potente Potions as though it were a baby. In 1993 she told Hermione Granger that Tomes and Scrolls stocked a book on Alucard. In 1994 she told Ron Weasley that every hippogriff book in the library was already out, all on the same ticket.

pages.title: The ghost of a tall witch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The ghost of a tall witch is one of the many ghosts who drift about the corridors of Hogwarts. Nothing is recorded of her name, her life or her death. She glided past Harry Potter and Ron Weasley one night in the Christmas holidays of 1991, while they were searching the castle for the Mirror of Erised.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry took Ron under the Invisibility Cloak to look for the room where he had found the mirror. They passed the ghost of a tall witch gliding the other way, and nobody else. Ron had just started moaning that his feet had died of cold when Harry saw the suit of armour and knew that they had found the room.

pages.title: Ron's grandfather
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A very old, battered wizard chess set
pages.html:
Ron Weasley's grandfather was the first owner of the wizard chess set that Ron plays with now. Like nearly everything Ron owns, it belonged to somebody else in the family first. The set is very old and battered, but Ron knows its chessmen so well that they do whatever he tells them.

The chess set

Wizard chess is just like Muggle chess, except that the pieces are alive and shout advice at their players, which makes a game feel a good deal like commanding an army. Which of his two grandfathers the set came from, Ron has never said.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, over the Christmas holidays of 1991, Ron went back to teaching Harry Potter wizard chess, playing with his grandfather's set. Harry played with a set Seamus Finnigan had lent him, whose pieces did not trust him an inch. In Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, the skill Ron had learnt on the old chessmen carried Harry and Hermione Granger across Professor McGonagall's giant chessboard, on the way to the Philosopher's Stone. In Chapter Thirteen Professor Dumbledore awarded Gryffindor fifty points for the best-played game of chess the school had seen in many years.

pages.title: Harry's grandparents
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Mr Evans; Susan Evans, born Susan Pevensie
In the Mirror of Erised, Christmas 1991
pages.html:
Harry Potter's grandparents on his father's side were Fleamont Potter and his wife, Euphemia. On his mother's side they were Mr Evans and his wife, Susan, who had been born Susan Pevensie.

The four of them

Fleamont made a fortune with Sleekeazy's Hair Potion. He and Euphemia both died of dragon pox before Harry was born. Susan had once been a crowned Queen of Narnia, and was the only one of the four Pevensies to survive the railway accident of 1949. Through her the blood of Aragorn and Arwen came down to Lily, then to Harry. Lord Voldemort killed her in October 1981, days before he came for Lily and James.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, at Christmas 1991, Harry looked into the Mirror of Erised. Beside his parents stood an old man with Harry's knobbly knees. Next to him was an old woman whose kind, lined smile spoke of old recipes and warm kitchens. Another old couple stood behind them. Harry took them for his two sets of grandparents, and every one of them was waving to him.

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt of his grandfather Fleamont, and knew his name although he had never heard it before.

pages.title: Harry's imagined brother and sister
infobox: A small boy and a smaller girl, holding hands
pages.html:
Harry's imagined brother and sister were the two children the Mirror of Erised showed Harry Potter in the Christmas holidays of 1991. A small boy and a smaller girl stood among his family, holding hands, gazing up at him. They were the little brother and sister he had always wished for. He has none: he is the only child of James and Lily Potter.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry stepped in front of the Mirror. He saw people all round him: his parents, two sets of grandparents and the two children. They waved and beckoned to him, glad to see him. When he put out his hand to touch his mother's, his fingers met cold glass. The Mirror shows the deepest desire of a person's heart, and Harry went back to it three nights running.

pages.title: Invisibility Cloak
infobox: Harry's Invisibility Cloak; James Potter's Invisibility Cloak
Potter family, magical object, Potter family heirloom, Peverell family
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Fluid, silvery grey cloth, like woven water
The Peverell Cloak: Peverell, then Pendragon, then Potter
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Invisibility Cloak is a cloak of fluid, silvery grey cloth, like water woven into material, that makes whoever wears it invisible. It belonged to James Potter, and came to his son Harry at Christmas 1991. It is far older than either of them: it is the Peverell Cloak, come down intact from the Peverell brother who first had it, through the Pendragons, to the Potters.

The Cloak

The Cloak hides its wearer completely, but it does not make him insubstantial: anyone under it is still solid, and can still be heard. It cannot fool a Dementor, nor the Marauder's Map, which shows whoever is underneath as plainly as anybody else.

It is a priceless family heirloom. In Harry's third year the only people who knew he had it were Ron, Hermione, Hagrid, Dumbledore and very probably Professor McGonagall. Dracina Malfoy did not.

James Potter's Cloak

James used it at Hogwarts mainly for sneaking down to the kitchens for food. Under it the Marauders slipped out of the castle every month to be with Remus Lupin, who often saw James vanish beneath it. Before he died, James left it in Dumbledore's keeping.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, the Cloak arrived at Christmas 1991 with an unsigned note in a narrow, loopy hand: 'Your father left this in my keeping before he died. It's time it came back to you. Use it well. A very merry Christmas to you.' Wearing it, Harry found the Mirror of Erised, and learnt that the Cloak did not stop him being solid. In Chapter Ten, on the night Norbert left, he and Hermione forgot it on top of the tower. At the end of the next chapter Harry found it folded neatly under his sheets, with a note pinned to it: 'Just in case.' In Chapter Thirteen Dumbledore admitted that he had sent it.

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, Harry wrapped Tom Riddle's diary in the Cloak and locked it at the bottom of his trunk. In Chapter Sixteen, when Dracina ransacked his dormitory and took the diary, she left the Cloak behind, having either not known what it was or not cared. Later in that chapter it hid him and Ron in a corner of Hagrid's hut on the night Hagrid was taken away. In Chapter Seventeen it took the two boys back down to the hut on their way into the Forest. Harry left it folded on Hagrid's table, since nothing in there could see them anyway, and fetched it again when they came out.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, Dumbledore warned the school that Dementors could not be fooled by tricks, disguises or even Invisibility Cloaks. In Chapter Eleven, when the Firebolt came at Christmas with no name on it, Ron guessed that it was from Dumbledore, who had given Harry the Cloak without putting his name to it either. 'That was my dad's,' said Harry. 'Dumbledore only passed it on.'

Twice that year Harry had to leave the Cloak at the foot of the chute under the one-eyed witch. The first time was in Chapter Fourteen, when Crabbe trod on its hem by the Shrieking Shack and Dracina saw Harry's head hanging in mid-air. The second was in Chapter Sixteen, when he dropped it down the chute to keep it out of Filch's sack. On the day Buckbeak was to be executed, Hermione went down and fetched it. 'Somebody has to look after you, Harry. It might as well be somebody sensible.'

In Chapter Seventeen, that same evening, Harry let the Cloak fall by the Whomping Willow when a great black dog leapt at him. In Chapter Eighteen Snape threw it off in the Shrieking Shack: he had found it at the foot of the Willow and followed them down the passage under it. When the fight was over, Lupin stowed it inside his robes. In Chapter Nineteen, when Lupin changed into his war form, the robes tore away in rags, with the Cloak somewhere among them.

In Chapter Twenty Harry, gone back three hours in time with Hermione, watched Snape snatch the Cloak up from the grass by the Willow and vanish under it. Later that night he saw Snape stoop over a heap of torn rags on his way down to the lake, then straighten up with something that poured over his arm like water. In Chapter Twenty-Two Lupin gave it back to Harry, with the Marauder's Map. He had found it before dawn, lying on the bed upstairs in the Shrieking Shack, folded very neatly. 'I have a fairly good idea who folds things as neatly as that. It wasn't Severus.'

pages.title: Mirror of Erised
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Ornate gold, on two clawed feet
The deepest, most desperate wish of the viewer's heart
Erised stra ehru oyt ube cafru oyt on wohsi
The last protection of the Philosopher's Stone, 1992
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Mirror of Erised is a magnificent mirror as tall as the ceiling, in an ornate gold frame standing on two clawed feet. It shows whoever looks into it the deepest, most desperate wish of their heart, and nothing else. It gives neither knowledge nor truth, which is the danger of it: men have wasted away in front of it, or gone mad, never knowing whether what they saw was real.

The inscription

A line of carved words runs round the top of the frame: Erised stra ehru oyt ube cafru oyt on wohsi. Read backwards, it says 'I show not your face but your heart's desire'. Harry could never make sense of it, however he read it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, at Christmas 1991, Harry came across the Mirror while hiding from Filch under his new Invisibility Cloak. It stood in a disused classroom, near a tall suit of armour, some five floors above the kitchens. In it he saw his parents waving at him, with two sets of grandparents, a little brother and a sister. He brought Ron the next night. Ron saw himself alone, older, as Head Boy, holding both the House Cup and the Quidditch Cup. On the third night Dumbledore was waiting for Harry. He explained what the Mirror showed and warned him that men had wasted away before it. Then he had it moved to a new home.

In Chapter Thirteen Harry met it again, deep under the school, as the last guardian of the Philosopher's Stone, with Quirrell gazing into it. Dumbledore had enchanted it so that only somebody who wanted to find the Stone, but not use it, could get it out.

In Book Two, Chapter One, back at Privet Drive in the summer of 1992, Harry felt as though he were standing in front of it again. The wizarding world had shown him something better, close enough to touch, and then he had had to walk away from it. In Chapter Nineteen Dracina Malfoy watched the Weasleys round Ginny's bed with the same longing Harry had once shown before the Mirror.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry was afraid that the man he had seen by the pillar in the Chamber of Secrets, whom he believed to be Christ, had been the Mirror again in a different frame: the thing he wanted most, which was not the same as the thing that was true. In Chapter Ten he remembered how it had shown him his family behind glass, a mother with his eyes, a father with his hair, grandparents, a little brother and a sister, until Dumbledore took it away. In Chapter Twelve, facing a boggart Dementor, he thought of his mother, who until then had been only a smiling face behind glass in an empty classroom. In Chapter Seventeen the same hard courage that had carried him down to Quirrell and the Mirror rose in him again.

pages.title: The screaming book
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The screaming book is a large black and silver book in the Restricted Section of the Hogwarts library. Open it, and it shrieks. Shutting it again does not stop it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, on Christmas night 1991, Harry Potter crept into the Restricted Section under his new Invisibility Cloak to look for Nicolas Flamel. A large black and silver book on the bottom shelf caught his eye. It was very heavy. He balanced it on his knee and let it fall open. At once it let out a piercing, blood-curdling shriek.

Harry slammed it shut, but the shriek went on and on, in one high, unbroken note. He knocked over his lamp, rammed the book back on its shelf and ran for it, passing Filch almost in the doorway.

pages.title: The Restricted Section
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The back of the Hogwarts library, behind a rope
A signed note from a teacher
pages.html:
The Restricted Section is the roped-off part at the back of the Hogwarts library. It holds the books of powerful Dark magic that are never taught at the school, and nobody may read them without a signed note from a teacher. Most of those notes go to older students studying advanced Defence Against the Dark Arts.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry wondered whether Nicolas Flamel might be in there. Dracina Malfoy came up behind him to point out that even her father could not get in without asking, and offered to help. On Christmas night he went in alone under his new Invisibility Cloak, with a lamp. One book had a dark stain down its cover that looked horribly like blood. He thought he could hear a faint whispering from the shelves, as though the books knew somebody was there who should not be. The first one he opened screamed.

pages.title: Hogwarts Library
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Tens of thousands of books on thousands of shelves
Open only with a note of permission signed by a teacher
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Hogwarts library holds tens of thousands of books on thousands of shelves. Most of them are open to any student. The books of the Restricted Section, which deal in powerful Dark magic that is never taught at Hogwarts, may be read only with a note of permission signed by a teacher.

The shelves

The library is kept by Madam Pince, who will not hand over a Restricted book without the proper signature. As a rule only older students studying advanced Defence Against the Dark Arts are allowed near those books. Among the other sections are the Arithmancy shelves and a section on Invisibility. A long table under the window is where the younger students sit. Moste Potente Potions, which holds the recipe for Polyjuice Potion, is kept in the Restricted Section.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger searched the library for a fortnight for the name of Nicolas Flamel. Harry wondered whether Flamel might be in the Restricted Section. He knew he would never get a teacher to sign for it.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Hermione told the others that the recipe for Polyjuice Potion was in Moste Potente Potions. It was bound to be in the Restricted Section, and there was only one way to get a book out of there: a note of permission, signed by a teacher. In the next chapter she got Gilderoy Lockhart to sign one.

Earlier in Chapter Ten, on his way out of the library, Harry saw Dracina Malfoy alone at the long table under the window, with a strange heap of books: two fat volumes of wizarding genealogy, with a battered picture book open on top. Its page showed a painted knight in silver armour, kneeling before a girl with long pale hair in a tower. When Dracina saw him looking, she slammed it shut so hard that Madam Pince shot out from behind her desk.

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Hermione was found Petrified near the library, together with Penelope Clearwater. In Chapter Eighteen, down in the Chamber of Secrets, Dracina remembered the painted book. She had slammed it shut so that Harry would not see it.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Hermione spent most of early 1994 in the library. In the first week of February Harry went there to look for her and found Dracina instead, at the far end past the Restricted Section. She was sitting at a table with nothing on it but one book and a pair of grey gloves. When she saw him coming, she shut the book face down.

pages.title: Weasley jumper
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Emerald green (1991); scarlet with a gold lion (1993)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
A Weasley jumper is the thick hand-knitted jumper that Molly Weasley makes for each of her children every Christmas. Since 1991 she has made one for Harry Potter too. His first was the first proper present he had ever been given.

The jumpers

Ron's jumper is always maroon, which he says he hates. In 1991 the twins' were blue, with a big yellow F on Fred's and a big yellow G on George's. Percy's had a P. Ron's had no letter at all: his mother, George supposed, reckoned he didn't forget his own name. In 1991 the jumpers came with a box of home-made fudge. Harry's in 1993 came with a dozen mince pies, a slab of Christmas cake and a box of nut brittle.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, on Christmas morning 1991, Ron went pink at the sight of a very lumpy parcel. 'She's made you a Weasley jumper,' he groaned. Harry's was emerald green, with a large box of home-made fudge, and he had never owned a knitted jumper in his life. 'Harry's is better than ours,' said Fred, holding it up. 'She obviously tries harder when you're not family.' For a moment Harry felt a hot little stab of something at Ron, who had a real mum to knit him jumpers, and who was moaning about it as if it were an insult. Then he caught the thought and held it still. None of it was Ron's fault.

In Book Two, Chapter One, Harry was still wearing the green jumper in July 1992, because he liked it, and it was still the best-made thing he owned. In Chapter Four, on the sofa at the Burrow, he sobbed out to Mrs Weasley that it had been the first proper present he had ever had. Ron had been moaning about his maroon one, and Harry had been so angry with him that he had wanted to hit him. He was still ashamed of it.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, Harry's jumper for Christmas 1993 was scarlet, with the Gryffindor lion worked across the chest in gold. Ron's was maroon again. Harry held his a moment longer than he needed to, then laid it flat on the bed and smoothed it once with his hand. Underneath it lay a long, thin parcel he had not noticed: the Firebolt.

pages.title: Wizard chess
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Alive: they move on command, fight and argue with their player
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Wizard chess is the wizarding form of chess. It is played by the same rules as Muggle chess, except that the pieces are alive. They move where they are told, drag one another bodily off the board, and argue with the player who commands them. Old sets are handed down in families, and a player whose pieces know him can run a game like a general.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, over the Christmas holidays of 1991, Ron Weasley went back to teaching Harry Potter on his grandfather's old, battered set, whose pieces did whatever Ron told them. Harry's set, lent him by Seamus Finnigan, did not trust him an inch, and its pieces kept shouting advice at him. On Christmas Day he lost spectacularly. In Book One, Chapter Nine, chess was the only thing Hermione Granger ever lost at, which Harry and Ron agreed was very good for her.

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the way to the Philosopher's Stone lay across a giant chessboard, whose stone pieces Professor McGonagall had brought to life. The white pieces had no faces. Ron, Harry and Hermione took the places of three black pieces. Near the end Ron let the white queen take him, leaving Harry free to checkmate the king, and she knocked Ron senseless. In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Dumbledore gave Gryffindor fifty points for the best-played game of chess the school had seen in many years.

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Ron beat Hermione during a free lesson, when the last Herbology lesson of term was cancelled for a blizzard. One of Ron's bishops dragged her knight off his horse and hauled him, kicking, off the board. Harry watched the little stone knight get up at the edge of the board and shake his tiny fist, calling for his horse. For no reason he could explain, it made him think of Dracina Malfoy.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Harry was losing to Ron as usual. A castle had just dragged his knight off the board, and his queen was looking at him with deep reproach, when he felt the pull of the diary under his bed. In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Ron sat up with Harry until nearly two in the morning, so that he would not lie awake thinking about Sirius Black. Harry lost four games in a row, badly. He knew perfectly well what was being done to him, and he let it be done.

pages.title: Wizard crackers
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A rear admiral's hat; several live white mice
pages.html:
Wizard crackers are the Christmas crackers of the wizarding world. They are nothing like the feeble Muggle kind, with its little plastic toys and flimsy paper hats. A wizard cracker goes off like a cannon in a cloud of smoke, and what comes out of it is a good deal more interesting.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, there were stacks of wizard crackers every few feet along the tables at the Hogwarts Christmas feast of 1991. Harry Potter pulled one with Fred Weasley. It went off like a cannon and swallowed them both in blue smoke. Out of the smoke burst a rear admiral's hat, followed by several live white mice. Up at the High Table, Dumbledore had traded his pointed hat for a flowered bonnet.

pages.title: The Farting Game
infobox: One wet afternoon in their first year
pages.html:
The Farting Game is a game that Harry Potter and Ron Weasley invented one wet afternoon in their first year at Hogwarts. The player cups his hands over his mouth and makes the biggest, wettest noise he can. The more the corridor echoes, the better.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, as the Christmas holidays of 1991 drew near, Harry thought he could do with a little time alone with Ron, doing lad things. He was very fond of Hermione Granger, but she had never approved of the Farting Game. She thought it disgusting, and said so. The boys had stopped playing it in front of her, to spare her feelings. With Hermione going home for Christmas, they would have the echoing corridors to themselves.

pages.title: Great Wizards of the Twentieth Century
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The great wizards of the twentieth century
pages.html:
Great Wizards of the Twentieth Century is a library book on the century's most famous witches and wizards. In December 1991 Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger searched it for Nicolas Flamel without success. A few weeks later they found out that Flamel was six hundred and sixty-five years old.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, the three of them had been hunting the library for Flamel ever since Hagrid let his name slip. He was not in this book, nor in Notable Magical Names of Our Time, Important Modern Magical Discoveries or A Study of Recent Developments in Wizardry. The trouble was knowing where to start, in a library of tens of thousands of books.

pages.title: Notable Magical Names of Our Time
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Notable Magical Names of Our Time is a reference book in the Hogwarts library on the famous witches and wizards of the present day. Nicolas Flamel is not in it, although he was very much alive in 1991.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, in December 1991, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger were hunting through the library for Flamel, whose name Hagrid had let slip. He was not in Great Wizards of the Twentieth Century, or in Notable Magical Names of Our Time. In Chapter Nine, in January 1992, Dumbledore's Chocolate Frog card put them on his trail at last. Hermione found him in a book she had borrowed weeks before for light reading, as the only known maker of the Philosopher's Stone.

pages.title: Important Modern Magical Discoveries
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Important Modern Magical Discoveries is a reference book in the Hogwarts library, given over to the advances wizards have made in recent times. It is one of the many books in which Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger looked for Nicolas Flamel in the winter of 1991. He was not in it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, the three of them had been hunting through the library for Flamel for a fortnight, in the odd minutes between lessons, ever since Hagrid let his name slip. He was not in Important Modern Magical Discoveries, nor in A Study of Recent Developments in Wizardry, nor in any of the others they tried. In Chapter Nine, after Christmas, Hermione found him at last in a book she had borrowed weeks before for a bit of light reading. Flamel was the only known maker of the Philosopher's Stone, aged six hundred and sixty-five. 'He's not exactly recent, is he, if he's six hundred and sixty-five,' said Ron.

pages.title: A Study of Recent Developments in Wizardry
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
A Study of Recent Developments in Wizardry is a library book on the newer advances in magic. In December 1991 Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger searched it in vain for Nicolas Flamel.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, the three of them were hunting the library for Flamel's name, which Hagrid had let slip. He was not in Great Wizards of the Twentieth Century, or Notable Magical Names of Our Time. Nor was he in Important Modern Magical Discoveries, or in this book.

In Book One, Chapter Nine, once they had found out that Flamel was six hundred and sixty-five years old, Ron saw why. 'And no wonder we couldn't find Flamel in A Study of Recent Developments in Wizardry,' he said. 'He's not exactly recent, is he, if he's six hundred and sixty-five.'

pages.title: Perenelle Flamel
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Perenelle Flamel is the wife of Nicolas Flamel, the only known maker of the Philosopher's Stone. In the school year 1991 to 1992 she was six hundred and fifty-eight years old, seven years younger than her husband. The two of them live quietly in Devon.

Life

Like her husband, Perenelle has lived for more than six centuries on the Elixir of Life that the Stone yields. When the Stone was destroyed in 1992, she was expected to die alongside him once the Elixir they had put by ran out. Albus Dumbledore believed that to Nicolas and Perenelle it would be rather like going to bed after a very, very long day.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, the old library book in which Hermione Granger found Nicolas Flamel gave Perenelle's age as six hundred and fifty-eight. It said she lived with him in Devon.

In Chapter Thirteen Dumbledore told Harry Potter that the Stone had been destroyed. The Flamels had enough Elixir put by to set their affairs in order, and after that they would die.

pages.title: Hermione's grandmother
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter 9
pages.html:
Hermione's grandmother is a Muggle, the mother of one of Hermione Granger's parents. Hermione stayed at her grandmother's house over Christmas 1991, during her first year at Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, back at school after the holidays, Hermione told Harry Potter a great deal about her Christmas. She described her parents, her grandmother's house and a dentistry conference in Harrogate, most of it twice.

pages.title: The Hufflepuff Seeker
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff Seeker of 1991 to 1992 played against Gryffindor in the match of 1992 that Harry Potter won in about five minutes. Nobody could remember the Snitch ever being caught so fast. The Seeker was also the subject of a rude chant.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Dean Thomas, who had grown up on the terraces at Upton Park, spent three evenings in the common room writing chants for the match. The third was about the Hufflepuff Seeker, and rhymed his name with something Hermione Granger pretended not to hear. Snape was refereeing, and gave Hufflepuff one penalty after another. Then Harry shot past Snape in a dive, missing him by inches, and pulled out with the Snitch in his fist. It was over in barely five minutes. The Gryffindors sang "Five minutes! Five minutes! You lasted five minutes!" as the Hufflepuff team drifted down to the grass, looking as though they were not quite sure what had happened to them.

pages.title: Philosopher's Stone
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Turns any metal into pure gold; yields the Elixir of Life
Gringotts, vault seven hundred and thirteen; then Hogwarts, 1991 to 1992
pages.html:
The Philosopher's Stone is a legendary alchemical substance that turns any metal into pure gold. It also yields the Elixir of Life, which makes whoever drinks it immortal. Many claims to the Stone have been made down the centuries, but the only one known to exist in modern times belonged to Nicolas Flamel. It was hidden at Hogwarts in the school year of 1991 to 1992, while Professor Quirrell tried to steal it for Lord Voldemort. When he had failed, Dumbledore and Flamel agreed that it should be destroyed.

Flamel's Stone

Flamel, the celebrated alchemist and lover of opera, made the Stone. He lived on its Elixir for centuries, and in 1992 was still living quietly in Devon with his wife, Perenelle.

In the summer of 1991 Rubeus Hagrid collected it from vault seven hundred and thirteen at Gringotts. On that very day somebody broke into the vault.

At Hogwarts

At Hogwarts the Stone lay beneath a trapdoor in the third-floor corridor, guarded by Hagrid's three-headed dog, Fluffy. Beyond him lay a chain of enchantments set by members of the staff, among them Professor McGonagall's giant chessboard and Quirrell's own. Last of all, Dumbledore hid the Stone inside the Mirror of Erised, where only somebody who wanted to find it, but not to use it, could get it out.

In June 1992 Quirrell got through every one of them as far as the Mirror, but he could not get the Stone out of it. Harry Potter followed him down, looked into the Mirror and felt the Stone drop into his own pocket.

Destruction

Afterwards Dumbledore told Harry that the Stone had been destroyed. He had had a little talk with Flamel, he said, and they had agreed that it was all for the best. The Flamels had enough Elixir put by to set their affairs in order. After that, they would die.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Hermione found the Stone in an old library book she had taken out weeks before for a bit of light reading. Nicolas Flamel, she whispered, was the only known maker of the Philosopher's Stone. The three of them concluded that Fluffy was guarding it, protected by further enchantments, Quirrell's among them, and that Snape was after it.

In Chapter Thirteen it proved to be 'a stone the colour of blood'. It had come from Gringotts vault seven hundred and thirteen in a grubby little package about two inches long. In the Mirror of Erised, Harry's reflection took it out of its pocket, winked at him and put it back. At the same moment Harry felt something heavy drop into his own real pocket. After Quirrell's attempt on it, the Stone was destroyed by agreement between Dumbledore and Flamel. 'So the Stone's gone?' Ron said, when he heard. 'Flamel's just going to die?'

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Ron reminded Harry that he had risked his neck on a giant chessboard for the Stone. He believed Dumbledore had known all along that the three of them were going after it. In Chapter Sixteen he reminded Harry that he had worked out the mystery of the Stone in his first year.

pages.title: Elixir of Life
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Immortality, for as long as the drinker keeps taking it
pages.html:
The Elixir of Life is the potion that the Philosopher's Stone yields, and it makes whoever drinks it immortal. The drinker must go on taking it to stay alive. Nicolas Flamel and his wife, Perenelle, lived on it for more than six hundred years.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Harry, Ron and Hermione found the Stone described in an old book. It would turn any metal into pure gold, and it yielded the Elixir of Life, which renders the drinker immortal. The same book gave Nicolas Flamel's age as six hundred and sixty-five. In Chapter Thirteen Lord Voldemort, reduced to mere shadow and vapour, told Harry that once he had the Elixir he would make a body of his own. After the Stone was destroyed in June 1992, Dumbledore told Harry that the Flamels had enough Elixir put by to set their affairs in order. Then they would die.

pages.title: Leg-Locker Curse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Curse, though no worse than a jinx
pages.html:
The Leg-Locker Curse, Locomotor Mortis, snaps its victim's legs together so tightly that they cannot be parted. The victim can hop, if he is determined, but he cannot walk. For all its name, it is no worse than a jinx, and a counter-jinx breaks it at once.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, in early 1992, Neville Longbottom toppled through the portrait hole into the Gryffindor common room with his legs stuck fast together. Everyone recognised the Leg-Locker Curse at once. He must have bunny-hopped the whole way up to the tower. Hermione jumped up and did the counter-curse. Neville told them that Dracina Malfoy had done it: she had said she was looking for somebody in particular to practise it on, but that he would do.

Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger got the idea from Dracina. They practised the curse in secret, then brought their wands to Harry's next Quidditch match, ready to use it on Snape the moment he showed any sign of wanting to hurt Harry. 'Don't forget, it's Locomotor Mortis,' Hermione muttered.

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Harry yelled 'Locomotor Mortis!' at Dracina herself. It was a jinx he had only ever seen her use on Neville, and it astonished him that he even knew it. Her legs snapped together. She went down on one knee on the cold floor of the Great Hall. A little later she broke it with a slash of her wand, the counter-jinx coming out of her in a snarl.

pages.title: Crackle-cough fit
pages.html:
A crackle-cough fit is a wizarding illness in which little sparks come out every time the sufferer coughs. By the account of Ron Weasley, who once had one, it is horrible.

Wizarding colds

It is one of a good many wizarding complaints that no Muggle doctor has ever heard of. Another is the sneezing slug cold.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter learnt that Professor Snape was to referee his next Quidditch match. Ron and Hermione Granger tried to talk him out of playing. Ron suggested he say he had a cold: a sneezing slug cold, perhaps, or a crackle-cough fit. ‘I had one of those once. It was horrible. You cough and these little sparks come out...’

pages.title: Dean Thomas's Quidditch chants
aliases: Can We Play You Every Week?
infobox: Can We Play You Every Week?; Five Minutes
pages.html:
Dean Thomas's Quidditch chants are the football terrace songs that Dean wrote for the Gryffindor stand in early 1992, in his first year at Hogwarts. They mocked Hufflepuff's colours, its badger and its famous patience. After the match came two more, Five Minutes and Can We Play You Every Week?

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Dean, who had grown up on the terraces at Upton Park, spent three evenings writing chants for the Hufflepuff match. From the front bench he led fifty Gryffindors through them: the Hufflepuffs had the colours of a wasp, their badger was good for digging a hole, and 'Loyal to losing, that's all that you do!' When Harry Potter caught the Snitch in barely five minutes, the stand sang 'Five minutes! Five minutes! You lasted five minutes!' As the Hufflepuffs drifted down to the grass it took up a slower, crueller one: 'Can we play you every week?' Professor McGonagall told him that would do. 'Yes, Professor,' said Dean, and did one more verse.

pages.title: Upton Park
infobox: Muggle, Football ground, London, West Ham United
pages.html:
Upton Park, properly the Boleyn Ground, is the football ground of West Ham United in the East End of London. The club has played there since 1904. The Chicken Run is its terrace along the east side of the pitch, where the supporters stand close enough to make every player hear them.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Dean Thomas, who had grown up on the terraces at Upton Park, spent three evenings writing Quidditch chants. He thought it a disgrace that a school with a stadium that size had never once had a decent chant in it.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, a big Ravenclaw sixth-year sneered that football was boring. Dean, going red, invited him to come down Upton Park on a Saturday, say it to the Chicken Run and see how far he got.

pages.title: Harrogate
pages.html:
Harrogate is a spa town in North Yorkshire, known among Muggles for its mineral waters, its Turkish baths and its conference halls. Over the Christmas of 1991 Hermione Granger's parents, who are both dentists, went to a dentistry conference there.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Hermione came back to Hogwarts after the Christmas holidays of 1991. She told Harry Potter a great deal about her Christmas: her parents, her grandmother's house and the dentistry conference in Harrogate, most of it twice.

pages.title: Devon
infobox: Nicolas and Perenelle Flamel; the Weasleys, at the Burrow; the Diggorys
pages.html:
Devon is a county in the south-west of England, a quiet green country of hills, lanes and small villages. Nicolas and Perenelle Flamel live there quietly. So do the Weasleys, whose crooked house, the Burrow, stands outside the village of Ottery St Catchpole.

Wizarding Devon

Several wizarding families live in the county. The Diggorys live near Ottery St Catchpole, not far from the Weasleys. The Flamels keep themselves to themselves elsewhere in the county.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Hermione Granger found Nicolas Flamel in an enormous old book she had taken out of the library weeks before for a bit of light reading. He had marked his six hundred and sixty-fifth birthday the year before. He lived quietly in Devon with his wife Perenelle, who was six hundred and fifty-eight.

In Book Two, Chapter Three, George Weasley told Harry Potter that the Burrow was a little way outside the village of Ottery St Catchpole. In Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the Weasleys drove from Devon to London to catch the Hogwarts Express, with Harry squeezed in among them. Mr Weasley muttered mile after mile about every pothole between Devon and London.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry worked out that the Weasleys' watch over him at school had been planned from home. Somebody in Devon had counted up five children in one castle and allocated them.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, at the end of the summer term of 1994, Hermione and Dracina Malfoy sent two thick letters by a single school owl. They were addressed to Mrs M. Weasley, The Burrow, Ottery St Catchpole, Devon. Mrs Weasley read all twenty pages without saying a word. Then she looked out of the kitchen window, east towards Surrey, and smiled.

pages.title: The broomshed
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Hogwarts grounds, near the Quidditch pitch
pages.html:
The broomshed is the shed in the Hogwarts grounds where brooms are put away after Quidditch, and where the school's own brooms are kept. Harry Potter was taking his Nimbus Two Thousand back there one evening in his first year when he saw Severus Snape slip off into the Forbidden Forest.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, in 1992, Gryffindor beat Hufflepuff in barely five minutes, with Snape as referee. Some time afterwards Harry left the changing room alone to put his Nimbus away in the broomshed, happier than he could ever remember feeling. On the way he saw a hooded figure come swiftly down the front steps of the castle, making for the Forest. He knew that prowling walk. It was Snape. Harry jumped back on his broom, followed him over the trees and, from the branches of a towering beech, overheard him threatening Professor Quirrell.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, at Christmas 1992, Ron Weasley told Harry about a way into the broom shed round the back of the pitch, where the lock was broken. Fred and George had been using it for years. With the snow lying thick over the grounds, the two of them had the whole white, empty pitch to themselves.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry had been riding one of the school brooms at practice for a month: an ancient Shooting Star that smelt of the broom shed and pulled to the left.

pages.title: Hufflepuff Quidditch team
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff Quidditch team plays for Hufflepuff House in yellow and black. In November 1993, under its new captain, Cedric Diggory, it beat Gryffindor by a hundred points.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, early in 1992, Hufflepuff lost to Gryffindor in barely five minutes, with Snape refereeing. As the match began, Dean Thomas led the Gryffindor stand in songs about them. The Hufflepuff stand, which did not, as a rule, get sung at, looked thoroughly bewildered. At the end the Gryffindors sang 'You lasted five minutes!' As the Hufflepuff team drifted down to the grass, not quite sure what had happened to them, Dean conducted a slower, crueller chant with his scarf, until Professor McGonagall told him that would do. In Chapter Ten the Hufflepuffs were still sore about Dean's singing.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, the dementors came onto the pitch in a storm, and Harry Potter fell fifty feet from his broom. Cedric Diggory caught the Snitch right after. He tried to call it off and offered a rematch, but Oliver Wood would not have it. Hufflepuff won by a hundred points. In Chapter Ten, at the end of the month, Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff, when Cedric lost the Snitch to a tiny Ravenclaw girl who went past him like a thrown dart.

pages.title: Pomona Sprout
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Pomona Sprout teaches Herbology at Hogwarts and is Head of Hufflepuff House. She is a squat, kindly little witch with earth on her robes and a patched hat over her flyaway hair. It was her Mandrakes that revived the victims of the Basilisk in 1993.

Teaching

Professor Sprout teaches in the greenhouses behind the castle. First-years work in Greenhouse One. Greenhouse Three holds more interesting and more dangerous plants. There her second-years repot Mandrakes, wearing earmuffs against their cries, and prune Abyssinian Shrivelfigs. By the third year they have moved on to Puffapods.

She was one of the teachers who set enchantments to guard the Philosopher's Stone in 1991 to 1992. Hers was the Devil's Snare beneath the trapdoor.

In the saga

On 2 September 1992 she was bandaging the Whomping Willow, which the Weasleys' flying car had battered the night before, and was visibly annoyed when Gilderoy Lockhart interfered. That year her Mandrakes were the cure for the Petrified. She cancelled the last Herbology lesson of the autumn term to put socks and scarves on them herself. In March 1993 she was delighted when they threw a wild party in Greenhouse Three, and she saw them ready in time for the victims to be revived at the end of the year.

When Dracina Malfoy screamed at Goyle over Christmas tea, Sprout half rose from the staff table. While Hagrid was in Azkaban, it was probably she who fed Fang. She also reminded Lockhart of his boast that he knew where the entrance to the Chamber was.

In the autumn of 1993, after Sirius Black's break-in, she somehow kept turning up on the front steps whenever Harry crossed the Entrance Hall. At Christmas dinner, passing the cream, she asked Minerva McGonagall comfortably where her young man with the three rules was now.
