He read the testimonials inside, among them Mr Ashby's: 'My brother-in-law always laughed at my wandwork. He has not laughed since Lesson Four, chiefly because he is presently a hatstand. Thank you, Kwikspell!'

pages.title: Egypt
pages.html:
Egypt is the country of the Nile, in the north-east of Africa, and the heir of Stygia. Every dark art that Europe knows came there by way of Egypt. It is also the place where the dead are weighed. Ra once ruled it as its sun god. Bill Weasley works there for Gringotts, breaking curses in the tombs.

Stygia's heir

Stygia was the old kingdom of sorcerers in the south, before the Ice Age ended and the Flood washed that world away. Egypt rose after it and inherited its craft. From Egypt the dark arts passed to Greece, then to Rome, then to England and the rest of Europe. A wizard who goes looking for the beginnings of his own magic finds Egypt, then Stygia, then nothing, because that is where the written record drowns.

The weighing of the dead

The dead are weighed in Egypt, and something still stands guard over the weighing. The tombs hold more than gold. Some of them hold things that sit up on their slabs and ask an intruder questions.

The Goa'uld Anubis took the name of the jackal-headed god of the dead, but it is not he who keeps watch over the weighing.

Ra

Ra, the greatest of the Goa'uld, once ruled Egypt as its sun god. Through the gate at Giza he carried Egyptians away to other worlds as slaves. Some five thousand years ago the people rose against him, with Thor, the son of Odin, fighting at their side, and Ra fled. The Egyptians buried his gate in the sand, where it lay until 1928.

Thor, the son of Odin, fought beside them in that rising. He came in a storm, a rare thing in Egypt, and broke Ra's guards while the people stormed the gate. Ra forbade the Goa'uld ever to speak of Earth again.

Apocalypse, the first of the mutants, was born at Akkaba in the years after the rising.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Bill Weasley was away in Egypt, working for Gringotts. In Chapter Fourteen Arthur and Molly Weasley went out to visit him there for Christmas 1992.

In Book Three, Chapter One, Arthur Weasley won seven hundred Galleons in the Daily Prophet Grand Prize Galleon Draw. The family spent it on a month in Egypt with Bill, in the summer of 1993, among the cursed tombs. Ron wrote to Harry that he should see what the Egyptian wizards put in the tombs. One had a curse on the door that turned you inside out if you said the password wrong.

In Chapter Four Fred and George told Harry that they had tried to shut Percy in a pyramid. Something all in bandages had sat up on its slab. It asked Percy whether he had lived with a true heart, and whether he was ready to have his heart weighed. 'And Percy answered,' said George. 'For about ten minutes. With examples.'

In Chapter Fourteen, in the spring of 1994, Ron spent ages in the Hogsmeade post office pretending to ask what it would cost to owl Bill in Egypt. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Sirius Black showed Harry and the others the crumpled cutting he had kept: the Daily Prophet photograph of the Weasleys in Egypt, with Scabbers on Ron's shoulder. It was how he had found out where Peter Pettigrew was hiding.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, the Muggle news reported that the American Egyptologist Dr Daniel Jackson had been declared dead after an accident at an excavation near Giza.

pages.title: Eton College
infobox: Eton, across the Thames from Windsor
pages.html:
Eton College is the most famous Muggle boarding school in England, at Eton, across the river Thames from Windsor. King Henry VI founded it in 1440. Justin Finch-Fletchley's name had been down for it before his Hogwarts letter came.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, Justin introduced himself to Harry Potter over the dragon-dung compost in Greenhouse Three. 'My name was down for Eton, you know.' Ron Weasley looked at Harry with his eyebrows up, waiting to be told what an Eton was.

In Chapter Ten Harry, remembering how Justin had turned on his heel at the sight of him in a corridor, thought bitterly: Eton boy, indeed. In Chapter Twelve Ernie Macmillan told his friends in the library that Justin had let slip to Harry that he was Muggle-born. Justin had even told Harry that he had had a place at Eton.

pages.title: Timbuktu
infobox: The southern edge of the Sahara, near the River Niger
pages.html:
Timbuktu is an ancient city in Mali, in West Africa, on the southern edge of the Sahara near the River Niger. In the Middle Ages it was a great centre of trade and learning. To the British it has long stood for the most remote place anyone can think of.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Ron showed Harry his Chudley Cannons bedspread and boasted that all the Chudleys were from England. 'What are those Muggles playing at, letting blokes from bloody Timbuktu play for English teams?' he said.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1994, Dracina wrote to Harry that Pansy Parkinson, who had never cared about Quidditch in her life, had suddenly taken up the Chudley Cannons. 'I just appreciate that they're all English,' Pansy had said. Harry knew exactly where she had got that from.

pages.title: Improper Use of Magic Office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery; the Statute of Secrecy
pages.html:
The Improper Use of Magic Office is the office of the Ministry of Magic that detects magic done where it should not be, and warns or punishes whoever is to blame.

Work

It watches above all for underage witches and wizards doing magic outside school. It can tell where a spell has been cast, but not who cast it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, on the evening of 31 July 1992, the Office detected a Hover Charm at number four, Privet Drive, at twelve minutes past nine. The spell was Dobby's, but the letter went to Harry Potter. Signed by Mafalda Hopkirk, it reminded him that underage wizards are not permitted to perform spells outside school. It cited the Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery of 1875 and Section 13 of the Statute of Secrecy. It ended: 'Enjoy your holidays!'

pages.title: Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office is the small office at the Ministry of Magic that deals with bewitched Muggle-made objects. Arthur Weasley heads it, with one colleague, an old warlock called Perkins. Ron Weasley calls it the most boring department there is.

The work

Its business is to stop bewitched Muggle-made things from ending up back in Muggle shops and houses. Ron's favourite example is a tea set that an old witch had been given by a formerly cursed French nobleman and his peasant wife. After her death it was sold to an antiques shop. When a little old Muggle lady served her friends tea from it, the whole set came alive and danced. The teapot sang. The old lady died of shock, and the office spent weeks on Memory Charms covering it up.

There are raids as well. One night's raids in the summer of 1992 turned up a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle, the work of Muggle-baiters. Lucius Malfoy thinks Arthur a disgrace to the name of wizards, and an ill-paid one. Arthur, who is mad about everything to do with Muggles, does not mind. It was awkward all the same when the head of the office was fined fifty Galleons in 1992 for enchanting a Muggle motor car.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the flying car, Ron told Harry where his father worked, and why it was boring. In Chapter Four Mr Weasley came home from nine raids with a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle to show for them. In Chapter Five Lucius Malfoy asked him in Diagon Alley whether they were paying him overtime. In Chapter Fourteen the Daily Prophet reported that Arthur Weasley, who heads the office, had been fined fifty Galleons over the car.

In Book Three, Chapter One, the Prophet named him again, as 'Arthur Weasley, 43, of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office', when he won its Grand Prize Galleon Draw and took his family to Egypt to visit Bill.

pages.title: Committee on Experimental Charms
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Committee on Experimental Charms is the office of the Ministry of Magic that deals with new, untried charms and the trouble they cause. Arthur Weasley, who has trouble enough of his own, is thankful that its cases are not his.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Arthur Weasley came home to the Burrow after a night of raids for the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office. He had found a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle. There had been some pretty nasty stuff that was not his department, he said. 'Mortlake was taken in for questioning about some extremely odd ferrets, but that's the Committee on Experimental Charms, thank goodness...'

pages.title: International Confederation of Warlocks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The International Confederation of Warlocks is the name under which the Statute of Secrecy is cited in the official letters of the Ministry of Magic. It is another name for the International Confederation of Wizards, which signed the Statute in 1689.

Section 13

Section 13 of the Statute makes any magic that risks the notice of Muggles a serious offence. The Ministry quotes it to any young witch or wizard caught doing magic in the holidays.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, the Ministry's warning letter to Harry Potter in July 1992 reminded him 'that any magical activity which risks notice by members of the non-magical community (Muggles) is a serious offence under Section 13 of the International Confederation of Warlocks' Statute of Secrecy'.

pages.title: Witch Weekly
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Witch Weekly is a popular wizarding magazine, read by witches all over Britain. It gives a Most Charming Smile Award, which Gilderoy Lockhart has won five times in a row.

The magazine

It runs to fashion, household charms and the doings of famous wizards. Pansy Parkinson reads it. Lockhart likes people to know that he does not talk about his awards.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart told Harry: 'I know, I know, it's not quite as good as winning Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award five times in a row, as I have.' Minutes later, at the start of the lesson, he introduced himself to the class as five times winner of the award: 'But I don't talk about that.' In Chapter Fifteen he was still signing himself five-times winner, on a card wishing Hermione Granger a swift recovery. In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1993, Pansy was reading Witch Weekly, and did not look up.

pages.title: Dark Force Defence League
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Dark Force Defence League is a wizarding society which, as its name says, stands against the Dark Arts. Its best-known member is Gilderoy Lockhart, who belongs to it as an Honorary Member, and who mentions it whenever he gives his name in full.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart introduced himself to his first Defence Against the Dark Arts class in September 1992 by pointing at his own portrait on the cover of Travels with Trolls. 'Gilderoy Lockhart, Order of Merlin, Third Class, Honorary Member of the Dark Force Defence League, and five times winner of Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award. But I don't talk about that.'

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Lockhart sent Hermione Granger a get-well card in the hospital wing, signed with the same titles. Ron Weasley snatched it out of the wastepaper basket by her bed and read it out in a high, gushing voice. Hermione said, in a huff, that she had decided she did not like Lockhart any more. She thought he was lying about a great many things.

pages.title: Headless Hunt
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A head that is properly off
Head Juggling, Head Polo, Horseback Head Juggling, Head Hockey
pages.html:
The Headless Hunt is a band of headless ghosts who ride ghost horses, led by Sir Patrick Delaney-Podmore. It admits only those whose heads came properly off. That is why it has turned Nearly Headless Nick away again and again.

The Hunt

Its members hack about the countryside on horseback with their heads under their arms. Their games include Head Juggling, Head Polo, Horseback Head Juggling and Head Hockey, none of which Nick could play. Nick's execution took forty-five blows with a blunt axe. At the end of it an inch of skin and sinew still held his head on.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, the Hunt turned Nick down again. 'Not that I wanted to join, you understand,' he told Harry Potter, with Sir Patrick's letter still in his hand. On Hallowe'en a hunting horn rang out at Nick's Deathday Party, and a dozen ghost horses burst out of the dungeon wall. On every one sat a rider with no head on his shoulders. Sir Patrick held his bearded head up high so that it could see the crowd, then mocked Nick in front of everyone.

Harry stood up for Nick, loud and clear: 'Nick's a great ghost.' Soon afterwards the Hunt began a game of Head Hockey. Nick tried gallantly to win his audience back, and gave up when Sir Patrick's head went sailing past his nose to loud cheers.

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, after the Duelling Club, Harry tried a joke. By stopping a snake from biting Justin Finch-Fletchley's head off, he said, he had saved Justin a job with the Headless Hunt. The joke did not land.

pages.title: Kwikspell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Kwikspell is a correspondence course in beginners' magic, for witches and wizards whose spells fizzle. Argus Filch, the Hogwarts caretaker, who is a Squib, takes it in secret.

The course

Its brochure comes in a large, glossy purple envelope with silver writing on it, and promises an all-new, never-fail, rapid-result, simple-to-learn method. One satisfied pupil, Mr L. Ashby of Kendal, writes: 'My brother-in-law always laughed at my wandwork. He has not laughed since Lesson Four, chiefly because he is presently a hatstand.'

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Harry Potter read the envelope while he waited in Filch's office. When Filch came back he saw that it had moved, went the colour of brick and flung it into a drawer. 'If I thought you'd read my private... not that it's mine... for a friend...' he spluttered. Harry lied that he had not, and Filch let him go unpunished.

pages.title: Malfoy family
aliases: the noble and ancient house of Malfoy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
William the Conqueror, to Armand Malfoy
pages.html:
The Malfoys are an old, rich pure-blood family of Dark wizards, who style themselves the noble and ancient house of Malfoy. They came over from Normandy with William the Conqueror, who gave Armand Malfoy his land in Wiltshire, and Malfoy Manor stands on it still. In 1994 the family is Lucius Malfoy, his wife Narcissa and their only child, Dracina, who is its heir.

History

The histories say that the big Norman wizarding families won William the Conquest with Dark magic, mostly, and that the old Anglo-Saxon families, who were light wizards, lost. The Malfoys have been Dark wizards from that day to this. They like to claim more than Normandy, all the same. Dracina was brought up to say that the Malfoys were in Britain before there was a Britain, and the family tree in the drawing room at the Manor takes up the whole wall.

The family counts its pride in centuries. Tom Riddle held that Malfoy blood was older even than the Potters', which is very old indeed. The Manor has forty bedrooms, peacocks on the lawn and portraits of the family's ancestors on every wall. Under the drawing-room floor there is a hidden room for the more precious Dark artefacts. Until 1993 the Malfoys also kept a house-elf, Dobby, whom Harry Potter tricked Lucius into freeing with a sock.

Other families think less of the Malfoys than the Malfoys think of themselves. Hagrid thinks less of them than most.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Hermione Granger explained that the Norman wizarding families had won William the Conquest with Dark magic. Dracina, overhearing, said that the Malfoys were in Britain before there was a Britain. When Hermione corrected her, citing Armand Malfoy and his land in Wiltshire, two spots of pink appeared on Dracina's cheeks.

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Fred Weasley told Harry from the driving seat of the flying car that the Malfoys had been Dark wizards all the way back to the Norman conquest. Harry had heard that before, from Hermione, with Dracina's cheeks going pink. Then he remembered Dracina talking of having a house-elf, during their detention in the Forbidden Forest. In Chapter Five, after Arthur Weasley's fight with Lucius in Diagon Alley, Hagrid told Arthur he should have ignored him: 'Rotten ter the core, the whole family, everyone knows that.'

In Chapter Fourteen Dracina, who had no idea that she was talking to Harry and Ron under Polyjuice Potion, boasted that the Ministry had raided the Manor the week before. Its men had walked right over the hidden room without finding it. In Chapter Eighteen Tom Riddle told Harry: 'The Potters are very old blood, Harry. Older than you know. And the Malfoys are older still.'

In Book Three, Chapter One, Dracina wrote to Harry that her father had forbidden them to correspond, because a Malfoy does not have friends among the Potters. In Chapter Seven her boggart, in her father's shape, sighed over her: 'There has not been a Malfoy who came second in eleven hundred years, and I had rather hoped that the first one would not be my only child.'

In Chapter Twenty-one, on the dock at Myst, Hermione called her spoilt. Dracina answered with the Manor: forty bedrooms, a wing of her own, a pony, peacocks on the lawn. Then she summed it up: 'It is the biggest, most beautiful cage in all Wiltshire, and I have lived in it all my life.'

In the Book Three Interlude John Constantine remembered his first day at Hogwarts in 1964. A small, stammering boy shook his hand very formally and gave his name as 'L-Lucius Malfoy'. Then he drew himself up: 'Of the n-noble and ancient house of M-Malfoy.'

pages.title: Weasley family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Burrow, near Ottery St Catchpole, Devon
Bill, Charlie, Percy, Fred, George, Ron, Ginny
pages.html:
The Weasleys are a large, red-haired pure-blood family who live at the Burrow, outside Ottery St Catchpole in Devon. Arthur Weasley has seven children with his wife, Molly: Bill, Charlie, Percy, Fred, George, Ron and Ginny. They are poor, every one of them has been in Gryffindor, and they have taken Harry Potter in as one of their own.

The family

Arthur is the son of Septimus Weasley and Cedrella Black. Molly was born a Prewett, and they married in 1969. Arthur heads the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office at the Ministry, which pays badly; most of the children's robes, books and wands are second-hand.

Bill, the eldest, is a curse-breaker for Gringotts in Egypt. Charlie works with dragons in Romania. Percy was a prefect, then Head Boy in 1993 to 1994. The twins, Fred and George, are the family's jokers. Ron is Harry's best friend. Ginny, the youngest and the only girl, came to Hogwarts in 1992.

Standing

For all their poverty, the Weasleys are one of the most prominent pure-blood families in Britain, which made Arthur, and his Muggle Protection Act, worth ruining. In 1992 Lucius Malfoy meant Tom Riddle's diary to end up with Ginny, so that Arthur's own daughter would be found attacking Muggle-borns. It ended up with Lucius's own daughter, Dracina, instead.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry saw how little money the family had: Mrs Weasley hoped to pick up a lot of Ginny's things second-hand. He learnt, too, that every one of them had been in Gryffindor. In Chapter Nineteen, in Lucius Malfoy's hearing, Dumbledore called the Weasleys one of the most prominent pure-blood families. He asked Lucius to imagine the effect on Arthur Weasley if his own daughter had been found attacking and killing Muggle-borns. It was very fortunate for the Weasleys, he observed, that the diary had ended up with Dracina.

pages.title: Lestrange family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Rodolphus Lestrange; Rabastan Lestrange; Bellatrix Lestrange, born Black
pages.html:
The Lestranges are an old pure-blood wizarding family, joined by marriage to the Blacks. The brothers Rodolphus and Rabastan Lestrange served Lord Voldemort as Death Eaters. Both are in Azkaban.

The family

Rodolphus Lestrange married Bellatrix Black, the sister of Narcissa Malfoy. She became as devoted a Death Eater as her husband or his brother Rabastan. After Voldemort's fall in 1981 the brothers joined Bellatrix and Barty Crouch the younger in torturing two Aurors, the Longbottoms, with the Cruciatus Curse. They hoped to learn where their master had gone. All four were sentenced to life in Azkaban.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Ron Weasley named the Lestranges, with the Blacks, as families who would rather marry their own sisters than a Muggle-born.

pages.title: Black family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Orion and Walburga Black; their sons Sirius and Regulus; Cygnus Black and Druella Rosier; their daughters Bellatrix, Andromeda and Narcissa
pages.html:
The Blacks are one of the oldest and proudest pure-blood families in wizarding Britain, whose motto is Toujours pur. Sirius Black is its most notorious son. His cousins, the Black sisters, married into the Lestrange and Malfoy families: Dracina Malfoy's mother, Narcissa, is one of them.

The family

Sirius was the elder son of Orion and Walburga Black. His younger brother, Regulus, followed the family into Lord Voldemort's service. Sirius went the other way, into Gryffindor, and became the best friend of James Potter.

The Black sisters

Cygnus Black and Druella Rosier had three daughters. Bellatrix and Narcissa were born within twelve months of each other. They started at Hogwarts together in 1971, in the same year as James Potter, Lily Evans and their cousin Sirius. At school both decided that James was theirs, and they feuded over him for years, until Lily won him.

Bellatrix married Rodolphus Lestrange and became one of Voldemort's most devoted Death Eaters. She has been in Azkaban since the end of the first war. Narcissa married Lucius Malfoy, and their daughter Dracina was born in 1980. The third sister, Andromeda, married the Muggle-born Ted Tonks, and the family struck her off.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Ron Weasley named the Blacks, with the Lestranges, as families who would rather marry their own sisters than a Muggle-born.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, Remus Lupin asked Harry Potter to remind him, when all this was over, to tell him about James and the Black sisters. Harry asked whether they were related to Sirius Black. 'Oh, yes,' said Lupin.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Harry told Dracina Malfoy that Sirius was innocent. 'Sirius Black,' she said at last. 'My mother's cousin. The mass murderer. Is innocent.'

pages.title: The Belmonts
infobox: Eastern Europe, near Wallachia and Transylvania
Leon, Sonia, Trevor, Christopher, Soleiyu, Simon, Juste, Richter, Julius
The Morris family, the Belnades, Alucard
pages.html:
The Belmonts are a family of vampire hunters who have been at war with Dracula since 1094, when Leon Belmont swore that his line would hunt the night for ever. Roughly once a century Dracula comes back. Each time he does, a Belmont takes down the whip called the Vampire Killer and goes up the mountain to his castle. In 1993 and 1994 the whip belonged to Julius Belmont. The blood of the Belnades witches has run in the family since Trevor Belmont married Sypha Belnades in the fifteenth century. For much of the nineteenth century the Belmonts themselves were missing, and their Morris kin carried the whip in their place.

Leon's oath

The family begins with Leon Belmont, a baron and knight of the late eleventh century. In 1094 he gave up his title to rescue his betrothed, Sara Trantoul, from the vampire Walter Bernhard. In the course of the rescue the alchemist Rinaldo Gandolfi's whip became the Vampire Killer. Then Leon's friend Mathias Cronqvist took Walter's soul for himself and rose as the vampire who would one day be called Dracula. Leon swore that his descendants would hunt him, and all his kind, for ever. Every Belmont since has been brought up to that oath.

The family's strength has not always made it welcome. Some time before 1476 the people of Wallachia grew frightened of the Belmonts' powers and drove them out. They took them back only when Dracula's armies came and there was nobody else who could stand against them.

The line of succession

The war has passed from parent to child for nine centuries. These are the Belmonts who carried it, in order.

Leon Belmont, 1094. The founder, a baron who had fought in the Church's wars. He gave up his title to rescue his betrothed, Sara Trantoul, from the vampire Walter Bernhard, and destroyed Walter with the newly made Vampire Killer. When his friend Mathias Cronqvist rose as a vampire, Leon swore the oath the family has kept ever since. For three and a half centuries after him the Belmonts hunted the night as he had sworn. Few of their names are recorded.

Sonia Belmont, 1450. Leon's descendant, and the first of the family to face Mathias under his new name of Dracula. His own son, Alucard, fought beside her. The Belmont chronicles hold that Alucard was the father of her son Trevor. Whatever the truth of it, Trevor was a mortal man, and so has been every Belmont since.

Trevor Belmont, 1476 to 1479. Sonia's son. When Dracula's armies came, the Church called him back to the Wallachia that had driven his family out. He destroyed Dracula in 1476 with Alucard, the pirate Grant DaNasty and the sorceress Sypha Belnades, whom he later married. He was still in the field in 1479, when he crossed paths with Hector, who had once been one of Dracula's Devil Forgemasters. Every Belmont after him descends from Trevor and Sypha together.

Christopher Belmont, 1576 and 1591. He destroyed Dracula in 1576, but the vampire survived as mist. Fifteen years later he came back and seized Christopher's son.

Soleiyu Belmont, 1591. Christopher's son and heir. Dracula carried him off at his coming-of-age feast and turned him into a demon to guard the newly risen castle. Christopher went after him, set him free and destroyed Dracula a second time. The line ran on from Christopher's house to Simon.

Simon Belmont, 1691 and 1698. In 1691 he fought his way through the castle and destroyed Dracula, but he took a curse from him in the battle. Seven years later, with the curse still on him, Simon gathered the scattered parts of Dracula's body and burned them in the ruins of the castle. When Dracula rose from the fire, Simon destroyed him too, and the curse lifted.

Juste Belmont, 1748. Simon's grandson, in whom Sypha's Belnades blood ran strongly enough for him to work magic. In 1748 he fought a revenant raised from Dracula's relics. The relics had possessed his friend Maxim Kischine, and the castle they raised held their friend Lydie Erlanger prisoner. Juste rescued them both.

Richter Belmont, 1792 and 1797. In 1792 the dark priest Shaft raised Dracula, and Richter destroyed him. He rescued the captives from the castle, among them the girl Maria Renard and Annette, whom he married. He vanished in 1796. In 1797 Alucard found him in the castle under Shaft's control and set him free.

The missing years. For much of the nineteenth century the Belmonts were missing, and others fought in their place. Nathan Graves fought in 1830. Shanoa of the Order of Ecclesia fought in the same century, and Cornell in 1844. In 1852 it was Reinhardt Schneider and Carrie Fernandez, a girl of Sypha's Belnades blood. The whip itself went to the Morris family, distant kin of the Belmonts. Quincy Morris died destroying Dracula in 1897. His son John carried the whip in 1917, and John's son Jonathan in 1944.

Julius Belmont, from the 1980s to 1999, and 2035 to 2036. Then the whip came back to the Belmonts. In 1993 and 1994 it was held by Julius Belmont, a man of about thirty who was actively hunting. In 1999, with Alucard beside him, Julius destroyed Dracula for good in the Demon Castle War. The war took his memory. He came back to the fight in 2035 and 2036 as the nameless hunter called J.

The war is therefore more than nine hundred years old, and more than five hundred under the name Dracula. The figure of about four hundred years that Hermione Granger gave in 1992 is wrong. She had it from Gilderoy Lockhart's Voyages with Vampires, which was mistaken, as Lockhart's books so often are.

Kin

The Morris family descends from the Belmonts by a distant line; Quincy Morris was a Texan. The Morrises held the Vampire Killer while the Belmonts were missing, and they paid for it. Quincy died of his wounds in 1897. John Morris carried the whip in 1917, with Eric Lecarde beside him, and died of it some years later. Without Belmont blood, anyone who calls on the whip's full power pays for it with his life, unless he has first mastered the whip. Jonathan Morris carried it in 1944 with the sorceress Charlotte Aulin. He won its full power by overcoming the spirit held in the whip itself, which met him in the shape of Richter Belmont, and so escaped his father's fate. After him the whip went back to the Belmonts.

The Belnades are the family of Sypha Belnades, the sorceress who fought beside Trevor in 1476 and married him. Through her, every Belmont since Trevor has Belnades blood. In Juste it came out strongly enough for him to work spells. Sypha's own family went on as the Belnades, and kept producing witches who fought beside the Belmonts. Carrie Fernandez was one, in 1852. Another was Yoko Belnades, a witch in the Church's service, who worked with Julius in 2035 and 2036.

Alucard, Dracula's dhampir son, has fought beside the family more often than anyone outside it: with Sonia in 1450, with Trevor in 1476, for Richter in 1797 and with Julius in 1999.

How they fight

The Belmonts fight with the Vampire Killer, holy water, crosses, axes and daggers. They learn how from their parents, who learnt it from theirs. The whip gives its full strength freely only to Belmont blood. The family has few dealings with the wizarding world, but it is not unknown there: Professor McGonagall counts Julius among her old friends.

Among the Kindred

To the Kindred the Belmonts are the most dangerous kind of mortal hunter: a family with a holy relic in its keeping. The best of them also have what the Kindred call True Faith: a faith strong enough to burn and repel the undead. A Belmont with the Vampire Killer in hand and that faith behind him can stand against vampires that no other mortal could face.

Dracula ignored the Masquerade at every return, raising his castle, his monsters and his armies of the dead in plain sight of mortals. The Camarilla, which has never been keen to fight him itself, has been content since its founding in 1435 to let the Belmonts deal with him. The Society of Leopold, the Catholic hunters who carry on the work of the Inquisition, honours the family but has never commanded it. The Belmonts answer to Leon's oath, and to God.

In the saga

In September 1992 Hermione Granger told Harry Potter about a family who had been hunting Dracula for about four hundred years. They were called the Belmonts, they had a whip, and every hundred years or so, when he came back, one of them had to go up the mountain. The true figure is longer: more than five hundred years under the name Dracula, and nine hundred since Leon.

On Halloween 1992 Professor McGonagall mentioned her old friend Julius, who had been in Transylvania for some years and always carried a whip. Gilderoy Lockhart's claim to know him as 'Julius Carrow' was false. By December 1993 Hermione had read the Belmont chronicles.

pages.title: Clan Ventrue
infobox: Can feed on only one kind of mortal
Hardestadt; Mithras; Jürgen the Sword-Bearer; the Master and the Aurelian line (Darla, Angelus, Drusilla, William the Bloody)
pages.html:
The Ventrue are the clan of kings, with old money and old manners. They think of themselves as royalty, and they run things, or believe they do. Besides leading the Camarilla, they sit on the boards of Muggle banks and in Muggle parliaments. On the rare occasions when the Kindred have dealings with the Ministry of Magic, it is a Ventrue who does the talking. The Aurelian line of the Master and Angelus is a Ventrue line, although it has never answered to the clan.

The founder

The clan descends from the Ventrue Antediluvian, one of the thirteen of the Third Generation. He was Embraced about 9300 BC by one of Cain's three childer in Enoch, the First City. He was among those who rose against the Second Generation and slew it, about 8990 BC. When Cain cursed the clans for that slaying, about 8980 BC, the curse he laid on the Ventrue was a narrowed hunger, bound for ever to one kind of prey.

What became of the founder afterwards is not known. No Ventrue will say whether he sleeps somewhere or was destroyed long ago, and it is likely that none of them knows. The Master, the fourth-generation Ventrue who founded the Aurelian line, claims that the Antediluvian sired him, which would make the Master one of the oldest Kindred walking. He will never reveal his sire's name. The clan has never been able to prove the claim, or to disprove it, which it finds very trying.

Gifts and curse

The Ventrue command with Dominate, which bends a mortal's will with a look and a word. They win loyalty and awe with Presence. They endure with Fortitude, shrugging off wounds that would destroy other Kindred, and bearing even fire a little longer than most. Like every power over the mind, their Dominate fails against a vampire of an earlier generation than their own, which is one reason the clan cares so much about lineage.

Their curse is a refined palate. Each Ventrue can feed from only one kind of mortal, and would starve sooner than drink from anybody else. One was known who could take blood only from priests; another, only from left-handed men with red hair. Others are bound to soldiers, to the rich, to virgins or to the people of a single nation. A new Ventrue learns the limit in the first nights after the Embrace, when other blood will not stay down.

The restriction governs only the blood of mortals. Animal blood will keep a Ventrue alive, though it gives little strength, and the blood of other vampires lies outside the curse altogether.

The clan of kings

The Ventrue choose their childer from among the powerful and the successful. In older centuries they took aristocrats and officers; in the modern nights, bankers, industrialists, lawyers or politicians. They prize breeding, manners and achievement, expecting a childe to have earned something before the Embrace. Inside the clan, rank follows age and lineage. Elders are owed deference, and favours are kept on account. The clan judges its own members in its own councils, and would never dream of letting an outsider do it.

They hold more princedoms in the Camarilla than any other clan, and they think of the sect as theirs to run. No Kindred work through mortals as much as they do. They own companies, sit on the boards of Muggle banks, have seats in Muggle parliaments and pull strings that few mortals ever see. The other clans call them the Blue Bloods, not always kindly.

Remus Lupin put it more simply. They think of themselves as the kings, he said: old money, old manners. They run things, or think they do.

From the Second City to Rome

After Cain departed into Nod, the Third Generation built the Second City and ruled it together. The Ventrue were among its lords until it fell to the wars of the founders and their childer. Then the clan's childer went west. In the ancient world they lived among the Greeks, and above all in Rome, which they claim to have guided from its early days. The Ventrue regard the Roman order of law, roads and Senate as their own design.

Rome's long war with Carthage was also a war between Kindred. Carthage was the city of the Brujah, where Kindred and mortals were said to live openly side by side. The Ventrue accused it of harbouring worshippers of the Devil among its vampires. Rome, guided by the Ventrue, destroyed the city in 146 BC, and the Brujah have never forgiven them. Under the Empire the Ventrue followed the legions across Europe. Mithras, a Ventrue whom Roman soldiers worshipped as a god, ruled the Kindred of London for centuries afterwards.

The Dark Ages

When Rome fell, the Ventrue did not. In the Middle Ages they were the lords of Europe's Kindred, ruling as feudal princes over cities and countryside. They held their domains from one another as vassals, with mortal kings and bishops for their creatures. In the east they fought the Tzimisce for the lands beyond the Elbe and the Carpathians. Jürgen the Sword-Bearer carried that war into the Baltic with the crusading knights of Germany.

The late Middle Ages went hard with them. The Inquisition burned vampires across Europe. The elders, the Ventrue foremost among them, saved themselves by giving their own childer to the fires. The young answered with the Anarch Revolt, striking at the elders in their havens. The Ventrue Hardestadt called the convocation of elders of 1435, from which the Camarilla grew and at which the Masquerade was proclaimed. At the Convention of Thorns, at Thornbury in England in 1493, the Ventrue made the peace on the elders' side.

They have led the Camarilla ever since. A minority of the clan went over to the Sabbat instead. These Ventrue antitribu think of themselves as the Sabbat's knights.

The modern nights and the Ministry

The Ventrue moved from land into trade, from trade into banking and from banking into industry. They have kept pace with every change in the mortal world's money since. In Europe and the Americas the princes of most great cities are Ventrue. On the Camarilla's Inner Circle the clan is the most powerful voice.

That position makes the Ventrue the clan that deals with the wizards. In 1900 the Camarilla came to an arrangement with the wizarding governments of the world, which came to the table through the International Confederation of Wizards. The British Ministry of Magic was one of the parties. The wizards would lend their wards and Muggle-Repelling Charms to help keep the Masquerade. These are the enchantments that hide Diagon Alley, Hogwarts and every wizarding house. In return, no vampire who answers to the Camarilla would ever hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard.

It is the Ventrue who very occasionally sit across a table from somebody at the Ministry, being polite about the agreement. The arrangement is old and fragile. It has held, more or less, because both sides have more to lose than to gain by breaking it. The Sabbat, which never signed it, has tried more than once to break it.

The Aurelian line

The Aurelian line is the clan's most famous bloodline, and the one it least likes to discuss. Its founder, the Master, is a fourth-generation Ventrue who claims the Antediluvian as his sire. He is too powerful to be bound to either the Camarilla or the Sabbat. He gathered a priesthood of vampires, the Order of Aurelius. From his blood came Darla, sired in the Virginia colony in 1609; Angelus, sired by Darla in Galway in 1753; Drusilla, sired by Angelus in London about 1860; and William the Bloody, sired by Drusilla in London in 1880.

Each of them carries the clan's curse in a form of its own. The Master can feed only on the devout. Darla can feed only on fair-skinned, dark-haired young men of confidence and drive, which describes Angelus exactly; her blood has been bound to that kind since 1609. Angelus can feed only on blonde, fair-skinned women of strength and beauty. That describes Darla, and it describes Buffy Summers, who became the Slayer in 1996, just as well. Drusilla feeds only on the frightened. William feeds only on those who fight back.

By the clan's standards the line is a scandal. The Master sired his favourite from a dying prostitute, not from among the powerful. His descendants, answering to no sect, ignored the Masquerade quite blatantly through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Angelus cut crosses into his victims' cheeks, and it was in all the broadsheets.

The Camarilla, the sect the Ventrue lead, often secretly supported or manipulated mortal hunters to bring Angelus down. The Society of Leopold was one of them, with hunters such as Daniel Holtz. None of the hunters knew whose money they were spending. The line's great days ended in 1898, when the Kalderash cursed Angelus with a soul. In 1937 the Master was sealed beneath a town in California, after a ritual went wrong.

Later nights

In 1997 the Master broke free of his prison beneath Sunnydale, California, when the Slayer Buffy Summers briefly died at his hands. She destroyed him the same night. Angel staked Darla that year. Drusilla sired her again in December 2000, and because of the particular manner of her siring she remained of the fifth generation.

In the saga

On 2 September 1992 Hermione Granger read in Voyages with Vampires that there were thirteen clans. At breakfast she told Harry Potter that the Ventrue were the ones who thought they were royalty. Later that autumn Gilderoy Lockhart told his class that he had fought an elder of the Clan Ventrue, a creature so old he had forgotten his own name and called himself only the Master. The fight was Lockhart's invention. The Master's lineage, by the Master's own claim, was not.

Remus Lupin described the Ventrue to Harry's class in October 1993, with their particular tastes in blood. Lavender Brown thought it ever so snobbish. 'It's a family failing,' said Lupin. Dracina Malfoy laughed, and looked to see whether Harry had laughed too.

pages.title: Aurelian bloodline
infobox: Darla, Angelus, Drusilla, William the Bloody
pages.html:
The Aurelian bloodline, the Aurelians for short, is the line of vampires from which Angelus came. It is the Ventrue line founded by the Master, and it takes its name from the Order of Aurelius, the priesthood of vampires that served him.

The line

The Master, a Ventrue of the fourth generation, sired Darla in 1609, in the Virginia colony. Darla sired Angelus in Galway in 1753. Angelus sired Drusilla in London about 1860, and Drusilla sired William the Bloody in London in 1880.

Like every Ventrue, each of them can feed from only one kind of mortal.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, at breakfast on the first morning of term in September 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter that there were thirteen clans of vampires. Among the Ventrue, the ones who think they are royalty, there had been one called Angelus, from the Aurelian bloodline, who went right across Europe in the seventeen hundreds.

pages.title: Royal Air Force
pages.html:
The Royal Air Force is Britain's Muggle air force, and the oldest independent air force in the world. It was formed on 1 April 1918, near the end of the Great War, and won the Battle of Britain in 1940. Oliver Wood's father served in it.

The Woods

Oliver Wood's father was in the RAF. Oliver once showed Harry a big magazine full of Muggle jet planes, then explained their payloads at length, with all the enthusiasm he gives to Quidditch results.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Fred Weasley, dripping in the changing room, described the Slytherins on their new brooms: 'Seven green blurs. That's all you can see. Seven green blurs, going past like something the Muggle air force would have.' This made Oliver perk up, since his dad had been in the RAF. George added that their own dad had a picture of a jump-jet in the shed, and that they go straight up.

pages.title: WWF
pages.html:
WWF, the World Wrestling Federation, is the American company that stages professional wrestling for Muggle television. Its shows reach Britain by satellite, and Dudley Dursley is devoted to them.

The wrestling

Its stars have included Hulk Hogan, the Undertaker, Bret Hart and the British Bulldog. The results are settled in advance, which its fans prefer not to dwell on. In August 1992 more than eighty thousand people filled Wembley Stadium to watch the British Bulldog beat Bret Hart.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter One, Harry remembered that Dudley had read nothing at all since the Dursleys had the Sky satellite dish put up and he discovered WWF.

pages.title: Nimbus Two Thousand and One
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Nimbus Two Thousand and One is a racing broom made by the Nimbus Racing Broom Company. It came out in August 1992 and left the old Two Thousand series standing. A month later Lucius Malfoy bought seven of them for the Slytherin Quidditch team, which has flown them ever since.

The broom

It is sleeker than the Nimbus Two Thousand, which had only come out the year before, and a great deal faster. It was the fastest broom on the market until the Firebolt came out the following year.

Every player on the Slytherin team has ridden one since the autumn of 1992, at Lucius Malfoy's expense. His daughter Dracina owns two of them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, the Slytherin team turned out on seven brand-new Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones, a gift from Lucius Malfoy a month after the broom came out.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, the Slytherins flew them in the November match against Gryffindor, much faster than Harry Potter's Nimbus Two Thousand. When Dracina threw her broom across a Bludger's path in front of Harry, the Bludger cracked its tail.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, the whole Slytherin team was still riding them, paid for by Lucius, as it had since the previous year.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, with Harry reduced to an old school Shooting Star, Dracina stepped into his path in the Entrance Hall. 'Potter, I've got a Nimbus. The Two Thousand and One.' She had two of them, she told him; he was to take the spare one for Saturday. 'It's entirely selfish. I've every intention of beating you in the spring, and I shan't enjoy it if people can say afterwards that you were on a broom out of a shed.' The broom reached him in the Owlery, roped in brown paper, with a note in small spiky handwriting: 'Mind the left-hand foot-rest, it goes if you kick it. D.'

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, once he had the Firebolt back, Harry returned the Nimbus to the Owlery in its brown paper, with a note that had taken him four drafts. Dracina rode the other one in the Quidditch final against Gryffindor in Chapter Fifteen.

pages.title: Cleansweep Five
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Cleansweep Five is an old racing broom from the Cleansweep Broom Company, long since overtaken by newer models. Fred and George Weasley, the Gryffindor Beaters, fly one each.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, the Slytherin team came on to the pitch with seven brand-new Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones, bought by Lucius Malfoy. Their captain, Marcus Flint, smiled nastily at the twins’ Cleansweep Fives. Dracina Malfoy suggested that Gryffindor might raise some gold for new brooms themselves. ‘You could raffle off those Cleansweep Fives. I expect a museum would bid for them.’

pages.title: The Weasleys' Ford Anglia
infobox: Arthur Weasley's Ford Anglia; Ford Anglia; Mr Weasley's car; The Ford Anglia
enchanted Muggle artefact, enchanted car, Weasley family
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Flight; cushioned seats; tyres that never go flat; an engine that runs on vegetable oil; a stretched boot and back seat; an Invisibility Booster (faulty)
pages.html:
The Weasleys' Ford Anglia is an old turquoise Muggle car, which Arthur Weasley bought rusty and enchanted in secret to fly. In September 1992 his son Ron flew it to Hogwarts with Harry Potter and crashed it into the Whomping Willow. It has lived wild in the Forbidden Forest ever since.

Enchantments

Mr Weasley is enormously proud of the car. On the morning of 1 September 1992 he kept Harry standing in the yard at the Burrow for twenty minutes, with a trunk in each hand, while he explained every charm he had ever put on it. Its seats carry a Cushioning Charm. Its tyres never go flat. Its engine runs on straight vegetable oil instead of petrol, with a further charm to stop Muggles noticing that it never needs filling up. The boot and the back seat have been stretched inside to hold far more than they should. 'Not a word to Molly,' Mr Weasley whispered, as he showed Harry the boot. On the dashboard is a large red button labelled Invisibility Booster, which is faulty.

Mrs Weasley would not hear of flying it. 'We aren't flying a Muggle car through broad daylight,' she told her husband. 'Think of the Statute of Secrecy, for Merlin's sake.'

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in August 1992, Fred, George and Ron flew the car to Privet Drive to rescue Harry Potter from the Dursleys, who had put bars on his window. They tied a rope round the bars and pulled them clean off the wall. In Chapter Nineteen Harry told Dracina Malfoy that Ron had come in a flying car and ripped them off.

In Book Two, Chapter Six, the barrier at King's Cross sealed itself against Ron and Harry on 1 September 1992. They flew the car north to Hogwarts instead. Over London the Invisibility Booster turned out to be faulty, and the car kept flickering back into sight. Six or seven Muggles saw it, as Severus Snape read out to them afterwards: two in London who were convinced they had seen an old car flying over the Post Office Tower, Mrs Hetty Bayliss of Norfolk, at her washing line, and Mr Angus Fleet of Peebles, who told the police.

Over the Hogwarts lake the engine died. The car came down into the Whomping Willow, which beat in the roof, and Ron's wand snapped in the crash. Then the car came to life by itself. It threw out their trunks and Hedwig's cage, then roared away into the Forbidden Forest with its one remaining door flapping.

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, late in the spring of 1993, Harry and Ron followed a trail of spiders into the Forest with Fang. In a clearing they found the car with its headlamps blazing. It had been roaming the Forest on its own for months. Its wings were scratched and plastered with mud. Where the door on Ron's side had been there was only a gap with a bit of bramble caught in it. It rolled forward to meet Ron like a big turquoise dog that had found its owner. 'The Forest's turned it feral...' said Ron.

Later that night it came thundering down into Aragog's hollow and scattered the spiders. It drove Harry, Ron and Fang out of the Forest on its own, losing a wing mirror to an oak on the way. At the edge of the trees it stopped to let them out. Then it reversed slowly back into the Forest and was gone. Arthur Weasley was never told.

pages.title: Floo powder
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Thrown on a fire, it turns the flames emerald green
The Floo Network, run by the Ministry of Magic
pages.html:
Floo powder is the glittering powder that witches and wizards use to travel by fire. A handful thrown into a fireplace turns the flames emerald green. The traveller steps into them, says the name of the destination clearly and is whirled away past a great many other grates until the right one comes.

Fires and grates

The fireplaces of wizarding Britain are joined together in the Floo Network, which the Ministry of Magic keeps in order. Speaking clearly matters. A traveller who mumbles, or coughs on the ash, may come out of a stranger's grate a long way from where he meant to be. A fire on the Network can also be used to call somebody, who may then climb out of it in person.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry travelled by Floo for the first time, from the Burrow, where the Weasleys keep their powder in a flowerpot on the mantelpiece. Mrs Weasley told him to speak clearly and to mind he got out at the right grate. He swallowed a lungful of hot ash, coughed out something like Diagon Alley and came out of the wrong grate altogether. He landed in a dim shop in Knockturn Alley, black with soot, with his glasses broken. Going home from the Leaky Cauldron that evening, he took his glasses off first and put them in his pocket.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, Snape took a handful of glittering powder from a jar on his own mantelpiece and flung it on the fire. ‘Lupin!’ he called into the flames. ‘I want a word!’ A few seconds later Lupin climbed out of the grate, beating the ash from his shabby robes.

pages.title: Hand of Glory
infobox: Dark artefact, Borgin and Burkes, occult
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (1998)
The hand of a hanged man, pickled and dried
Light for its holder alone; with the proper words, enchanted sleep on a household
pages.html:
A Hand of Glory is the withered, pickled hand of a hanged man, made to hold a candle or to be one. Wizards know it as a burglar's curiosity, sold in Knockturn Alley, that gives light only to the person holding it. The old thieves of Europe knew better. Lit in a house at night with the proper words, it keeps everybody in the house asleep until it is put out.

The artefact

A Hand of Glory is made from the hand of a man hanged on the gallows. It is cut from the body, then pickled and dried. The common sort, of the kind Borgin and Burkes sells, has a candle set in its palm. Finer and older examples have each finger made into a candle itself. Whatever the kind, its flame gives light to the holder alone, which is why Mr Borgin calls it the best friend of thieves and plunderers.

Wizards have decided that it is no more than that. They have forgotten what the old thieves of Europe always knew. Lit in a house at night, with the proper words, a Hand of Glory keeps everyone in the house asleep until the flame is put out. If one finger will not light, somebody in the house is still awake.

Constantine's Hand

John Constantine owns a Hand of Glory cut from a hanged man on the gallows of Prague two hundred years ago. It is not the cheap sort that Borgin sells. Each of its brown, shrivelled fingers has been made into a candle. He bought it years ago from a dealer in Prague's Old Town, for more money than he cared to think about, and he swore at the time that he would never use it. Before August 1993 he had already used it four times.

In August 1993 he lit it in the dark hall of Shacklewell House in New Mexico. ‘Let those who rest more deeply sleep,’ he whispered. ‘Let those awake their senses keep...’ One by one the dead fingers caught, burning with a thin, greasy, yellow flame that gave light to nobody but him. The thumb would not light. The owner of the house, Ephraim Shacklewell, had never been able to sleep, and he was indeed awake.

In the saga

In the summer of 1992, in Borgin and Burkes, a Hand of Glory lay on a cushion in a glass case while Harry hid in a cabinet nearby. Dracina pointed at the withered thing. ‘Ewwww, what is that disgusting thing, Father?’ she asked.

Mr Borgin hurried over to explain, sounding deferential and defensive at once. With a candle inserted, he said, it gave light only to the holder; it was the best friend of thieves and plunderers. He tailed off at Dracina's look of disgust. Lucius Malfoy laid a hand on his daughter's shoulder, quite gently. ‘I hope my daughter will amount to more than a thief or a plunderer, Borgin,’ he said. Then he added that if her school marks did not pick up, that might indeed be all she was fit for.

In August 1993 John Constantine used his own Hand of Glory to rob Shacklewell House.

pages.title: The cursed opal necklace
infobox: cursed object, Borgin and Burkes, Dark object
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Cursed; has claimed the lives of nineteen Muggle owners to date
pages.html:
The cursed opal necklace is a necklace of opals laid out on black velvet in Borgin and Burkes. A small card beside it gives fair warning. The necklace is cursed, and has so far claimed the lives of nineteen Muggle owners.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Dracina Malfoy darted to the glass case in Mr Borgin's shop and stood over the necklace with her hands pressed together. Harry, watching from inside a black cabinet, had never seen her look so plainly delighted by anything. She had drawn breath to call her father over when she read the card beside it. Caution: Do Not Touch. Cursed. Has Claimed the Lives of Nineteen Muggle Owners to Date. She pouted.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, writing to Harry Potter in August 1994 about his relatives, she brought it up again. 'Besides all that, Mr Borgin still has an opal necklace in his shop with a card on it that says it has killed nineteen Muggle owners. I have always thought twenty a rounder number.' Harry laughed at that, until it occurred to him that she was probably not joking.

pages.title: The black cabinet in Borgin and Burkes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The black cabinet in Borgin and Burkes is a big black cabinet, deep in dust, which stands in the shop on Knockturn Alley. Harry Potter hid in it in the summer of 1992.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry's first journey by Floo powder went wrong, and he came out of the fireplace in Borgin and Burkes. Just before the Malfoys came in, he shot into the cabinet and pulled the doors to, leaving a crack to see through. It was a hundred years deep in dust, and he had to give his whole attention to not sneezing.

Through the crack he watched Lucius Malfoy do his business with Mr Borgin. Dracina wandered about the shop, looking at things, until she found herself looking straight at the cabinet. She walked up to it and put out her hand for the handle. 'Come, Dracina!' said her father at the counter, and she turned away.

pages.title: The vanishing cabinet
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hogwarts, the floor above Filch's office
pages.html:
The vanishing cabinet was a large black-and-gold cabinet at Hogwarts, which Argus Filch held to be extremely valuable. In October 1992 Peeves dropped it onto the floor above Filch's office, at Nearly Headless Nick's urging, and it was wrecked.

Vanishing cabinets

Vanishing cabinets are made in pairs. Whatever is shut inside one comes out of the other, however far apart the two may stand.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Argus Filch caught Harry Potter dripping mud from his Quidditch robes and marched him down to his office to be punished. Before Filch could finish writing him up, Nearly Headless Nick persuaded Peeves to crash the cabinet right over the office. Filch hurried off to see, leaving Harry alone with a Kwikspell envelope on the desk.

Filch came back triumphant. 'That vanishing cabinet was extremely valuable!' he was saying to Mrs Norris, with relish. 'We'll have Peeves out this time, my sweet.' Harry got away without so much as a detention. He owed Nick for it, so he agreed to go to Nick's Deathday Party on Hallowe'en.

pages.title: Tom Riddle's diary
infobox: Dracina's diary; Riddle's diary; The small black book
Dracina Malfoy, Dark object, dark artefact, dark magic
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
A newsagent's on Vauxhall Road, London
1993, by Harry Potter with the sword, in the Chamber of Secrets
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Tom Riddle's diary was a cheap black notebook into which the sixteen-year-old Tom Riddle poured a piece of himself. Lucius Malfoy planted it in 1992, and it was his own daughter who picked it up. It possessed Dracina Malfoy for months and opened the Chamber of Secrets through her, until Harry Potter destroyed it in the Chamber.

Description and making

The diary is small and thin, with a shabby black cover worn pale at the corners, like something bought for a few pence in a junk shop. The name T. M. Riddle is stamped on the back in worn gold. Printed inside the back cover is the name of a newsagent's on Vauxhall Road, London. Its pages look blank, and neither Aparecium nor a Revealer will show anything on them. It stays spotless even when a bottle of ink is smashed over it.

Riddle made it in 1943, the year he opened the Chamber of Secrets and a girl died in a bathroom, so that his sixteen-year-old self would be preserved inside it. It is a Horcrux: a piece of a soul poured into a vessel, to wait, whisper and be carried. It was made so that whoever carried it would love it and hold it ever tighter, until they could not let go. In this it is a crude copy of the One Ring. Ambrose Greyhame recognised it at once as made in the same way as the gold ring he had once known.

Powers

Ink written in the diary sinks into the page, and the memory inside writes back in a neat, sloping hand. It can draw a reader through a page into Riddle's memory, as it drew Harry into 13 June 1943.

It breeds a craving in anyone who writes in it, leaving them sick while they have it and desperate without it. It feeds on what they pour into it, until it can move their hands and walk them about while they believe themselves asleep.

1992 to 1993

Lord Voldemort instructed Lucius Malfoy to plant the diary on Ginny Weasley. At Flourish and Blotts in August 1992 Lucius slipped it into Ginny's old Transfiguration book. When the brawl there was over, Dracina Malfoy gathered up the spilled books in one sweep. She pressed one into Ginny's hands and stuffed the rest into her own bag. The small black book was among them, and it went home with her.

From the first days of term she was seen writing in it, then stopping, waiting and reading, with her lips moving. She called its voice Tom, her understanding friend. That autumn she grew pale, sleepless and withdrawn. She lost hours. She could not eat, and she woke in places she did not remember, with red marks on her hands. Through her the memory opened the Chamber, set the Basilisk on the school and wrote on the walls.

On Christmas night 1992 Harry, disguised as Gregory Goyle, took the diary from the Slytherin common room. It felt cold against his chest. He felt a strong urge to write in it, and resisted, locking it in his trunk wrapped in his Invisibility Cloak. Deprived of it, Dracina ransacked the dungeon and raved in the Great Hall about a thief who had taken her 'precious'.

Harry later wrote in it himself. It answered him by name, told him that Dracina wrote about him constantly, and asked whether he had noticed 'what's underneath'. In the spring his dormitory was ransacked and the diary taken back to Dracina. The next morning she appeared radiant, and perfectly well.

In the Chamber at the end of the year the memory took solid form, revealed itself as Lord Voldemort and insisted that the diary could not be destroyed. Harry drove the sword through it. Black ink gushed out like blood, and Riddle dissolved, screaming.

Afterwards

Lucius learned only in McGonagall's office that his own daughter had carried the diary, and he went white. Harry hid his sock inside the ruined book and handed it back to him. Lucius tossed the sock carelessly aside, and in doing so freed his house-elf, Dobby. The pierced diary went home with Lucius.

Dracina was possessed by it for months, which in public passed as her being 'unwell'. It wrote itself into her head until there was hardly any of her left. Harry suspects that the Garou who attacked them in June 1994 could still smell it on her. She has wanted to tell Harry something about it since June 1993.

pages.title: Ginny Weasley's diary
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Ginny Weasley's diary is a pink diary with a lock, a present from her mother, which Ginny has kept for years. It is a perfectly ordinary diary, which is more than could be said for the other diary at large at Hogwarts in Ginny's first year.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the Weasleys’ car had already gone back twice, for George’s fireworks and Fred’s broom, when Ginny shrieked that she had left her diary on her bed. It had to turn back a third time.

In Chapter Sixteen, after Riddle’s diary vanished from Harry’s dormitory, Ron mentioned that Ginny was always writing in a diary of her own, every night, under the covers. ‘Had it for years. Mum gave it her. Pink thing, with a lock.’ He laughed at the idea that his sister could have turned out Harry’s trunk, but the laugh came out a little uncertain.

pages.title: Ron Weasley's wand
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Fourteen inches, willow, one unicorn tail-hair (1993)
pages.html:
Ron Weasley's first wand was a hand-me-down from his brother Charlie, chipped along its length, with the unicorn hair at its core nearly coming out of the tip. It snapped nearly in two when Ron crashed his father's flying car into the Whomping Willow on 1 September 1992. Mended with Spellotape, it spent the rest of that year doing almost anything except what Ron asked of it.

After the Willow

Patched up, the wand crackled, sparked and smoked. Later it took to blowing great purple bubbles, then to whistling like a kettle. Its spells went wrong, or nowhere, or on to Ron.

In the tunnels beneath the school in 1993, Gilderoy Lockhart used it to cast a Memory Charm. The charm backfired and brought the tunnel roof down. After that Ron had no wand at all.

In the summer of 1993 he got a new one: fourteen inches, willow, with a single unicorn tail-hair.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron dug the wand out of his trunk to show Harry. It had seen better days. It was chipped along its length, and something white gleamed at the tip. 'The unicorn hair's nearly coming out.'

In Book Two, Chapter Six, the wand snapped nearly in two in the crash on 1 September 1992, with the tip hanging off by a few splinters. In Chapter Seven Ron patched it with borrowed Spellotape. It crackled and sparked at odd moments all the same.

In Chapter Eight it leapt out of his hand in Charms and hit tiny Professor Flitwick squarely between the eyes. On Saturday 5 September, on the Quidditch pitch, Ron pointed it at Dracina Malfoy after she had called Hermione a Mudblood. A jet of green light shot out of the wrong end and hit Ron himself in the stomach. He spent the rest of the morning belching up slugs.

In Chapter Fifteen it blew great purple bubbles that floated off round the classroom. In Chapter Eighteen it had started to whistle like a kettle. 'Can you imagine me sitting exams with this?' Down in the tunnels under the school, Gilderoy Lockhart got hold of it to cast a Memory Charm, without noticing that it was held together with Spellotape. The charm backfired and brought the tunnel down. After that Ron had no wand.

In Chapter Nineteen, at one in the morning in the hospital wing, Harry sat on the end of Dracina Malfoy's bed and argued with her. He told her that one of her claims was like saying Ron's wand was brilliant because it kept blowing up. Dracina took him at his word. 'Weasley's wand is brilliant. It's the most dangerous object in this castle. It took out a whole tunnel.'

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Ron showed Harry its replacement. 'Brand-new wand. Fourteen inches, willow, containing one unicorn tail-hair.'

pages.title: Hagrid's pink umbrella
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The pieces of Hagrid's snapped school wand
pages.html:
Hagrid's pink umbrella is the flowery pink umbrella that Rubeus Hagrid keeps about him. Hagrid is not supposed to do magic, since he was expelled from Hogwarts in his third year and his wand was snapped in two. The umbrella does a fair amount of it all the same.

What it can do

On the night of Harry Potter's eleventh birthday in 1991, when Hagrid came for him at the hut on the rock in the sea, he used the umbrella to give Dudley Dursley a curly pig's tail. In Diagon Alley he tapped the bricks in the wall behind the Leaky Cauldron with its tip to open the archway.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1992, Harry noticed the umbrella leaning against the back wall of Hagrid's hut, while Hagrid was owning up to giving his enormous pumpkins a bit of help. Harry had a strong suspicion that Hagrid's old school wand lived inside it, since Hagrid was not meant to do magic. He had been expelled in his third year, and Harry had never found out why. Any mention of it made Hagrid clear his throat and go mysteriously deaf.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, Harry sat on a wall in Magnolia Crescent, certain that he would be expelled himself for blowing up Aunt Marge. He thought of what had been done to Hagrid fifty years before. Hagrid had been innocent, but his wand had been snapped all the same. All he had left of it, Harry reckoned, were the pieces hidden inside that pink umbrella.

In Chapter Eleven, in December 1993, Harry could not bring himself to ask Hagrid why he had never once mentioned Sirius Black. Hagrid was the only person who had ever come for him, on an island in the sea, with a pink umbrella and a squashed birthday cake in his coat.

pages.title: Harry's photograph album
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
June 1992, at the end of Harry's first year
Under his pillow at Privet Drive; in his bedside cabinet at Hogwarts
James and Lily Potter's wedding, with Sirius Black as best man
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Harry's photograph album is the leather-bound album of wizard photographs of his parents that Rubeus Hagrid made for Harry Potter at the end of his first year. Hagrid filled it by writing to everybody who had ever known Lily and James Potter. Harry can recite every photograph in it, in order, page by page.

The photographs

The photographs move, as wizard photographs do. James and Lily stand together by a lake. In a garden, James has his arm round Lily while she laughs at something out of the picture. Lily holds a baby with black hair who keeps trying to grab her nose. Later in the album comes the wedding photograph, with a third figure laughing beside the couple, one hand on James's shoulder: the best man, Sirius Black.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Hagrid gave Harry the album in June 1992. It was bound in handsome leather. Its wizard photographs showed his parents by a lake, in a garden, and his mother holding a black-haired baby who kept trying to grab her nose.

In Book Two, Chapter Three, locked in his bedroom at Privet Drive in the summer of 1992, Harry kept the album under his pillow. When Ron, Fred and George Weasley came for him in their father's flying car, it was among the first things he passed out through the window.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, in December 1993, Harry dug the album out of his bedside cabinet at Hogwarts, looking for one picture. He had just learnt that Sirius Black had been his father's best friend. In the wedding photograph he found him: the best man, young, handsome and laughing, with the same laugh as James. Harry had only ever seen that face in the Daily Prophet, as a waxy ruin.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, Harry watched a Muggle news report from a protest outside the United Nations in New York. A woman of about forty spoke to the camera. She had long dark red hair and green eyes. Harry's heart gave an odd lurch, because she looked the way the girl in his album might have looked if she had lived to be forty and had a hard time of it.

pages.title: The Weasley kitchen clock
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The clock on the wall of the Burrow's kitchen has one hand and no numbers. Round its rim, where the numbers ought to be, are written such things as Time to make tea, Time to feed the chickens and You're late.

Description

It hangs on the wall of a small, rather cramped kitchen, with a scrubbed wooden table and chairs in the middle. It does not so much tell the time as tell the household what ought to be done about it. Books stand three deep along the mantelpiece, with titles such as Charm Your Own Cheese, and an old wireless sits by the sink.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Harry Potter sat on the very edge of a kitchen chair at the Burrow and looked about him. He had never been inside a wizard's house before. The clock with one hand was one of the first things he saw.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, at Christmas 1993, Ron told Harry by the fire that he was on Mrs Weasley's list. For a moment Harry could see the whole Burrow waiting for him: the ghoul, Mrs Weasley's mince pies and the one-handed clock that told you when it was time to feed the chickens.

pages.title: The Burrow's kitchen mirror
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Over the kitchen mantelpiece, the Burrow
Telling Harry to tuck his shirt in
pages.html:
The mirror over the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow is a talking mirror with firm views on dress. In the summer of 1992 it told Harry Potter to tuck his shirt in every time he went past it.

Talking mirrors

Talking mirrors are common in wizarding houses, and few of them keep their opinions to themselves. The one over the basin in room eleven at the Leaky Cauldron took a similar interest in Harry's hair a year later.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, the mirror told Harry, 'Tuck your shirt in, young man, honestly, the state of you,' every single time he passed it. The Weasleys, who had lived with it all their lives, thought nothing of it.

pages.title: Self-Shuffling playing cards
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ron Weasley's bedroom at the Burrow
pages.html:
Self-Shuffling playing cards are a wizarding pack that shuffles itself, which saves the dealer the trouble. A pack is the sort of thing found lying about in any wizarding household with children in it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, a pack of Self-Shuffling playing cards lay on the floor of Ron Weasley's bedroom at the Burrow. Ron's room is a small one at the top of the house, and very orange, since nearly everything in it is in the colours of the Chudley Cannons.

pages.title: Howler
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Shouts its message in the sender's voice, magnified a hundred times
pages.html:
A Howler is a scarlet envelope that delivers a telling-off in the sender's own voice, magnified until it fills a room. Left unopened, it begins to smoke at the corners. Opened, it shouts its message at enormous volume and then bursts into flames.

Receiving one

A Howler is the wizarding way of being furious with somebody at a distance, in front of everybody. The wisest course is to open it at once and get it over with. Neville Longbottom once ignored one from his grandmother, and it was horrible.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, the Weasleys' owl Errol brought Ron a Howler from his mother at breakfast in the Great Hall. Ron and Harry had flown his father's car to school the day before. Mrs Weasley's voice, a hundred times louder than it ever was in the kitchen at the Burrow, rattled the plates on the table and shook dust out of the rafters. Ron slid so far down in his chair that only his crimson forehead showed above the table.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, two days after Sirius Black got into Gryffindor Tower with Neville's list of passwords, Neville's grandmother sent him one. A huge barn owl brought it down the Gryffindor table at breakfast, and Neville ran for the doors holding it out at arm's length. It went off in the Entrance Hall. His grandmother's voice, magnified until it rattled the suits of armour, told him that he had disgraced the entire family. Everybody else within half a mile heard it too.

pages.title: Dr Filibuster's Fabulous Wet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Light when wet; give off no heat
pages.html:
Dr Filibuster's Fabulous Wet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks are wizarding fireworks that will light even when they are wet. They give off no heat at all. Fred and George Weasley are seldom without some.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry came across the twins in Gambol and Japes, in Diagon Alley. They were stocking up on Filibuster fireworks with Lee Jordan.

In Chapter Six, on the last night of the summer of 1992, they filled the Burrow’s kitchen for half an hour with red and blue stars that bounced from the ceiling to the walls, while Mrs Weasley pretended to be cross. The next morning the car had to turn back because George had forgotten his.

In Chapter Nine they found out what happens when you feed one to a Salamander. It shot into the air and whirled round the Gryffindor common room like a Catherine wheel, spitting tangerine stars, until it dived into the fire.

In Chapter Twelve Harry lit one of Fred’s with his wand and lobbed it into Goyle’s cauldron in Potions. Swelling Solution went up in a fizzing green fountain over half the class. Dracina Malfoy got a faceful, and her nose blew up like a balloon. In the uproar Hermione slipped out of the dungeon, coming back with the front of her robes bulging.

In Chapter Nineteen, on the Hogwarts Express home in June 1993, Harry and his friends set off the very last of the twins’ stock.

pages.title: Ogden's Old Firewhisky
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Ogden's Old Firewhisky is the best-known brand of firewhisky in wizarding Britain. Firewhisky is a strong spirit that burns all the way down, which is rather the point of it. It is sold by the bottle or by the glass, and it is not for children.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Gilderoy Lockhart went through the answers to the quiz about himself that he had set his class. He reminded them that in chapter twelve of Wanderings with Werewolves he named his ideal birthday gift as harmony between all magic and non-magic peoples. 'Though I wouldn't say no to a large bottle of Ogden's Old Firewhisky!' Of all the things he said about himself that year, it was one of the few that nobody had any reason to doubt.

pages.title: Spellotape
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Spellotape is the wizarding answer to sticky tape. It will hold almost anything together, though, as Ron Weasley found, it cannot make a broken wand behave.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Ron patched his broken wand with borrowed Spellotape. It had snapped nearly in two in the Whomping Willow on 1 September 1992. The tape held the two halves together. It did nothing at all for the wand's behaviour, which for the rest of the year was sparking, smoking and backfiring.

pages.title: Colin Creevey's camera
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Melted inside, in the autumn of 1992
pages.html:
