According to the legend, only Slytherin's true heir could open the Chamber. He would release the horror inside and purge the school of all who were unworthy to study magic. The purge was only a story. In truth Slytherin kept the Basilisk, the king of serpents, to defend Hogwarts from Muggles.

A Basilisk's stare kills. Seen indirectly, through a camera, a mirror or a ghost, it only Petrifies, which is why nobody died of it in the school year of 1992 to 1993.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after the Chamber was opened at Hallowe'en 1992, Professor Binns told Harry Potter's class the legend. ‘It is generally held to be some sort of monster,’ he said, ‘which the heir of Slytherin alone can command.’ He thought the whole thing perfect nonsense.

On the way out of that lesson Hermione Granger said that whatever had attacked Mrs Norris might not be human, since even Professor Dumbledore had been unable to cure her. Over the months that followed it Petrified pupils, and even a ghost.

In Chapter Eighteen Harry learnt from a page in Hermione's fist that the monster was a Basilisk, travelling through the castle's pipes. In the Chamber, Tom Riddle told him that he had worked it through Dracina Malfoy, who had been writing in his diary. ‘I opened the Chamber with her mouth. I set the Basilisk on the Mudbloods with her voice.’ She remembered none of it.

Harry killed the Basilisk with Andúril, the sword that came to him out of the Sorting Hat. The flaming blade went through its neck as it turned on Dracina, who lay senseless on the stone.

pages.title: Pure-blood
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A witch or wizard of wholly magical descent
pages.html:
A pure-blood is a witch or wizard of wholly magical descent, with no Muggle or Muggle-born blood in the family for generations. Pure-blood prejudice holds that such people are better than everybody else.

The prejudice

The histories trace it to Salazar Slytherin, who mistrusted children whose parents were not magical. The tale that he meant his heir to purge the school of them is only a legend. Not every pure-blood family holds with the prejudice: the Weasleys are as pure as the Malfoys, and want nothing to do with it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Professor Binns told Harry Potter's class that Slytherin had wanted the school to take only children of magical families. In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Ernie Macmillan told Harry that his family went back nine generations of witches and wizards, every single one. Harry told him: ‘Those ideas are bloody dreadful and need to change.’

pages.title: Parseltongue
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Salazar Slytherin; Lord Voldemort; Harry Potter
pages.html:
Parseltongue is the language of snakes, and a witch or wizard who can speak it is called a Parselmouth. The gift is very rare. Because Salazar Slytherin was famous for it, most wizards take Parselmouths for dark wizards.

The language

To anybody who cannot speak it, Parseltongue sounds like hissing. A Parselmouth hears it as plain speech, and often speaks it without noticing that he has changed language at all. The gift ran in Slytherin's line down to Lord Voldemort, his last living descendant.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club, Harry Potter spoke Parseltongue to the snake Dracina Malfoy had summoned without realising he was doing it. He was trying to save Justin Finch-Fletchley from it, but most of the school took it for egging the snake on. Afterwards Harry found he could not speak it unless he was face to face with a snake.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, he opened the sink with it, and then the serpent wall of the Chamber, managing it only when he imagined that the carved snakes were alive. In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, Albus Dumbledore explained that Voldemort had passed some of his own powers into Harry on the night he gave him the scar: ‘Not, I think, on purpose.’

pages.title: Petrification
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Mrs Norris, Colin Creevey, Justin Finch-Fletchley, Nearly Headless Nick, Hermione Granger, Penelope Clearwater (a Ravenclaw prefect)
pages.html:
Petrification is the state of being frozen stiff while still alive. Petrified victims lie as though they had been stuffed, with their eyes open, knowing nothing of what goes on around them, until a Mandrake draught revives them.

The Basilisk

In 1992 and 1993 the Petrifications at Hogwarts were the work of the Basilisk of Salazar Slytherin, whose direct gaze kills. Those who met its eyes only indirectly were Petrified instead of killed. Colin Creevey saw it through his camera, Justin Finch-Fletchley through a ghost, and Mrs Norris only its reflection in the water on the floor. Hermione Granger and Penelope Clearwater, a Ravenclaw prefect, saw it in a mirror. Nearly Headless Nick, who took the full force of it, could not die a second time. He turned black and smoky. He hung flat and still, six inches above the floor.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Harry Potter came upon Justin Finch-Fletchley Petrified in a dark corridor, with Nearly Headless Nick floating black and smoky beside him. In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Professor McGonagall announced that the Mandrakes were ready for cutting and that the Petrified would be revived that night.

pages.title: Staff magic
infobox: The elder art behind wand magic
pages.html:
Staff magic is an older art than wand magic, worked with a staff instead of a wand. Few living wizards can still do it. Most think it a quaint old country thing, like Morris dancing, if they think of it at all.

Ambrose's pupils

Ambrose Greyhame, who is Gandalf, found the young Albus Dumbledore skimming stones in the river at the bottom of the lane at home, the summer he was eleven. Albus had been sent out of the house for setting fire to the curtains. Ambrose asked him whether he had ever thought what he could do with a good stick, and Albus told him that a stick was for hitting things with. Ambrose spent the next six summers proving him wrong. In the last of them, in 1899, he taught Greta Grindelwald as well. She took to it faster than Albus did, and one morning she turned the whole river to light, just to see whether she could.

By Dumbledore's reckoning there are not five wizards living who can do what Ambrose taught him with a staff, Mad-Eye Moody perhaps among them. Even the Unspeakables have forgotten it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, by the fire in Dumbledore's study, the two old friends remembered those summers. ‘A wand’s a fine thing,’ said the old man. ‘A wand’s a staff that’s gone to town and learned manners. But it’s good to remember where it came from.’

pages.title: Early medieval magical cultures of Britain
infobox: Southern sorcerers, druids, Viking families, Picts
pages.html:
In the early Middle Ages Britain had several wizarding worlds, not one. Each had its own way of doing magic, and each was sure that the others were frauds.

The traditions

The southern sorcerers of London and the old Roman towns worked in the classical manner: Latin, Greek, a great deal of geometry. The druids held the Midlands, Wales and the North. Their magic, Brythonic, Cymric or Cornish, was made of song, stone and season. The sorcerers and the druids could not stand each other. Viking families stayed on in the North-East after Jorvik fell to the Saxons, and stopped calling themselves Norse. The Picts of Scotland had their own magic, all knots and tattoos.

Hogwarts

They fought about it for centuries. Hogwarts, founded in 990, was the first place where they were all made to sit in one room, and even then it was two hundred years before they would marry each other. Wand magic as it is done now did not settle into anything a modern wizard would recognise until the eighteenth century.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Hermione Granger explained all this to Harry Potter in the library.

pages.title: Football
pages.html:
Football is the Muggle game played by two teams of eleven with a single ball, which only the goalkeepers may handle. It is far and away the most popular game in Muggle Britain.

Among wizards

It has a few devoted followers in the wizarding world. Dean Thomas, who grew up among Muggles, supports West Ham. Arthur Weasley is mad on it, according to his son Ron. Plenty of other wizards think it boring, because nobody flies.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, at a Quidditch match in 1992, the Gryffindor stand roared out a song to a tune Dean said he had learnt on the terraces at West Ham, with Dean on his seat at the front conducting. Later in the match he stood on his seat again and held up a red card at Dracina Malfoy. A Ravenclaw sixth-year sneered that football was boring, and Dean began to climb over the seat. Ron got between them: ‘Twenty-two of them, and only one ball, it’s dead clever when you think about it.’

pages.title: The Slayer
infobox: One at a time, as a rule
After the Ice Age, by a ritual drawing on the power of the Solar Exalted
Far less than an Exalted; far more than any mortal hunter
pages.html:
The Slayer is the Chosen One: one girl in each generation, given the strength and skill to fight vampires as well as demons. The first was made after the Ice Age, by an ancient ritual that drew on the dwindling power of the Solar Exalted. As a rule there is only ever one at a time. When she dies, the next is called. In the early 1990s the Slayer was a girl whose name is not recorded. Buffy Summers, her successor, was called in 1996.

The first Slayer

The Slayer was made in the ages after the Flood, when the ice had gone back. The childer of Cain had begun to spread out across the world by then.

A band of men of an ancient people in Africa, whom the Watchers remember as the Shadow Men, worked a ritual that reached into the power of the Solar Exalted. These were the sun-chosen champions of an elder age, whose might was even then dwindling out of the world. The Shadow Men bound what they could draw of it into a girl.

She was the first Slayer. Every Slayer since has inherited that power.

Why a girl

The men who made her chose a girl on purpose. Even in that age the world had its heroes. They were men, who went out to hunt the darkness in its own places.

A girl would draw the monsters to herself as no man could. They would come to her thinking her easy prey, and find otherwise.

So the Slayer was made to be the other half of the work. She is not the hero who rides out to find the darkness. She is the one who stays, guarding the streets, the town she lives in and the people near her against whatever comes for them. While the heroes of every age have gone out hunting, she has held the line at home.

Nature

A girl chosen to be the Slayer is far stronger, faster and tougher than any human. She heals quickly, fights by instinct and sometimes dreams of things that are true.

Her power is a thin share of what the Solar Exalted once had, and she is nothing like the match of one of them. She is still far stronger than any mortal hunter of the dark, from the inquisitors of the Society of Leopold to the Imbued, the hunters who began to appear at the end of the century.

The line of Slayers

A Slayer cannot pass the power on by choice. It moves only at her death, to the next girl in line, somewhere in the world.

The Watchers' Council finds and trains them. It is an old society of Muggle scholars and occultists in London. Each Slayer is given a Watcher of her own.

Few Slayers live long. William the Bloody killed one, Xin Rong, in Beijing in 1900. He killed another, Nikki Wood, in New York in 1977. Drusilla killed the Slayer Kendra Young in Sunnydale in 1998.

In the 1990s

Through the early 1990s the Slayer was a girl whose name has not come down. In 1996 her successor was called: Buffy Summers, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl in Los Angeles, whose years in Sunnydale, California, began in 1997.

In the spring of 1997 Buffy drowned. She was dead for only a short time before she was revived, but it was long enough for the power to move on, and Kendra Young was called. For the first time there were two Slayers. When Kendra died in 1998, the line went on through her.

In the saga

In the autumn of 1992 Gilderoy Lockhart told his Defence Against the Dark Arts class that he had once spent a fortnight being trained in close combat by the Slayer. 'The Slayer, Mr Finnigan. The Chosen One. There is only ever one at a time, you know, and she was kind enough to show me a few of her little tricks. A wonderful girl. Hit like a troll.'

The training never happened. Harry Potter, lying on the floor as Lockhart's defeated vampire, had no idea what a Slayer was. He thought it sounded like a title in a fairy story.

pages.title: Gaia
infobox: The living Earth, as the Garou know it
The Garou and the other shapeshifting peoples
pages.html:
Gaia is the name the Garou give to the living Earth, and to the spirit of everything that grows on it. They believe she made them to be her warriors. Every Garou is whelped into her war against the corruption they call the Wyrm.

In Garou belief

To the Garou, Gaia is the Earth Mother: the world itself, with its forests, waters and creatures, together with the spirit that lives in them. They teach that the three great powers they call the Triat, the Wyld, the Weaver and the Wyrm, once worked in balance within her. The Weaver's madness and the Wyrm's corruption, they say, have left her wounded. She is a mother under siege. The Garou call themselves her children and her soldiers. The other shapeshifting peoples were made, they say, to serve her in other ways.

Gaia's places are the caerns, holy sites where her spirit lies close to the surface: rings of stones, old springs, groves where the trees seem to watch. The Garou guard them jealously. From the caerns they can step sideways out of the world into the spirit world, the Umbra.

Her ally in the heavens is Luna, the moon. Every Garou is born under one of Luna's phases, and its sign fixes the Garou's part in life. Silver, the moon's metal, is the one thing a Garou cannot bear.

The war for Gaia

The Garou measure everything in creation by whether it is sound timber or rot. They fight for Gaia by finding the rot and destroying it, whether it is poisoned land, a corrupted spirit or a servant of the Wyrm. Many of them believe the war is in its last days, which they call the Apocalypse.

Remus Lupin is both a Garou and a Christian. He fights the same war, and he holds that all dark magic comes from a single source.

In the saga

In the autumn of 1992 Minerva McGonagall told Harry Potter that the Garou serve something they call Gaia, which she supposed was the Earth. They were at war, she said, with something they call the Wyrm, which she supposed was everything else.

She warned him about places that were very old and very green, such as a ring of stones or a spring in a wood. If he ever found himself in one, he should leave the way he came and touch nothing, because it would be one of their places.

pages.title: The Wyrm
infobox: Lucifer; Satan; Morgoth; the First of the Fallen; Mephisto
The corruption that eats at the world from underneath
Dark magic; dementors; vampires; the Black Spiral Dancers
pages.html:
The Wyrm is the Garou's name for the corruption that eats at the world from underneath, wears a thousand shapes and has servants everywhere. Every Garou is born enlisted in the war against it. It is no blind force but a person: the being whom Scripture calls Satan, the elder days knew as Morgoth and the lords of Hell call the First of the Fallen. All dark magic comes from him.

In Garou belief

The Garou teach that three great powers work through creation: the Wyld, which makes new things, the Weaver, which gives them pattern, and the Wyrm, which once cleared away whatever had served its time. In their telling the Weaver went mad and bound the Wyrm in its web. The Wyrm went mad in turn and became the Corruptor.

To the Garou everything in creation is either sound timber or rot, and the Wyrm is the rot. They can smell it in a place, in an object or in a man. They smell it in dark magic, in dementors and in Dark wizards. When a Garou senses it, the urge to root it out and destroy it at once is very hard to resist. Light magic is free of it: Animagus magic, for one, is not Wyrm-touched at all.

There were once fourteen tribes. One of them went over to the Wyrm whole, every man, woman and whelp of it. Its members dance a spiral in the Wyrm's service, and are known as the Black Spiral Dancers. As for wizards, the Garou have little love for them, and suspect them of playing with the Wyrm's fire.

One being

Behind the Garou's telling stands a single being. The Wyrm is Lucifer, the first of the angels to rebel, who brought discord into the great Music before the world was made. In the elder days he was Melkor, until Fëanor named him Morgoth. He is Satan in Scripture, and in the age of heroes he has walked the world as Mephisto, buyer of souls. Dark magic began with his rebellion. It is his craft, and the dementors are his work. After the Flood his servant Lilith led Cain into the blood magic that turned him into the first vampire, and her bargain put every vampire under his will.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the autumn of 1992, Professor McGonagall told Harry Potter in a window alcove that not every werewolf was bitten. They call themselves the Garou, she said, and think of themselves as soldiers. 'They serve something they call Gaia, which I suppose is the Earth, and they're at war with something they call the Wyrm, which I suppose is everything else.'

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1993, Professor Snape told the third years that the Garou are born enlisted in a war 'against a corruption that eats at the world from underneath, that wears a thousand shapes and has servants everywhere'. They have a name for the rot, he said. 'They can smell it, they claim... in a place, in an object.' His eyes came to rest on no one. 'In a man.' There had been fourteen tribes, he told them, until one went over, whole, to the very thing the other thirteen were whelped to fight. In Chapter Ten Harry remembered McGonagall's words while Remus Lupin talked about dementors the way a soldier talks about the other side.

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Lupin said that Peter Pettigrew smelt of dark magic. 'Of his master. Of the Wyrm! It reeks, it's vile!' Before the Wolfsbane Potion, he explained, he had been at risk of transforming the moment he sensed anything that smelt of the Wyrm. In Chapter Nineteen, under the full moon, the Garou that Lupin had become breathed Harry in, long and slow, as though it had found two smells on him. Then it growled: 'Wyyyrrrm.' It said the same to him in Chapter Twenty, in the Forest.

In Chapter Twenty-Two Lupin told Harry that he could smell the Wyrm everywhere at Hogwarts. He guessed that this might have been purposeful, 'from the one all dark magic originates from'.

pages.title: Crinos
infobox: Five forms: Homid, Glabro, Crinos, Hispo, Lupus
pages.html:
The Crinos is the war form of the Garou, the third and most terrible of their five shapes. It is neither wolf nor man, about nine feet tall, and the sight of it causes the Delirium. It is the shape that wizards' grandmothers could not remember seeing.

Description

A Garou in its war form stands on two legs like a man and is mostly shoulders. It has a wolf's head, yellow eyes, and black claws like carving knives on real, fingered hands. Its arms hang past its knees. Its chest is as broad as a door. Heat comes off it in waves, and it smells of wet dog with hot iron underneath.

It can take a troll apart like bread, go through trees rather than round them, and burst an iron manacle by pulling on it. In this shape speech all but leaves it. What comes out of its chest is a grinding growl that is very nearly a word.

Very little troubles a Crinos. Three Stunners do no more to it than a cat's sneeze would, and most wounds heal while one watches. Silver is the exception. It burns, and silver wounds do not close. The wounds a Crinos deals must heal the slow way, without magic, or not at all.

The Delirium

Muggles who see a Crinos forget it, go mad, or both, and most wizards fare little better. The mind will not hold the sight. Minerva McGonagall once watched an Auror, a war hero, see one come round the corner of a barn. He dropped his wand and stood there weeping like a child.

Use

The Garou wear the war form at will, moon or no moon. It is the shape their rage drives them towards, all the same, and to take it is to surrender to instinct. It is the form in which they fight the Wyrm. It is also the form in which a Garou that loses hold of its rage does its worst harm.

The other four shapes run from the human Homid, through the heavy Glabro, to the Hispo, a wolf the size of a pony, and the Lupus, an ordinary wolf. A Crinos can fold down into the Hispo to run.

In the saga

Minerva McGonagall named the Crinos to Harry Potter in the autumn of 1992. In 1993 the boggart in the Hogwarts staffroom took the shape of a bloodied war form for Remus Lupin's class. In November 1993 Severus Snape drew one above the desks in cold light.

In June 1994 Lupin took his war form on the castle lawn when he missed his Wolfsbane Potion. Harry burned its muzzle with a silver Sickle, and its claws raked his left arm, leaving four pale lines. Lupin said afterwards that in his war form he is still himself, and remembers everything.

pages.title: The Delirium
infobox: The sight of a Garou in its war form
The mad, the dying and those with a certain grounding
pages.html:
The Delirium is what the sight of a Garou in its war form does to the mind. Muggles who see one forget it, go mad, or both, and most wizards fare little better. It is the reason the Garou have stayed hidden for thousands of years. It is also the reason that wizarding scholarship on werewolves is a tale for frightening children.

Effect

The Delirium begins as fear, and not the cold fear of a dementor. It comes up hot from the very back of the skull, from the part of a person that remembers being small in the dark while something big went hunting. The body tries to run and to fold up at once. Then the mind refuses what it saw. It closes over the place the way water closes over a stone. What grows back is a lie the witness believes to the end of his life: he was set upon by a bear, or a big dog, or his neighbour went mad at the full moon and had to be shot. He will swear to it, and he will swear it to the clerk who writes the textbook.

Not everybody takes it the same way. Some freeze where they stand, some run and a few lash out, but nearly all of them explain it away afterwards. The few on whom it has no hold are the mad, the dying and those with a certain grounding. Others can sometimes fight it if they know what is happening to them. Bravery and training are no protection. Minerva McGonagall once watched an Auror, a war hero, see a Garou come round the corner of a barn, drop his wand and stand there weeping like a child.

Origin

Many Garou hold that the Delirium is the memory of the Impergium: the three thousand years after the ice when they culled mankind. Every human, they say, still carries that hunted terror. Whatever its source, it is the chief protection of the Veil, which the Litany forbids any Garou to lift.

In the saga

McGonagall named the Delirium to Harry Potter in the autumn of 1992, and Severus Snape described it in his lecture of November 1993. In June 1994 Remus Lupin changed on the lawn. Harry felt the Delirium take hold of him and heard a reasonable voice in his head insisting that it was a bear. He refused it, telling himself that it was Lupin and that he had seen it happen. Ron Weasley kept telling Harry to get away from the bear. Hermione Granger could not look at the creature, and she recited Snape's lesson under her breath. Peter Pettigrew curled up in the grass. Only Sirius Black seemed untouched. He walked up to the creature as steadily as a man crossing a road.

pages.title: Apparition
infobox: A crack like a breaking branch
pages.html:
Apparition is the magic of travelling from one place to another in an instant, by deciding that one is no longer where one was and is now somewhere else. It is how most wizards travel these days. They arrive with a crack like a breaking branch and a faint smell of singed air.

The art

Apparition is hard to learn and dangerous to get wrong. A careless or tired wizard can arrive in pieces, leaving part of himself behind, and one who does not know where he is going can end up inside solid rock. The Ministry of Magic lets nobody Apparate until they have passed a test at seventeen.

Hogwarts is protected by more than walls. Nobody can Apparate into the castle, and nobody can Disapparate inside it.

History

The first wizards ever to meet the D'ni came upon them by Apparition. In 1541 a few wizards were travelling, unknown to him, in the army of Francisco Vásquez de Coronado. They slipped away to try long-distance Apparition across the New Mexico desert. One night they arrived by mistake in the D'ni cavern deep underground, and very nearly ended up inside the rock.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame came up the road from Hogsmeade on foot, in the dark, with the first of the snow. He could have Apparated like most wizards, but he had always liked to walk the last mile to anywhere.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, after Sirius Black broke into the castle, a Ravenclaw wondered whether he knew how to Apparate. Hermione Granger pointed out that nobody could Apparate into Hogwarts. In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine could have Apparated to Hogsmeade, in theory. After the day he had had, he would have arrived in several instalments, not all of them in the right order.

In Chapter Twenty the Aurors outside Black's locked door reminded one another that you cannot Disapparate inside Hogwarts. In Chapter Twenty-One Hermione told Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy the story of Coronado's wizards. 'Underground?' said Harry. 'Blimey. They were lucky they didn't end up in the rock.' They very nearly had, Hermione told him.

pages.title: Moste Potente Potions
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Powerful potions, the Polyjuice Potion among them
pages.html:
Moste Potente Potions is a large, mouldy book of powerful potions, kept in the Restricted Section of the Hogwarts library because of what some of them do. It holds the recipe for the Polyjuice Potion.

Contents

Its illustrations are worse than its recipes. One shows a man who appears to have been turned inside out, and looks rather surprised about it; another shows a witch with several extra pairs of arms growing out of the top of her head. The Polyjuice Potion has a page of its own, with drawings of people halfway through turning into other people. A footnote describes a curse from the fifteenth century that boils the blood, starting at the feet.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the autumn of 1992, Hermione Granger got Gilderoy Lockhart to sign a note for the book without reading what it was. Madam Pince held the note up to the light, but it passed. Hermione, Harry Potter and Ron Weasley pored over the damp, foxed pages in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom. The recipe called for lacewing flies, leeches, fluxweed, knotgrass, powdered Bicorn horn, shredded Boomslang skin and a piece of the person to be turned into.

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Hermione assured everybody that Peter Pettigrew would not get far if he tried to escape. She knew at least four spells that would kill a man slowly. One was in a footnote in Moste Potente Potions, the book she had got out of the Restricted Section for the Polyjuice. A Muggle-baiter in Shropshire, the footnote said, had taken nine hours to die of it, awake for every one of them. Sirius Black said hoarsely that he liked her. 'Everybody likes her,' said Harry, 'until she gets to the footnotes.'

pages.title: Flying with the Cannons
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ron Weasley to Harry Potter, Christmas 1992
pages.html:
Flying with the Cannons is a book of interesting facts about the Chudley Cannons, the Quidditch team Ron Weasley supports. Ron gave it to Harry Potter for Christmas in 1992, their second year. Its pictures move: little wizards in bright orange robes whizz in and out of them on broomsticks.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, it was among Harry's presents on Christmas morning 1992, with Hagrid's treacle fudge and Hermione Granger's eagle-feather quill.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in August 1994, Harry woke from a nightmare at Privet Drive. He found the book where he had dropped it when his eyes had started to close. He watched one of the tiny orange figures swerve round two Bludgers to put the ball through a hoop fifty feet high. Then he shut it with a snap. Not even Quidditch could hold his attention just then.

pages.title: Dean Thomas's slimy snake chant
infobox: One from the terraces at West Ham
pages.html:
Dean Thomas's slimy snake chant was a terrace song mocking the Slytherins' bought brooms and their manhood, sung at the Gryffindor match against Slytherin in the autumn of 1992. Two hundred Gryffindors roared it, then the other houses joined in, until Professor McGonagall stopped it. A second version, aimed at Dracina Malfoy, cost her the Snitch.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Dean had been working on it since the summer holidays, on the backs of envelopes and in the margins of his Potions notes. For three weeks he took Gryffindors aside one at a time to teach it, until there was hardly a Gryffindor in the castle who did not know every word. It went to a tune he said he had learnt on the terraces at West Ham. As the brooms rose, two hundred voices roared it from the Gryffindor stand, while Dean stood on his seat at the front, conducting with a rolled-up programme.

The verse said the Slytherins came up from the dungeons with brand-new shiny brooms their daddies had paid for. Then came the chorus: 'I'm a slimy snake, I've got no balls.' By the second chorus the Hufflepuffs and Ravenclaws had picked it up. By the third it was coming from three sides of the stadium, while the stamping made the stands shake. The Slytherin stand went berserk. Professor McGonagall seized Lee Jordan's megaphone. If she heard one more word, she thundered, Gryffindor would lose fifty points.

Dean sat down, deeply disappointed. Later in the match, when Dracina had seen the Snitch and was a foot from it, he rose again with new words: 'She's a slimy snake, she's got no Snitch.' It called her Daddy's girl, who could not catch a thing. Dracina's hand faltered. She turned right round on her broom to scream at the stand that her father sat on the Board of Governors. McGonagall took twenty points from Gryffindor. By the time Dracina turned back, the Snitch had gone.

pages.title: Oh Potter, the plotter
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Harry Potter, as the supposed Heir of Slytherin
High kicks and a final bow
pages.html:
'Oh Potter, the plotter' is the song Peeves the poltergeist made up in December 1992, when half of Hogwarts believed Harry Potter was the Heir of Slytherin. He sang it in crowded corridors for months, and later worked out a high-kicking dance to go with it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Harry was found standing over the Petrified bodies of Justin Finch-Fletchley and Nearly Headless Nick. Peeves bobbed overhead, grinning, and burst into song: 'Oh Potter, the plotter, he's at it again'. The next line accused Harry of stiffening the students and now the dead men. That was as far as Peeves got before Professor McGonagall barked at him to get out. He shot away backwards down the corridor with his tongue stuck out at Harry.

In Chapters Fifteen and Sixteen, the song went on into 1993. Peeves kept popping up in crowded corridors to sing it. He worked out a dance to go with it, with a great deal of high kicking and a final bow. By March, nearly four months after the attack, he had finally got bored with it.

pages.title: The knight and the tower picture book
infobox: A knight in silver armour, kneeling, offering his sword hilt first to a girl with long pale hair in a tower
pages.html:
The knight and the tower picture book is a big, battered children's picture book, of the kind small children are given at Christmas. Dracina Malfoy was reading it in the Hogwarts library in November 1992, open at a picture of a knight in silver armour kneeling before a girl with long pale hair in a tower. When Harry Potter saw it, she slammed it shut.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Harry saw Dracina sitting alone in the library, with the picture book open on top of two volumes of wizarding genealogy. In the picture, the knight was holding his sword out to the girl, hilt first. Dracina slammed the book shut so hard that Madam Pince shot out from behind her desk, swept it under the genealogies and glared at him with her face burning. 'What, Potter?'

pages.title: The Malfoy genealogies
infobox: The Malfoy crest, on the spine of one
pages.html:
The Malfoy genealogies are two fat volumes of wizarding genealogy in the Hogwarts library, one of them with the Malfoy crest on its spine.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, in November 1992, Harry Potter passed Dracina Malfoy sitting alone in the library behind a strange heap of books. The two volumes of genealogy lay at the bottom of it. On top, open, lay a children's Christmas picture book showing a knight kneeling to a girl in a tower. When Dracina saw Harry looking, she slammed the picture book shut and swept it under the genealogies.

pages.title: Books on the Aurelian line
pages.html:
Hermione Granger had read three books on the Aurelian line by the autumn of 1992. All three agree that the Master, the ancient vampire at the head of the line, has been trapped since 1937.

What they say

The Aurelians descend from the Master, who sired Darla. Darla sired Angelus, Angelus sired Drusilla, and Drusilla sired William the Bloody. In 1937 the Master tried to open the Hellmouth beneath a small town in California. The ritual went wrong, and he has been sealed beneath the town ever since.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Gilderoy Lockhart told his class how he had fought the Master in Eastern Europe. Hermione put up her hand: 'Because I've read three books on the Aurelian line, and all three of them say the Master's been trapped since nineteen thirty-seven. Under a town in California.' She could not see how he had fought him in Eastern Europe, unless it was before 1937, in which case he would not have been born. There was a very long silence. At last Lockhart said brightly that the Master must have sent a psychic projection of himself, and gave her five points.

pages.title: Dumbledore's letter to Ambrose Greyhame
infobox: Harry Potter's scar; the Philosopher's Stone; the chessboard, the potions and Quirrell
pages.html:
Dumbledore's letter to Ambrose Greyhame was a long letter that Albus Dumbledore wrote in his slanting hand in the summer of 1992, to his old friend across the sea. Ambrose Greyhame is the name Gandalf goes by. The letter told him about Harry Potter's scar, then about the Philosopher's Stone: the chessboard, the potions and Quirrell, with his dark passenger.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, in December 1992, Ambrose watched Harry duelling in the Great Hall at Hogwarts. He had known about the scar already. He had read about it in a letter, a long letter, in a slanting hand, that had come to him across the sea the summer before. It was not the scar he was looking at, though. It was the boy's face, which put him in mind of a tall, weather-stained man in the dark corner of an inn, long ago.

The next day he told Dumbledore about it. 'I knew about the Stone. You told me, in your letter.' The letter had made him think Harry a brave boy, and a lucky one. 'But to see him. To see him with my own eyes...' Harry had the very look, he said. 'My old friend would be most proud of him.'

pages.title: Dumbledore's note to Ambrose
pages.html:
Dumbledore's note to Ambrose was a note Albus Dumbledore left on his desk in December 1992, for his friend Ambrose Greyhame to find. It said that he was at the Ministry with Fudge in a flap, invited Ambrose to make himself at home and forbade him to feed Fawkes Fizzing Whizbees.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose went up to the Headmaster's office after watching the duel in the Great Hall. Albus, he knew, had a sweet tooth. He tried pear drop, Acid Pop, Fizzing Whizbee, peppermint humbug and Cockroach Cluster on the gargoyle before sherbet lemon worked. 'Every time,' he said fondly. The office was empty. On the desk lay a note in the same slanting hand as the summer's letter: 'Ministry. Fudge in a flap again. Back by morning, I hope. Make yourself at home, my friend, I know you will anyway. Do NOT feed Fawkes the Fizzing Whizbees, they give him hiccups.' The old man laughed, then settled into the chintz armchair by the fire to light his pipe.

pages.title: Exploding Snap
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Exploding Snap is a wizarding card game, played much like Muggle snap, except that the cards blow up without warning. It is a favourite in Gryffindor Tower, where it is usually played as loudly as possible.

The game

The cards can go off at any moment, with a bang and a cloud of smoke. A game usually ends with cards all over the room and the players' eyebrows singed.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, over Christmas 1992, Harry Potter, Hermione Granger and the Weasleys had Gryffindor Tower to themselves. They could play Exploding Snap as loudly as they liked without anybody complaining. In Chapter Seventeen, needing the common room empty, Harry and Ron Weasley lost to the twins on purpose, game after game, as fast as they could. It was long past midnight before Fred and George went up to bed. In Chapter Nineteen the friends played it on the Hogwarts Express home.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, Ron was drawn into a game with Seamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas. The cards went off in Seamus's face twice. In Chapter Fourteen Neville Longbottom, at a loose end, offered Harry a game; Harry had other plans. In Chapter Sixteen, with the exams coming, Percy Weasley confiscated Lee Jordan's cards.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, on the train home in June 1994, Harry, Ron and Hermione played until they all had singed eyebrows. Then Dracina Malfoy looked into the compartment. 'Exploding Snap,' she said. 'How terribly sophisticated.' She bent down to flick the top card with one fingernail, and the whole pack went off at once. In the smoke, Harry felt something small, folded very tightly, being pushed into his hand.

pages.title: International Warlock Convention of 1289
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Included a sub-committee of Sardinian sorcerers, which met that September
One of Professor Binns's dullest lectures
pages.html:
The International Warlock Convention of 1289 was a meeting of the wizards of several nations in the late thirteenth century. Its proceedings included a sub-committee of Sardinian sorcerers, which met in the September of that year. At Hogwarts it is remembered chiefly as the subject of one of Professor Binns's dullest lectures.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, in November 1992, Binns was half an hour into a remarkably dull account of the Convention when Hermione Granger put up her hand. It seemed to be the first raised hand he had noticed in a century and a half. She asked him about the Chamber of Secrets. Binns told her that he dealt in facts, not in myths and legends. Then he went back to his notes: 'In the September of that year, a sub-committee of Sardinian sorcerers...' He faltered. Hermione's hand was up again.

pages.title: The Medieval Assembly of European Wizards
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A three-foot History of Magic composition, set in November 1992
pages.html:
The Medieval Assembly of European Wizards was a gathering of the wizards of Europe in the Middle Ages. Its history is taught in History of Magic at Hogwarts, where in November 1992 Professor Binns set the second-years a composition on it three feet long.

The wizards of medieval Britain

In the early Middle Ages there was no single wizarding world, not even in Britain. The southern sorcerers, round London and the old Roman towns, worked in the classical manner. Their incantations were Latin and Greek, with a great deal of geometry. The druids of Wales, the Midlands and the North sang their magic, working it through stone as well as the turning seasons. The two lots could not stand each other. The Viking families of the North-East had their own ways. So did the Picts of Scotland, whose magic was all knots and tattoos.

Every one of these peoples thought that it alone had real magic. They fought about it for centuries. Hogwarts, founded in 990, was the first place where they were made to sit down in the same room. Even then it was another two hundred years before they would marry one another, and wand magic did not settle into the form wizards know today until the eighteenth century.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Ron Weasley sat at the back of the library measuring his composition, which was still eight inches short. Hermione Granger had done four feet seven inches in tiny writing. She was also writing out Harry Potter's for him, whatever Ron said about it, and explaining it as she went, because Harry ought at least to know what was in it. Harry understood more of it in two minutes from her than in two months from Binns.

pages.title: The meltwater flood
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 13
The end of the Ice Age
Whole countries, with the black towers and serpent temples by the warm seas
pages.html:
The meltwater flood was the hundred-year flood that came down out of the north at the end of the Ice Age, when the ice that had lain a mile thick on the mountains went back at last. It drowned whole countries. It was the Flood of Noah.

The flood

The ice went back groaning and cracking. Its meltwater came down from the north in a flood that went on for a hundred years. The drowned countries took with them the black towers by the warm seas. With them went the temples where men had worshipped a great serpent and fed it. The sorcerers who had learnt their magic from the thing in those temples went under too, having paid dearly for it. So ended the Hyborian Age, and Stygia with it.

Afterwards a few frightened families huddled round small fires on cold new shores. They had nothing at all, and nobody to teach them anything except what they could find out for themselves. To them God sent Gandalf. He sat by their fires and taught the first of them the first words of magic: how to call a flame, how to ask the rain to wait, how to heal a cut. Above all he taught them how to tell that a voice offering power out of the dark is never the voice of a friend.

Cain, who could not die, came through the water. Not long after it, Lilith led him into the blood magic by which he became the first vampire.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame, who is Gandalf, walked up to Hogwarts through the snow in December 1992. At the gates he thought of how far back it all went: to the ice going back, to the flood and to the few frightened families on the cold new shores, by whose fires he had once sat.

pages.title: Previous opening of the Chamber of Secrets
aliases: the last time the Chamber was opened
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The previous opening of the Chamber of Secrets was the one that came before the attacks of 1992 to 1993, about fifty years earlier, in 1943. A Muggle-born girl died, a student was expelled for it and the whole affair was kept quiet. In 1992 almost nobody at Hogwarts knew more than that. Most of what was known came from hints and rumour.

What happened

The Chamber was opened in 1943 by Tom Riddle, a fifth-year Slytherin and the heir of Slytherin. Its Basilisk attacked several students before it killed one, a Muggle-born Ravenclaw girl called Myrtle. Riddle framed the third-year Rubeus Hagrid, with his pet spider Aragog, and Hagrid was expelled. The Headmaster, Professor Dippet, could not bear the shame of it, so the girl's death was put about as an accident. Riddle was given a special award for services to the school, and told to keep quiet.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, at Christmas 1992, Harry Potter sat in the Slytherin common room disguised by Polyjuice Potion as Gregory Goyle, with Ron Weasley as Crabbe. Dracina Malfoy told them that her father would tell her nothing about the last time the Chamber was opened, fifty years before. He knew all about it, though, and he said that it had all been kept quiet. Reading between the lines of his hints, she had gathered that a Muggle-born had died. The culprit, she said, had been expelled, and was probably rotting in Azkaban.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Riddle's diary gave Harry its own account and drew him into its memory of 13 June 1943. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber itself, the memory of Riddle showed him who he really was: Lord Voldemort.

pages.title: Aragog
infobox:
Rubeus Hagrid raised by
Mosag wife
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A domed web in a hollow deep in the Forbidden Forest
pages.html:
Aragog is a giant spider who lives with his enormous family in a hollow deep in the Forbidden Forest. The young Rubeus Hagrid raised him from an egg. In 1943 he was wrongly blamed for the death of a girl at Hogwarts, and in 1993 he told Harry Potter the truth of it.

Origins

Aragog is an Acromantula, a spider from the jungles of a distant country that grows to an enormous size and can talk. A traveller gave him to Hagrid as an egg. Hagrid, then a boy at Hogwarts, hatched him and kept him in a cupboard in the castle, feeding him on scraps from the tables. Aragog never saw any part of the castle but that cupboard.

In 1943 Tom Riddle caught Hagrid trying to smuggle him out. The girl who had died when the Chamber of Secrets was opened was laid at Aragog's door, and Hagrid was expelled for it. Aragog fled into the Forest, where he has lived ever since. Hagrid found him a wife, Mosag, and still visits him. Aragog's children by Mosag, with their own children after them, now fill the hollow in their hundreds.

Aragog is the size of a small elephant. There is grey in the black of his body and legs. His eight eyes have gone milky white with blindness.

In the saga

In 1993 Hagrid told Harry and Ron to follow the spiders. They led the boys straight to Aragog's hollow. He told them that he had never harmed a human being, out of respect for Hagrid. The monster in the Chamber, he said, was the creature his kind fear above all others, and he would not name it. When he had sensed it moving through the castle, he had begged Hagrid to let him go. Then he gave the two boys to his children: 'My sons and daughters do not harm Hagrid, on my command. But I cannot deny them fresh meat.' The Weasleys' flying car, which had been living wild in the Forest, came crashing through the trees to rescue them.

In their own words

My sons and daughters do not harm Hagrid, on my command. But I cannot deny them fresh meat.Aragog · B2 Ch17

pages.title: Professor Dippet
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Very old and frail, bald but for wispy white tufts above his ears
pages.html:
Armando Dippet was the Headmaster of Hogwarts in the 1940s, before Albus Dumbledore. He was in charge of the school in 1943, when the Chamber of Secrets was opened and a girl was killed. He could not bear people knowing that such a thing had happened under his nose, so the death was put about as an accident.

Headmaster

By 1943 Dippet was a very old, frail wizard, bald except for a few wispy white tufts above his ears. Albus Dumbledore taught Transfiguration under him. That year the monster of the Chamber went for one student after another, and in the end it killed the Ravenclaw girl now known as Moaning Myrtle. The Ministry talked of closing the school. Rubeus Hagrid was expelled for it on Tom Riddle's word, though Dumbledore persuaded Dippet to keep Hagrid on at the castle to be trained as gamekeeper.

When Riddle was leaving school two years later, he asked Dippet whether he might stay on as a teacher. Dippet told him he was too young. Dumbledore succeeded Dippet as Headmaster.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Tom Riddle's diary told Harry Potter that the Chamber had been opened in Riddle's fifth year. The Headmaster at the time, Professor Dippet, could not bear the shame of it, or people knowing that such a thing had happened at Hogwarts under his nose. So it was put about that the girl had died in some sort of accident. According to Riddle, he was given a very handsome trophy with his name engraved on it, and told to keep quiet.

Then the diary drew Harry into the Headmaster's office on 13 June 1943, at sunset. There was no phoenix, and none of Dumbledore's whirring silver instruments. Dippet sat hunched over a letter by the light of a single candle. Riddle, a sixteen-year-old prefect, had written asking to stay at the castle over the summer rather than go back to his Muggle orphanage. Dippet was kind about it, but he refused: with the attacks going on, it would be very foolish to let Riddle stay on alone in the castle. Between themselves, he added, the Ministry was even talking about closing the school altogether. Riddle asked what would happen if somebody were caught. Dippet sat up with a squeak, but Riddle said he knew nothing about the attacks, and Dippet sank back in his chair, looking faintly let down.

pages.title: Daphne Greengrass
infobox:
Dracina Malfoy friend
Pansy Parkinson friend
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (June 2003)
The Greengrasses, a pure-blood family; a younger sister, Astoria
pages.html:
Daphne Greengrass is a Slytherin witch in Harry Potter's year, and one of Dracina Malfoy's few real friends. She is a quiet, watchful girl, whom Dracina likes chiefly because she usually says nothing.

Character

Daphne comes of an old pure-blood family, the Greengrasses, and has a younger sister, Astoria. She was one of the friends Lucius Malfoy chose for his daughter, and one of the few Dracina actually likes.

She says little and notices a great deal. On the Hogwarts Express in September 1993 she remarked, quite mildly, that Dracina had been gone for twenty minutes. Her tongue is sharp when she cares to use it. On Hallowe'en morning she suggested to Harry that he might faint into the butterbeer, and she choked when Dracina praised Professor Lupin's lessons to him.

At Hogwarts

In the spring of 1993, while Dracina was ill, Daphne sat beside her in Potions. At the carriages at the end of that term she asked her what the matter was, because Dracina was crying. After Buckbeak's attack in September 1993 she left a box of Chocolate Frogs at Dracina's bedside. When Dracina paid her formal call on Harry in the hospital wing in November, Daphne giggled through the whole visit as though she were watching a play.

In 1994 she stayed at the Slytherin table when Dracina went over to inspect Harry's Firebolt. After Buckbeak's verdict she stood with Pansy Parkinson in Care of Magical Creatures, a little apart from Dracina. On the castle steps, the day after Sirius Black's escape, she held Dracina back by both arms when Dracina lunged at Pansy, and let go only when Dracina asked her to. She chattered with Pansy about the theory that Black had turned into a bat. On the train home she pulled Pansy away from Ron Weasley by the elbow.

pages.title: Penelope Clearwater
infobox: Ravenclaw, prefect, Hogwarts student, Basilisk victim, Prefect
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Penelope Clearwater is a Ravenclaw prefect with long, curly hair, and Percy Weasley's girlfriend. In 1993 the Basilisk Petrified her beside Hermione Granger near the library. She had been looking round a corner with a small mirror, which is why she lived.

Percy

Penelope was in the same year at Hogwarts as Percy, a sixth-year when the Basilisk struck. She left school with him in the summer of 1994. For a long time nobody knew about them. They wrote to each other all through the summer of 1992 and met all over the school in secret. Ginny Weasley once walked in on them kissing in an empty classroom.

By 1993 the secret was out. Percy keeps a photograph of her, in which she hides her face under the frame because her nose has gone blotchy. She bears his lectures with great patience.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, on Christmas night 1992, a Ravenclaw girl with long curly hair came up out of the dungeons into the Entrance Hall. Harry and Ron, disguised by Polyjuice Potion as two Slytherins, asked her the way to their common room. 'Your common room?' she said stiffly. 'I'm in Ravenclaw.' In Chapter Sixteen Harry found her Petrified in the hospital wing, a sixth-year girl with long, curly hair, and knew her for the Ravenclaw they had stopped by mistake. George Weasley told him her name, and that Percy was in a state.

In Chapter Eighteen Harry worked out what must have happened. Hermione, who had just realised that the monster was a Basilisk, must have warned her to look round corners with a mirror first. A small round mirror had been found beside the two of them. In Chapter Nineteen Ginny told Harry and Ron that Penelope was Percy's secret girlfriend.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, Ron grumbled that Percy was accusing him of dripping tea on his photograph of her. At King's Cross Percy strode over to her with his chest thrown out, so that she could not miss his shiny Head Boy badge. In Chapter Ten he went down to Hogsmeade with her.

In Chapter Thirteen, before the Ravenclaw match of March 1994, Penelope weighed Harry's Firebolt expertly across one finger. 'Now, now, Penny, no sabotage!' said Percy. 'I'm a Ravenclaw prefect, Percy, not a highwayman.' They had ten Galleons on the match. 'He was very confident at the time,' said Penelope. Gryffindor won, and she lost the bet.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, at breakfast in June 1994, Percy held forth about Sirius Black's escape and the proposals he meant to make about Magical Law Enforcement. Penelope nodded patiently and went on eating her toast.

In their own words

I'm a Ravenclaw prefect, Percy, not a highwayman.Penelope Clearwater · B3 Ch13

pages.title: Mosag
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A hollow deep in the Forbidden Forest
pages.html:
Mosag is a giant spider, an Acromantula, and the wife of Aragog. Rubeus Hagrid found her for him after Aragog fled into the Forbidden Forest in 1943. Their children, and their children's children, now fill a hollow deep in the Forest in their hundreds.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, Harry Potter and Ron Weasley followed the spiders into the Forest in 1993, as far as Aragog's hollow. Aragog told them how Hagrid had protected him when he was blamed for the death of a girl, and how Hagrid still visited him. 'He even found me a wife, Mosag, and you see how our family has grown, all through Hagrid's goodness...'

pages.title: Olive Hornby
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Teasing Myrtle about her glasses; being haunted for it
pages.html:
Olive Hornby was a Hogwarts student in the 1940s. On the day in 1943 that Myrtle died, Olive had been teasing her about her glasses. When Myrtle came back as a ghost, she haunted Olive for it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, in 1993, Moaning Myrtle told Harry Potter, with deep relish, how she had died. She had hidden in a cubicle in the girls' bathroom because Olive Hornby was teasing her about her glasses. The door was locked, and she was crying, when she heard somebody come in. It was a boy, saying something in a strange language. Then she saw a pair of great big yellow eyes, and her whole body seized up. "And then I came back. I was determined to haunt Olive Hornby, you see. Oh, she was sorry she'd ever laughed at my glasses."

pages.title: Marjorie Dursley
infobox: Aunt Marge; Marge; Marge Dursley; Marjorie; Miss Marjorie Dursley; Uncle Vernon's sister

Vernon Dursley brother
Ripper favourite dog, dog
Colonel Fubster friend who minds her dogs
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999); first mentioned in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (June 1997)
The country, where she breeds bulldogs
Dudley Dursley (nephew); Harry Potter (no blood relation)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Marjorie Dursley, known to the family as Aunt Marge, is Vernon Dursley's sister: a bulldog breeder from the country who has bullied Harry Potter on every visit of his life. In August 1993 she insulted his parents once too often, and Harry's anger blew her up like a balloon.

Description

Marge is large, beefy and purple-faced, with a moustache. She lives in the country, where she keeps twelve bulldogs. Ripper is her favourite. When she travels, a friend of hers, Colonel Fubster, minds the dogs for her.

She is no blood relation of Harry's. She dotes on Dudley, giving him money and presents. Harry has had dog biscuits from her for Christmas.

Earlier visits

At Dudley's fifth birthday party Marge whacked Harry's shins with her walking stick. On her last visit before he went to Hogwarts she let Ripper chase him up a tree in the back garden at Privet Drive. She kept him there until past midnight. Her gloating is one of the voices Harry still hears in his head.

The visit of 1993

Marge came to Privet Drive by train on 31 July 1993, for about a week. She complained that between Didcot and Reading she had been the only English person in her carriage. Harry was under orders to pretend that he went to St Brutus's Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys, so he played a dull-witted boy who said 'nuffink'. Marge approved of the cane, and urged extreme force. She said that Khan Noonien Singh's people had been 'made in a laboratory'. She mocked the Power Rangers as coloured clowns dressing up in California.

Then she compared Lily Potter to a defective bitch in dog breeding: if there was something wrong with the bitch, she said, there would be something wrong with the pup. Her wineglass exploded in her hand. She blamed her own grip.

On the last evening, with Vernon pouring her brandy, she called Lily a bad egg. She called James a wastrel and a scrounger. They had died, she said, drunk in a car crash. Harry's rage inflated her until she floated up to the ceiling. Two members of the Accidental Magic Reversal Squad punctured her and modified her memory, so she remembers nothing of it. Lucius Malfoy heard of the matter at the Ministry. He observed with distaste that the woman was still breathing.

In Harry's dream

In Harry's dream of August 1994 Marge was the maid in the house on the hill. She wore a black dress with a frilly apron, and she poured gravy until it flooded the table, never once looking up. The old man at the head of the table called her Marjorie. When spoken to, she answered: 'Couldn't say, sir. Never saw him, sir. I never see anything, sir.'

In their own words

Couldn't say, sir. Never saw him, sir. I never see anything, sir.Aunt Marge (in Harry's dream) · B4 Ch1

pages.title: The Masons
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Masons are a rich Muggle builder and his wife, who came to dinner with the Dursleys at Number Four, Privet Drive, on 31 July 1992. Vernon Dursley hoped to sell Mr Mason an enormous order of drills. The evening ended in disaster.

The dinner party

Harry Potter was sent upstairs with bread and cheese while the Dursleys laid the table. Dobby the house-elf, who was waiting in Harry's bedroom, wrecked the evening. First he brought Aunt Petunia's pudding crashing down in the kitchen. Then an owl from the Ministry of Magic, which blamed Harry for Dobby's magic, dropped a letter on Mrs Mason's head. The Masons left in a fury. The bars went up on Harry's window the next morning.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapters One and Two, the Dursleys rehearsed every minute of the evening, which Dobby then wrecked.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Tom Riddle told Harry that he had seen the whole evening in Harry's memories, down to the bars going up the morning after.

pages.title: The Polkisses
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Piers Polkiss, Dudley Dursley's best friend
pages.html:
The Polkisses are a Muggle family of Little Whinging. Their son, Piers, is Dudley Dursley's best friend. When the Polkisses started going to church, Aunt Petunia took her own family once, at Christmas, because she was not going to be outdone.

Piers

Piers Polkiss is a thin boy with a face like a rat. He is one of Dudley's gang, and as a rule the one who holds the victim still while Dudley does the hitting.

The Christmas service

The Dursleys are not churchgoers. They have been perhaps twice in Harry Potter's memory, and the first time was to keep up with the Polkisses. It was Christmas, and Harry was seven. He stared up at a stained-glass window all through the carols. He did not go inside a church again for years.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, in the hospital wing after the Chamber of Secrets, Harry remembered that Christmas and the window he had stared at through the carols. In Book Three, Chapter One, he counted up the Dursleys' visits to church: once because the Polkisses had started going, and once for a churchwarden who might buy drills.

pages.title: Saint George
infobox: Killing the dragon that was eating a kingdom's daughters
pages.html:
Saint George is the knight who killed the dragon, a saint of the Church and the patron saint of England. Every wizarding child knows his story from the picture books, where he stands next to Merlin. Wizards hold that he was one of them. Whether his strength came from his own magic or from God is another matter, and even wizards do not agree about it.

The saint

In the Church's tradition George was a soldier who was put to death for his faith in Christ under the emperor Diocletian, about the year 303. He is the patron saint of England, kept on 23 April, and his red cross on white is the English flag. The story tells of a dragon that was eating a kingdom's daughters. George rode out against it, killed it with his lance and brought the princess home.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, as Harry Potter charged the Basilisk in the Chamber of Secrets, he thought of the stained-glass window in the church Aunt Petunia had once taken him to at Christmas: the painted knight going in under the dragon's neck, while a lady in white waited in the corner. A strength that was not his own went into his arms. Dracina Malfoy came round to see Harry standing over her with the dead monster at his feet, and she saw Saint George.

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, she lay in the hospital wing remembering the picture books, where George stands next to Merlin. In the wall hanging her mother keeps in the east drawing room at Malfoy Manor, he has black hair. Of course Harry was Saint George, she thought. He was her knight.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Lucius Malfoy told Harry that in Dracina's latest telling of the Chamber he was the second coming of Saint George himself. Harry's own doubt later sneered at him: ‘Who do you think you are? Saint George?’ In Book Three, Chapter Seven, after he had seen her boggart, Harry reflected that Dracina had a Saint George on the drawing-room wall, a manor and a father. He began to think that the two of them were more alike than he had supposed.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry asked Trelawney whether George, who had a window in a Little Whinging church, was a Muggle story too. She told him George had been a wizard, who slew his dragon by magic and let the Muggles credit their God. Harry had thought of that same window as he fought the Basilisk, and he put her answer to the Fat Friar. The Friar agreed that George was a wizard, but said that Harry was in a better position than she was to judge whose strength had killed the dragon.

pages.title: Jesus Christ
aliases: The man by the broken pillar
the man by the broken pillar
the man by the fallen pillar
the man in the white robe
infobox: Aslan; Christ; Jesus; Our Lord; The man by the broken pillar

Harry Potter watched over him, appeared to him
God Son, Father
Christian faith, Christianity, Chamber of Secrets
The east window of St Michael's Church, Little Whinging
pages.html:
Jesus Christ is the Son of God, crucified and risen, at the centre of the Christian faith. In Narnia he is Aslan. In June 1993 he stood by a fallen pillar in the Chamber of Secrets and watched the dying Harry Potter with pride. Harry and Dracina Malfoy both saw him. Harry knew the face from a church window.

Life

Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem, in the reign of the emperor Augustus, and grew up in Nazareth. He was baptised by John in the Jordan. Satan tempted him for forty days in the wilderness. Then he preached the kingdom of God through Galilee, healing the sick and calling fishermen to follow him. Among them was Simon, whom he named Peter.

One night on the lake of Galilee he came to his disciples walking on the water. Peter climbed out of the boat to go to him, but began to sink. Christ caught him by the hand: 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' When Peter asked how often he must forgive his brother, Christ told him 'until seventy times seven'.

In Jerusalem he found the Temple turned into a market. He made a whip of cords and drove out the money changers, overturning their tables. He was betrayed, condemned under Pontius Pilate and crucified. On the third day he rose from the dead. He showed his wounds to his disciples, and Thomas, who would not believe until he had put his fingers in them, believed.

Remus Lupin told Harry that Christ himself made sure that Christianity was given to everyone, 'whether they like it or not. Whether they're even aware of it or not.'

Aslan

In Narnia he is Aslan, the great Lion, the son of the Emperor-beyond-the-Sea, who sang Narnia into being. When the White Witch held the land in a hundred years of winter, he came back. He gave himself up to die on the Stone Table in the place of the traitor, Edmund Pevensie. He rose again by a deeper magic from before the dawn of time. He broke the Witch's power, then crowned the four Pevensies kings and queens at Cair Paravel.

He told Edmund and Lucy that he had another name in their own world. They must learn to know him by it.

Susan Pevensie, Harry Potter's grandmother, was the last of the crowned Pevensies left alive after the railway accident of 1949. She came back to Christ after the death of her brothers and sister, moved above all by the courage of Aslan.

In the Chamber of Secrets

In June 1993 Harry beheaded the basilisk and stabbed Tom Riddle's diary. Then the venom came back, and he fell beside Dracina Malfoy. A man was standing a little way off by the fallen pillar, watching him. He was fair-skinned, with long brown hair past his shoulders and a brown beard, in a plain white robe with nothing on it.

He did nothing. He looked warm, kind and sad. He looked at Harry with pride, as somebody who had always known Harry could do this, and knew he would have to do it again. Harry asked him silently to get Ginny and Dracina out. The man's face changed into something that might have been a smile. Earlier, as Harry lay dying, a warmth like being held had come over him, and a fatherly voice had said, 'Your work is not yet done, my child.'

Dracina, trying to raise Harry, looked up and saw the man too. When she looked back, he was gone. In the hospital wing she described him to Harry before he had said a word. They found that they had both seen him. Only the two of them knew.

Harry knew the face. He had seen it once before, when he was seven, in a stained-glass window, through a gap in the carols. He thought it was how his father would have looked at him, if he had had one.

It was Christ, though Harry could only be almost sure. At King's Cross he crossed himself, clumsily, in front of everybody. Through the months that followed he half talked himself into calling it the venom, or a bang on the head, and the doubt helped to wreck his first attempts at the Patronus. He wondered whether touching the man's sleeve would have made him certain.

In the spring of 1994 Harry told the Fat Friar what he had seen. The Friar believed him, but told him that 'nobody finds Christ, young Potter. He was there before you went down into the Chamber. He's here now... All you did, down there, was notice Him.' The Friar added: 'He was proud of you, Harry Potter. You saw it yourself.'

The window at St Michael's

The tall stained-glass window over the altar of St Michael's Church in Little Whinging shows Christ in a white robe, his hands held out, with long brown hair and a short brown beard. It is the face Harry stared at all through the Christmas service when he was seven. It is the same kind, grave face he saw in the Chamber.

On his first evening at Evensong, in July 1994, the window glowed like coloured fire, although the sun was setting on the other side of the church. Its light came down the whole length of the nave to lie across his hands in the back pew. 'You planned this, didn't you,' Harry murmured to it. The figure did not answer, and Harry took that as a yes.

Faith in Christ among wizards

Lily Potter believed in Christ with all her heart. The witches and wizards around her tutted at it; some of them snickered. After her marriage she brought Remus Lupin to faith. Then she brought James, who took to talking about Christ and God. Sirius Black came to believe only in Azkaban.

Lupin's own Patronus memory is of something done for him that he had no right to and could never have earned, by Somebody a good deal older than Dumbledore, to whom Lily introduced him. Lupin taught that a cross in the hand of somebody who believes in Jesus Christ is a different thing altogether from a stick of wood. Vampires do not like it. On the Hogwarts lawn in June 1994 he and Black said the evening collect together, ending 'for the love of thy only Son, our Saviour, Jesus Christ'.

Leaving on Buckbeak that night, Sirius told Harry that Lily would want him to sort things out with Christ. The vicar of St Michael's talks about Jesus as if he were an old friend. At the church door in the summer of 1994 he told Harry that Our Lord was very proud of him.

pages.title: The MI6 agent McGonagall dealt with
pages.html:
The MI6 agent McGonagall dealt with was a charming officer of the Secret Intelligence Service who once lied to Professor Minerva McGonagall's face. He did it brazenly, for the last and very final time. Whatever she did to him then, she has not forgotten it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, early in 1993, Gilderoy Lockhart told McGonagall outside her classroom that he had frightened the culprit into shutting the Chamber of Secrets for good. McGonagall said nothing whatever. Her nostrils went very thin as she thought about what she had done to that charming MI6 agent. When Lockhart had gone, she said something under her breath in a language Harry Potter did not recognise. It sounded Russian. It did not sound like a compliment.

pages.title: The bald man in the white suit
infobox: Vast and bald, in a white suit
In a picture in Vernon Dursley's study
pages.html:
The bald man in the white suit is the vast man in a picture in Vernon Dursley's study at number four, Privet Drive. Two enormous bodyguards stand behind him. Vernon speaks of him, with deep respect, as a very successful American businessman.

Identity

The picture does not name him. The description fits Wilson Fisk of New York in every particular: a vast, bald man in a white suit who passes for a respectable businessman, and whom the city's underworld knows as the Kingpin.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, in 1993, Harry Potter sat behind Dracina Malfoy in Potions while she held court, with Pansy Parkinson on one side and Daphne Greengrass on the other. Crabbe and Goyle stood behind her stool with their arms folded, like the two enormous bodyguards Harry had once seen in the picture in Uncle Vernon's study.

pages.title: The Armenian warlock
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ugly and old, with no dress sense
pages.html:
The Armenian warlock is an ugly old wizard who once rid a village of werewolves. Gilderoy Lockhart tracked him down, got him to tell exactly how he had done it, took the credit and wiped his memory.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Harry Potter and Ron Weasley went to Lockhart's office with what they had found out about the Chamber of Secrets. They found him packing to run. When Harry shouted that he had written the books, Lockhart told him to use a little common sense: 'Who wants to read about some ugly old Armenian warlock, even if he did rid a village of werewolves? He'd look simply dreadful on a cover. No dress sense whatsoever.' Then he drew his wand to wipe their memories too, and Harry disarmed him.

pages.title: The witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee is the woman who really did the deed that Gilderoy Lockhart boasted of. Lockhart tracked her down, got her to tell him exactly how she had done it, took the credit and wiped her memory. She does not remember it herself.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Lockhart admitted it to Harry Potter and Ron Weasley while he packed to run. His books would not have sold a quarter as well, he said, if people had not believed he had done it all himself: 'And the witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee had a hairy chin. I mean, really...' There had been work involved, he insisted. He had to track these people down, find out exactly how they had done it, and then Memory Charm them so that they would not remember doing it.

pages.title: The woman who ran Riddle's orphanage
infobox: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (16 July 2005)
pages.html:
The woman who ran Riddle's orphanage was Mrs Cole, the matron of Wool's Orphanage in London, where Tom Riddle was born on the last night of 1926 and grew up. According to Riddle, she used to lock the little ones in the coal cellar for hours.

Wool's Orphanage

Riddle's mother, Merope Gaunt, came there to give birth to him and died soon afterwards. Tom grew up there, and loathed it. Even after he went to Hogwarts in 1938 he had to spend his holidays there, and he hated going back.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, the memory of the sixteen-year-old Riddle tried to win Harry Potter over by telling him about it. 'There was a woman who ran it who used to lock the little ones in the coal cellar. In the dark. For hours. I was five years old the first time.'

pages.title: Tom Riddle's father
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Riddle House, on the hill above Little Hangleton
Tom Marvolo Riddle, later Lord Voldemort
pages.html:
Tom Riddle's father, also called Tom Riddle, was a handsome Muggle, the son of the family in the big house on the hill above Little Hangleton. His son, who became Lord Voldemort, was named Tom after him.

Life and death

Merope Gaunt, a witch of the decayed Gaunt family, bewitched him into running away with her. He left her before their son was born and went home to his parents. In the summer of 1943 his sixteen-year-old son came to Little Hangleton. With his uncle Morfin's wand he murdered his father and grandparents in the house on the hill.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, inside the memory kept in his diary, the sixteen-year-old Riddle told Professor Dippet, the Headmaster, that his father had been a Muggle. His mother, he said, had lived just long enough to give him his names: 'Tom, after my father. Marvolo, after her own father.'

In Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Harry threw it back at him: 'Tom after your father. Your Muggle father.'

pages.title: Tom Riddle's mother
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Gaunts, last descendants of Salazar Slytherin
Tom Marvolo Riddle, later Lord Voldemort
The last night of 1926, in a Muggle orphanage in London
pages.html:
Tom Riddle's mother, Merope Gaunt, was a witch of the decayed Gaunt family, the last descendants of Salazar Slytherin. She died almost as soon as her son was born. He grew up to be Lord Voldemort.

Life

She grew up in a hovel near Little Hangleton. While her father was in Azkaban, she bewitched Tom Riddle, the handsome son of the family in the big house on the hill, into running away with her. He left her before the baby came. On the last night of 1926 she came to a Muggle orphanage in London, where she gave birth to a son. She lived just long enough to name him Tom, after his father, and Marvolo, after her own. She died within the hour.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, in a memory kept in his diary, the sixteen-year-old Riddle told Headmaster Dippet: 'My mother died almost as soon as I was born, sir. They told me at the orphanage that she lived just long enough to give me my names. Tom, after my father. Marvolo, after her own father.'

pages.title: Marvolo
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Gaunts, last descendants of Salazar Slytherin
pages.html:
Marvolo Gaunt was the father of Tom Riddle's mother, Merope, and the head of the Gaunt family, the last descendants of Salazar Slytherin. His grandson Tom Marvolo Riddle, who became Lord Voldemort, carries his name.

The Gaunts

By Marvolo's time the Gaunts had nothing left but their blood, their pride and a few heirlooms. They lived in a hovel near Little Hangleton, and they spoke Parseltongue. While Marvolo was in Azkaban for attacking Ministry officials, Merope ran off with Tom Riddle, the handsome Muggle son of the family in the big house on the hill. Marvolo never saw his grandson.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, in the memory kept in his diary, the sixteen-year-old Riddle told the Headmaster, Professor Dippet, how he had come by his names: 'They told me at the orphanage that she lived just long enough to give me my names. Tom, after my father. Marvolo, after her own father.'

In Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Harry threw the names back at him. Tom was after his Muggle father, Marvolo after his grandfather: 'You're a half-blood, Tom. Just like me.'

pages.title: The traveller who gave Aragog to Hagrid
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
An egg, to the young Rubeus Hagrid
pages.html:
The traveller who gave Aragog to Hagrid is the unknown wanderer who handed the boy Rubeus Hagrid an egg from a distant land. Out of it hatched the Acromantula Aragog.

Aragog
