Acromantulas are giant spiders that can talk, and they come from the jungles of Borneo. Their eggs are not supposed to be traded at all, which is the sort of thing that has never troubled Hagrid. While he was still a boy at school, he raised Aragog in a cupboard in the castle on scraps from the table. When Aragog was blamed in 1943 for the death of a girl, Hagrid protected him, and he has lived in the Forbidden Forest ever since. Hagrid still visits him, and he even found him a wife, Mosag.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, in the spring of 1993, Aragog told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley, deep in the Forbidden Forest: 'I was not born in the castle. I come from a distant land. A traveller gave me to Hagrid when I was an egg.'

pages.title: The Hufflepuff prefect scratched by Dracina
infobox: Three long scratches down one cheek, Boxing Day 1992
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff prefect scratched by Dracina is a big, worried-looking Hufflepuff prefect who stayed at Hogwarts over Christmas 1992. On Boxing Day he tried to take hold of Dracina Malfoy's arm in the Great Hall, and she scratched him down the cheek.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, on Boxing Day 1992, the day after Harry Potter took Tom Riddle's diary, Dracina woke and turned the Slytherin dungeon upside down looking for it. Then she came up to breakfast in her nightdress, with her school cloak buttoned up wrong over the top and her feet bare on the cold stone. Pansy Parkinson came running in after her, with two or three other Slytherins and the prefect, who must have met them on the stairs. Dracina flung a plate of toast against the wall, then a jug of milk. When the prefect tried to take hold of her arm, she whirled round and scratched three long red lines down his cheek. He let go with a yell.

Dumbledore told the Hall that Miss Malfoy had contracted an uncommon complaint called Morrigan's Fever, and that nobody was to hold anything she said or did against her. He looked very hard over his half-moon spectacles at the Slytherin table, then at the Hufflepuff prefect with the scratched face, and then, for rather longer, at Harry.

pages.title: The portrait of the sleeping wizard
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 15
A corridor near the hospital wing, Hogwarts
pages.html:
The portrait of the sleeping wizard hangs in a corridor near the hospital wing at Hogwarts. Its wizard is usually asleep in his chair.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Harry visited Hermione in the hospital wing, where she was recovering from the Polyjuice Potion with whiskers and a tail. He fled without telling her who was in the next bed. He was halfway down the corridor outside when he heard the curtain rings dragged back, a short, shocked silence, and then a shriek: 'WHAT IS SHE DOING HERE?!' It rang off the stone walls, so loud that the sleeping wizard fell clean out of his chair. The next bed was Dracina Malfoy's.

pages.title: The Ravenclaw first-year in the Charms corridor
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 17
pages.html:
The Ravenclaw first-year in the Charms corridor was a girl who burst into tears there one morning in 1993, because somebody had dropped a book behind her. It was during the fear that took hold of Hogwarts after Albus Dumbledore was suspended as headmaster.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, Harry Potter saw the whole school frightened. A first-year Ravenclaw burst into tears in the middle of the Charms corridor at the sound of a dropped book. A group of Hufflepuffs had taken to walking down corridors with their backs pressed to the wall, so that nothing could come at them from behind. Even Dean Thomas, who was afraid of nothing, sat on the end of his bed one night with a lit wand, watching the dormitory door.

pages.title: The grim-faced Valentine dwarf
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Gilderoy Lockhart, as a Valentine's Day cupid
pages.html:
The grim-faced Valentine dwarf was one of the dozen sour-looking dwarfs Gilderoy Lockhart hired to deliver Valentines at Hogwarts on 14 February 1993. They wore golden wings and carried little golden harps. This one sang a Valentine to Harry Potter on a crowded staircase.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, the dwarf caught up with Harry on the stairs to Charms, kicking his way through a queue of first-years. He grabbed Harry's bag, which split clean in half, spilling everything.

When Harry ran for it, the dwarf tackled him and sat on his ankles. Then he sang, in a surprisingly sweet, deep voice, of a boy with eyes like the first green of spring.

Ron Weasley, who had held it in heroically, gave up and laughed until he cried. Dracina Malfoy, who had watched Harry's face all through the song, turned on Ron in a fury. Among the things spilt from Harry's bag was Tom Riddle's diary. Dracina picked it up, but Percy Weasley plucked it out of her hands and gave it back to Harry.

In Chapter Sixteen Harry thought again about the singing Valentine, and about her face while the dwarf sang it. The song had spoken of a girl who was silver, and Dracina was the only girl he knew with silver eyes.

pages.title: The second Valentine dwarf
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter Fifteen
Ginny Weasley's Valentine to Harry Potter
Much worse than the first dwarf's
pages.html:
The second Valentine dwarf was another of the cupids Gilderoy Lockhart hired for Valentine's Day 1993. He sang Ginny Weasley's Valentine to Harry Potter, twice as loudly as the first dwarf had sung his, and a great deal worse.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, only minutes after the first singing Valentine, he came barrelling up the stairs, shoving Crabbe out of the way with his harp. He planted himself in front of Harry, scowling, and struck up before anyone could stop him. The song compared Harry's hair to a raven at night, and his eyes to a frog in the light.

At the back of the queue of first-years, Ginny went so red that she was practically glowing. Dracina Malfoy saw her. All the fury that had been building in Dracina swung round from Harry on to Ginny. ‘That one was yours, wasn't it?’ she said. She mocked the frog in the light and the arm on behind. Ginny burst into tears and ran. Percy Weasley sent Dracina to her lesson.

pages.title: The girl at the river in Dumbledore's memory
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The river at the bottom of the lane, Godric's Hollow
pages.html:
The girl at the river in Dumbledore's memory is Greta Grindelwald, whom Albus Dumbledore loved, as she was in the summer of 1899. Down at the river at the bottom of the lane in Godric's Hollow, she once turned the whole of it to light, just to see if she could.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, in December 1992, Dumbledore talked with Ambrose Greyhame about the girl who had taken to Ambrose's staff-magic faster than he had. 'Do you remember the morning she turned the whole river to light? Just to see if she could? I thought it was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen.'

In Chapter Nineteen Harry Potter put his hand on Dracina Malfoy's shoulder while she sobbed out the story of the diary. Only Dumbledore looked straight at the two of them. He was thinking of a river at the bottom of a lane on a summer afternoon, and of a girl who had turned the whole of it to light just to see if she could. He wept without a sound.

pages.title: The old woman in the church
infobox: In church during the carols, when Harry Potter was a child
pages.html:
The old woman in the church is the only person Harry Potter had seen make the sign of the cross before he made it himself. He saw her do it during the carols, when he was a child.

Christmas

Harry was seven. It was the one Christmas Aunt Petunia took the family to church, because the Polkisses went and she was not going to be outdone. All through the carols Harry stared up at a stained-glass window of Christ.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, at the end of his second year, Harry stopped on the concourse at King's Cross and made the sign of the cross for the first time. He did it clumsily, not sure he had got it the right way round. He had only ever seen it done once, by an old woman in a church, through the gap in the carols, a long time ago.

pages.title: Aragog's hollow
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Aragog's hollow is the home of the giant spider Aragog and his enormous family, deep in the Forbidden Forest. It is a vast bowl cleared of trees, open to the stars, with a misty domed web at its centre.

The colony

Aragog has lived there since 1943, when he was found in the castle and blamed for the death of a girl. Hagrid found him a wife, Mosag. Their children and grandchildren now fill the hollow in their hundreds, spiders the size of carthorses. They do not harm Hagrid, on Aragog's orders. Nobody else has that protection.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, in 1993, Harry and Ron followed the spiders down into the hollow on Hagrid's word. Aragog told them that he had never harmed a human, and that the thing in the castle was a creature his kind fear above all others. Then he gave them to his children. Mr Weasley's wild flying car came thundering down into the hollow with its headlamps blazing, and carried them off through the trees.

pages.title: The newsagent's on Vauxhall Road
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The newsagent's on Vauxhall Road is a Muggle shop in London. Its name is printed in tiny letters inside the back cover of Tom Riddle's diary, which Riddle bought there as a boy.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Harry opened the diary at the back and found the name. 'He must have been Muggle-born, then,' he said slowly. To have bought a diary there, he reasoned, Riddle must have grown up among Muggles: it was a Muggle shop in a Muggle street. Harry was half right. Riddle had grown up in a Muggle orphanage in London, but he was a half-blood, the son of a Muggle father and a witch.

pages.title: Riddle's Muggle orphanage
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Tom Riddle, born there on 31 December 1926
pages.html:
Riddle's Muggle orphanage was the London children's home where Tom Riddle was born and brought up. His mother, Merope Gaunt, came to its door on the last night of 1926. She gave birth to him there, named him and died within the hour.

The orphanage

It was known as Wool's Orphanage. Riddle lived there until he went to Hogwarts in 1938, and he had to go back every summer afterwards. It was a hard place for a small child. The woman who ran it locked the little ones in the coal cellar, in the dark, for hours at a time, while the big boys tormented the smaller children.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, deep in the Chamber of Secrets, the memory of Tom Riddle from the diary told Harry Potter that he had grown up in a place like Privet Drive, only worse. 'There was a woman who ran it who used to lock the little ones in the coal cellar. In the dark. For hours. I was five years old the first time.' He spoke of the big boys too. Then one summer, he said, he had found out what he could do, gone home and made them sorry.

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt that number four, Privet Drive, was an orphanage, and always had been, with iron bars on every window. Aunt Petunia sat inside, dressed in black, with a bunch of keys at her belt, writing in a big ledger. His mother, he knew in the dream, had come to its door on the last night of the year, in the snow. She had lasted just long enough to have him and to tell them what he was to be called. Then she had died, in a narrow iron bed under the stairs.

pages.title: Albania
pages.html:
Albania is a small, mountainous country on the Adriatic coast of the Balkans. Its forests are deep enough to hide a great deal; in 1993 Lord Voldemort was hiding in them.

History

For forty years after the Second World War it was the most closed country in Europe, under the Communist dictator Enver Hoxha, who died in 1985. Wizards have known its forests longer. Helena Ravenclaw fled there with her mother's diadem, and the young Quirinus Quirrell met Voldemort there on his travels.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, Dumbledore asked Lucius Malfoy how Lord Voldemort could have come to enchant Dracina at all, when his sources placed him in hiding in the forests of Albania.

pages.title: Whitechapel
infobox: The murders of 1888; Professor McGonagall's fight with William the Bloody
pages.html:
Whitechapel is an old, poor, crowded district of the East End of London. Muggles know it best for the murders of 1888, whose killer was never caught.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, warning Harry away from the Chamber of Secrets, Professor McGonagall told him that she had 'tangled with William the Bloody himself, in a cellar in Whitechapel'. She had come out of that one with her life and very little else. William the Bloody is the vampire better known as Spike, sired in London in 1880 by Drusilla.

In the Interlude of Book Three, in the summer of 1993, the kit John Constantine took to Shacklewell House in New Mexico included a small glass bottle of earth from a churchyard in Whitechapel.

pages.title: Númenor
infobox: Island kingdom of Men in the western sea
Drowned under the sea late in the Second Age
Elendil and his line, Aragorn, and through him Harry Potter
pages.html:
Númenor was the great island kingdom of Men in the West, raised from the sea at the start of the Second Age and drowned beneath it at the end. Aragorn's line came out of it. Albus Dumbledore has told Harry Potter that the protection his mother gave him is 'the magic of Elves, Harry. And of Númenor', and that it lives in his blood.

History

When Morgoth was overthrown at the end of the First Age, the Valar raised a star-shaped island out of the sea between Middle-earth and the Undying Lands. It was the reward of the Edain, the Men who had fought him. Elros, brother of Elrond, chose to be counted among Men, and he became its first king, Tar-Minyatur. The Númenóreans were granted lives three times as long as other men's. They grew wise and mighty, the greatest mariners in the world, though they were forbidden to sail west out of sight of their own shores.

In time they came to envy the Elves their deathlessness. Sauron was brought to Númenor as a captive, and became counsellor to Ar-Pharazôn, the last king. He set up a temple to Morgoth there and persuaded the king to make war on the Undying Lands. The world was changed, and Númenor went down under the sea.

Elendil the Faithful escaped with his sons in nine ships to Middle-earth, where they founded Arnor and Gondor. Aragorn was their heir. In The Lord of the Rings, Númenor is long gone before the story begins. It appears chiefly as a name in old songs and in the blood of Aragorn's people.

The Elves called it Atalantë, the Downfallen. It is the Atlantis of the old story: the great island of the West that grew proud and was swallowed by the sea. Two kingdoms under the sea now claim the name of Atlantis, and neither has the right to it. No living man or woman knows the whole truth of it except Albus Dumbledore.

Dumbledore suspects that the Ancients, the builders of the Stargates, were somehow related to Númenor, though he cannot work out exactly how, or how they could have left Earth to build their empire among the stars.

In Harry Potter's blood

At the end of the summer term of 1993, on the castle steps, Dumbledore explained why Harry had to go back to Privet Drive. Lily Potter's protection, he said, was old magic, older than anything he could do: the magic of Elves and of Númenor. It lived in Harry's blood, as it did in his aunt's. Harry had never heard the word. He found it in Dudley's copy of The Lord of the Rings, and read the book to find out what it meant.

At Aunt Marge's table in August 1993, the phrase 'the blood of Númenor' came into his head unbidden. Whatever it meant, he thought, it was better than Marge and better than Vernon. In June 1994, in the tunnel from the Shrieking Shack, the words came back to him as he explained to Sirius Black why he could not come and live with him. The protection was in his blood, as it was in Aunt Petunia's, and it held only while he lived where she lived.

Aragorn gives the line Númenor, as Arwen gives it the Elves. Harry descends from both through his mother, by way of Susan Pevensie. Dumbledore knows it, and so does Lord Voldemort. Lying awake in June 1994, Harry knew Númenor by then as the drowned kingdom across the sea that Aragorn's family came from. He had no idea what it had to do with number four, Privet Drive.

pages.title: The church Aunt Petunia took Harry to
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 19
St Michael's, at the end of Magnolia Crescent, Little Whinging
Christmas 1987, when he was seven; Evensong from July 1994
Saint George and the dragon, with a lady in white; Christ in a white robe, over the altar
pages.html:
The church Aunt Petunia took Harry to was St Michael's, the small, old Anglican church at the end of Magnolia Crescent in Little Whinging. The Dursleys went there one Christmas, when Harry Potter was seven, because the Polkisses had started going and Petunia was not going to be outdone. For years afterwards it was the only church Harry had ever been inside.

The church

Harry sat squashed into the end of a pew next to Dudley. One of the stained-glass windows showed Saint George on a painted horse, going in under the dragon's neck with his lance couched, while a lady in white waited in the corner. The window over the altar showed a man in a white robe, with long brown hair and a short brown beard, his hands held out. Harry stared up at it all through the carols. Once, through a gap in the singing, he saw an old woman make the sign of the cross. The Dursleys had no time for that sort of thing.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, as Harry ran at the Basilisk with the sword blazing in his hands, a small, calm part of him noted that this was how it must have looked in the picture in that church: the painted knight going in under the dragon's neck, with the whole window lit up gold behind him.

In Chapter Nineteen, in the hospital wing after the Chamber of Secrets, Harry and Dracina Malfoy spoke of the man in white they had both seen in the Chamber. He had been there when Harry was dying, and he had looked at Harry as though he were proud. Harry had seen that face before, he realised, in a stained-glass window in the church Aunt Petunia had taken them to. For one wild moment he thought it was Jesus Christ, then told himself not to be stupid. Dracina, for her part, lay thinking of Harry as Saint George. At King's Cross afterwards Harry made the sign of the cross, clumsily, the way he had once seen the old woman do it.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry asked Professor Trelawney whether Saint George was a Muggle story as well. 'There's a window of him, in Little Whinging, with the dragon.' Saint George, she told him, had been a wizard.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, at the beginning of July 1994, Harry pushed open the door of St Michael's at last and looked up at the window over the altar. It glowed like coloured fire, though the sun was setting on the other side of the church. Harry knew that window. He had sat under it at seven, and he had seen the same kind, grave face a year ago, looking down at him in the Chamber of Secrets.

pages.title: Potter family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
King Arthur (as a Pendragon); Henry, Fleamont, James and Harry Potter
pages.html:
The Potters are an ancient wizarding family, of whom Harry Potter is the last. They were kings before they were Potters. The line runs back through the Pendragons, King Arthur's house, to Ignotus Peverell, the brother who was given the Cloak of Invisibility. The Cloak has come down the family intact.

Peverell, Pendragon, Potter

The most famous of the Pendragons was King Arthur. After his time, Dark wizards who followed Morgana hunted his descendants, so the family took the name Potter to hide behind. It worked so well that the wizarding world forgot what the name was hiding.

The descent is no secret. Anybody who walks into the right archive can trace it straight back to Arthur; it is obscure only because almost nobody bothers to look. Lucius Malfoy, who keeps his own family tree on his drawing-room wall, has looked. Harry knows nothing of it.

The later Potters

Henry Potter sat on the Wizengamot. In the Great War he caused an uproar by publicly condemning the Minister for Magic, Archer Evermonde, who had forbidden wizards to help the Muggles. His son Fleamont multiplied the family fortune many times over with Sleekeazy's Hair Potion. Fleamont's son James, a Gryffindor, married Lily Evans. Voldemort murdered them both at Godric's Hollow on 31 October 1981. Their son Harry survived.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Tom Riddle told Harry that the Potters were very old blood, older than he knew. In Book Three, Chapter One, Dracina Malfoy wrote that her father had forbidden her to write to Harry, because a Malfoy does not have friends among the Potters.

In Chapter Four Lucius told Harry himself: 'The Potters go back a very long way. Further than you have been told. Potters have been kings before they were Potters. When there was a king worth the name, and that was not an accident either.' He meant every word of it. The king worth the name was Arthur.

pages.title: Death Eaters
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The Dark Mark, burnt into the left forearm
Lucius Malfoy; Severus Snape (former); Bellatrix, Rodolphus and Rabastan Lestrange; Walden Macnair; Peter Pettigrew; Regulus Black
pages.html:
The Death Eaters are the followers of Lord Voldemort, who is their master. Many of them began as pure-blood students who talked in low voices about what ought to be done with Muggle-borns. Together they became the army that terrorised wizarding Britain until Voldemort fell in 1981. Each of them bears his mark, burnt into the arm.

Origins

In Lucius Malfoy's schooldays a set with old names and cold eyes sat together in the Slytherin common room. They talked in low voices about Muggle-borns, whom they called Mudbloods, and about what ought to be done with them. Later they had a name for themselves. Later still they had a master, and a mark burnt into their arms to prove it.

John Constantine, who was sorted into Slytherin on the same night as Lucius, had known even then where that road went. It was a mug's game, and Lucius should have known better. After leaving Hogwarts in 1971 Lucius joined Voldemort and took the Dark Mark on his left forearm: a skull, with a serpent coming out of its mouth.

The first war

Through the 1970s the Death Eaters murdered Muggles, Muggle-borns and any witch or wizard who stood against them. Voldemort fell on 31 October 1981 at Godric's Hollow. Afterwards some of his followers went to Azkaban. Bellatrix Lestrange was sentenced to life there, with her husband, his brother and Barty Crouch the younger, for torturing two Aurors, the Longbottoms.

Many others stayed free by pretending to have seen the error of their ways. Walden Macnair escaped prosecution altogether, and found work for the Ministry killing dangerous beasts.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Harry Potter raised the sword over Tom Riddle's diary. 'I wonder what your followers think about you?' he asked. For one moment there was no master of the Death Eaters, only Tom Riddle, sixteen years old, with his mouth open and nothing coming out of it.

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, Harry learnt why Peter Pettigrew had hidden for twelve years as a rat. Voldemort's followers in Azkaban believed Pettigrew had double-crossed them. Many others were still free, pretending to have seen the error of their ways.

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine remembered how Lucius Malfoy had drifted away from him at school, to sit with the cold-eyed set in the Slytherin common room.

pages.title: MI6
pages.html:
MI6, properly the Secret Intelligence Service, is the British government's Muggle intelligence service abroad. Its most famous officer is James Bond, agent 007, who had a romance with Minerva McGonagall from 1960 to 1962.

History

The service was founded in 1909, as the foreign section of the new Secret Service Bureau. Its chief signs himself C. The government would not admit until 1992 that the service existed at all.

McGonagall worked alongside Bond before she began teaching. Their romance ended when she found out how much he had lied to her, and she has not forgotten it. Since the 1980s he has been held without trial in an American prison, under the name of John Mason.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Professor McGonagall told her class that she had once turned a vault's worth of gold into beetles, a very long time ago, for a gentleman she was working alongside. He was a Scottish Muggle: 'He had a desk at a very dull-sounding office near the river, though he was seldom at it.' The gentleman was Bond.

In Chapter Fifteen, faced with Gilderoy Lockhart, Professor McGonagall said nothing whatever. Her nostrils went very thin as she thought about what she had done to 'that charming MI6 agent who so brazenly lied to her face for the last and very final time'.

pages.title: Revealer
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
A Revealer is a bright red rubber, like the ones used to rub out pencil, which makes invisible ink show itself. Rubbed over a page, it brings out any writing hidden there in invisible ink. Hermione Granger bought hers in Diagon Alley.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Hermione thought the blank pages of Tom Riddle's diary might be written in invisible ink. When Aparecium brought out nothing, she dug in her bag for her Revealer. 'It's a Revealer,' she said. 'I got it in Diagon Alley.' She rubbed it hard on the page for the first of January, then on the first of February, the inside covers and the page for her own birthday. Nothing appeared. Harry said nothing at all: he had not told either of his friends that the diary had already written back to him.

pages.title: Eagle-feather quill
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A little box lined with green velvet
pages.html:
The eagle-feather quill is the long, dark, glossy quill that Hermione Granger gave Harry Potter for Christmas 1992, in a little box lined with green velvet. It was the quill he used when he first wrote in Tom Riddle's diary.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, it came among Harry’s Christmas presents, with a tin of treacle fudge from Hagrid and Flying with the Cannons from Ron. That evening, with Tom Riddle’s diary open on his knees, he found his hand drifting towards it. He wanted very badly to dip it in ink and write something on the blank page, just to see whether anybody would write back. In Chapter Fifteen he gave in. He picked up the quill from his bedside table, dipped it in ink and wrote Hello at the top of the first page.

pages.title: Harry's Gryffindor scarf
infobox: 1993, by Dracina Malfoy, from Harry's trunk
pages.html:
Harry's Gryffindor scarf is the long scarlet and gold scarf that Harry Potter wears to Quidditch matches. In 1993 it went missing from his dormitory at the same time as Tom Riddle's diary. The next time Harry saw it, it was wound three times round Dracina Malfoy's neck in the Chamber of Secrets.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Harry came up to his dormitory in 1993 to find his things thrown all over the room and every pocket of his robes turned inside out. The scarf, which should have been on its hook at the end of his bed, was nowhere to be found. Riddle's diary had gone too, although his Invisibility Cloak was still at the bottom of the trunk. It was Dracina Malfoy who had turned out his trunk, after Neville Longbottom let her into Gryffindor Tower for the second time. She took the scarf with the diary.

For a while Harry and Ron wondered about Ginny Weasley. She had come down to breakfast one warm, bright morning with a long Gryffindor scarf wound three times round her neck. 'And what would she want your scarf for?' said Ron.

In Chapter Eighteen Harry found Dracina in the Chamber of Secrets, standing with her head bowed between the feet of the great statue, in a long scarlet and gold scarf wound three times round her neck. He knew that scarf. He had lost it. She still had it on at the very end, when Harry, too weak to speak, tried to tell her that it was his scarf.

pages.title: Medal for Magical Merit
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Medal for Magical Merit is an award given at Hogwarts. An old one in the trophy room has Tom Riddle's name engraved on it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, early in 1993, Harry went down to the trophy room at break to look at the Special Award for Services to the School that Tom Riddle had won fifty years before. Hermione came because she was interested. Ron came very unwillingly: he had polished the silver there in a detention the term before, and said he had seen enough of the trophy room to last him the rest of his life.

Riddle's shield, tucked away at the back of a corner cabinet, did not say why it had been given. 'Good job, too,' said Ron. 'Or it'd be twice the size and I'd still be in here scrubbing it.' They did find Riddle's name on an old Medal for Magical Merit, though, as well as on a list of former Head Boys.

pages.title: Order of Suspension
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Board of Governors of Hogwarts
pages.html:
The Order of Suspension was the document by which the Board of Governors removed Albus Dumbledore from Hogwarts in 1993, while the Chamber of Secrets stood open. It bore the signatures of all twelve governors. Lucius Malfoy delivered it himself.

The governors' power

The appointment of the Headmaster is a matter for the governors, not the Ministry of Magic, and so is his suspension. Lucius reminded Cornelius Fudge of this when Fudge protested that suspending Dumbledore was the very last thing they wanted just then. The suspension did not last. Dumbledore was back at Hogwarts before the end of the school year.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Lucius Malfoy came to Hagrid's hut on the night Fudge arrived to take Hagrid away. He drew a long roll of parchment from inside his cloak. 'This is an Order of Suspension. You will find all twelve of our signatures on it.' Dumbledore told him that if the governors wished him to go, then naturally he would step aside.

pages.title: Hair-Raising Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Hair-Raising Potion does to the hair what its name suggests. Rat tails are among its ingredients, although few second-years can remember how many.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Snape set an essay on it. Ron was just saying that he wished he had asked Hermione how many rat tails went into a Hair-Raising Potion, when an angry outburst from the floor above stopped them both. Later Harry used the unfinished essay as his excuse to slip away from Ron for a while.

pages.title: Love Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Besots the drinker with whoever gave it
As long as the doses keep coming
pages.html:
A love potion makes the drinker besotted with whoever gave it, for as long as the doses keep coming. It cannot make real love, only a powerful infatuation.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, on Valentine's Day 1993, Gilderoy Lockhart told the school to pop along and ask Professor Snape how to mix up a Love Potion. Snape looked as though the first student to ask him would be made to drink something very different.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, at breakfast in the Leaky Cauldron on 1 September 1993, Mrs Weasley told Hermione and Ginny about a love potion she had made as a young girl. A boy had followed her round the whole of the Easter holidays with a look on his face like a spaniel. She had kept topping him up: 'Three drops in his pumpkin juice, every morning, for a fortnight.' When Ginny asked whether it wore off, Mrs Weasley said, 'Eventually.' She looked down the table at Mr Weasley. 'Or he decided he didn't need it. One of the two.' Hermione stopped laughing a second before the others did.

pages.title: Flesh-Eating Slug Repellent
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Rubeus Hagrid, for the school cabbages
pages.html:
Flesh-Eating Slug Repellent keeps flesh-eating slugs off vegetables, which they will otherwise ruin. It can be bought in Knockturn Alley, which is not where most people go for their garden supplies.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry came out of the wrong grate into Knockturn Alley in August 1992 and ran into Hagrid there. Hagrid growled that he had been looking for Flesh-Eating Slug Repellent, since the slugs were ruining the school cabbages. In Chapter Sixteen, after the diary had shown Hagrid accused of opening the Chamber of Secrets fifty years before, Ron asked about that meeting. Harry answered at once that Hagrid had been buying slug repellent. For the cabbages, he said.

pages.title: Aparecium
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Aparecium is a revealing charm that makes invisible ink show itself. The caster taps the page with a wand and speaks the incantation.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, early in 1993, Harry, Ron and Hermione sat looking at the diary of T. M. Riddle, which seemed to have nothing written in it. Harry had not told the others that it had already written back to him. 'It might be in invisible ink!' Hermione whispered. She tapped the diary three times and said 'Aparecium!' Nothing happened. Undeterred, she dug a bright red Revealer out of her bag and rubbed it hard on the page for the first of January. Nothing happened then either.

pages.title: Wand-Lighting Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Lights the tip of the wand
pages.html:
The Wand-Lighting Charm, Lumos, makes the tip of a wand shine like a torch. It is one of the first charms a young witch or wizard learns, and one of the most often used. Cast suddenly, close to the eyes of a creature of the night, it can blind as well as light.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, in 1993, Harry Potter lit his wand with Lumos to show Ron and himself the path into the Forbidden Forest. Ron did not light his, in case it went off or turned into a frog. In Chapter Eighteen Harry lit it again in the tunnel beneath Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, on the way to the Chamber of Secrets.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in August 1993, he cast it in Magnolia Crescent, the night he ran away from Privet Drive. The tip of his wand burst into light so sudden and white that it half blinded him. It lit up a huge black dog standing in the gap between a garage and a fence. In Chapter Ten he lit his wand in the secret passage to Honeydukes, at the bottom of the stone slide. In Chapter Thirteen Ron cast Lumos and found Crookshanks sitting in the fork of a tree.

In Chapter Seventeen, on the night of the full moon in June 1994, Harry fumbled for his wand under the Whomping Willow, blinking blood out of his eyes, and lit it. Its light showed him the great black dog dragging Ron into a wide gap between the roots. In Chapter Nineteen, later the same night, the Garou had Harry on his back in the grass, its jaws open over his face. He jabbed his wand straight up. 'Lumos!' The light went into its eyes like a pair of pins, because its pupils had opened huge and black for the night. It reared back with a yelp, and Harry rolled free.

pages.title: Vanishing Spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
The Banishing Charm, which sends a thing away
pages.html:
The Vanishing Spell makes its target disappear altogether. It belongs to Transfiguration, and it grows harder the more complicated the thing to be vanished. It is easily muddled with the Banishing Charm, which sends a thing away from the caster rather than out of existence.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, in September 1992, Harry Potter found himself clamped under Gilderoy Lockhart's arm, and wished he knew a good Vanishing Spell.

In Chapter Fifteen, in February 1993, in Hermione Granger's first Transfiguration lesson back from the hospital wing, Professor McGonagall asked the class the difference between a Vanishing Spell and a Banishing one. Hermione's hand went up as quick as a reflex, then stopped halfway and came down again. Neville Longbottom put up his own hand very slowly and gave the right answer. 'Quite right, Mr Longbottom, five points,' said McGonagall, and Neville went pink to his ears.

pages.title: Banishing Spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Sends an object flying away from the caster
pages.html:
The Banishing Spell sends an object flying away from the caster. It is the reverse of the Summoning Charm. It is easily muddled with the Vanishing Spell, which makes a thing disappear altogether, and Professor McGonagall makes sure her students know the difference.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Hermione Granger came back from the hospital wing at the beginning of February 1993, cured at last of the cat's fur her Polyjuice Potion had given her. In her first Transfiguration lesson back, Professor McGonagall asked the class about the difference between a Vanishing Spell and a Banishing one. Hermione's hand went up, as quick as a reflex. Then, halfway up, it stopped. It came down again. Neville Longbottom put his own hand up, very slowly, and gave the right answer.

pages.title: Entrancing Enchantments
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Professor Flitwick, according to Gilderoy Lockhart
pages.html:
Entrancing Enchantments are charms that captivate or beguile. Gilderoy Lockhart once told the whole school that Professor Flitwick knew more about them than any wizard alive.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, on Valentine's Day 1993, Lockhart announced that his card-carrying cupids would spend the whole day delivering the school's valentines. He urged everybody to ask Professor Snape how to mix up a Love Potion, or else to try Professor Flitwick. 'He knows more about Entrancing Enchantments than any wizard alive, the wicked old rascal!' Flitwick put his face in his hands. Snape looked as though the first student to ask him about Love Potions would be made to drink something very different.

pages.title: Dracina's healing charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter Nineteen
pages.html:
Dracina's healing charm is a charm for cuts that Dracina Malfoy learnt from her mother, Narcissa. Touched to a wound three times, it stops the bleeding, closes the cut and then all but erases it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, in the Chamber of Secrets in 1993, Ginny Weasley came round with a cut at her temple that was still bleeding. Harry Potter had no idea what to do about a cut. Dracina came over, trying very hard to look contemptuous. 'Oh, for Merlin's sake,' she said. 'Give her here.' She knelt, turned the cut to the light and drew her wand. 'Mother taught me this last year. I used to fall off my pony.'

At the first touch of her wand the bleeding stopped. At the second the edges of the cut drew together. At the third there was nothing left but a thin pink line. 'Thank you,' Ginny whispered.

Something went across Dracina's face, there and gone in a second. 'Don't mention it,' she said stiffly. 'Really. Don't.'

pages.title: Basilisk
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A chicken's egg, beneath a toad
Fifty feet long; killed by Harry Potter in 1993
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Basilisk, known also as the King of Serpents, can reach gigantic size and live many hundreds of years. The Basilisk of the Chamber of Secrets was Salazar Slytherin's own, kept to defend Hogwarts from Muggles. It slept beneath the school for nearly a thousand years. Tom Riddle loosed it on the school's pupils in 1943, and again through his diary in 1992 to 1993. Harry Potter killed it in 1993.

Nature

A basilisk is hatched from a chicken's egg beneath a toad. Besides its venomous fangs it has a murderous stare, and anybody who meets its eye dies on the spot. Those who catch the stare only indirectly, through a camera, a mirror or a ghost, are Petrified instead. Spiders flee before it, for it is their mortal enemy. The basilisk itself flees only from the crowing of the rooster, which is fatal to it. Only a Parselmouth can command one.

The Basilisk of the Chamber

Salazar Slytherin set his Basilisk on the Muggles who came against Hogwarts. The quarrel with Godric Gryffindor that followed drove him from the school. He left the serpent sleeping inside a colossal statue of himself in the Chamber of Secrets. The story that he meant it to purge the school of the unworthy is only legend.

It moved about the castle through the plumbing. In 1943 it killed Myrtle in a girls' bathroom, and Hagrid's spider Aragog was blamed for her death. In 1992 to 1993 it Petrified Mrs Norris, Colin Creevey, Justin Finch-Fletchley, Nearly Headless Nick, Hermione Granger and Penelope Clearwater, all of whom saw it indirectly. Colin saw it through his camera, Justin through Nick. Hermione and Penelope saw it in a mirror. Its shed skin, a vivid poisonous green, lay coiled across the tunnel to the Chamber and showed it to be at least twenty feet long. It was fifty.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Harry heard its voice in the walls because he speaks Parseltongue: 'Come... come to me... let me rip you... let me tear you... let me kill you...' In Chapter Nine he heard it again: '... I smell blood... I SMELL BLOOD!' In Chapter Eighteen he prised a page torn from an old library book out of the Petrified Hermione's fist. It described the Basilisk. Underneath, in Hermione's hand, was a single word: Pipes.

In the Chamber, Riddle summoned it from the mouth of Slytherin's statue: 'Speak to me, Slytherin, greatest of the Hogwarts Four.' Harry ran from it between the pillars with his eyes on the floor. It caught his right arm just below the shoulder with a fang as long as his arm. Fawkes dropped the Sorting Hat into his hands, and out of it Harry drew a sword. When the Basilisk's stare met his, it struck a golden heat like the opened door of a furnace and went no further. Harry drove the sword through its lower jaw and shattered a fang. Maddened with pain, it went for the unconscious Dracina Malfoy at the feet of the statue. Harry planted himself over her and cut off its head with a single stroke.

Afterwards, in Chapter Nineteen, Harry thought of it as a fifty-foot snake. Dracina, through whom Riddle had worked all year, could hardly take it in. 'I made a Basilisk come out of a wall, Potter, with my voice, while I was asleep...' In Book Three, Chapter One, Harry remembered lying on the floor of the Chamber with its venom in his arm, and a warm voice saying Your work is not yet done, my child.

In Chapter Four Lucius Malfoy told Harry that he had heard the story of the Chamber of Secrets eleven times. 'In the most recent version the Basilisk was eighty feet long and you were the second coming of Saint George himself. I expect by Christmas the Basilisk will have had wings.' In Chapter Nine Dracina announced that the safest place to sleep was beside the boy who had saved her life from a basilisk. Ron Weasley pointed out that she was the one who had unleashed it. In Chapter Fourteen Ron reminded Harry that he had slain a basilisk. In Chapter Fifteen Harry remembered planting his feet on either side of Dracina with the sword raised, and a strength in his arms that was not his own.

In Chapter Twenty, kneeling in the stream with his shield failing, Harry felt the same warmth that had come to him at the bottom of the Chamber with the venom burning in his arm. In Book Four, Chapter Two, he recalled how one of its fangs had laid his right arm open just below the shoulder.

pages.title: Giant spiders of the Forbidden Forest
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A hollow deep in the Forbidden Forest
pages.html:
The giant spiders of the Forbidden Forest are the children of Aragog and Mosag, with their own children after them: hundreds of eight-eyed black spiders the size of carthorses, living in a hollow deep in the Forest. They click their pincers when they speak. On Aragog's order they never harm Hagrid, who raised their father from an egg. Anybody else who wanders in is food.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, as Hagrid was being taken away to Azkaban, he let fall that anybody looking for answers had only to follow the spiders. In Chapter Seventeen, in May 1993, Harry Potter spotted a line of them hurrying away from the castle towards the Forest, because the creature they feared above all others was loose in the pipes. One night soon afterwards he and Ron Weasley followed them deep into the Forest with Fang, until spiders the size of carthorses carried them down into Aragog's hollow.

Aragog told them the truth about 1943. Then he gave them to his children. 'My sons and daughters do not harm Hagrid, on my command. But I cannot deny them fresh meat, when it wanders so willingly into our midst.' The Weasleys' old car, which had been living wild in the Forest, came thundering down into the hollow, headlamps blazing, horn screaming, and carried the boys away. Harry yelled several things out of the window about the spiders' mothers and their legs. 'Follow the spiders,' said Ron weakly. 'I'll never forgive Hagrid for that.'

pages.title: Abyssinian Shrivelfig
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Its peeled fruit, in the Shrinking Solution
pages.html:
The Abyssinian Shrivelfig is a magical plant grown in the greenhouses at Hogwarts. It needs regular pruning, and its fruit, peeled, goes into the Shrinking Solution.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, in May 1993, Professor Sprout set the second years to pruning Abyssinian Shrivelfigs. It was a very quiet lesson. There were two empty places in the class, Justin Finch-Fletchley's and Hermione Granger's, since both of them had been Petrified. Harry Potter went to tip an armful of withered stalks on to the compost heap and came face to face with Ernie Macmillan, who apologised for ever having suspected him. Ernie then came to work at the same Shrivelfig as Harry and Ron Weasley, bringing his friend Hannah Abbott. Snapping off dead twigs, he wondered aloud whether Dracina Malfoy might be Slytherin's heir. A little later Harry hit Ron over the back of the hand with his pruning shears, and pointed. A line of large spiders was hurrying across the earth towards the Forest, like people late for a train.

pages.title: Dwarfs
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hogwarts on Valentine's Day 1993; the Leaky Cauldron
pages.html:
Dwarfs are a small, bearded, short-tempered people who live among the wizards of Britain. They will take paid work, though they seldom look as if they enjoy it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, on Valentine's Day 1993, Gilderoy Lockhart clapped his hands at breakfast. In tramped a dozen very sour-looking dwarfs. They wore golden wings. They carried little golden harps, and every one of them looked as though he would like to hit somebody with his. All day they barged into lessons to deliver Valentines, which drove the teachers wild. Late in the afternoon a particularly grim-faced dwarf kicked his way through a queue of first years to reach Harry Potter on the stairs to Charms. He split Harry's bag in half, brought him down by the knees and sat on his ankles to sing him his Valentine. A second dwarf followed with another, and sang it twice as loud.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, a party of raucous dwarfs at the Leaky Cauldron sat at the table next to a party of wild-looking warlocks in bearskins. The two had been feuding since the tenth century, over a ritual that was meant to turn the beards of the dwarfs' ancestors to gold and had only made them itch. Harry watched a dwarf throw a kipper. When he wondered at a quarrel of a thousand years, the landlord put him right. 'Eleven hundred, young sir, if you ask the dwarfs,' said Tom. 'Nine-fifty if you ask the warlocks. They can't agree on that either.'

pages.title: Nephilim
aliases: the mighty men which were of old
infobox: Third-year Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts
pages.html:
The Nephilim are the giants of Genesis 6, born when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men: 'mighty men which were of old, men of renown'. Those of the elder days were under no sentence of immortality, and the Flood took them. Creatures called Nephilim have troubled the wizarding world within living memory all the same. They ate friends of Minerva McGonagall's while she was learning wards.

In Scripture and tradition

Genesis records that 'there were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men'. It was in that age that God saw the wickedness of man, and sent the Flood.

The Book of Enoch tells how the Watchers, angels who left their proper place, took wives of the daughters of men. Their children were great giants. The giants ate up all that men could grow, and then turned to devouring men themselves.

After the Flood the spies whom Moses sent into Canaan reported seeing the sons of Anak, 'which come of the giants'. Beside them, the spies said, they had been as grasshoppers.

The Nephilim of Genesis 6 were under no sentence of immortality, as Cain was, and the Flood took them.

In the wizarding world

Nephilim are taught in third-year Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts. Late in the spring of 1993, in a Transfiguration lesson, Professor McGonagall told her second-years to revise. When she was learning wards, she said, placing them as she learnt them, she had bitterly regretted never paying attention in class, as Nephilim snatched and ate her friends around her. She would make sure they did not make her mistake.

Ron Weasley asked what a Nephilim was. 'Never you mind, Mr Weasley,' she said. He would learn about them in his third year, in Defence Against the Dark Arts, by which time they would be mercifully free of Lockhart. Then she winced, very slightly, at what she had said. In September 1993 Harry Potter caught the same knowing look on her face, and remembered the morning she had said Nephilim.

Shortly before Christmas 1993, in the Three Broomsticks, McGonagall reminded Cornelius Fudge that he had read her file, 'especially those bits'. Fudge's legs shuddered. He declared that 'at least we know those parasite creatures and those Nephilim won't be bothering us again'. Professor Flitwick said, 'Hear, hear.' The Ministry considers the matter closed.

pages.title: Wraiths
pages.html:
Wraiths are the restless dead: souls that have not passed on, held to the world of the living by their Fetters, the people, places and things they cannot let go. They walk the Shadowlands, a grey country lying just behind the living world on the far side of a veil called the Shroud.

The dead

Every wraith carries a dark half of its own, its Shadow, which longs to drag it down into Oblivion. The places where wraiths walk are dangerous ground for the living.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, in 1993, Professor McGonagall told Harry Potter that whatever was in the Chamber of Secrets, she would not go in after it alone, not even now. She had faced Garou, she said. ‘I have walked through places where Wraiths walk and come out the other side.’

pages.title: Elves
infobox: The Firstborn of Ilúvatar; the Eldar
Rivendell, Lothlórien, Mirkwood, the Grey Havens
pages.html:
The Elves were the Firstborn, the deathless people of the elder days: tall, graceful folk who sang under the stars. The things they made were so beautiful that men went to war over them. They have passed out of the world, taking their craftsmanship with them, but their blood runs on through Arwen's line to Lily Potter and her son.

History

The Elves woke beside the water of Cuiviénen, in the far east of Middle-earth, before the Sun had ever risen. They were the first of the Children of Ilúvatar. Many of them made the Great Journey into the West, to Valinor. Among those were the Noldor, the greatest craftsmen there have ever been, whose prince Fëanor made the Silmarils. Others stayed behind in Middle-earth as the Sindar and the Silvan Elves. All through the First Age they fought Morgoth, the being Scripture calls Satan.

In the Second Age the Elven-smiths of Eregion, led by Celebrimbor, learnt the craft of rings. Sauron worked among them in a fair disguise and learnt it too, which is why the One Ring could be made at all. Through the Third Age the Elves lived in Rivendell, Lothlórien and Mirkwood. When it ended, most of those who were left took ship from the Grey Havens into the West. Those who stayed behind faded.

A few of them lingered at the Grey Havens long after the rest had gone. In the days of King Arthur the Elves there forged Excalibur, and the Lady of the Lake, who was one of them, gave it to him. The Havens are the Avalon of the legends.

Their craftsmanship went with them. That is why the One Ring can never be made again: the missing part is not knowledge but a people.

Elves and house-elves

The house-elves of the wizarding world, such as Dobby, are another people altogether. When Harry Potter heard Dumbledore speak of the magic of Elves in June 1993, he thought of Dobby at once, and knew that was not what Dumbledore meant. The Elves he found in Dudley's copy of The Lord of the Rings were tall and graceful. They sang under the stars, lived for ever and made things so beautiful that men went to war over them.

When Gandalf first saw Dracina Malfoy's silver eyes, which shone like starlight on still water or mist on a river at dawn in a very old wood, he was reminded of a face he had known long ago. It belonged to a prince of the forest folk, Legolas of Mirkwood.

The magic of Elves

Dumbledore told Harry that his mother had come down from Elves. The protection she gave him by dying for him, he said, was the magic of Elves and of Númenor. It lives in Harry's blood, as it does in his aunt Petunia's. Harry's elven blood comes from Arwen, by way of his mother and his grandmother, Susan Pevensie.

Reading of Rivendell in August 1993, Harry felt a light come off the Elves, as though the pages had been left in the sun. It was the first thing he had read since his Hogwarts letter that made him feel there was somewhere people were simply good, and did not have to be ashamed of it. In June 1994, in a clearing in the Forbidden Forest, he felt something very old come up through him and turn his shield white. He remembered Dumbledore's words: 'Old magic, Harry. The magic of Elves.'

pages.title: Morrigan's Fever
infobox: A cover for Dracina Malfoy's breakdown
pages.html:
Morrigan's Fever is an uncommon, curable complaint that brings on fits of delirium, wild fancies and a great deal of distress. Those who suffer from it are not to be held responsible for anything they say or do while it lasts. In 1993 Albus Dumbledore used it to cover Dracina Malfoy's breakdown.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, after Dracina's breakdown, Dumbledore told the whole school in the Great Hall that Miss Malfoy had contracted Morrigan's Fever. He looked very hard at the Slytherin table, then at Harry, and said he trusted that nobody would hold anything she had said against her. The Weasley twins had never heard of it. ‘Morrigan’s Fever,’ said Fred Weasley, after a moment. ‘Ever heard of it, George?’

Dracina herself, sitting up in the hospital wing, told Harry Potter that it was very rare and very aristocratic. ‘Only the best families get it.’

pages.title: Muggle Studies
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Optional subject, from the third year
pages.html:
Muggle Studies is the Hogwarts subject that teaches witches and wizards about the non-magical world. It is an option taken up in the third year.

The subject

Many students think it an easy option. Hermione Granger, who is Muggle-born, took it up in 1993 anyway, to Ron Weasley's disbelief. Her essays have included Explain Why Muggles Need Electricity.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Percy Weasley told Harry Potter that he did not agree that Muggle Studies was an easy option. Every witch and wizard ought to understand the non-magical world, he said, especially if they were going to work alongside it, as his father did every day.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Ron Weasley could not see why Hermione was taking it at all: ‘You’re Muggle-born! Your mum and dad are Muggles! You already know all about Muggles!’ By Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Ernie Macmillan reckoned she had never missed a single Muggle Studies class, though half of them were at the same time as Divination.

pages.title: Care of Magical Creatures
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Optional subject, from the third year
pages.html:
Care of Magical Creatures is the Hogwarts subject that teaches students to look after magical beasts, and to come away from them alive. It is an option taken up in the third year, and its lessons are held out of doors.

The subject

Until 1993 it was taught by Professor Kettleburn, who retired that summer, as Dumbledore put it, ‘in order to enjoy more time with his remaining limbs’. Since then it has been taught by Rubeus Hagrid, the school's gamekeeper, who loves every creature he has ever met. His first lesson brought out the hippogriffs. Later his third-years met fire crabs at the paddock, where Hermione Granger had her eyebrows singed.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, as Harry Potter chose his third-year subjects, Percy Weasley told him that Charlie, always more the outdoors sort, had gone in for Care of Magical Creatures. Charlie went on to work with dragons in Romania.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, at the start-of-term feast in 1993, Dumbledore announced that Hagrid would take Kettleburn's place, in addition to his gamekeeping duties.

pages.title: Arithmancy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Optional subject, from the third year
pages.html:
Arithmancy is the magical study of numbers, and one of the optional subjects Hogwarts students may take up in their third year. It is taught by Professor Vector.

The subject

The work is done on charts, with columns of numbers and lines ruled between them in four colours. It has a reputation for being hard. Hermione Granger, who took it up in 1993, says it is wonderful, and her favourite subject.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, as the second-years chose their subjects for the coming year, Neville Longbottom sat in a corner surrounded by letters from his relations. He kept asking anybody who came near him whether Arithmancy sounded harder than the Study of Ancient Runes.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, at breakfast on the first day of lessons in 1993, Ron Weasley found Arithmancy on Hermione's timetable at nine o'clock, at the same time as Divination and Muggle Studies. In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry Potter picked up one of her charts and said it looked terrible. ‘Oh no, it’s wonderful!’ said Hermione earnestly. ‘It’s my favourite subject!’ Harry never found out what was wonderful about it.

pages.title: Study of Ancient Runes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Optional subject, from the third year
pages.html:
The Study of Ancient Runes is the Hogwarts subject that teaches students to read the runic scripts of the old magical world. It is an option taken up in the third year.

The subject

It is mostly translation, done with rune dictionaries. Hermione Granger took it up in 1993, along with every other option on offer, and works with two dictionaries open at once.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, in the spring of 1993, Neville Longbottom wondered aloud whether Arithmancy sounded harder than the Study of Ancient Runes. Hermione was already sitting in a corner of the common room, reading Ancient Runes Made Easy.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Harry saw one of her rune translations under her elbow, with three different dictionaries holding its corners down.

pages.title: Sign of the Cross
infobox: Christian gesture of prayer and blessing
Forehead, chest, left shoulder, right shoulder
pages.html:
The sign of the Cross is the gesture by which a Christian marks himself with the cross of Christ, as a prayer or a blessing. In the Western form the right hand touches the forehead, then the chest, then the left shoulder and the right.

History

It is very old, and goes back to the early Church, when Christians traced a small cross on their foreheads with the thumb. In the East the right shoulder is touched before the left.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, in June 1993, Harry Potter made the sign of the Cross for the first time in his life, in the middle of the concourse at King's Cross. He did it clumsily, unsure that he had it the right way round. He felt very silly about it, but he knew what he had seen down in the Chamber of Secrets. He had only ever seen it done once, by an old woman in a church during the carols, long ago. Please, he thought, though he did not know to whom. Please. Just get me through it. God was listening all the same.

pages.title: Christianity
infobox: The Church of England, among others
pages.html:
Christianity is the faith of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. For centuries it lived in harmony with the wizarding world of Britain, until the witch-hunts. Since the Statute of Secrecy of 1692 most wizards have scorned it as a Muggle thing, though every one of them still keeps Christmas.

Beliefs and practice

Christians believe in one God, the maker of heaven and earth. They believe in His Son, Jesus Christ, who was crucified, rose from the dead and will come again. They hope for the resurrection, when everything is given back.

In England the established Church is Anglican. Its Evening Prayer, or Evensong, ends with an old collect, which opens: 'Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us'. The prayer goes on, 'from all perils and dangers of this night; for the love of thy only Son, our Saviour, Jesus Christ.' Remus Lupin calls Christianity a gift, 'given to everyone, whether they like it or not'. Christ himself, he says, made sure of it.

Wizards and the Church

The old magic of Britain was bound up with the old religion of druids and standing stones. When the missionaries came, many of the early monks were wizards. Half the healing charms in use today come from the monasteries, and some monasteries were all but magical schools with a cross on the roof.

The Fat Friar, a Benedictine of the earliest Hogwarts days, remembers that half the boys who left the school went into the Church. They were Muggle-born boys, mostly. The girls went home to be the wise woman of the village, and the priest would nod to her on his way out of Mass. Many wizards believed that God had given them magic on purpose, as a gift to be held in stewardship.

An old rule of the Church held that anybody who believed one creature could be changed into another, except by God, was next door to a heretic. The wizards read it the other way about. The Church never minded herbs, physic or reading the stars. What it condemned was calling up spirits and bargaining with things in the dark. The Friar agrees: that, he says, is idolatry.

In Britain witchcraft became a felony, a crime against one's neighbour, not a heresy. On the Continent it went a great deal worse. The Dominican Johannes Nider wrote, in a book about ants, that witches were an army: a secret church with the Devil for its bishop. In 1486 two more Dominicans published the Malleus Maleficarum. After that, witchcraft was an organised heresy and a pact with the Devil. Inquisitors and witch-finders followed.

Wizards live long. They keep talking portraits and ghosts, so they remember: there are people at Hogwarts who watched their friends burn. When the Statute of Secrecy came in, in 1692, the wizarding world hid from the Church in particular. It threw out God and angels as it went. Bathilda Bagshot's A History of Magic treats Christianity as the main reason wizards and Muggles stopped mixing. Hogwarts has no chapel, and nobody says grace.

Wizards still keep Christmas every year, with trees, crackers and carols, without the least idea whose feast it is. The Fat Friar has watched them do it for five hundred years. He believes it is God's own joke.

Believers and scoffers

Susan Pevensie, Harry Potter's grandmother, was an Anglican. Her daughter Lily believed in Christ with all her heart. She did not stop when witches and wizards tutted at her. After her marriage Lily brought Remus Lupin to faith, then James. Peter Pettigrew went through the forms.

Sirius Black refused until Azkaban. There he came to believe through the Bible passages printed in The Quibbler: 'I'd rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than dwell in the tents of wickedness.' He held on to a cross of two grey splinters bound with blanket thread.

Harry grew up at Privet Drive, among people who thought religion was something old people and Americans did. He came to faith between June 1993 and June 1994. From July 1994 he went to Evensong at St Michael's every Sunday. The vicar there, an old man called Ambrose Greyhame, is Gandalf, though Harry does not know it. Ron Weasley began thinking about God at the Ravenclaw match, after seeing Harry's Patronus.

Most British wizards scorn it. Seamus Finnigan laughed when Harry asked about signs. Professor Trelawney laughed too, and denied that God exists. Even Ron at first thought it was a Muggle thing. Hermione Granger does not believe, but she would rather sit next to somebody who wonders than somebody who laughs. She is writing a paper on Christian influences on wizardry.

Faith against the dark

As Remus Lupin told his third-years, a cross in a coward's hand is a stick of wood. In the hand of somebody who believes in Jesus Christ it is a different thing altogether. Vampires do not like it. Cain's curse was pronounced by God, and the sign belongs to God.

Dementors are repulsed by true faith. The Patronus Charm draws on light derived from God. Lupin's own crosses are wooden, because silver burns him. Lily kept 'Be ye angry, and sin not' written up on the wall of her flat.

pages.title: Dracina's singing Valentine
aliases: There's a boy with eyes like the first green of spring
infobox: There's a boy with eyes like the first green of spring
Unsigned; implied to be Dracina Malfoy
'She is silver and stubborn and wild as a flame.'
pages.html:
Dracina's singing Valentine was the first of two singing Valentines delivered to Harry Potter on 14 February 1993. It told of a boy who was locked away and rose from the dark, watched since autumn by a girl who would wait at her window till he was grown. It was not signed. Everything about it points to Dracina Malfoy.

The song

The song began 'There's a boy with eyes like the first green of spring'. It went on to say that he had been locked away and taught not to sing. 'But he rose from the dark like a lark on the wing.' His heart was a lantern that burned in the cold. Somebody had watched him since autumn first fell, who had noticed him always and knew him too well.

The second half spoke to him directly. He was to be brave, though he did not know her name. She was silver, stubborn, as wild as a flame, and she would pull down the stars if anybody tried to take him away. 'She will wait at her window. She'll wait till you're grown.' It ended with her holding him so close he would forget he was free, when he climbed up the tower and finally saw.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Gilderoy Lockhart covered the walls of the Great Hall with pink flowers for Valentine's Day. Then he sent a dozen sour-looking dwarfs, dressed as cupids, round the school to deliver the Valentines. At breakfast he winked first at Harry, then at a thin, pale, silent girl at the very end of the Slytherin table, and tapped the side of his nose. Late in the afternoon a grim-faced dwarf caught up with Harry on the stairs to Charms with a musical message: 'In person. Special delivery. Professor's orders. Says he's taken a personal interest.' In the struggle Harry's bag split. The dwarf brought him down, then sat on his ankles to sing.

He sang in a surprisingly sweet, surprisingly deep, surprisingly tuneful voice. Dracina had been standing quite still a few steps above, her hands clasped, watching Harry's face. When Ron Weasley, crying with laughter, asked who in their right mind could have written that, all the colour came up into her face. She turned on Ron like a snake striking. Harry, who had not spoken to her for weeks, said that whoever had sent it must be off their head. Dracina flinched as if he had slapped her.

Quotations

She is silver and stubborn and wild as a flame.The grim-faced Valentine dwarf · B2 Ch15

pages.title: Ginny's singing Valentine
aliases: His hair is as black as a raven at night
infobox: His hair is as black as a raven at night
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Ginny's singing Valentine was the second singing Valentine delivered to Harry Potter on 14 February 1993. Ginny Weasley wrote it. It praised his raven-black hair, his frog-green eyes and his defeat of You-Know-Who. Her brothers Fred and George went on singing it to tease him.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, a second dwarf came barrelling up the stairs to Charms just after the first had sung, and struck up before anybody could stop him. His voice was much worse than the first one's. He sang twice as loud: 'His hair is as black as a raven at night, And his eyes are as green as a frog in the light.' Harry, it went on, was ever so brave, ever so kind, had once caught the Snitch with his arm on behind, and had beaten You-Know-Who when he was small.

At the back of the queue of first years Ginny went so red that she was practically glowing, with both hands over her mouth. Dracina Malfoy saw her. 'That one was yours, wasn't it?' Frog in the light, she jeered; with his arm on behind. It was not a poem, she said, but the scribble of a stupid, silly, pathetic little girl. Ginny burst into tears and ran. Percy Weasley, in a voice Harry had never heard him use, sent Dracina to her lesson.

That night Harry went to bed early, partly because he could not stand to hear Fred and George singing His hair is as black as a raven at night one more time.

Quotations

His hair is as black as a raven at night, And his eyes are as green as a frog in the light.The second Valentine dwarf · B2 Ch15

pages.title: The Basilisk page
aliases: the page from the old library book
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
In Hermione's fist, while she lay Petrified
pages.html:
The Basilisk page is a page torn out of a very old library book, describing the Basilisk, the King of Serpents. Hermione Granger wrote one word beneath it, 'Pipes', and had it clenched in her fist when the Basilisk Petrified her.

The text

The page says that the Basilisk, known also as the King of Serpents, may reach gigantic size and live many hundreds of years. It is born from a chicken's egg, hatched beneath a toad. Besides its venomous fangs it has a murderous stare, and all who are fixed with the beam of its eye suffer instant death. It warns: 'Spiders flee before the Basilisk, for it is their mortal enemy.' The Basilisk itself flees only from the crowing of the rooster, which is fatal to it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Harry Potter worked the page out of Hermione's fingers in the hospital wing, while Ron Weasley kept watch. It explained everything at once, down to the killing of Hagrid's roosters. Harry pointed at the word Hermione had written. 'Pipes,' he said. 'Pipes, Ron. It's been using the plumbing. I've been hearing the voice in the walls...'

Quotations

Spiders flee before the Basilisk, for it is their mortal enemy.The Basilisk page · B2 Ch18

pages.title: Her skeleton will lie in the Chamber for ever
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Dracina Malfoy, possessed by Tom Riddle's diary
On the wall, directly under the first message
pages.html:
Her skeleton will lie in the Chamber for ever was the second message of the heir of Slytherin, written on 29 May 1993 directly under the first. It announced that Ginny Weasley had been taken into the Chamber of Secrets. The hand that wrote it was Dracina Malfoy's, possessed by Tom Riddle's diary. The ink was Ginny's blood.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Harry Potter and Ron Weasley were hiding in a wardrobe in the staff room when Professor McGonagall came in. 'The heir of Slytherin,' she said, 'has left a second message. Directly under the first. Her skeleton will lie in the Chamber for ever.' The student was Ginny. Ron slid down the inside of the wardrobe until he was sitting among the shoes. Snape added that one of his own Slytherins had not answered the register either.

In the Chamber, Tom Riddle told Harry how it had been done. Ginny had followed them down, so he had Dracina deal with her: all he had needed was a bit of her blood. He pointed at the cut on Ginny's temple. 'And then I walked her back up, of course, to leave a little note on the wall. One does like to be tidy.'

pages.title: Ancient Runes Made Easy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Ancient Runes Made Easy is an introduction to the study of runes. Hermione Granger was reading it in the Gryffindor common room in the spring of 1993, on the day Tom Riddle's diary was stolen from Harry Potter's dormitory.

Description

Ancient Runes is one of the optional subjects a Hogwarts pupil chooses at the end of the second year, to begin in the third. This is the book for anybody who wants a head start, which describes Hermione exactly.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Harry and Neville Longbottom found the boys' dormitory ransacked. Riddle's diary was gone, with Harry's match scarf. Harry and Ron Weasley hurried down to tell Hermione, who was sitting by herself in a corner of the common room, reading the book. She looked appalled. Only somebody in Gryffindor could have done it, she whispered, since nobody else knew the password.

pages.title: The painted book of the knight in the tower
infobox: A knight in silver armour kneeling before a girl in a tower, holding out his sword
pages.html:
The painted book of the knight in the tower is a big, battered picture book in the Hogwarts library. Dracina Malfoy slammed it shut in November 1992 so that Harry Potter would not see the picture it was open at: a knight in silver armour kneeling before a girl in a tower, holding out his sword to her.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Harry saw it lying open on top of two volumes of wizarding genealogy, and Dracina slammed it shut.

In Chapter Eighteen, at the bottom of the Chamber of Secrets in May 1993, Dracina woke in time to see Harry cut the head off the Basilisk. He stood over her with the sword, filthy, bleeding and shining. He looked like something out of the painted book: the knight in silver armour, holding out his sword. Only he was not kneeling in a tower. He was standing between her and the dark, with the dead Basilisk at his feet. It was Saint George, she thought, and he had just slain the dragon.

pages.title: The book that makes you speak in limericks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Its reader speaks in limericks for life
pages.html:
The book that makes you speak in limericks is a cursed book that leaves anybody who reads it speaking in limericks for the rest of his or her life. Fred and George Weasley told Harry Potter about it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, early in 1993, Harry Potter sat looking at Tom Riddle's diary, which had just written back to him. It had to be enchanted, he thought. He had heard of books that bit, books that screamed and books you could not stop reading once you had started. Fred and George Weasley had told him about one that made you speak in limericks for the rest of your life. But he had never heard of a book that wrote back.

pages.title: Lockhart's get-well card
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hermione Granger, in the hospital wing
pages.html:
Lockhart's get-well card was a large gold card that Gilderoy Lockhart sent Hermione Granger in the hospital wing early in 1993. It was signed 'your devoted teacher', with every one of his titles after his name, and it ended up in her wastepaper basket.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Hermione was still in the hospital wing after her Polyjuice Potion went wrong. Harry Potter spotted something gold sticking up out of the bin by her bed. Ron Weasley snatched it out of the bin and read it aloud in a high, gushing voice. It wished dear Miss Granger a swift and complete recovery, from her devoted teacher. Then came all his titles, down to his five Most Charming Smile Awards. Hermione announced that she no longer liked Lockhart, because she thought he was lying about a great many things. On the stairs afterwards, Ron said he was going to need a bath.

pages.title: The opening of the Chamber of Secrets (1943)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Tom Riddle, the heir of Slytherin
Myrtle, a Muggle-born Ravenclaw, in June 1943
pages.html:
The opening of the Chamber of Secrets in 1943 was the first known opening of the hidden Chamber that Salazar Slytherin built beneath Hogwarts. Tom Riddle opened it in his fifth year, and its monster attacked several students before it killed one, the girl who became Moaning Myrtle. Riddle framed Rubeus Hagrid and his spider Aragog. Hagrid was expelled, the death was passed off as an accident and the real heir of Slytherin walked away unpunished, with a special award for services to the school.

The opening

Riddle was an orphan, raised in a Muggle orphanage in London. He was a Parselmouth, and at Hogwarts he found out that he was the last descendant of Salazar Slytherin. He found the Chamber, whose entrance lay in a girls' bathroom, and loosed its Basilisk on the school.

In June 1943 a Muggle-born Ravenclaw called Myrtle locked herself in a cubicle of that bathroom to cry. She heard a boy come in, speaking a strange language. When she opened the door to tell him to go away, she saw a pair of great yellow eyes, and died.

The cover-up

After the death the Ministry talked of closing Hogwarts altogether. Riddle did not want to go back to the orphanage. On 13 June 1943 he caught the third-year Rubeus Hagrid with the young Acromantula he was keeping in a box, and denounced him. Hagrid was expelled, and his wand was snapped, though Albus Dumbledore saw to it that he was kept on as gamekeeper.
