In Chapter Ten, that December, he went anyway, without a form, by the secret passage from the one-eyed witch to the cellar of Honeydukes.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, on the Hogwarts Express home in June 1994, Harry opened a letter from Sirius. Folded up inside it was a note: 'I, Sirius Black, Harry Potter's godfather, hereby give him permission to visit Hogsmeade at weekends.' Harry was sure that would be good enough for Dumbledore.

pages.title: Knight Bus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Emergency transport for the stranded witch or wizard
Eleven Sickles; thirteen with hot chocolate; fifteen with a hot-water bottle and a toothbrush
pages.html:
The Knight Bus is a violently purple triple-decker that serves as emergency transport for the stranded witch or wizard. It is summoned by holding out a wand hand at the side of the road, and it arrives out of nowhere with a bang. It will go anywhere at all, so long as it is on land; underwater it can do nothing.

The bus

Instead of seats it has brass bedsteads beside its curtained windows, with candles burning in brackets by each bed. It does not so much drive as leap, a hundred miles at a time, with a noise like a bomb going off. In between leaps it careers along the roads while lampposts, pillar boxes and bins jump out of its way.

The fare is eleven Sickles wherever the passenger is going. In 1993 thirteen Sickles bought hot chocolate as well. Fifteen bought a hot-water bottle and a toothbrush. It is a no-smoking bus, as a brass plate on the door says, and as the conductor, Stan Shunpike, tells every passenger who forgets. Ernie Prang drives.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, the Knight Bus very nearly ran Harry over in Magnolia Crescent on the summer night in 1993 when he ran away from Privet Drive. A moment before, it had been somewhere in Wales. From Surrey it jumped back into Wales, to Abergavenny, then on to Anglesey and Aberdeen. At dawn it put Harry down outside the Leaky Cauldron on Charing Cross Road.

One other passenger was awake that night: a man in a crumpled grey suit and a long tan raincoat, with one hand resting flat on a carrier bag beside him. Every time the bus banged he swore under his breath, steadily, with his feet braced against the bedstead opposite. He was John Constantine. In the Interlude of Book Three he flagged the bus down in Liverpool a little after eleven, with the Myst linking book in a white Tesco carrier bag, and asked for Hogsmeade. Stan charged him eleven Sickles, mentioned that thirteen would get him hot chocolate, and made him put out his cigarette. It was not the last time that night.

From Liverpool the bus went to Nottingham, where a large witch in a fur hat got on, then to Wales, then to Surrey for Harry. After Abergavenny, Anglesey and Aberdeen it stopped on Charing Cross Road to let Harry off. Hogsmeade was right at the bottom of Stan's list, so Constantine sat on past Aberdeen and past London, all the way to the end.

In Chapter Fourteen Hagrid booked two beds on the Knight Bus to take himself and Buckbeak to London for the hippogriff's hearing.

pages.title: Percy's Head Boy badge
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Percy's Head Boy badge is the silver badge Percy Weasley received when he was made Head Boy of Hogwarts in the summer of 1993. He was the second of the Weasley brothers to hold the post, after Bill. He was enormously proud of it, which is exactly why his younger brothers could not leave it alone.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, on 31 August 1993, the new badge went missing at the Leaky Cauldron, where the Weasleys were spending the last night of the holidays. 'My Head Boy badge is gone,' said Percy, rounding on Harry. While Percy took apart the room he shared with Ron, the twins crouched on the landing, heaving with laughter. They had taken it. 'We've been improving it,' Fred whispered to Harry. The badge now read Bighead Boy.

In Chapter Thirteen, on the night Sirius Black got into Gryffindor Tower, Percy somehow found time to put the badge on over his pyjamas before ordering everybody back upstairs. In Chapter Sixteen, keeping the common room silent before the exams, he patrolled it every evening with the badge polished until it hurt to look at.

pages.title: The Ministry cars
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Enchanted cars, lent by the Ministry of Magic
pages.html:
The Ministry cars were two old-fashioned dark green cars, lent by the Ministry of Magic, which took the Weasleys, Harry Potter and Hermione Granger to King's Cross on 1 September 1993. They looked like ordinary cars. They could slide through gaps that no ordinary car could.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, Mr Weasley waited outside the Leaky Cauldron for the two cars, then marched Harry across the pavement to the first of them. Each was driven by a furtive-looking wizard in a suit of emerald velvet. On the way to King's Cross they slid through gaps that Uncle Vernon's new company car certainly could not have managed. At the station the drivers found everybody trolleys, unloaded the trunks and touched their hats to Mr Weasley.

pages.title: Hagrid's gourd vine
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Six
Over the door of Hagrid's hut
pages.html:
Hagrid's gourd vine was a great fat gourd vine that Rubeus Hagrid grew over the door of his hut in a single night, to give a bit of shade to the step for his first class. By evening it was dead.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, Hagrid stood waiting at his door for his first Care of Magical Creatures lesson in September 1993, beaming, in a pool of cool green shade. Over the door hung something new: a vine with leaves the size of umbrellas. The lesson went badly, for the hippogriff Buckbeak hurt Dracina Malfoy. By evening the vine hung off the porch in black, slimy rags. Its gourds had gone soft. A fat white grub the size of Harry's thumb sat quite still on the doorstep, as if it were resting after a long day's work.

The sight made Harry furious, for no reason he could name, and he would have trodden on the grub if Hermione had not been in the way. Inside, they found Hagrid drinking at his table. 'Me vine's gone,' he said. 'Did yeh see? Grew it las' night. Fer a bit o' shade on the step, fer the class. Come up in a night an' gone in a night. Some grub.'

Harry said that he would have squashed it. 'Wha' for?' said Hagrid. 'It's a grub, Harry. Can' be cross with a grub fer bein' a grub.' He had sat for half an hour feeling sorry for the vine, he said, but he would be sorrier for any one of the hippogriffs out in the dark, or the children up at the castle, than for a hundred vines. 'Even her. Even Malfoy. Didn' want her hurt. Never wanted that. Yeh don' get ter pick which ones yeh're sorry for.'

The Book of Jonah tells of a gourd like it, which God made to grow up over the prophet in a single night to shade him. At dawn the next day God sent a worm to smite it, and it withered.

pages.title: Gobstones
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The stones squirt a nasty-smelling liquid at a player who loses a point
From plain stone to solid gold
pages.html:
Gobstones is a wizarding game rather like marbles, in which the stones squirt a nasty-smelling liquid into a player's face whenever he loses a point. Sets range from the ordinary to the solid gold. Hogwarts has its own Gobstones Club; Eileen Prince, Severus Snape's mother, was once captain of the school team.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry Potter needed a good deal of self-control in Diagon Alley not to buy a handsome set of solid gold Gobstones. He kept reminding himself that he had five years to go at Hogwarts, and how it would feel to ask the Dursleys for money for spellbooks.

In Chapter Eleven, at Christmas 1993, Harry raged that the grown-ups had told him about Quidditch, about Gryffindor, about gobstones, but never about Sirius Black. Ron Weasley, trying to head off a visit to Hagrid, suggested chess, or Gobstones, since Percy had left a set. In Chapter Fifteen Ron kept watch at the end of a corridor, pretending to read a notice about Gobstones. In Chapter Sixteen, as June drew near, everybody wanted to be out on the lawns, or playing Gobstones in the shade of the beech trees. Nobody could, because the exams were almost upon them.

pages.title: Lunascope
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Following the moon without moon charts
pages.html:
A lunascope is a wizarding instrument for following the moon. Its great selling point is that it does away with moon charts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry was living at the Leaky Cauldron and spending his days in Diagon Alley. He ate under the brightly coloured umbrellas outside the cafés, where the other diners showed one another what they had bought. One wizard was showing off a new lunascope: 'it's a lunascope, old boy, no more messing around with moon charts, see?'

pages.title: The moving galaxy model
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Model of the galaxy in a glass ball
A shop in Diagon Alley, August 1993
pages.html:
The moving galaxy model is a perfect working model of the galaxy inside a large glass ball. Harry Potter saw it in a shop in Diagon Alley in August 1993 and was sorely tempted by it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry was spending the last weeks of the summer at the Leaky Cauldron, with the whole of Diagon Alley to look at and a money bag freshly filled at Gringotts. He was sorely tempted by the galaxy model, which would have meant he never had to take another Astronomy lesson. He kept his hands off it, and off a handsome set of solid gold Gobstones, by reminding himself that he had five years to go at Hogwarts. He did not want to have to ask the Dursleys for money for spellbooks.

pages.title: Quick-Quotes Quill
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
A Quick-Quotes Quill is an enchanted quill that stands upright on the parchment and writes down whatever is said near it, with no hand to guide it. It writes very fast, and not always faithfully: what goes down on the page tends to be livelier than what was actually said. Journalists of the more sensational sort are fond of them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, Dracina Malfoy did an impression of Hermione Granger for the Slytherin table in the Great Hall, with one arm shooting straight up in the air. Afterwards Harry told Hermione that Dracina had got her hand all wrong. Ron, catching on, said the voice was wrong too. 'It's not high. It's fast. It's like a Quick-Quotes Quill on fire.'

pages.title: Butterbeer
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Butterbeer is a hot, sweet wizarding drink, served foaming in tankards at the Three Broomsticks in Hogsmeade. It tastes a little like butterscotch. On a cold day it seems to warm every bit of a person from the inside.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, the Weasleys had told Harry all about Hogsmeade: the only all-wizard village in Britain, a sweetshop that had to be seen to be believed and a pub where, according to Percy, third-years were technically allowed Butterbeer. Percy himself did not approve.

In Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry drank his first, at the Three Broomsticks with Ron and Hermione. By the third swallow his hands had thawed. Then Cornelius Fudge came in with the teachers. Ron and Hermione pushed Harry under the table at once. He ended up on his knees on the floor, holding an empty tankard, with Butterbeer running down his neck.

In Chapter Twelve, after one of their lessons, Professor Lupin brought out two bottles from the Three Broomsticks. ‘Butterbeer!’ said Harry, without thinking. ‘Yeah, I like that stuff!’ It was a plain admission that he had tasted it before. Harry said that Ron and Hermione had brought him some back from Hogsmeade. Lupin handed the bottle over anyway.

In Chapter Thirteen, after Gryffindor beat Ravenclaw, Fred and George came back with crates of it for the party. Neville, after one and a half, became the most confident person in Gryffindor Tower.

pages.title: Pepper Imps
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The eater smokes at the mouth
pages.html:
Pepper Imps are tiny black sweets sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. They are sold as making you breathe fire. In practice they make the eater smoke at the mouth, which most people find quite good enough.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron Weasley listed Pepper Imps among the delights of Honeydukes: they make you smoke at the mouth.

In Chapter Eight, on Hallowe'en 1993, Ron and Hermione came back from Hogsmeade with an armful of sweets for Harry, who had not been allowed to go. Harry picked up a packet of tiny black Pepper Imps.

In Chapter Ten, in December, Harry got into Honeydukes himself and found them on the shelf of odd sweets under the sign Special Effects, sold as breathe fire for your friends.

pages.title: Chocoballs
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Chocoballs are great fat chocolates sold at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade. Each is full of strawberry mousse and clotted cream.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the way to school on 1 September 1993, Ron described Honeydukes to Harry with a dreamy look on his face. They had everything there, he said. Pepper Imps made you smoke at the mouth. There were great fat Chocoballs full of strawberry mousse and clotted cream. There were sugar quills, too, which you could suck in class while looking as though you were thinking what to write next.

pages.title: Sugar quills
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Sugar quills are sweets made to look like quills, sold at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade. Their great advantage is that they can be sucked in class. Anybody watching will think the eater is only thinking about what to write next.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron Weasley named them among the things he most wanted from Honeydukes: 'really excellent sugar quills, which you can suck in class and just look like you're thinking what to write next...'

pages.title: Levitating sherbet balls
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Lifts the eater a few inches off the ground
pages.html:
Levitating sherbet balls are the massive sherbet balls sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. Anyone sucking one floats a few inches off the ground until it is gone.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express in September 1993, Ron listed them among the wonders of Honeydukes for Harry's benefit. '...and massive sherbet balls that make you levitate a few inches off the ground while you're sucking them,' he said, paying no attention whatever to Hermione. In Chapter Ten, in December, Harry saw them in the shop for himself.

pages.title: Cauldron Cakes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
From the sweet trolley on the Hogwarts Express
pages.html:
Cauldron Cakes are wizarding cakes sold from the sweet trolley on the Hogwarts Express, along with Chocolate Frogs, Pumpkin Pasties and the rest.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, Harry bought some of everything on the trolley on his first journey to Hogwarts, Cauldron Cakes among them. In Book Three, Chapter Five, on 1 September 1993, he bought a large stack of them from the trolley witch. Professor Lupin was fast asleep in the corner of the compartment, so the witch said that if he was hungry when he woke, she would be up at the front with the driver. Harry passed one to Hermione.

pages.title: Rat tonic
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Rat tonic is a restorative for pet rats, sold in small red bottles by the Magical Menagerie in Diagon Alley. Ron Weasley bought one for Scabbers on 31 August 1993. Scabbers was still taking it on the night he vanished.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, the witch at the Magical Menagerie told Ron that an ordinary garden rat could not be expected to live much longer than three years. When he would not hear of a replacement, she brought the tonic out from under the counter. Ron said he would take it. At that moment Crookshanks sprang off the top of the highest cage at Scabbers, who bolted out of the shop with Ron after him. Hermione Granger came out carrying the cat, whom she had just bought, and slapped the bottle into Ron's hand. 'That reminds me, you forgot your rat tonic.'

That night at the Leaky Cauldron Ron could not find it, and thought he must have left it in the bar. Harry went down and found it lying under the table where they had sat. He waited until he heard the Weasleys' bedroom door close, then took it back upstairs to Ron.

In Chapter Twelve, on the evening Harry got his Firebolt back, Ron offered to carry the broom up to the dormitory, saying he had to give Scabbers his rat tonic. Moments later he came running down the stairs, dragging a bloodstained bedsheet. Scabbers had gone.

pages.title: Flame-Freezing Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Turns flames into a mild, pleasant warmth
Saving genuine witches and wizards at the stake, 1300 to 1400
pages.html:
The Flame-Freezing Charm turns the heat of a fire into a mild and rather agreeable warmth. In the fourteenth century it made the witch burnings of medieval Europe almost pointless. Nearly all of the thousands put to the stake had no magic at all. The few genuine witches or wizards among them simply cast the charm, shrieked convincingly for the crowd and came to no harm.

The burnings

Between 1300 and 1400 the Muggles of Europe lived in terror of witchcraft, yet they were almost wholly unable to detect it. When the fire was lit under a real witch, the charm did the rest. All the condemned had to do was scream for the benefit of the onlookers.

Wendelin the Weird enjoyed the tickly feeling so much that she let herself be caught forty-seven times, under a variety of names and hats.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, Harry Potter sat at his desk in Privet Drive writing a History of Magic essay: Witch Burning in the Fourteenth Century Was Completely Pointless. Discuss. He copied down what Bathilda Bagshot's A History of Magic had to say about the charm, and then he wrote about Wendelin the Weird.

In Chapter Sixteen, in June 1994, while they waited outside the classroom for their History of Magic exam, he told Hermione Granger that he meant to do the burnings properly this time. He would not stop at the Flame-Freezing Charm and Wendelin letting them burn her forty-seven times because she liked the tickly feeling. He would put in what Florean Fortescue had told him about why the Muggles were so frightened, as well as the Fat Friar's account of the long years before it all went wrong.

pages.title: Braking Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The Firebolt, which has an unbreakable one
pages.html:
A Braking Charm is the charm built into a broomstick that lets its rider stop. On a fast racing broom it matters a great deal. The Firebolt has an unbreakable one.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1993, a week after he had arrived at the Leaky Cauldron, Harry Potter found a crowd in Quality Quidditch Supplies. They were gathered round a new podium, on which stood the most magnificent broom he had ever seen. The notice beside it promised a handle of ash with a diamond-hard polish, a tail of individually selected birch twigs and an acceleration of 150 miles an hour in ten seconds. It also promised an unbreakable Braking Charm. The price was on request.

pages.title: A Charm to Cure Reluctant Reversers
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Curing a broom that will not fly backwards
pages.html:
A Charm to Cure Reluctant Reversers is a broomstick charm for brooms that are unwilling to fly backwards. It is printed on page twelve of the Handbook of Do-It-Yourself Broomcare.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, Aunt Marge came to stay at Privet Drive. Harry Potter got through her visit by thinking about his Handbook of Do-It-Yourself Broomcare whenever she started on him. It gave him such a glazed look that she decided he was mentally subnormal. At the dinner table he tried his very hardest to remember page twelve. The thing he wanted to say to Aunt Marge, about which of the two of them was healthy-sized, was right there on his tongue.

pages.title: Transfiguration Today
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Albus Dumbledore, while still a student
pages.html:
Transfiguration Today is a learned wizarding journal of Transfiguration. Albus Dumbledore had papers published in it while he was still a student at Hogwarts. Its articles are taken seriously enough to start arguments over breakfast.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry Potter watched a group of venerable-looking wizards at breakfast in the Leaky Cauldron arguing over the latest article in Transfiguration Today. One of them grew so cross about it that he turned his toast into a hedgehog, and had to be helped.

pages.title: Unfogging the Future
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Palmistry, crystal balls, bird entrails; tea-leaf symbols on pages five and six
pages.html:
Unfogging the Future is the Divination textbook for third years at Hogwarts, by the celebrated Seer Cassandra Vablatsky. It is a thick, black-bound guide to the basic methods of fortune-telling: palmistry, crystal balls and bird entrails among them. The symbols for reading tea leaves are on pages five and six.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the manager of Flourish and Blotts climbed a set of steps to fetch Harry Potter a copy, calling it a very good guide to all the basic methods. Harry was not listening. He had seen another book on a table nearby, Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming, with a black dog as large as a bear on its cover.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, at the first lesson, Trelawney told the class to find the tea-leaf symbols on pages five and six. Harry read Ron Weasley's cup with its help. A bent little cross meant trials and suffering. A sun meant great happiness. So, Harry told him, Ron was going to have an awful time, and be really happy about it.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Hermione Granger stood up in the middle of a lesson, crammed the book into her bag and walked out of Divination for good. In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Neville Longbottom sat on the stairs before the examination with the book open on his knees at the chapter on crystal-gazing.

pages.title: Predicting the Unpredictable: Insulate Yourself Against Shocks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Predicting the Unpredictable: Insulate Yourself Against Shocks is a fortune-telling book, for those who would like some warning of the worst. It is stocked in the Divination corner at the back of Flourish and Blotts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the manager of Flourish and Blotts led Harry Potter to the back of the shop to fetch him Unfogging the Future. A small table there was stacked with fortune-telling books, among them Predicting the Unpredictable and Broken Balls: When Fortunes Turn Foul. On a display nearby Harry saw Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming, with a black dog as large as a bear on its cover. The manager advised him not to read it, or he would start seeing death omens everywhere.

pages.title: Broken Balls: When Fortunes Turn Foul
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Broken Balls: When Fortunes Turn Foul is a fortune-telling book on what to do when the omens turn bad. In August 1993 it was stacked with the other Divination books in the back corner of Flourish and Blotts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry Potter went to Flourish and Blotts for his copy of Unfogging the Future by Cassandra Vablatsky. The manager led him into the back of the shop, to a corner given over to fortune-telling. A small table there was stacked with volumes such as Predicting the Unpredictable: Insulate Yourself Against Shocks and Broken Balls. Harry hardly noticed them. A moment later his eyes fell on Death Omens.

pages.title: Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A black dog, as large as a bear, with gleaming eyes
pages.html:
Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming is a book of Divination about the signs that foretell a death. Its cover shows a black dog as large as a bear, with gleaming eyes. In August 1993 it reminded Harry Potter of the dog he had seen in Magnolia Crescent.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry was buying Unfogging the Future at Flourish and Blotts when his eyes fell on the book. The manager saw what he was staring at. 'Oh, I wouldn't read that if I were you,' he said lightly. 'You'll start seeing death omens everywhere. It's enough to frighten anyone to death.' Harry went on staring at the cover. A slow cold crept down his back, just as it had on the wall in Magnolia Crescent.

In Chapter Six, when Professor Trelawney found the Grim in his teacup, the dog on the front of the book was the first thing he thought of. The dog in Magnolia Crescent, as it turned out, was Sirius Black.

pages.title: Invisible Book of Invisibility
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Two hundred, by Flourish and Blotts
pages.html:
The Invisible Book of Invisibility is a book that lives up to its title rather too well. Flourish and Blotts once bought two hundred copies of it, at great expense, and never found a single one. What it says is anybody's guess.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the manager of Flourish and Blotts was trying to keep about a hundred copies of The Monster Book of Monsters from tearing one another to pieces in an iron cage. Poking them apart with a walking stick, he told Harry Potter that he was never stocking them again. He had thought the shop had seen the worst when it bought two hundred copies of the Invisible Book of Invisibility. They had cost a fortune, he said, and they never found them.

pages.title: Intermediate Transfiguration
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Intermediate Transfiguration is the Transfiguration textbook set for Hogwarts third-years, a step on from the simpler work of their first two years in Professor McGonagall's classroom.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, it was on Harry Potter's book list for his third year. He asked for it at Flourish and Blotts, along with The Standard Book of Spells, Grade Three, barely aware of what he was saying. He had just seen Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming on a display table, with a black dog as large as a bear on its cover, and the dog had looked oddly familiar. He left the shop ten minutes later with his new books under his arms, bumping into people all the way back to the Leaky Cauldron.

pages.title: The Standard Book of Spells, Grade Three
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Bought at Flourish and Blotts, August 1993
pages.html:
The Standard Book of Spells, Grade Three is the Charms textbook for third years at Hogwarts. It is the third volume of Miranda Goshawk's graded series, the next after Grade 2.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the book was on Harry Potter's third-year list. Harry was staying at the Leaky Cauldron, and he bought it at Flourish and Blotts together with Intermediate Transfiguration. He asked for them in a daze. A moment before, he had seen a black dog as large as a bear on the cover of Death Omens, and it had looked oddly familiar. He walked back to the Leaky Cauldron ten minutes later with his new books under his arm, bumping into people all the way.

pages.title: Sites of Historical Sorcery
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Places of magical history in Britain
The inn of the 1612 goblin rebellion; the Shrieking Shack
pages.html:
Sites of Historical Sorcery is a guide to the places of magical history in Britain. According to its entry on Hogsmeade, the village inn was the headquarters of the goblin rebellion of 1612, and the Shrieking Shack is supposed to be the most severely haunted building in Britain.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1993, Hermione Granger asked Ron Weasley whether he knew much about Hogsmeade. Ron only wanted to talk about Honeydukes. When Hermione pressed on eagerly with what Sites of Historical Sorcery had to say, he went on describing sherbet balls that make you float, plainly not hearing a word. Harry Potter, who had no signed permission form, said heavily that she would have to tell him about it when she had found out.

pages.title: Accidental Magic Reversal Squad
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The Minister for Magic, by Cornelius Fudge's account
pages.html:
The Accidental Magic Reversal Squad is the branch of the Ministry of Magic that undoes magical accidents, above all those that Muggles might notice. It is a subsection of the Department of Magical Accidents and Catastrophes.

Work

Its members are sent out whenever a spell goes wrong where it should not, whether it is a child's accidental magic or a grown wizard's mistake. They reverse the damage, and the memories of any Muggles who saw it are modified so that nobody remembers a thing.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry Potter blew up his Aunt Marge at Privet Drive in August 1993 and ran away. Within a few hours two members of the Squad had been sent to the house. Cornelius Fudge gave Harry the news at the Leaky Cauldron at dawn: 'Miss Dursley has been punctured and her memory has been modified. She has no recollection of the incident at all.'

Later in the same conversation Harry, who was busy flattering the Minister, told him: 'I'd never have thought of a Reversal Squad. I didn't even know there was one.' Fudge explained that it was a subsection of the Department of Magical Accidents and Catastrophes, under his own overall direction, before he caught himself and changed the subject.

pages.title: Department of Magical Accidents and Catastrophes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The Accidental Magic Reversal Squad; the Obliviators; the Muggle-Worthy Excuse Committee
pages.html:
The Department of Magical Accidents and Catastrophes is the department of the Ministry of Magic that puts magical accidents right and keeps them from Muggle eyes.

Work

Its Accidental Magic Reversal Squad undoes spells that have gone wrong. Its Obliviators modify the memories of Muggles who have seen what they should not. Its Muggle-Worthy Excuse Committee thinks up the explanations, such as burst gas mains.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Cornelius Fudge told Harry Potter at the Leaky Cauldron that the Accidental Magic Reversal Squad was a subsection of the department, under his own overall direction.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Fudge spoke in the Three Broomsticks of what he had seen in 1981, on the day Sirius Black was taken: 'I was Junior Minister at Magical Catastrophes in those days, and I was one of the first to reach the scene after he did it, after he...'

pages.title: International Confederation of Wizards
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The International Confederation of Wizards is the body through which the wizarding governments of the world deal with one another. It signed the International Statute of Wizarding Secrecy in 1689. In 1900 it was through the Confederation that those governments came to terms with the Camarilla. Its head is called the Supreme Mugwump, an office that Albus Dumbledore holds.

History

The Confederation signed the Statute of Secrecy in 1689, and in 1692 the Statute came into force. From then on the witches and wizards of every nation withdrew into hiding, each government answering for its own people.

In 1900 the wizarding governments of the world, meeting through the Confederation, made an agreement with the Camarilla. The wizards would lend the vampires their own concealment magic to help keep the Masquerade. In return, no vampire who answers to the Camarilla would ever hunt or feed on a witch or wizard. Britain's Ministry of Magic was one of the parties.

In 1932 Greta Grindelwald tried to make herself leader of the Confederation by trickery. She failed in front of the whole wizarding world.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, on the Knight Bus in the summer of 1993, Harry Potter read in Stan Shunpike's newspaper that Cornelius Fudge had come under sharp criticism from within the Confederation. He had briefed the Muggle Prime Minister on Sirius Black's escape, a step unprecedented in peacetime. 'I had no choice, and I'd do it again,' Fudge said. The Ministry's warning letter to Harry the summer before had cited Section 13 of the same Statute of Secrecy.

pages.title: Obliviators
infobox: Memory Charms on Muggles who have seen magic
pages.html:
The Obliviators are the witches and wizards of the Ministry of Magic whose work is making Muggles forget. When a Muggle sees magic, they are sent to change the memory with a Memory Charm, so that the Statute of Secrecy holds.

The work

They belong to the Department of Magical Accidents and Catastrophes. Done well, their work leaves nothing behind: the Muggle remembers a quiet evening, a gas leak or a bad dream. The vampires keep their own secret far more harshly.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry asked Lucius Malfoy in Diagon Alley about Spider-Man. Lucius assured him that if such a man existed, the Wizengamot would have heard of him: 'We have Obliviators for a great deal less than climbing walls.' In Chapter Eight Lupin told his class that any vampire who lets a Muggle see what it is will be hunted down and destroyed by the others, who are far less gentle about it than the Obliviators.

pages.title: British National Party
pages.html:
The British National Party, the BNP, is a far-right political party in Britain, founded by John Tyndall in 1982. Vernon Dursley holds a membership card, which he would very much rather nobody knew about.

The party

The party campaigns against immigration, and only white Britons may join it. In September 1993 it won its first seat on a local council, in the East End of London, to a national outcry.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, on Harry Potter's thirteenth birthday, 31 July 1993, Uncle Vernon announced that Aunt Marge was coming to stay for a week. She was to be told that Harry went to St Brutus's Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys. Harry followed Vernon to the front door and asked him to sign his Hogsmeade form. 'And why should I do that?' sneered Uncle Vernon.

A couple of weeks earlier Vernon's BNP membership card had fallen out of his wallet. Harry had put it back exactly where he had found it, then said nothing for a fortnight, for precisely this moment. What if he let something slip in front of Marge, he wondered aloud: that membership card, for instance? All the purple drained out of Vernon's face from the top down. 'Y-you never mind that, boy,' he said hoarsely. Harry asked what the neighbours would think.

Vernon gave in. 'I'll sign the bloody form, you cursed child, just do what I say about Marge!' He never did sign it. On the last evening of her visit Harry blew Aunt Marge up and ran away.

pages.title: Grunnings
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Grunnings is a firm that makes drills. Vernon Dursley is its director, and he can talk about it for as long as anybody will let him.

The firm

Mr Dursley works in an office on the ninth floor, where he always sits with his back to the window.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter One, in the summer of 1992, Vernon set his heart on a huge order from a rich builder, Mr Mason, who was coming to dinner with his wife. After dinner Vernon meant to steer the conversation round to drills, and he hoped to have the deal signed before the News at Ten. In Chapter Two the evening went badly wrong. An owl dropped a letter on Mrs Mason's head, and she ran out of the house shouting about lunatics. Her husband followed, and the deal went with him.

In Book Three, Chapter Two, on the last evening of Aunt Marge's stay in the summer of 1993, Vernon bored them all through the lemon meringue pie with a long talk about Grunnings, his drill-making company.

pages.title: Irish International Side
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The Irish International Side is Ireland's national Quidditch team. In 1993 it ordered seven Firebolts, the fastest racing broom in the world, and it went into the 1994 World Cup as favourite.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry Potter squeezed into the crowd at Quality Quidditch Supplies in Diagon Alley to see the new Firebolt on its podium. 'Irish International Side's just put in an order for seven of these beauties!' the proprietor told the crowd. 'And they're favourites for the World Cup!'

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley wrote to Harry in August 1994 that Ireland would play Bulgaria in the final on Monday night.

pages.title: St Michael's Church (Little Whinging)
aliases: the church at the end of Magnolia Crescent
infobox: Little Whinging, Christianity, church, Christian faith, Church of England, Anglican
End of Magnolia Crescent, Little Whinging, Surrey
Christ in a white robe, over the altar
pages.html:
St Michael's is the small, old Anglican church at the end of Magnolia Crescent, round the corner from Privet Drive in Little Whinging. Its vicar is Gandalf, under the name of Ambrose Greyhame. Since July 1994 Harry Potter has gone to Evensong there every Sunday.

Description

The church has a squat stone tower, circled by screaming swifts in summer, and dark old yew trees. The way in is through a lych-gate, the roofed gateway where a coffin once rested on its way to burial, with a bench inside it. The noticeboard advertises a jumble sale and Evensong on Sundays at 6.30 p.m. Somebody practises the organ, badly.

Inside, the church is small, old and cool. It smells of stone, furniture polish, candles and old hymnbooks. Over the altar is a tall window of old stained glass. It shows Christ in a white robe, with long brown hair and a short brown beard, his hands held out. The congregation at Evensong numbers perhaps fifteen or twenty, nearly all of them elderly, who come chiefly to catch up with one another.

The church is dedicated to Michael the archangel. In the Revelation he fought the dragon, 'that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan'. Michael cast him out of heaven. Gandalf told Harry that the church had been there rather longer than he would think.

Harry Potter and St Michael's

Harry was taken inside once, at Christmas when he was seven, because the Polkisses had started going and Aunt Petunia would not be outdone. He sat at the end of a pew beside Dudley, staring up at the window all through the carols. He saw an old woman make the sign of the cross. In June 1993, in the Chamber of Secrets, he recognised the face in that window.

In the summer of 1993 he walked to St Michael's four times, and each time he stood on the pavement looking at the door without going in. On the fourth evening, in late July, he found a very tall old man in sandals and socks on the bench inside the lych-gate. The old man had been counting his visits. He told Harry that the door was open, and that nobody would ask him for a ticket. When Harry looked back, he was gone. That autumn Trelawney's talk of the Grim, which haunts churchyards, made Harry think of the lych-gate, 'right outside the door I didn't open'.

A week after he came home in July 1994, Harry walked through the lych-gate. He had finished The Lord of the Rings the night before. He pushed the door open while the congregation was saying 'Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord'. Nothing happened, except that the door creaked and an old lady in the back pew gave him a kind, short-sighted smile. The vicar who climbed into the pulpit was the old man from the bench. The window over the altar glowed like coloured fire, though the sun was setting on the other side of the church. Its light reached all the way to the back pew and lay across Harry's hands. The vicar preached on 'Be ye angry, and sin not'.

Harry has gone every Sunday since. Nobody in the congregation speaks to him. The vicar, though, comes down to the back pew after every service to ask how he is getting on. On Harry's second Sunday he gave him a little black Bible.

pages.title: Magnolia Crescent
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Round the corner from the end of Privet Drive
pages.html:
Magnolia Crescent is a street in Little Whinging, just round the corner from the end of Privet Drive. St Michael's Church stands at the far end of it. It was in the Crescent, on the night he left the Dursleys in the summer of 1993, that Harry Potter first saw the great black dog that was Sirius Black.

The street

The Crescent is a street of big square houses with pebbledashed walls, garages and high larch-lap fences. At night one of its streetlamps buzzes. At the end of the road the church stands among dark yew trees, behind a lych-gate, and its noticeboard advertises a jumble sale.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, in July 1993, Harry walked up Magnolia Crescent to St Michael's three times, stood on the pavement looking at the door and went home again. The fourth time, his feet took him to the lych-gate at the end of it on their own.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, on the night he ran away from Privet Drive, Harry sat down on the garden wall of number two. He was sure that something was standing in the dark gap between the garage and the fence behind him. He lit his wand. In the gap stood something far, far too big. He stumbled back, fell over his trunk and landed in the gutter.

In the Book Three Interlude, the Knight Bus stopped dead in the quiet street, which smelt of cut grass and creosote. It picked Harry up from the pavement under a buzzing streetlamp, with John Constantine already aboard. In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry remembered the dog in the gap from the night he was nearly run over by a bus.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, Sirius told Harry that he had been there in his dog form. 'I was in that gap by the garage, at the end of Magnolia Crescent, when round the corner you came.' In the same chapter Harry wondered whether the church at the end of the Crescent was just a building with yew trees round it and a noticeboard about a jumble sale.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, in the summer of 1994, a week after he came home, Harry walked to the end of Privet Drive one Sunday evening. He turned the corner into Magnolia Crescent and went to Evensong at St Michael's.

pages.title: Wisteria Walk
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
Wisteria Walk is a street in Little Whinging, Surrey, between Privet Drive and Magnolia Crescent. Mrs Arabella Figg, the Squib who used to mind Harry Potter whenever the Dursleys went out, lives there.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, Harry went out after dinner because the house was too hot. He walked down Privet Drive, along Wisteria Walk and up Magnolia Crescent, the way you do when you are not going anywhere in particular. His feet took him on to the lych-gate at the end of it all, as they always seemed to.

In Chapter Three, after he had blown up Aunt Marge, Harry dragged his trunk round the corner into Wisteria Walk, past the identical hedges, cars and dark front windows, talking furiously to himself out loud.

pages.title: Brittany
infobox: Hermione Granger, in the summer of 1993
pages.html:
Brittany is the great peninsula of north-western France, where Hermione Granger spent a holiday with her parents in the summer of 1993. Rennes, its chief city, has a wizarding shop so well hidden that, as Hermione said, you would never find it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, Hermione wrote to Harry Potter from Brittany for his thirteenth birthday. She found it lovely, though the Muggle history there was terrible. There had been witch trials everywhere, and she had been to three museums about them, all of which had got nearly everything wrong. In the shop at Rennes she had found him a Broomstick Servicing Kit. She sent it with Hedwig, who had turned up on the balcony of her hotel three nights before, looking very pleased with herself, and would not leave.

In Chapter Two, sending Hedwig off to look for Ron Weasley in Egypt, Harry reminded her that she had found Hermione in France without anyone asking her to. In Chapter Three, on the night he ran away from Privet Drive, he thought of his friends and his heart sank. Ron was in Egypt, and Hermione was in Brittany.

pages.title: Dervish and Banges
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Dervish and Banges is the shop in Hogsmeade for magical instruments. As well as selling them, it will test them and mend them. A man there also deals in second-hand broomsticks.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express, Harry Potter's pocket Sneakoscope went off, and Ron Weasley suggested getting it looked at in Hogsmeade. 'They sell that sort of thing in Dervish and Banges, magical instruments and stuff. Fred and George told me.' In Chapter Eight it was one of the places Ron went with Hermione Granger on the first Hogsmeade weekend, which Harry had to miss.

In Chapter Ten, after Harry's Nimbus was destroyed, Hermione offered to put her Christmas money towards a second-hand Cleansweep from the man in Dervish and Banges, so that Harry would have a proper broom for the Ravenclaw match. Harry would not hear of it.

pages.title: Shrieking Shack
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A tunnel from the Whomping Willow
The most haunted building in Britain
pages.html:
The Shrieking Shack is a lonely, boarded-up house on the hillside above Hogsmeade, said to be the most severely haunted building in Britain. It is not haunted at all. It was built for the young Remus Lupin, so that he would have somewhere safe to go at the full moon while he was at Hogwarts, and the screams the villagers heard there were his.

History

When Lupin came to Hogwarts in 1971, Albus Dumbledore had the house built for him at the far end of a secret tunnel from the school grounds. The Whomping Willow was planted over the mouth of the tunnel, so that nobody could come across him while he was dangerous. Once a month, at the full moon, he was smuggled out of the castle and down the tunnel to transform. With nothing else to attack, he bit and clawed at himself in his rage. The villagers heard the screaming and took it for violent spirits.

Dumbledore encouraged the story that the place was haunted. It has been silent for years, but the villagers still do not dare go near it. Its entrances are sealed, and even the Hogwarts ghosts avoid it.

The house

It stands on its own, a little higher up the hill than any house in the village, with every window boarded over. Its garden has run wild, all brambles and rank grass. Inside, the wallpaper hangs in mouldy strips. Every stick of furniture is smashed. Downstairs, old claw marks have been ripped right through the plaster to the brick, a foot above Harry Potter's head. Upstairs there is a bedroom with a dusty four-poster bed.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter that the Shrieking Shack was supposed to be the most severely haunted building in Britain. In Chapter Eight Percy Weasley said that one naturally ought to see it, though Harry, with no signed form, could not go. In Chapter Ten, on Harry's first secret visit to Hogsmeade in December 1993, Ron and Hermione suggested going up to it, until Ron, whose teeth were chattering, thought of a Butterbeer at the Three Broomsticks instead.

In Chapter Fourteen, on a bright, blowy day in March 1994, Harry slipped into Hogsmeade under his Invisibility Cloak. He and Ron climbed the slope beyond the village to look at the Shack. 'Some say a mad old wizard chopped people to bits in the shack in the 70s,' Ron told him, sounding exactly like a tour guide. Even the Hogwarts ghosts avoided the place, he said, and all its entrances were sealed. Then Dracina Malfoy came over the brow of the hill with Crabbe and Goyle. Harry, invisible, threw mud at her. When Crabbe trod on the hem of the Cloak, it slid off Harry's face, and Dracina saw his head hanging in the air with nothing underneath it.

In Chapter Seventeen, at the end of the school year, a great black dog dragged Ron down between the roots of the Whomping Willow. Harry and Hermione followed him along the tunnel behind Crookshanks, coming up at last into the Shack. The furniture was smashed, the wallpaper hung in strips and the windows were boarded over. Upstairs Crookshanks lay purring on the four-poster, and Ron lay on the floor beside it with a broken leg. The dog was Sirius Black, an Animagus, who was waiting behind the door. In Chapter Eighteen Lupin told them the truth about the house.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, before dawn on the morning after Sirius's escape, Lupin went back to the Shack for his things. He found Harry's Invisibility Cloak on the bed upstairs, folded very neatly.

pages.title: Florean Fortescue's Ice Cream Parlour
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Sundaes; its owner's knowledge of medieval witch-burnings
pages.html:
Florean Fortescue's Ice Cream Parlour stands in Diagon Alley, with tables outside in the sunshine. Its owner, Florean Fortescue, knows a great deal about medieval witch-burnings. In August 1993 he helped Harry Potter with his summer homework and gave him a free sundae every half an hour.

Florean on the burnings

Florean holds that most of the people who burnt witches were not wicked, only frightened. In his telling, the crops had failed, the baby had died and a woman down the lane had said something odd. 'Frightened people do the most dreadful things in the world, and they're still only frightened people.' He does not think that excuses it. But if you want to understand it, he says, you start there.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry sat outside Florean's day after day in August 1993, finishing his essays in the sunshine while Florean read them upside down over his shoulder. Not long afterwards, when Lucius Malfoy had him nodding along to the idea that blood is a fact, something at the back of his head said They were frightened, in Florean's voice. It stopped him nodding. On the last day of the holidays Harry found Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger at one of Florean's tables, waving frantically.

In Chapter Fifteen Harry remembered that he had finished his History of Magic summer essay sitting outside Florean Fortescue's. In Chapter Sixteen every scrap of what Florean had taught him about the medieval witch-hunts went into his History of Magic exam.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, Harry watched the anti-metahuman protests in New York on the news. Looking at the angry faces, he thought of Florean leaning over his essay the summer before, with a knickerbocker glory in his hand. The Muggles who burnt witches had not been monsters, Florean had told him. They had been frightened. These people were frightened too.

pages.title: The Apothecary
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Apothecary is the shop in Diagon Alley where Hogwarts students buy their potion ingredients. It smells of bad eggs and rotten cabbage, but it is so fascinating inside that most people forgive it.

The shop

Barrels of slimy things stand on the floor. Jars of herbs, dried roots and bright powders line the walls. Bundles of feathers, strings of fangs and snarled claws hang from the ceiling. Unicorn horns are among the dearest things on sale; beetle eyes go by the scoop.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Hagrid brushed the soot off Harry Potter so hard that he nearly knocked him into a barrel of dragon dung outside the Apothecary.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry went to the Apothecary to replenish his store of potion ingredients before the new school year. Later that month, walking off his temper, he went up the Alley past it, past the cauldron shop and Eeylops Owl Emporium, where the owls blinked at him in the dark.

pages.title: Eeylops
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Eeylops Owl Emporium is the owl shop in Diagon Alley, a dim place full of soft hooting and blinking eyes. It sells tawny owls, screech owls, barn owls, brown owls and snowy owls. Rubeus Hagrid bought Hedwig there on 31 July 1991, as a present for Harry Potter's eleventh birthday.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry walked up the Alley past Eeylops, where the owls blinked at him out of the gloom. He spent a good deal of that month reading, some of it on the steps outside the shop.

pages.title: Magical Menagerie
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Crookshanks, to Hermione Granger, on 31 August 1993
pages.html:
The Magical Menagerie is a cramped, noisy pet shop in Diagon Alley, where every inch of wall is hidden by cages. Hermione Granger bought her cat Crookshanks there on 31 August 1993, the last day of the summer holidays.

The stock

The shop sells purple toads, a jewelled tortoise, poisonous orange snails, ravens and a rabbit that keeps turning into a silk top hat. There are humming balls of fur, and black rats that skip with their own tails. The witch behind the counter advises customers on the care of their animals. An ordinary common or garden rat, she told Ron Weasley, cannot be expected to live longer than three years or so.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, on 31 August 1993, Ron Weasley brought his rat Scabbers in to be looked at. A huge orange creature leapt from the top of the highest cage, landed on Ron's head and went for the rat. 'NO, CROOKSHANKS, NO!' cried the witch. While Ron and Harry Potter chased Scabbers down the street, Hermione Granger bought the enormous ginger cat.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, at Christmas 1993, Harry remembered the witch's warning that rats go about three years. In Chapter Thirteen Hermione said that Ron had never forgiven Crookshanks for landing on his head.

pages.title: Ollivander's
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
382 BC, by the sign over the door
pages.html:
Ollivander's is the wandmaker's shop in Diagon Alley, and nearly every young witch or wizard in Britain goes there for a first wand. The peeling gold letters over its door say that the Ollivanders have been making fine wands since 382 BC.

The shop

It is a narrow, shabby place. A single wand lies on a faded purple cushion in the dusty window. Inside there is room for little more than one spindly chair, while thousands of narrow boxes are stacked to the ceiling. Mr Ollivander, an old man with wide, pale eyes, remembers every wand he has ever sold. He holds that the wand chooses the wizard, so a customer may try a great many before the right one answers. Harry Potter bought his there in the summer of 1991: holly with a phoenix feather, eleven inches.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, Ron Weasley wrote to Harry from Egypt that he was getting a new wand. 'A proper one, from Ollivander's, since the old one blew up with Lockhart in it.' In Chapter Four, at the end of that August, Ron had it at last: fourteen inches, willow, with one unicorn tail-hair.

pages.title: Abergavenny
pages.html:
Abergavenny is a market town in the old county of Monmouthshire, in south-east Wales, where the Gavenny runs into the Usk. It sits in a ring of hills on the edge of the Brecon Beacons, the Sugar Loaf and the Skirrid among them. Its Norman castle saw a notorious massacre at Christmas 1175, when William de Braose murdered the Welsh lords he had invited to dinner.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, the Knight Bus stopped at Abergavenny to set down old Madam Marsh, who was going to see her grandson. He was seven on Sunday, she said, and he had a bicycle. Stan Shunpike carried her cloak down the stairs with his arms out, ready to catch her, and told her to wish the boy a happy birthday from Stan. Harry suspected that Stan had worked out exactly who he was somewhere around Abergavenny.

The Book Three Interlude tells the same stop from the side of John Constantine, who was on the bus that night.

pages.title: Aberdeen
pages.html:
Aberdeen is a city on the north-east coast of Scotland, between the mouths of the Dee and the Don. It is called the Granite City, from the grey stone it is built of. Since the 1970s it has been the capital of the North Sea oil industry.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, the Knight Bus jumped from Anglesey to Aberdeen in a single bound on the night it carried Harry Potter to London. Stan Shunpike, who had just remembered Harry's hot chocolate, spilt it all over his pillow. A dodgy-looking passenger with a Liverpool accent sat on through Aberdeen with his hand on his bag; he was John Constantine. Somewhere around Aberdeen, Harry decided that he liked Stan.

pages.title: Anglesey
pages.html:
Anglesey is the large island off the north-west coast of Wales, across the Menai Strait from the mainland. The Welsh call it Môn, Mam Cymru, the mother of Wales, because its fields once fed the country.

History

It was the last stronghold of the druids, whom the Roman governor Suetonius Paulinus put to the sword there in AD 60 or 61. Two bridges now cross the Strait: Telford's suspension bridge of 1826 and Stephenson's Britannia Bridge of 1850.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, the Knight Bus passed through Anglesey on the night it carried Harry Potter to London. It then jumped straight to Aberdeen, which is how Harry came to have hot chocolate all over his pillow. The Book Three Interlude tells the same night from the seat of John Constantine, who was on the bus with him.

pages.title: Charing Cross Road
pages.html:
Charing Cross Road is a street in the West End of London, long known to Muggles for its bookshops. Between a big bookshop and a record shop stands the Leaky Cauldron, the small, grubby wizarding pub that leads through to Diagon Alley. Most of London has never noticed it in its life.

The Leaky Cauldron

Witches and wizards pass through the pub on their way to the shops. Muggles walk straight past it without seeing it. Rubeus Hagrid first brought Harry Potter this way in the summer of 1991, to buy his school things.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, the Knight Bus brought Harry to London after he had run away from Privet Drive. It set him down on Charing Cross Road outside the Leaky Cauldron, where Cornelius Fudge was waiting for him. In the Book Three Interlude John Constantine, who had been riding the same bus, watched the boy get off just before dawn. John had not been inside the Leaky Cauldron since 1971. He did not intend to go in now.

pages.title: Birmingham
infobox: 30 July 1993, on the Bull Ring shopping centre
pages.html:
Birmingham is a large Muggle city in the West Midlands of England. On the afternoon of 30 July 1993 its city centre was evacuated for six hours while a giant creature attacked the Bull Ring shopping centre.

The Bull Ring attack

The creature was pink and enormous, with far too many arms. Eyewitnesses said it looked like a starfish the size of a double-decker bus. It came up out of the canal basin near Gas Street and went for the Bull Ring. The Power Rangers, the team from California, came straight over and engaged it with their combat vehicle shortly after four o'clock. Nobody was killed, though a number of shoppers were treated for shock. West Midlands Police asked anyone who knew where the creature had come from to come forward.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, on 31 July 1993, the news at Privet Drive showed film of the fight taken from a helicopter. Dudley Dursley watched it with a sausage halfway to his mouth, his eyes gone round and shining. It was, Harry thought, the first time he had ever seen Dudley want to be anything.

In Chapter Four, walking down Diagon Alley with Lucius Malfoy, Harry spoke up for the Muggles who help. He told Lucius that he had seen the Power Rangers on the news in Birmingham, fighting a starfish the size of a bus in a shopping centre. They had no magic at all, not a drop, and they went to stand in front of it all the same.

pages.title: North Tower
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A spiral staircase, then a silver ladder through a trapdoor
pages.html:
The North Tower is one of the high towers of Hogwarts, and one of the hardest to reach. At the very top of it is the Divination classroom, where Professor Sybill Trelawney teaches. There is no door. A narrow spiral staircase ends on a little landing, and the only way on is through a round trapdoor in the ceiling, from which a silver ladder slides down.

The Divination room

A brass plate screwed to the trapdoor reads 'Professor S. Trelawney. Divination'. Above it is a hot, dim, stuffy room that looks less like a classroom than somebody's crowded attic made over into a tea room. Twenty or more little round tables are jammed together inside, each ringed with chintz armchairs or squashy pouffes. The curtains are kept drawn, and every lamp has a dark red scarf thrown over it. A fire burns under the cluttered mantelpiece, boiling a big copper kettle and giving off a heavy, sickly perfume. The shelves round the walls are crammed with feathers, candle-ends, greasy packs of cards, crystal balls by the dozen and more teacups than Harry Potter had ever seen in one place.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on the first morning of lessons in September 1993, Ron Weasley found Divination on his timetable. 'Divination's right at the top of North Tower,' he said. 'That's miles.' None of the three friends had ever been up that corner of the castle. By the seventh staircase they were lost, until the knight Sir Cadogan led them the rest of the way. The stair came out on a landing crowded with the class. The trapdoor swung open as if it had heard Harry ask how they were to get up, and the silver ladder slid down to his feet.

In Chapter Eight, by the autumn, Harry had come to dread the hours in that hot, scented, crowded little room. He spent them squinting at shapeless brown splodges in the bottoms of teacups, while Professor Trelawney's enormous swimming eyes filled up every time they landed on him.

In Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, the class moved on to crystal balls. Hermione Granger, who had somehow missed Cheering Charms, was waiting under the silver ladder looking extremely harassed. Up in the stuffy tower room every little table held a ball glowing with milky mist. When Professor Trelawney saw something moving in Harry's, he asked her politely whether it was a dove, since he would like to know which sort of sign it was before he started panicking. Ron fell off his pouffe. Then Professor Trelawney told Hermione that she had never met a student whose mind was so hopelessly mundane. 'I give up! I'm leaving!' said Hermione. She stamped over to the trapdoor, booted it open and climbed out of sight. Afterwards they found her sitting on her bag at the bottom of the North Tower staircase. 'I've never felt better,' she announced.

pages.title: Metropolis
infobox: Home of Superman; the Daily Planet; LexCorp
pages.html:
Metropolis is the great American city that Superman has called home since 1938. Half of it was torn up in 1992 in the fight in which Doomsday killed him. In May 1994 its downtown was flattened by sonic torpedoes fired by Lex Luthor's aide, so that the news now speaks of ‘what remains of Metropolis’.

Superman's city

Metropolis has been Superman's city for more than half a century. He worked there as Clark Kent, a reporter on the Daily Planet, whose building was crowned by a great globe. There, too, Lex Luthor built LexCorp into the most powerful company in the city, with its headquarters in a tall L-shaped tower.

The city is home to a branch of S.T.A.R. Labs and to a police Special Crimes Unit for superhuman trouble. It also has a rough district called Suicide Slum. No other city has seen so many battles fought over its roofs. For most of the century its people regarded that as the price of having Superman.

It was in Metropolis, in front of the Daily Planet, that Superman and Doomsday killed each other on 18 November 1992. The fight tore up half the city. Superman was buried there, in a memorial tomb in Centennial Park, before his return in 1993.

The fall of downtown

In May 1994 Superman and the authorities hunted down Lex Luthor. His deceptions had been exposed, and his body was failing. Beneath Metropolis he had hidden sonic torpedoes reverse-engineered from the weapons left behind by the alien invasion of 1988.

Luthor was persuaded not to fire them, but his aide, Dr Sydney Happersen, launched them anyway. Superman and his allies stopped most of them. The rest flattened downtown, destroying the Daily Planet building, LexCorp's tower and a great many others. Happersen died in Superman's arms.

The city has had little time to rebuild between the two disasters, and insurers have often refused to pay. By the summer of 1994 its people were among the angriest in the country. ‘Who pays for Metropolis?’ was being carried on placards in New York.

In the saga

In August 1993 Harry Potter recalled that Superman had died fighting ‘some grey monstrous thing out of nowhere that had torn up half an American city called Metropolis’.

On 20 August 1994 the news reported protests overnight in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and ‘what remains of Metropolis’. A man in a suit with a black eye shouted at the cameras that Doomsday had knocked his building down in 1992. He had rebuilt, and then in May ‘some lunatic in a lab coat flattened downtown with torpedoes left over from the alien invasion’. ‘Every time they fight over Metropolis,’ he said, ‘we're the ones underneath!’

pages.title: New Delhi
infobox: The forces of Khan Noonien Singh, late July 1993
pages.html:
New Delhi is the capital of India. In late July 1993, after a siege of eleven weeks, it fell to the forces of Khan Noonien Singh, the foremost of the Augments. The Indian government withdrew to Bangalore, and Delhi has been in Khan's hands ever since.

The Augment War

In March 1994, under a United Nations mandate, the largest multinational force assembled since the Gulf War crossed the front line south of Delhi. American, Russian, British and French troops fought side by side for the first time since 1945. They were expected to reach the city within a month. They were withdrawn in June, having advanced eleven miles. By August 1994 Khan's territory stretched from Bengal to the Gulf, and was home to roughly a quarter of the world's population.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in late July 1993, the television news reported that Khan's forces had completed their advance on New Delhi, ending a siege of eleven weeks. The man on the screen stood on a balcony above a crowd, with his chin up and his eyes half closed. In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, Harry Potter thought of the man on the balcony in Delhi the summer before, and his face went hot.

pages.title: St Brutus's Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Marjorie Dursley; the neighbours of Privet Drive
pages.html:
St Brutus's Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys is the school the Dursleys say Harry Potter attends. Uncle Vernon calls it a first-rate institution for hopeless cases. By the summer of 1994 they had been telling the neighbours for three years that Harry spent his terms there, since the truth was not to be thought of.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, Uncle Vernon told Harry that they had told his sister Marge he attended St Brutus's. He was to stick to that story, or there would be trouble. Harry pointed out how hard it would be to keep up in front of Aunt Marge. With a little blackmail besides, he got Uncle Vernon to promise to sign his Hogsmeade form if he behaved himself.

At tea Aunt Marge asked where it was they sent him. 'St Brutus's,' said Uncle Vernon promptly. 'It's a first-rate institution for hopeless cases.' Then Marge barked across the table: 'Do they use the cane at St Brutus's, boy?' Harry said that they did. 'All the time. Got all the marks from it and everything.' It earned him the first approving nod Uncle Vernon had given him in twelve years. It was for lying about being beaten.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, the Dursleys had been telling the neighbours for three years that Harry spent his terms at St Brutus's.

pages.title: St Grogory's
infobox: Muggle school, Little Whinging, Muggle, school
pages.html:
St Grogory's is the primary school in Little Whinging where Harry Potter and his cousin Dudley Dursley were pupils until 1991. Harry remembers it mostly for the ways in which it let him down. It was also where, without paying it much attention, he learnt the Lord's Prayer and heard a verse of Scripture that came back to him years later.

Harry at St Grogory's

Dudley's gang made sure that nobody at school would be Harry's friend. A teacher once held up his school jumper in front of the whole class to show them what neglect looked like. The same teacher let Dudley off for breaking Harry's glasses in the playground, because boys will be boys. A dinner lady slipped Harry an extra bread roll every day for a fortnight, until Aunt Petunia came in to complain about the jumper; after that the dinner lady never looked at him again. Once, running from Dudley's gang, Harry found himself on the roof of the school kitchens, and the Dursleys had a very angry letter from the headmistress.

Morning assembly was where Harry stood through the Lord's Prayer, with Dudley pinching him or kicking his chair from the row behind.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the memory of that teacher came up with the rest of Harry's anger, in a hot, tight knot under his ribs. In Chapter Thirteen he remembered the dinner lady. Her turning away had hurt more than all the people who had never been kind to him in the first place.

In Chapter Fourteen, watching Remus Lupin at the foot of the marble staircase, Harry knew from St Grogory's assemblies the shape of the words his lips were making: 'as we forgive those who trespass against us'. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, the words 'Be ye angry, and sin not' went round in Harry's head. He had heard them long ago in assembly at St Grogory's, with Dudley kicking the back of his chair.

pages.title: Cedric Diggory
infobox: Hufflepuff, Hufflepuff Quidditch team, Seeker, Quidditch captain, Hogwarts student
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
Amos Diggory, of the Ministry of Magic
pages.html:
Cedric Diggory (born 1977) is a Hufflepuff, tall, handsome and thoroughly decent. He became his house's Quidditch captain and Seeker in 1993. In November 1993 he caught the Snitch just as Harry Potter fell from his broom. As soon as he found out what had happened, he tried to have the match played again.

Background

Cedric is the only son of Amos Diggory, who works at the Ministry of Magic in the Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures. The family lives near Ottery St Catchpole, not far from the Weasleys. His wand came from Ollivander's: ash, with a unicorn hair core, twelve and a quarter inches long.

He is liked all over the school, not only in his own house. Alicia Spinnet called him strong and quiet.

In the saga

In 1993, as a fifth-year, Cedric became Hufflepuff's new captain and Seeker. The Gryffindor match that November was played in a hurricane. When the dementors came onto the pitch, Harry fell from his broom, and at that moment Cedric caught the Snitch. Hufflepuff won by a hundred points. Once Cedric learnt what had happened, he offered a rematch, which Oliver Wood refused. At the end of November he lost the Snitch to a small Ravenclaw girl.

When he met Harry again in 1994 he admired the Firebolt's hand-finished tail without touching it. He said he was sorry about the Whomping Willow smashing Harry's Nimbus. He explained that he had asked for the November match to be replayed because he had not known Harry had fallen. 'Honestly, I'd have felt better if he'd let me give it back.' Harry decided that Cedric was everything Gilderoy Lockhart had only pretended to be.

In their own words

Honestly, I'd have felt better if he'd let me give it back.Cedric Diggory · B3 Ch13

pages.title: Montague
infobox: Slytherin, Slytherin Quidditch team, Chaser, Hogwarts student, Quidditch
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Montague is a Chaser on the Slytherin Quidditch team, playing alongside Marcus Flint. In 1994 he helped Flint dream up the fake-dementor prank at the Ravenclaw match, and he was one of those who pushed Dracina Malfoy into it.

Soft on Potter

From November 1993 Flint, Montague and half the Slytherin team kept saying that Dracina had gone soft on Potter. She went and sat with the Gryffindors at their practices, they said; whose side was she on? Montague said it to her face in the common room, in front of everybody.

With Flint he worked out a prank for the Ravenclaw match in March 1994. Figures in stolen hooded robes would stand up as dementors below Harry's broom while he reached for the Snitch. Flint said that if Dracina would not help, he would write to her father himself. She agreed, she told Professor Snape afterwards, only to make them stop before her father heard about it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, the Slytherins passed the Gryffindor team on the path to the pitch. Dracina, her arm still in its sling, put on a show of brave suffering for Harry's benefit. She swayed very slightly, so that Montague had to put out a hand to steady her.

In Chapter Fourteen, after the Ravenclaw match, Dracina told Snape how the prank had come about. 'It was Flint's idea. Flint's, Montague's, half the team's.'

In Chapter Fifteen, in the final against Gryffindor, Montague cut across in front of Katie Bell and grabbed her head instead of the ball. Katie spun head over heels in the air. Madam Hooch swooped on Montague with a furious telling-off, and Katie scored the penalty. Later Montague scored for Slytherin, making it seventy points to twenty. When the match was lost he stood at the edge of the pitch kicking the turf.

pages.title: Bellatrix Lestrange
infobox:
Narcissa Malfoy sister
Sirius Black relative, cousin
Black family (implied), Black family, Death Eaters
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (July 2000)
pages.html:
Bellatrix Lestrange, born Bellatrix Black, is the sister of Narcissa Malfoy and a cousin of Sirius Black. She is one of Lord Voldemort's most devoted Death Eaters. Since the end of the first war she has been in Azkaban, in the cell next to her cousin's.

Early life

Bellatrix was born into the House of Black, one of the oldest pure-blood families in Britain, whose motto is Toujours pur. She was a daughter of Cygnus Black and Druella Rosier. She and her sister Narcissa were born within twelve months of each other. They started at Hogwarts together in 1971, in the same year as James Potter, Lily Evans and their cousin Sirius. Bellatrix was the black-haired sister, Narcissa the fair one. Their other sister, Andromeda, married the Muggle-born Ted Tonks, and the family cast her out.

Both girls fell for James Potter. Professor Flitwick remembers them feuding across his Charms classroom for years, with hexes and flowers. Remus Lupin remembers them in the entrance hall, trying to hex each other's eyebrows off over James, while James stood between them looking bewildered. It ended only when Lily Evans came along and won him. Flitwick says that neither sister ever quite forgave anybody afterwards. Around the time of the Potters' wedding Sirius was still 'putting out the fires from Bella'.

Death Eater

Bellatrix married Rodolphus Lestrange, of another old pure-blood family. She followed Voldemort with a fanatic's devotion, and after his fall in 1981 she refused to renounce him. She tortured the Aurors Frank and Alice Longbottom with the Cruciatus Curse, hoping to learn where their master had gone. With her were her husband, his brother Rabastan and Barty Crouch the younger. All four of them were sentenced to life in Azkaban.

In the saga

Bellatrix spent twelve years in the cell next to Sirius Black's. Sirius says that she went completely round the twist. When he speaks of 'Bella', he says the name the way people at funerals say the names of the dead.

On Myst Island in 1994 Sirius met a woman who talked in riddles, who was dreadfully sad about something and had a lovely laugh when you could get it out of her. She reminded him of Bella, as Bella had been before she went mad. Later he saw Harry Potter caught between Dracina Malfoy and Hermione Granger. 'Bella and Cissy,' he murmured, to nobody in particular. 'Bella and Cissy, all over again. God help the boy.'

pages.title: Dracina Malfoy's grandmother Black
infobox: Bellatrix Lestrange; Andromeda Tonks; Narcissa Malfoy
A silver serpent brooch with emerald eyes
pages.html:
Grandmother Black is Dracina Malfoy's grandmother on her mother's side, born Druella Rosier. The silver serpent brooch with two emerald eyes that Dracina wore in her plaits at Hogwarts in 1993 had once been hers. Dracina said it was worth more than Goyle's house.

Family

She married Cygnus Black, of the House of Black, whose motto is Toujours pur. They had three daughters. Bellatrix and Narcissa were born within twelve months of each other. They were in the same year at Hogwarts as James Potter. Bellatrix married Rodolphus Lestrange. Andromeda married the Muggle-born Ted Tonks, and the family struck her off. Narcissa married Lucius Malfoy, and their only child is Dracina.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1993, Dracina found after Potions that the brooch had gone from her plaits. 'It was Grandmother's, it was Grandmother Black's, it's worth more than your house, Goyle...' Peeves turned up wearing it on his bow tie, crowing that he had found it by the dungeon steps.
