Professor Lupin's Waddiwasi charm shot a wad of chewing gum up his nose. Peeves tore the brooch off as he fled and flung it into a fire bucket. The whole class burst out laughing, Slytherins and all. Dracina knelt by the bucket and fished it out with her good arm.

Later Harry found himself thinking of a skitter of silver and green on the dungeon steps. He thought, too, of the blank look on Hermione Granger's face just before she said how sorry she was. He told himself not to be stupid, since Hermione had been with him all day. Everything points to Hermione as the one who took it.

pages.title: Dracina's paternal grandfather
infobox: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (16 July 2005)
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's paternal grandfather, Abraxas Malfoy, is Lucius Malfoy's father. By the family's account he was never second at anything. It was from him that the young Lucius learnt the blood prejudices he repeated in the Slytherin common room.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, Dracina faced the boggart in Remus Lupin's Defence Against the Dark Arts class, and it became her father. It told her coldly that she was second in Potions behind a Mudblood, second in Charms and beaten to the Snitch. ‘Your grandfather was never second at anything,’ it said. There had not been a Malfoy who came second in eleven hundred years, it went on, and it had rather hoped that the first one would not be its only child.

pages.title: Dracina's cousin
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's cousin is a relation of hers who said something at dinner in the summer of 1993 that Dracina thought worth repeating. Nobody knows what it was. The one person she told was not listening.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, Harry Potter was brewing two Shrinking Solutions at once in Potions, his own and Dracina's, because she said her arm was too badly hurt for her to work. She talked to him the whole time about the summer: her mother's roses at the Manor, a peacock that had got into the orangery, and something her cousin had said at dinner. Harry said ‘mm’ and counted drops. After ten minutes she told him he had not heard a single thing she had said.

pages.title: Peter Pettigrew
infobox:
Pettigrew's mother mother
Sirius Black school friend, former friend
Scabbers rat form
Lord Voldemort master
James Potter betrayed friend
Ron Weasley owner of his rat form
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (June 1997), as Scabbers
The Marauders; the Order of the Phoenix (as a spy); servant of Lord Voldemort
Order of Merlin, First Class (awarded in the belief that he was dead)
pages.html:
Peter Pettigrew is the wizard who betrayed James and Lily Potter to Lord Voldemort. He was their Secret-Keeper, and he gave them up. Then he faked his own death, framed Sirius Black for it and hid for twelve years as the Weasley family's pet rat, Scabbers. He escaped again in June 1994, on the very night it had been foretold that the Dark Lord's servant would set out to rejoin his master.

School and the Marauders

At Hogwarts Peter was a plump boy who trailed after James Potter and Sirius Black, worshipping them both. Professor McGonagall remembers that he was always hopeless at duelling. With Remus Lupin, the four of them were the Marauders, and Peter, who was called Wormtail, helped to make the Marauder's Map. When James and Sirius became Animagi to keep Lupin company at the full moon, Peter needed their help to manage it. His shape was a rat. Being the smallest, he could slip under the Whomping Willow's branches to press the knot that froze it.

After the Potters married, Peter followed Lupin and James into the Christian faith, though in form only. He was never serious about it. He performed it well enough to satisfy everybody all the same, Lily included. Sirius, the honest unbeliever of the group, always doubted that Peter was truly faithful. Peter has always attached himself to powerful protectors.

The betrayal

For a year before the Potters died, Peter had been passing information to Voldemort. When they went into hiding under the Fidelius Charm, Sirius persuaded them at the last moment to make Peter their Secret-Keeper instead of himself, believing that nobody would ever suspect him. Peter gave them up. On 31 October 1981 Voldemort came to Godric's Hollow.

The next day Sirius cornered him in a street full of Muggles. Peter yelled, for the whole street to hear, 'Lily and James, Sirius! How could you?' Then, with a wand he had been holding behind his back, he blew the street apart, killing everyone within twenty feet of him. He cut off his own finger and fled into the sewers as a rat. The world believed that Sirius had killed thirteen people with a single curse, Peter among them.

The biggest piece of Peter ever found was the finger. It was sent to his mother in a box, together with the Order of Merlin, First Class, which the Ministry had awarded him after his supposed death. Sirius went to Azkaban for the murders.

Scabbers

Peter spent the next twelve years as a rat, hiding from Voldemort's old supporters, who believed he had double-crossed them. The Weasleys took him in as Percy's pet. Later he was handed down to Ron, the definitive Weasley hand-me-down, and for three years he slept in Harry Potter's dormitory. In 1991, on the Hogwarts Express, he bit Gregory Goyle on the knuckle.

In 1993 the Daily Prophet printed a photograph of the Weasleys in Egypt, with the rat on Ron's shoulder and a toe missing from his front paw. The newspaper reached Sirius Black in Azkaban, and Sirius knew him at once.

Hermione's cat, Crookshanks, saw through him from the start. In early 1994, realising that the cat was hunting him, Peter fled. He left blood and ginger hairs on Ron's sheets. It was his second faked death, and it cost Ron his friendship with Hermione for weeks. Harry, Ron and Hermione found him again, very much alive, in a milk jug in Hagrid's hut on the day of Buckbeak's execution.

In the saga: unmasked

In the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Sirius Black and Remus Lupin forced Peter back into his own shape. He was a very small man, with thin, colourless hair, a bald patch, sagging grey skin, a sharp nose and small, watery eyes. Where his first finger should have been, there was a stump. He reeked so strongly of dark magic and the Wyrm that Lupin was nearly driven into his war form.

Peter cringed, begging Ron, Hermione and Harry for mercy. He told Harry that he looked just like his father. He pleaded with Sirius that Voldemort would have killed him. It was Harry who stopped Sirius and Lupin from killing him, so that he could be handed over to the dementors as proof of Sirius's innocence.

They bound and gagged him. Then they chained him between Lupin and Ron to march him up to the lawn. When the full moon rose and Lupin changed, Peter seized Lupin's dropped wand. He struck down Ron and Crookshanks. Then he turned into a rat and escaped.

In the saga: afterwards

That afternoon, at the end of Harry's Divination examination, Professor Trelawney had fallen into a trance. She foretold that the Dark Lord's servant would break free that night to rejoin his master, and help him return to power. Dumbledore told Harry afterwards that by sparing Peter's life he had created a bond between them: Peter owes him a debt. James, Dumbledore said, would have spared him too.

In their own words

Harry... Harry... you look just like your father... just like him...Peter Pettigrew · B3 Ch18
You don't understand! He would have killed me, Sirius!Peter Pettigrew · B3 Ch18

pages.title: Pettigrew's mother
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
His Order of Merlin, First Class; his finger, in a box
pages.html:
Pettigrew's mother is the woman whose son, Peter Pettigrew, was believed to have been murdered by Sirius Black in November 1981. The Ministry of Magic sent her his Order of Merlin, First Class, together with his finger in a box. The finger was the biggest piece of him anybody could find.

The truth

The Ministry was wrong. Peter had blown the street apart himself, cut off his own finger and escaped down the sewers as a rat. He was unmasked in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, and he got away again that same night.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, in December 1993, Ron Weasley tried to frighten Harry Potter out of going after Black: 'Listen... you know what Pettigrew's mother got back after Black had finished with him? Dad told me. The Order of Merlin, First Class, and Pettigrew's finger in a box. That was the biggest bit of him they could find.'

pages.title: Madam Rosmerta
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Sirius Black and James Potter as schoolboys
pages.html:
Madam Rosmerta keeps the Three Broomsticks, the inn at Hogsmeade where Hogwarts students drink Butterbeer. She is a curvy woman with a pretty face, a quick smile and a laugh that carries over the noise of a full bar. She wears sparkly turquoise high heels. She has kept the inn long enough to remember Sirius Black and James Potter as a schoolboy double act.

The Three Broomsticks

The Three Broomsticks is warm, crowded, smoky and cheerful, with a fire roaring at one end. Madam Rosmerta serves at the bar herself, and brings the drinks to the tables on a tray. In December 1993 Ron Weasley went slightly red at the sight of her, and straightened his scarf on his way up to the bar. The teachers of Hogwarts drink there, and so does the Minister for Magic, Cornelius Fudge, who calls her 'm'dear'.

In the autumn of 1993 the dementors sent to guard Hogwarts against Sirius Black searched the village twice, house by house. They frightened off half her trade. By December a Ministry notice warned that dementors would patrol the streets of Hogsmeade every night after sundown until Black was caught. It was no better for business.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, on the last Hogsmeade weekend before Christmas 1993, Harry Potter was hiding under a table behind the Christmas tree in the Three Broomsticks when Madam Rosmerta sat down with Fudge, Professor McGonagall, Professor Flitwick and Hagrid. She complained to Fudge about the dementors. 'They've frightened off half my trade. It's very bad for business.'

Of everyone who might have gone over to the Dark Side, she said, she would have put Sirius Black last on the list. She remembered him as a boy, in her pub. You never saw him without James Potter. 'Sirius Black and James Potter! What a double act they were.' Then she heard Fudge tell the whole story of the Potters' betrayal, and of the street where Black was supposed to have laughed among the bodies.

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Harry remembered that afternoon: the Minister telling Madam Rosmerta and a table full of teachers how worried he was, without doing anything whatever about it.

In their own words

Sirius Black and James Potter! What a double act they were.Madam Rosmerta · B3 Ch10

pages.title: Davey Gudgeon
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Nearly losing an eye to the Whomping Willow
pages.html:
Davey Gudgeon was a Hogwarts student in the early 1970s who nearly lost an eye to the Whomping Willow. The tree had been planted in 1971, Remus Lupin's first year at the school. After Davey's accident, nobody was allowed near it.

The Willow

The Willow was planted over the mouth of the secret tunnel to the Shrieking Shack, the way the young Lupin was smuggled out of the castle at the full moon. The students soon made a game of it, getting as close as they dared to touch the trunk.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in November 1993, the Willow had smashed Harry Potter's Nimbus Two Thousand to pieces. Professor Lupin told Harry that the tree had gone in during his own first year. There was a game people used to play, he said, getting as close as they dared. In the end a boy called Davey Gudgeon came within an inch of losing an eye, and after that they were not allowed near it.

pages.title: Derek
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Derek is a Hogwarts student who started at the school in September 1993. He was one of the handful of students who stayed at the castle over Christmas that year.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, he was one of two first-years at the Christmas lunch of 1993. The House tables had been cleared to the walls, and a single round table was laid for a dozen in the middle of the Great Hall. The company included Dumbledore, McGonagall, Snape, Sprout, Flitwick and Filch, the last in a tailcoat so old that it had gone green at the seams. It so overawed the two first-years that they stopped eating. Derek was the smaller of the two. Dumbledore turned on him, beaming. "Derek. Have you had any of these chipolatas? They are particularly good this year."

pages.title: The other first-year at Christmas lunch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The other first-year at Christmas lunch was one of two first-years who stayed at Hogwarts over Christmas 1993; Derek was the other. The company at the table so overawed the pair that they stopped eating.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, the House tables had been cleared to the walls for Christmas lunch, and a single round table was laid for a dozen in the middle of the Great Hall. Dumbledore sat there with McGonagall, Snape, Sprout and Flitwick, along with Filch in an ancient tailcoat gone green at the seams. Apart from Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, there were only three pupils. One was a Slytherin fifth-year with a face like a wet Tuesday. The other two were first-years, so overcome by the company that they had stopped eating. Derek was the smaller of them. Nothing more is recorded of the other.

pages.title: The Slytherin fifth-year at Christmas lunch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Christmas lunch in the Great Hall, 1993
pages.html:
The Slytherin fifth-year at Christmas lunch was one of the very few pupils who stayed at Hogwarts over Christmas 1993. The fifth-year sat through the meal with a face like a wet Tuesday.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, so few people were left in the castle on Christmas Day that the House tables had been cleared to the walls. A single round table stood in the middle of the Great Hall, laid for a dozen. Dumbledore sat at it with Professors McGonagall, Snape, Sprout and Flitwick. Filch had come too, buttoned into a tailcoat so old that it had gone green at the seams. Besides Harry and his friends there were only three pupils. Two were first-years so overcome by the company that they had stopped eating. The third was the gloomy Slytherin fifth-year.

pages.title: The Honeydukes shopkeeper
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Very large, with a shining bald head
pages.html:
The Honeydukes shopkeeper is a very large, bald wizard who works at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. Honeydukes is run by Ambrosius Flume, and its owners live over the shop.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry Potter climbed up into the Honeydukes cellar through the secret passage from the statue of the one-eyed witch at Hogwarts. A voice called down the cellar stair for another box of Jelly Slugs, and a pair of heavy boots came down past him. Harry hid behind the largest crate while the shopkeeper shifted boxes at the far wall, grunting. Then Harry crept up the wooden stair on his toes. Looking back from the top, he saw only a very large backside and a shining bald head, both buried to the shoulders in a box marked SLUGS, JELLY, 144. He slipped through the door behind the counter, and nobody noticed.

Later that afternoon Hermione Granger worried that Sirius Black might use the same passage. Ron Weasley pointed out that the owners would hear a break-in. "They live over the shop!"

pages.title: The old wizard at the Hogsmeade quill shop
infobox: A little shop at the end of Hogsmeade that sells nothing but quills
pages.html:
The old wizard at the Hogsmeade quill shop runs a little shop at the end of the village that sells nothing but quills: hundreds of them, eagle, peacock and phoenix. He lets his customers try them all, and never minds if they leave without buying anything.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Harry Potter had no signed permission form, so he could not go to Hogsmeade. Dracina Malfoy told him it was very unfair. Hogsmeade itself was not much, she said, only a village, but she thought he would have liked the quill shop best of all. She had been going to show him. "Next time, perhaps." Harry said yes, next time, when Black was caught: in about fifty years, when he would have a beard and need a quill to sign his pension.

pages.title: The Ravenclaw Seeker
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 10
Beating Cedric Diggory to the Snitch, November 1993
pages.html:
The Ravenclaw Seeker is the tiny Ravenclaw girl who beat Cedric Diggory to the Snitch at the end of November 1993, when Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff. She went past him like a thrown dart.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry Potter watched the match from the stands between Ron and Hermione Granger. He saw big, steady, decent Cedric, who had offered Gryffindor a rematch, lose the Snitch to her. Ravenclaw's win put Gryffindor back in the race for the Cup. Harry found himself on his feet, roaring, while Ron did the arithmetic beside him at the top of his voice.

Harry did not learn her name that day. When Gryffindor played Ravenclaw in March 1994, the Ravenclaw Seeker was Cho Chang, a fourth-year who barely came up to Harry's chin. Oliver Wood had hoped she would not be fit, since she had had some problems with injuries.

pages.title: The Muggle woman with the dog
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The hotline on the Muggle news
pages.html:
The Muggle woman with the dog saw Sirius Black not far from Hogwarts in the autumn of 1993, while she was out walking her dog. She rang the number they had been putting on the television.

The sighting

To the Muggles, Black was an ordinary convict who had broken out of a Muggle prison. The Muggle news had given out a special hotline for anyone who saw him. She did not know what she was looking at, but she rang it. By the time the Ministry of Magic got there, he was gone without a trace.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, Seamus Finnigan leaned across in Potions to pass on the news from that morning's Prophet to Harry Potter and Ron Weasley, rather enjoying himself. Dracina Malfoy, who had been sitting beside Harry for an hour, said nothing, but Harry felt her go still at his elbow.

pages.title: The second-year Hufflepuff
pages.html:
The second-year Hufflepuff is a Hogwarts boy whom Vincent Crabbe and Gregory Goyle started on in a corridor in the autumn of 1993. Dracina Malfoy stopped them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Dracina was being nice to everybody, which Harry Potter found very hard to account for. When Crabbe and Goyle started on the Hufflepuff in the corridor, in front of Harry, she stopped them: leave him alone, he's not worth the bother. It was not exactly kind. It was a great deal kinder than Crabbe and Goyle had ever been told to be.

pages.title: The social worker
pages.html:
The social worker came once to Number Four, Privet Drive, with a folder, while Harry Potter was growing up there. She never came back.

Privet Drive

She looked at Harry once in the Dursleys' front room, with her head on one side, then went away. Whatever she made of him, nothing changed.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, lying in the hospital wing after the dementors came to the Quidditch pitch, Harry dreamt of paying back everyone who had hurt him, with Dracina Malfoy at his shoulder. When the social worker came, it was Dracina who said that one, Harry, that one especially.

pages.title: The young man with the three rules
aliases: the young man with the three rules
pages.html:
The young man with the three rules was Minerva McGonagall's partner on a mission into Siberia in the winter of 1966, and on a number of others after it. He was about her own age, and she is not permitted to tell anybody his name. He was Big Boss, the soldier who had brought Operation Snake Eater to its end two years before.

Siberia

The target was a village forty miles past the last road, full of men who had been doing something to the people in the valley below for the better part of thirty years. The Ministry of Magic declined to recognise that the place existed. Somebody had to go. McGonagall went, with nobody but him. There were nine of them. Two, she holds, is the right number. They waited four days in the snow, until the men came out to them because they were bored.

The three rules

He taught her three things, and she has found no reason since to amend any of them. The first is that you do not announce yourself: a wand held out in front of you at a doorway is a declaration of intent, and also a thing to be grabbed. The second is that most people are beaten by the weather and their own appetites before anybody fights them at all. The third is that the most dangerous moment in any engagement is not the beginning but the moment after you believe you have won, when the heat is still in you and your judgement is not. He put it better, she says. The hard part is not learning to carry a weapon; it is learning to put it down.

Afterwards

The two partners did a number of such things together. In 1972 his genome was taken without his knowledge to make Solid Snake and Liquid Snake. McGonagall knows nothing of it. She has had no word of him in some years. The silence is hers as much as his: they have been estranged since 1984, over what he did to the man who became his decoy.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, at Christmas dinner in 1993, Professor Flitwick asked McGonagall about a scar on the back of her hand. She answered with Siberia, the young man and his three rules, looking straight down the table at Harry Potter as she gave them. When Professor Sprout asked where her young man with the three rules was now, McGonagall was a moment answering.

‘I have not had word of him in some years,’ she said. ‘We did a number of these things together, in the end. He was the better of the two of us, and it did him no good whatever; the people who use men like that use them up.’ Then she told Sprout to eat her pudding before it went cold. Harry had caught the look on her face before she turned it away. It belonged to somebody talking about a person who had died, or had gone somewhere they could not be written to.

pages.title: The man in white by a pillar
infobox: Long brown hair, a beard, a plain white robe
pages.html:
The man in white by a pillar is the figure Harry Potter saw in the Chamber of Secrets in 1993, standing by a fallen pillar in a plain white robe and looking at him with pride. He was Jesus Christ.

The vision

He was a grown man with fair skin, long brown hair that fell past his shoulders and a brown beard. He stood quite still with his hands at his sides, looking down at Harry, who had fallen beside Dracina Malfoy with the Basilisk's venom in him. Harry knew the face. He had stared at it all through the carols in a stained-glass window, on the one Christmas Aunt Petunia took the family to church, when he was seven.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Harry saw the man as he lay on the floor of the Chamber. He looked warm, kind and sad. He was looking at Harry with pride, as though he had always known that Harry could do it.

In Chapter Nineteen Dracina Malfoy told Harry in the hospital wing that she had seen the man too, standing by the broken pillar. For one wild moment Harry thought of the church window, and of who the man might be.

In Book Three, Chapter One, in July 1993, Harry was still telling himself that there was a perfectly rational explanation for a man in a white robe in a sewer.

In Chapter Seven Harry thought about Dracina, who had everything a person could want and still lay awake trying to be good enough for her father. At least he had always known that the Dursleys were wrong. He had had Hogwarts, Ron, the Weasleys and a man in white by a pillar to tell him so.

In Chapter Twelve, in January 1994, Harry had spent seven months calling the man a trick of concussion, out of embarrassment.

pages.title: Cain
infobox:
Abel brother
Adam father
Lilith deceived by
painting, Biblical, Bible, vampire, Christianity, Genesis
Immortality, burning in sunlight, endless wandering
Enoch, Irad and Zillah (the Second Generation)
The thirteen Antediluvians of the Third Generation, founders of the clans, and every vampire since
pages.html:
Cain, the elder son of Adam and Eve, is the first murderer and the first vampire. For killing his brother Abel he was cursed by God to be immortal, soulless and burned by the sun. He wandered through the Ages of Middle-earth and the Hyborian Age. Because he could not die, he came through Noah's Flood. Shortly after the Flood a servant of Morgoth called Lilith tricked him into learning blood magic, and from that bargain the first vampires came. Cain became the vampire of the First Generation. The thirteen clans were born from his grandchilder, the Third Generation. He is the man in the cracked painting of two brothers at their altars, in the disused fourth-floor corridor at Hogwarts.

The murder and the curse

Cain was a tiller of the ground, and his brother Abel a keeper of sheep. When both brought offerings, God had respect for Abel's and not for Cain's. He warned Cain that sin lay at his door, that its desire was for him, and that he must rule over it. Cain rose up against his brother in the field and killed him. God cursed him from the ground that had drunk Abel's blood. He sent him out to wander in the land of Nod, east of Eden, and set a mark upon him, so that nobody who found him would kill him.

The sentence had three parts. Cain was to live for ever. Sunlight would repel him and burn him. He would wander without rest or home for ever. What it meant beneath those three was soullessness, and every vampire since has carried the same verdict.

All this happened before the ages of Middle-earth. Cain was walking the world long before the Istari came over the sea, before the Rings were made, before there was any Stygia. Through every one of those ages he was no vampire. He was only a cursed, deathless, sun-shy wanderer, with no soul and no powers.

The wandering

Cain went out from the presence of the Lord to dwell in the land of Nod, east of Eden, and he never stopped walking. He walked through all the Ages of Middle-earth, from the First to the long Fourth, then through the Thurian Age and the Hyborian Age that came after. All that time the burning God had laid on him kept him from the day. He saw kingdom after kingdom of Elves and Men rise up, then fall. He watched Stygia gather the craft of Morgoth. He was part of none of it.

He was not yet a vampire. He had the curse and nothing else: no thirst, no Disciplines, no Beast. That distinction is the hinge of his whole history.

Noah's Flood and Lilith

The Flood that ended the Ice Age, the Flood of Noah and the ark, did not take him. God had already sentenced him to live, and God does not revoke His own sentences. Cain could not drown. The Nephilim, who were under no such sentence, perished in the water.

Shortly after the water had gone down, Cain met Lilith. She told him that she was Adam's first wife, the woman made before Eve who would not bow. That was a lie. She was a powerful immortal servant of Morgoth, whom men call Satan, and she had come for him on her master's errand. She showed him the power in his own cursed blood and taught him blood magic. With it he strengthened himself, drank, and passed his curse to others. He believed he was being given relief from his sentence. In fact he was being recruited. The craft bound Cain to Morgoth's power and will. Through Cain it bound every vampire who would ever descend from him.

From that moment Cain was a vampire as the Kindred know vampires. The Beast was inside him. He had the hunger for blood, the Disciplines of the Blood and the power to make others of his kind by the Embrace. He was the first of them. The Kindred count him alone as the First Generation.

The First City and the clans

Cain went out again into Nod, and for a time he was alone with his blood. Then he took three childer, Enoch, Irad and Zillah, who were the Second Generation. With them, and with the mortals who gathered to them, he built a city. He named it Enoch after his eldest childe. It was the First City, and its vampires ruled it openly as gods.

The Second Generation sired childer of their own, thirteen of them. Cain, seeing what the blood was becoming, forbade any more. These thirteen were the Third Generation, the Antediluvians. From them come the thirteen clans: the Brujah, Gangrel, Malkavian, Nosferatu, Toreador, Tremere, Ventrue, Lasombra, Tzimisce, the Assamites, the Followers of Set, the Giovanni and the Ravnos. The Tremere later took the place of the Salubri's founder by diablerie. The Giovanni come down through Cappadocius, whose line Augustus Giovanni later usurped.

The Kindred still call the Third the Antediluvians, and say that they were sired before the Flood. In truth the whole line began after Noah's Flood. The name records only how old the Kindred believe themselves to be.

In time the First City fell. The Third Generation rose against their sires and slew the Second. Cain cursed the clans for it, laying on each its own weakness, then departed into the wilderness of Nod. He has not ruled his get since. His words were gathered in the Book of Nod, together with the prophecies of the end of the Kindred that they call Gehenna. The Sabbat honour him as the Dark Father, and wait for the day the Antediluvians wake to devour their descendants. The Camarilla officially count him a legend. The Kindred cannot agree whether he still walks the earth.

Whatever the clans believe, they belong to the same inheritance as their founder. Every drop of their blood came down from Cain's bargain with Lilith. Every one of them stands under the will of Morgoth, whether it knows it or not.

In the saga

In early November 1993 Harry Potter passed a big, dark canvas, cracked all over, in a disused corridor on the fourth floor. It showed two brothers in rough clothes at stone altars on a bare hillside. One offering burned cleanly, its smoke rising in a straight white feather. The other had sunk to embers. Its smoke crawled along the ground like a grass snake, while its keeper glared over his shoulder. 'His burned and mine didn't,' the painted man complained. He said that a patient thing had lain at his door-sill since the first day the smoke went wrong, wanting him, while a voice told him to rule over it. Then he told Harry, 'You're angry, boy. I can always tell. It's a smell in your blood, like rain coming. Mind the door-sill.'

On the Saturday that November when Harry lay in the hospital wing, the same man came into his dreams. He was tall, in rough clothes, with a still, ruined face and the smell of very old blood. From a doorway he watched Harry take his revenge on the Dursleys, and he never said a word. Harry told him that if he meant to stand there all night he could make himself useful and mend a broom. The man laughed, a rusty, startled sound that nobody had heard for longer than there had been writing. Then a beam of clean white light came down through the ceiling of number four, Privet Drive. It fell on him the way a hand falls on a shoulder, and he burnt. He went up like the smoke on his brother's altar, white, straight and clean.

When Harry described the man, Remus Lupin went the colour of the wall, with a low note sounding in his chest, and could not say who he was. He would say only that a man visited in his dreams by such a thing would once have gone to seek God, or at least a priest. The painting and its warning came back to Harry in Divination in the spring of 1994.

In their own words

His burned and mine didn't.Cain · B3 Ch9
You're angry, boy. I can always tell. It's a smell in your blood, like rain coming. Mind the door-sill.Cain · B3 Ch9

pages.title: Abel
aliases: the brother at the accepted fire
pages.html:
Abel was the younger son of Adam and Eve, a keeper of sheep, and the first man ever to be murdered. His brother Cain killed him in a field because God had accepted Abel's offering and turned Cain's away. The curse God laid on Cain for it, of deathlessness, soullessness and the burning sun, set him wandering through the ages. Long afterwards, when the Flood had gone down, that curse made him easy prey for Lilith, and the first vampire was the result.

Life and death

Abel kept sheep while Cain tilled the ground. When the time came, each of them brought God an offering: Cain the fruit of the ground, Abel the firstlings of his flock and the fat of them. God had respect to Abel's offering but not to Cain's, and He warned the angry Cain that sin lay at his door. Cain talked with his brother all the same. When they were in the field, he rose up against Abel and killed him.

Abel's blood cried out to God from the ground, which is why God cursed Cain from the earth that had drunk it. Adam and Eve had another son afterwards, Seth, whom Eve called God's gift in Abel's place.

In the saga

There is a cracked painting of the two brothers in a disused corridor on the fourth floor at Hogwarts. In it Abel stands with his back turned, in the clean light of his accepted offering, its smoke going up in a single straight white feather to the top of the frame. The painter gave him no face at all.

Harry Potter, walking past it in November 1993, understood with a prickle up his spine that there was a reason for that, and that the reason had already happened, somewhere beyond the edge of the frame. When Cain burned in Harry's dream later that month, he went up the way Abel's smoke did: white, straight and clean, in one feather.

pages.title: David
infobox: Killing Goliath; sparing Saul; the Psalms
pages.html:
David was the shepherd boy of Bethlehem who became King of Israel. He killed the giant Goliath with a stone from his sling, and many of the Psalms are his. From his line came Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

Life

The prophet Samuel anointed him while he was still a shepherd lad, the youngest of the sons of Jesse. King Saul grew jealous of him and hunted him through the hills for years. Twice David had the king at his mercy, and twice he spared him. In those years, too, Abigail turned him back from vengeance on her husband, Nabal, with a soft answer. After Saul's death he reigned as king, first at Hebron and then at Jerusalem.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter of a shepherd lad who was promised great things. A mad old king who feared him hunted him all over the hills for years. Twice the shepherd had the old king asleep at his mercy, and twice he spared him. Then a rich fool refused his men bread, and the patient shepherd swore that by morning there would be no male thing left alive in the fool's house. Only the fool's wife, kneeling in a ravine, turned him back. The shepherd blessed her advice all his days, said the Friar, because she had kept him from carrying a morning's work for the rest of his life. 'Wrath pays its wages in the morning, young Potter, and it always pays in full.' The Friar named nobody, but the shepherd is David.

pages.title: Saul
infobox: Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin
On Mount Gilboa, by his own sword
pages.html:
Saul, the son of Kish, was the first King of Israel. The prophet Samuel anointed him, but he lost the Lord's favour by disobedience, and an evil spirit troubled him.

Saul and David

Jealous of the young David, who had killed Goliath, Saul hunted him through the hills for years. Twice David had him at his mercy, and twice he spared him. Saul died on Mount Gilboa, falling on his own sword after the Philistines had beaten Israel. David reigned after him.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter of a mad old king who feared a shepherd lad and hunted him all over the hills. 'A patient man, this shepherd. Twice he had the old king asleep at his mercy, and twice spared him. The soul of patience.' The Friar named nobody, but the old king is Saul.

pages.title: Nabal
infobox: Maon, with his flocks at Carmel
About ten days after refusing David
pages.html:
Nabal was a rich, churlish farmer of Maon, in the hill country of Judah. He refused bread to David's men after they had guarded his flocks all season, which very nearly cost every male in his household his life. His wife, Abigail, saved them.

The fool

His name means fool. While Abigail was turning David back, Nabal held a feast fit for a king and got very drunk. When she told him in the morning what had happened, his heart died within him. About ten days later he was dead.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter of a rich fool of a farmer who refused the shepherd's men bread and insulted them to their faces. When Ron Weasley asked what became of the fool, the Friar said he had dropped dead inside a fortnight with no help from anybody, 'as fools generally contrive to'. The reckoning had come anyway, without the shepherd's hand on it. The Friar named nobody, but the fool is Nabal.

pages.title: Abigail
infobox: Maon, in the hill country of Judah
Turning David back with a soft answer
pages.html:
Abigail was the wife of Nabal, a rich, churlish farmer of Maon, and afterwards a wife of King David. When David swore to destroy her husband's household, she rode out alone to meet him, though he had four hundred men behind him. She brought bread, wine and two hundred fig cakes. She knelt before him in the road, and with a soft answer she turned him back.

The soft answer

Nabal had refused bread to David's men, who had guarded his flocks all season without taking so much as a lamb. He insulted them to their faces as well. David swore that by morning there would be no male thing left alive in Nabal's house. Abigail got down from her donkey in the mouth of a ravine and talked to him softly. He heard her, and he turned his whole company round. He blessed her advice, because she had kept him that day from shedding blood with his own hand. When Nabal died about ten days later, David sent for her and made her his wife.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter her story. The fool's wife, he said, was a clever woman married to a fool. She rode down the mountain alone, against four hundred swords coming up it, with bread, wine and two hundred fig cakes; the story, he said, is very particular about the fig cakes. She knelt in the road at the mouth of the ravine and talked to the shepherd softly. 'No sword was drawn and no charm was cast, for they had none in those days.' Though the Friar named nobody, the woman in his story is Abigail.

pages.title: Binky
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Binky was Lavender Brown's pet rabbit, still only a baby, who was killed by a fox in October 1993. The news reached Lavender at Hogwarts in a letter on 16 October 1993, the very date Professor Trelawney had told her to dread. To Lavender that was the day Binky died, and the proof that Trelawney had the Sight.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Lavender was crying in the queue outside Transfiguration, with Parvati Patil's arm round her. 'She had a letter from home this morning,' whispered Parvati. 'It's Binky. Her rabbit. A fox got him.' Lavender wailed that she should have known. 'It's the sixteenth of October!' Professor Trelawney had said so, and it had come true.

Hermione Granger could not leave it alone. Had Lavender really been dreading Binky being eaten by a fox? Was Binky an old rabbit? 'He was only a baby!' Lavender sobbed. Then, Hermione asked, why would she have been dreading him dying? Binky had not even died that day, she pointed out; Lavender had only heard about it that day.

Ron told Lavender to take no notice, because Hermione didn't reckon anybody's pets mattered except hers. Ron and Hermione did not say a word to each other for the rest of the lesson. Harry, watching Lavender with her head on her arms, found himself thinking that Dracina Malfoy was right, and that Hermione could be really nasty.

pages.title: Augusta Longbottom
infobox: Mrs Longbottom; Neville's grandmother; Neville's gran
pages.html:
Augusta Longbottom is a pure-blood witch, the mother of the Auror Frank Longbottom. She is also the grandmother of Neville Longbottom, and his guardian. She has brought him up herself ever since 1981, when his parents were tortured into madness.

Life

In 1981 four Death Eaters, Bellatrix Lestrange among them, tortured Frank and his wife Alice with the Cruciatus Curse until they lost their minds. They have been in St Mungo's Hospital ever since. Augusta took their small son home and raised him. She still takes him to visit them.

She is a severe, old-fashioned witch. She wears a tall hat with a stuffed vulture on top of it, a long green dress, a fox-fur scarf and a big red handbag. She measures her grandson against his parents, and often tells him he is practically a Squib. For years the family feared he was one. When he was eight, his Great-uncle Algie dangled him out of an upstairs window by the ankles and let go by accident. Neville bounced, and his grandmother cried with joy.

She never let Neville near a broomstick. In his first year she sent him a Remembrall. She once sent him a Howler, which he ignored, with horrible results.

In the saga

On 31 August 1993 Harry saw her outside Flourish and Blotts, telling Neville off for losing his booklist. That autumn she sent Neville's Hogsmeade permission form straight to Professor McGonagall. Professor Trelawney warned Neville not to count on his grandmother's health. When Neville's boggart took the shape of Professor Snape, he defeated it by dressing it in her clothes.

In March 1994 Sirius Black broke into Gryffindor Tower with the list of passwords Neville had lost. Two days later Augusta sent Neville a Howler. It told him, and everybody within half a mile, that he had disgraced the family.

pages.title: The great black dog
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Magnolia Crescent, August 1993; the Quidditch pitch, November 1993
Sirius Black, in his Animagus form
pages.html:
The great black dog was the huge, gaunt animal that seemed to follow Harry Potter through the autumn of 1993. He saw it first in Magnolia Crescent, then in the stands at Hogwarts. Each time it appeared something nearly killed him, and he came to believe it was the Grim, the worst omen of death there is. It was Sirius Black.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, during Gryffindor's match against Hufflepuff in November 1993, Harry flew high over the north stand and looked down at the topmost row of seats, empty all match in the rain. The dog stood there quite still, enormous and black, watching him. Minutes later the Dementors came on to the pitch, and Harry fell from his broom.

In Chapter Ten Harry remembered that he had seen it before, in Magnolia Crescent, just before he was nearly hit by a bus. Ron had gone white to the lips over that one, and Hermione had given him the statistics on big black dogs in rural Scotland. This time he told nobody. He believed it was the Grim.

Like the dog in Magnolia Crescent, it was Sirius Black in his Animagus shape.

pages.title: Boggart
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Unknown; none has ever been seen alone
pages.html:
A boggart is a shape-shifter that takes the form of whatever frightens the person looking at it most. Nobody knows what one looks like on its own, because nobody has ever seen one alone. Narcissa Malfoy calls it something that wears your fear like a coat. Laughter finishes it, through the charm Riddikulus.

Nature

Boggarts like dark, shut-in places: wardrobes, the space under a bed, the cupboard under the sink. Remus Lupin once met one that had made its home in a grandfather clock. A boggart does not so much turn into something as reach into the person in front of it, find the greatest fear there and wear it. A crowd muddles it, because it cannot decide whom to frighten first. One that tried to frighten two people at once turned itself into half a slug. Driven off, it bursts into threads of grey smoke. The threads can run back together and slide away under the nearest door, for a boggart is never quite gone until it is gone.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in September 1993, Lupin took his third years to the staffroom, where a boggart had got into the wardrobe. Hermione Granger called it a shape-shifter. Dracina Malfoy, putting up her hand in a lesson for the first time Harry had ever seen, put it in her mother's words: 'Something that wears your fear like a coat because it hasn't got a shape of its own.' Lupin said her mother sounded like a sensible woman.

The boggart became Snape for Neville Longbottom, who put it in a long green dress, a vulture hat and a crimson handbag. It became a mummy for Parvati Patil and a banshee for Seamus Finnigan. Confused, it was a rat, then a rattlesnake, then a bloodshot eyeball. It was a severed hand for Dean Thomas. For Dracina it was her father, Lucius, telling her she was second at everything and not a real Malfoy. She wept, then turned him into a tramp in odd wellingtons asking for 20p, and laughed until she could not breathe. It was a spider for Ron Weasley.

Lupin stepped in front of Harry Potter before the boggart could reach him. Neville finished it off. Lupin handed out points, ten of them to Slytherin for Dracina, 'five for the boggart and five for her coat'. Only Harry saw the grey threads run back under the wardrobe door. What came out next was a blood-soaked Garou, nine feet tall, and it looked past the class at Lupin as though it had known him all his life. Lupin gave it stumpy legs the length of teacups. It toppled on to its chin. 'Oh, bother.'

In Chapter Eight Lupin told Harry why he had not let him face it: he had thought it would turn into Lord Voldemort. In Chapter Twelve Lupin found another boggart in Mr Filch's filing cabinet and brought it to Harry's Patronus lessons, where it became a dementor. Going backwards into its packing case, it was for half a second something else: tall, stooped and shaggy. Harry did not take it in.

In Chapter Sixteen a fresh boggart waited in a trunk at the end of Lupin's exam. For Harry it was a dementor, which he dressed in Oliver Wood's soaking Quidditch robes. For Hermione it was Professor McGonagall telling her she had failed everything. Dracina's, by all accounts, told her she had come second.

pages.title: Dhampir
infobox: As a rule, a thin-blooded vampire of the last generations and a mortal
Mortal at the last, with something of the vampire
Connor, the human son of Angel and Darla
pages.html:
A dhampir is the child of a vampire, half one thing and half the other. He is mortal at the last, but he is born with something of the vampire's strength, senses and long life, without its whole curse. By the laws of the blood only the thin-blooded of the last generations, the weakest of all the Kindred, can father or bear a child, and dhampirs are their children. The two best known, Alucard and Blade, are exceptions to that rule in different ways.

The laws of the blood

The Kindred do not bring new life into the world. The stronger the blood, the further a vampire is from anything a living body does. An elder can no more father a child than a stone can.

Only at the far end of Cain's line, among the thin-blooded of the fifteenth generation and after, is the blood so weak that something of the living body survives the Embrace. A few of them can father children on mortal women. A few can conceive and carry a child, though the bodies of the dead were never meant for it. Such a pregnancy is hard on them.

What they bear is a dhampir. A dhampir is born alive, grows up and in the end dies, as mortals do. He needs no blood to live, but the vampire's inheritance shows in him all the same. He is stronger and tougher than an ordinary man. Many dhampirs share some gift of the parent's clan.

No other kind of power can take hold of a dhampir. He can never become a werewolf, a mage or any of the other kinds of creature that walk the world.

Old tradition

Balkan and Romani tradition holds that a dhampir can see vampires that others cannot, which fits him above all other men to hunt them. In the old Serbian and Albanian lands a dhampir might make his living destroying them, going from village to village wherever the dead had been troubling the living.

The Time of Thin Blood

The Kindred's own prophecies speak of a Time of Thin Blood that will come before Gehenna. That is the last night, when the Antediluvians are to rise to devour their children. The birth of children to the thin-blooded is counted among its signs.

For that reason elders have hunted the thin-blooded and their dhampir children, as have the cults that wait for Gehenna. Most dhampirs who know what they are keep it to themselves.

Alucard

Alucard, born Adrian, is the son of Dracula by his wife, Lisa, a witch. By the laws of the blood he should not exist, because Dracula is of the fourth generation, as far from the thin-blooded as any vampire walking.

But Dracula's blood came to him through the Crimson Stone, which set him at the fourth generation against every ordinary rule of diablerie. Nothing about that blood has ever obeyed the rules.

Alucard has a vampire's strength and speed. He can take the shape of a bat, a wolf or mist, and he has lived for more than five hundred years. He turned against his father, fought beside Trevor Belmont in 1476 and destroyed Dracula himself in 1797.

Blade

Blade, born Eric Brooks in London in 1929, is a dhampir of another kind, since no vampire fathered him. His mother, Tara Brooks, was in labour when the vampire Deacon Frost, posing as a doctor, fed on her. She died, and the child was born with the vampire's taint in his blood.

He has a dhampir's strength and senses. No vampire can sire him, he ages far more slowly than other men, and he walks in daylight, so that the Kindred call him the Daywalker. He has hunted them all his life.

Connor

Connor, the son of the vampires Angel and Darla, born in 2001, was no dhampir. His parents, of the sixth and fifth generations, were far too strong in the blood to have a child at all. He was conceived and born wholly human, by a direct act of God.

In the saga

In December 1993 Hermione Granger told Ron Weasley about Alucard: 'He was a dhampir, half one of them, half not. He hunted his own father.' The library's copy of the book on him had pages missing, with the illustrations cut out, so she meant to buy it at Tomes and Scrolls. Ron announced that he was going to go and be sick with excitement in the dormitory.

pages.title: Red Cap
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Places where blood has been spilt
Anything that has carried a great deal of blood
pages.html:
Red Caps are squat, goblin-like Dark creatures that lurk wherever blood has been spilt, in the cellars of old castles or the shell holes of forgotten battlefields. Given the chance, they will club a lost traveller to death in the dark.

Habits

Red Caps can smell old blood, and they keep well away from anything that has carried a great deal of it. Simple charms and jinxes will drive them off.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Professor Lupin brought a Red Cap to class in a cage. It flung itself at the bars whenever anybody moved, but it took one look at Lupin and went to the very back of the cage, where it lay flat on its belly for the rest of the lesson. ‘They can smell old blood,’ Lupin told the class. ‘It's what they live on. Anything that's carried a great deal of it, they keep well away from.’ Nobody in the class knew then what Lupin was.

In Chapter Sixteen Red Caps crouched in the potholes of the obstacle course Lupin set for his third-years' examination in June 1994. When Ron Weasley went waist-deep into the marsh, it took Lupin and two Red Caps to pull him out. The Red Caps were not trying to help.

pages.title: Kappas
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Scaly and monkey-like, with webbed hands
The water held in the hollow of its head
pages.html:
The kappa is a Japanese water demon that lives in shallow ponds and rivers. It looks like a scaly monkey. It has webbed hands, which it uses to drown anybody unwise enough to wade into its water.

Dealing with a kappa

A kappa carries water in a hollow on the top of its head, and its strength comes from that water. The way to beat one is to trick it into bowing, so that the water spills out. A kappa can also be persuaded to leave a person alone if it is thrown a cucumber with that person's name carved into it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Professor Lupin taught kappas to Harry Potter's class in Defence Against the Dark Arts. They came straight after Red Caps, and before the vampires he began in the second week of October.

pages.title: Grindylow
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Sickly green, with little pointed horns
Its fingers, very strong but very brittle
pages.html:
A grindylow is a small water demon, sickly green, with little pointed horns, green teeth and long, thin, spidery fingers. It lurks in the weed at the bottom of lakes and ponds, grabbing at anything that comes within reach. Its fingers are very strong but very brittle, so the trick is to break its grip.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, on Hallowe'en 1993, Remus Lupin had a grindylow delivered for his next lesson and kept it in a tank in his office. When Harry Potter came in, it pressed itself against the glass, making faces at him and flexing its long, thin, spidery hands. 'Water demon,' said Lupin. 'He shouldn't give us much trouble. Not after the kappas. The thing is to break his grip. See those fingers? Very strong. And very brittle.' The grindylow showed its green teeth and went to bury itself in a clump of weed. In Chapter Nine, when Snape took the class, the tank sat covered at the front of the room like a shrouded coffin. Snape dismissed grindylows, along with Red Caps, as first-year matter.

In Chapter Sixteen a grindylow lurked at the bottom of the paddling pool in Lupin's exam. Harry kicked it off his ankle without even looking down. Dracina Malfoy had it off hers with one sharp jab of her wand before it had properly got hold. In Chapter Twenty-Two the tank stood empty when Lupin packed to leave, and he carried it away under his arm.

pages.title: Hinkypunk
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A frail, smoky, one-legged thing no bigger than a cat
pages.html:
A hinkypunk is a thin, frail, smoky little creature with one leg, no bigger than a cat, which seems to be made out of wisps of fog. It carries a small lantern. At night it hops along ahead of travellers on soft ground, just far enough in front to look like the light of a house, and leads them into the bog.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1993, Hermione Granger protested to Snape that the class was due to start hinkypunks, not werewolves. In Chapter Ten, in November, Lupin came back and taught them. He brought one in a glass tank. It looked, Harry Potter thought, as if a strong word would blow it out. 'People follow the light,' said Lupin. 'They always follow the light.' Then it threw itself at the glass with a noise like a boot coming out of mud, and Lavender Brown shrieked.

In Chapter Sixteen a hinkypunk bobbed about the marsh in Lupin's exam, waving its lantern hopefully towards the deepest part of the bog. Harry ignored it altogether. It led Ron Weasley so cleverly astray that he ended up waist-deep in the marsh. It took Lupin and two Red Caps to pull him out. The Red Caps were not trying to help. When it waved its lantern at Dracina Malfoy, she gave it such a withering look that it went out.

pages.title: Banshee
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A woman with floor-length black hair and a face like a skull
pages.html:
A banshee is a dark creature in the shape of a woman, with black hair down to the floor and a green-white face like a skull. Its cry is a long, high, howling shriek that does not seem to belong in the world. In the old stories of Ireland, to hear one is to know that somebody is about to die.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Break with a Banshee was among the books by Gilderoy Lockhart that the second years had to buy. In Chapter Seven Lockhart told his class that he had not got rid of the Bandon Banshee by smiling at her. In Chapter Eight Hagrid said that if one word of Lockhart's banshee story was true, he would eat his kettle. Hagrid's kettle was safe. In Chapter Eighteen Lockhart admitted that somebody else had done it. 'And the witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee had a hairy chin. I mean, really...'

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in September 1993, Seamus Finnigan's boggart took the shape of a banshee: a woman with black hair down to the floor and a green-white face like a skull. Her shriek made every hair on Harry Potter's head stand up. When Seamus cast Riddikulus, she clutched her throat and made a noise like a creaking gate, because her voice had gone. 'Did you see me with that banshee?' Seamus was shouting afterwards.

pages.title: Manticore
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A man's head, a lion's body and a scorpion's tail
pages.html:
The manticore is a Greek beast with the head of a man, the body of a lion and the tail of a scorpion. It is as dangerous as the Chimaera. Its sting kills at once, and it is said to croon softly to itself as it devours its prey.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, in the Christmas holidays of 1993, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger searched the records of wizarding law for a case that might save Buckbeak. They found a manticore of 1296 that had been cleared of savaging a woodcutter. It had not been found innocent. It had been cleared because the Committee could not find anybody willing to fetch it in.

pages.title: Goa'uld
infobox: Spinal parasite; The possessing parasites; Goa'uld symbiote
Stargate SG-1, 'Children of the Gods' (27 July 1997); Ra in Stargate (film, 28 October 1994)
Humans, and the Unas before them
pages.html:
The Goa'uld are serpent-like parasites that enter a living host through the back of the neck. They coil round the spine and rule the body from within, while the host looks on. For thousands of years they passed themselves off as the gods of Egypt and of many other peoples. Minerva McGonagall killed one long ago and keeps it in a glass case over her fire.

Nature

A mature Goa'uld is about the length of a forearm, grey-white and segmented like a thin eel. It has a fringe of fins down its back, and its head opens four ways into a mouth lined with needle teeth. It goes in through the flesh, usually at the back of the neck. Then it wraps itself round the spine, lies along it and speaks with the host's mouth. The host is still in there, quite awake, watching, with no say in anything any more.

There are two plain signs. When a Goa'uld is angry or proud, which is most of the time, the host's eyes shine brightly, like lamps. The voice comes out doubled, as though two people were speaking at once, one of them very much further down. No Transfiguration will separate host from symbiote. McGonagall tried, and in the end only a knife answered.

A Goa'uld is born carrying the memories of its ancestors. Its blood holds traces of naquadah, which lets it work Goa'uld devices and sense its own kind. Hosts are kept young by the sarcophagus, which can heal the dying and raise the dead, though it corrodes the mind with use. Goa'uld larvae cannot survive long outside water or a host. They are matured in the Jaffa, a warrior people bred to carry them in a pouch in the belly.

History

The Goa'uld came from a world of water, where their first hosts were the Unas. Through the Stargate they found Earth. They took humans, who made far better hosts, and carried them off to other worlds as slaves, soldiers or miners. In Egypt they ruled as gods. Ra was the greatest of them, with Egypt as his seat, until the people rose against him, drove him off and buried his gate.

Thor, the son of Odin, fought beside the Egyptians in that rising, and it is partly because of him that the Goa'uld have shunned Earth ever since. Ra forbade any Goa'uld to speak of it. The ban still holds in every Goa'uld court, although every Goa'uld remembers the place, since each is born with the memories of its ancestors. For some four thousand years afterwards Thor hunted them wherever they came near the North, until the Protected Planets Treaty; he gave no quarter to Goa'uld, host or Jaffa. A System Lord who hears thunder in a clear sky has been known to turn his fleet round.

Some, such as Kali, Olokun and Amaterasu, came to Earth quietly in defiance of Ra's ban, keeping well away from the North.

They have invented very little of their own. Their ships, their weapons and the gates themselves were all taken from older peoples. Across the galaxy the strongest Goa'uld rule as the System Lords, a quarrelsome council of tyrants who make war on one another as readily as on anyone else. Asgard holds them back from certain worlds under the Protected Planets Treaty. A small faction, the Tok'ra, share their hosts willingly and fight the System Lords in secret.

Among the stars

The Goa'uld are not alone among the stars, though they prefer to behave as if they were. Their domains fill much of the galaxy, and they travel them chiefly through the Stargates, which is one reason the greater powers have so often overlooked them. Because of Ra's ban, they also know less about Earth and its heroes than almost anyone else in the galaxy.

The Kree and the Skrulls

Their oldest neighbours, and the ones they like least, are the Kree. Until 1992 the Kree Empire was ruled from Hala, in the Greater Magellanic Cloud, by the Supreme Intelligence, a vast living computer made of the greatest Kree minds. For thousands of years its frontier has rubbed against the Goa'uld's at the edge of the galaxy.

Long ago a Goa'uld took the body of a Kree officer. The Supreme Intelligence answered by burning the world where it had happened down to the bedrock, Kree garrison and all. The Goa'uld have not tried it again. The Kree Accusers, who are judge and executioner in one, have since put more Goa'uld to death than anyone except Thor.

The Skrulls, who can take any shape they please, have fought the Kree for longer than anyone can remember. They have also, at one time or another, had spies in the courts of most of the System Lords. Every System Lord's court has been searched for Skrulls at least once, and somebody perfectly ordinary has usually been put to death in the process.

When the Kree and the Skrulls fought over Earth from 1971 to 1972, the Goa'uld stayed well out of it. They would not go near Earth for anybody's war.

The Shi'ar

The Shi'ar, a proud, bird-like people whose empire lies far beyond the galaxy, never thought the Goa'uld worth conquering. In 1992 the Shi'ar broke the Kree Empire and took what was left of it. When they came to the Kree frontier, they found Goa'uld ships already there, picking over the wreckage. The Shi'ar Imperial Guard drove them off in an afternoon. Lilandra, the Shi'ar Majestrix, is said to have asked afterwards who the Goa'uld were, and to have lost interest when she was told.

The Green Lantern Corps

For thousands of years the Goa'uld were one of the oldest unsolved problems of the Green Lantern Corps. The Guardians of the Universe would act against slavers who crossed open space, so the Goa'uld learnt to move their slaves through the Stargates instead, where no Lantern was watching.

It did not help that the motherships of the System Lords are covered in gold. Until 1994 a Lantern's ring had no power over anything yellow. The Goa'uld, who never knew why the Lanterns so seldom troubled their ships, put it down to their own divinity.

Hal Jordan, whose sector held Earth, never met a Goa'uld in his life, because the Goa'uld never came there. The destruction of the Corps at the turn of 1994 went almost unnoticed among them. They had never understood it in the first place.

The New Gods

The System Lords, who also call themselves gods, regard the New Gods of Apokolips and New Genesis as rivals in the same trade. The New Gods do not regard them at all, with one exception.

Darkseid, the Lord of Apokolips, once took an interest in them. A Goa'uld commands its host's body from within, and every Goa'uld is born with the memories of all its ancestors; it struck Darkseid that the Anti-Life Equation might be hidden somewhere in those memories. He had DeSaad bring the whole court of a lesser System Lord to Apokolips, and take their minds apart one by one.

DeSaad found nothing but vanity, and a great many memories of Thor. The System Lord's name has since been struck from every Goa'uld record, which is how the Goa'uld deal with embarrassment.

Krypton

Long before Krypton exploded, a Goa'uld ship found it. Under their own red sun the Kryptonians were very little different from human beings, and the Goa'uld thought they had found a world of perfect hosts. Instead they found the Eradicator, the ancient machine the Kryptonians had built to keep their world closed against outsiders. It destroyed the ship before it could land.

Krypton's last son has never met a Goa'uld. Under a yellow sun no symbiote could get through the skin at the back of Superman's neck, and it is probably as well for the symbiote that none has tried.

Apocalypse

Apocalypse, the first of the mutants, was born in Egypt some five thousand years ago, in the years after the rising against Ra. He grew up among desert raiders in the ruins of a god's rule. He has said ever since that only the strong deserve to survive, and to him Ra's fall proved only that Ra had not been strong enough.

At least one Goa'uld, coming quietly to Earth in the centuries after Ra, tried to take him as a host. It went in at the back of his neck. Apocalypse, who can reshape every cell of his body at will, closed round it, and the Goa'uld never learnt what had become of it.

Other powers

Galactus, who eats worlds, once ate one that belonged to a System Lord, together with the System Lord. It is the only time the Goa'uld are known to have prayed, and nobody is sure to whom.

In 1988 the Dominators invited the Goa'uld to join their Alliance against Earth. The System Lords refused without giving a reason. The Dominators thought them cowards. After the Daxamites turned on the Alliance under Earth's sun, a good many Dominators came round to the Goa'uld's view.

The Watcher, who lives on Earth's Moon, has watched the Goa'uld for as long as there have been Goa'uld, and has never once interfered. The Goa'uld take this as a compliment.

Thanos, the Mad Titan, was born on a moon of Saturn, which the Goa'uld count as one more reason to keep away from that part of the sky.

On Earth in the twentieth century

McGonagall, an Unspeakable of the Department of Mysteries, confronted one in its host 'a long time ago and a very long way from here'. She had the help of the man she will not name, Big Boss, who was better with the knife than she was. The host died. So did the creature, which she had stuffed and kept.

The Ministry of Magic waged a campaign against what it calls 'those parasite creatures', and it considers the matter closed. It is not closed. Jack O'Neill learnt that the Goa'uld exist in 1994, on the Abydos mission. In 1997 they came back, and Muggles fought them through the gate found in Egypt. The Ministry did not notice.

It was Apophis who came. Ra's death in 1994 had left a gap at the head of the System Lords, and Apophis was quickest to fill it. He knew the people of Earth had killed Ra, and he had heard that Thor seemed to be busy elsewhere, although nobody among the Goa'uld knew where. They know nothing of the Replicators. In 1997 he broke Ra's old ban and came through the Stargate to Earth. The Goa'uld have taken a close interest in Earth ever since.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Five: in McGonagall's office Harry saw a long glass case on a bracket over the fire, lit from inside. It held a stuffed grey-white segmented thing with fins down its back and a mouth that opened four ways at once. He thought it the most horrible object he had ever seen in a teacher's office.

Book Three, Chapter Eight: teaching the limits of Transfiguration, McGonagall described creatures that take up residence inside a person, without naming them. She told the class that she had once tried to separate one from its host. A knife had done it instead, with the help of a man she would not name. The host had died. She had kept the creature as a reminder that some problems cannot be solved with a wand. Harry thought at once of the case.

Book Three, Chapter Ten: at the Three Broomsticks, McGonagall reminded Cornelius Fudge that he had read her file. Fudge said that at least 'those parasite creatures and those Nephilim' would not be bothering them again.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, McGonagall suggested to Gilderoy Lockhart a parasite of the vocal cords, which spread by language through Russian soldiers in Afghanistan and conscripts in Africa. That is a different organism, met in the same years of her work.

pages.title: Puffapod
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Fat and pink, full of shiny beans
The beans burst into flower when dropped
pages.html:
The Puffapod is a magical plant with fat pink pods full of shiny beans. A bean that is dropped bursts into flower at once. That makes the plant a cheerful thing to work with, and a hazard to anybody careless with the pods.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger worked on the same Puffapod in Herbology, although Ron was not speaking to Hermione. They split the fat pink pods and tipped the shining beans into a wooden bucket. Ron missed the bucket. The beans burst into a mass of pale, nodding flowers the moment they hit the warm floor, and Professor Sprout cried out to him to be careful.

In Chapter Fourteen, in March 1994, Ron came out of Greenhouse Three grumbling about a Puffapod that had gone off in his face.

pages.title: Darla
aliases: The pale lady from the colonies
the pale lady from the colonies
infobox: The pale lady from the colonies
Buffy the Vampire Slayer, 'Welcome to the Hellmouth' (10 March 1997)
1609, in the Virginia colony, by the Master; sired again in 2000 by Drusilla
Fifth (unchanged by her second siring in 2000)
Young men with fair skin and dark hair, of confidence and drive
1997, by Angel; died again in 2001, giving birth to Connor
pages.html:
Darla is a vampire of the Aurelian line, a Ventrue of the fifth generation, sired by the Master in the Virginia colony in 1609. She was the pale lady from the colonies who sired Angelus in a Galway alley in 1753. For a century and a half the two of them were the terror of Europe. She was destroyed in 1997 and raised as a mortal woman in 2000, then sired again by Drusilla. In 2001, by a direct act of God, she bore Angel a living son, Connor. She died to give him life.

The colony, 1609

Her name before she was sired is not recorded. In 1609 she was a woman of the young English colony in Virginia, earning her living as a prostitute. She was dying of syphilis when the Master came to her deathbed in the guise of a priest. She asked him for salvation, and he gave her the only kind he had. She took the name Darla, and she has used no other since.

By the standards of her clan the choice was a scandal. The Ventrue sire their childer from among the powerful and the successful: princes, bankers, men of affairs. The Master sired his favourite from a dying prostitute in a colonial stockade. He never cared what the rest of the Ventrue thought of it. After him, neither did she.

The blood of the fifth generation

Every step away from Cain thins the blood. Darla stood only five steps from him, closer than all but a handful of the vampires walking the world in her century.

The blood of the fifth generation is the blood of the great elders. It mends what would destroy a younger vampire, and it holds more power than lesser blood can carry. No vampire of a later generation can bend her mind, though she can bend theirs.

Of the gifts of her clan she used Presence most. Men followed her into alleys without asking why. Vampires older in years than her childe stepped aside for her in the street. She had the Ventrue command of other minds, as well as the Ventrue endurance. In four centuries she seldom needed either for long.

One kind of blood

Like every Ventrue, Darla can feed from only one kind of mortal, and she would starve sooner than drink from anybody else. Hers is young men with fair skin and dark hair. They must be men of confidence and drive.

It is a very close description of Angelus. Her blood was bound to that kind from the night of her siring in 1609, more than a century before Liam of Galway was born. When she saw him outside a tavern in 1753, fair-skinned, dark-haired and sure of himself, she saw exactly what her blood had always wanted. She did not let him go.

The Order of Aurelius

For a century and a half she was the jewel of the Master's court, the priesthood of vampires called the Order of Aurelius. She hunted for him in the colonies as well as in the Old World.

In 1753, in Galway, she saw a handsome, drunken linen merchant's son outside a tavern. She beckoned him into an alley and sired him. He became Angelus.

In 1760 she brought him to London to be presented to the Master in his lair beneath the city. Angelus laughed at a lord of the night who lived in the sewers and called it piety. When he walked out, Darla went with him. The Master never forgave either of them.

The Scourge of Europe

For decades afterwards the two of them cut a path across Europe, he at the front and she beside him. In May 1764 they came to the house of the hunter Daniel Holtz in York while he was away. They killed his wife and infant son, then turned his daughter. Holtz pursued them across Europe for nine years. He never caught them.

Like the Master and Angelus, Darla was unaligned. She paid no attention to the Masquerade. Her line did more to endanger it than any other of its age. That is why the Camarilla, the sect her own clan leads, quietly paid for the hunters who chased her.

Angelus's childe Drusilla joined them about 1860, and Drusilla's childe William the Bloody in 1880. For some years the four of them were the most feared company of vampires in Europe.

The gift and the curse

In 1898, in Romania, Darla gave Angelus a girl of the Kalderash as a present. She was the clan's favourite daughter. For that the elders cursed him with a new soul.

When Darla found what he had become, she cast him out. Then she went to the clan's camp. She offered an elder the lives of his wife and daughters if the curse were taken back. It was not. While she argued, Drusilla and William went through the camp, killing everyone they found.

In 1900, in Beijing during the Boxer Rising, Angel found her again and asked to come back. She tested him with a baby taken from a missionary family. He could not kill it. He fled with it through a window, and she knew that Angelus was gone. She did not look for him again.

Sunnydale

In the twentieth century she returned to the Master, sealed since 1937 beneath Sunnydale in California, and served him while he waited to rise.

In 1997 a new Slayer, Buffy Summers, came to the town. Darla meant to kill her, and to wound Angel in doing it. Angel staked her in the Slayer's own house.

A second life

In 2000 the Los Angeles law firm Wolfram and Hart raised her from the dust as a mortal woman, meaning to use her against Angel. She came back with her old disease. Within weeks she was dying of it again.

When Drusilla sired her again in December 2000, Darla should by every rule of the blood have risen as Drusilla's childe. She would then have been of the eighth generation, three steps further from Cain than before. Because of the particular manner of her siring, she did not. Her blood came back to her as the Master had given it, of the fifth generation, and with it came the same hunger.

That winter the two of them went through Los Angeles together. Early in 2001 Angel set them both alight and left them to burn. They lived.

Connor

Early in 2001 Angel and Darla lay together, on a night of despair, not of happiness, so that the curse held. Months later she found that she was carrying his child.

By every law of the blood it could not be. Of all the Kindred, only the thin-blooded of the last generations can father or bear children. What they bear are dhampirs, half one thing and half the other. Angel was of the sixth generation and Darla of the fifth. Their blood was far too strong ever to bring forth a child.

It was an act of God: a direct intervention, a miracle, done for a purpose of His own. The child grew in her as a living human boy, not a dhampir, with a soul of his own. While she carried him his soul shone through her, so that Darla felt remorse for the first time since 1609.

A vampire's body could not deliver a living child. On a rainy night in November 2001, in an alley in Los Angeles, she staked herself. As she crumbled to dust the child was born alive. Angel named him Connor.

In the saga

Darla is the pale lady from the colonies in the account Hermione Granger read to Harry Potter and Ron Weasley from Blood Nobility: The Great Kindred Lineages in the autumn of 1993. She was the woman who beckoned Angelus into an alley in 1753, so that he was never alive again. Afterwards she went with him across Europe, through the years Hermione summed up in three words: 'Decades of blood.' The book does not name her.

pages.title: Kathy
infobox: Liam (Angelus), her brother; their father, a linen merchant
pages.html:
Kathy was the little sister of Liam of Galway, who became the vampire Angelus. In 1753 she saw her dead brother standing in the moonlight at the window, believed he had come back to her as an angel and let him in. He killed her with the rest of the household. It was from her mistake that he took his name.

The girl at the window

Kathy was the younger child of a Galway linen merchant. She adored her brother Liam, whatever their father thought of him. When Liam died in 1753, sired in an alley by Darla, she believed him safe in Heaven.

He came back to the house that same night and stood at the window in the moonlight. A vampire cannot cross the threshold of a home unless someone inside invites him in. Kathy, who thought her brother had returned to her as an angel, opened the door to him.

Her death

He killed the whole household, servants included, and Kathy with them. Their father he saved for last. No one was left alive to bury them.

The name Angelus comes from the angel she thought she saw.

In the saga
