He went up like the smoke on his brother's altar, white, straight and clean, in one feather, to the top of the frame.

In Chapter Fifteen, staring into a crystal ball in Divination in the spring of 1994, Harry found the painting bobbing up in his emptied mind: one column of smoke going up straight and white, the other crawling along the ground. Mind the door-sill.

pages.title: Ginny's get-well card
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Harry Potter, in the hospital wing, November 1993
pages.html:
Ginny's get-well card is the homemade card that Ginny Weasley brought Harry Potter in the hospital wing in November 1993, after his fifty-foot fall from his broom. It has a scarlet lion on the front, and it sings.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Ginny came on the Sunday, just before lunch, scarlet in the face, and put the card into Harry’s hands without a word. It was lumpy with glue, and the scarlet lion on the front had clearly given her a good deal of trouble. When he opened it, it sang a get-well song in a high, thin, piercing voice that grew louder the longer it was open. Harry shut it, sat on it and finally wedged it under his bowl of fruit, where it went on humming through the apples. Dracina Malfoy, arriving for her own visit soon afterwards, took in the singing fruit bowl along with the rest of him.

pages.title: The sword from the hat
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Andúril, the sword of Elendil reforged
pages.html:
The sword from the hat is the blade that Harry Potter drew from the Sorting Hat in the Chamber of Secrets in June 1993, and with which he killed the Basilisk. Hogwarts knows it as the Sword of Gryffindor. It is in truth Andúril, the sword of Elendil, reforged long ago for Aragorn. Gandalf gave it to Godric Gryffindor, who was one of Aragorn's descendants. Harry worked out what it was during his third year at Hogwarts, and has told nobody.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry lay in the hospital wing in November 1993, after the dementors had brought him down at the Hufflepuff match. He reached for the thing he had found in June, when the sword came out of the hat. It had gone up through him like a flame along a fuse. It was what had made him stand in front of Quirrell, then in front of a basilisk fifty feet long, without stepping back.

Later in the chapter, alone with the Marauder's Map, he remembered Professor McGonagall's office in the small hours of that June morning, with the sword still lying on the desk. Mr Weasley had said there that you should never trust anything that could think for itself, if you could not see where it kept its brain.

pages.title: The two painted monks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A landscape painting near Sir Cadogan's portrait, Hogwarts
pages.html:
The two painted monks live in a landscape painting at Hogwarts, not far from the entrance to Gryffindor Tower, which Sir Cadogan guarded in 1993. They were guests at the Christmas party he held in his frame that year.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, on Christmas Day 1993, Sir Cadogan was guarding Gryffindor Tower in place of the Fat Lady. For his Christmas party he had got in a pair of monks from a nearby landscape, along with three previous headmasters of Hogwarts. His fat dappled pony came too. It had been given something out of a bucket, and was swaying gently. When Harry Potter and Ron Weasley reached the portrait after lunch, Sir Cadogan saluted them with a flagon.

pages.title: The three former headmasters
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The three former headmasters are portraits of past Heads of Hogwarts who were guests at Sir Cadogan's Christmas party in 1993, in his frame at the entrance to Gryffindor Tower. Like the other painted Heads, they can leave their own frames to visit other pictures about the castle.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, on Christmas Day 1993, Harry Potter and Ron Weasley came back to the tower after lunch to find Sir Cadogan having a Christmas party of his own. He had got in a pair of monks from a nearby landscape, three previous headmasters of Hogwarts and his fat dappled pony. Sir Cadogan pushed up his visor and saluted the two boys with a flagon. Ron gave the password, "Scurvy cur". "And the same to you, sir!" roared Sir Cadogan, as the portrait swung forward.

pages.title: The painted dinner party
infobox: A painting in the third-floor gallery, Hogwarts
pages.html:
The painted dinner party is a company of diners in a painting in the third-floor gallery at Hogwarts. Just after Hallowe'en 1993, Professor McGonagall came down the gallery looking for a portrait to guard Gryffindor Tower. Rather than answer her, the entire party got up and left through the back of its own canvas.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Sirius Black had slashed the Fat Lady at Hallowe'en, and she had been found two floors up, wedged behind a cypress tree in a painting of Tuscan hills. The news had gone round every frame in the castle by breakfast. Painted people, it turned out, could be frightened just like real ones. Portraits all over Hogwarts were standing-room only, because their occupants had crowded in with friends for safety. When McGonagall went down the gallery on the third floor asking for a volunteer, the dinner party walked out on her. Only one picture in the whole school offered, and that was Sir Cadogan.

pages.title: Ogre
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Possibly in the Three Broomsticks, Hogsmeade, at Hallowe'en 1993
pages.html:
Ogres are large, brutish creatures of roughly human shape. Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger believed they saw one in the Three Broomsticks at Hogsmeade in 1993, which surprised nobody who knew the place.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, Aunt Marge insulted Harry Potter's mother at the Dursleys' table. Harry reflected that whatever his mother had come down from, it was a great deal better than whatever had produced Uncle Vernon and Aunt Marge. He had a strong suspicion that it was ogres.

In Chapter Eight Ron and Hermione came back from their first visit to Hogsmeade, at Hallowe'en 1993, with an armful of sweets for Harry. One of them told him: ‘We think we saw an ogre, honestly, all sorts go in the Three Broomsticks...’

pages.title: Vampire clans
infobox: The Antediluvians of the Third Generation
A gift and a curse of the blood
pages.html:
Vampires are divided into clans, thirteen by the old count, though the count changes. Every clan descends from one of the vampires of the Third Generation, the grandchilder of Cain. Each carries its founder's gift and its founder's curse in the blood.

Blood and generation

Vampires count their descent by generation. Cain is the First. His childer were the Second, and theirs, the founders of the clans, were the Third. The older the blood, the stronger it is, and the less of a person is left in it. Vampires of the Fourth and Fifth Generations are called Methuselahs. The first vampire lies so far back that many vampires can no longer agree who he was.

The thirteen

The Ventrue think of themselves as kings. They have old money and old manners. They sit on the boards of Muggle banks and in Muggle parliaments. Occasionally one of them sits across a table from somebody at the Ministry of Magic, being polite about the agreement. Each of them can feed from only one kind of person, such as priests or left-handed men with red hair. They would starve sooner than drink from anybody else.

Every Malkavian is mad, because the blood makes them so. Some are mad the way Peeves is mad, some the way a very clever man is mad who has seen something he should not have. The madness spreads to anybody who talks with one for long enough.

The Tzimisce of the Carpathians shape bone and flesh like wax. One can come at an enemy as a great wolf made out of men. Struck, it does not fall down: it comes apart and walks off in several directions. The Nosferatu are twisted into monstrous shapes by the Embrace, and live hidden beneath the cities, trading in secrets.

The rest are the rebellious Brujah, the Gangrel who run as wolves, the Toreador who live for beauty, the Tremere sorcerers, the Lasombra masters of shadow, the Assamite assassins, the Ravnos tricksters, the Giovanni necromancers and the Followers of Set, who worship their founder as a god.

Sects and the blood bond

Seven clans founded the Camarilla, which keeps the Masquerade. The Lasombra and the Tzimisce lead the Sabbat. Vampires without a clan are called Caitiff.

Some vampires can take hold of a mind just by looking into it. Worse, a mortal who drinks a vampire's blood three times, a few drops each time, will love that vampire for the rest of his life, whether he wants to or not. He will never know the difference. This is the blood bond. Lupin calls it the cruellest thing they do.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, in September 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter that there were thirteen clans of vampires, among them the Ventrue, who think they are royalty. One of them, she said, was Angelus, of the Aurelian bloodline. She described the Nosferatu to him over breakfast, in rather more detail than he wanted with a kipper in front of him.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Gilderoy Lockhart boasted of beating a Methuselah of the fourth generation, of Clan 'Tzi-mi-see', who came at him in the shape of a great wolf made out of men. Professor McGonagall murmured to Harry that it was Tzimisce, three syllables, not four. That, she said, was not how one killed one of the fourth generation: not with a wand held so, nor with a wand at all. In Chapter Eleven Lockhart made Harry stand at the front of the class as his Tzimisce, then added to the tale an elder of Clan Ventrue who called himself the Master. Afterwards McGonagall gave Harry a message for him. 'If Professor Lockhart asks you to play a vampire again, you may tell him from me that a Tzimisce doesn't fall down when you hit it. It comes apart and walks off in several directions.'

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in October 1993, Remus Lupin taught Harry's class the clans: thirteen by the old count, each with its gift and its curse, descended from somebody so old that vampires can no longer agree on the first. He described the Ventrue, then warned the class above all about the Malkavians. 'So. If you ever meet a beautiful, charming, slightly odd person at a party who seems to know things about you that they can't possibly know... make your excuses. Early.' He ended with the blood bond. In Chapter Fourteen Neville Longbottom offered to help Harry with Malkavians, which he had studied for a family matter.

pages.title: Werewolf Registry
pages.html:
The Werewolf Registry is the Ministry of Magic's register of werewolves. It is built on the belief that the full moon makes a wolf of a man, so it watches the werewolves of Britain only around the full moon.

A grain of truth

There is only a grain of truth in the belief. The Garou change whenever they choose, into any of five shapes. What the moon does is raise the tide in them, so that on the nights about the full every one of them is harder to hold. Fenrir Greyback has never put his name on the Registry.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Professor Snape, taking Lupin's class, told them that the Ministry had built its Registry on that grain of truth. Hermione Granger put her hand up. If the Garou can change whenever they choose, she said, 'then the whole Registry is pointless, isn't it, because the Ministry only ever watches them on the full moon'. Snape took five points from Gryffindor for her trouble.

pages.title: Cho Chang
infobox: Ravenclaw, Hogwarts student, Ravenclaw Quidditch team, Seeker, Scottish, Quidditch
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
pages.html:
Cho Chang is a Scottish witch in Ravenclaw House, a year above Harry Potter, and the Ravenclaw Seeker. She is small, very fast and very pretty. In the Ravenclaw match of 1994 she marked Harry closely, which drew the attention of both Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy.

Quidditch

Cho is small, with long dark hair, and flies a Comet Two Sixty. She has supported the Tutshill Tornados since she was six. Before the Ravenclaw match Oliver Wood warned the team that she had been troubled by injuries. She can read a dive off a rival's shoulders.

In the match, in March 1994, she took one look at Harry's Firebolt and stopped hunting the Snitch. Instead she marked Harry, blocking him at every turn, all of it perfectly legal, until he feinted a dive and left her eighty feet below the game. She was the first to point at the fake dementors.

In the saga

Harry noticed that Cho was pretty, and was irritated with himself for noticing. After the match she told him that his dive had been evil, and that she would not fall for it next time. The next morning, after Dracina had given her a long, still look, Cho's bag split open on the marble staircase, smashing all her ink bottles. It was Seamus Finnigan who passed the story on to Harry.

When Cho wished Harry luck before the Quidditch final, Dracina snapped her quill in two, and Hermione went stiff. Ron, watching the war that was developing between the two girls, feared for her.

In their own words

That dive on Saturday was evil, you know.Cho Chang · B3 Ch14

pages.title: Roger Davies
infobox: Ravenclaw, Hogwarts student, Ravenclaw Quidditch team, Quidditch captain, Chaser
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Roger Davies is the captain of the Ravenclaw Quidditch team and one of its Chasers. In 1994 he was a big fifth-year, built like a rower, and very hard to stop once he had the Quaffle.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, Ravenclaw played Gryffindor in March 1994. Madam Hooch told Wood and Davies to shake hands. From the start Harry knew it was going to be a hard match. Davies barged Angelina Johnson off her line with his shoulder, quite legally. From the restart the Ravenclaw Chasers came down the pitch all three abreast, passing sideways in short, quick bursts, a formation Harry had never seen a school team use. Davies flicked the Quaffle past Oliver Wood's elbow into the top of the hoop.

Watching from above, Harry saw that the Ravenclaw Chasers turned the same way every time, into Davies, because he was the big one and they were all watching him. He sent Fred and George forward. George's first Bludger missed Davies by a foot, but it made him flinch just as he passed. The pass went wide, straight to Angelina, who was waiting on the outside exactly where Harry had told her to be.

Later Davies scored three goals in six minutes, every one of them hard, and brought Ravenclaw back to seventy points against Gryffindor's eighty. It was not enough. Harry caught the Snitch, and Gryffindor won the match.

pages.title: Derrick
infobox: Slytherin, Hogwarts student, Slytherin Quidditch team, Beater
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Derrick is a gigantic Slytherin Beater, partnered by Bole. In the 1994 final one of his Bludgers, meant for Harry Potter, hit Dracina Malfoy instead.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, early in the final, Derrick sent a Bludger whizzing past Harry's right ear. He and Bole closed in on Harry from opposite sides, but Harry shot straight upwards at the last moment. The two Beaters smashed into each other with a horrible crunch. Later, when Oliver Wood was left unguarded, Derrick and Bole drove both Bludgers into his stomach.

Once Derrick sent a Bludger at Harry out of the sun. Dracina swerved across in front of him, and it hit her on the shoulder with a thud that Harry heard from ten feet away. She swayed on her broom, white to the lips, then straightened up without a sound. Harry decided that Derrick must have mis-hit it.

pages.title: Bole
infobox: Slytherin, Hogwarts student, Slytherin Quidditch team, Beater
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Bole is a Beater on the Slytherin Quidditch team, partnered by Derrick. He played in the final against Gryffindor in 1994, the dirtiest match Harry Potter had ever flown in.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, early in the final, Bole and Derrick closed in on Harry from opposite sides with their clubs raised. Harry shot straight upwards at the last moment. The two Beaters smashed into each other with a horrible crunch. Gryffindor's lead drove the Slytherins half mad. Bole whacked Alicia Spinnet with his club, then swore he had mistaken her for a Bludger. George Weasley paid him back with an elbow across the nose.

Later the Weasley twins went to guard Katie Bell, leaving Oliver Wood alone at the hoops. Bole and Derrick saw it at once. They drove both Bludgers into Wood's stomach, one after the other. After the match Bole stood scowling up at the Cup.

pages.title: Hobday
infobox: Filius Flitwick teacher who paid his debt
Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Twelve
Nine Galleons, paid by Professor Flitwick (December 1993)
pages.html:
Hobday is a big fifth-year Slytherin. In December 1993 Professor Flitwick quietly paid a gambling debt of nine Galleons for him. In February 1994 he was caught pinning a first-year against the wall of the Entrance Hall over two Sickles.

The two debts

On 11 December 1993 Hobday went to Professor Flitwick's office in some distress. He had lost nine Galleons of his father's money at cards to a seventh-year, which is forbidden at Hogwarts. He could not pay it, and he had a week to find it. Flitwick paid the seventh-year out of his own pocket. He told nobody. He did not write to Hobday's father, and Hobday was not expelled. Flitwick told him at the time that he expected nothing whatsoever in return.

There are seventeen Sickles to the Galleon, so Hobday had been let off a hundred and fifty-three Sickles. The first thing he did with the rest of his winter was to threaten a child over two. It was the parable of the unforgiving servant over again: the servant who was forgiven ten thousand talents, then took a fellow servant by the throat over a hundred pence.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in February 1994, a shout from the doors to the dungeons made the whole Entrance Hall turn. Hobday had a first-year held up against the wall by the front of his robes, with the boy's feet clear of the floor. Two of Hobday's friends stood by looking embarrassed. The boy owed him two Sickles. He had promised to pay on Thursday, and it had been a fortnight. When the boy squeaked that he would get the money off his brother at Easter, Hobday told him to get it tonight, or he would have the boy's owl off him to sell.

Then Professor Flitwick came out of the Great Hall at a run, like a hornet arriving at a picnic. Hobday dropped the boy at once, and the boy bolted up the marble staircase. Flitwick drew himself up to his full height, which brought him roughly level with Hobday's elbow. In a voice that carried to every corner of the Hall, he told the story of the nine Galleons. Hobday went the colour of wet parchment. Flitwick asked him whether he knew how many Sickles there were in nine Galleons. Hobday did not answer.

'There are a hundred and fifty-three,' said Flitwick. 'My office, eight o'clock. Go away.'

Dracina Malfoy had watched the whole thing with her eyebrows up. 'Well,' she said. 'That was educational. A hundred and fifty-three. Do you suppose he'd worked that out beforehand, or is he simply like that?' Harry Potter could only look at the place where Hobday had been standing.

pages.title: The first-year bullied by Hobday
pages.html:
The first-year bullied by Hobday is a Hogwarts boy who owed two Sickles to Hobday, a big fifth-year Slytherin, in February 1994. He promised to get the money off his brother at Easter.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in February 1994, Hobday had the boy pinned against the wall of the Entrance Hall by the front of his robes, with his feet clear of the floor. Hobday bellowed that he had promised Thursday, and that it had been a fortnight. "I haven't got it!" squeaked the boy. He swore he would get it off his brother at Easter. Hobday told him to get it that night, or he would have the boy's owl off him to sell.

Then Professor Flitwick came out of the Great Hall at a run, and Hobday dropped the boy at once. The boy grabbed his bag and bolted up the marble staircase. Flitwick went on to remind the whole Hall that in December he had paid Hobday's own gambling debt of nine Galleons out of his own pocket. Nine Galleons, Flitwick pointed out, came to a hundred and fifty-three Sickles.

pages.title: The Malfoy eagle owl
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Malfoy eagle owl is Ganymede, the great eagle owl of Malfoy Manor. He belongs, strictly, to Narcissa Malfoy. For nearly three years he has carried Dracina Malfoy's parcels of sweets to Hogwarts every week.

Description

He is enormous, dark and barred. He has ear tufts like horns and eyes the colour of marmalade. He makes plain what he thinks of the places he is sent to.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, at midnight on 31 July 1993, he swept into Harry Potter's bedroom at Privet Drive with Dracina's birthday letter tied to his leg with green ribbon. He looked round the room with an expression of the deepest disdain, and did not wait for a reply.

In Chapter Fourteen Harry knew him at once when he came down over the Slytherin table at breakfast. He dropped a thick envelope from Lucius Malfoy, sealed in green wax, in front of Dracina, then swept straight out again without waiting for so much as a bacon rind.

pages.title: Security trolls
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Male, as far as Harry Potter could tell
The seventh-floor corridor outside the Fat Lady's portrait
pages.html:
The security trolls are a gang of enormous, sullen male trolls that Hogwarts hired in March 1994 to guard the Fat Lady, the portrait at the entrance to Gryffindor Tower. From then on they paced the corridor outside her frame at all hours, grunting at one another.

Why they were hired

At Hallowe'en 1993 Sirius Black slashed the Fat Lady's portrait when she would not let him into Gryffindor Tower, and she fled her frame. The knight Sir Cadogan guarded the entrance in her place. In March 1994 Black got past him too, with a whole week's passwords read off a little piece of paper, so Sir Cadogan was sacked.

The Fat Lady came home beautifully mended, though the faint lines of the stitching still showed if anybody looked closely, which she did not like them doing. She was in a terrible state of nerves. She flatly refused to go back to work unless somebody stood guard over her, so the castle hired the trolls.

The trolls

They are enormous, sullen, thoroughly unpleasant creatures. Each carries a club, and they like to hold their clubs up side by side, like boys comparing conkers. As far as Harry Potter could tell, they were all male. At least, he reflected, they did not go wandering into the ladies' loo, which was more than could be said for the last troll to get into the castle.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, the trolls took up their post on the seventh floor. It was Neville Longbottom who had written down the week's passwords and left them lying about, so Professor McGonagall had forbidden every Gryffindor to tell him the new one. Every evening he had to sit on the cold flagstones outside the portrait, hugging his knees, until somebody came along to let him in. The trolls stood over him the whole time, leering. After a week of it Harry took pity on him and told him the password, Victis, in a low voice, so that the trolls would not hear.

By Chapter Sixteen, in June 1994, the Fat Lady had taken a great fancy to them and was flirting with them outrageously. On the day of the Divination examination she had put on her best pink silk to flutter her eyelashes at the largest, who was picking his teeth with a splinter of the banister. She told him that he had the most expressive eyebrows. The troll grunted.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, at breakfast in the last days of term, Crabbe and Goyle sat at the Slytherin table nodding slowly at whatever anybody said, like the security trolls who had guarded the Fat Lady's portrait since the spring.

pages.title: The Ravenclaw sixth-year with the fleece
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 12
A soaked sheepskin on dry stone
pages.html:
The Ravenclaw sixth-year with the fleece is a witch whom Harry Potter found lying on the front steps of the castle one evening in late February 1994, testing a sheepskin. It was soaked, while the stone round it stayed bone dry. She meant to repeat the test the other way round before she would believe it.

The test

She lay flat on her stomach with a lantern, touching the fleece with two fingers in a careful grid, muttering numbers over a notebook. There was no dew that night, and the glass had been rising since four. She had had the fleece out for two hours, and it was wet. Nothing in the physical world could account for it, which delighted her.

The next night she meant to do it the other way round: dry fleece, wet stone, with everything else exactly the same. One result on its own proved nothing, she said. It could be a fluke, or the stone, or her wanting it. 'Then I'll believe it,' she told Harry, 'and not before. Anybody who tells you that's faithless has never had to write a thing down.' Gideon had asked for the same sign twice, the other way about the second time.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry was on his way to the Owlery, where a broom was waiting for him, when he came on her outside the oak doors. Ron had gone back for his scarf. Harry stopped, because it was not possible to walk past, and asked whether she was all right. She told him to shush.

When she went back to her grid, Harry stood on the gravel in the wind for some time. He had never asked for his own sign twice. He had never asked for it even once. He had been handed a single piece of parchment and had built a whole winter on it, without ever once putting it to the test.

In their own words

Anybody who tells you that's faithless has never had to write a thing down.The Ravenclaw sixth-year with the fleece · B3 Ch12

pages.title: The Hufflepuff boy who went through the ice
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff boy who went through the ice is a thin second-year who walked thirty feet out on the frozen lake in January 1994. He was doing well until he looked down. Then he panicked, and fell through to his chest.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in January 1994, Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy were on the bank when a shout went up. The boy was out past the reeds, going along as though the lake were a floor. At thirty feet he turned to wave. He saw what was under his feet, four inches of ice over a hundred feet of black lake, and whatever had been holding him up stopped. He took two running steps and went through with a crack like a gun. An enormous sixth-year Hufflepuff hauled him out. He was carried towards the castle, blue, wrapped in four cloaks, with his teeth going like a telegraph.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, in June 1994, as Harry faced the dementors by the lake, he remembered the boy. Harry did not look down.

pages.title: The sixth-year Hufflepuff who pulled the boy from the ice
infobox: Pulling a second-year out of the frozen lake, January 1994
pages.html:
The sixth-year Hufflepuff who pulled the boy from the ice is an enormous Hufflepuff who, in January 1994, lay flat on the frozen lake at Hogwarts to haul out a second-year who had gone through. Then he told him off for looking down.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, the boy went into the lake up to his chest. The sixth-year lay flat on his stomach, grabbed him by the robes and hauled him out. The two of them came off the lake in an undignified sliding tangle, to the sound of the whole bank shouting at once. As the boy was carried up the lawn towards the castle, the sixth-year kept saying it, to nobody, with the particular fury of fright. "Why did you look down? You were all right. You were all right the whole way, you daft little idiot. You were fine till you looked down."

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, in June 1994, Harry Potter remembered the big Hufflepuff carrying the boy up the lawn, and what he had said. The words helped Harry cast his Patronus.

In their own words

You were fine till you looked down.The sixth-year Hufflepuff who pulled the boy from the ice · B3 Ch12

pages.title: Lizzie
pages.html:
Lizzie is a first-year Hufflepuff who started at Hogwarts in September 1993. At the start of February 1994 a cut went right through her forearm, and Madam Pomfrey healed it in about four seconds. Her friend Mary would not believe it until she had touched the scar.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in the first week of February 1994, Lizzie came out from between the library shelves with her sleeve pushed up to the elbow, arguing with Mary. The cut had gone all the way through, she said, yet Madam Pomfrey had mended it in about four seconds. Mary still wanted to touch it. "Fine," said Lizzie, and thrust out her arm. "Go on, then. Put your finger on it." Mary pressed two fingers into the thin white line, then gave in. "I'm sorry, Lizzie. All right. I believe you." Lizzie told her she was an awful friend. They went off between the shelves arm in arm, with Madam Pince hissing at them from the desk.

pages.title: Mary
pages.html:
Mary is a first-year Hufflepuff who started at Hogwarts in September 1993. In February 1994 she would not believe that her friend Lizzie's arm had healed until she had touched the scar. Then she said sorry.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in the first week of February 1994, the two friends came out from between the library shelves, arguing. A cut had gone right through Lizzie's forearm, and Madam Pomfrey had healed it in about four seconds. Mary was not saying Lizzie was lying, she said; she only did not believe that a cut could go all the way through somebody's arm on Tuesday and be gone by Friday. She wanted to touch it. She took her friend's wrist, quite seriously, like a healer, and pressed two fingers into the thin white line. Then her face went quiet. "Oh," she said. "I'm sorry, Lizzie. All right. I believe you." When Lizzie called her an awful friend, Mary humbly agreed, and they went off between the shelves arm in arm.

In their own words

I'm sorry, Lizzie. All right. I believe you.Mary · B3 Ch12

pages.title: The Hufflepuff who knocked over Hermione's bag
infobox: Eleven inches taller than Hermione Granger
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff who knocked over Hermione's bag is a second-year Hufflepuff boy, eleven inches taller than Hermione Granger. In the spring of 1994 he caught the strap of her bag with his elbow outside the Charms classroom. One look from her had him on his knees, picking up her homework.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, on a Friday morning in the corridor outside Charms, the boy was running late and caught the strap of Hermione's bag with his elbow as he dashed past. The bag went flying, and two hours' worth of Arithmancy homework went skating across the flagstones. He began to stammer an apology. Harry Potter, three feet away, found that he had taken a step backwards without meaning to. Hermione did not shout. She stood perfectly still, with wisps of bushy hair escaping from her ponytail, and gave the boy a long, flat, patient look, as though he were a wasp she had not yet decided whether to swat. The boy went white to the lips. He said sorry three more times, got down on his knees and gathered up every last sheet in the right order.

pages.title: The Hufflepuff who dropped her Remembrall
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff who dropped her Remembrall is a second-year Hufflepuff girl. In the spring of 1994 Harry Potter made her jump by shouting on the stairs, and she dropped it. A Remembrall is a glass ball the size of a large marble, full of smoke that turns red when its owner has forgotten something.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Hermione Granger missed Charms after her fight with Dracina Malfoy on the castle steps, and she was not at lunch either. On the stairs up to Gryffindor Tower, Ron Weasley asked anxiously whether Harry thought Malfoy had done something to her. "No," said Harry. It came out a great deal louder than he had meant. The second-year Hufflepuff on the landing above jumped and dropped her Remembrall. Malfoy would not go sneaking about, he said, more quietly but just as fiercely. If she wanted to have a go at Hermione, she would do it to her face.

pages.title: The two Hufflepuffs at the steps fight
infobox: The fight between Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy, spring 1994
pages.html:
The two Hufflepuffs at the steps fight were two students dawdling at the bottom of the front steps of Hogwarts in the spring of 1994, when Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy fought there. When it was over, they went off to tell everybody they knew.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Dracina's voice rose as she accused Hermione of poking her nose into business that was not hers, and the two Hufflepuffs stopped dawdling to stare. The girls rolled down the last of the steps in a tangle of black robes. Hermione's bag split, Dracina's plaits came down, and somebody screamed: one of the Hufflepuffs, perhaps, or Pansy Parkinson. When Dracina had gone inside, with Pansy scurrying after her, the two Hufflepuffs decided the show was over. They slunk off round the side of the castle to tell everybody they knew.

pages.title: The leek-eared duellists
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A fourth-year Gryffindor; a sixth-year Slytherin
Neighbouring beds in the hospital wing, with leeks growing out of their ears
pages.html:
The leek-eared duellists were a fourth-year Gryffindor and a sixth-year Slytherin who fought each other in a corridor at Hogwarts in the spring of 1994, before the Quidditch final. Both of them ended up in neighbouring beds in the hospital wing, each with a bunch of leeks growing out of his ears.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, by the end of the Easter holidays of 1994, feeling between Gryffindor and Slytherin was running higher before the final than anyone could remember. Fights kept breaking out in the corridors. This one was the worst of them.

pages.title: Walden Macnair
infobox:
Lucius Malfoy old friend
Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures employer
Rubeus Hagrid antagonist
Ministry of Magic, executioner, Executioners' Union, Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
Executioner, Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
Executioners' Union; formerly a Death Eater
pages.html:
Walden Macnair is the executioner employed by the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures at the Ministry of Magic, and an old friend of Lucius Malfoy. In June 1994 he was sent to Hogwarts to behead the hippogriff Buckbeak. He was cheated of his work.

Background

Macnair is tall and burly, with a thin black moustache. He served Lord Voldemort as a Death Eater in the first war, and escaped prosecution after his master's fall. Afterwards he found work at the Ministry in which he could still kill things. He is a member of the Executioners' Union.

In the saga

On the day of Buckbeak's appeal in June 1994, Macnair stood on the front steps of Hogwarts stroking his axe. Dracina Malfoy fled at the sight of him.

At sunset, as the axe fell, a small hooded figure flew Buckbeak away from under his nose, and the blade buried itself in a tree. The rider was Dracina, who had lured the hippogriff with a dead ferret. She did it in front of the Minister for Magic.

Macnair raged in Hagrid's pumpkin patch. 'I'm lodging a formal complaint, Hagrid, on behalf of the Executioners' Union!' he yelled. 'Nobody pays a man for a job he never done!' He accused Hagrid of planning it and insulted his giant mother. Hagrid threw him into the pumpkins, where he lay howling for Hagrid's arrest. On the walk back up to the castle he complained to the Minister that his axe had gone blunt on the tree. Later that night he went to fetch the dementors to give Sirius Black the Kiss.

In their own words

Nobody pays a man for a job he never done!Walden Macnair · B3 Ch16
I'm lodging a formal complaint, Hagrid, on behalf of the Executioners' Union!Walden Macnair · B3 Ch20

pages.title: The elderly Committee member
aliases: the old wizard from the Committee
pages.kind: Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
infobox: Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
pages.html:
The elderly Committee member was a very old wizard from the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures, who came to Hogwarts in June 1994 for the appeal of the hippogriff Buckbeak. He was so old that he seemed to be shrivelling up before Harry Potter's eyes, and he complained that he was getting too old for this.

The Committee

The Committee belongs to the Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures at the Ministry of Magic. It hears cases against creatures thought to be dangerous, and it keeps an executioner of its own. In 1994 it was Walden Macnair, an old friend of Lucius Malfoy's.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, he came out of the castle behind Cornelius Fudge with the executioner. He squinted down the lawn towards Hagrid's cabin and spoke in a thin, quavering voice: ‘Dear, dear, I’m getting too old for this... Two o’clock, isn’t it, Fudge?’ At sunset, when the party came down the castle steps to the cabin, the doddery old wizard brought up the rear with Macnair and his axe.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, he came down to the cabin for the execution itself, with Dumbledore, Fudge and Macnair. Inside, he suggested that Hagrid might do better to stay indoors for it. When Buckbeak was found to be gone, he sat down rather suddenly on an upturned bucket and fanned himself with his hat.

pages.title: The St Grogory's dinner lady
infobox: St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
An extra bread roll every day, for a fortnight
pages.html:
The St Grogory's dinner lady served school dinners at Harry Potter's primary school in Little Whinging. For a fortnight she slipped him an extra bread roll every day. Then Aunt Petunia came in to complain about the jumper, and after that the dinner lady never looked at him again.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, trudging back up to the castle after the Ravenclaw match in March 1994, Harry remembered her. He had let himself hope where Dracina Malfoy was concerned, and the old voice in his head was reminding him why he should not have. The dinner lady's kindness had hurt more than all the people who had never been kind to him in the first place. It was part of the lesson the Dursleys had drummed into him from the time he could walk: kindness is the first half of something.

pages.title: The St Grogory's teacher
infobox: St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
pages.html:
The St Grogory's teacher taught at Harry Potter's primary school in Little Whinging. When Dudley Dursley broke Harry's glasses with his fist in the playground, this teacher let Dudley off, because boys would be boys.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, after the Ravenclaw match in March 1994, the memory came back to Harry with a string of others as he walked up the lawn. There were the old socks wrapped in newspaper for his sixth birthday, the sweet Dudley held out then snatched back, and the dinner lady who stopped looking at him. Together they made up the oldest lesson he had: nobody was nice to you for nothing, and hoping always cost you.

pages.title: Septima Vector
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Septima Vector teaches Arithmancy at Hogwarts. It is the study of the magical properties of numbers, and one of the optional subjects open to pupils from their third year.

Arithmancy

Arithmancy is worked through long, complicated number charts, and it is reckoned one of the hardest of the optional subjects. Pupils choose it at the end of their second year, alongside Divination, Care of Magical Creatures, the Study of Ancient Runes and Muggle Studies, or instead of them. In the spring of 1993 Neville Longbottom went round the common room asking anybody who came near him whether Arithmancy sounded harder than Ancient Runes. Hermione's Arithmancy book is Numerology and Grammatica, a vast volume full of number charts.

Hermione Granger, who has no patience with Divination, counts Arithmancy among her favourite subjects. Her charts are columns of numbers with lines ruled between them in four colours. Ron Weasley once saw her Arithmancy homework by accident, and said it gave him a headache for two days.

In the saga

Hermione took Arithmancy with Professor Vector from September 1993, as part of a timetable that put her in more than one classroom at the same hour. One morning in September her timetable had her in Divination, Muggle Studies and Arithmancy, all at nine o'clock. Early in 1994 Harry picked up one of her charts and said that Arithmancy looked terrible. Hermione told him otherwise: 'It's my favourite subject!'

About the same time Ron overheard Hermione discussing with Vector, 'that Arithmancy witch', a lesson she seemed to have attended while she was somewhere else entirely. In June she sat the Arithmancy exam at nine o'clock on the Monday morning, at the same time as Transfiguration. The explanation was the Time-Turner that Professor McGonagall had obtained for her from the Ministry of Magic. McGonagall had sworn her to keep it secret.

pages.title: The old man who visited early Hogwarts
infobox: Hogwarts, one winter in its earliest years
Very tall, very old; a grey hat with the point fallen over
pages.html:
The old man who visited early Hogwarts was a very tall, very old traveller who came up out of the valley on foot one winter, in the snow, when the school was so new that its hall had only half a roof and no gate. He was Gandalf, who had gathered the four founders in the first place. The Fat Friar, who met him as a boy, never asked his name.

The visit

The hall door opened for him before anybody had touched it. He wore a grey hat with the point fallen over, and boots that had walked a very long way. He carried a stick taller than he was. The Friar thought him older than the hills, and in all the centuries since he has not had cause to change his mind.

He sat half the night by the kitchen fire with a crowd of muddy first-years, smoking and telling them stories. Magic, he told them, was a gift, given long ago to men who needed it by Somebody who had never given up on them. Most people had long since forgotten who had passed it on. You are not the first to carry it, he said. Don't let anybody tell you it's yours to do as you like with.

It was a lesson the Friar never forgot. In his day half the lads who left the school went into the Church, and most wizards believed, as he did, that God had given them magic on purpose, to be used in His service.

Who he was

The old man was Gandalf. He had gathered Rowena Ravenclaw, Godric Gryffindor, Helga Hufflepuff and Salazar Slytherin when they were young, standing them in the mud on the crag above the lake. He taught all four of them while the school took shape. These days he goes by the name of Ambrose Greyhame and is the vicar of St Michael's Church in Little Whinging. Harry Potter met him on the lych-gate bench there in July 1993, and still has no idea who he is.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry asked the Fat Friar why wizards hated the Church. The Friar told him that most wizards of his own day had believed God gave them magic on purpose. When Harry asked who had told him so, the Friar remembered the old man by the kitchen fire. Harry had an odd feeling that he had heard about this man before, though he could not think where. He asked the old man's name. 'Do you know,' said the Friar, 'I never asked. It didn't seem the sort of thing you asked him.'

Later in the same talk the Friar told Harry that the door had always been open. Nobody was going to ask him for a ticket. Harry's head jerked up. The old man on the lych-gate bench had said exactly that to him in the summer, and Harry said so. 'Did they?' said the Friar mildly. 'Sensible fellow.'

pages.title: The Flash
aliases: the man in the red suit
infobox: Jay Garrick (from 1939); Barry Allen (1956 to 1985); Wally West (since 1985)
pages.html:
The Flash is the name carried by three of the world's fastest men. Jay Garrick took it in 1939. Barry Allen, the Flash of the Justice League's early years, died in 1985 in the Crisis. Wally West, who as a boy had run beside Barry, has been the Flash ever since. In August 1994 he stood behind Superman at the United Nations, a man of about forty-five.

Jay Garrick

The first Flash was Jay Garrick, a college student who gained his speed in a laboratory accident. He came to public notice at the end of 1939 in a red shirt with a lightning flash and a winged metal helmet. He was a founder of the Justice Society in 1940, and he retired with it in 1951.

A wartime enemy's sorcery kept him young for half a century. In July 1994, during Zero Hour, Extant aged him in moments to his true years, about seventy-four. The Society disbanded soon after.

Barry Allen

In 1956 a Central City police scientist, Barry Allen, was soaked in chemicals by a bolt of lightning. He found that he could run faster than sound. He took the name of the Flash from Jay Garrick, whom he had admired as a boy. His red suit, with the lightning flash on the chest, has been the Flash's ever since.

Barry was a founder of the Justice League. He died in 1985 in the Crisis, the battle nobody has ever properly explained. So far as anyone can say, he ran himself out of existence destroying a weapon aimed at the world, and he was never seen again.

Wally West

Wally West, the nephew of Barry Allen's wife, Iris, was given the same powers in 1959 by a repetition of the same accident, when he was about ten. He ran beside Barry as Kid Flash for a quarter of a century. After Barry's death he took up his name and his costume.

Wally has served in the Justice League in its various forms. In 1994 he serves under Superman.

The name

In Britain the name of the Flash has an unfortunate echo, since it is also the name of a well-known household cleaner. At least one British newsreader has said so on air.

In the saga

In the spring of 1994, watching Hermione leave a room at speed, Harry Potter remembered once seeing a man in a red suit on the Dursleys' television, on the news from America. He had been running so fast that the cameras could only catch a streak of light. The newsreader had said he was called after the same stuff Aunt Petunia used on the kitchen floor.

On 20 August 1994 the Flash stood behind Superman at the Security Council. He was not the Flash of Dudley's old annuals, who had died in 1985 in a battle nobody had ever properly explained, but the boy who used to run beside him, grown into a man of forty-five or so.

pages.title: History of Magic classroom
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The History of Magic classroom at Hogwarts belongs to Professor Binns, the only ghost on the staff. It smells of a hundred years of his chalk dust.

The room

Binns comes into his lessons through the blackboard. He fell asleep in front of the staff-room fire long ago, and the next morning he got up to teach as usual, leaving his body behind in the armchair.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Remus Lupin held Harry Potter's Patronus lessons there, at eight o'clock on Thursday evenings; the room, he said, should be large enough. On the first evening the room was dark and cold. It smelt of a century of chalk dust. Harry lit the lamps along the walls with his wand. Lupin arrived with a big packing case roped at the corners, which held a boggart. He got it on to Binns's desk with a thump that raised dust.

pages.title: The Fat Friar's priory
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 15
On the Wash, in eastern England
The Fat Friar, for a few hundred years
By King Henry VIII, for the lead off its roof
pages.html:
The Fat Friar's priory was a Benedictine house on the Wash, on the east coast of England, where the Hufflepuff ghost known as the Fat Friar was a monk in life. After his death he haunted it for a few hundred years. Then King Henry VIII pulled it down to sell the lead off the roof, and the Friar came home to Hogwarts.

History

In the Friar's young days, he said, half the boys who left Hogwarts went into the Church, Muggle-borns mostly, since a monastery would gladly take a boy who could set a broken leg by looking at it. Most monks were ordinary men who got up in the dark to sing. The wizards among them believed, as the Friar did, that God had given them magic on purpose, and that using it to heal was a kind of prayer.

The priory fell in the Dissolution of the Monasteries in the late 1530s, when the King's men stripped the abbeys and priories of England of everything that could be sold. Lead from the roofs fetched a great deal of money.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry Potter found the Fat Friar at the window of the corridor that leads down to the kitchens, and asked him about God. The Friar told him that he was a good deal older than the fourteenth century, whatever the records said. 'I spent a few hundred years haunting my own priory, on the Wash, until King Henry pulled it down to sell the lead off the roof. I came home to Hogwarts after that.' He was strictly a monk, he added. The friars came along a couple of hundred years after he had died, but the name had stuck.

pages.title: Afghanistan
pages.html:
Afghanistan is a mountainous, landlocked country between Iran, Pakistan and the former Soviet republics of Central Asia. Professor McGonagall knows it from her own work, and seldom speaks of it.

History

The Soviet army invaded in December 1979 and fought the mujahideen in its mountains for nearly ten years, withdrawing in 1989. During the war a parasite of the vocal cords, a strain that spreads by language, went through the Russian soldiers there. McGonagall has seen it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, McGonagall assured Harry that the Philosopher's Stone was secure. She knew what she was talking about, she said: she had once spent a very long night in the dark outside Kandahar, making certain her camp was properly warded against creatures he would learn about in his third year.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry put Kandahar in the drawer in his head marked later, along with Kosovo and a place called Zanzibar Land. In Chapter Ten, over the Petrified Mrs Norris, McGonagall asked Lockhart whether he had considered 'a parasite of the vocal cords'. It had spread, she said, through Russian soldiers in Afghanistan and conscripts in Africa.

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, McGonagall watched the boys of Harry's dormitory march him down to breakfast as an escort for his new Firebolt. Over her toast she muttered: 'More protective than those absolute glaikits in Afghanistan.' A glaikit, in Scots, is a fool.

pages.title: Silver Arrow
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Circles back to hover over a fallen rider
pages.html:
The Silver Arrow is an old broomstick that has not been made for many years. It was one of the first true racing brooms, made by Leonard Jewkes. It had one habit its riders never forgot: if they fell off, it would circle back to hover over them until help came.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, examining Harry Potter's Firebolt, Madam Hooch thought its slim handle reminded her of the old Silver Arrows. 'A pity they've stopped making them. I learnt to fly on one, and a very fine old broom it was too.' If you came off one at a hundred feet, she said, it would circle back to hover over you until somebody came. She spoke from experience.

pages.title: Time-Turner
aliases: the golden object on Hermione's chain
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A tiny glittering hourglass on a fine gold chain
Each turn takes the wearer back one hour
Professor McGonagall, with the Ministry's leave
pages.html:
A Time-Turner is a magical device that carries its wearer back through time. Hermione Granger wore one all through the school year of 1993 to 1994, so that she could go to lessons held at the same hour. On the night of 6 June 1994 she used it to take herself and Harry Potter back three hours.

Description

Hermione's Time-Turner is a tiny glittering hourglass on a gold chain as fine as a thread. Each turn of the hourglass takes the wearer back an hour. Anyone inside the chain travels too.

Time-Turners are rare, and the Ministry of Magic does not let them out lightly. Before Hermione could have one, Professor McGonagall had to write all sorts of letters to the Ministry. She had to tell it that Hermione was a model student, who would never use it for anything except her studies.

How it works

A Time-Turner cannot change what has happened. Professor McGonagall explained it to Hermione as best she could: from the traveller's point of view, the time has already happened. The traveller must also take great care not to be seen. 'It's quite simple if you have a grasp of quantum mechanics, Harry,' Hermione told him. Harry had no such grasp.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, on the first morning of the exams, Hermione sat at breakfast twisting the chain she had been worrying at since the start of term. She drew out an inch of it while she watched Dracina Malfoy at the Slytherin table. Something small and golden glinted at the end of it, just under the edge of her collar. 'Do you know,' she said, in a strange, soft voice, 'it would be so easy. Nobody would ever know.' Then she stopped dead, with a sharp, angry little movement, and pushed the chain back inside her robes.

When Harry asked what the thing was, she said shortly that it was a present from a friend of the family. Twice more that week he saw her hand creep up to her collar while she glared across the Great Hall at Dracina, and each time she snatched it away again, as if the chain had burnt her. Only a Time-Turner could explain how she had been at lessons and exams held at the same hour.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Dumbledore locked Harry and Hermione into the hospital wing at five minutes to midnight on 6 June 1994. His last words were: 'Miss Granger, three turns should do it. Good luck.' Hermione flung the chain round Harry's neck as well as her own. She turned the tiny hourglass three times, which took them back three hours. She had got the Time-Turner from Professor McGonagall on the first day back, she explained, and had used it all year to get to all her lessons. Later that night Harry had to tell Dracina about it, which was the last thing Hermione had ever wanted.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, on the train home, Hermione told her friends that she had dropped Muggle Studies. 'That Time-Turner, it was driving me mad. I've handed it in.'

pages.title: Dracina Malfoy's grandmother's brooch
infobox: From a fire bucket, by Dracina herself
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's grandmother's brooch is the silver serpent clasp, with emerald eyes, that Dracina inherited from her grandmother Black and wears in her hair. In September 1993 it went missing from her plaits. She was sure that Hermione Granger had taken it, and she was right.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, the brooch vanished on the day Dracina came back to lessons after Buckbeak’s attack. Peeves turned up wearing it on his bow tie, then flung it into a fire bucket, and Dracina fished it out with her sleeve soaked to the shoulder. Hermione told her she was so sorry about it.

In Chapter Ten, in front of Harry, Dracina let Hermione know what she suspected. She was glad Hermione had been so concerned for her arm, she said, back when her jewellery kept finding its way into Hermione’s bag. In Chapter Fourteen, when a letter she had written vanished from the table by her bed, Dracina told Harry that it must have been Granger. ‘She had my grandmother’s brooch in September, I know she did; she’d take a letter.’ In Chapter Fifteen she told Hermione to her face that she knew about the brooch.

In Chapter Twenty, in the Forest in June 1994, Hermione owned up. She had taken the brooch out of Dracina’s hair in a corridor and left it on the dungeon steps, where Peeves would find it. ‘I fished it out of a fire bucket, Granger. It took a week to dry.’ In Chapter Twenty-One Hermione offered to be her friend, if Dracina could forgive her for the brooch, the ribbons and the rest.

pages.title: Dracina's Easter egg
pages.html:
Dracina's Easter egg is the dark chocolate egg, as big as a Quaffle, that Harry Potter found on his pillow on Easter Sunday 1994. Dracina Malfoy had made it herself, and she wanted him to know it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry woke to find it on his pillow, wrapped in green tissue paper. He had never been given an Easter egg in his life. A thin gold line ran round its middle where the halves joined, and a golden Snitch was painted on one side. On the other side, in letters of white icing so small that he had to hold it up to the window, was a message: I made it myself. Truly. D. He had no idea how she had got it into a guarded tower.

Hermione spotted it at breakfast and went rigid. She wanted to take it straight to Professor McGonagall, in case it was cursed. Harry would not let her. She tried three revealing charms on it at the Gryffindor table, and nothing happened. Ron snapped off a piece and ate it. ‘If I die,’ he said thickly, ‘tell Mum it was worth it.’

He did not die. Harry broke off a piece for himself. Over at the Slytherin table Dracina had been watching him all through breakfast. As he bit into the chocolate, she went pink to the roots of her hair.

pages.title: Neville's password list
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A whole week of Sir Cadogan's passwords to Gryffindor Tower
pages.html:
Neville's password list was the scrap of paper on which Neville Longbottom wrote down a whole week of Sir Cadogan's passwords to Gryffindor Tower. He lost it. Sirius Black used it to walk straight past Sir Cadogan into the tower.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, Ron woke in the night to find Sirius Black beside his bed. Sir Cadogan told Professor McGonagall proudly that the man had had the whole week's passwords and had read them off a little piece of paper. 'Which person,' she said, in a voice that was not steady, 'which abysmally foolish person wrote down this week's passwords and left them lying around?' Neville, standing at the foot of the stairs in his fluffy slippers, slowly put up a shaking hand.

In Chapter Fourteen McGonagall banned Neville from Hogsmeade for the rest of his school career, gave him a detention and forbade everyone in Gryffindor Tower to tell him the password. Every evening he sat on the cold flagstones outside the portrait until somebody let him in. Two days after the break-in his grandmother sent him a Howler.

In Chapter Eighteen Black explained that Crookshanks had stolen the passwords for him from a boy's bedside table. 'Ugh... bloody Neville,' Harry murmured.

pages.title: Crystal ball
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
A crystal ball is a globe of crystal, full of a softly glowing milky mist, into which a Seer gazes to see what is coming. Professor Trelawney calls it the Orb. She teaches it to her third-years at Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, early in 1994, Professor Trelawney brought out the crystal balls sooner than she had planned. ‘The fates have informed me that your examination in June will concern the Orb, and I am anxious to give you sufficient practice.’ Harry asked whether the prophets of the Bible, who saw visions without any crystal ball, counted. Trelawney told him that those were desert folk tales. ‘A true Seer does not require a burning bush.’

After fifteen minutes of gazing into the mist, Ron had seen only a burn on the table, where somebody had spilt a candle. A little later he announced that the meaning was obvious: there was going to be loads of fog tonight. When Professor Trelawney bent over their ball, she saw the Grim in it again, stalking towards Harry. Hermione told her not to start on that ridiculous Grim again. Trelawney said that her mind was hopelessly mundane. Hermione crammed her books into her bag, announced that she gave up and stamped out through the trapdoor.

pages.title: The Saint George window
infobox: A knight, a dragon and a lady in white
pages.html:
The Saint George window is a stained-glass window in a church in Little Whinging. Aunt Petunia took the family there one Christmas. The window shows a painted knight, a dragon, and a lady in white in the corner.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, as Harry ran at the Basilisk in the Chamber of Secrets with the sword blazing in his hands, some small, calm part of him thought of the picture in that church. There was the painted knight on the painted horse, going in under the dragon's neck with his lance couched. The whole window was lit up gold behind him, while the lady stood in the corner in white and waited.

In Chapter Nineteen Harry remembered the visit itself. He had been seven. Aunt Petunia had taken them all that once, at Christmas, because the Polkisses went and she was not going to be outdone.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry remembered thinking of the window as he ran at the Basilisk. In Divination he asked Professor Trelawney whether Saint George was a Muggle story as well. She told him that George had been a wizard, a knight of the old school with a lance in one hand and his wand in the other. He slew his dragon by magic, she said, and let the Muggles believe it had been their God. When Harry told the Fat Friar, the Hufflepuff ghost, the Friar agreed that George was a wizard. As for whose strength he had killed his dragon with, the Friar said that Harry was in a rather better position to judge than Professor Trelawney was.

pages.title: Fudge Flies
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Fudge Flies are a wizarding sweet. Scabbers, Ron Weasley's rat, was particularly fond of them, as Ron made sure everybody knew once Scabbers had gone.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, after Scabbers had vanished, apparently eaten by Crookshanks, Ron spent a whole evening telling Dean Thomas at great length about the Fudge Flies Scabbers used to like. Across the room, Hermione’s quill stopped moving.

At the party after Gryffindor beat Ravenclaw, Harry was trying to coax Hermione over for some food when Ron called across the common room: ‘If Scabbers hadn’t just been eaten, he could have had some of those Fudge Flies. He used to really like them-’ Hermione burst into tears. She snatched up her enormous book and fled up the girls’ staircase.

pages.title: Fizzing Whizzbees
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Fizzing Whizzbees, also spelt Fizzing Whizbees, are sherbet balls sold at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade that lift whoever sucks one a few inches into the air. Since they come from Hogsmeade, Argus Filch regards them as contraband.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, the feud between Gryffindor and Slytherin boiled over one last time, on the Saturday after the Quidditch final. Filch was sent round every dormitory in the castle with a list of forbidden objects as long as his arm. Harry raced off to hide his Invisibility Cloak down the chute in the one-eyed witch's hump. When he got back to Gryffindor Tower, Filch was tipping out Ron's trunk on to the floor. He confiscated a packet of Fizzing Whizzbees.

pages.title: Arresto Momentum
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Arresto Momentum is the charm that slows a falling object, or a falling person, so that it comes down gently. It is a charm that takes practice: in an emergency it must be cast quickly, and at a moving target.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, in March 1994, Dracina Malfoy admitted to Professor Snape that she had helped with the fake-dementor prank at the Ravenclaw match. She had made the others let her go on top, so that she would know the very second anything went wrong. She had her wand out the whole time.

For a week before the match she had practised Arresto Momentum in an empty classroom every night, on cushions, on a broom and on a suit of armour, until she could do it in her sleep. She meant to catch Harry Potter if her prank made him fall. 'If he'd fallen, I'd have caught him. I would have.'

As it turned out, Harry did not need catching. He sent a Patronus at the three figures below him instead.

pages.title: Cheering Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Leaves the target giddy and happy
pages.html:
A Cheering Charm leaves the person it hits giddy, happy and inclined to laugh at nothing. Overdone, it can leave them laughing for an hour.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in 1994, Professor Flitwick had his third-years practising Cheering Charms in pairs. It was the best Charms lesson they had ever had. Within ten minutes Neville was giggling helplessly into his sleeve, while Ron left Harry beaming at the ceiling in a happy, silly daze. Flitwick hinted that the charms would come up in the examinations.

They did. In Chapter Sixteen, in June, Harry was so nervous that he slightly overdid his. Ron, his partner, went off into fits of hysterical laughter and had to lie down in an empty classroom. It was a full hour before he was calm enough to try the charm himself.

pages.title: Hurling Hex
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Makes a broomstick buck and try to throw its rider
pages.html:
A Hurling Hex is laid on a broomstick to make it buck and try to throw its rider. It is the curse anybody would suspect on a broom that arrives as a present with no name attached.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, Harry Potter was sent a Firebolt for Christmas 1993 without a card. Hermione Granger, afraid it had come from Sirius Black, told Professor McGonagall, who took it away to be stripped and tested.

In Chapter Twelve, in February 1994, Harry asked McGonagall about the broom after every Transfiguration lesson. On the twelfth occasion she answered before he had opened his mouth. 'No, Potter, you can't have it back yet. We've checked for most of the usual curses, but Professor Flitwick believes the broom might be carrying a Hurling Hex. I shall tell you once we've finished checking it.' In the end Madam Hooch and Flitwick found nothing wrong with it. McGonagall gave it back to him with every twig in place.

pages.title: Unforgivable Curses
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The Imperius Curse, the Cruciatus Curse and the Killing Curse
pages.html:
The Unforgivable Curses are the three darkest curses there are: the Imperius Curse, which controls its victim; the Cruciatus Curse, which tortures; and the Killing Curse. Using any of them on another human being earns a life sentence in Azkaban. They work only when the caster means them with his whole heart.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Harry Potter asked Remus Lupin, at one of their lessons against the dementors, why the Patronus Charm needed a memory when no other spell did. Most magic draws on what a wizard can do, Lupin told him, but a very small number of spells draw on what he is. 'You cannot cast an Unforgivable Curse by learning it. Everybody knows the words. Say them with your whole heart behind them, meaning them, wanting them, and the curse works; say them without, nothing happens at all, which is the single most merciful fact in our entire body of law. Dark magic of that order asks the caster for something out of his soul, takes it, then does not give it back.'

pages.title: Revealing Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Makes hidden writing, enchantments or curses show themselves
pages.html:
A Revealing Charm makes whatever is hidden on or in an object show itself, whether that is invisible writing or a curse waiting to go off. There are several of them, each looking for something different.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry Potter woke on Easter Sunday 1994 to find a chocolate egg the size of a Quaffle on his pillow. Somebody had painted a golden Snitch on one side. On the other, in tiny letters of white icing, it said I made it myself. Truly. D. It was from Dracina Malfoy.

Harry took it down to breakfast, which was a mistake. Hermione Granger went rigid at the sight of it. Things did not just appear on people's beds, she said, not with Sirius Black on the loose; it could be cursed. Harry would not let her take it to Professor McGonagall. So she whipped out her wand and tried three different revealing charms on the egg, one after another, while half the Gryffindor table looked on. Nothing happened. Ron broke off a piece and stuffed it into his mouth. 'If I die,' he said thickly, 'tell Mum it was worth it.' He did not die.

pages.title: Confusing Concoction
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The Confusing Concoction is a potion for muddling the mind, which turns a deep, smoky blue when it is brewed correctly. Its ingredients include scurvy-grass, which curdles it if overdone, and exactly two sprigs of sneezewort. It is stirred anticlockwise.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, it was the third-years' Potions exam. Dracina Malfoy, working across the gangway from Harry, had hers the right smoky blue already, while his stayed as thin as tea. Without moving her lips she coached him: too much scurvy-grass, two sprigs of sneezewort, not three, then stir it anticlockwise. Snape, standing behind Harry, asked silkily whether she was assisting Potter. Dracina did not even look up. 'I was telling him he's hopeless. He doesn't seem to have heard me.' Snape bent over her cauldron and pronounced it excellent. Against Harry's he wrote something on his clipboard that looked suspiciously like a zero.

pages.title: Sleekeazy's Hair Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
By Pansy Parkinson to Dracina Malfoy, early 1994; refused
pages.html:
Sleekeazy's Hair Potion smooths and tames unruly hair. It was invented by Fleamont Potter, Harry Potter's grandfather, and it made the Potters far richer than they had ever been. It is sold in bottles.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, early in 1994, Dracina Malfoy came running back from Hogsmeade with her silver-blonde hair hanging round her face in thick, dripping ropes of mud. Crabbe had already blundered into the Slytherin common room, dripping green, with a muddled story about ghosts, Potter's head and the Weasleys' bedroom. So Pansy Parkinson came straight along with a towel to wait in the passage outside Snape's office. She also brought a bottle of Sleekeazy's Hair Potion, which she held out like a peace offering the moment Dracina stepped into the passage. Dracina would not have it. 'Leave it.'

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt of a row of little glass jars labelled Sleekeazy's on a sideboard, behind the gleaming white hair of his grandfather, Fleamont.

pages.title: Undetectable Poisons
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 12
pages.html:
Undetectable Poisons are the poisons that leave no trace of themselves in the victim. They are part of the Potions course at Hogwarts, where poisons are taught alongside their antidotes. Early in 1994 Professor Snape set Harry Potter an essay on them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry sat grinding through his essay on Undetectable Poisons for Snape at the table next to Hermione Granger's. She was visible only as a quantity of hair over the top of a tower of books.

pages.title: Fire crab
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
A large tortoise with a jewelled shell
Shoots flames from its rear end
pages.html:
The fire crab looks like a large tortoise with a heavily jewelled shell. When it is attacked it shoots flames from its rear end, which makes it a lively subject for a Care of Magical Creatures class.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Hermione Granger had her eyebrows singed by fire crabs at the paddock in Care of Magical Creatures. Ron Weasley had heard her talking to Professor Vector about an Arithmancy lesson held at the same time, and he held up the fire crabs as proof that she could not have been there. 'She was with us in Care of Magical Creatures, we were up at the paddock with the fire crabs, she had her eyebrows singed.' Hermione was, in fact, using a Time-Turner to get to all her classes.

pages.title: Kneazle
infobox: Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them (12 March 2001)
Cat-like, with spotted or speckled fur, large ears and a lion's tail
Knows an untrustworthy person on sight
pages.html:
The Kneazle is a small magical cousin of the cat, with spotted or speckled fur, outsize ears and a tail like a lion's. It is clever, independent and sometimes bad-tempered. A Kneazle that takes to a witch or wizard makes an excellent pet. It can tell at once when somebody is not to be trusted, and it will lead its owner safely home when they are lost.

Kneazles and cats

Kneazles can breed with ordinary cats, and a licence is needed to keep a pure one. Hermione Granger's cat Crookshanks is part Kneazle, which explains a good deal about him.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, during the Defence Against the Dark Arts exam in June 1994, Harry Potter put his arm round Hermione Granger, who had gone to pieces in front of the boggart. Dracina Malfoy told Hermione that it meant nothing. ‘He'd do it for a kicked Kneazle,’ she said. ‘Potter's kind to anything pathetic.’

pages.title: Fanged Geranium
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
The Fanged Geranium is a magical plant with a mouthful of small, sharp teeth. It is grown in the Hogwarts greenhouses, and handling one without being bitten is part of the Herbology examinations.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, in June 1994, the third years sat their Herbology exam out in the greenhouses, with the sun blazing down through the glass. By the end of it half the class had sunburnt necks. A Fanged Geranium bit Neville Longbottom twice. 'Only twice,' he said, looking at his hand with something like pride. 'I thought it'd be loads more.'

pages.title: Dementor's Kiss
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The soul sucked out and eaten
pages.html:
The Dementor's Kiss is the last and worst weapon of the dementors. A dementor lowers its hood only to use it, clamping its jaws upon the victim's mouth to suck out the soul.

What it does

The Kiss does not kill. The body goes on living while the heart and brain still work. But it is an empty shell, with no sense of self, no memory, nothing. There is no chance of recovery. The soul is not sleeping, nor waiting somewhere to be fetched: the dementor has eaten it, and it will not be given back at the end, when everything else is. Its place is filled by something that is never the victim's own, such as a beast of the kind a vampire carries.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Remus Lupin explained the Kiss to Harry Potter over butterbeer after a Patronus lesson. Of all the things the Ministry had ever licensed, he said, it was the one he would walk to London to stop. Harry asked why the soul would not be given back. ‘Because the thing has eaten it,’ said Lupin. ‘Ask me a happier question.’ The Daily Prophet had reported that morning that the Ministry had given the dementors permission to perform the Kiss on Sirius Black if they found him. Harry, to his own surprise, was pleased.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Black had been caught and locked away upstairs. The Kiss had been authorised. Earlier that night it had very nearly been performed on Harry himself, down by the lake.

pages.title: Seventy times seven
pages.html:
Seventy times seven is the answer Jesus gave when Peter asked how often he ought to forgive a brother who sinned against him: not seven times, but seventy times seven. The sum comes to four hundred and ninety. The point is to lose count.

The saying

It is in the Gospel of Matthew, in the eighteenth chapter. Jesus followed it with the parable of a servant whose master forgave him a vast debt, and who then had a fellow servant thrown into prison over a small one.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, after a Patronus lesson early in 1994, Remus Lupin told Harry Potter a story about a man who asked his teacher how many times he ought to forgive somebody, and suggested seven. ‘Seventy times seven, said the teacher.’ Harry worked it out as four hundred and ninety. Lupin replied: ‘I’ve always understood that the idea was to lose count.’ When Harry asked about people like Snape, Lupin admitted that he found it difficult every single day. It was written down, he said, if Harry ever went looking.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the saying moved Harry to forgive Dracina Malfoy on the castle steps. In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, it helped him not to mind too much that Hermione Granger had lied to him twice in one night.

pages.title: Christmas
pages.html:
Christmas is the feast of the birth of Christ, kept on the twenty-fifth of December. Every witch and wizard in Britain keeps it too. They put up trees, pull crackers and sing carols, though hardly any of them have the least idea whose feast it is.

Father Christmas

The old man in red who brings the presents is Father Christmas. In Narnia, where the White Witch had kept it winter for a hundred years with no Christmas at all, he came back in 1940 as her power broke.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in Divination in the spring of 1994, Harry Potter asked Professor Trelawney why wizards kept Christmas. She told him it was a very ancient festival of the turning year, which the Muggles had borrowed from wizards and dressed up in their own little stories. Wizards kept it for the feasting, the giving and the light in the darkest days. Harry pointed out that it had Christ in it, and that it was His birthday. Trelawney waved it away: ‘Names are merely labels, dear. The Inner Eye looks beneath them.’

The Fat Friar told Harry, in the same chapter, that wizards laugh at God all year round, then sing His carols on the twenty-fifth because they like the tunes. He had watched them do it for five hundred years. ‘I’ve come to believe it’s a joke. His joke, I mean.’

pages.title: Natural magic
infobox: Herbs, physic, reading the stars for sowing
pages.html:
