The dock was furred with weed and rotten through. The brass switch had gone green, and the clock had stopped at a quarter past two behind cracked glass. Moss had crept up the pillars, ivy had got in at the windows, and the library's books were burnt or burst with damp. Both stands were empty. Harry, not knowing it, stood on the same planks where the Stranger had once arrived. The grey sea made him think of drowned Númenor. He judged that the island was the whole of that world, and tiny.

On the dock Hermione and Dracina quarrelled. Dracina broke down. By the end of it the two girls were friends, and rivals as well. Harry, standing apart, heard none of it. They followed Sirius's footprints up the path to the library, where Sirius sat against the wall beneath the map. A woman had kept him company there; she was Yeesha. The four of them went home one at a time by the small leather book.

Book 4: In the summer of 1994 Hermione found the island in the Muggle computer game Myst, new, clean and sunlit. Everything was where she had seen it with Harry: the dock, the ship, the gear, the clock tower, even the library with the map. She sent Harry photographs of the screen, with copies to Dracina, who replied that she did not need a Muggle box to remember the island, because she had been there.

pages.title: Greta Grindelwald's fortress prison
infobox: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (21 July 2007)
pages.html:
Greta Grindelwald's fortress prison is Nurmengard, a black fortress in the mountains of Austria. She built it to hold her enemies, and she carved her own words over its gate: For the Greater Good. Since Albus Dumbledore defeated her in 1945, she has been its prisoner herself.

History

During her war Greta filled Nurmengard with the witches and wizards who stood in her way. When Dumbledore beat her in their duel of 1945, she was shut up in its topmost cell. She has been there ever since, for nearly fifty years, under her own motto.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in his office in the summer of 1993, Dumbledore told John Constantine that he had asked braver men than John to go to their deaths, and would do it again if he must, 'for the greater...' He stopped dead in the middle of the phrase. John knew the words. He had seen them once, carved over the gate of the black fortress in the mountains of Austria that was now Greta's prison. He had heard whispers in the pubs he drank in that she had once been far more than an enemy to the young Dumbledore, and he had never believed them until then.

pages.title: Hell
infobox: The First of the Fallen, who is the Devil
The Second and the Third of the Fallen
Dukes and Great Earls, Andromalius among them
Runs wrongly: an hour can last a year
pages.html:
Hell is the realm of the Devil, where he rules over the fallen angels and the damned. To its lords he is the First of the Fallen, the eldest and greatest of them all. The Second and the Third of the Fallen rule beneath him. Time does not run properly there: an hour can last a year, and a year can go past in an hour.

Visitors

John Constantine, the Liverpool occultist, has been there more than once. On one visit he was carried down in a lift made of screaming. He has sat across a card table in Soho from a Duke of Hell, who shortly afterwards lost his shirt. In 1991 he sold his soul separately to the Second and the Third of the Fallen, so that the First could not collect it without starting a war in Hell.

In August 1993, to get past the wards of a house in New Mexico, John drew the seal of Andromalius, a Great Earl of Hell whose particular talent is catching thieves and returning stolen property.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, riding the Knight Bus in August 1993, John thought of the places he had been where time did not work properly. There had been Hell, more than once. When the name of Harry Potter rang a faint bell, he remembered the baby of 1981 who had done for Voldemort. Then he remembered that he had been busy with something in Hell for a while afterwards, and had forgotten all about it.

pages.title: The Styx
pages.html:
The Styx is the river that bounds the underworld of the ancient Greeks, the land of the shades. Charon the ferryman takes the dead across it in his boat, for a coin. The gods of Olympus swore their most binding oaths by its water.

In the saga

In the Interlude of Book Three, riding the Knight Bus in the summer of 1993, John Constantine reflected that he had sailed the Styx, been carried down to Hell in a lift made of screaming, and once driven a hearse over the Pennines in a snowstorm, with the corpse sitting up in the back giving him directions. None of it had been as bad as the Knight Bus.

pages.title: The poisoned quarry in mid-Wales
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 19
Above a village in the hills of mid-Wales
Poisoned a whole valley for thirty years
Remus Lupin's pack of Garou, most of them Fianna
pages.html:
The poisoned quarry in mid-Wales stands above a village in the hills. For thirty years it poisoned the whole valley below, and things crawled out of its slag heaps that were no longer animals. The Garou pack Remus Lupin found in those hills put them back where they came from.

The pack

To the Garou, poison of that kind is the Wyrm's work. Lupin's pack were mostly Fianna, one of the thirteen tribes. They still send for him now and then, as they did at Christmas 1993.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, in June 1994, Lupin told Harry, Ron and Hermione about the years he had spent where wizards do not go. In the end he had found a pack in the hills of mid-Wales. 'Fianna, most of them, Hermione,' he said. 'It's one of the thirteen tribes. I could see you were about to ask.' They had done good work, and he told them about the quarry quite simply, the way he might have described a school trip. But he had never been one of them: he had been bitten, not born, and he was a wizard besides.

pages.title: MACUSA
aliases: the Magical Congress of the United States of America
Magical Congress of the United States of America
infobox: Magical Congress; Magical Congress of the United States of America
Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them (film, November 2016)
The Woolworth Building, New York (by the 1920s)
pages.html:
MACUSA, the Magical Congress of the United States of America, governs the witches and wizards of America. It was founded in 1693, in the aftermath of the Salem witch trials. From 1790 to 1965 it kept American wizards apart from No-Majs under Rappaport's Law, the strictest separation anywhere in the wizarding world.

Founding

MACUSA was founded in 1693, after the Salem witch trials. In those trials the Scourers, a band of corrupt wizard bounty-hunters, had helped the Puritans hunt down real witches and wizards, along with a great many innocent No-Majs. The new Congress was set up to break the Scourers, and to deal with the wizarding criminals who had fled Europe for the colonies. Its first President was Josiah Jackson.

Some of the Scourers escaped into the No-Maj world, where they married and settled. They passed down to their descendants a hatred of magic, which American wizardry has had to reckon with ever since.

Rappaport's Law

In 1790 Dorcus Twelvetrees, the daughter of a MACUSA official, gave away the secrets of the Congress to a No-Maj called Bartholomew Barebone, who was descended from Scourers. President Emily Rappaport answered with the law that bears her name. It forbade American witches and wizards to befriend or marry No-Majs. It also made every wand in the country subject to permit. It was not repealed until 1965.

For 175 years the law shaped American wizardry. Some families kept to it rigidly, while others broke it quietly. The stage magician Zatara broke it in public every night of his career, doing real magic for No-Maj audiences who took it for illusion. He broke it again by marrying a No-Maj, Sindella. MACUSA pursued him for years without ever convicting him, because no No-Maj who had seen him perform would believe that the magic was real.

In the twentieth century

In 1900 MACUSA was among the wizarding governments of the world that made an agreement with the Camarilla, through the International Confederation of Wizards. Wizards lend their own concealment spells to help keep the Masquerade, while Camarilla vampires never hunt or feed on wizards.

By the 1920s MACUSA sat in the Woolworth Building in New York, under President Seraphina Picquery. Through the age of the costumed heroes it kept the American wizarding world out of sight. It was content to let No-Majs take any magic they happened to see for the powers of metahumans, or for the tricks of the stage. Zatara's half-blood daughter, Zatanna, went on to do much the same thing on stage as her father had. MACUSA has left her alone since 1965.

After the repeal American wizards were free to deal with No-Majs again, and some of them made fortunes at it. One was the father of Ephraim Shacklewell, who sold a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona through front companies. The Congress never quite managed to prove that the companies were his.

In the saga

In August 1993 John Constantine posed as a MACUSA officer of "Magical Security, Artefacts Division" to take the Linking Book to Myst Island from Ephraim Shacklewell. He signed the receipt "J. Lennon, MACUSA". He reckoned that Dumbledore could have taken the house apart brick by brick, but would have had MACUSA on the doorstep by breakfast and a diplomatic incident by lunch.

pages.title: Delta Green
infobox: Officially closed in 1970; still at work
pages.html:
Delta Green is a secret American organisation that would prefer nobody knew its name. It hunts things that ought not to exist, and it takes the dangerous objects they leave behind into its own keeping.

History

Delta Green grew out of the American government's raid on the town of Innsmouth, Massachusetts, in 1928. It was officially shut down in 1970. It went on all the same, without anybody's leave, as a conspiracy of agents inside the government who still answer its call.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine took the Myst book from Shacklewell House in New Mexico, at Albus Dumbledore's request. In America, he reflected, a thing like that usually drew flies. There was the organisation that would prefer you did not know its name was Delta Green, with their nice suits and their nasty smiles. There was whatever was left of Majestic 12, if anything was, and there was even the SCP Foundation. John had got in and out before any of them had done more than park a van up the road.

pages.title: Majestic 12
infobox: The crash at Roswell, New Mexico
pages.html:
Majestic 12 is a secret American committee of twelve men, said to have been set up on President Truman's orders in 1947 to deal with the crash at Roswell, New Mexico. By 1994 it was far from clear that anything was left of it.

Roswell

Something came down near Roswell in July 1947, and the American government has never been entirely frank about what it was. In the trophy room of Shacklewell House, a wizarding house in New Mexico, a lump of twisted grey metal is labelled NO-MAJ FLYING SAUCER (FRAGMENT), ROSWELL, N.M., 1947. John Constantine thought it half a hubcap off a Ford, and he knew a Mi-go who would have had a chuckle about it.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine counted whatever was left of Majestic 12, if anything was, among the American groups that a thing like the Myst book usually drew, like flies. The others were Delta Green and the SCP Foundation.

pages.title: SCP Foundation
pages.html:
The SCP Foundation is a secret organisation that collects dangerous things and locks them away. Its name stands for its motto: Secure, Contain, Protect.

The Foundation

Everything it holds gets a number, a cell and a file. Its catalogue runs to dangerous objects, dangerous people and the occasional demon, each graded by how hard it is to hold: Safe, Euclid or Keter. A council known as the O5 runs it. In America it has rivals in the same trade, among them Delta Green and whatever is left of Majestic 12, if anything is.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine reflected that in America a thing like the Myst linking book usually drew flies. The SCP Foundation was one of them: 'those nutters with their cells, their numbers and their filing cabinets', who collected dangerous things the way little boys collected football cards. He was gone from New Mexico with the book before the Foundation or any of its rivals had done more than park a van up the road.

pages.title: The watchers in the black van
infobox: A mile from the Cleft, New Mexico
A black van with no number plates
pages.html:
The watchers in the black van were the unknown people in a black van with no number plates, parked with its lights off beside the road a mile from the Cleft, in August 1993. Nobody knows who they were.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, on his way to Shacklewell House, John Constantine passed the dig at the Cleft. A mile further on stood the van, at the side of the road with its lights off. He walked past it without turning his head, though he could feel somebody watching him through the tinted glass. At sunrise, coming back with the book, he found it still waiting where he had left it. He lit a cigarette and gave it a cheery little wave as he went by. Nobody in it so much as turned a head.

America has several outfits that collect dangerous things, among them Delta Green, whatever is left of Majestic 12 and the SCP Foundation. Constantine was in and out before any of them had done more than park a van up the road.

pages.title: The Cleft dig
infobox: John Loftin, Elias Zandi, Dr Richard Watson
pages.html:
The Cleft dig is the small, quiet excavation in the New Mexico desert that has been opening up the lost cavern of D'ni since 1988. It is run by a handful of well-meaning amateurs with clipboards, which in John Constantine's experience is the most dangerous combination in the world.

History

In 1987 the artefact hunter John Loftin found tunnels under the desert, with great digging machines standing in them that nobody living had built. On 19 March 1988 he took Elias Zandi down, and the tunnels led them to D'ni. Zandi had the money. He brought in Dr Richard Watson, and the three of them began to explore the cavern.

In 1993 there was not much to see above ground: a wire fence, a hand-painted sign about a geological survey, a couple of tents, a caravan and a ladder going down into a deep crack in the earth. Things were coming up out of the hole all the same, books among them. Most went straight out of the back door to whoever would pay for them. One, the linking book to Myst Island, was sold to Ephraim Shacklewell for fifty dollars. The diggers founded the D'ni Restoration Council in 1997.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, Constantine passed the dig at night on his way to Shacklewell House. Somewhere under it, his reading said, there was a cavern big enough to hold a city, and a city still in it.

pages.title: Fianna
infobox: The Celtic peoples and their descendants
pages.html:
The Fianna are one of the thirteen tribes of the Garou, the tribe of the Celtic lands. They are bards, poets and warriors. They keep the oldest songs of their people, and they fight the Wyrm with joy. The pack that took in Remus Lupin in the hills of mid-Wales was mostly Fianna.

Totem and ways

The Fianna follow Stag, the spirit of the wild hunt, of pride and of the greenwood. They are passionate in everything: in drink, in love, in grief and in battle. Galliards are especially honoured among them, for their songs and stories carry the history of the Garou from before the coming of writing. The Fianna are generous hosts and terrible enemies, slow to forget an insult but quick to forgive a friend. Their rites are full of music.

The Fianna are close to the Wyld and to the old powers of their islands. They are on easier terms than most Garou with the Fair Folk who once walked there. They share their name with the war-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill in the old Irish tales. Their Kinfolk are the Irish, the Scots and the Welsh, with all their descendants across the world.

Homelands and history

The tribe's heart is in Ireland, Scotland and Wales. Its oldest caerns lie among standing stones, holy wells and hollow hills. Its songs tell of ancient wars in Ireland against the Fomorians, the monstrous servants of the Wyrm. They tell, too, of the long feud with the Get of Fenris, which began with the Viking raids. When the Celtic peoples crossed the sea to America and elsewhere, the Fianna went with them. They are now found wherever the Irish and the Scots have made their homes.

Place in the world

Among the tribes the Fianna are respected for their courage and their lore. They are teased for their tempers and their drinking. Like other Garou they have little love for wizards, who in their view play with the Wyrm's fire. Their sacred places in the hills, the rings of stones and the springs in old woods, are best left untouched by any witch or wizard who comes across them.

In the saga

After the deaths of James and Lily Potter in 1981, Remus Lupin left the wizarding world for years. In the end he found a pack in the hills of mid-Wales, mostly Fianna. They were good people in their way, and did good work. Above one village a quarry had been poisoning a whole valley for thirty years, and things that were no longer animals had crawled out of its slag heaps. The pack put them back where they came from.

The pack still sends for Lupin now and then. It did at Christmas 1993, when Albus Dumbledore told the Hogwarts table that Lupin was unwell. It never let him forget, though, for a single day, that he was biteborn, bitten rather than born, which the tribes hold to be no true Garou. He was a wizard too, which was worse. Lupin told Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger about the pack in June 1994.

pages.title: Shacklewell family
pages.html:
The Shacklewells are an American pure-blood wizarding family. They have been in America since a great-great-grandfather stepped off a ship in Boston with a wand in his pocket and a price on his head. For most of that time they were not rich.

Fortune

The money came in the 1960s, after Rappaport's Law was repealed. Ephraim Shacklewell's father sold a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona as a miracle cleaning fluid, through a string of front companies. MACUSA never quite managed to prove it.

Ephraim has spent the money since on Shacklewell House, a vast pink adobe mansion in the Spanish style, hidden in the New Mexico desert behind the look of a derelict filling station. It has a fountain shaped like a Thunderbird, a swimming pool shaped like a Golden Snitch and the most expensive wards that MACUSA's own security men could be bribed into building. In his trophy room he kept the D'ni linking book to Myst Island, which he had bought for fifty dollars from a man who dug it out of the Cleft.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, before he burgled Shacklewell House in August 1993, John Constantine did his reading on the family. They were pure-blood all right, he concluded, but the money was new. Ephraim, who could never sleep, caught him in the trophy room, wearing a silk dressing gown and a hairnet. John passed himself off as an officer of MACUSA. He signed the receipt J. Lennon and left by the front door with the book, while Ephraim waved him off from the step.

pages.title: Sirius Black's wooden cross
infobox: Two splinters of grey bed-frame wood, bound with thread from a blanket
pages.html:
Sirius Black's wooden cross was the cross he made for himself in his cell in Azkaban. It was two splinters of grey wood from his bed-frame, bound together crosswise with a thread pulled from his blanket, and it hung on a dirty string. He clung to it for twelve years. He lost it in June 1994, on the night his godson learnt the truth about him.

Faith in Azkaban

Sirius had never believed in God. That had been Lily, he said, and her mother Susan before her, who made sure her children were godly. Remus went to Him first, after Lily and James were married. Then James started on it too, and so, after a fashion, did Peter Pettigrew.

In Azkaban Sirius had nothing else: not a single happy memory, only the things Lily used to say to him. He made the cross from two splinters of his bed frame and held on to it like a life raft. His thumb rubbed it for years, until the centre was worn smooth and dark.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seventeen, the cross fell out of Black's robes while Harry fought him in the Shrieking Shack. It lay in the dust by his collar in a blade of moonlight: two splinters of bed frame, bound crosswise with a bit of thread, very small and plain.

In Chapter Eighteen, telling Harry that he had as good as killed Lily and James by persuading them to change their Secret-Keeper, Black fished the cross out from the neck of his robes. He pressed it to his mouth, murmuring into it. My fault... my fault... my most grievous fault... Later, when Hermione asked how he had got out of Azkaban without Dark Magic, he drew the little cross out on its dirty string and held it up in the moonlight. Harry saw it properly for the first time. 'I... I never used to believe in it. God... and all that. That was all Lily.' He had held on to it, he said, like a life raft.

In Chapter Nineteen, the string snapped somewhere in Black's fight with the Garou. By the time he was a man again, crouched at the water's edge, the cross was gone.

In Chapter Twenty-One, Harry found Sirius in the ruined library on Myst Island. As Sirius got up off the floor, his hand went to the place over his heart and closed on nothing. He had lost it down by the lake, he told Harry, when the dementors came. 'Never mind. I don't suppose He needs it to find me.'

pages.title: Remus Lupin's cross
infobox: Plain wood, on a leather cord
pages.html:
Remus Lupin's cross is a little plain wooden cross on a leather cord, which Lupin wore under his shirt from the day James and Lily Potter were married. On the night of the full moon in June 1994 it fell from his neck as he changed, and Harry Potter held it up to the Garou. At the end of that term Lupin gave it to Harry to keep, and Harry has worn it ever since.

The cross

Lupin came to faith through Lily Potter after she married James, the first of the friends to follow her. He has worn a cross ever since their wedding. It has to be wooden, because silver burns him. He keeps a box of them at home, and can easily carve another.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, with the wolf gnawing at him from the inside, Lupin's hand crept up to his collar. It closed round the cross under his shirt. Harry saw his lips move, and guessed the words. Deliver us from evil.

In Chapter Nineteen, out on the grass under the full moon, the cord snapped as his neck thickened in the change. The cross flew out of his collar and came to rest beside Harry's hand. Harry snatched it up and shoved it into his pocket. When the Garou came for him, he held the cross up between himself and the creature, although he did not even know whether he believed in God. Its nostrils twitched at the scent of it, and for a moment Harry thought he saw Lupin again, far down in its yellow eyes. Whatever it smelt on Harry was stronger than the cross.

In Chapter Twenty, the cross went warm in Harry's inside pocket just before his shield turned white. Afterwards, in the Forest, he found it still faintly warm. He pressed it into Lupin's cold hand, then closed the fingers round it one at a time.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, packing to leave Hogwarts, Lupin drew the mended cord over his head and gave the cross to Harry. 'I think this one would rather go with you. It seems to work rather better in your pocket than it ever did round my neck.'

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry woke from a dream in the summer of 1994 holding the cross so hard that its edges had bitten red marks into his palm. It was warm. In Chapter Two he remembered a night at the end of July when his lamp went out and the moon lit his book until he reached the end of the chapter. The cross had been warm against his chest the whole time.

pages.title: The Myst linking book
aliases: the Linking Book for Myst Island
the book in the Tesco bag
infobox: MYST; Myst; The Myst Island linking book

Atrus writer
John Constantine stole it for Dumbledore
Tall, thick and heavy; cracked brown leather; MYST in tarnished gold
Atrus; Ephraim Shacklewell (as he believed); held for Atrus by Albus Dumbledore
pages.html:
The Myst linking book is the linking book for Myst Island, written by Atrus. It came out of the excavation of the D'ni cavern and was sold for fifty dollars to an American wizard collector. In the summer of 1993 John Constantine stole it back for Albus Dumbledore, carrying it across Britain in a Tesco carrier bag. In June 1994 it carried Sirius Black out of Flitwick's office to Myst Island. Harry, Hermione and Dracina followed.

Description

The book is big, old and heavy, a tall, thick volume bound in brown leather that has cracked with age, its corners rubbed pale. Across the front, in tarnished gold, is the single word MYST. Inside are thick, creamy pages. The left-hand page is blank. On the right is a dark oblong like a little window, and in it a picture moves. It shows a greenish grey sea seen from high above. The view sweeps in towards an island with dark pines, a wooden dock, the mast of a sunken ship, an enormous stone gear half buried on the hill and a squat stone clock tower standing in the water. Through thin plastic the panel shows as a soft greenish flicker, like a television left on in another room. When the book falls open, its picture pulls at the onlooker like a current, inviting him to put out his hand.

History

Atrus wrote the book for Myst Island, the Age his grandmother Anna had written as a home for the family. When he escaped Riven by leaping into the Star Fissure, he linked to Myst as he fell. The book went on falling, out of Riven and down to Earth. He had meant it to be destroyed, and it troubled him to think whose hands might one day hold it. Early in the nineteenth century a traveller from the surface found it. He laid his hand on the picture and arrived on the island's dock with nothing in his hands. The book stayed behind, as such books do.

In the twentieth century it came out of the excavation of the D'ni cavern. Like a great many things from that dig, it went out of the back door. A digger sold it for fifty dollars to Ephraim Shacklewell, a rich pure-blood wizard of Shacklewell House in New Mexico. He put it on a red velvet cushion in the last glass case of his trophy room, next to a piece of hubcap labelled as a Roswell flying saucer. Its card read NO-MAJ PICTURE BOOK (NATIVE?). CHARMED PHOTOGRAPH INSIDE, MOVES. FROM THE DIG. $50. He never touched it.

In the summer of 1993 Dumbledore sent an owl to John Constantine in a Soho pub. The letter, in green ink, asked him to bring the book to Hogwarts before the middle of August, without opening it or looking at it for longer than he must. The job was meant to square an old account between them over a stolen Deluminator. Constantine buried his wand in the desert. He slipped past the wards of Shacklewell House with salt, chalk, his own blood and a Hand of Glory, then took the book. It fell open in his hands and pulled at him; he slammed it shut. He left a Jackie Collins paperback on the cushion in its place. When Shacklewell caught him, he passed himself off as an officer of MACUSA and wrote him a receipt signed J. Lennon. He came home to Liverpool by the old crossroads and took the Knight Bus north, with the book in a Tesco carrier bag under his hand all night. At the end of the journey he laid it on Dumbledore's desk. Dumbledore told him that the book belonged, as it always had, to the very old acquaintance who wrote it, who would be extremely glad to know it was safe. It would go back to him with the small leather linking book: one way there and one way home.

In the saga

Book 3: On the Knight Bus in the summer of 1993 Harry saw the greenish flicker through the plastic. Whatever the dodgy bloke opposite was doing with a book in a Tesco bag, he decided, he wanted no part of it. A jolt of the bus had knocked the cover back an inch, and Constantine pressed it shut through the plastic.

In June 1994 the book lay closed in the middle of the blotter on Flitwick's desk, where Dumbledore had left it, with Sirius Black's grubby grey fingermarks round the cover. Sirius had touched it and gone to Myst Island, out of reach of the dementors. Harry remembered the Knight Bus. Hermione recognised the book as D'ni. As the Aurors rattled the door handle she opened it. She, Harry and Dracina put their hands on the picture together. When Hermione came back by the small book, the big one was still lying open on the desk with its picture moving, so that any Auror could have followed them. She closed it and left it on the desk for Dumbledore to find.

pages.title: The small leather linking book
infobox: No bigger than a pocket diary; plain dark leather; untitled; heavy and warm
The Stranger's family; Albus Dumbledore; Harry Potter
pages.html:
The small leather linking book was written long ago by Atrus for the traveller known as the Stranger. It was to take him home from Myst Island after he had done Atrus a very great service. The Stranger never used it. It came down through his family to Albus Dumbledore, who gave it to Harry Potter in June 1994. It carried Hermione, Sirius Black, Dracina and Harry home from Myst before Atrus's daughter Yeesha took it back.

Description

The book is hardly bigger than a pocket diary. It is square, bound in plain leather gone dark and soft with handling, with nothing on the cover or the spine, neither a title nor a name. It is oddly heavy for its size and faintly, steadily warm, like the last of a fire in a grate. It grows warmer in the hand. Its first page is blank, and on the page opposite is a little dark window holding a moving picture.

History

Atrus wrote the book for the Stranger early in the nineteenth century, after the Stranger had freed him from his sons' trap. It was to lead from Myst Island back to this world. The Stranger never used it. He went home by another road, through Riven's Star Fissure, taking the book with him, and he kept it. His family handed it down for a great many years, from one person who did not know what it was to the next. At last it came to Dumbledore, who kept it in the drawer of his desk.

Dumbledore showed it to John Constantine in the summer of 1993, beside the Myst linking book Constantine had just brought him. Both books, he said, would go back to their writer when the time was right: one way there and one way home.

In the saga

Book 3: In the hospital wing at five minutes to midnight in June 1994, Dumbledore put the book into Harry's hands. It was not to be opened, read or touched until the proper time, he said, and Harry would know when that was. There would be another book waiting in the office, to be read first. 'The right book, Harry, can carry you into another age entirely.' It had been written, he added, by a very old acquaintance, a great deal older than himself, with far steadier handwriting. Harry put it in the inside pocket of his robes, next to Lupin's cross. In Flitwick's office he noticed a small plain leather book on a low shelf, between two fat volumes on Charms, with nothing on its spine. It was rather like the one in his pocket. He gave it no second thought.

On Myst Island Hermione remembered the book. Opened, its picture showed Flitwick's office: the books from floor to ceiling, the library steps, the low desk, the candle still burning and the big brown book on the blotter. Hermione concluded that Dumbledore had planned everything. Harry kept it buttoned in his pocket until they had found Sirius. In the library they used it one at a time, Hermione first, then Sirius, then Dracina, each of them catching it before it hit the floor. Harry went last. The book fell to the library floor behind him and lay open on the dusty boards.

Then Yeesha appeared in the corner. She picked the book up and knew it as the one her father had written for a stranger, lost to him for longer than she had been alive. It had come home. She tucked it into her robe, said 'Shorah' and stepped sideways out of the world.

pages.title: Linking book
infobox: Touch the moving picture to travel to the place shown
The Myst linking book; the small leather linking book; the red and blue books of Myst Island
pages.html:
A linking book is a D'ni book, written by the Art, that carries its reader to another place, usually another world, called an Age. It holds a moving picture of where it leads, and whoever lays a hand on the picture goes there. The book itself never goes with him.

Description and use

A linking book is written in D'ni script, with special inks and paper made for the purpose. Its first page is usually blank. The page opposite holds a dark oblong, like a little window set into the paper, and in it a picture of the destination moves. The picture sweeps in towards the place, as a bird might see it coming down to land, and it pulls at whoever looks at it, like a current round the ankles. Laying a hand on it carries the reader there at once, with a moment of blackness and a soft rushing sound.

The book that brings a traveller into an Age always stays behind, wherever he was when he used it. The only way out of an Age is therefore another linking book, one that leads somewhere else; a traveller without one is stranded for ever. A linking book need not lead to a new world at all. It may just as well lead to another place in the same world, or from an Age back to Earth.

Kinds of book

The D'ni distinguished the descriptive book, in which an Age was written and could be altered, from the linking books that merely led to it. A prison book, or trap book, is a linking book that leads nowhere. Whoever uses it is held inside, his face flickering on the page, until somebody else uses it and takes his place. For a time Atrus's sons were held in two prison books on Myst Island, Sirrus in a red one and Achenar in a blue. In 1806 Gehn was tricked into a prison book on Riven.

Since the Fall

When the D'ni died, their books lay in the empty cavern for two centuries. Since the digging began in the 1980s, books from near the Cleft have turned up in junk shops and in rich men's glass cases, waiting for somebody to open one for a look at the picture. A working linking book in a private American collection is dangerous in a way its owner seldom understands. In 1993 Albus Dumbledore had John Constantine take the Myst linking book from one such collection, because he would rather nobody else ever came to understand it.

In the saga

Book 3: Constantine had read that the book stays where it is when its user goes, and Dumbledore confirmed it to him. In June 1994 Hermione recognised the big brown book on Flitwick's desk as a D'ni linking book. She, Harry and Dracina linked to Myst Island with three hands on the picture together. On the island she worked out what that meant: they could leave only by another book. Harry still had the small leather book Dumbledore had given him. Because the book drops when its user vanishes, Hermione had the four of them, Sirius Black included, go one at a time, each catching the book before it hit the floor.

pages.title: The Art
infobox: Books written in D'ni script with special inks and paper
Lost with the D'ni, more or less
pages.html:
The Art is what the D'ni called the writing of books that link to other worlds. They always gave it a capital letter, like a name. A good enough Writer could describe a world, which the D'ni called an Age, so precisely that a book would carry its reader there. The Art uses no wand and nothing a wizard would call a spell. No wizard understands it.

How it works

A Writer of the Art describes an Age in a descriptive book, written in D'ni script with inks and paper made for the purpose. If the description is precise enough, the book links to a world that matches it. A linking book is then made for that Age. It has a dark panel on its right-hand page, where a moving picture of the Age appears. Whoever lays a hand on the picture is carried there, and the book stays behind.

A descriptive book can be added to after an Age has been reached, and a Writer can change an Age by writing into it. Careless or contradictory writing makes an Age unstable. Gehn's Ages were full of flaws. His Age of Riven slowly broke apart in spite of everything Atrus wrote to hold it together. The D'ni Guild of Maintainers existed to inspect new Ages, keeping D'ni safe from the mistakes of its own Writers.

Doctrine and heresy

The D'ni priests taught that a Maker had made every world that could possibly exist. There were millions upon millions of them, growing off each other like the leaves of an enormous tree. A Writer created nothing. He described a world so exactly that the book found the one that matched, somewhere among all the others, and made a link to it.

Hardly any D'ni behaved as though they believed it. They had been writing for so long, and were so clever, so powerful, that many of them treated the worlds they wrote as their own property, peoples included. Some came to believe that they had made them. The priests called that belief heresy. Gehn held it all his life; his son Atrus kept to the old teaching. Anna thought that nobody among the D'ni had ever really questioned the Art, and that their pride in it destroyed them.

Science or magic

The D'ni always insisted that the Art was not magic but a science, a very difficult one, with rules, like mathematics. Anna, a Muggle with no magic of her own, learnt the Art and practised it. She could not prove them wrong. The few wizards who have studied the subject still argue about it. The Spanish wizards who stumbled into the cavern in 1541 thought the D'ni were not magical at all.

The D'ni teaching about branching worlds is close to a Muggle theory in physics. In 1957 the American physicist Hugh Everett proposed that the universe branches whenever something could happen in more than one way, an idea later called the Many Worlds interpretation.

After the Fall

When the plague of A'Gaeris killed nearly all the D'ni about 1788, the Art was lost with them, more or less. Anna knew it, and so did her son Gehn. Her grandson Atrus knows it still. He has been writing linking books for more than a century and a half. Albus Dumbledore has exchanged a few letters with Atrus about the Art. Dumbledore's were rather long; the replies were short, very courteous and written in a far steadier hand.

In the saga

Book 3: John Constantine had come across the words in one of the few scraps of reading there were to be found on the D'ni. He recognised them when Dumbledore used them in 1993. In June 1994, on the dock on Myst Island, Hermione explained the Art to Harry and Dracina. She went by way of Anna's journal and Hugh Everett, until Dracina, freezing, asked her to get to the point. Before linking home, Dracina told Harry that if he stayed behind she would come back for him. She would learn the Art herself if she had to.

pages.title: Deluminator
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997), as the Put-Outer; named the Deluminator in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (21 July 2007)
Sucks every light in a street into itself
pages.html:
The Deluminator is Albus Dumbledore's device for taking away light. It looks like a silver cigarette lighter. One click sucks every light in a street into it, and another click puts them back.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine remembered how he had come to steal it. In 1985 a very old demon that fed on light turned up, and John needed something that could take the light away from it before it took the world’s. The Deluminator was the only thing he knew of that could do it. He gatecrashed a Ministry dinner for the purpose and stole it out of Dumbledore’s own pocket.

He gave it back the very next week, scorched on one side, with the demon safely put away for a thousand years. He tried to apologise in the back room of the Hog’s Head, with a goat looking in at the window. Dumbledore let him get about three words out, then shouted him down. He threatened to turn John’s liver into a pair of slippers. Afterwards he put the whole business away in his desk drawer, like a good cheque saved for a rainy day.

Eight years later, in 1993, it rained. Dumbledore’s letter asking John to fetch a book from New Mexico ended with a reminder: I think of you often. I think of my Deluminator, too. When John reached his office, Dumbledore admitted that he had been annoyed. John told him he had been bloody livid. Dumbledore saw no difficulty in the theft he was now asking for, since the Deluminator had belonged to him and the book did not belong to Mr Shacklewell.

pages.title: Sickle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Twenty-nine Knuts; seventeen Sickles to the Galleon
pages.html:
The Sickle is the silver coin of wizarding money. It is worth twenty-nine bronze Knuts, and seventeen Sickles make one gold Galleon. Like all wizarding coins, it is minted by the goblins of Gringotts.

Silver

Being silver, a Sickle will burn a Garou. On the night of the full moon in June 1994, a single one, left over from a Hogsmeade weekend, did exactly that.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine took the Knight Bus from Liverpool to Hogsmeade. The fare was eleven Sickles, wherever he was going. He had been a wizard for thirty years, near enough, and had never got the hang of wizards' money: twenty-nine Knuts to a Sickle, seventeen Sickles to a Galleon. He found the eleven, mostly in the lining of his coat.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, with the Garou coming at him across the grass, Harry Potter put his hand in his pocket. Under the little cross his fingers found a silver Sickle, left over from Hogsmeade. He threw it with a Seeker's throw, quick and flat from the wrist. It struck the creature on the end of its muzzle with a hiss like water dropped on a hot stove, and it burned. It left a wound that never healed: a black, smoking mark the size of a coin, which would not close.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, when Lupin left Hogwarts, the black mark was still on the end of his nose, where Harry's Sickle had struck him.

pages.title: Knut
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The silver Sickle; the gold Galleon
pages.html:
The Knut is the smallest coin in wizarding money, a little bronze piece. Twenty-nine Knuts make one silver Sickle, and seventeen Sickles make a gold Galleon.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, Harry spent eleven silver Sickles and seven bronze Knuts on sweets from the trolley on the Hogwarts Express.

In the Interlude of Book Three, John Constantine counted out his Knight Bus fare from a handful of coins collected all over the world. He had been a wizard for thirty years, near enough, and had never got the hang of wizarding money. Twenty-nine Knuts to a Sickle and seventeen Sickles to a Galleon seemed to him like something a mad uncle had made up at Christmas to keep the children quiet.

pages.title: Dragot
pages.html:
The Dragot is a coin of wizarding America. Dragots are heavy and bronze, stamped with an eagle that looks as though it would like a fight.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, John Constantine sorted through a handful of loose change under the headlamps of the Knight Bus while Stan Shunpike waited for his fare. Money stuck to him wherever he went. Among the coins were three American Dragots, a Japanese coin with a hole in the middle and a token from a launderette in Peckham. In thirty years as a wizard John had never got the hang of wizards’ money. In the end he found the eleven Sickles he needed, mostly in the lining of his coat.

pages.title: The Quibbler
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
The Quibbler is a wizarding magazine of the odder sort, edited by Xenophilius Lovegood. It reached Sirius Black in Azkaban. The old Bible passages it printed became all he had there, and they led him to faith.

The magazine

It prints what other papers will not: creatures nobody else has seen, and theories nobody else believes. Sirius Black thinks Lovegood a smart man who knows his nargles.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Black told Harry Potter that he normally had only The Quibbler in his cell. It was the Quibbler, he said, that had put in the mad old Bible passages. They were all he had among those godless, miserable people. One verse above all kept him: I'd rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than dwell in the tents of wickedness. Once he truly believed it, the dementors stopped coming.

pages.title: Lost Civilisations of the Ancient World
infobox: The lost peoples of the ancient world
A footnote on D'ni linking books
pages.html:
Lost Civilisations of the Ancient World is a history of peoples who have vanished from the earth. A footnote in it is one of the places where Hermione Granger read about the linking books of the D'ni.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Hermione, Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy were trapped in Professor Flitwick's office in June 1994, with Ministry Aurors just outside the door. A big book lay on the desk. Hermione put her hand flat on its cover and whispered that she knew what it was. She had read about such things in at least three books, and there was a footnote in Lost Civilisations of the Ancient World. It was a D'ni linking book, she said, and there was no time to explain. She asked Harry whether he trusted her. He said yes at once. Dracina hissed that she was sure it was a fascinating footnote, but that in about three seconds there would be Aurors in the room. There was a rattle at the door handle. Hermione opened the book.

pages.title: Snape's werewolf essay
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
How to recognise one in each of its five shapes; how to kill it
pages.html:
Snape's werewolf essay was the homework Professor Snape set Harry Potter's class in November 1993, when he took Remus Lupin's lesson. Writing it led Hermione Granger to realise that Lupin was a Garou. Lupin believed Snape had set it in the hope that somebody would.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Snape set two rolls of parchment, by Monday morning, on the ways to recognise one of them in each of its five shapes, and the ways to kill it. In Chapter Ten Lupin told the class that nobody need hand it in, to the dismay of Hermione, who had finished hers on the Saturday.

In Chapter Seventeen, in the Shrieking Shack, Lupin asked Hermione how long she had known what he was. 'Ages,' Hermione whispered. 'Since I did Professor Snape's essay...' 'He'll be delighted,' said Lupin coolly. 'He assigned that essay hoping someone would realise what my struggles meant. The signs were always there. I'm painfully aware of that.'

pages.title: Buckbeak's notice of execution
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
pages.html:
Buckbeak's notice of execution was the official notice by which the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures condemned the hippogriff Buckbeak to death. Cornelius Fudge, the Minister for Magic, read it aloud in Hagrid's hut on 6 June 1994. Hagrid signed it, as did the executioner, Walden Macnair. The sentence was never carried out: Dracina Malfoy took the hippogriff from under the executioner's axe.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, after the appeal was lost, Fudge told Hagrid that they had to read him the official notice of execution, which he and Macnair would then sign. Outside, Harry Potter, who had turned back time with Hermione Granger, crept through the pumpkin patch to Buckbeak while Fudge read. The hippogriff Buckbeak, 'hereafter called the condemned', was to be beheaded on the sixth of June at sundown by the Committee's appointed executioner, Walden Macnair. Harry bowed, Buckbeak bowed back, and Harry set to work on the knot that tied him to the tree. It jammed half undone, and Buckbeak would not budge. Then a small cloaked figure ran out from behind the cabin to throw him a dead ferret. Buckbeak lunged for it, the knot gave way, and Macnair's axe buried itself in the tree where his neck had been. The rider on his back, as he climbed into the red evening sky, was Dracina Malfoy.

pages.title: Dumbledore's letter to John Constantine
infobox: Summer 1993, in a pub in Soho
To bring Ephraim Shacklewell's book to Hogwarts before mid-August, unopened
pages.html:
Dumbledore's letter to John Constantine was the letter in green ink that sent Constantine to New Mexico in the summer of 1993. It asked him to bring a book held by Ephraim Shacklewell to Hogwarts before the middle of August, without opening it. Its closing lines were a reminder of an old debt: 'I think of you often. I think of my Deluminator, too.'

The letter

The owl found John in the back bar of a pub in Soho at two o'clock on a Tuesday afternoon. Nobody knew about that pub, which was the first bad sign. The second was the ink, which was green.

It began: 'I do hope that this finds you well, or at any rate alive. I understand that in your case these are not always the same thing.' The book was at Shacklewell House, New Mexico, some miles south of the place the diggers called the Cleft. It did not belong to Mr Shacklewell, who did not understand it, and Dumbledore would very much prefer that nobody else ever came to understand it either. John was not to open it, nor look at it for longer than he must. There was a postscript: 'I am told that you may find Mr Shacklewell's wards troublesome. I am quite sure that you will not.'

The Deluminator

In 1985 John had needed something that could take the light from a demon that fed on it. The only thing he knew of was Dumbledore's Deluminator, so he stole it out of the Headmaster's own pocket at a Ministry dinner. He gave it back the next week, a little scorched, and tried to say sorry in the back room of the Hog's Head. Dumbledore shouted him down. Then he put the whole business away in his desk drawer, like a man saving a good cheque for a rainy day. I think of you often meant I have not forgotten. Eight years later, it rained.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John read the letter three times, then folded it up very small to put in his inside pocket, next to his wand. He did as he was told, as he always did in the end with Dumbledore, which was what he hated most of all. He came away from New Mexico with the book, a big, heavy, old one bound in brown leather, with Myst stamped on the front in gold. In August 1993 he was carrying it to Hogwarts on the Knight Bus, in a thin white carrier bag.

Quotations

I am told that you may find Mr Shacklewell's wards troublesome. I am quite sure that you will not.Albus Dumbledore · B3 Interlude

pages.title: Dracina's letter to her father
pages.html:
Dracina's letter to her father was the letter about Buckbeak that Dracina Malfoy wrote to Lucius Malfoy in September 1993. She told Harry Potter she had decided not to send it. Somebody took it while she slept, and the hearing that condemned Buckbeak followed. Hermione Granger believed for months that Dracina had posted it herself.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, on the night of 6 June 1994, Dracina rescued Buckbeak herself, right in front of Macnair and Fudge. Walking back through the Forest afterwards, Harry said he had known all along she would make it right. Hermione thought he was being used. 'She still sent that letter, Harry.' Dracina had told him in Potions that she would not send it, Hermione pointed out, and then at Christmas there had been a complaint, a Committee, an executioner. 'You don't get an execution out of a letter nobody posted.' Harry said that somebody had taken it while Dracina was asleep. She had told him so, and he believed her.

Later that night Hermione owned up to Dracina about her brooch and her ribbons. 'I didn't take your letter, though,' she said. 'I never touched it. That part wasn't me.' Dracina was left quite at a loss. It had in fact been Pansy Parkinson, who confessed on the castle steps the next day, in Chapter Twenty-Two, and was forgiven.

pages.title: Lighten our darkness
infobox: Prayer; the third collect at Evensong
Lily Potter; Remus Lupin; Sirius Black
pages.html:
'Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord' is the opening of an old evening prayer of the Church of England, the third collect at Evensong. Lily Potter used to say it. Remus Lupin and Sirius Black said it together on the lawn at Hogwarts in June 1994. Her son, who had never heard it before, found that he liked it.

The prayer

The collect asks God to lighten the dark and to defend those who pray from all perils of the night, for the love of His only Son. It is far older than the Prayer Book. The Church of England took it from an ancient Latin service book in 1549, and it has been said at Evening Prayer ever since.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, Lupin and Black were walking Peter Pettigrew up the dark lawn from the Shrieking Shack. Lupin's voice had begun to go wrong. Black asked him to say it with him, the way Lily used to. In a voice that seemed to cost him a great deal, Lupin said, 'Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord.' 'And by thy great mercy defend us,' said Black. 'From all perils and dangers of this night,' said Lupin. They said the last part together, very low. Harry Potter had never heard the words before. They sounded very old to him, and he liked them; for a little while the night seemed smaller. A few minutes later the moon came out.

In Chapter Twenty, the words came back to Harry in a clearing in the Forbidden Forest, with Lupin in his war form tearing at his shield and Dracina Malfoy crouched behind him in the stream. The cross in his inside pocket had gone warm. A moment later his shield turned white.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, on a Sunday evening a little over a fortnight after the night on the lawn, Harry walked to St Michael's for Evensong. He stopped in the porch, not quite daring to go in. From the other side of the door came an old man's voice, leading a handful of others in the same prayer. Harry took a deep breath and pushed the door open. He did not burst into flames. He slid quietly into the back pew instead, and stayed to listen.

pages.title: Doctor Who
infobox: By the BBC, from November 1963 to 1989
pages.html:
Doctor Who is a Muggle television programme about the Doctor, a Time Lord who travels through time and space in a police box that is bigger on the inside. The BBC broadcast it from 1963 to 1989. Dudley Dursley watched the old episodes on video on Saturday afternoons.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, on the evening of 6 June 1994, Harry Potter had gone back in time with Hermione Granger. He wondered whether they could simply run in and grab Peter Pettigrew. Hermione was horrified. Harry finished the thought for her: 'Catastrophically harm the timeline. Yeah I know. I watched a bit of Doctor Who back in the day, Hermione. At least I tried to.'

He had tried, often, perched on the very end of the sofa at Privet Drive, until Aunt Petunia noticed him and flapped him out of the room with a rolling pin.

pages.title: Kojak
infobox: Telly Savalas, as Lieutenant Theo Kojak
pages.html:
Kojak is an American television police series about Lieutenant Theo Kojak of the New York police, a bald detective in sharp suits with a weakness for lollipops. John Constantine learnt most of his American accent from it.

The series

Telly Savalas played Kojak for five seasons, from 1973 to 1978, and the series was shown in Britain too. Kojak sucked lollipops in place of cigarettes. He greeted friends and suspects alike with 'Who loves ya, baby?'

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, Constantine broke into Shacklewell House in New Mexico to fetch a book for Albus Dumbledore. When Ephraim Shacklewell caught him in the trophy room, he passed himself off as an officer of MACUSA's Magical Security, Artefacts Division. He said it in the best American he could manage, which he had mostly learnt off Kojak.

pages.title: Harry Hunting
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Behind the shops in Little Whinging
pages.html:
Harry Hunting was the favourite game of Dudley Dursley's gang, played every summer behind the shops in Little Whinging. Harry Potter was the quarry. Dudley and his friends, Piers Polkiss among them, did the hunting.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, on the night of 6 June 1994, Sirius Black asked Harry in the tunnel from the Shrieking Shack whether everything was all right with his aunt and uncle. Harry thought of the cupboard under the stairs, where he had slept for ten years, and of the cat flap in his bedroom door. He thought of Dudley's gang playing Harry Hunting, every summer, behind the shops. He wanted to tell Black everything. Then Lupin called from up ahead that Crookshanks had found the way out, and the moment had gone.

pages.title: Wand-Extinguishing Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The Wand-Extinguishing Charm, Nox, puts out the light that the Wand-Lighting Charm has lit at the end of a wand. It is one of the shortest spells there is, and on a dark night it can matter as much as any.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seventeen, in June 1994, Harry Potter and Hermione Granger crept up the stairs of the Shrieking Shack with their wands lit. On the landing they breathed 'Nox' together, and their wandlight died.

In Chapter Nineteen, later that night, Harry blinded the Garou with a Lumos, scrambled away through the grass and threw himself into the black shadow behind a boulder. 'Nox,' he breathed, and the light at the end of his wand went out. He pressed his back against the cold stone. He tried not to breathe at all while the creature hunted for him on the other side.

pages.title: Ferula
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Binds a broken limb to a splint with bandages
pages.html:
Ferula is a healing charm for broken limbs. It conjures bandages that wind themselves round the limb and strap it tight to a splint, so that the patient can stand on it until somebody can mend the bone properly.

Use

Ferula mends nothing. It is first aid, the sort of spell that is worth knowing because the person who needs it is usually a long way from a hospital wing.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Remus Lupin used it on Ron Weasley's broken leg. He admitted that he could not mend bones nearly as well as Madam Pomfrey, so he touched his wand to the leg and said 'Ferula'. Bandages spun up Ron's leg and strapped it to a splint. Ron tested it very cautiously and found that it held.

pages.title: Mobilicorpus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Lifts and carries an unconscious body
pages.html:
Mobilicorpus lifts an unconscious body and carries it along upright, a few inches above the floor, as though it hung from invisible strings. It is a practical spell, though not a dignified one for the body concerned.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in June 1994, Severus Snape lay out cold in the Shrieking Shack after three Disarming Charms had hit him at once. Remus Lupin thought it best not to revive him until they were safely back in the castle. 'Mobilicorpus,' he muttered. Snape was jerked upright, as though strings had been tied to his wrists, his neck and his knees. His head lolled horribly, like a puppet's, and his feet dangled a few inches above the floor.

'Can we keep him like that?' said Harry. Nobody answered, although Sirius Black's mouth twitched.

pages.title: Impediment Jinx
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
The Impediment Jinx, cast with the word Impedimenta, slows down or stops whatever it hits. Against a person, or a small creature, it is one of the most useful defensive spells there is. Against something big and angry enough, it does very little.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, on the night of the full moon in June 1994, Hermione Granger turned on the Garou that was attacking Harry Potter in the grounds of Hogwarts. Her face had gone white and savage. Her Impedimenta hit the creature in the shoulder. It staggered one step sideways, no more.

In Chapter Twenty, in the Forbidden Forest, she cast it again, between two Stunners. All three spells might as well have been snowflakes.

pages.title: Incarcerous
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
Binds the target with thick ropes shot from the wand
pages.html:
Incarcerous shoots thick ropes from the end of a wand. They lash themselves round the target and bind it fast. They will hold a man. They will not hold everything.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, on the night of the full moon in June 1994, Hermione Granger used it on the Garou that was attacking Harry Potter in the grounds of Hogwarts. Thick ropes burst from her wand, lashing themselves round its arms and chest. The creature flexed its shoulders, and the ropes snapped like cotton thread.

pages.title: Severing Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
The Severing Charm, Diffindo, cuts whatever it strikes as cleanly as a knife. It is most often used on cloth, rope or paper. Against a living creature it opens a wound.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, on the night of the full moon in June 1994, Hermione Granger turned it on the Garou that was attacking Harry Potter in the grounds. 'Diffindo! Don't you TOUCH him! Don't you dare touch him!' The charm struck the creature on the flank. A thin dark line opened in the grey fur, as neatly as if it had been drawn with a ruler. Then the edges simply crept back together, and within seconds there was no mark at all.

Professor Snape had warned the class of exactly this, in a lesson on werewolves in November 1993 (Book Three, Chapter Nine). Silver burns them, he had said, but 'very little else troubles them at all, and what does, they heal while you stand watching.'

pages.title: Entrail-Expelling Curse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
The Entrail-Expelling Curse is a killing curse of the messier sort. It was invented in the seventeenth century by Urquhart Rackharrow, a rather vicious-looking wizard whose portrait hangs in St Mungo's Hospital.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Hermione Granger told the room that she knew at least four spells that would kill a man, and slowly, too. She dismissed this one at once.

'There's the Entrail-Expelling Curse, of course, but that's very messy, and over far too quickly to be much use.'

Peter Pettigrew made a faint gurgling noise behind his gag.

pages.title: Desiccation Hex
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Eighteen
Draws the water out through the skin
pages.html:
The Desiccation Hex draws all the water out of the victim through the skin, very gradually, until the victim shrivels up like a prune. The tongue goes first, so that the victim cannot scream. It can kill.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Peter Pettigrew lay tied up and gagged on the floor. Hermione Granger explained, with shining eyes, that she knew at least four spells that would kill a man slowly. By the time she reached the Desiccation Hex, Sirius Black's mouth had fallen slightly open. Professor Lupin had shut his eyes, the way teachers do when they are counting to ten.

'The tongue goes first, which is clever, actually, because it means he can't scream.' If he were a rat at the time, she pointed out, it would be quicker still. She had worked out the timings once, just in case. It was all a matter of body weight.

'Thank you, Hermione,' said Lupin politely, opening his eyes. 'That is... extremely thorough. I'm quite sure Peter has taken the point. Perhaps we might save the rest of it for another time? Ideally,' he added, 'a long time from now, and after your O.W.L.s.'

pages.title: The blood-boiling curse
infobox: Boils the blood, starting at the feet
pages.html:
The blood-boiling curse is a fifteenth-century curse that boils its victim's blood, starting at the feet and working upwards. It is recorded in a footnote in Moste Potente Potions, a book from the Restricted Section of the Hogwarts library. According to the footnote, a Muggle-baiter in Shropshire took nine hours to die of it, and he was awake for every one of them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Peter Pettigrew lay tied up and gagged on the floor. Hermione Granger observed brightly that he would not get far if he tried to escape. She knew at least four spells that would kill a man, slowly, and this was the second. She had found it while making Polyjuice Potion in her second year. Remus Lupin shut his eyes, the way teachers did when they were counting to ten.

pages.title: The curse banned in 1612
pages.html:
The curse banned in 1612 is a curse that kills, outlawed so long ago that hardly anybody now knows its countercurse. That, in Hermione Granger's opinion, is what makes it the really interesting one.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, it was the fourth curse on the list Hermione gave Peter Pettigrew, after the Entrail-Expelling Curse, the blood-boiling curse and the Desiccation Hex. 'The fourth one is the really interesting one, because it was banned in 1612, so hardly anybody knows the countercurse.' She had just begun to explain it when Remus Lupin opened his eyes. 'Thank you, Hermione,' he said politely. 'That is... extremely thorough.' He suggested they save the rest for another time, ideally after her O.W.L.s. Ron, going pinker by the second, asked her to remind him never to forget her birthday.

pages.title: Jelly-Legs Jinx
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Turns the victim's legs to jelly
pages.html:
The Jelly-Legs Jinx turns its victim's legs to jelly. The knees buckle and give way, so that the victim generally ends up on the floor. It is a schoolyard jinx, and a cruel one at the top of a staircase.

In the saga

The Book Three Interlude, which follows John Constantine in August 1993, looks back on his years at Hogwarts, where he was a Muggle-born in Slytherin. The other students made him pay for it. At Hallowe'en they locked him in a broom cupboard in the dungeons and forgot to let him out until the next lunchtime. In his second year, 1965 to 1966, somebody put a Jelly-Legs Jinx on him at the top of the marble staircase, in front of half the school.

pages.title: Anti-Cheating Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Anti-Cheating Charms are the charms that examiners put on the quills used in Hogwarts examinations. Together with wards round the Great Hall, set to catch notes, whispers and copied answers, they are meant to make cheating impossible.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine remembered his schooldays in the 1960s. He was clever enough to pass every examination honestly. It took far less effort to cheat, though, and it was safer, because a cheat knew what was coming. The examiners put Anti-Cheating Charms on the quills; John worked out how to get round them in his second year. They put wards round the Hall; he found the gaps in them the way water finds the gaps in a roof. He was never once caught. Everybody knew anyway.

pages.title: Unlocking Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Unlocking Charm, Alohomora, opens locks with a tap of the wand. It is quick, simple and known to every wizard who ever wanted to be somewhere he was not supposed to be. For exactly that reason, any decent ward is built to notice it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Five, in the autumn of 1991, Harry, Ron, Hermione Granger and Neville Longbottom were caught out of bed at midnight. Peeves bellowed for Filch, and they ran for it down the Charms corridor, straight into a locked door. Hermione snatched Harry's wand, tapped the lock and whispered, 'Alohomora!' The door swung open just ahead of Filch. On the other side of it was the forbidden corridor on the third floor, with a three-headed dog in it. In Chapter Twelve, on the night they went after the Philosopher's Stone, her Alohomora would not open the door beyond the flying keys at all.

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine came to Shacklewell House in the New Mexico desert to take the Linking Book to Myst Island. Every ward on that house had been built by wizards to keep out wizards. It would know an Unlocking Charm the moment one was cast. John left his wand buried in the desert. He went in with chalk, salt and a Hand of Glory instead.

pages.title: Disillusionment Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
Makes the subject blend into whatever is behind it
pages.html:
The Disillusionment Charm makes a person or thing take on the look of whatever is behind it, like a chameleon, until it can hardly be seen. It is not true invisibility, and a well-made ward can tell when one has been cast.

The charm

To the person being disillusioned, it feels as if somebody has broken a cold egg over the top of their head. A disillusioned wizard who keeps still is very hard to see. Once he moves, a sharp eye may catch the shimmer.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine stood outside Shacklewell House in New Mexico and weighed up its wards. They had been built by wizards to keep out wizards. They would be watching for wand magic. They would know an Unlocking Charm the moment one was cast, and they would scream the house down at a Disillusionment Charm.

pages.title: The Animagus-revealing spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Forces an Animagus in animal shape back into human form
pages.html:
The Animagus-revealing spell forces an Animagus who is hiding in animal shape back into human form. It shows as blue-white light. Remus Lupin and Sirius Black used it together in June 1994 to unmask Peter Pettigrew, who had spent twelve years as a rat.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Ron Weasley at last handed over his rat, Scabbers. 'Together?' said Black quietly. 'I think so,' said Lupin, and on the count of three both wands blazed with blue-white light.

Scabbers hung in the air, writhing, then fell to the floorboards. A second flash came, brighter than the first, and it was like watching a tree grow, speeded up. Seconds later a very small man was crouching where Scabbers had been. It was Peter Pettigrew. His smell reached Lupin a moment later, and it very nearly drove him into his war form on the spot.

pages.title: Wolfsbane Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
Suppresses a Garou's compulsion to transform and to destroy the Wyrm
Aconite, also called wolfsbane or monkshood
pages.html:
The Wolfsbane Potion is a very recent, very difficult discovery that holds down a Garou's war form. As long as he keeps taking it, the instinct to transform is suppressed, along with the compulsion to root out and destroy the Wyrm at once; neither is ever quite gone. Severus Snape brewed it for Remus Lupin throughout the school year of 1993 to 1994.

Effects

A Garou who takes the potion regularly can keep his human shape and his self-command, even in places or company that would otherwise drive him into his war form. The compulsion is suppressed, not cured. It never truly goes away, and the drinker must still master it.

Before the potion was discovered, a bitten Garou such as Lupin was liable to transform the moment he sensed anything that smelled of the Wyrm. He could not always control himself when he did. Even with the potion, Lupin judged himself a danger to every witch and wizard at Hogwarts. The castle's teaching mixes dark magic with light, and he could smell the Wyrm everywhere there.

Against a strong enough reek of the Wyrm the potion only just holds. Snape's Dark Mark sets every instinct Lupin has against him. The potion is the only reason Lupin can bear to stand in the same room as the man who brews it.

Brewing

The potion was invented by Damocles Belby. Its chief ingredient is aconite, the plant also called monkshood and wolfsbane. Snape asked Harry Potter the difference between those two names in his first Potions lesson in 1991; there is none.

It is particularly fiddly to make, and not many wizards can brew it. It is drunk from a smoking goblet over the days around the full moon. It tastes revolting, it smells like burnt grass while it simmers, and it must never be sweetened, because sugar stops it working.

In the saga

In 1993 Snape brewed a whole cauldron of the potion for Lupin, and brought it to his office in a smoking goblet. Harry Potter saw Lupin drink it there in October. At Christmas 1993 Albus Dumbledore asked Snape whether he had made up Lupin's potion again. In early 1994 it simmered in Snape's office, while Lupin struggled to stay downwind of the man brewing it.

Lupin explained what the potion was for in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994. That night he had left his office before Snape brought the goblet. Missing his dose under the full moon, he transformed on the lawn, and Hermione Granger understood at once that this was the reason.

pages.title: The Shacklewell scouring potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Interlude
pages.html:
The Shacklewell scouring potion is the magical cleaner that made the Shacklewells rich. Ephraim Shacklewell's father sold it to the copper mines of Arizona, through a string of front companies, as a miracle cleaning fluid. The Magical Congress of the United States of America never quite managed to prove it.

The fortune

The Shacklewells had been in America for generations without ever being rich. The trade only became possible after 1965, when MACUSA did away with Rappaport's Law, which had kept American wizards from having anything to do with No-Majs. Ephraim has spent the money since on Shacklewell House in New Mexico, its pool and its very expensive wards.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine broke into Shacklewell House for the Myst book. Caught in the trophy room, he passed himself off as a MACUSA officer and told Shacklewell that the book would be confiscated. 'We'll say no more about the business with the copper mines.' Shacklewell, weak with relief, handed it over.

pages.title: True Faith
infobox: Real belief in God, truly held
pages.html:
True Faith is real belief in God, held so completely that the things of darkness cannot bear it. A cross in the hand of somebody who truly believes in Jesus Christ will hold a vampire off, and dementors are repulsed by such faith. In a coward's hand, as Remus Lupin puts it, a cross is a stick of wood.

Nature

What matters is the believer, not the object. A cross works against vampires because God pronounced their curse, and the sign belongs to Him, while the thing in front of it belongs to His enemy. It is no use at all to somebody who does not believe in it. True Faith is rare. It cannot be pretended, and no spell will put it into anybody.

Against dementors

In Azkaban Sirius Black made himself a little cross of grey wood: two splinters bound together crosswise with a twist of thread pulled from a blanket. He had never believed in God. That had been Lily's, and her mother Susan's before her. But he remembered the things Lily used to say, along with the mad old Bible passages printed in The Quibbler. He held on to that cross like a life raft. It did nothing for him at first. When he began truly to believe, the dementors stopped coming to him. 'They're repulsed by True Faith, Sirius,' said Lupin, in the voice he used in lessons.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in October 1993, Lupin taught Harry Potter's class the ground rules of defence against vampires. When the class came to crosses, his eyes went very briefly to Harry. 'A cross in a coward's hand is a stick of wood. In the hand of somebody who believes in Jesus Christ, it's a different thing altogether. They don't like that at all. Nobody's ever really explained why.' In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Sirius told Harry how the dementors had stopped coming to him once he believed, and Lupin gave the reason.

In Chapter Nineteen, with the transformed Lupin standing over him, Harry remembered the lesson. He did not even know whether he believed in God, but he held up Lupin's cross anyway, because there was nothing else. It stopped the creature for a moment. Whatever it smelt on Harry was stronger. Later, with the dementors closing round the lake, Harry wondered whether there was anybody up there at all. Lupin's cross in his pocket was a stick of wood. His Patronus wavered and fell apart.

In Chapter Twenty Harry stopped looking down, and the Patronus that came out of him on the far side of the lake destroyed the dementors outright. In Chapter Twenty-Two the Fat Friar told him that he had touched God. 'You reached out, and He was there.'

pages.title: Old magic
aliases: the magic of Elves and of Númenor
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The blood of Aragorn and Arwen, through Lily Potter
Protects Harry while he calls his aunt's house home
Albus Dumbledore, Lord Voldemort and Gandalf
pages.html:
Old magic is Albus Dumbledore's name for the protection Lily Potter laid on her son when she died for him. It is older than anything Dumbledore can do: 'the magic of Elves, Harry. And of Númenor'. It lives in Harry's blood, as it does in his aunt's. It is the inheritance of Aragorn and Arwen, come down to Lily through the Pevensies.

Lily's protection

When Voldemort came for Harry in 1981, Lily Potter died for him. Her death put a protection on him that no other mother's death has done in all Dumbledore's experience. In June 1992, in the chamber under the trapdoor, Quirinus Quirrell found that he could not touch Harry's bare skin without his own hands blistering.

Afterwards Dumbledore told Harry that some hold Muggle-born magic to be the recessive power of a magical ancestor. He had reason to believe, he said, that Lily was descended from a very powerful line of magic indeed. He would not say which, because the knowledge would put Harry and his friends in danger.

At the end of the summer term of 1993, on the castle steps, Dumbledore told him more: 'Old magic. Older than anything I can do. The magic of Elves, Harry. And of Númenor. It lives in your blood, and it lives in hers.'

Lily's blood lives on in her sister Petunia. So Harry is protected while he lives under Petunia's roof, for as long as he can call that house his home.
