The Coast City man is a big man in a baseball cap who spoke at the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994. He held a photograph of his wife and two little girls against his chest. They died with his parents when Coast City was destroyed in 1993.

Coast City

He was in San Diego on the day it happened. He drove back up the coast that night and found no city at all, only a hole with a machine in it, where seven million people had lived. The thing that did it, he said, had worn the S and called itself Superman. It was the Cyborg Superman. Mongul's forces had destroyed the city for him.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he spoke to the camera in a flat voice: 'So you tell me. You tell me how I'm supposed to know the difference. Because I can't. Nobody can.'

In their own words

So you tell me. You tell me how I'm supposed to know the difference. Because I can't. Nobody can.The Coast City man at the UN protest · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The old man in the cardigan at the UN protest
infobox: Had a heart attack in December 1965
pages.html:
The old man in the cardigan is a small, very upright New Yorker who leans on a stick. At the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994 he told the cameras that he had watched superhumans fight over his head for fifty-four years.

Fifty-four years

He was sixteen in 1940, when the first of them, the Sub-Mariner, came out of the sea and tore up his street. The Sub-Mariner threw a fire engine through the front of the pharmacy. The next year he came back with the water behind him, and the old man's father drowned on the steps going down to the trains.

Just before Christmas 1965 the sky over Manhattan caught fire, because something had come to eat the world. It was Galactus, the devourer of worlds. People said afterwards that the Fantastic Four had talked him out of it. On the second day of the sky fire, the old man's wife had a heart attack.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he looked straight into the camera with watery old eyes. 'Not one of them ever asked us. Not one. Not once.'

In their own words

Not one of them ever asked us. Not one. Not once.The old man in the cardigan at the UN protest · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The Bellevue nurse at the UN protest
infobox: Eleven patients in the blackout of August 1993
pages.html:
The Bellevue nurse is a young intensive-care nurse from Bellevue Hospital in New York. In August 1994 she spoke at the protest against superhumans outside the United Nations, looking as though she had come straight from a shift.

The blackout

She was on duty in intensive care at Bellevue on the night of the great blackout of August 1993. The lights, the monitors, the ventilators and even the generators all went off at once. She and two other nurses bagged the patients by hand in the dark all night, but they could not go fast enough.

The blackout was the work of one mutant, Magneto, who put out the lights all over the world for a night from his space station, Avalon.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, she told the cameras: 'We lost eleven people on my floor. Eleven. That was one mutant. One man, up in a space station, having a tantrum.' She shook her head. 'And they want us to say thank you to the rest.'

pages.title: The Metropolis man with the black eye
infobox: Knocked down by Doomsday in 1992; rebuilt
pages.html:
The Metropolis man with the black eye is a man in a suit who pushed his way to the microphone at the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994. His part of Metropolis has been flattened twice in two years.

Twice in two years

Doomsday knocked his building down in 1992, in the battle that ended with Superman's death. He rebuilt. Then in May 1994, as he put it, 'some lunatic in a lab coat flattened downtown with torpedoes left over from the alien invasion'. The man in the lab coat was Dr Sydney Happersen, Lex Luthor's chief scientist. Nobody, the man shouted, was even paying for it.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter saw him on the news at Privet Drive. 'Every time they fight over Metropolis, we're the ones underneath!' he shouted. Similar protests were reported that night in Los Angeles, in Chicago and in what remained of Metropolis.

In their own words

Every time they fight over Metropolis, we're the ones underneath!The Metropolis man with the black eye · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The woman in the headscarf
pages.html:
The woman in the headscarf was one of the crowd protesting against superhumans outside the United Nations in New York, in the small hours of 20 August 1994. She was crying.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, she was one of the last faces in the report that Harry Potter watched at Privet Drive. Most of the people there, the reporter said, had a story to tell. Hers went untold. Looking at the crowd, Harry thought of what Florean Fortescue had said of the Muggles who burnt witches: they had been hurt, and they had hit back at whatever was nearest.

pages.title: The boy in the Friends of Humanity T-shirt
pages.html:
The boy in the Friends of Humanity T-shirt was a teenager among the crowd protesting against superhumans outside the United Nations in New York, in the small hours of 20 August 1994. He was shouting something that could not be made out, with tears running down his face.

The protest

The Friends of Humanity is an American movement against mutants and other superhumans. Its banner, held up by a dozen people, said FRIENDS OF HUMANITY in neat red letters. More than twenty thousand people had gathered, chanting 'No more capes!', after word spread of Superman's appearance before the Security Council the afternoon before.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he was among the last faces in the report, which Harry Potter watched on the Dursleys' television. Looking at the crowd, Harry thought of what Florean Fortescue had told him about the Muggles who burnt witches. They had been frightened, as these people were.

pages.title: The fireman with the helmet
pages.html:
The fireman with the helmet was one of the crowd protesting against superhumans outside the United Nations in New York, in the small hours of 20 August 1994. He stood on his own at the edge of the crowd, saying nothing at all, holding up a helmet.

The protest

More than twenty thousand people had gathered there after Superman spoke to the Security Council, watched by mounted police and a line of officers with riot shields. Their placards read HUMANS FIRST, NO MORE CAPES, REMEMBER COAST CITY and WHO PAYS FOR METROPOLIS? Nobody said whose helmet it was.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he was one of the last faces in the report that Harry Potter watched at Privet Drive that morning.

pages.title: The young man in the loud shirt
pages.html:
The young man in the loud shirt is a shopkeeper in Angel Grove, California. The Power Rangers saved his life from a ten-storey monster, and then their giant robot destroyed his shop. He spoke to the Muggle news in August 1994.

Interview

He was the last face in a report on public anger at superhumans, squinting on a street corner in bright sunshine under the caption ANGEL GROVE, CALIFORNIA. After all the darkness that had gone before, the sunshine looked very strange. He was not against the Rangers, he said. They had saved his life, from a thing ten storeys high with a head like a pumpkin with teeth. But their robot had gone through four buildings on his block to get to it. The buildings were empty, because the Rangers always get everybody out first. His shop had been in one of them, though, and his insurance would not pay. 'There's a clause. Superhuman combat. You never even hear about it until it's your roof.'

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: his interview closed the report on the protests outside the United Nations. Dudley demanded of the television why anybody would be against people who saved people's lives. Harry did not answer. He did not think he could have explained it to Dudley, and he was not sure he could have explained it even to himself.

In their own words

Superhuman combat. You never even hear about it until it's your roof.The young man in the loud shirt · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The pumpkin-headed monster
infobox: A head like a pumpkin with teeth
pages.html:
The pumpkin-headed monster was a giant ten storeys high, with a head like a pumpkin with teeth. It attacked Angel Grove, California, and the Power Rangers fought it there. Their robot went through four buildings on one block to reach it.

The attack

The Rangers got everybody out first, as they always do. All the same, their giant robot went through four empty buildings on one block to get to the monster. One of those buildings held the shop of a young man who said afterwards that the Rangers had saved his life. His insurance, he said, would not pay, because of a clause excluding superhuman combat.

Most of the monsters the Rangers fight in Angel Grove are made by Rita Repulsa's servant Finster. When one of them is losing, Rita makes it grow to giant size with her wand.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: the young man in the loud shirt described the monster on the Muggle news of 20 August 1994: 'That thing was ten storeys high. It had a head like a pumpkin with teeth.'

pages.title: Cyborg Superman
aliases: The false Superman of Coast City
infobox: The false Superman of Coast City; Hank Henshaw
Adventures of Superman #466 (May 1990), as Hank Henshaw; Adventures of Superman #500 (June 1993), as the Cyborg Superman
Life force held captive on Apokolips since spring 1994
pages.html:
The Cyborg Superman is Hank Henshaw, a former astronaut whose mind outlived his body. In 1993 he appeared wearing Superman's symbol and claiming to be Superman, back from the dead. With Mongul's forces he destroyed Coast City and its seven million people, standing in the sky while it was done.

Hank Henshaw

Henshaw was the commander of the space shuttle Excalibur, which was struck by a burst of radiation in orbit in 1990. The crew, his wife Terri among them, came back changed. Henshaw's own body broke down altogether. His mind survived by passing into machinery, first the computers of LexCorp and then whatever metal he could gather round himself. Terri, horrified at what he had become, died soon afterwards.

Henshaw blamed Superman for all of it. He left Earth in the Kryptonian birthing matrix that had once carried the infant Kal-El. In his years in space he learnt a great deal about Krypton, and about the man he hated.

The false Superman

He came back in 1993, after Superman's death, in a body half flesh and half steel. It was built so closely on Kryptonian lines that tests seemed to show he was Superman himself, rebuilt. He was one of four figures who wore the S that year. He had made an alliance with Mongul, and in the summer of 1993 Mongul's warship bombed Coast City out of existence while the Cyborg Superman hovered above. In the crater they built a great machine, Engine City, the first of two that were meant to turn Earth into a new Warworld.

The real Superman returned that August. He met the Cyborg in the ruins of Coast City, with Hal Jordan, Steel, Superboy and Supergirl beside him. Superman destroyed the Cyborg's body, and Hal Jordan beat Mongul.

Afterwards

Henshaw was not finished. In the spring of 1994 he surfaced again on Apokolips, at the time of Doomsday's second rampage. Darkseid compressed what remained of his life force into a small sphere, and kept it.

The public has not forgotten his crime. The thing that destroyed Coast City wore Superman's symbol and used his name. Because of it, many people no longer trust themselves to tell Superman from an impostor. ‘Remember Coast City’ has become a slogan against all superhumans.

In the saga

Outside the United Nations, on the night of 19 August 1994, a man who had lost his wife, his daughters and his parents at Coast City told a television reporter about the thing that did it. It had been wearing the S, he said; it had said it was Superman, and it had stood up in the sky while they did it. ‘You tell me how I'm supposed to know the difference,’ he said. ‘Because I can't. Nobody can.’

pages.title: The Watchtower
pages.html:
The Watchtower is the Justice League's station on the Moon, and it is still only half built. The League has worked from it since it lost its New York embassy in June 1994 and its United Nations charter in July. On 19 August 1994 Superman told the Security Council that the Watchtower was ready.

Bases of the League

The League has had a string of headquarters. Its first, from 1960, was the Secret Sanctuary, a cave in a hollowed-out mountain near Happy Harbor, Rhode Island. It was given up in 1969, after Snapper Carr, tricked by the Joker, let slip where it was.

From 1970 the League worked from a satellite in orbit 22,300 miles above the Earth, which its members reached by teleporter. From 1984 it worked from a bunker in Detroit. Under its United Nations charter, from 1987, it kept embassies in New York, Paris and Moscow, with diplomatic standing.

The move to the Moon

In June 1994 the New York embassy was destroyed in an attack. In July the United Nations suspended the League's charter. The League had no secure base left on Earth, and no standing among the nations either.

So it withdrew to the Moon, to a station it had begun to build there and had not finished. From there, a month later, Superman offered the League's services to the Security Council.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994 the news showed Superman telling the Security Council, ‘The Justice League is ready. The Watchtower is ready. We can be in Belgrade within the hour.’ The newsreader explained that since July the League had been operating from a half-built station on the Moon, which it called the Watchtower. Harry Potter waited for her to smile, and she did not.

pages.title: Wonder Woman
aliases: The woman in red and gold with a tiara
infobox: The woman in red and gold with a tiara; Diana; Princess Diana of Themyscira; Diana Prince
The Justice Society; the Justice League (a founding member)
pages.html:
Wonder Woman is Diana, princess of the Amazons of Themyscira. She came out into the world of men in 1941 and has fought beside its heroes ever since. She does not age, so that in 1994 she looks no older than she did half a century ago, and she stands at Superman's side in the Justice League.

Themyscira

Diana was born on Themyscira, the hidden island of the Amazons, a nation of immortal women who turned their backs on the world of men in ancient Greece. Her mother, Queen Hippolyta, shaped her out of clay from the island's shore. The goddesses of Olympus gave the child life. They gave her gifts as well: strength, speed, wisdom and beauty. She was the only child ever born on the island.

In 1941 an American intelligence officer called Steve Trevor crashed on Themyscira. Hippolyta decreed a contest to choose the Amazon who would take him home and stay on as the island's champion in the world of men. Diana was forbidden to enter. She entered in disguise, and won.

In the world of men

She came to public notice in America late in 1941, on the eve of the country's entry into the war, dressed in red and gold, with a gold tiara on her dark hair. She carries a golden lasso that makes anyone it binds tell the truth. Her silver bracelets turn bullets aside, and her tiara can be thrown as a weapon.

From 1942 she served with the Justice Society, first as its secretary, later as a full member. At the turn of 1960 she was one of the founders of the Justice League. In 1968 she gave up her powers for a time and left the League. Once she had them back, she proved herself all over again in a series of trials watched by the other members, who took her back in 1976.

Accounts of the Crisis of 1985 to 1986 disagree about what became of her at the end of it. Some witnesses say she was struck down and went back to the clay she had been made from. Yet she was seen in the world afterwards, quite unchanged. Since then she has acted as Themyscira's emissary, carrying the Amazons' message of peace to the governments of the world and to the United Nations. In 1987 she stopped the war god Ares, who was goading the great powers towards nuclear war. In 1991 she fought the sorceress Circe in the war among the gods that spilt over onto the Earth.

1994

At the turn of 1993, with Superman dead, Wonder Woman called the League together again and led it through the months of mourning. Since his return she has served under him once more. On 19 August 1994 she stood behind him at the Security Council in New York, looking no older than she did in the annuals and newspaper photographs of decades before.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994 Harry watched the news of the Security Council session. Among the heroes Superman had brought with him he recognised a tall woman in red and gold, with a gold tiara on her dark hair. He knew her from the annuals Dudley had collected when he was small, and she looked no older than she did in them.

pages.title: Green Lantern
infobox: Alan Scott (from 1940); Hal Jordan (1959 to 1994); Guy Gardner; John Stewart; Kyle Rayner (since January 1994)
A ring that turns the wearer's will into green light
The Green Lantern Corps, under the Guardians of the Universe on Oa
pages.html:
Green Lantern is the name borne by the heroes who wield green power rings. Most of them have been members of the Green Lantern Corps, the police force of the Guardians of the Universe. Earth's most famous Green Lantern, Hal Jordan, wore the ring from 1959 until he vanished at the turn of 1994. Since January 1994 the name has belonged to a young man called Kyle Rayner.

Alan Scott

The first man on Earth to be called Green Lantern was Alan Scott, a railway engineer who survived a bridge disaster in 1940 by the light of a mysterious green lantern and made a ring from its metal. His ring was magic, and had nothing to do with the Corps. It had no power over wood. He was one of the founders of the Justice Society in 1940.

In July 1994, during Zero Hour, the time-mad Extant aged the rest of the Justice Society to its true years. Alan Scott's ring held, and he alone of them came through unchanged.

The Corps

On the planet Oa, at the centre of the universe, the immortal Guardians of the Universe divided creation into 3,600 sectors and set a Green Lantern to guard each one. Each Lantern was chosen for the ability to overcome great fear. Each was given a ring that turns the wearer's will into shapes of green light, and the rings were charged from lanterns linked to the great Central Power Battery on Oa. For most of the century the rings had no power over anything yellow, a weakness their enemies soon learnt to use.

The Goa'uld were among the Corps' oldest problems. They moved their slaves through the Stargates rather than across open space, where the Lanterns could see them, and their gold-covered motherships were safe from any ring with the yellow weakness. Hal Jordan, whose sector held Earth, never met one, because the Goa'uld kept away from Earth.

In 1959 the dying Green Lantern of Earth's sector, Abin Sur, crashed in California, and his ring chose Hal Jordan, a test pilot of Coast City. Hal served for thirty-four years. Other Earthmen served beside him, among them the brash Guy Gardner and the architect John Stewart.

In 1977, when Thanos meant to snuff out the stars, the Guardians sent the Corps to stand guard over the ones he had marked.

The fall of the Corps

In 1993 Coast City was destroyed with everyone in it, and Hal Jordan broke. When the Guardians rebuked him for using his ring to try to raise the city again, he flew to Oa, took the rings of the Lanterns who tried to stop him, and drained the Central Power Battery into himself. The Guardians died; the Corps was finished. Hal Jordan vanished.

One Guardian, Ganthet, survived, and came to Earth with the last ring. In January 1994 he gave it to Kyle Rayner, a young artist in Los Angeles, who has been Green Lantern ever since. Kyle wears a mask the public had never seen before, and he serves in the Justice League under Superman.

In July 1994 Hal Jordan returned as Parallax, the power behind Zero Hour, and tried to remake history. He was stopped at the beginning of time, and vanished again.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994 Harry Potter saw a young Green Lantern behind Superman at the United Nations. He wore a mask Harry had never seen before, and he had turned up out of nowhere in January, after the old one vanished.

pages.title: Martian Manhunter
infobox: The green-skinned man; J'onn J'onzz; John Jones
pages.html:
The Martian Manhunter is J'onn J'onzz, a green-skinned Martian who was brought to Earth in 1955 and stranded here. He is a telepath and shape-shifter of great strength. He was a founder of the Justice League, and he is its longest-serving member. In August 1994 he stood behind Superman at the United Nations so still that he might have been carved.

Mars

J'onn J'onzz was a Martian of the green race, a people of telepaths and shape-shifters. Their civilisation died long ago of a plague that spread through their minds and set them burning. His wife, M'yri'ah, died of it with their daughter, K'hym. He is the last of them.

Earth

He came to Earth in 1955, drawn across space by the experimental teleportation beam of a scientist, Dr Saul Erdel. Erdel died of the shock of seeing him, and with him died the only means of sending J'onn home.

J'onn took human shape and the name of John Jones. For years he worked as a police detective, while in his own form he fought crime as the Manhunter from Mars.

Even that form is a compromise. His true Martian shape is taller, thinner and stranger than the one the public knows. The heavy-browed green man is the face he chose so as not to frighten people.

The Justice League

At the turn of 1960 he was one of the seven founders of the Justice League. Of all its members he has stayed the longest.

When Aquaman broke up the old League in 1984 and moved it to Detroit, J'onn went with him. He served there until the Detroit League came to an end in 1987. When the League was rebuilt that year, after Darkseid's attack on public trust, he was again among its founders and its steadiest member. He has served in it, in one form or another, ever since.

In 1993, while Wonder Woman led the League through the months of mourning for Superman, J'onn led a smaller task force of his own. In 1994 he is among the League's core members under Superman.

Powers

The Martian Manhunter has strength comparable to Superman's. He flies, reads minds and speaks into them. He changes his shape and his size at will. He can turn invisible, or pass through solid matter.

Fire is his great weakness, as it was the death of his people. In public he appears as a tall, heavy-browed green man with red eyes. Less dangerously, he has a weakness for chocolate biscuits.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994 Harry Potter saw him on the news, among the League behind Superman at the United Nations: a huge man with green skin and a heavy brow, standing so still that he might have been carved.

pages.title: Batman
infobox:
Bruce Wayne first Batman
Dick Grayson second Batman
Terry McGinnis third Batman
Bruce Wayne; Dick Grayson; Terry McGinnis
pages.html:
Batman is the masked vigilante of Gotham, at work there since 1939 and a founding member of the Justice League. Three men have worn the cowl. The first was Bruce Wayne, the second Dick Grayson, and the third is Terry McGinnis, who was already Batman by 1993. The public knows that Batman has been more than one man, but not who any of them were.

The first Batman

Batman first came to public notice in Gotham in 1939: a man in a grey and black costume who hunted criminals by night. He wore a bat's cowl over his face, with a cape like a bat's wings. Behind the mask was Bruce Wayne, heir to the Wayne fortune, who had seen his parents murdered in the street as a boy and had trained for years to make war on crime. He had no powers. He had his mind, his body, his money and a cave full of equipment under Wayne Manor.

From 1940 he had a boy partner, Robin. Together they fought a gallery of enemies who became famous across the world, the Joker first among them. At the turn of 1960 Batman was among the founders of the Justice League, where he was valued for his detective work and his planning as much as for his fighting.

Three Batmen

Bruce Wayne gave up the cowl at last. It passed to Dick Grayson, the first Robin, who had grown up beside him and had worked under his own name of Nightwing since 1984. After Dick Grayson the cowl went to a third man, Terry McGinnis, whom Bruce Wayne guides from the cave beneath the manor.

None of these changes was ever announced. Gotham noticed that its Batman moved differently, fought differently and at last dressed differently. Slowly the public understood that more than one man had carried the name. It has never learnt who they were.

The Batman of the 1990s

The Batman of 1994 works in a Gotham of towers, neon and flying traffic, with gangs of Jokerz in the streets. He is black all over, with a red bat across his chest. He flies, too, on wings and rocket boots built into a powered suit. Like the men before him he never goes anywhere in daylight. When Superman addressed the United Nations in August 1994, Batman did not stand with the rest of the Justice League.

In the saga

Watching the news on 20 August 1994, Harry Potter noticed that Batman was not with the League at the United Nations. Batman never went anywhere in daylight. Besides, the Batman people talked about these days was black all over, with a red bat on his chest, and he flew.

pages.title: Bruce Wayne
pages.html:
Bruce Wayne was the first Batman, the man who put on the cowl in Gotham in 1939 and kept it on for decades. He has long since retired. He is an old man now, living at Wayne Manor, and from the cave beneath it he guides the third Batman, Terry McGinnis. The public has never known that he was Batman at all.

Early life

Bruce Wayne was the only son of Thomas Wayne, a Gotham doctor, and his wife Martha, heirs to one of the city's great fortunes. One evening, when Bruce was a boy, he and his parents were walking home from the cinema. A thief stopped them in an alley and shot both his parents dead in front of him. Bruce swore on their memory to spend his life fighting the kind of criminal who had killed them.

He spent his youth getting ready, studying under teachers all over the world. He learnt science, criminology and detection. He learnt gymnastics, every form of fighting, disguise and escape. The family butler, Alfred Pennyworth, brought him up and stayed at his side for the whole of his career.

The cowl

Bruce Wayne became Batman in 1939. He chose the bat because he believed criminals were a superstitious and cowardly lot. To the city he was a rich and idle playboy; by night he was its most feared vigilante. In 1940 he took in the orphaned circus acrobat Dick Grayson, who became his partner, Robin. At the turn of 1960 he was a founder of the Justice League with Superman, Wonder Woman and the others.

His career ended one night when he was already an old man. In the middle of a rescue his heart failed him, and he snatched up a gun to save himself. He had sworn never to use one. He put the cowl away for good, and it passed first to Dick Grayson.

Retirement

In retirement Bruce Wayne lived alone at Wayne Manor with a dog for company. His company, meanwhile, became Wayne-Powers, under the control of Derek Powers. Then the teenager Terry McGinnis found his way into the cave. Terry's father had just been murdered by Derek Powers's men. Terry stole the last Batsuit Wayne had built, went after the killers and took up the war on crime. Wayne, angry at first, came to accept him and became his mentor. Now he watches the third Batman's patrols on the cave's monitors, talks to him by radio and lends him the knowledge of half a century.

Character

Bruce Wayne is driven, secretive and difficult. Age has not softened him, and Terry McGinnis would be the first to say so. He has never killed and never wanted to. He is a brilliant detective and a brilliant engineer. Every suit, vehicle and device the three Batmen have used came out of his workshop.

pages.title: Dick Grayson
pages.html:
Dick Grayson was the first Robin, the boy who fought beside Batman from 1940. He later worked under a name of his own, Nightwing, and when Bruce Wayne gave up the cowl, Dick became the second Batman. The public knows Robin and Nightwing well enough. It has no idea that the boy wonder of 1940 grew up to be Gotham's second Batman.

Robin

Dick Grayson was born into the Flying Graysons, a family of trapeze artists who travelled with Haly's Circus. When he was a boy, his parents fell to their deaths in front of him. A gangster, Tony Zucco, had sabotaged their rigging because the circus would not pay him protection money. Bruce Wayne, who had watched his own parents die, took the boy in as his ward and trained him.

In 1940 Dick appeared at Batman's side as Robin, in red, green and yellow: an acrobat who laughed while he fought, which Batman never did. He was the first of the costumed partners, and for years the most famous boy in America.

The Titans and Nightwing

In 1964 Robin founded the Teen Titans with Wally West, who was Kid Flash, and Aqualad. They were the young partners of famous heroes, and they wanted to work out of their mentors' shadows. Dick led the team for many years. Growing up meant growing away from Batman. In 1984 he gave up the name of Robin and took a new one, Nightwing, with a costume of his own. The name came from an old Kryptonian legend that Superman had once told him.

The second Batman

When Bruce Wayne put the cowl away for good, Dick Grayson took it up and became the second Batman. Gotham was not told. His time as Batman ended before 1993, by which time the cowl had passed to Terry McGinnis. How it ended, and why, is not generally known.

pages.title: Terry McGinnis
pages.html:
Terry McGinnis is the third Batman, a young man from Gotham who was already wearing the cowl by 1993. He works at night in a powered nanotech suit, black with a red bat across the chest, in a Gotham of towers, neon, flying traffic and Jokerz gangs. His mentor is the retired Bruce Wayne.

Origin

Terry McGinnis grew up in Gotham, the elder son of Warren and Mary McGinnis, who had separated. His younger brother is called Matt. Terry was a troubled teenager with a record for fighting.

One night, running from a gang of Jokerz, he found himself in the grounds of Wayne Manor. The old Bruce Wayne came out and fought beside him, then collapsed. Terry got him back into the house, and there he found his way into the cave beneath it.

That same night Terry's father, an engineer at Wayne-Powers, was murdered by Derek Powers's men. He had discovered that the company was making a nerve gas for use as a weapon. Terry took the last Batsuit Bruce Wayne had built and went after his father's killers. Wayne was angry at first. In time he came to accept the boy, and became his mentor.

Batman

The suit Terry wears is the most advanced of all the Batman suits. It is black, with a red bat across the chest. It multiplies his strength, glides on retractable wings, flies on rocket boots and can hide him from sight.

He patrols a Gotham of high towers and neon. Flying cars crowd the air, and gangs dressed in imitation of the long-dead Joker run the streets. Wayne watches from the cave and talks him through his cases, with a great black dog called Ace at his feet.

Terry brought down Derek Powers. Powers had been poisoned by his own nerve gas, and the radiation that saved his life turned him into the radioactive killer Blight.

Like the Batmen before him, Terry does not go about in daylight. He works with the Justice League, but he does not appear with it in public. The public knows only that Batman has been more than one man.

In the saga

Watching the news in August 1994, Harry Potter reflected that the Batman people talked about these days was black all over, with a red bat on his chest, and that he flew.

pages.title: Gotham
infobox: Towers, neon, flying traffic, Jokerz gangs
pages.html:
Gotham is the city on the American East Coast that has belonged to Batman since 1939. It has long been known for its corruption, its crime and its peculiar criminals. By 1993 it had become a city of high towers, neon and flying traffic, with gangs of Jokerz in its streets. At night the third Batman, Terry McGinnis, patrols it.

The old city

Gotham grew into one of the largest cities in the United States, with old money and grand buildings at the top of it. At the bottom were poverty and organised crime. The Waynes were one of its great families, and Wayne Manor stands just outside the city. For most of the century Gotham was notorious for corrupt police, mob rule and a run of costumed criminals unlike anywhere else, many of whom ended up in Arkham Asylum. The worst of them was the Joker, the clown-faced murderer who first appeared in 1940.

For many years the one honest man at the top of the city's police was Commissioner James Gordon, who worked with the first Batman. By the 1990s the commissioner was his daughter, Barbara Gordon.

Batman has worked in Gotham since 1939, always at night. Three men have worn the cowl, and the city has known all three, though never by name.

Gotham in the 1990s

By 1993 the old city had been built over and up. Its skyline is a crowd of towers lit in neon, with flying cars filling the air between them. The streets below belong to the gangs. The best known are the Jokerz, young people in clown paint who take their style from the Joker, though he is long dead. Wayne Enterprises has become Wayne-Powers. The city's Batman is Terry McGinnis. He wears a black suit with a red bat across the chest, and he flies.

In the saga

Nobody Harry Potter knows has yet been to Gotham. On 20 August 1994 Harry noticed that Batman was not with the Justice League at the United Nations, since Batman never went anywhere in daylight.

pages.title: Coast City
infobox: Home of Hal Jordan and Ferris Aircraft
Summer 1993, by Mongul's forces for the Cyborg Superman
pages.html:
Coast City was a Californian city of about seven million people, and the home of Hal Jordan, the Green Lantern. In the summer of 1993 Mongul's forces destroyed it, acting for the Cyborg Superman, who wore Superman's symbol and claimed his name. Where the city stood there is now a crater with a machine in it. ‘Remember Coast City’ has become a slogan against superhumans.

The city

Coast City lay on the Pacific coast of California, north of San Diego. It was an aviation town, the home of Ferris Aircraft, where the test pilot Hal Jordan was working when he received his Green Lantern ring in 1959. For thirty-four years it was Green Lantern's city, as Metropolis was Superman's.

Destruction

In the summer of 1993, while the world was still mourning Superman, the Cyborg Superman and his ally Mongul chose Coast City as the site of the first of their engines. Mongul's warship bombed the city out of existence with nearly everyone in it. The Cyborg Superman, wearing the S, hung in the sky above it while it was done. In the crater their machinery built Engine City, which was meant to be the first step in turning Earth into a new Warworld.

In August 1993 the real Superman, returned from the dead, fought them in the ruins with Hal Jordan, Steel, Superboy and Supergirl. The engine was stopped. Nothing could bring the city back. Hal Jordan had lost his home and everyone in it. He tried to use his ring to make Coast City again, and the reprimand that followed from his masters on Oa led to his fall at the turn of 1994.

Remember Coast City

The destruction of Coast City did more than anything else to turn public opinion against superhumans. Because the killer had looked like Superman, the survivors could no longer trust the real one. ‘Remember Coast City’ was among the slogans carried outside the United Nations in August 1994.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994 the Dursleys' television showed a big man in a baseball cap at the protest in New York, holding a photograph of his wife and two daughters. He had been in San Diego for work on the day. Driving back up the coast that night, he found ‘a hole, with a… with a machine in it’, where seven million people had lived. ‘The thing that did it was wearing the S,’ he said.

pages.title: Sydney Happersen
aliases: The man in the lab coat
the lunatic in a lab coat
infobox: The man in the lab coat; Dr Sydney Happersen
Firing the sonic torpedoes that flattened downtown Metropolis, May 1994
pages.html:
Dr Sydney Happersen was Lex Luthor's chief scientist and aide at LexCorp. He was the man in the lab coat who in May 1994 fired the sonic torpedoes that flattened downtown Metropolis, after Luthor himself had agreed not to. He died in Superman's arms moments later.

Life

Happersen worked for Lex Luthor from at least 1987. He was one of the scientists who did LexCorp's most secret work, and he saw to the details that Luthor did not want to know about.

Among them were the sonic torpedoes. Luthor had them reverse-engineered from the weapons left behind by the alien invasion of 1988, and buried beneath Metropolis as a last resort. For years Luthor treated Happersen with contempt, and Happersen took it.

May 1994

In May 1994 Superman cornered Luthor. Luthor's cloned body was failing, and his deceptions had been exposed. Superman asked him whether he really wanted Metropolis to remember him as the man who destroyed it, and Luthor agreed not to fire.

Happersen fired the torpedoes anyway. Superman and his allies stopped most of them. Those that got through flattened downtown Metropolis, the Daily Planet building among it.

Happersen died in Superman's arms. He alone had known exactly where all the torpedoes lay.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994 a protester in a suit, with a black eye, told the news outside the United Nations that Doomsday had knocked his building down in 1992. Then in May, he said, ‘some lunatic in a lab coat flattened downtown with torpedoes left over from the alien invasion. Nobody's even paying for it!’

pages.title: Thunderstrike
aliases: The blond Avenger with the mace
infobox: The blond Avenger with the mace; Eric Masterson; Eric Kevin Masterson
Human, empowered by an Asgardian mace
pages.html:
Thunderstrike is Eric Masterson, an American architect who once served as Thor and now carries an enchanted mace that Odin gave him. With Thor away fighting Asgard's war against the Replicators, the big blond man with the mace has taken his place among the Avengers. He stood with them at the United Nations in August 1994.

Thor's partner

Eric Masterson was a divorced architect in New York, with a young son called Kevin, when he first crossed paths with Thor in 1988. The following year he was mortally injured in one of Thor's battles. To save his life Thor merged with him, so that Masterson could change into Thor and back again.

In late 1991 Odin banished Thor himself. Masterson was given Thor's form, strength and hammer to serve in his place. For more than a year he was Thor, as well as an Avenger, in his own right.

The mace

When Thor came back at the end of 1992, Masterson gave up the hammer. Odin rewarded him with a mace of Asgardian make, called Thunderstrike, and Masterson took its name as well. When he strikes the mace he becomes a powerfully built, long-haired blond warrior with the strength and toughness of an Asgardian. He flies by hurling the mace and holding on to it. He can also draw blasts of energy from it.

Since Thor was called away to Asgard's war with the Replicators, Thunderstrike has stood among the Avengers in his place.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: on the news of 20 August 1994 Harry sees the Avengers at the United Nations, behind Superman. Compared with the Avengers on Dudley's old lunchbox, the man with the hammer has been replaced by a big blond man with a mace.

pages.title: War Machine
infobox: The Avenger in gunmetal armour; James Rhodes; Jim Rhodes; James Rupert Rhodes; Rhodey
Variable Threat Response Battle Suit (War Machine)
pages.html:
War Machine is James Rhodes, a former United States Marine and Tony Stark's oldest friend, who wears a heavy gunmetal armour bristling with guns. With Stark retired, Rhodes has taken the place of the red and gold Iron Man among the Avengers. He was with them at the United Nations on 19 August 1994, when the Security Council heard Superman.

Rhodes and Stark

James Rupert Rhodes grew up in Philadelphia. He flew helicopters for the Marines in Vietnam, and it was there that he met Tony Stark, who had just escaped from his captors in his first, crude armour. The two of them fought their way out of the jungle together. Afterwards Rhodes became Stark's personal pilot, and the closest friend Stark had.

In 1983 Stark went back to the bottle and lost control of his company. Rhodes put on the Iron Man armour himself and wore it for the next two years. Most of the world never knew that a different man was inside. It was Rhodes, as Iron Man, who was carried off to Battleworld with the other heroes in the Secret Wars of 1984. The same year he helped to found the West Coast Avengers. He gave the armour back to Stark in 1985.

War Machine

By 1992 Stark's nervous system was failing. He faked his own death that year and left Rhodes his company, together with a new suit he had built, heavier than anything he had worn himself. This was the Variable Threat Response Battle Suit, gunmetal grey and silver. It carried a rotary gun on one shoulder, a missile launcher on the other and weapons built into both forearms. Rhodes wore it under the name War Machine.

Stark came back early in 1993. Rhodes, who had mourned him, did not easily forgive being lied to, and he kept the armour. Stark has since retired, and Rhodes has taken his place among the Avengers.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: on the news Harry watched on Saturday 20 August 1994, the Avengers stood a little apart from the Justice League at the Security Council. Harry noticed that they looked nothing like the Avengers on Dudley's old lunchbox. The red and gold armour had been replaced by a heavier gunmetal suit bristling with guns, with a different man inside it.

pages.title: The Hulk
infobox: Hulk; Bruce Banner; Robert Bruce Banner; Joe Fixit
A gamma bomb test, New Mexico
pages.html:
The Hulk is the huge green creature that the physicist Bruce Banner turns into, a being of almost limitless strength whose rampages have left a long trail of wreckage across America. Few superhumans frighten ordinary people more. At the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994, somebody carried a sheet that read HULK KILLED MY DAD.

Origin

Dr Bruce Banner was a nuclear physicist, working on the gamma bomb for the American military at a desert base in New Mexico. During the test in 1962 a teenager, Rick Jones, drove on to the range. Banner ran out to pull him clear and was caught in the blast himself. That night he changed for the first time into a huge grey brute, and soon afterwards the creature turned green. At first the change came at nightfall. Later it came with anger, fear or pain, and the angrier the Hulk becomes, the stronger he gets.

General Thaddeus 'Thunderbolt' Ross, the commander of the base, spent years hunting the Hulk with the American army. All that time Banner was in love with the general's daughter, Betty.

History

The Hulk was one of the five founders of the Avengers in 1963, but he left within weeks, and for most of the time since he has been hunted rather than welcomed. He has taken many forms. There has been the savage, childlike green Hulk; for a few years in the early 1980s, a Hulk with Banner's own mind; a cunning grey Hulk who worked as a Las Vegas enforcer under the name of Joe Fixit; and, from 1991, a single Hulk in whom Banner's personalities had been merged.

In 1984 he was among the heroes taken to Battleworld in the Secret Wars. That summer the dream-demon Nightmare broke Banner's mind. The savage Hulk smashed his way across America to New York, where he fought the city's heroes, Thor among them, through the streets and across Central Park. A family's picnic was one of the things in his way. In the end Doctor Stephen Strange banished him to another dimension.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: at the protest outside the United Nations, shown on the news of 20 August 1994, somebody has painted a big green fist on a sheet, with HULK KILLED MY DAD in dripping black paint beneath it. A woman of about forty with dark red hair and green eyes, who reminds Harry of his mother, tells the camera what happened ten years before. On a Saturday in the summer of 1984 she was having a picnic in Central Park with Danny and Mikey when the Hulk came through the trees, fighting somebody she never identified. He was not even looking at them. He picked up a car and threw it. It landed on Danny and Mikey. Mikey was six, and wearing his new red shoes.

She breaks down. Then she screams that Khan is just the same as all the superhumans they want to send against him, and that they all need to be punished. Harry recognises the anger in her face as his own.

pages.title: The Sub-Mariner
infobox: The Invaders; the All-Winners Squad; later the Defenders and the Avengers
pages.html:
The Sub-Mariner is Namor, prince of the undersea kingdom of Atlantis and one of the earliest superhumans of the century. In 1940 he came out of the sea and tore up a street in New York. In 1941 he came back with the water behind him and flooded it. For more than half a century since he has been by turns the surface world's enemy and its ally. Nobody has ever been quite sure which to expect.

Birth and nature

Namor was born in 1920, the son of an American sea captain, Leonard McKenzie, and of Fen, a princess of the Atlanteans. They are a blue-skinned people who breathe water, and their kingdom lies under the Antarctic sea. Namor is a hybrid of the two races, and a mutant besides.

He can breathe both air and water. He is immensely strong, and he flies by means of small wings on his ankles. He ages far more slowly than an ordinary man, but his strength fades if he is kept too long out of the water. He grew up among his mother's people, who taught him to see the surface world as the enemy that was poisoning and plundering the sea.

New York and the war

Namor came to public notice in 1939. In 1940 he attacked New York itself, wrecking streets and fighting the android Human Torch in the skies above the city. In 1941 he came back with the sea behind him and flooded it.

Once America was in the war, he turned on the Axis instead. He fought beside Captain America and the Human Torch in the Invaders until 1945. In 1946 he was one of the All-Winners Squad.

Later years

Some time after the war he lost his memory and vanished. In 1962 Johnny Storm of the Fantastic Four found him living as a derelict in a flophouse on the Bowery, and restored his memory. He went home to find his kingdom in ruins, wrecked by the surface world's nuclear tests, and attacked the surface world again. Later, still in a temper, he came upon a block of Arctic ice that a band of Inuit were worshipping, and threw it into the sea. Inside it was Captain America. It drifted south to where the Avengers found him.

He has since ruled Atlantis. He has fought beside the Fantastic Four and the Avengers about as often as he has fought them. In 1971, with Doctor Stephen Strange and the Hulk, he formed the loose band called the Defenders. In 1985 he joined the Avengers. In the early 1990s, to the surprise of a good many people, he ran a business empire on the surface.

Namor holds that his kingdom is the true Atlantis, heir to the island that went down in the Cataclysm in the days of Kull, and he will not hear the same claim from Aquaman's people. Neither kingdom is the Atlantis of the old story, which was Númenor.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: at the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994, a small, upright old man in a cardigan, leaning on a stick, tells the camera that he was sixteen in 1940 when the first one came out of the sea. The Sub-Mariner, they called him. He tore up the old man's street and threw a fire engine through the front of the pharmacy. The next year he came back with the water, and the old man's father drowned on the steps going down to the trains. He ends by looking straight into the camera: 'I have watched them fight over my head for fifty-four years. Not one of them ever asked us. Not one. Not once.'

pages.title: Fantastic Four
infobox: Reed Richards, Susan Storm, Johnny Storm, Ben Grimm
The Baxter Building; later Four Freedoms Plaza, New York
Turning Galactus away from Earth, December 1965
pages.html:
The Fantastic Four are a family of four superhuman explorers and adventurers based in New York. They came to public notice in 1961, and they have never hidden who they are. They are remembered above all for the days just before Christmas 1965, when the sky over Manhattan caught fire because something had come to eat the world. The Fantastic Four, it was said, talked it out of it.

Origin

In 1961 the scientist Reed Richards took an experimental rocket into space without permission. With him went his fiancée Susan Storm, her teenage brother Johnny and his friend the pilot Ben Grimm. Cosmic rays poured through the ship's thin shielding. When they crashed back to Earth, each of them had changed.

Richards could stretch his body into any shape, and called himself Mister Fantastic. Sue, the Invisible Girl, could vanish from sight, and later learnt to throw up force fields that nobody could see. Johnny could burst into flame and fly, as the Human Torch. Grimm had become a huge, rock-skinned, enormously strong creature, the Thing, and he could not change back.

They decided to use their powers together. Unlike most of their kind they never wore masks. From their headquarters at the top of the Baxter Building in Manhattan, they became as much celebrities as heroes.

History

Their oldest enemy is Victor von Doom, Reed's rival at university, who first attacked them in 1962. That year they also found the Sub-Mariner living as a derelict in a Bowery flophouse, his memory gone. Giving it back to him had consequences for New York. Reed and Sue were married in 1965. Their son Franklin was born in 1968.

In December 1965 the Watcher, an alien observer sworn never to interfere, set the sky over Manhattan ablaze to hide the Earth from the Silver Surfer, the herald of Galactus. It did not work. Galactus came to devour the planet's energy. The sculptor Alicia Masters turned the Surfer against his master. Johnny Storm crossed the depths of Galactus's ship to bring back the Ultimate Nullifier, a weapon Galactus himself feared. With it in his hand, Reed persuaded Galactus to leave the Earth alone.

In 1984 Reed, Johnny and Ben were among the heroes carried off to Battleworld in the Secret Wars. There Ben found that he could change from one shape to the other at will. He stayed behind on Battleworld for a time, and She-Hulk took his place in the team. In 1987 the family moved into a new headquarters, Four Freedoms Plaza.

They have grown older in the ordinary way since that first flight. By 1994 Johnny Storm, the teenager of 1961, is a man in his late forties.

The family met the Inhumans in the autumn of 1965. Crystal served in the team from 1968 to 1970, and Medusa in 1973.

In late 1961 four Skrulls took the Fantastic Four's shapes to turn the public against them. Reed Richards sent their fleet home and turned the four into cows.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: at the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994, an old man in a cardigan tells the camera that just before Christmas in 1965 the sky caught fire over Manhattan, because something had come to eat the world. The Fantastic Four talked it out of it, they said. His wife had a heart attack on the second day. He has watched superhumans fight over his head for fifty-four years, he says, and not one of them ever asked.

pages.title: Justice Society

Disbanded after Zero Hour; its surviving members are elderly and retired

The Flash (Jay Garrick), Green Lantern (Alan Scott), the Atom (Al Pratt, killed in Zero Hour), Hawkman and Hawkgirl, Hourman (Rex Tyler, killed in Zero Hour), Doctor Mid-Nite (killed in Zero Hour), Starman (Ted Knight), the Sandman, Wildcat, Johnny Thunder
pages.html:
The Justice Society was the world's first association of costumed heroes, founded late in 1940 at the request of President Roosevelt. It fought through the Second World War, much of it within the President's All-Star Squadron. In 1951 it disbanded rather than unmask before a committee of Congress. Its members, whose ageing had been slowed by a wartime enemy's sorcery, came back to the work in the 1960s. They spent six years out of the world from 1986 and returned in 1992. In July 1994, during Zero Hour, the time-mad Extant took back the years its members had been spared since the war. Three of them died, and the rest were aged in moments to their true years. The survivors disbanded the Society, and by August 1994 the news remembers it chiefly as history.

Founding, 1940

Between 1938 and 1940 a great many masked, costumed adventurers appeared across America: the mystery men, as the papers called them. Superman had been the first, in 1938, and Batman had followed in Gotham in 1939. Most of the others worked alone in their own cities. The Justice Society was the first time a number of them agreed to work as one body.

Eight heroes founded it late in 1940. The Atom was Al Pratt, a college student of about twenty with no powers beyond his fists and his training. Doctor Fate was Kent Nelson, then thirty-two, a sorcerer brought up by the Babylonian Lord of Order Nabu after the tomb at Ur killed his father in 1920. The Flash was Jay Garrick, a student of about twenty who had gained his speed in a laboratory accident. Green Lantern was Alan Scott, a young railway engineer whose magic ring had been made from the metal of a mysterious green lantern.

Hawkman was Carter Hall, an archaeologist who fought with ancient weapons and a belt that let him fly. Hourman was Rex Tyler, a research chemist whose Miraclo pill gave him an hour of great strength. The Sandman was Wesley Dodds, a wealthy man who hunted criminals by night in a gas mask. The Spectre was Jim Corrigan, a police detective murdered by gangsters in 1940 and sent back as a spirit of vengeance.

They came together at the President's request. That autumn several of them, working separately, had broken a Nazi scheme to prepare an invasion of Britain. Franklin D. Roosevelt asked them to go on working together for the country's defence. The Flash was the Society's first chairman. Hawkman succeeded him in 1941, and he chaired it for most of the decade.

Superman and Batman, already the most famous of all, were made members as a mark of honour. They joined its cases when they were needed. From the start the Society kept a custom: a member who became famous enough to work on his own account gave up his full place and kept only his name on the roll. That way the places went to those who needed them most. The result was a line-up that changed constantly through the 1940s.

The war years, 1941 to 1945

In 1941 the Flash and Green Lantern gave up their full places in this way. Johnny Thunder joined that summer, a hapless young man who could summon a genie-like Thunderbolt with a word. At the turn of 1942 Hourman stepped back, and two new men came in. One was Doctor Mid-Nite, the blinded physician Charles McNider, who could see in the dark. The other was Starman, the astronomer Ted Knight, with his gravity rod.

Wonder Woman, the Amazon princess Diana, came to public notice late in 1941. In 1942 she became the Society's secretary, and soon afterwards a full member. Being an Amazon, she aged not at all.

After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, Roosevelt called every mystery man in the country into a single body for the duration of the war. This was the All-Star Squadron. It made its headquarters in the Perisphere, the great globe left standing on the grounds of the 1939 World's Fair at Flushing Meadows in New York. The Society's members served in it while keeping their own meetings and their own name. Among the Squadron's other members were Liberty Belle, Johnny Quick, Robotman, Firebrand and Commander Steel. Amazing-Man joined them in 1942. For a few months in 1942 the Society itself served as the Justice Battalion, an extension of the American armed forces.

The Society never carried the war into Europe in force. Adolf Hitler held the Spear of Destiny, the lance that pierced the side of Christ on the cross. With it he could bend to his will any hero of great power who entered the lands the Axis held, above all those touched by magic. Japan held the Holy Grail, to the same effect in the Pacific. So the Society's strongest members fought the war at home, on the seas and at the edges of occupied territory. Their enemies were saboteurs, spies and the Axis's own superhuman agents. Captain America and the Invaders went where the Squadron's mightiest could not, into occupied Europe.

Among the Society's enemies was the Dark witch Greta Grindelwald. Because of the Spear, its members who were touched by magic could not go into the Axis lands. The Society fought her only where her war spilt over those borders.

During the war the Society also fought the sorcerer Ian Karkull, a master of shadow and time. The energies released at his defeat soaked into its members, and into several of those closest to them. Nobody understood it for many years, but from then on they aged far more slowly than other people. Doctor Fate and his wife, Inza, were kept young besides by Nabu's own power.

The membership went on changing. The Spectre gave up his place. In 1945 the Flash and Green Lantern returned as full members. Mister Terrific (Terry Sloane) and Wildcat (the heavyweight boxer Ted Grant) fought beside the Society in the war years. The Squadron did not outlast the peace, but the Society did.

The last years, 1945 to 1951

After the war the Society carried on as a band of friends who answered the call when it came. In 1947 it first met the Injustice Society, a union of its own worst enemies. The same year it had help from Black Canary, a young Gotham florist named Dinah Drake who fought crime in fishnet and leather. In 1948 she became a member. Wonder Woman remained its secretary.

In 1951 the Society was summoned before the Joint Un-American Activities Committee, a committee of both houses of Congress. Under Senator O'Fallon, the committee asked its members to unmask, so that their names could be cleared of suspicion. They refused. Nearly every member retired immediately afterwards, and the Society disbanded.

Most of the founders were then men in their thirties and forties. The heroes who had always worked alone, among them Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman, carried on through the 1950s. The Society as a body was finished.

The 1950s

Through the 1950s the Society's members lived as private citizens. Jay Garrick married Joan Williams. Alan Scott ran a broadcasting company in Gotham. Carter Hall married Shiera Sanders, Hawkgirl, who had fought beside him since 1941. Rex Tyler ran his chemical company. Dinah Drake married the detective Larry Lance, and their daughter, Dinah Laurel, would one day take up her mother's name.

In the second half of the decade a new generation of heroes appeared. The Martian Manhunter came to Earth in 1955. In 1956 Barry Allen, a Central City police scientist who had read about Jay Garrick as a boy, gained the same speed. He took the name of the Flash in Jay's honour. In 1959 Hal Jordan received a power ring of the Green Lantern Corps, a different thing altogether from Alan Scott's. At the turn of 1960 seven heroes founded the Justice League, the Society's successor in all but name.

The return, 1961 to 1985

In 1961 Barry Allen sought out Jay Garrick in Keystone City, and the two Flashes fought side by side. The meeting drew Jay and several of his old colleagues back into action. In 1963 the Society re-formed. Its members were in their forties and fifties by then. Karkull's energies, though, had left them looking and moving like much younger people.

From 1963 the Society and the Justice League joined forces nearly every summer. The custom lasted more than twenty years. Some of the Society's names had passed to younger heroes in the meantime. Besides the new Flash and the new Green Lantern, there was a new Atom, Ray Palmer, from 1961. There was a new Hawkman too, Katar Hol of the planet Thanagar, so the joint cases often had two men of the same name side by side. In 1969 Dinah Drake's daughter joined the League as the new Black Canary.

In the mid-1970s younger heroes joined the Society itself, among them Power Girl and the Star-Spangled Kid, Sylvester Pemberton. In 1979 Mister Terrific was murdered during one of the summer cases with the League. He was the first of the wartime heroes to die in action since the Society re-formed. In 1983 the Society's children and heirs formed a team of their own, Infinity Inc. Alan Scott's twins, Obsidian and Jade, were among them. So was the Halls' son Hector, the Silver Scarab.

The Crisis and Ragnarok, 1985 to 1992

The Society fought through the Crisis of 1985 to 1986. The skies of the world turned red, and Barry Allen, the Flash who had brought the Society back together, was killed. Like everybody who was there, its members do not agree about what they saw.

In 1986 most of them left the world altogether. Eleven of them passed into a realm outside time. There they fought the battle of Ragnarok, the twilight of the gods of the north, over and over without end, so that it would not break out upon the Earth. They were the Atom, Doctor Mid-Nite, the Flash, Green Lantern, Hawkman, Hawkgirl, Hourman, Johnny Thunder, the Sandman, Starman and Wildcat. Doctor Fate, the Spectre, Power Girl and the Star-Spangled Kid stayed behind.

So the Society was absent in the winter of 1986 to 1987, when President Reagan grounded every costumed hero in America. It was absent, too, for the founding of the new Justice League in 1987, which Doctor Fate joined. Kent Nelson's long service ended that year. The helmet of Fate passed to others until he and Inza returned to life in younger bodies in 1991.

In 1992 the absent members were brought home, and others were sent to take their places in the endless battle.

The last stand, 1992 to 1994

On their return the members took up the work again as a team. They were Jay Garrick, Alan Scott, Al Pratt, Rex Tyler, Charles McNider, Ted Knight, Ted Grant, Wesley Dodds and Johnny Thunder. Carter Hall came back with them, and so did his wife, Shiera.

Most of them had been in their twenties or thirties in 1940. By 1994 they were in their seventies and eighties; Jay Garrick was about seventy-four. They still fought like people half their age. Through 1992 and into 1993 they often acted together.

In July 1994 time itself broke down in the catastrophe called Zero Hour. At Vanishing Point, beyond the end of time, the Society made its last stand against the time-mad Extant. He took back the years that Ian Karkull's energies had held off since the war. The Atom (Al Pratt), Hourman (Rex Tyler) and Doctor Mid-Nite (Charles McNider) died of it. Jay Garrick, Ted Knight, Wesley Dodds, Johnny Thunder and Ted Grant were aged in moments to their true years. Ted Grant suffered a heart attack. Kent Nelson and his wife, Inza, were aged to their true years. Both were torn from the power of Fate. Carter and Shiera Hall were merged into a single being. Only Alan Scott, whose ring held, came through unchanged.

When time was begun again early in August, the survivors were old in body as well as in years. They agreed that the Society's day was done, and they disbanded it. It had no part in the joint statement of the Avengers and the League on the Augment War, nor in Superman's appeal to the Security Council that month. On the news its name came up only as history, as the first time a government had tried to rein in its heroes.

The Society and the world

No team of heroes was ever closer to the government of the day than the Justice Society in its first years. It was formed at Roosevelt's request. It served the war effort as the Justice Battalion, and its members made up the core of the All-Star Squadron, the President's own wartime gathering of every mystery man in the land. It worked with the armed forces and the federal police. It spent the war hunting fifth columnists, saboteurs and Axis agents on American soil.

The limits of what it could do were set by the Spear of Destiny. Hitler held the Spear, and Japan the Grail. So the war that Americans fought overseas was fought by ordinary soldiers and a few heroes such as the Invaders, while the most powerful beings on Earth spent it on the home front. It is the reason the Second World War was not ended in a week, and the reason it was won at the cost it was.

The Society also met the war's ugliness at home. In February 1942 the Squadron was sent to Detroit to head off violence at the opening of the Sojourner Truth Homes, a housing project built for Black war workers. A white mob had gathered there against the new tenants. The Squadron found the anger being stirred up by an agitator who called himself the Real American. Afterwards Will Everett, the Black athlete known as Amazing-Man, joined the Squadron, so that America would see Black and white heroes standing together.

The Society's end belongs to the years after the war. Committees of Congress searched Hollywood, the universities and the government for communists, while Senator Joseph McCarthy made a career of accusation. In 1951 the Joint Un-American Activities Committee demanded that the Society's members unmask. They would not, and they gave up the work instead. It was the first time a government tried to bring costumed heroes to heel.

It was not the last. In 1986 President Reagan grounded every costumed hero in America for a winter, and in 1994 the United Nations suspended the Justice League's charter. The Society's own members were absent for the second of these, and they played no part in the third. By 1994 they are a living link to the war and to the Roosevelt years. The pollsters' rising hostility to metahumans, as the word now is, has seldom touched them.

Line-ups

Founding line-up, 1940: the Atom (Al Pratt), Doctor Fate (Kent Nelson), the Flash (Jay Garrick), Green Lantern (Alan Scott), Hawkman (Carter Hall), Hourman (Rex Tyler), the Sandman (Wesley Dodds) and the Spectre (Jim Corrigan). Superman and Batman were made members as a mark of honour.

The war years, 1941 to 1945: Johnny Thunder joined in 1941. Doctor Mid-Nite and Starman followed at the turn of 1942. Wonder Woman became secretary in 1942, then a full member, and Hawkgirl served too. The Flash, Green Lantern and Hourman stepped back for a time, keeping only their names on the roll. The Flash and Green Lantern returned as full members in 1945. Mister Terrific and Wildcat fought beside them. All of them served in the All-Star Squadron.

1948 to 1951: the line-up of the last years, with Black Canary (Dinah Drake) a member from 1948. The Society disbanded in 1951.

From 1963: the surviving founders and wartime members re-formed the Society. Power Girl and the Star-Spangled Kid joined them in the mid-1970s.

1992 to 1994: the Flash (Jay Garrick), Green Lantern (Alan Scott), the Atom (Al Pratt), Hawkman, Hawkgirl, Hourman (Rex Tyler), Doctor Mid-Nite (Charles McNider), Starman (Ted Knight), the Sandman (Wesley Dodds), Wildcat (Ted Grant) and Johnny Thunder.

Deaths, retirements and successors: Jim Corrigan was already dead when he joined. The Spectre still walks. Mister Terrific was murdered in 1979. Extant killed the Atom (Al Pratt), Hourman (Rex Tyler) and Doctor Mid-Nite (Charles McNider) in Zero Hour in July 1994. The Society disbanded after it. Kent Nelson was struck down in 1987. The helmet passed to Eric and Linda Strauss. After the Nelsons' return in 1991 it passed to Inza Nelson. By 1993 it had fallen asleep.

The name of the Flash passed to Barry Allen in 1956 and to Wally West in 1985, though Jay Garrick never gave it up. The name of Green Lantern was taken in 1959 by Hal Jordan of the Corps, whose ring had nothing to do with Alan Scott's. Younger men took the names of the Atom and Hawkman in 1961. Dinah Drake's daughter took the name of Black Canary. Wonder Woman left for the Justice League, which she helped to found at the turn of 1960. She serves in it under Superman in 1994.

In the saga

On Saturday 20 August 1994 the news on the Dursleys' television reported Superman's appeal to the Security Council and the suspension of the Justice League's charter. Then the newsreader observed that this was not the first time governments had tried to rein in superhumans. In 1951, she said, the Justice Society had disbanded rather than unmask before a committee of Congress. In 1986 President Reagan had grounded every costumed hero in America for an entire winter.

pages.title: Wolverine
infobox: Logan; James Howlett; Patch; Weapon Ten
pages.html:
Wolverine, who calls himself Logan, is a Canadian mutant with a healing power so strong that he has lived for about a century without growing old. Long claws spring from the backs of his hands. He was the subject of Weapon X, the tenth attempt of the Weapon programme, which laced his skeleton with unbreakable metal. When he first came to public notice in 1974 he was already a very old man, though nobody looking at him would have guessed it.

The long life

He was born James Howlett in Alberta in the late nineteenth century, the sickly son of a wealthy family. His powers first showed on the night he saw his father murdered. He ran away and took the name Logan. For most of the next hundred years he lived as a frontiersman, a soldier, a spy and a mercenary. He fought in both world wars, meeting Captain America in 1941 along the way, and lived for a time in Japan. Canadian and American intelligence both made use of him. Most of this is hidden even from him, because his memories were later tampered with and replaced.

His mutation heals almost any wound in moments. It shields him from poison and disease, as well as slowing his ageing almost to nothing. He has the senses of an animal and, since boyhood, three bone claws in each forearm.

Weapon X

Some time before 1974 Logan was taken into Weapon X, the tenth project of the long, secret super-soldier programme whose first success had been Captain America. At a facility in the Canadian Rockies its scientists bonded adamantium, an almost indestructible metal, to his whole skeleton and his claws. They wiped his memory and wrote him a new one, to make him a killer they could control. He broke out, killing many of his captors, and ran wild in the woods. It was the Hudsons, James and Heather, who found him there. They brought him back to himself.

He went to work for Department H, a branch of the Canadian government. He came to public notice in 1974, when he was sent against the Hulk and a Wendigo in the Canadian wilderness. In 1975 Professor Charles Xavier recruited him into the new X-Men, and he has been the team's most famous member ever since, as well as its most troublesome.

Avalon, 1993

In August 1993, after Magneto's global blackout, the X-Men went up to his space station, Avalon. There Wolverine very nearly gutted Magneto, who in his rage tore the adamantium out of Wolverine's body. Only the healing power kept him alive. That was how he learnt that his claws had been his own bone all along. Soon afterwards he left the X-Men to recover alone.

pages.title: Sentinels
infobox: About three times that of a man
Mothballed; a proposal to revive them is before the Senate
pages.html:
The Sentinels are giant robots, three times the height of a man, with blank metal faces and glowing eyes. They were built to find and detain mutants inside the United States. The world first saw them in 1965, when two of them smashed into a television studio in the middle of a debate. After a series of incidents in the 1980s they were mothballed. In August 1994 a proposal to revive them and send them against Khan came before the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Trask's Sentinels

The first Sentinels were the work of the anthropologist Dr Bolivar Trask, who believed that mutants would one day enslave ordinary humanity. In 1965 he went on television to warn the public, in a debate with Professor Charles Xavier, and unveiled his robots to prove that humanity could defend itself. They broke into the studio and carried people off. Before the year was out the Sentinels and the Master Mold, the great machine that built them, had decided that the surest way to protect humanity from mutants was to rule it. Trask died destroying the Master Mold.

Sentinels can fly, and they are programmed to detect the mutant gene. They are armed with beams, restraints and gas. Each generation has learnt from the last.

Later generations

In 1969 Trask's son Larry built a second generation. More were built in the 1970s for a private programme under the scientist Stephen Lang. Others followed in the early 1980s, made by the industrialist Sebastian Shaw for a government programme concerned with mutants. The most advanced of them all, Nimrod, appeared in the mid-1980s.

Most Sentinels have been painted purple and blue. They hunt as readily by night, with searchlights, as by day. The incidents of the 1980s led to the programme being mothballed.

The 1994 proposal

After the failure of the spring campaign in India, supporters of the programme argued in 1994 that a new generation of Sentinels could be sent against Khan's forces without risking American lives. Critics pointed out that the machines had been built for quite a different purpose: to find and detain mutants, at home. Mutant rights groups called the proposal a licence to hunt. The Pentagon, which was still paying for the Indian campaign, would not say where the money was to come from. The White House said that no decision had been taken.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: the Muggle news of 20 August 1994 reports that the Senate Armed Services Committee will hear evidence the following week on reviving the Sentinel programme. It shows juddering film in black and white from 1965 of a bald man in a wheelchair arguing politely with a big, fierce man in a suit. Then a robot smashes through the back wall of the studio, with a second behind it. One of them reaches down, quite slowly, and picks up a running man the way Dudley might pick up a toy soldier. Newer film, in colour, shows a purple and blue Sentinel flying low over a small town at night, sweeping a white beam across the streets while people throw themselves into doorways.

Harry goes cold. He wonders what a machine built to hunt down people born with powers would make of a wizard, especially the sort who shouts into a telephone, and decides it would pick him up before he got his wand out.

pages.title: Professor X
aliases: The bald man in the wheelchair
infobox: The bald man in the wheelchair; Charles Xavier; Charles Francis Xavier; Professor Xavier; Professor Charles Xavier
Xavier's School for Gifted Youngsters; the X-Men (1963)
pages.html:
Professor X is Charles Xavier, the bald telepath in the wheelchair who founded the X-Men. He has spent his life arguing that mutants and ordinary people can live together in peace. In 1965 he was putting exactly that case, politely, to Dr Bolivar Trask in a television studio, when Trask's Sentinels smashed through the wall.

Early life

Charles Francis Xavier was born in the early 1930s to a rich family in Westchester County, New York. His father, a nuclear researcher, died when Charles was a boy. His mother then married his father's colleague, Kurt Marko, whose son, Cain, bullied Charles without mercy and grew up to be the unstoppable Juggernaut. Charles's telepathy showed itself in childhood, and his hair had all fallen out while he was still young.

He served as a soldier in Korea and afterwards studied genetics. In the 1950s, in a hospital in Haifa, he made friends with a survivor of the death camps, Erik Lehnsherr, who would become Magneto. The friendship broke over the question that has shaped both their lives ever since: whether mutants should make peace with humanity or rule it. Some years later, in the Himalayas, an alien would-be conqueror brought a block of stone down on him. He lost the use of his legs, and has used a wheelchair ever since.

The dream

In 1963 Xavier opened his School for Gifted Youngsters in the family mansion, and made his first pupils into the X-Men. He has led them ever since against Magneto and every other threat to his hope of peace. He does it with his own telepathy, and with Cerebro, the machine that magnifies it so that he can find mutants wherever they are.

In the mid-1980s, badly hurt, he left Earth for several years with Lilandra, the ruler of the alien Shi'ar Empire, to recover. He put his school in Magneto's charge, which astonished nearly everyone who knew them both. He came back in 1991.

While he was away, Deathbird seized Lilandra's throne. He helped Lilandra fight for it until 1991.

In August 1993, after Magneto's blackout, Xavier went up with the X-Men to the space station Avalon. He ended the battle there by going into his old friend's mind and shutting it down, leaving him in a coma.

At the end of 1992 Stryfe shot Xavier with a techno-organic virus, and Apocalypse cured him.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: the Muggle news of 20 August 1994 shows juddering film in black and white of a television studio in 1965. In it a bald man in a wheelchair argues politely with a big, fierce man in a suit, until a giant robot smashes through the back wall. A second follows it.

pages.title: Bolivar Trask
aliases: The big fierce man in the suit
infobox: The big fierce man in the suit; Dr Bolivar Trask; Trask
pages.html:
Dr Bolivar Trask was the American anthropologist who designed the Sentinels, the giant robots built to hunt mutants. In 1965, while debating Professor Charles Xavier on live television, he unveiled them, and two of them smashed through the studio wall. Before the year was out his machines had turned on the humanity they were meant to protect. Trask died destroying them.

Life

Trask was a respected anthropologist, a big, forceful man. He became convinced that mutants were a new species, and that sooner or later they would enslave ordinary humanity. In 1965 he took his warning to the public on television, in a debate with Professor Charles Xavier. To prove that humanity could defend itself, he revealed the Sentinels he had secretly built. The robots broke into the studio and seized people in front of the cameras.

Trask had given the Sentinels, and the great machine that built them, the Master Mold, a single duty: to protect mankind from mutants. They decided that the surest way to do it was to rule mankind themselves, and they made Trask their prisoner. Seeing at last what he had done, he destroyed the Master Mold late in 1965 and died in the explosion.
