Catherine Langford recruited Daniel Jackson, a young Egyptologist whose career had just collapsed, to read the cover stones. He saw that the symbols on the gate were constellations, and he identified the missing seventh symbol. The gate opened on to Abydos, a desert world where Ra still ruled a people taken from Egypt thousands of years before.

A team under Colonel Jack O'Neill went through, with orders to destroy the gate with a nuclear device if they found a threat. Ra was killed when the bomb was sent up to his ship. Jackson stayed on Abydos with the wife he had married there. On Earth he was declared dead after what was announced as an accident in a shaft near Giza.

Later history

The gate did not stay quiet for long. In 1997 the Goa'uld came back through it, and the programme was reopened, this time with teams sent out to other worlds. The best known of them was SG-1. From then on Earth's struggle with the Goa'uld was fought by Muggle soldiers and scholars, through a gate found in Egypt.

It was Apophis who came. He had been taking over Ra's domains since Ra's death, he knew that Earth had killed Ra, and he had heard that Thor was busy elsewhere. His Jaffa killed the soldiers guarding the gate and carried one of them off.

In 1939 Ba'al, come back from 2008, tried to keep the gate from reaching America; Cameron Mitchell shot him aboard the ship that carried it, the Achilles.

In the saga

The gate has not been named in the saga. The Muggle news of 20 August 1994 (Book Four, Chapter Three) reported Daniel Jackson's death beneath the Giza plateau and said nothing more. The wizarding world knows nothing of the gate. The Ministry of Magic believes that 'those parasite creatures' will not be bothering it again (Book Three, Chapter Ten). It did not notice when they came back.

pages.title: Ra
infobox: The Abydos expedition of Jack O'Neill and Daniel Jackson
pages.html:
Ra was the greatest of the Goa'uld, the Supreme System Lord, who ruled Egypt as its sun god thousands of years ago. His slaves rose against him and drove him off Earth, but he kept his hold on Abydos. In 1994 he was destroyed above Abydos by the first American expedition through the Stargate.

Ruler of Egypt

Ra came to Earth in the remote past and took a human host, a young boy, whose body he kept youthful for thousands of years in the sarcophagus. Egypt was his seat. He ruled it as a god, with guards in the masks of Horus and Anubis. He came and went in a great pyramid-shaped ship. The pyramids were built in the likeness of its landing places. Through the gate at Giza he took Egyptians to other worlds as slaves.

The people of Egypt rose against him at last, and Ra fled. They buried his Stargate under the sand, with cover stones declaring it sealed and buried for all time. There it lay until Professor Paul Langford's expedition dug it up in 1928.

When the people of Egypt rose against him, Thor, the son of Odin, came down in a storm to fight beside them. He broke Ra's guards and struck Ra's ship with lightning as it rose from the desert. Ra never forgave the Egyptians or Thor, and he could not bear to have it spoken of. He forbade any Goa'uld to mention Earth again, and the System Lords have kept the ban.

Lord of the System Lords

Away from Earth Ra remained the foremost of the System Lords, the ruling council of the Goa'uld, and the others feared him. Hathor was his queen, and Heru'ur was their son. On Abydos his slaves mined naquadah for him. They were forbidden to read or write, so that they would not remember where they had come from.

Death

In 1994 an expedition from Earth came through the gate to Abydos under Colonel Jack O'Neill, with Daniel Jackson to read the inscriptions. Ra seized their nuclear device. He meant to send it back to Earth through the gate, with its power magnified by naquadah. The Abydonians rose against his guards. O'Neill and Jackson sent the armed bomb up to his ship through the transport rings. Ra tried to escape into orbit and was destroyed with his ship.

His death left a gap at the head of the System Lords, and others hurried to fill it.

Apophis was the quickest. With Ra gone there was nobody left to enforce his ban on Earth, and in 1997 Apophis came through the gate to Earth himself.

In the saga

Ra has not appeared or been named in the saga. The Abydos mission against him took place in 1994, the year in which Book Four begins. Egypt, where the Weasleys spent the summer of 1993, was his old seat. It is one of several reasons why Egypt has never been quite as innocent a place for a holiday as it looks.

pages.title: Jack O'Neill
infobox: Blackjack; Jack Blackjack O'Neill; Jack 'Blackjack' O'Neill; Colonel Jonathan O'Neill
United States Air Force, special operations
pages.html:
Colonel Jack 'Blackjack' O'Neill is a United States Air Force special-operations officer. Minerva McGonagall mentored him in the 1980s, and he has been her close friend ever since. He has never known that she is a witch. In 1994 he led the expedition through the Stargate to Abydos, and learnt the hard way that the Goa'uld exist.

Career

O'Neill made his name in covert special operations for the Air Force, the kind of work that is never reported, and he earned the nickname Blackjack. He is dry, impatient with officialdom and quicker than he lets anyone see. He is fiercely loyal to the men under him.

He married Sara, and they had a son, Charlie. Shortly before the Abydos mission Charlie shot himself by accident with his father's pistol. O'Neill blamed himself. His marriage broke under it. He had retired from the service, with no wish to go on living, when the Air Force called him back.

McGonagall

On one of her sabbaticals from Hogwarts in the 1980s, Minerva McGonagall's work as an Unspeakable put her alongside O'Neill, and she mentored him. Whatever she taught him, she taught in Muggle terms. He never knew that she was a witch, or that a magical world exists.

They are still close friends, and they still write to each other. Neither can tell the other anything about their work, or in practice about their lives. Theirs is a friendship conducted round two large silences. He knows that she cannot talk. He has no idea how much. He is one of the 'great many friends in the Muggle world' that Molly Weasley meant when she said that she knew where McGonagall had been and who she knew.

O'Neill was not with McGonagall when she confronted a Goa'uld symbiote and its host. That was Big Boss. O'Neill knew nothing of the Goa'uld until 1994. By then McGonagall had killed one and kept it over her fire. She could not tell him.

Abydos

In 1994 O'Neill was given command of the first team through the Stargate. Daniel Jackson went with them to read the symbols, and O'Neill carried secret orders to destroy the gate with a nuclear device if they met a threat. On Abydos he found Ra and his Jaffa guards. He also found Skaara, a boy of the Abydonians, who attached himself to O'Neill. Without either of them quite intending it, Skaara taught him to want to live again.

With Jackson he sent the armed bomb up to Ra's ship, and the Goa'uld died in orbit. O'Neill brought the survivors home and left Jackson on Abydos. In his report he said that Jackson was dead and that the gate on Abydos had been destroyed. Neither was true.

Later years

In 1997 the Goa'uld came back through the gate. O'Neill was recalled to command SG-1, the team that carried the war to them across the galaxy.

It was Apophis, who had been taking Ra's place among the System Lords since O'Neill killed Ra. On Abydos he took Skaara, the boy who had taught O'Neill to want to live again, as a host for his son.

In 2002 Ba'al tortured him to death many times over, reviving him each time in the sarcophagus.

In the saga

O'Neill has not appeared or been named in the saga. McGonagall's letters to him run on through the years of Harry's schooling. So in 1994 she is writing to a man in mourning for his son, about none of the things that matter to either of them.

pages.title: James Bond
infobox: Bond; John Mason; John Patrick Mason; 007
Casino Royale (novel, 13 April 1953); on screen in Dr. No (5 October 1962); as John Mason in The Rock (7 June 1996)
MI6, agent 007; former SAS captain as Mason
Wolfburg Penitentiary, in isolation, without trial
1996, to lead a team back into Alcatraz
pages.html:
James Bond is a Scottish agent of MI6, codenamed 007. From 1960 to 1962 he had a romance with Minerva McGonagall, which ended when she found out how much he had lied to her. Under the name of John Patrick Mason he is also the only man ever to escape from Alcatraz. He has been held in isolation at Wolfburg Penitentiary, without trial, since the mid-1980s, which covers all of Harry's years at Hogwarts so far. He was not brought out until 1996.

McGonagall

From 1960 to 1962, before she began teaching, Minerva McGonagall worked alongside Bond and had a romance with him. Once he needed a great deal of gold to go missing in a hurry, and she turned a vault's worth of it into beetles for him. He had a way of asking, she said, that one found hard to refuse. She ended the affair when she discovered that he had lied to her about a great many things. She has never forgotten the lying.

They kept in touch after the break until late in 1962, when he went undercover as John Mason and was locked up on Alcatraz. Her contact with him ended there.

John Mason and Alcatraz

In late 1962, as John Mason, a former SAS captain trained by MI6, Bond stole the microfilm on which J. Edgar Hoover kept the secrets of the American establishment. He was caught. He refused to say where he had hidden it, and he was sent to Alcatraz without trial. Early in 1963, before the prison closed on 21 March, he escaped from it, the only man ever to do so. The United States government has claimed him ever since.

Active service

His missions as 007 fall on these dates. On Crab Key, off Jamaica, he destroyed Dr Julius No, an agent of SPECTRE who had been toppling American rockets (5 October 1962). He brought the Soviet cipher clerk Tatiana Romanova and the Lektor decoding machine out of Istanbul on the Orient Express, past SPECTRE's assassins (10 October 1963). He stopped Auric Goldfinger's attempt to irradiate the gold at Fort Knox (17 September 1964). Off Nassau he recovered two atomic bombs that SPECTRE's Emilio Largo had stolen from a NATO bomber (9 December 1965). In Japan he found the base inside a volcano from which Ernst Stavro Blofeld's SPECTRE had been stealing American and Soviet spacecraft (12 June 1967). He followed a diamond-smuggling ring through Las Vegas to Blofeld, and to the laser satellite the diamonds had been gathered to build (17 December 1971).

After December 1971 he was recaptured as Mason and sent to San Quentin, from which he escaped in February 1976. In 1983, older and long thought past it, he was called back to recover two cruise missiles stolen by SPECTRE (7 October 1983).

Wolfburg

After 1983 he was recaptured once more. He has been held ever since in isolation at Wolfburg Penitentiary, without trial, the government's prisoner on and off for more than thirty years.

In 1996 renegade Marines under General Francis Hummel seized Alcatraz, threatening San Francisco with rockets of VX gas. Bond was brought out of Wolfburg to take a team back in, as the only man who had ever found a way off the island.

In the saga

Book Two, Chapter Seven: while Harry was trying to turn a beetle into a button, McGonagall told the class that she had once turned a vault's worth of gold into beetles, a very long time ago. When Seamus Finnigan asked why, she said it had been for a gentleman she was working alongside: 'A Muggle. Scottish. He had a desk at a very dull-sounding office near the river, though he was seldom at it.' She had not heard from him in a good many years. She expected, she said, that he had retired somewhere warm and was lying about it. Something like fondness crossed her face.

Book Two, Chapter Fifteen: when Gilderoy Lockhart took the credit for shutting the Chamber, McGonagall said nothing whatever. Her nostrils went very thin as she thought about what she had done to 'that charming MI6 agent who so brazenly lied to her face for the last and very final time'.

Through all of Harry's years at Hogwarts so far, Bond has been a prisoner at Wolfburg, a long way from anywhere warm.

pages.title: Alcatraz
pages.html:
Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay, which from 1934 to 1963 held the most secure federal prison in the United States. Only one man ever escaped from it: John Mason, early in 1963.

The Rock

The island lies more than a mile from the shore, in cold water with fierce currents. It held the most troublesome men in the federal system, Al Capone among them. It was costly to run, and the prison closed on 21 March 1963.

John Mason

Mason, a former SAS captain trained by MI6, was in truth James Bond. In late 1962 he stole the microfilm on which J. Edgar Hoover kept the secrets of the American establishment. He would not say where he had hidden it, so he was sent to Alcatraz without trial. Early in 1963, weeks before the prison closed, he escaped.

In 1996 renegade Marines under General Francis Hummel seized the island, threatening San Francisco with rockets of VX gas. Mason, as the only man who had ever found a way off it, was brought out of prison to take a team back in.

pages.title: San Quentin
infobox: Point San Quentin, Marin County, California
pages.html:
San Quentin is the oldest prison in California, on Point San Quentin at the edge of San Francisco Bay, north of the city. James Bond, the British agent, was held there under the name of John Mason in the 1970s, until he broke out in February 1976.

John Mason

The prison opened in 1852 and keeps the state's condemned men. The Americans had wanted Mason back ever since 1963, when he became the only man ever to escape from Alcatraz. After December 1971 they caught him again and sent him to San Quentin. In February 1976 he escaped from there too.

pages.title: Wolfburg Penitentiary
infobox: John Patrick Mason (James Bond), in isolation since the mid-1980s
pages.html:
Wolfburg Penitentiary is an American federal prison. Since the mid-1980s it has held John Patrick Mason in isolation, without trial. Mason is the only man ever to escape from Alcatraz, and he is in truth James Bond of MI6.

Its prisoner

Mason was first locked up without trial on Alcatraz in 1962, for stealing the microfilm of J. Edgar Hoover's secret files, and escaped from it in 1963. In the 1970s he was recaptured and sent to San Quentin. He broke out in February 1976. After 1983 he was taken once more, and this time he was sent to Wolfburg. By 1994 the American government had held him, or hunted him, for more than thirty years without once bringing him to trial.

He came out in 1996, when renegade Marines seized Alcatraz. The government needed the only man who had ever found a way off the island.

pages.title: Saint Peter
infobox: Peter; Simon Peter; Simon son of Jonah; Cephas
Fisherman, of the lake of Galilee
Crucified at Rome under Nero, by tradition
pages.html:
Saint Peter was a fisherman of Galilee who became the chief of Christ's apostles. In June 1994 the Fat Friar told Harry Potter the story of Peter's walk on the water. It is the key to how Harry's Patronus killed dementors: Peter walked on the water until he looked down.

Life

Simon, son of Jonah, was fishing on the lake of Galilee with his brother Andrew when Jesus called the two of them to follow him. He would make them, he said, fishers of men. Christ named Simon Cephas: Peter, the rock. Upon that rock, he said, he would build his church. He gave Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

One night in a storm the disciples saw Christ walking towards their boat on the water. Peter asked to come to him. He climbed out of the boat. He walked on the water towards Christ until he saw the wind and the waves. Then he was afraid. He began to sink, and Christ caught him by the hand: 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?'

It was Peter who first confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God. It was Peter, too, who asked how often he must forgive his brother, to be told 'until seventy times seven'.

On the night of the betrayal he denied Christ three times before the cock crowed, and wept bitterly. After the resurrection Christ asked him three times whether he loved him. Each time Peter said yes, and Christ told him to feed his sheep. Peter led the apostles after Pentecost. By tradition he was crucified at Rome under Nero, head downwards, at his own request.

In the saga

In January 1994, standing by the frozen lake with Dracina Malfoy, Harry watched a small Hufflepuff walk far out across the ice as though it were a floor. Then he looked down, and went straight through. The boy who hauled him out said, 'You were fine till you looked down.'

In March Lupin told Harry the seventy-times-seven story without naming either party. He said he would very much like Harry to go looking for where it was written down.

In June 1994 Harry's stag Patronus crossed the lake as though the lake were a floor. The next day the Fat Friar told him the story of Peter on the water. Harry, the Friar said, had stopped looking down. When Harry asked whether the Hufflepuff on the ice had been a sign meant for him, the Friar laughed: God does not often speak so clearly. Then he told Harry that wondering whether he was too thick to hear it was the very doubt that made Peter sink.

pages.title: Dark Mark
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Death Eaters, Severus Snape and Lucius Malfoy among them
pages.html:
The Dark Mark is the sign of Lord Voldemort, burnt into the left forearm of each of his Death Eaters. It is horrific dark magic. It links whoever bears it directly to Voldemort himself.

The bearers

Severus Snape bears the Mark, and so does Lucius Malfoy. To Remus Lupin, who is a Garou, it reeks of the Wyrm. Every instinct he has tells him to take his war form and tear Snape apart. Only the Wolfsbane Potion lets him stand in the same room.

Lucius knows that his own Mark will compel him to fight Harry Potter on his master’s behalf, and that this will hurt his daughter. It is the real reason he stands against anything between Dracina and Harry, though the boy has grown on him more than he will ever admit. Dracina believes that her father simply disapproves of Harry.

The sign in the sky

During Voldemort's first rise his followers sent the same sign into the sky, a skull with a serpent coming out of its mouth, over every house where they had killed.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in Diagon Alley in August 1993, Lucius Malfoy told Harry that he had forbidden Dracina to write to him. As they walked on, his free hand went to his own left forearm, gripped it hard through the sleeve and let go, as if it had remembered something.

In Chapter Eight, when Snape came into Lupin’s office with a smoking goblet, every hair on Lupin’s forearms stood on end and his lip came up off his teeth. It lasted no more than a moment.

In Chapter Fourteen Dracina told Snape why she had joined in her teammates’ trick with the dementors at the Ravenclaw match. As she talked, Snape’s right hand moved, without his seeming to notice it, to grip his own left forearm through the sleeve.

pages.title: J. R. R. Tolkien
infobox: Professor at Oxford; scholar of Old English
The Hobbit (1937); The Lord of the Rings (1954 to 1955)
pages.html:
J. R. R. Tolkien was an English scholar of old languages who wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. Most people take his books for stories. They are in fact history, the history of the elder days of the world: of the Elves, of Númenor and of the War of the Ring.

Life

Tolkien was born in South Africa in 1892. He was brought up in Birmingham by his mother, a convert to the Catholic Church, until she died when he was twelve. He fought on the Somme in 1916, and most of his close friends were killed in the war. For more than thirty years he taught at Oxford, where his friends included C. S. Lewis.

The Hobbit came out in 1937. The Lord of the Rings, which took him twelve years to write, followed in three parts in 1954 and 1955. He died at Bournemouth in 1973.

His record

Tolkien's record of the elder days has its gaps. It is vague about the two Blue Wizards and never settles what became of them. The reason is simple. Five Istari were sent out, and one of the Blue Wizards, Zordon, was sent off the world entirely, to Eltar. Nobody who could have written it down ever saw him again.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, Harry Potter found an enormous copy of The Lord of the Rings, all three parts bound into one, among Dudley Dursley's unwanted Christmas presents. Dudley had been using it to prop up a wobbly table. Harry read it all through his third year.

In Chapter Twenty-One, on Myst Island in June 1994, the empty grey sea made him think of Tolkien's drowned kingdom of Númenor, lying somewhere under a grey sea in the West. Later that night he thought of it again. Dumbledore had once told him that the magic of Elves and of Númenor lived in his blood. Harry knew Númenor from Tolkien by now, as the kingdom across the sea where Aragorn's family had come from. What it had to do with him, he had no idea. He finished the book in Chapter Twenty-Two, in July 1994.

pages.title: Francisco Vásquez de Coronado
infobox: Governor of New Galicia, in New Spain
1540 to 1542, in search of the Seven Cities of Cíbola
pages.html:
Francisco Vásquez de Coronado was a Spanish Muggle explorer who led an army north out of New Spain in search of the Seven Cities of Cíbola, which were said to be made of solid gold. They did not exist. In 1541 his army was in New Mexico, and a few wizards in its ranks became the first wizards ever to meet the D'ni.

The expedition

Coronado was the young governor of New Galicia when he marched north in 1540. The first of the golden cities turned out to be a Zuni village of stone and mud. His men searched the deserts of the north for two years. He came home in 1542 with nothing, and died in Mexico City in 1554.

The wizards in his army

Coronado never knew that a few of his men were wizards. In New Mexico they slipped away to try long-distance Apparition across the desert. One night they Apparated somewhere they had not meant to go, and found themselves in the D'ni cavern.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy the story. 'The first wizards who ever met them were Spanish. It was in 1541. They were with Coronado.'

pages.title: Hugh Everett
pages.html:
Hugh Everett was an American Muggle physicist. In 1957 he proposed that the universe branches into every possibility, with each branch as real as the rest, an idea later called the Many Worlds interpretation.

Life

Everett set the idea out in his doctoral thesis at Princeton in 1957, and hardly anybody took it seriously. He left physics to work for the Pentagon, calculating what a nuclear war would do. His theory found an audience only in the 1970s. He died of a heart attack in 1982, at the age of fifty-one.

The D'ni teaching

His theory comes very close to what the D'ni priests taught: that every world that could possibly be already exists, and a Writer creates nothing. He only describes a world so exactly that his book finds one to match.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione Granger explained Everett's theory to Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy. 'There was an American physicist called Hugh Everett, in 1957. He said that whenever something tiny could happen more than one way, it actually happened every way at once.'

pages.title: Erwin Schrödinger
infobox: The Schrödinger equation; the cat in the box
pages.html:
Erwin Schrödinger was an Austrian Muggle physicist, one of the founders of quantum physics, who shared the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1933.

Life

Schrödinger was born in Vienna in 1887. He left Germany in disgust when the Nazis came to power, worked for many years in Dublin and died in Vienna in 1961.

The cat

In 1935 he asked his colleagues to imagine a cat shut in a box with a flask of poison and a little radioactive material. If a single atom decays, the flask breaks and the cat dies. By the rules of quantum physics the cat is both alive and dead until somebody opens the box. Schrödinger meant it to show how absurd those rules looked when applied to cats.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione Granger mentioned a book of her father's, In Search of Schrödinger's Cat, and began to explain. 'Schrödinger's cat is a sort of thought experiment, you see, with a cat in a box, a bottle of poison and a little bit of radioactive…' Dracina Malfoy, who was freezing, stopped her there.

pages.title: Ludwig van Beethoven
infobox: Nine symphonies, many of them written as his hearing failed
pages.html:
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer who spent most of his working life in Vienna. Much of his greatest music was written after he had gone deaf. Mr Granger, Hermione's father, plays him on compact disc.

Life

Beethoven was born in Bonn in December 1770 and moved to Vienna at twenty-one. He began to lose his hearing before he was thirty. By the time his Ninth Symphony was first played, in 1824, he could not hear the applause, and one of the singers had to turn him round to see it. He died in Vienna in 1827.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Hermione Granger wrote to Harry Potter in August 1994 about the new computer her father had bought, and the CD-ROMs that came with it. 'They're like the compact discs Dad plays his Beethoven on, only they hold pictures as well as sound.' One of them was Myst.

pages.title: Ronald Reagan
infobox: President of the United States, 1981 to 1989
Grounding every costumed hero in America, 1986
pages.html:
Ronald Reagan was the fortieth President of the United States, from 1981 to 1989. In 1986 he grounded every costumed hero in America for an entire winter.

President

Reagan was Governor of California before he won the White House in 1980. Two months into his first term he survived an assassination attempt. Since leaving office in January 1989 he has lived in retirement in California.

The grounding

In 1986 Darkseid, the Lord of Apokolips, set out to turn America against its heroes through his agent Glorious Godfrey, who went before the cameras as the preacher G. Gordon Godfrey. Coming so soon after the Crisis, the campaign found a frightened audience. Reagan issued an executive order forbidding every costumed hero in America to act. Early in 1987 Godfrey was faced down at a great march on Washington, and the order was lifted.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, the news on the Dursleys' television recalled earlier attempts to rein in superhumans. 'In 1986 President Reagan grounded every costumed hero in America for an entire winter.'

pages.title: Manfred Wörner
infobox: West German Minister of Defence, 1982 to 1988
pages.html:
Manfred Wörner was a German statesman and the Secretary-General of Nato from 1988 until his death on 13 August 1994. He died a week before British television reported Augment forces within forty miles of Belgrade.

Life

Wörner was a Christian Democrat from Stuttgart and a jet pilot in the air force reserve. He was Helmut Kohl's Minister of Defence from 1982 to 1988, then the first German to lead Nato, through the end of the Cold War. In his last years, ill with cancer, he went on working while the alliance argued over how hard to bomb the Bosnian Serbs. His deputy, Sergio Balanzino, took over as acting Secretary-General.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, the news on the Dursleys' television reported the Augment advance in the Balkans. 'Nato's acting Secretary-General, who took over only last weekend after the death of Manfred Wörner, has called the alliance's ambassadors to an emergency meeting.' Diplomats described the mood as close to despair.

pages.title: J. Edgar Hoover
infobox: Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, 1924 to 1972
pages.html:
J. Edgar Hoover ran the Federal Bureau of Investigation for nearly half a century, from 1924 until his death in 1972. He kept files on everybody in America who mattered. The most dangerous of his secrets were kept on a microfilm, which James Bond stole in late 1962.

The Director

Hoover became head of the Bureau of Investigation in 1924, at the age of twenty-nine, and turned it into the FBI. Presidents came and went. Hoover stayed, and it was widely believed that he stayed because of what was in his files.

The microfilm

In late 1962 James Bond, working as John Patrick Mason, a former captain in the SAS, stole the microfilm on which Hoover kept the secrets of the American establishment. He was caught. He refused to say where he had hidden it, and he was locked up on Alcatraz without trial. He has never told anybody where it is.

pages.title: Sirius's tropical birds
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Sirius's tropical birds are the large, gaudy birds that brought Sirius Black's letters to Harry Potter at Privet Drive in the summer of 1994. Neither letter came by owl. Sirius never said where he was, in case somebody got hold of the letters.

Description

Hedwig thoroughly disapproved of them. She let them drink from her water dish with the worst possible grace before they flew off again. Harry, for his part, liked them. They made him think of palm trees and hot white beaches. He could not imagine dementors lasting long in bright sunshine, which perhaps explained why Sirius had headed south.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in August 1994, two letters had come from Sirius since Harry got home, both by tropical bird. Harry kept them hidden under the loose floorboard beneath his bed. Both sounded cheerful, and in both Sirius told him to get in touch if ever he needed to. In his reply Harry wrote: 'Thanks for your last letter. That bird was enormous; it could hardly get through my window.'

pages.title: The Chudley Cannons' Keeper
pages.html:
The Chudley Cannons' Keeper guards the goal hoops for the Chudley Cannons, the Quidditch team in bright orange that came bottom of the Prime League. In the summer of 1994 Pansy Parkinson wrote to Dracina Malfoy about the Keeper four times in a single fortnight.

Pansy's Keeper

Pansy had never cared for Quidditch in her life. The Cannons happen to be Ron Weasley's team, and Pansy has a crush on Ron, which he has not noticed.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Dracina Malfoy complained about Pansy in a letter to Harry Potter. Pansy, who used to take a novel to the Slytherin matches, had suddenly taken up the Cannons. She had a poster of them over her bed, in an orange that clashed with everything she owned. Dracina's verdict on the team was short: ‘They came bottom, Harry. Bottom.’ Pansy had also written to her four times that fortnight about their Keeper.

pages.title: Ireland (Quidditch team)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Ireland's national Quidditch team reached the final of the 1994 Quidditch World Cup, which is being held in Britain. It plays Bulgaria on the night of Monday 22 August 1994. Every one of its players is Irish, which Ron Weasley thinks only right.

The team

Known in the Quidditch world as the Irish International Side, the team went into the tournament as favourites, on the seven Firebolts it had ordered in 1993. Its Chasers are Troy, Mullet and Moran. Its Seeker is Aidan Lynch.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley sent Harry Potter word in August 1994 that his father had got tickets for the final. Ron was a bit miffed that England had not brought the Cup home this time. 'But Ireland are all right. They're all Irish at least.'

pages.title: Bulgaria (Quidditch team)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Bulgaria's national Quidditch team reached the final of the 1994 Quidditch World Cup, which is being held in Britain. It plays Ireland on the night of Monday 22 August 1994.

The team

Its Seeker is Viktor Krum, who at eighteen is already counted among the finest Seekers in the world.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, a note from Ron Weasley reached Harry Potter at Privet Drive in August 1994: 'DAD GOT THE TICKETS. Ireland versus Bulgaria, Monday night.' Arthur Weasley had got prime seats through his connections at the Department of Magical Games and Sports. As Mrs Weasley told the Dursleys, Britain had not hosted the Cup for thirty years.

pages.title: Middle-earth
infobox: The First, Second and Third Ages of the elder days
The Ice Age and the Flood, which drowned its memory
The Lord of the Rings, taken for a novel
pages.html:
Middle-earth is the world of the elder days. In it Morgoth made war on Elves and Men, as Sauron did after him, while the Istari walked its roads. Its ages were real. They came before the Hyborian Age and the Flood, which washed away nearly all knowledge of them, so that they reach the present only as a novel somebody wrote.

The ages

In the First Age the Elves and the Fathers of Men fought Morgoth, the being Scripture calls Satan, in the north-west of the world for the Silmarils. The age ended when the Valar overthrew him in the War of Wrath, and the lands of Beleriand went down under the sea. In the Second Age the Men of the West lived on Númenor, and Sauron forged the One Ring. That age ended with the drowning of Númenor and the Last Alliance.

In the Third Age the realms in exile rose, then dwindled, and the Istari came. It closed with the War of the Ring, the destruction of the Ring, the crowning of Aragorn and the departure of the Elves over the Sea. The Fourth Age was the dominion of Men. Through every one of those ages Cain, already cursed, walked the world as a deathless wanderer with no powers at all.

Gandalf belongs to those ages, and remembers them well. He remembers the hobbits who taught him much of the art of not being noticed. He remembers Aragorn, whom he crowned, and a prince of the forest folk with an infuriating habit of keeping score.

How it was forgotten

After the ages of Middle-earth came the Hyborian Age, and after that the Ice Age, whose ending brought the Flood. Nothing came through the water whole. Recorded history has spent the time since forgetting the rest. The great ages survive only as story: Conan as a legend, Arthur as half-history and Middle-earth as a novel. A wizard who goes looking for the origins of his craft finds Egypt, then Stygia, then nothing, because that is where the written record drowns.

So The Lord of the Rings, written by J. R. R. Tolkien and published in the 1950s, is a history book that hardly anybody in either world knows to be one. Tolkien's record of the Blue Wizards goes vague because one of them, Zordon, went off the world entirely, and nobody who could have written it down ever saw him again.

Its inheritance

Two things came down out of the elder days into the present. One is the dark craft of Morgoth. Stygia kept it, the Flood scattered it, and every dark wizard since has inherited some broken piece of it.

The other is a bloodline. Harry Potter descends through his mother from Aragorn and Arwen. That is what Dumbledore means when he speaks of the magic of Elves and of Númenor in Harry's blood. The sword Harry drew from the Sorting Hat in 1993 was Andúril, which Aragorn carried in the War of the Ring.

pages.title: Dracina's Nimbus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Dracina's Nimbus is the spare racing broom that Dracina Malfoy lent Harry Potter in his third year, while his Firebolt was being taken apart for jinxes. He gave it back the moment the Firebolt returned.

In the saga

The broom is a Nimbus Two Thousand and One, the model the whole Slytherin team has flown since 1992. Dracina has two. In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, at the end of February 1994, she stopped Harry in the Entrance Hall and offered him the spare for the Ravenclaw match, so that he would not have to fly the school’s old Shooting Star. It was not charity, she said. It was entirely selfish, since she meant to beat him in the spring. Harry, who had sworn he would never ride anything with Malfoy money in it, said yes.

It arrived at the Owlery two evenings later, wrapped in brown paper, with a note: Mind the left-hand foot-rest, it goes if you kick it. D. He never took it out of its paper. On the Thursday before the match Professor McGonagall gave him his Firebolt back, and he sent the Nimbus back to Dracina by school owl. His note had taken four drafts: Got my own back off McGonagall, so you’d better have this one. Thanks anyway. It was decent of you. H.

pages.title: Sonic the Hedgehog
infobox: Dudley Dursley, until the summer of 1994
pages.html:
Sonic the Hedgehog is a Muggle computer game, made by Sega for its Megadrive, about a blue hedgehog who runs faster than anything alive. Dudley Dursley owned a copy until the summer of 1994, when he threw his Megadrive out of the window.

The game

Sonic races through hills, caves and factories at tremendous speed, collecting gold rings as he goes. His enemy is the round, moustached Doctor Robotnik, who has shut the island's animals up inside robots. The game came out in June 1991 and sold in enormous numbers.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry Potter told Sirius Black in a letter that Dudley had been caught smuggling doughnuts into his room, against his diet. When his parents threatened his pocket money, he threw the Megadrive out of the window. Harry thought it rather stupid, since Dudley now had neither Sonic the Hedgehog nor Shinobi to take his mind off things.

pages.title: Shinobi
infobox: Dudley Dursley, until the summer of 1994
pages.html:
Shinobi is a Muggle computer game, made by Sega, about a ninja called Joe Musashi who fights his way through a gang of criminals with throwing stars and a sword. Dudley Dursley owned one of the Shinobi games until the summer of 1994.

The games

The first Shinobi appeared in the arcades in 1987. Three more followed on the Megadrive: The Revenge of Shinobi in 1989, Shadow Dancer in 1990 and Shinobi III in 1993. Which of them Dudley had is not recorded; Harry Potter called it only 'that Shinobi game'.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry wrote to Sirius Black that Dudley, whose diet was not going well, had been caught smuggling doughnuts into his room. Told that his pocket money would be cut, Dudley had thrown his Megadrive out of the window. That left him without Sonic the Hedgehog or Shinobi to take his mind off things.

pages.title: The Ventrue Antediluvian
infobox: About 9300 BC, in Enoch, by one of Cain's three childer
pages.html:
The Ventrue Antediluvian is the founder of Clan Ventrue, and one of the thirteen vampires of the Third Generation from whom every clan descends. What became of him is not known.

The founder

He was Embraced about 9300 BC in Enoch, the First City, by one of Cain's three childer. The Third Generation are called the Antediluvians, although all thirteen were in fact Embraced after the Flood. About 8990 BC he was among those who rose against the Second Generation and slew it. Cain cursed the clans for that slaying about 8980 BC, then departed into Nod. The curse he laid on the Ventrue was a narrowed hunger: each of them can feed on only one kind of mortal.

Afterwards the thirteen built the Second City and ruled it together, the Ventrue among its lords, until it too fell to their wars. No Ventrue will say whether he sleeps somewhere or was destroyed long ago, and it is likely that none of them knows.

The Master's claim

The Master, the fourth-generation Ventrue who founded the Aurelian line, claims that the Antediluvian sired him. If the claim is true, the Master is among the oldest vampires walking. He will never reveal his sire's name. The clan has never been able to prove the claim, or to disprove it.

pages.title: The Dursleys' Christmas present
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Dursleys' Christmas present to Harry Potter in 1991, his first Christmas at Hogwarts, was a fifty-pence piece. They sellotaped it to a note. Harry gave it to Ron Weasley.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry woke on Christmas morning 1991 to a pile of presents, although he had never once been given a Christmas present before. A very small parcel held a note: We received your message and enclose your Christmas present. From Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia. Sellotaped to the note was a fifty-pence piece. 'That's friendly,' said Harry. Ron, though, was fascinated by the coin, and Harry told him to keep it.

pages.title: The hooded stranger in the Hog's Head
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Never seen; he kept his hood up
pages.html:
The hooded stranger in the Hog's Head was the cloaked man who lost a dragon egg to Rubeus Hagrid at cards in the spring of 1992. Over the game he got out of Hagrid that music would send Fluffy to sleep. He was Quirinus Quirrell, who carried Lord Voldemort on the back of his head.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Hagrid told Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger how he had come by the egg. 'Las' night. I was down in the village havin' a few, an' got into a game o' cards with a stranger. Think he was glad ter be shot of it, ter be honest.'

In Chapter Twelve Hagrid admitted that he had never seen the man's face, since he had kept his hood up the whole time. The stranger had kept buying him drinks, and Hagrid had told him how to calm Fluffy down: 'Jus' play him a bit o' music an' he goes straight off ter sleep...'

In Chapter Thirteen, face to face with Quirrell, Harry understood at last who had been under the hood. Afterwards Hagrid sobbed that it was all his fault: 'I told the evil git how ter get past Fluffy! I told him!'

pages.title: The man who sold Fluffy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The man who sold Fluffy is the stranger from whom Rubeus Hagrid bought his three-headed dog in 1990, a year before Fluffy went to guard the Philosopher's Stone at Hogwarts. Hagrid met him in a pub. He had a caravan and a funny voice, so Hagrid decided he was Greek. Harry Potter suspected that he was nothing of the kind.

Fluffy

Hagrid named the dog himself, and in 1991 he lent him to Albus Dumbledore. For the next school year Fluffy stood guard over the trapdoor in the forbidden third-floor corridor. Where the man had found a three-headed dog in the first place is not recorded.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1991, Hagrid told Harry, Ron and Hermione where the dog had come from: 'Bought him off a Greek chappie I met down the pub las' year. Well, I think he was Greek. He had the caravan and funny voice the greeks have.' Harry had a growing suspicion that Hagrid was not describing a Greek at all. In Chapter Twelve he decided that the man had been a Traveller.

pages.title: The idol from Romania
pages.html:
The idol from Romania was a present that Charlie Weasley sent to his brother Percy from Romania, where Charlie works with dragons. Their mother took it away from Percy. It had too many tentacles for her liking.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, lying in the hospital wing in June 1992, Harry Potter remembered hearing the story of the idol, which had happened the year before. Mrs Weasley had had to take it off Percy. Too many tentacles.

pages.title: The seven-bottles riddle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A roll of paper beside the bottles
The potions chamber on the way to the Philosopher's Stone
pages.html:
The seven-bottles riddle is the rhyming riddle on a roll of paper beside the seven bottles in the potions chamber, Professor Snape's defence of the Philosopher's Stone. Snape wrote it in verse of his own. Hermione Granger solved it in June 1992.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, Hermione snatched up the roll of paper as soon as the two fires had trapped her with Harry Potter. It began: 'Before you, danger; safety at your back.' Hermione let out a great sigh and smiled. 'Brilliant,' she said. 'This isn't magic. It's logic. It's a puzzle.' She read it through several times, then walked along the row of bottles, pointing at each in turn. Something very bright came into her face as she worked, which Harry could not have named. At last she clapped her hands. The smallest bottle would get them through the black fire, towards the Stone.

pages.title: The Sorting Hat song (1991)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Sorting Hat song of 1991 is the short new song the Sorting Hat sang before the Sorting on 1 September 1991, the year Harry Potter came to Hogwarts.

The song

The Hat admitted it was patched and plain, but boasted that there was no cleverer hat anywhere. Nothing was hidden, it said, in any head it had ever worn, whatever that head had done. It sent the bold to Gryffindor and the fair of heart to Hufflepuff. The quick of wit went to Ravenclaw, while the cunning thrived in Slytherin. It ended by telling the first-years to try it and never fear, since it had never yet been wrong.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, a tear near the Hat's brim opened like a mouth, and it burst into song. The Hall applauded, and the Hat bowed to each table in turn. Harry felt neither bold nor quick-witted. If the Hat had mentioned a house for those who felt slightly sick, he would have known exactly where he belonged.

pages.title: Dean Thomas's terrace chants
pages.html:
Dean Thomas's terrace chants are the football songs Dean has been writing for the Gryffindor stand since his first year at Hogwarts. Dean grew up on the terraces at Upton Park, and he holds that a school with a stadium that size ought to have proper chants. His teachers do not agree.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, in early 1992, he wrote chants against Hufflepuff for the match that Professor Snape refereed. One ended 'Loyal to losing, that's all that you do!' When Harry Potter caught the Snitch almost at once, the stand sang 'Five minutes! Five minutes! You lasted five minutes!'

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the autumn of 1992, his chant against Slytherin, to a tune from West Ham, had a chorus that ran 'I'm a slimy snake, I've got no balls'. Two hundred Gryffindors roared it, then the other houses took it up, until Professor McGonagall stopped it. A later verse, about the Malfoys, called Dracina Malfoy Daddy's girl, with Daddy's gold and Daddy's brooms. It made her miss the Snitch.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, he taught Gryffindor a chant about badgers digging their burrows, to a tune he swore everybody in Muggle Britain knew. Hufflepuff answered it to the same tune, five hundred voices strong.

pages.title: Pottyhead
infobox: Her only insult for him in their first year
pages.html:
Pottyhead was the insult Dracina Malfoy used for Harry Potter, and the only one, through their whole first year at Hogwarts. She coined it on the spot when he rejected her.

The insult

It is not much of an insult, as Harry told her himself. What made it remarkable was what she left unsaid. Harry had handed her a whole stock of insults that would really have hurt, and she never used a single one. She stuck to Pottyhead.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Dracina first called Harry a pottyhead, and Ron Weasley laughed until he had to wipe his eyes. In Book One, Chapter Six, on the Quidditch pitch, Harry asked her whether that was the best she had got. In Book One, Chapter Seven, he noticed that she had never once used the crueller insults he had given her that night.

In Book One, Chapter Ten, dragged off down a dark corridor at night, she screamed it over and over: ‘I hate you, Pottyhead! I hate you!’ Harry was standing under his Invisibility Cloak, closer to her than she ever knew.

pages.title: The fall of Jorvik
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter 12
The Norse völvas of Jorvik; the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London
pages.html:
The fall of Jorvik in 954 ended the wizarding war between the Norse völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. It came when the Anglo-Saxons took Jorvik, the Viking city of York, which brought the last Norse kingdom in England to an end.

The war

Jorvik had been a Viking city since the Danes took York in 866. Its witches were völvas, Norse seeresses who worked their magic with staff and song. In the south, round London and the old Roman towns, the last Hellenic sorcerers still worked magic the classical way. Their incantations were Latin and Greek, with a great deal of geometry thrown in. Neither side thought the other's magic was the real thing.

In Muggle history the end came in 954, when the Northumbrians drove out Jorvik's last king, Eric Bloodaxe. He was killed at Stainmore, and King Eadred of England took his kingdom for his own. The Viking families of the North-East did not leave. They simply stopped saying they were Norse. Thirty-six years later Hogwarts was founded, the first place where all the quarrelling magical peoples of Britain were made to sit down in the same room.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the last of the first-years' examinations in the summer of 1992 was an hour of History of Magic on this war. Harry Potter was rather proud of having got the date, 954, to stay in his head.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, explaining the early Middle Ages to Harry in November 1992, Hermione Granger told him that the Viking families of the North-East had not left when the Saxons took Jorvik. They had just stopped saying they were Norse.

pages.title: The Yorkshire lady found in a chimney
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
pages.html:
The Yorkshire lady found in a chimney is the ghost of a lady from Yorkshire whose body was found in a chimney in 1812, when it was swept. Her own steward had bricked her up inside it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, she was one of the famous ghosts Hermione Granger named in October 1992, when Ron Weasley asked her who would be at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party.

pages.title: The quartered monk
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
pages.html:
The quartered monk is the ghost of a monk of Glastonbury who was hanged, drawn and quartered by Henry the Eighth's men, so that he comes in four pieces. He is Brother Aldric, who hid Glastonbury Abbey's books from the King's commissioners in a cave on the Tor.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party on 31 October 1992, the quartered monk told Hermione Granger where Glastonbury's books were hidden. She took about thirty seconds to write the answer down, then came running after Harry and Ron, glowing. 'He told me!' she said.

pages.title: The cursed tea set
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A formerly cursed Muggle French nobleman and his peasant wife
A Muggle woman, who died of shock
pages.html:
The cursed tea set was a set of china that came alive in a Muggle house, danced, talked, and frightened a Muggle woman to death. It had belonged to an old witch, who was given it by a formerly cursed Muggle French nobleman and his peasant wife.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter the story in the flying car, to explain what his father's office did. The old witch died the year before, and her tea set was sold to an antiques shop. A little old Muggle lady bought it, took it home and tried to serve her friends tea in it. The pieces came alive. They started dancing and speaking to one another. The old lady died of shock, while the other people went mad.

Arthur Weasley worked overtime for weeks. There are only two of them in his office, Arthur and an old warlock called Perkins. They had to use Memory Charms, among other things, to cover it up.

pages.title: Dracina's knight-and-princess picture book
infobox: A knight kneeling to a girl in a tower
pages.html:
Dracina’s knight-and-princess picture book is a big, old, battered picture book of the kind small children are given at Christmas. Dracina Malfoy had it with her at Hogwarts, and did not want it seen.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Harry passed Dracina at a library table, alone, behind two fat volumes of wizarding genealogy, one with the Malfoy crest on its spine. Open on top of them was the picture book. Its page showed a painted knight in silver armour kneeling before a girl with long pale hair in a tower, holding out his sword to her hilt first. When she saw him looking, Dracina slammed the book shut so hard that Madam Pince shot out from behind her desk. She swept it under the genealogies and glared at him, her face burning.

In Chapter Twelve, watching a little stone knight on a chessboard, Harry thought of it again. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Dracina looked up at Harry standing over her with the sword, between her and the dark, with the Basilisk dead at his feet. He looked like the knight from the painted book, except that he was not kneeling in a tower.

pages.title: Peeves's song
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
'Oh Potter, the plotter, he's at it again'
pages.html:
Peeves's song is the mocking song Peeves the poltergeist sang about Harry Potter while the Chamber of Secrets was open. It is better known by its first words, 'Oh Potter, the plotter'.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, in December 1992, Peeves burst into it over the Petrified bodies of Justin Finch-Fletchley and Nearly Headless Nick: 'Oh Potter, the plotter, he's at it again'. Professor McGonagall sent him packing. He went on singing it in crowded corridors through the early months of 1993, and later added a dance with a great deal of high kicking.

pages.title: The wall messages
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A wall of the second-floor corridor, Hogwarts
The memory in Tom Riddle's diary, through the possessed Dracina Malfoy
pages.html:
The wall messages were the two warnings from the Heir of Slytherin daubed on a wall of the second-floor corridor at Hogwarts in the school year 1992 to 1993. They were the work of the memory in Tom Riddle's diary, which wrote them with the hand of the girl it had possessed, Dracina Malfoy.

The messages

The first appeared on Hallowe'en 1992. It was daubed between two tall windows in letters a foot high, and it glimmered red in the torchlight: ‘THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS HAS BEEN OPENED. ENEMIES OF THE HEIR, BEWARE.’ Filch's cat, Mrs Norris, hung Petrified from a torch bracket beside it.

The second appeared directly under the first when Ginny Weasley was taken into the Chamber in the summer term of 1993: ‘Her skeleton will lie in the Chamber for ever.’

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger found the first message on Hallowe'en night. Hermione screamed when she saw Mrs Norris. When the feast ended, students came pouring into the corridor from both ends. Dracina Malfoy pushed her way to the front and shouted, ‘Enemies of the heir, beware! You'll be next, Mudblood!’ Nobody noticed the red stain down the side of the finger she was pointing with, not even Harry. In Book Two, Chapter Ten, the message was still there, with Filch's empty chair against the wall below it.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Professor McGonagall told the staff that a student had been taken into the Chamber itself. The heir had left a second message, she said, directly under the first. The student was Ginny Weasley.

pages.title: The pyramid mummy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Four
Wrapped in bandages, lying on a slab
Whether a visitor has lived with a true heart
pages.html:
The pyramid mummy is a bandaged guardian of the dead that lies on a slab in an Egyptian pyramid. When anybody comes in uninvited, it sits up to question them. Have they lived with a true heart? What have they done with the years given them? Are they ready to have their heart weighed?

The weighing of the heart

In old Egyptian belief, the heart of the dead is weighed against the feather of truth. Only a heart as light as the feather may pass on into the life beyond.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the Weasley twins told Harry Potter at the Leaky Cauldron how they had tried to shut Percy in a pyramid in Egypt that summer. They got him through the door before their mother spotted them. The mummy sat up on its slab. It asked Percy whether he had lived with a true heart, what he had done with the years given him and whether he was ready to have his heart weighed. ‘And Percy answered,’ said George. ‘For about ten minutes. With examples.’ The mummy lay back down. Fred thought it would rather have had the eternal dark.

Their brother Bill, a curse-breaker for Gringotts, had told them that it did that to everyone who went in uninvited. They were lucky it was only asking questions, he said; most people came out of there a lot quieter than they went in.

pages.title: Lizzie and Mary
pages.html:
Lizzie and Mary are two first-year Hufflepuffs, close friends, who started at Hogwarts in September 1993. In February 1994 a cut that went right through Lizzie's forearm was healed by Madam Pomfrey in four seconds. Mary would not believe it until she had touched the mark.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in the first week of February 1994, the pair came out from between the library shelves in the middle of an argument, loud enough to bring Madam Pince's head up behind her desk like a vulture's. Mary was not saying Lizzie was lying, she said; she only could not believe in the healed arm until she had touched it. So Lizzie held it out. Mary pressed two fingers into the thin white line, then left them there for a long moment. "I'm sorry, Lizzie. All right. I believe you." The two of them went off between the shelves arm in arm.

Dracina Malfoy had been watching from her table with Harry Potter. "What," she said, "in the name of Merlin was that?" "Hufflepuffs," said Harry. "They're like a sort of weather," said Dracina.

Harry had been about to ask her about a Ministry letter he had built six weeks of suspicion on, without ever once asking to touch the thing. After watching the two Hufflepuffs, he told her it would keep.

pages.title: The boy on the lake ice
pages.html:
The boy on the lake ice is a thin Hufflepuff second-year who walked thirty feet out on the frozen lake at Hogwarts in January 1994, on ice only four inches thick. He was doing perfectly well until he looked down, and then he went through.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, the lake had frozen hard in the second week of January 1994. Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy were on the bank fifty yards off when a knot of Hufflepuffs began roaring. The boy had gone out past the reeds with his arms straight out from his sides, laughing, white-faced with it. At thirty feet he turned to wave, and looked down. He floundered, took two steps at a run and went through to the chest. An enormous sixth-year Hufflepuff lay flat on the ice to haul him out. Afterwards, as they carried him up to the castle, the sixth-year kept demanding furiously, "Why did you look down?"

pages.title: Dracina's dragon-hide gloves
pages.html:
Dracina's dragon-hide gloves are the pair of black, supple, lined Quidditch gloves that Narcissa Malfoy sent her daughter, and that Dracina passed on to Harry Potter in December 1993. Harry was fairly sure they had cost more than everything he was wearing put together.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Dracina had taken to watching Gryffindor’s evening practices, moving a little closer each night until she was sitting in the Gryffindor stand itself. One night in the sleet she rose as Harry came past and held out a small flat parcel. ‘Mother sent these. Dragon-hide. They were going spare.’ She would rather he did not lose his fingers before he had to play Slytherin, she said. It would make the victory less satisfying.

Hermione called down from two rows up that his drink was getting cold. Dracina told her it was very loyal of her, like a dog with a Thermos. Harry was left standing between them in the sleet, with the gloves in one hand and the flask in the other.

In Chapter Fourteen Dracina told Professor Snape that her teammates had been saying she was soft on Potter ever since the hospital wing and the gloves.

pages.title: The Buckbeak letter
infobox: Dracina Malfoy, with her left hand
Lucius's complaint against Buckbeak was upheld
pages.html:
The Buckbeak letter was the four-page letter Dracina Malfoy wrote to her father from the hospital wing in September 1993, after the hippogriff Buckbeak slashed her arm. She wrote it with her left hand, then decided not to send it. Pansy Parkinson sent it all the same, believing it was what Dracina wanted, and Lucius Malfoy's complaint against Buckbeak was upheld.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, lying awake in the hospital wing with her arm aching, Dracina made up her mind to write to her father first thing in the morning. She would use her left hand and make the injury look worse than it was. She would use the words bone, scar and permanent. Father would do what Father did, which was make things happen to people.

In Chapter Seven, in Potions, she apologised to Harry for what she had said about Hagrid. She had dropped it all, she told him. 'I had written to Father, if you must know, I sat up all night, it was four pages. And then I didn't send it.'

In Chapter Ten, two months later, Pansy stood in the hospital wing, visiting Harry, and looked at the bare table by the bed that had been Dracina's. Nobody else knew that four pages had once lain on it. Nobody else knew who had taken them to the Owlery, thinking it was what a friend would want. Pansy had found out in Potions, two tables away, what her friend had really wanted. She had said nothing about it to anybody.

In Chapter Eleven, a letter to Hagrid told him that the official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy had been upheld. Reading it, Harry remembered Dracina at his elbow in the dungeon in September, telling him she had not sent anything. From then on he believed she had lied to him.

In Chapter Fourteen, Lucius wrote to thank his daughter. He had put her four pages in front of the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures, and had the hearing brought forward on the strength of them. Dracina told Professor Snape that she had written back, begging her father to drop it, but that once Father had decided a thing, it happened. Walking back to the Slytherin common room, she told Pansy that somebody had taken the letter off the table by her bed while she slept. 'I'm going to find out who.' Pansy followed her with a towel.

In Chapter Fifteen, Dracina told Harry the whole story. She had written the letter in a rage, on the night he came to the wing to tell her she was horrible, and in the morning she could not send it.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, on the front steps of the castle, Pansy broke down and confessed. 'I thought you wanted the letter sent,' she sobbed. 'I thought… I thought you left it and I was being helpful. I'm so sorry.' Since the spring Dracina had blamed Hermione Granger. Now Daphne Greengrass had to hold her back by both arms. 'You didn't even ASK,' Dracina shouted. 'You nearly RUINED EVERYTHING!'

pages.title: The green bloke on the news
infobox: On the Muggle television news, by 1992
pages.html:
The green bloke on the news is a green superhuman whom Harry Potter had seen on the Muggle television news by the summer of 1992. Harry mentioned him in the same breath as Superman. He never said who he meant.

Candidates

The news in those years had more than one green figure to show. The Hulk, Bruce Banner's huge green other self, had been wrecking parts of America since 1962. J'onn J'onzz, the green-skinned Martian Manhunter, was a founder of the Justice League.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1992, Ron Weasley and the twins came for Harry in the flying car. They found him behind the bars that Uncle Vernon had paid a man to put on his window. Harry told Ron: 'Unless you can get Superman on the phone, or that green bloke I saw on the news, I reckon I'm stuck.' 'Who's Superman?' said Fred, interested.

pages.title: The dwarf and warlock feud
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 4
A beard-to-gold ritual that only made the dwarfs' beards itch
1,100 years by the dwarfs' count; 950 by the warlocks'
pages.html:
The dwarf and warlock feud, better known as the beard-gold feud, is a quarrel over a ritual that was supposed to turn the beards of the dwarfs' ancestors to gold. It made them itch instead. The dwarfs say the feud has lasted 1,100 years; the warlocks say 950. They cannot agree on that either.

The feud

The quarrel began in the tenth century. Nobody now remembers what the ritual was for, only that it failed. The two sides still carry it on whenever they meet.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, a party of warlocks in bearskins and a party of dwarfs breakfasted at neighbouring tables in the Leaky Cauldron, throwing kippers at each other. Tom, the innkeeper, explained the two counts to Harry Potter. Nobody, he said, remembered what the ritual had been for. 'That's the thing about carrying a grudge, Mr Potter. You carry it. Not the other fellow. He's gone home and put his feet up. Heavy things, grudges.'

pages.title: The Prewetts
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
The Prewetts are an old pure-blood wizarding family, the family Molly Weasley was born into. Her brothers, Fabian and Gideon Prewett, were killed fighting Death Eaters in the first war against Voldemort.

The family

It took five Death Eaters to kill Fabian and Gideon. Their sister, Molly, had married Arthur Weasley in 1969, and her sons know of a face she once wore, the morning she came back from the Prewetts'. Bill told the twins about it. They know what it means: somebody's house is about to be taken apart.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, when Harry was set on going after Sirius Black, Fred and George Weasley told him that he had the face on. It was the one their mother had worn the morning she came back from the Prewetts', the time Bill had told them about. Fred explained what it meant: 'The one that means somebody's getting their house taken apart.'

pages.title: The social worker with the folder
pages.html:
The social worker with the folder visited Number Four, Privet Drive, once, while Harry Potter was growing up there. She looked at Harry in the Dursleys' front room with her head on one side, then went away, and never came back.

Privet Drive

Harry was used to grown-ups believing the Dursleys. His teachers at St Grogory's believed them. So did the dinner lady and the lady from the council. The social worker went away and left things exactly as they were.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in the hospital wing, Harry dreamt of taking revenge on everyone who had hurt him, with Dracina Malfoy standing very close at his side. When the social worker with the folder came, Dracina said that one, Harry, that one especially. He did, and she laughed her real laugh, with her hand over her mouth.

pages.title: The teachers at St Grogory's
infobox: St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
pages.html:
The teachers at St Grogory's taught Harry Potter at his Muggle primary school in Little Whinging. They believed Dudley Dursley every time.

Harry's teachers

One of them held up Harry's school jumper in front of the class to show them what neglect looked like, then let Dudley off for breaking Harry's glasses. Another shut Harry in the stock cupboard for something Dudley had broken.

At assembly the school said the Lord's Prayer, with Dudley pinching Harry from the row behind or kicking the back of his chair.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in Diagon Alley in August 1993, the memory of the jumper came back to Harry with his anger. In Chapter Ten, lying in the hospital wing, he dreamt of paying back everyone who had hurt him. The teachers from the primary school came, and Dracina Malfoy, at his shoulder, told him to go on.

pages.title: Hermione Granger's parents
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Mr and Mrs Granger are the Muggle parents of Hermione Granger. Both are dentists, with a surgery of their own, and both are atheists, like their daughter.

The family

Nobody in either family has ever had any magic. The Grangers learnt that their only child was a witch when her Hogwarts letter came in 1991, which was a great surprise to all three of them. They write to her every week during term.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, they went with Hermione to Diagon Alley in August 1992. Arthur Weasley was delighted to meet two real Muggles. He insisted on taking them to the Leaky Cauldron for a drink, towing them up the street in a way that looked to the Grangers a good deal more like a kidnapping. Both Grangers were left shaking after Lucius Malfoy insulted them and Arthur fought him in Flourish and Blotts.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, talking with Harry about why Hogwarts has no chapel, Hermione told him plainly: 'I'm an atheist. My parents are.'

In Chapter Twenty-One, on the dock at Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione told Dracina Malfoy what it had been like to find that half the castle thought her dirt because of her parents: 'Because they're dentists who fill people's teeth, and they love me.'

pages.title: Abydos
pages.html:
Abydos is a desert world at the far end of the Stargate found at Giza. Ra kept a people taken from ancient Egypt there as his slaves, to mine naquadah for him. In 1994 the first expedition from Earth reached it, Ra was destroyed in the sky above it, and Daniel Jackson stayed behind.

World and people

Abydos is a world of sand and wind under a hard sun. Its gate stands inside a great pyramid in the open desert, a long walk from Nagada, the walled town where the Abydonians live. They are descended from Egyptians whom Ra carried through the gate thousands of years ago, and they still speak a form of the ancient Egyptian tongue. Their beasts of burden are mastadges, big shaggy animals that haul loads across the dunes. They mined naquadah for Ra, whom they worshipped as their god.

Ra forbade them to read or write, so that they would forget where they had come from. Their history survived only in hidden chambers, whose inscriptions told of Ra's coming, of the rising on Earth that drove him out and of the gate that had been buried behind him. The elder of Nagada is Kasuf. His daughter Sha'uri and his son Skaara are among the young people who rose against Ra.

One of the inscriptions shows a storm over the desert, with a giant in it holding a hammer. The Abydonians do not know who he was.

The 1994 expedition

In 1994 a United States Air Force team under Colonel Jack O'Neill came through the gate, with Daniel Jackson to read its symbols. When the Abydonians saw the Eye of Ra on the amulet Jackson carried, they bowed down before the strangers. The people of Nagada took them in, and Kasuf gave Sha'uri to Jackson as his wife.

When Ra arrived in his ship, the Abydonians took up arms against his guards for the first time in their history. O'Neill and Jackson sent the expedition's bomb up to Ra's ship. He was destroyed in the sky above them.

Jackson chose to stay with Sha'uri and her people. O'Neill told his superiors that the gate on Abydos had been destroyed, so that the Abydonians would be left alone.

Apophis

In 1997 Apophis, who had been taking over Ra's domains since Ra's death, came to Abydos. He took Sha'uri as a host for his queen, Amaunet, and Skaara as one for his son, Klorel.

In 2003 Anubis destroyed Abydos. Oma Desala had already raised its people beyond his reach, Skaara among them.

In the saga

Abydos has not been named in the saga. The only trace of it is the reported death of Daniel Jackson beneath the Giza plateau, on the Muggle news of 20 August 1994 (Book Four, Chapter Three). The death was a cover story for his going there.

pages.title: Amaterasu
infobox: Amaterasu, the sun goddess of Japan
pages.html:
Amaterasu is a Goa'uld System Lord who was worshipped in Japan as the goddess of the sun. In 2004 she came to Earth with Lord Yu and Camulus to ask for help against Ba'al. She went home without it. By early 2005 she and Yu were gathering their armies for a last stand. What became of her is not known.

The sun goddess

Amaterasu came quietly to Japan, against Ra's ban. On islands at the far eastern edge of Asia she was a very long way from the North, which suited her.

The Japanese worshipped her as the goddess of the sun. They told how she once shut herself away in a cave, in anger at her brother, until the other gods lured her out. The emperors of Japan claimed descent from her.

The embassy to Earth

Earth's defeat of Anubis in 2004 left the System Lords in disarray. To avoid open war among themselves, they agreed to divide his territories and his armies evenly. Ba'al learnt where Anubis had been making his Kull warriors, and he took the place for himself.

That summer Camulus asked Earth for talks. The System Lords sent him to Stargate Command with Amaterasu and Lord Yu, to ask for Earth's help against Ba'al. Amaterasu said what the others had been thinking. Asgard, she pointed out, had not come to Earth's aid when Anubis attacked it, and nobody had heard from Asgard for a long time. Ba'al was convinced that Asgard could no longer exercise its power in the galaxy, and he meant to take the protected planets for himself.

After a thousand years of keeping the treaty for fear of Asgard, the System Lords were beginning to wonder whether there was anything left to fear. Daniel Jackson, who knew perfectly well where Asgard's strength had gone, told her that Earth talked to Asgard all the time. Earth was now keeping up Asgard's bluff for it.

The System Lords offered Earth the means to build a fleet of ships as good as their own motherships. Elizabeth Weir, who led Earth's side, declined. Amaterasu then wondered aloud what Ba'al would think if he heard that Earth's great Ancient weapon was temporarily out of commission. He would come to take Earth for himself, Camulus observed. Earth would have to destroy him, and the System Lords would have to give Earth nothing at all.

When the talks broke down, the System Lords secretly sent a ship to test Earth's defences. Earth held the delegates prisoner. The ship never came, because Ba'al destroyed it on its way. Weir then let them go, judging them more use fighting Ba'al than sitting in a cell. Camulus stayed behind to ask for asylum. As she left, Amaterasu asked Weir to 'make sure Camulus knows he will forever be branded a traitor and a coward'.

The last stand

By early 2005 Ba'al had killed or broken one System Lord after another. The Tok'ra reported that Amaterasu and Lord Yu were rallying their armies for what would probably be their last stand. The free Jaffa were moving against her as well. Bra'tac said that they had allies within the ranks of Amaterasu's own Jaffa, ready to help when they struck.

Then the Replicators began a full-scale invasion of the galaxy. By then the System Lords knew exactly what had kept Asgard so busy. The Ancient weapon on Dakara destroyed every Replicator in the galaxy. Yu was dead by then. Ba'al fled from the free Jaffa at Dakara, and the rule of the Goa'uld collapsed.

What became of Amaterasu in all this was never recorded.

pages.title: Ancients
infobox: Human beings raised to the order of the Maiar
The Stargates; outposts across the galaxy
A city that could sail between the stars
Not to meddle in the affairs of the living
pages.html:
The Ancients are the builders of the Stargates, a people of human beings who long ago rose to a higher plane of existence and became Maiar, spirits of the same order as Gandalf, in the service of God. Nobody knows when they were mortal. They left the Stargates behind them, with outposts and weapons scattered across the galaxy. They also left the memory of a city that could sail between the stars, which myth has confused with Atlantis.

The builders

The Ancients built the Stargates, the great rings that open a passage from one world to another, and set them in a network across the galaxy. The Goa'uld did not make a single one. They found the gates, as they found most things. Then they used them to carry their slaves and armies from world to world.

The Ancients also left outposts, machines and stores of knowledge on many worlds. Their language survives in inscriptions, and it looks a little like Latin, which has misled more than one scholar. In 1999 one of their repositories forced its knowledge into the head of Jack O'Neill, who could neither use it nor bear it for long. Asgard took it out again.

Ascension

At some time nobody can now fix, the Ancients ceased to be mortal. They rose to a higher plane of existence and became Maiar, spirits of the same order as Gandalf, in the service of God. They are the only mortals known to have been raised to that order, apart from the few whom Oma Desala has helped to follow them.

As Maiar they keep one rule above all: they do not meddle in the affairs of the living. They are hard on those of their number who break it. Oma Desala, who helps those she judges worthy to rise, has been in trouble with the rest of them more than once.

The worst of it was Anubis. The Devil gave him the power to deceive Oma, and she began to help him rise before she saw what he was. A being as wicked as a Goa'uld could never finish that journey. He was left halfway, in torment, and the Ancients would not admit him.

In 2002 Oma raised Daniel Jackson, who was dying. For a year he was one of them, until he tried to interfere and was sent back, without his memories. In 2003 she raised the people of Abydos beyond Anubis's reach before his weapon fell on their world.

Before they came to this galaxy, the Ancients lived in another, which takes its name from them: the Alteran galaxy. There the Ori, Maiar who had followed Melkor and been cast out with him, set themselves up as gods. The Ancients who would not worship them left.

The city

The Ancients once had a city that could sail between the stars. It could rest on the sea, or sink beneath it and rise again. More than one story of a shining city lost under the waves began with it.

Long ago, at a time nobody can now fix, it stood on Earth, where the Antarctic ice now lies. Then it rose and went out among the stars. It is believed to lie now in another galaxy.

Atlantis

Myth has mixed the city up with Atlantis, and so have nearly all the people who think they know where Atlantis was. Two kingdoms under the sea claim the name. The Sub-Mariner's people, under the Antarctic sea, say that they are the true Atlantis, the heirs of the island that went down in the Cataclysm in the days of Kull. Aquaman's Atlantis, the kingdom of his mother's people, says the same of itself. Each disputes the other's claim, loudly.
