Neither is right. The Atlantis of the old story, the great island kingdom of the West that grew proud, made war on the powers of the West and was swallowed by the sea, was Númenor. The Elves called it Atalantë, the Downfallen. Both undersea kingdoms are real, and both are old, but neither is the place the story remembers.

No living man or woman knows the whole truth of it except Albus Dumbledore.

Dumbledore suspects that the Ancients were somehow related to Númenor. He has never been able to work out exactly how. Nor, if he is right, can he see how they left Earth to build an empire among the stars and make the Stargates.

On Earth

The Ancients left an outpost on Earth itself, under the Antarctic ice. In 2004 Anubis came for it, believing that Earth held the secrets of the Ancients, and he was right. Jack O'Neill, carrying their knowledge in his head for the second time, reached the outpost first. From its chair he sent out the drone weapons that destroyed Anubis's fleet.

They also left a weapon on Dakara that could wipe out every living thing in the galaxy. In 2005 Earth turned it on the Replicators instead.

pages.title: Anezka
infobox: Vampire (Kindred); for eight centuries a ghoul
pages.html:
Anezka is a Bohemian nun of Prague who nursed the wounded crusader Christof Romuald in 1141, and loved him. The Tzimisce took her and made her the ghoul of the Methuselah Vukodlak. She seemed to turn against Christof, and spent more than eight hundred years at her master's side. All that time she worked in secret against his waking, and prayed for Christof to come back. When Christof destroyed Vukodlak in New York in 1999, he Embraced her so that she would not die. She became his childe.

The nun of Prague

Anezka was a young nun in Prague in 1141. When the French knight Christof Romuald was wounded in battle there, she nursed him back to health in a church. The two of them fell in love, though neither said so. Their vows stood between them, and she kept hers.

That same year Christof was Embraced into Clan Brujah, and the faith he had shared with her broke. Anezka's did not.

Vukodlak's ghoul

In the war between the Tremere and the Tzimisce, the Tzimisce took her. At Vyšehrad, their castle above Prague, she was made the ghoul of the Methuselah Vukodlak. He was an elder of the clan who lay sleeping beneath the castle, and he meant to rise above the ancestors of every clan. His blood kept her from growing old. With it came the bond that such blood brings.

When Christof came to Vyšehrad for her, she turned from him and went to wake her master. Before she could, mortal forces stormed the castle and brought it down. The elders of the Tzimisce bound Vukodlak in a sleep of their own. Anezka stayed at his side.

Eight hundred years

For more than eight centuries she lived on Vukodlak's blood. She served his followers, who counted her one of his creatures. She was nothing of the kind. All that time she worked in secret against his waking, undoing what she could of the work of those who meant to raise him. Every night she prayed for Christof to come back.

In 1999 Vukodlak's followers carried him to New York and hid him beneath the Cathedral of Flesh. Anezka went with him. By then she lived only by the Methuselah's blood. When Christof found them, Vukodlak offered her to him, if Christof would serve him. Christof refused. Thrown into the tunnels beneath the Cathedral, he found the Wall of Memories. In it he saw what she had done for eight hundred years.

The Embrace

Christof went back up into the Cathedral and destroyed Vukodlak. With her master gone, Anezka had no blood left to keep her. Without it the centuries she had been spared would have taken her at once. Christof was reconciled with her. He Embraced her so that she would not die, and she rose of Clan Brujah, of the tenth generation: his childe.

In later years Kindred who saw a beautiful, quiet woman at Christof's side often took her for a Tzimisce. Eight centuries of a Tzimisce Methuselah's blood leave their mark. She never troubled to correct them.

pages.title: Anubis
infobox: The jackal-headed god of the Egyptian dead
Stranded halfway between ordinary life and a higher plane, in endless torment
The power to deceive Oma Desala
Lord Yu, SG-1, the Tok'ra, Asgard
Held by Oma Desala in a struggle without end, from 2005
pages.html:
Anubis is a Goa'uld whom the other System Lords banished long ago, for crimes so terrible that even they could not stomach them. They believe him dead. He is not. The Devil gave him the means to deceive Oma Desala, one of the Ancients, into helping him rise to a higher plane of existence. No being as wicked as a Goa'uld could ever finish that journey, and the Devil knew it: Anubis was left halfway, in a state of endless torment. From 2001 he made war on the System Lords, the Tok'ra and Earth with what he had brought back. In 2005 Oma Desala, the Ancient who had helped him, took him out of the world, and he was not seen again.

Banishment

Anubis took his name from the jackal-headed god of the Egyptian dead, whose mask Ra's own guards wore. Whatever it is that keeps watch over the weighing of the dead in Egypt, it has never been him.

What he did to earn his banishment the Goa'uld prefer not to say. The Tok'ra say only that his crimes were unspeakable, even by the standards of the Goa'uld, which are not high.

The System Lords cast him out of their council, swore that he should never return and then tried to kill him. They believed they had succeeded. It was all so long ago that by 2002 only Yu, the oldest of them, was left of the System Lords who had done it.

Between the planes

While the System Lords believed him dead, Anubis set out to raise himself to a higher plane of existence, as the Ancients had done long before. The Ancients were human beings of a far older age, the builders of the Stargates. Those of them who ascended became Maiar, spirits of the same order as Gandalf, in the service of God.

No Goa'uld could make that journey, and Anubis knew it. He went to the Devil for help, and the Devil gave it gladly. The gift was a single power: the power to deceive Oma Desala, one of the Ancients, who helps those she judges worthy to rise. With it Anubis made her believe that he was worthy, and she began to help him.

The gift was a trick, and meant to be one. Anubis had believed that he could rise to stand near God, and near the Devil himself. The Devil does not forgive that sort of presumption in a parasite. He knew that a being as wicked and corrupt as a Goa'uld could never make the journey properly, however far it was helped along.

By the time Oma saw what Anubis was, it was too late for her to stop him on her own. He rose halfway and no further. He was left between ordinary life and the higher plane, neither one thing nor the other. It is a state of horror and endless torment. It was exactly what the Devil had intended.

The Ancients would not admit him, and they never quite forgave Oma for having helped him on his way.

He kept some of the knowledge he had gained. That knowledge, much of it the Ancients' own, made him the most dangerous Goa'uld there has ever been.

The return

Anubis came back after the deaths of Apophis and Cronus. At first he worked through underlords, among them Osiris, Zipacna and Tanith. In 2001 Tanith forced the Tollan, a people far more advanced than Earth, to build weapons for destroying Earth through the Stargate. The Tollan Narim blew the weapons up, and Tanith's ships laid Tollana waste.

In 2002 Osiris came before the System Lords in council on his behalf. Anubis, Osiris said, would destroy Earth as his gift to them if they took him back. Since he was not a System Lord, the Protected Planets Treaty did not bind him. They voted to take him back by six votes to one, with only Yu against. At the same time his underlord Zipacna fell on the Tok'ra base on Revanna, and very few of the Tok'ra there survived.

That year Anubis did a thing no other Goa'uld would have dared. Over Adara II, one of the protected worlds, the weapons of an Asgard ship made no impression on his shields, and Thor himself, who had come to drive him off, was taken prisoner. Anubis put a device into Thor's head that joined his mind to the ship's computers, meaning to read everything he knew.

Thor turned the link against him. Through it he let Jack O'Neill and Teal'c out of their cell. He guided them through the ship, which they crippled, and SG-1 got him away. Anubis withdrew when more Asgard ships arrived. He had learnt enough from Thor's mind by then to copy the way Asgard beams people from place to place, as well as its holograms.

Later in 2002 he used a weapon of the Ancients to hold open a wormhole to Earth's Stargate, pouring energy into it until it would explode with force enough to destroy the planet. O'Neill carried the gate away into space on Earth's new fighter, where it exploded harmlessly, while Teal'c, Bra'tac and Rya'c destroyed the weapon itself.

Abydos

Anubis built a great new ship with a weapon powered by the six Eyes of the Goa'uld. By 2003 he had five of them. The sixth, the Eye of Ra, was hidden on Abydos.

SG-1 found the Eye first. Yu had at last persuaded the other System Lords to act together, and their fleet came to face him. Daniel Jackson, whom Oma Desala had raised to a higher plane the year before, offered Anubis the Eye if he would leave Abydos alone for ever. Anubis agreed.

Once he had the Eye he destroyed most of the System Lords' fleet with his new weapon. Then he turned it on Abydos anyway. When Jackson struck at him, Oma Desala held Jackson back. The weapon fell on Abydos, but its people were already gone. Oma had raised them beyond his reach before it struck, Skaara among them.

Langara and the Kull

Later in 2003 SG-1 destroyed the weapon aboard Anubis's ship. Yu, whose mind was going, called off the attack that should have finished it.

Anubis took Jonas Quinn prisoner and read his mind. It led him to Langara, Jonas's home, and to its naquadria. He seized Kelowna while his Jaffa stripped the planet of the mineral. There Ba'al, now at the head of the System Lords' fleet, caught him and destroyed his ship. Anubis escaped in a pod.

He devised a new kind of soldier, the Kull warriors, armoured, nearly impossible to kill and utterly loyal to him. He made them on Tartarus, with a healing device of the Ancients and symbiotes without memories, born of a queen who served him. Later that year SG-1 got into Tartarus with Jacob Carter's help. They killed the queen, along with his servant Thoth, which slowed the making of more.

Earth

In 2004 Anubis came for Earth itself. He believed it held secrets of the Ancients, and he was right: there was an outpost of theirs under the ice of Antarctica.

He sank American warships from orbit, then appeared as a hologram in the White House to demand that Earth surrender to its god. The President of the United States offered to discuss the terms of Anubis's surrender instead.

Then the whole of his fleet came. Jack O'Neill, who carried the knowledge of the Ancients in his head at the time, reached the outpost first. From its chair he sent out its drone weapons, which destroyed Anubis's fleet, flagship and all.

Anubis did not die with it. Later that year what was left of him reached Earth aboard the International Space Station and passed from one body to another inside Stargate Command, trying to get to the gate. He went through at last in the body of a Russian officer, Colonel Alexei Vaselov, who had offered himself to spare the others. Samantha Carter had changed the address, so the gate sent him to a frozen world.

Dakara

Anubis got away from the frozen world. In secret he took back his forces from Ba'al, who from then on ruled the Goa'uld in his name.

He wanted the weapon that the Ancients had left on Dakara, which could destroy every living thing in the galaxy. Being what he was, he would survive it. Earth turned the weapon on the Replicators first, with Ba'al's help. In 2005 Anubis took Dakara back from the free Jaffa all the same, and he dialled every Stargate in the galaxy.

Oma Desala stopped him. Taking responsibility at last for the harm she had let loose, she rose against him and drew him away from the world into a struggle that neither of them can win. She cannot defeat him. But so long as she fights him he must fight back, and he can harm nobody else.

The weapon on Dakara fell silent. His Kull warriors stopped fighting and stood about, quite lost, as though nobody were telling them what to do any more.

Character

Anubis killed servants who failed him, as a lesson to the rest. He broke his word whenever it suited him, as Abydos found out. After his return he called himself a true god, in speeches grand even by the standards of the Goa'uld.

The other System Lords are cruel because cruelty is useful to them. Anubis was cruel in a way that frightened even them, and in the end he meant to kill every living thing in the galaxy except himself.

pages.title: Apocalypse
infobox: About 3000 BC, at Akkaba in Egypt
Command of every cell of his body
Unknown since early 1993, when he was left for dead on the Moon
pages.html:
Apocalypse is the first of the mutants. He was born in Egypt some five thousand years ago, in the years after the rising against Ra, and he has lived ever since by a single law: only the strong deserve to survive. He has added to his powers with the machines of the Celestials. He has slept away most of the centuries since his birth in hidden chambers, and each time he wakes he sets out to test the world, with four Horsemen to help him. Earth's heroes first met him in 1986. Nobody has known where he is since the beginning of 1993, when he was left for dead on the Moon.

Akkaba

En Sabah Nur was born about five thousand years ago at Akkaba, a settlement in Egypt, in the years just after the rising against Ra. Ra, the greatest of the Goa'uld, had ruled Egypt as its sun god until his slaves rose against him. Thor, the son of Odin, had come down in a storm to fight at their side, and Ra had fled. The Egypt the child was born into was a country getting used to the absence of its god.

He was born with grey skin and blue lips. The people of Akkaba took one look at him and left him in the desert to die.

He was found by Baal, the chief of the Sandstormers, a tribe of raiders who lived off the desert and whatever crossed it. This Baal was a mortal man, no kin to the Goa'uld System Lord Ba'al. The name means ‘lord’, and a great many men have borne it. Baal saw strength in the child. He raised him as his own son and named him En Sabah Nur, which means ‘the First One’.

The Sandstormers lived by one law, which Baal taught the boy before anything else: the strong survive, while the weak do not. En Sabah Nur grew up among them in the ruins of a god's rule. He drew his own lesson from Ra's fall, and he has never changed it. Ra had not been driven out because he was a tyrant. He had been driven out because he was not strong enough.

The First One

Baal died while En Sabah Nur was still young. The Sandstormers were attacked by the soldiers of a general called Ozymandias, and Baal, badly wounded, took refuge with the boy in a cave. Before he died he showed him what lay hidden there: machines left on Earth by the Celestials, the space gods who visited it before history began.

En Sabah Nur went into the royal city as a slave. There Ozymandias's sister, Nephri, took a liking to him, until she saw his true face and turned from him in disgust. His rage woke his powers to their full height. He gave himself a new name, Apocalypse, and from then on he did not grow any older.

He turned Ozymandias into a creature of living stone, blind, but able to see what is to come. Ozymandias has served him ever since. Then Apocalypse withdrew into the desert, vowing to return one day to test the strong and weed out the weak.

Powers and the machines of the Celestials

Apocalypse commands every cell of his body. He can make himself as tall as a house, grow his hands into blades or cannon, put out wings or close up any wound he is given. He is enormously strong, very hard to hurt and harder still to kill, since he can put himself back together after injuries that would kill anyone else.

The Celestials' experiments on the first human beings produced three new peoples: the Eternals, the Deviants and the mutants. Apocalypse has spent five thousand years studying the machines they left behind. He thinks of himself as tending what they planted, which in his view mostly means weeding it.

Like the Goa'uld, he rules by machines he did not make. Unlike the Goa'uld, he has taken the trouble to understand his.

The long sleeps

Apocalypse does not stay long in the world. He wakes, tests it and sleeps again, sometimes for centuries, while his body renews itself in one of the sanctuaries he keeps hidden about the world. Between sleeps he has gone about the earth in the guise of one god or another. He has set nation after nation at war, which he holds to be good for them.

His children, and their children after them, became Clan Akkaba, named after the village that left him to die. The clan has worshipped him as a living god for thousands of years. It watches over him while he sleeps, and wakes him when it must.

For his wars he chooses four servants at a time, named after the riders in the Revelation: War, Famine, Pestilence and Death. He calls them his Horsemen. He gives each of them new powers, which they pay for by belonging to him.

In 1859 he woke in London. There he gave a scientist called Nathaniel Essex the powers that made him Mister Sinister. Essex repaid him with a plague made to kill nobody but Apocalypse, who was obliged to go back to sleep to recover. Apocalypse forgave him with a warning, which is more than most people get.

The Goa'uld

After Ra's fall most of the Goa'uld kept away from Earth, since Ra had forbidden any of them to speak of it. At least one did not. Coming quietly to Earth in the centuries after Ra, it tried to take Apocalypse as its host, and it went in at the back of his neck, as the Goa'uld do.

Apocalypse, who can reshape every cell of his body at will, simply closed round it. The Goa'uld never learnt what had become of it. Apocalypse has never said, although it is a fair guess that he did not think it strong enough.

X-Factor

Apocalypse came to notice in 1986. That year the five original X-Men came together again as X-Factor, passing themselves off at first as hunters of mutants for hire. Early on they fought a band called the Alliance of Evil over Michael Nowlan, a mutant who could strengthen the powers of others. The master of the Alliance was Apocalypse.

He invited X-Factor aboard his ship, which hung unseen above Manhattan. He told them that their dream of peace did nothing to make mutants grow strong. They turned him down.

He chose four new Horsemen. Pestilence was Plague, one of the Morlocks, the mutants who live in the tunnels under New York. War was Abraham Kieros, a paralysed former soldier. Famine was Autumn Rolfson, an angry girl who wanted power over other people. The place of Death he kept for a man who had lost everything.

That man was Warren Worthington, the Angel, one of X-Factor's own founders. Late in 1986 killers working for Mister Sinister massacred the Morlocks, and Warren's wings were ruined in the fighting. In the spring of 1987 they had to be cut off. Soon afterwards the private plane he was flying blew up, and the world believed he was dead.

Apocalypse had taken him out of the plane at the last moment. He offered Warren new wings, but the price was Warren himself. By the end of 1987 Warren was the fourth Horseman, Death, with blue skin and wings of razor-edged metal.

At the start of 1988 the Horsemen fell on New York. Death fought his old friends until Bobby Drake, Iceman, tricked him into believing that he had killed him, and Warren turned on his master. With his help X-Factor beat the Horsemen. They took Apocalypse's ship for their headquarters.

Warren kept the blue skin and the metal wings. In 1989 he took a new name, Archangel. Few of Apocalypse's enemies hate him as Warren does.

Nathan

In 1991 Apocalypse's servants, the Riders of the Storm, carried off Nathan, the small son of Scott Summers, X-Factor's Cyclops. Apocalypse took the child to his stronghold on the Moon. There he infected him with a techno-organic virus, a sickness that turns living flesh into machinery.

X-Factor followed him to the Moon. They beat his Riders, wrecked his machines and seemed to have killed Apocalypse himself. Nathan was dying all the same.

A woman called Askani came out of the future, saying she had been sent to save the boy. Scott gave her his son. She took him away with her, nearly two thousand years ahead, where he might be cured.

His stronghold on the Moon was the Inhumans' city, whose people he had enslaved, and the Royal Family fought beside X-Factor.

Cable and Stryfe

Nathan grew up in the age that Askani came from, nearly two thousand years from now, in which Apocalypse rules the Earth. He spent his life fighting him. He came back to the twentieth century in 1990 as a grown man, with a metal arm where the virus had taken hold, under the name Cable. He took charge of a band of young mutants, the New Mutants, who became X-Force in 1991.

In case Nathan died of the virus, Askani's followers had made a clone of him while he was still a baby. Apocalypse's servants stole the clone. Apocalypse raised him as his heir, meaning one day to move into his body. The clone grew up believing that he was the real Nathan, abandoned by his parents. He called himself Stryfe.

When the time came, Apocalypse tried to pass into Stryfe's body. Nathan broke the bond between them, and Apocalypse's old body, with nowhere to go, withered away. That is the end of Apocalypse, nearly two thousand years from now.

Scott Summers saw it. In 1994, soon after he married Jean Grey, the two of them were drawn into that future in spirit. They spent twelve years there raising Nathan under other names, before they were returned to their own bodies.

The Moon

Stryfe followed Cable into the past. At the end of 1992 he shot Professor Xavier with a bullet carrying the virus, wearing Cable's face to do it. Then he had Scott Summers and Jean Grey carried off to Apocalypse's old base on the Moon.

Apocalypse had never fully recovered from his defeat of 1991, and his servants had woken him before he was ready. Stryfe caught him unawares and stabbed him in the chest. Apocalypse went to the X-Men for sanctuary. As the price of it he cured Xavier of the virus.

On the Moon his own servants, the Dark Riders, who had gone over to Stryfe, beat him almost to death. Archangel found him there. Apocalypse asked him to finish it. Warren refused, and left him to die.

Cable dragged Stryfe into a whirlpool of time, and the two of them vanished. Cable came back. Stryfe did not.

Nobody has seen Apocalypse since early in 1993. Nobody who knows him believes that he is dead.

Later years

Apocalypse came back early in 1995. Five years later he very nearly found himself a new body. He meant to take the body of a young mutant of enormous power, but Scott Summers gave himself up in the boy's place, and for months the two of them shared one body.

Early in 2001 Jean Grey tore Apocalypse out of her husband, and Cable destroyed what was left of him. He came back from that too, as he has come back from every death anyone has ever given him.

pages.title: Apophis
infobox: Apophis, the serpent of Egypt, enemy of the sun
Bra'tac; then Teal'c, who turned against him in 1997
2001, when his ship fell on Delmak
pages.html:
Apophis is one of the Goa'uld System Lords, the serpent god whose Jaffa wear the helmets of snakes. For thousands of years he was the rival of Ra, and when Ra died above Abydos in 1994 he moved faster than any of the others to take Ra's worlds. In 1997 he broke Ra's old ban on Earth and came through the Stargate, which began SG-1's long war with the Goa'uld. He lost two fleets in that war, as well as his queen, his son and his freedom. Every time, he came back stronger, until the Replicators finished him in 2001.

Ra's rival

Apophis takes his name from Apep, the great serpent of Egyptian story, who was the enemy of the sun. His host is an Egyptian scribe, whom he took thousands of years ago and has kept young in the sarcophagus ever since. The man is still in there, as every host is, although it was a very long time before anybody heard from him.

The priests of Egypt told how the serpent lay in wait every night for the boat that carried Ra through the underworld, and how every night he was beaten back. The story was a tidier version of the truth. For thousands of years Apophis was Ra's rival among the System Lords. Neither of them ever quite managed to destroy the other, and neither ever stopped trying.

They could still make common cause when it suited them. Long ago both of them joined the alliance that brought down Sokar, once among the mightiest of the System Lords. When the Egyptians rose against Ra, with Thor fighting beside them, Ra fled Earth and forbade any Goa'uld to speak of it again. Apophis kept the ban with the rest. He had no more wish to meet Thor than they had.

Chulak and the First Primes

Apophis rules from Chulak, the home world of the Jaffa. His personal guard, the Serpent Guard, wear helmets shaped like the heads of snakes. Every Jaffa in his service bears the mark of the serpent on his forehead, and for his First Prime it is set in gold.

For many years his First Prime was Bra'tac, the old master of the Jaffa of Chulak. Bra'tac served him faithfully, and believed privately that he was no god at all. He kept the belief to himself. In 1984 he was one of those whom the Beyonder carried off to Battleworld in the Secret Wars, so that a servant of Apophis stood for a while among the heroes of Earth.

Bra'tac's successor was his best pupil, Teal'c. Teal'c's father, Ronac, had been First Prime to the System Lord Cronus, who killed him for losing a battle that could not have been won. The boy was sent with his mother to Chulak in disgrace. There he grew up under Bra'tac's teaching to serve Apophis, and he rose to be the highest of his warriors. As First Prime he led the raids by which Apophis took hosts and slaves from worlds such as Cartago. He also came to share his old master's doubt.

Thor

Towards the end of the tenth century Apophis did something the System Lords seldom do: he made common cause with his rivals. With Heru'ur, Ra's own son, and with Ba'al, he brought his fleet against the worlds of Asgard, on the reckoning that Thor could not be everywhere at once.

Thor met the three fleets above a dead world on the edge of Goa'uld space, which the Jaffa still will not name. Apophis saw what was happening to the other two. He turned his own round before the end, and his was the only one of the three to survive. It was the worst defeat the Goa'uld had ever suffered. The Protected Planets Treaty followed soon afterwards.

Apophis does not speak of it. Every Goa'uld is born with the memories of its ancestors, so every Goa'uld remembers Thor. Apophis remembers him twice over.

After Ra

In 1994 the Tau'ri, as the Goa'uld call the people of Earth, destroyed Ra above Abydos. For the first time in thousands of years the System Lords had no Supreme System Lord, and Ra's worlds had no master. Apophis was quickest. He took more of Ra's domains than any of the others, and he took them first.

He had also learnt that it was the Tau'ri who had killed Ra. Earth was a nuisance again, and Ra was no longer there to forbid its name. As for Thor, Apophis had heard only what all the System Lords had heard: that the Thunderer seemed to be busy somewhere else. He did not know where, or why. Asgard had taken great care that he should not.

Earth

In 1997 Apophis came through the Stargate to Earth himself, the first System Lord to come openly in more than a thousand years. The gate stood in an American military base deep inside a mountain in Colorado. Five airmen were playing cards in front of it when it opened. His Jaffa seized one of them, Airman Carol Weterings, and Apophis looked her over. Then he had the other four shot. By the time the base's soldiers reached the gate room, he was going back through the gate with her.

The attack brought Colonel Jack O'Neill back into the service. It also sent him back to Abydos, whose gate he had reported destroyed in 1994. While his team was there, Apophis's Jaffa came through that gate as well. They seized Sha'uri, the wife of Daniel Jackson, and her brother Skaara, the boy who had taught O'Neill to want to live again. On Chulak, Apophis gave Sha'uri to his queen, Amaunet, as her host, and Skaara to his son, Klorel.

O'Neill's team followed them to Chulak and was taken prisoner there. Apophis's First Prime, Teal'c, was ordered to kill the prisoners. He turned on his master instead, escaped with them through the gate to Earth and joined O'Neill's new team, SG-1. From then on he was shol'va, the traitor, to every Goa'uld. Bra'tac became one of Earth's closest allies.

Apophis had come for hosts. What he had actually done was to remind Earth that the Goa'uld existed, and to show the Goa'uld that Earth would fight. From then on the System Lords took a close interest in Earth, and Earth, through SG-1, took a close interest in them.

The motherships

Early in 1998 Apophis came back in force. He and Klorel brought two motherships against Earth, the great pyramid-shaped ships of the Goa'uld, with an army aboard. SG-1 had already got on to his ship before it left. So had Bra'tac, who was still in Apophis's service. The old master threw in his lot with them, and together they planted explosives in both ships.

Both ships blew up above Earth. SG-1 escaped in death gliders and was picked up by an American space shuttle. Apophis and Klorel got away through the Stargate on board. Everything else was lost: the ships, the army and most of Apophis's standing among the System Lords. Hardly anybody on Earth ever knew how close it had come.

Apophis spent the rest of the year trying to make up for it. He kidnapped Teal'c's son, Rya'c, turned the boy's mind to his own service and hid in him a sickness meant to kill every living thing on Earth. SG-1 found the boy in time and broke the hold on his mind.

That summer Sha'uri bore Apophis a son. Amaunet had lain quiet inside her while she carried him, so that the child would live. A child of two Goa'uld hosts is called a Harcesis. It is born with all the knowledge of the Goa'uld in its head, and Goa'uld law forbids it. Sha'uri's father, Kasuf, hid the boy on Abydos, and Apophis was led to believe that Heru'ur had stolen him.

Sokar and Netu

Without his fleet Apophis was easy prey. Sokar, the old enemy whom he had once helped to bring down, caught him, tortured him to death, then revived him in the sarcophagus and began again.

Early in 1999 Apophis escaped in a death glider and crashed on a distant world, where SG-1 found him dying. He begged them for sanctuary, and they took him to Earth. Sokar fired a beam through the wormhole at the iris that guards Earth's gate, and he showed his face on it to demand Apophis back. Apophis died in the infirmary. Before the end his host, the Egyptian scribe, was able to speak for himself for the first time in thousands of years. When he died, Daniel Jackson said the rites of the dead over him. Then the body was sent through the gate to Sokar, who put it back in the sarcophagus.

In the summer of 1999 SG-1 found a world where Apophis had been training humans in the uniforms of Earth's teams to slip into the base in Colorado. They were still drilling for him months after his death on Earth, until SG-1 showed them a recording of his death and they gave him up. That autumn Amaunet tried to kill Daniel Jackson with her hand device, and Teal'c killed her to save him.

Sokar had sent Apophis down to Netu, the prison moon of Delmak, which he had made over in the likeness of Hell. Apophis did not stay a prisoner. He passed himself off as the First Prime of Bynarr, the underlord who kept the moon for Sokar, then killed Bynarr and began to raise the prisoners against their master.

A few weeks after Amaunet's death SG-1 came to Netu to rescue Jacob Carter, the host of the Tok'ra Selmak, whom Sokar had caught. Apophis captured them and tortured them for anything they knew that might help him against Sokar. The Tok'ra settled the matter with a bomb. It destroyed Netu, together with Sokar's ship in orbit above it, and Sokar died with his ship. SG-1 escaped with Jacob Carter. So did Apophis, who took Sokar's leaderless forces on Delmak for his own. He had come back from the dead with a larger army than he had ever had.

Heru'ur

Apophis's chief rival was now Heru'ur, Ra's son, who had once stood beside him against Asgard. While Apophis was still rebuilding, Heru'ur went after his son. Early in 2000 two of Heru'ur's motherships chased Klorel to Tollana, where the Tollans' guns destroyed them both. Klorel came down there in a death glider. The Tollans put him on trial, and their judges ruled that Skaara had the better right to his own body. The Tok'ra took Klorel out of him, and Klorel was sent away to a Goa'uld world.

That summer SG-1 destroyed a new kind of mothership that Apophis was building on a distant world. By the autumn of 2000 he and Heru'ur commanded the two largest armies the Goa'uld had. Together they could have overthrown every other System Lord. At war, they would have ruined each other. They agreed to meet alone in the Tobin minefield, a belt of floating mines left by a people long extinct, to talk of an alliance.

Heru'ur brought a gift to seal the bargain. It was Teal'c, who had been betrayed on Chulak by a Jaffa named Rak'nor and handed over to be broken by Heru'ur's torturer, Terok. Teal'c would not break. Rak'nor watched him hold out, and changed his mind. He struck Terok down, set Teal'c free and sent the senseless Terok across to Apophis in Teal'c's place.

Apophis had not come alone either. A whole fleet of his lay hidden close by under cloak. When he found that he had been cheated of Teal'c, he brought it out and destroyed Heru'ur's ship, with Heru'ur aboard. He took Heru'ur's fleet and Jaffa for his own. With them, and with Sokar's, he now led the largest army of any Goa'uld alive.

The Replicators

Early in 2001 Apophis brought his fleet to Vorash, the world where the Tok'ra had their base. SG-1 and the Tok'ra met him there with the mothership SG-1 had lately taken from Cronus. They dropped a Stargate into Vorash's sun with its wormhole open to a black hole, and the sun exploded. The blast destroyed Apophis's fleet. It threw his own ship, and SG-1's with it, into another galaxy. Teal'c, whom Apophis had taken prisoner in the battle, went with him.

Far from home, the Replicators found him. A strange ship attacked his. The Replicators came aboard from it, killing his Jaffa as they went. Apophis escaped in a cargo ship with Teal'c, whom he had revived in the sarcophagus and persuaded that he was once again his loyal First Prime. With Teal'c's help he took SG-1's ship and set a course for Delmak, his new home. He had brought the Replicators with him.

They took that ship too, and drove it towards home far faster than it had ever been built to go. SG-1 wrecked its sublight engines, so that it could not slow down when it came out of hyperspace, then got away with Teal'c in the cargo ship. The mothership fell on Delmak out of the sky. Apophis was still aboard, shut in his command chamber while the Replicators swarmed over him. He did not get out.

That was the end of Apophis, who had escaped Thor, Earth and Sokar in turn. The ship that killed him had once been Cronus's. His death also gave the System Lords their first sight of the Replicators, and the first hint they had of the war that had kept Thor so busy for so long.

pages.title: Asgard
infobox: The Protected Planets Treaty, with the Goa'uld System Lords
pages.html:
Asgard is the realm of the Aesir, the long-lived people whom the Norse worshipped as gods. It is ruled by Odin All-Father, and Thor is his son. Asgard is also a power among the stars, one that the Goa'uld System Lords fear. It holds the Protected Planets Treaty with them and is at war with the Replicators, which is why Thor is absent from Earth in 1994.

The Realm Eternal

Asgard is one of the Nine Worlds held in the branches of the World Tree, Yggdrasil. It is joined to Earth, which its people call Midgard, by Bifrost, the Rainbow Bridge, which the watchman Heimdall guards. Its golden city is ruled by Odin, with his wife Frigga beside him. Among its people are Thor; his adopted brother Loki, a scheming sorcerer; Balder the Brave; the warrior Sif and the Warriors Three.

The Aesir are far stronger and longer-lived than humans, though they are not immortal. They keep their youth by eating the golden apples of Idunn. The Norsemen knew them as gods. The old stories of Thor, Odin and Loki are memories of them. Asgard came to the notice of the modern world in 1962, soon after Thor did, and the Avengers have fought there more than once since.

The Protected Planets Treaty

The Asgard High Council holds a treaty with the Goa'uld System Lords, the parasites who rule much of the galaxy. Under it the Goa'uld must leave alone the worlds it names. Its terms bind Asgard as well. Asgard may not use its own technology to advance the peoples it protects, and a serious breach on one world could free the Goa'uld to attack all of them.

One protected world, Cimmeria, is home to a people descended from Norsemen. There Thor left a device known as Thor's Hammer, which seizes any Goa'uld who comes through the stargate. Earth is not one of the protected worlds.

The treaty came out of Thor's wars with the Goa'uld. He fought beside the Egyptians when they drove Ra off Earth some five thousand years ago, and for thousands of years afterwards he hunted the Goa'uld wherever they came near the North. He ended the war by destroying the combined fleets of Apophis, Heru'ur and Ba'al. The System Lords fear Asgard, but Thor they fear in particular. It is said in Asgard that their first demand was that he should not be present at the signing.

The Replicator war

The Replicators are machines built of small identical blocks, which join together into larger forms like insects. They feed on metal and technology. They copy whatever they take in, multiplying without end, and the more advanced the technology they take, the more dangerous they become. They have overrun worlds that belonged to Asgard, and they adapt to its weapons as fast as it can design new ones.

Asgard's fleet fights them under Thor's command. The war has become Asgard's first concern, and it has left Asgard less able to enforce its treaty with the Goa'uld. It also keeps Thor away from Earth. In his absence Eric Masterson, who once served as Thor himself, carries Odin's gift, the mace Thunderstrike, among the Avengers.

The Goa'uld have never been told of the war, and Asgard means to keep it that way. It goes on showing its ships over the protected worlds as though its fleet had nothing else to do. The System Lords, who do not know the truth, still believe Asgard could crush any of them that broke the treaty, and it is that belief, more than Asgard's ships, which keeps the protected worlds safe.

pages.title: Ba'al
infobox: Baal, the storm god of Canaan
The coasts of the North, about 1000 BC
Thor, Lord Yu, SG-1, the Tok'ra
Shot dead by Cameron Mitchell in 1939, having travelled there from 2008
Taken from its host by the Tok'ra, 2008
pages.html:
Ba'al is a Goa'uld System Lord, and the cleverest of them by some distance. The Canaanites worshipped him as Baal. About 1000 BC he raided the coasts of the North in defiance of Ra's ban on Earth, and Thor followed him home. He has kept the ban ever since. From 2002 he was one of SG-1's most persistent enemies: he tortured Jack O'Neill to death many times over, led the System Lords against Anubis and outlived every one of them. He died in 1939, shot through the head by Cameron Mitchell, having gone back there from 2008 to change history.

Baal of Canaan

Ba'al took his name from Baal, the lord of storms whom the Canaanites worshipped, as did the Phoenicians. He came to them quietly, in defiance of Ra's ban, as a few of the bolder Goa'uld did, and he kept well away from the North.

His worship spread along the eastern shores of the Mediterranean. It lasted for centuries after he had stopped coming, and the prophets of Israel spent a good deal of their time denouncing it.

The raid on the North

About 1000 BC Ba'al grew bolder. He thought Ra's ban one of Ra's vanities, so he sent his ships to the coasts of what is now Norway to carry off people as slaves and hosts.

Thor met them on the shore. He killed every Jaffa who set foot on the beach, and he brought one of the ships down into the sea with his lightning. Then he followed the rest of them home. On the world where Ba'al kept his palace he freed the captives, broke the palace open and killed every Goa'uld he could find in it. Ba'al himself escaped.

Some time afterwards Thor sent him a jar. In it was the symbiote of one of his underlords.

Ba'al has kept Ra's ban ever since. He is not a Goa'uld who needs to be told anything twice. He had learnt to keep away from Earth. He had not yet learnt to keep away from Thor.

The war of the 990s

In the 990s Ba'al joined Apophis and Heru'ur in one of the very few alliances the System Lords have ever managed. The three of them brought their fleets together to strike at the worlds of Asgard, reasoning that Thor could not be everywhere at once.

Thor met them above a dead world on the edge of Goa'uld space. Ba'al's fleet was one of the two he destroyed, and Thor went down after its survivors to finish them on the ground. Apophis saved his own fleet only by running. Ba'al lived, as he generally does.

About the year 1000 the System Lords asked Asgard for terms, and the Protected Planets Treaty was the result. Asgard says, and the System Lords deny, that their first demand was that Thor should not be present at the signing. Earth was left off the list.

The summit and Jack O'Neill

By 2002 Apophis and Cronus were both dead. The other System Lords had spent months fighting over their worlds, and when they met in council to make peace, it was Ba'al who presided. Osiris came before them as the envoy of Anubis, whom they had banished long before and believed dead. Ba'al put Anubis's return to the vote. It passed by six votes to one, with only Yu against.

Ba'al's own lo'taur, his favoured human slave, warned Yu that Yu's slave was not to be trusted. He was quite right: the slave was Daniel Jackson in disguise.

Later that year Ba'al's Jaffa caught Jack O'Neill as he ran for the Stargate on the world of Ba'al's secret fortress. O'Neill was carrying a Tok'ra, Kanan, who had been blended with him to save his life. Kanan had once spied in Ba'al's household, where he had fallen for Ba'al's lo'taur, Shallan. He had used O'Neill's body to go back for her. When they were caught, Kanan abandoned O'Neill's body, leaving O'Neill to answer for him.

Ba'al wanted to know what Kanan knew. At the fortress he had been studying gravity in secret, and he pinned O'Neill to a wall with one of his gravity fields. Then he dropped knives into the field until O'Neill died. He revived him in the sarcophagus and began again. The next time he used acid. O'Neill was killed and brought back many times.

Earth had no ship that could reach the fortress. Instead it sent its plans to Yu, who had every reason to want the place destroyed, asking him to strike at its power first. Yu's ships bombarded it from orbit, the power failed and O'Neill escaped with Shallan.

The war against Anubis

In 2003 the System Lords put their fleets together against Anubis under Lord Yu, who was by then too far gone to lead them. Teal'c and Oshu, Yu's First Prime, persuaded Ba'al to take command. His fleet caught Anubis's great ship above Langara and destroyed it, although Anubis escaped in a pod.

Ba'al used the ships he had been given against Anubis to make himself greater than any of the others, which surprised nobody who knew him. On Erebus, a world he had lately taken, Jaffa who would not change masters mined naquadah for his new motherships until the fumes killed them. Bra'tac was among them, with Teal'c's son Rya'c, until SG-1 got them out.

Later that year he got hold of a computer virus that Earth had made to disable Stargates. He altered it, spread it through the whole network of gates and attacked his rivals while their gates were dead. He had the largest fleet of any System Lord, so he gained more from it than anybody.

Supreme Commander

Anubis's fleet was destroyed over Earth in 2004. To keep the peace, the System Lords divided his worlds among themselves. Ba'al, however, found Tartarus, where Anubis had made his Kull warriors, and took them for himself.

Yu, Camulus and Amaterasu went to Earth to ask for help against him. While they talked, Ba'al destroyed the ship they had come in. Camulus begged Earth for asylum. Ba'al got him all the same, by pretending to hold SG-1 prisoner and offering to trade them for him. Camulus was not seen again. When Moloc was killed later that year, Ba'al took his domain as well.

By 2005 he had conquered or cowed most of the other System Lords, and he called himself the Supreme Commander of the Goa'uld. In truth he was a servant. Anubis had returned in secret and taken back his forces. From then on Ba'al ruled in his name, which he disliked very much.

That year the Replicators came into the galaxy. The Goa'uld found out at last what had been keeping Asgard so busy, and it was not good news. The machines tore through the fleets of the System Lords. Yu was killed by one of them at the very meeting where Ba'al's envoy, Selkhet, had come to offer the last of the High Council terms.

Ba'al was losing too, so he came to Earth by hologram to ask for help. He told Earth of the weapon the Ancients had left on Dakara, which could wipe out every living thing in the galaxy, and warned that Anubis meant to use it. With his help Samantha Carter and her father, Jacob, turned the weapon on the Replicators instead. Ba'al gave them a means of dialling every Stargate in the galaxy at once, so that it struck everywhere together.

It was the end of the Goa'uld empire all the same. When Ba'al moved to take back Dakara, rebel Jaffa stormed his ship, and he saved himself by beaming away. Jaffa all over the galaxy saw one of their gods run, and stopped believing. Anubis kept Ba'al alive so that he could watch the end of everything. Then Oma Desala took Anubis out of the world, and Ba'al was left as the last of the System Lords.

The clones

With his armies gone, Ba'al went to Earth, the world whose ban he had kept for three thousand years. There was nothing left to keep. He set himself up as a businessman, bought companies and took over the Trust, a secret society of rogue intelligence agents that the Goa'uld had already got into. He also made copies of himself, each of whom claimed to be the real one.

In 2005 he warned Earth that he would destroy one of its cities if anybody tried to take him. SG-1 tried anyway. The bomb turned out to be a whole new skyscraper in Seattle, built with naquadah through its frame, and Earth's ship Prometheus beamed it into space before it went off. Gerak, a Jaffa leader, caught a Ba'al and put him to death on Dakara in front of Teal'c. It was one of the clones.

The clones went on scheming for years. In 2006 one of them set about brainwashing the new Jaffa High Council until Teal'c killed him. Others stole Stargates. Later that year a Ba'al crashed a ship on Earth and gave himself up, saying that his clones had turned on him. SG-1 rounded up twenty of them before they all escaped together, taking with them a list of the gate addresses of the Ancients.

In 2007 a Ba'al seized Adria, who led the armies of the Ori. He gathered the other clones in one place and killed them with poison, then put one more into Adria to take her as a host. SG-1 killed the Ba'al behind the plot. The Tok'ra took the one in Adria out of her, but as they did it he poisoned her with the last of his strength.

The last Ba'al

In 2008 the Tok'ra took the last of the clones from its host on their own homeworld, after reading aloud the list of Ba'al's crimes, which took three hours. The clone told SG-1 that they had made a terrible mistake. The real Ba'al was still at large, and he had planned for this.

He had. The real Ba'al had gone back through time, by way of an outpost for watching the sun on the world of Praxyon, to 1939. That year the Stargate was crossing the Atlantic to America in the hold of a freighter, the Achilles. Ba'al came through it with his Jaffa, killed the crew and left a bomb to sink the ship.

For a little while he succeeded. History ran differently: the gate lay frozen in the Arctic, there was no Stargate programme, and Ba'al, who knew what was coming, made himself master of the Goa'uld. He took Qetesh as his queen and Teal'c as his First Prime. He chose to deceive the people of Earth rather than slaughter them, having been impressed by them the first time round. Qetesh grew suspicious of how much he knew and killed him with a sword.

Cameron Mitchell was one of three members of SG-1 who had slipped through the change. He went back to 1929, the nearest year he could reach, and waited ten years. When the gate on the Achilles opened in 1939 he was waiting in the hold with a Thompson gun beside the ship's bosun. They shot the Jaffa as they came through. Then Mitchell shot Ba'al through the head.

History went back to its proper course. On the Tok'ra homeworld the extraction went ahead without a hitch, and nobody there ever knew what had happened. So the last of the System Lords died in the hold of a freighter in the Atlantic, at the hands of a man who had waited ten years for him.

Character

Ba'al does not believe that he is a god. Among those who already know the truth he does not trouble to pretend, and he suspects that most other Goa'uld do not believe it either. He is dry, patient and quick. He keeps a short, neat beard, and he dresses well.

He prefers a trick to a battle. Unlike most of his kind he likes to do his own work. He experimented with gravity himself, and he knows the workings of the Stargate network better than any other Goa'uld.

He is entirely selfish but never stupid. When something threatens the whole galaxy, Ba'al is usually the first Goa'uld to notice, if only because he lives in it too.

pages.title: Bahro
infobox: The cavern of D'ni and its Ages
When the Tablet was given to them
pages.html:
The Bahro are a hidden race of beings, not human, who lived in the cavern of D'ni before the D'ni came. The D'ni took the cavern from them and made them slaves. Yeesha, the daughter of Atrus, calls them the Least, and she has worked for their freedom.

The name

Bahro is a D'ni word, and an insulting one, usually rendered as beast people. The D'ni and their Ronay ancestors used it for peoples who were not human. In Terahnee, the lost sister realm of D'ni, it was the word for slaves.

Bondage

The beings who bear the name lived in the great cavern under New Mexico before the D'ni arrived, nearly ten thousand years ago. The D'ni took the cavern from them and enslaved them. There are signs that they were once hunted for sport.

The D'ni bound the Bahro with a stone Tablet whose holder could command them. The Bahro move between places, and even between worlds, without books. They answer to symbols drawn on slates. Long after the Fall of D'ni, when the city stood empty, they stayed on in its shadows. Screams in the dark of the cavern have been put down to them.

The Grower

A prophecy among them spoke of a Grower who would restore D'ni. Yeesha came to believe that she was the one. She unlocked the Tablet, chose wrongly with it and lost the power to use it. In the end the Tablet was given to the Bahro themselves, and their bondage was over.

In the saga

The Bahro have not appeared in the saga. They belong to the hidden life of the cavern, which the small group of Muggles digging under New Mexico in the 1990s have only begun to uncover.

pages.title: Barry Allen
pages.html:
Barry Allen was the second Flash, the red-suited speedster of Central City. He came to public notice in 1956, helped to found the Justice League and died in 1985 in the Crisis, in a battle nobody has ever properly explained. Wally West, his nephew by marriage, has carried the name ever since.

The police scientist

Barry Allen was a police scientist in Central City, a careful and famously unhurried man. One night in 1956 a bolt of lightning smashed through his laboratory window and drenched him in a rack of chemicals. Afterwards the most unhurried man in the Central City police found that he could move faster than sound.

He made himself a red costume with a lightning flash on the chest, which folded away into a ring. He took the name of the Flash from Jay Garrick, the Justice Society hero he had admired as a boy. In 1961 he met Jay in person, and helped to bring him back into action with several of his old team.

At the turn of 1960 Barry was among the founders of the Justice League. He married the reporter Iris West, whose young nephew Wally had been given the same powers by the same freak accident in 1959, and he trained the boy as Kid Flash. He fought a long line of enemies, among them Captain Cold, Gorilla Grodd and, worst of all, Professor Zoom, who murdered Iris in 1979. In 1983 Barry killed Zoom to stop him from murdering again, and he stood trial for it.

Death

Barry Allen died in 1985, during the Crisis. Those who were there say that he was captured and escaped. Then he ran faster than he had ever run, to destroy a weapon aimed at the world, and he went on running until there was nothing left of him but his costume. Like everything about the Crisis, the details are uncertain. The world knew only that the Flash was gone, and soon afterwards that the boy who had run beside him had taken up his name.

In the saga

On 20 August 1994, watching the news at the Dursleys', Harry Potter reflected that the Flash of Dudley's old annuals had died in 1985, in a battle nobody had ever properly explained. The Flash now standing behind Superman was the boy who used to run beside him.

pages.title: Bastet
infobox: Bastet, the cat goddess of Egypt
Killed in Ba'al's war on the System Lords, by early 2005
pages.html:
Bastet is a Goa'uld System Lord who was worshipped in Egypt, long ago, as a goddess with the head of a cat. Among the Goa'uld she is known for treachery, which in that company is saying a good deal. In 2002 she sat at the council of the System Lords that took Anubis back among them. She was killed in Ba'al's war on the other System Lords, and was dead by early 2005.

The cat goddess

Bastet was one of the Goa'uld who ruled in Egypt in Ra's day. The Egyptians knew her as a goddess with a cat's head, the protector of the home, of women in childbirth and of secrets. She left Earth with the rest of them when the Egyptians rose against Ra, about 3000 BC. Afterwards she kept Ra's ban on speaking of Earth, as all the System Lords did, and she is not known ever to have gone back.

The Egyptians went on worshipping her for thousands of years without her. Her chief city was Bubastis, in the Nile delta, where her temple stood and the cats sacred to her were buried by the thousand.

Sobek

Bastet's best-known treachery was carried out with Kali the Destroyer. The two of them made a treaty with Sobek, a Goa'uld who had taken the name of the crocodile god of Egypt. Then they turned on him at the feast held to celebrate it, when he had let his guard down. It is said that his head still decorates Bastet's palace.

Lord Yu, the oldest of the System Lords, knew the story perfectly well. In 2002 he still reckoned Bastet and Kali his likeliest allies.

The council at Hasara

In 2002 the System Lords met under truce on a space station in the Hasara system, which they counted as neutral ground. For months an enemy none of them could name had been attacking their worlds. He struck only with his ships, never with troops on the ground, and none of them knew who he was.

Bastet brought the nearest thing to evidence. When her outpost on Zeldor was attacked, her First Prime had disabled one of the enemy's ships and boarded it. Its Jaffa fought to the death. Most of them had been in the service of Cronus or Sokar, she told the council, but one bore the mark of Olokun. Olokun, who was sitting with the rest of them, took it very badly.

The enemy turned out to be Anubis, whom the System Lords had cast out long before. He sent Osiris to the council to ask for his old place among them. Bastet had lost two motherships to him, and she said so. She voted to take him back all the same. Only Yu voted against.

Ba'al's war

By 2003 Yu was failing, and the combined fleet he led against Anubis was failing with him. Teal'c of SG-1 and Oshu, Yu's First Prime, went looking for another System Lord to take the command. Ba'al refused it with contempt. Teal'c wondered aloud whether they should ask Bastet instead. Ba'al promptly changed his mind. It was probably the most useful thing Bastet ever did for anybody, and she was not even there.

After Earth defeated Anubis in 2004, Ba'al took Anubis's Kull warriors for himself and turned them on the other System Lords. Their Jaffa were no match for the Kull. Early in 2005 the Tok'ra reported that Bastet was dead.

pages.title: Biteborn
infobox: Garou made by the bite rather than born
pages.html:
The biteborn are Garou made by the bite rather than born. It is rare. A Garou in any of its shapes can pass the change by biting, at any hour, though it does not pass with every bite. The Litany frowns on it, and most Garou never do it. Those who make others by the bite on purpose mostly serve the Wyrm. The tribes despise the biteborn as no true Garou, though by every measure that matters they are Garou. Remus Lupin is biteborn.

The bite

The Garou are a born people. The blood runs quiet for generations in Kinfolk families, human and wolf. Then a child is born who has it, and the First Change wakes it.

But there is a second way in. A Garou in any of its shapes can make another by the bite, upon anyone and at any hour. Severus Snape put it plainly to the Hogwarts third-years in 1993: 'They are born. Or a man is bitten.'

It happens rarely. The change does not pass with every bite, and very few Garou will ever try to pass it. The Litany frowns on making Garou by the bite. A Garou of the thirteen tribes who did it would answer to his sept for it. The great exception is the fallen tribe, the Black Spiral Dancers. They make others by the bite deliberately, and they are extremely particular in their choosing.

Garou in every measure

Whatever the tribes say of them, the biteborn are Garou. A biteborn wears all five shapes at will, from the man to the wolf, with the nine-foot war form between. He carries the rage that sits in every Garou like fire in a lamp. The moon raises its tide in him as in any other.

He has a birth sign, and the work that goes with it. He can learn the Gifts of the spirits and step sideways into the spirit world. He can smell the Wyrm in a place, an object or a man. Silver burns him. Those who see him in his war form suffer the Delirium. The Litany binds him, and Gaia accepts him. By every measure the Garou themselves use, a biteborn is a Garou.

'Not true Garou'

The tribes despise them all the same. The Garou set great store by blood and breeding. They care about Kinfolk lines, the names of ancestors, the tribe a whelp is born into and the moon it is born under. A biteborn has none of that by birth.

Many Garou call the biteborn not true Garou. They are made things, the tribes say, the fruit of a crime against the Litany. Very likely they carry the taint of whatever bit them, since most Garou who make others by the bite belong to the Wyrm.

A biteborn is given the worst work and the least thanks. He is passed over for rank, and spoken over at moots. He must prove at every turn what a born Garou is simply assumed to be. Few septs will take one at all. The contempt is close kin to the way the Garou treat the metis, the malformed children of two Garou. In some septs it is worse, for a metis was at least born of the People.

The Wyrm's biteborn

The Black Spiral Dancers are the one people among whom the biteborn are common. They choose with care, children above all. They raise them apart from their families, and turn them to the Wyrm before they are grown. Fenrir Greyback, the Spiral Dancer who bit Remus Lupin, seeks out the children of wizards, so that one day there will be enough of his kind to overwhelm wizards altogether.

It is the Spiral Dancers' biteborn that the tribes have in mind when they say a bitten Garou carries the taint of the thing that bit him. It is also why a biteborn of the thirteen tribes, like Lupin, must spend his life proving that he does not.

Remus Lupin

Remus Lupin was bitten as a very small boy by Greyback, in revenge on his father. He has been Garou ever since.

After 1981 he found a pack in the hills of mid-Wales, mostly of the Fianna, which fought beside him and still sends for him. It never let him forget, for a single day, that he was bitten rather than born. Worse, he was a wizard.

He is still himself in his war form, and remembers everything he does in it. He holds his rage in check with the Wolfsbane Potion, his faith and a great deal of prayer. In June 1994 Harry Potter saw him take that war form in the grounds of Hogwarts.

pages.title: Black Furies
infobox: Greece, Asia Minor and the shores of the Black Sea
Avenging wronged women and children; guarding the wild
pages.html:
The Black Furies are one of the thirteen tribes of the Garou: a tribe of women, risen from ancient Greece and the lands about the Black Sea. They guard the wild places of the world. They take vengeance on those who prey on women and children.

Totem and ways

The Furies follow Pegasus, the winged horse, a spirit of wild places, freedom and righteous anger. They take their name from the avenging spirits of the old Greek stories, and they count the Amazons among their ancestors. Their members are women born to the tribe's Kinfolk. Sons who prove to be Garou are given to other tribes to raise, most often to the Children of Gaia. Only the male metis stay among the Furies, tolerated rather than honoured.

They are fierce, proud and disciplined. They are devoted to the Wyld above the other powers of creation, because they see in it the untamed strength that the Weaver's order and the Wyrm's corruption both seek to crush. Their rites honour Gaia, as well as the moon in her three aspects of maiden, mother and crone.

Homelands

The tribe's oldest caerns lie in Greece, in Asia Minor and about the Black Sea. They are mountain sanctuaries, sacred groves or caves that were holy before the first temples were built. Over the centuries the Furies spread through the Mediterranean and Europe, then across the oceans. Wherever they go, they make a point of seeking out the wild places that nobody else defends.

Place in the world

Among the Garou the Black Furies are respected as warriors and feared as judges. They hunt down men who harm women and children, whether or not those men serve the Wyrm. They are closest to the Children of Gaia, who raise their sons. They are slow to trust any tribe they think proud or domineering, and slowest of all to trust the Get of Fenris.

pages.title: The Black Widow
infobox: Black Widow; Natasha Romanoff; Natalia Romanova
The Soviet Union, in the late 1930s
The Avengers (from 1973; chairwoman since 1992); formerly the Champions of Los Angeles; formerly the KGB
pages.html:
The Black Widow is Natasha Romanoff, born Natalia Romanova. She was a Soviet agent who came to America in 1964 to destroy Tony Stark, broke with her masters and became one of the Avengers. She has been the team's chairwoman since 1992, and in August 1994, a woman in her mid-fifties, she still holds the chair.

The Soviet agent

Natalia Romanova was trained as a spy in the Soviet Union. In 1964 she was sent to the United States to sabotage the work of the armaments maker Tony Stark, whose Iron Man was then the face of American power. She worked against him for two years. In that time she drew the young archer Hawkeye into her schemes. He fell in love with her, and slowly she came to return it.

Her husband, the test pilot Alexi Shostakov, had been reported dead, and her masters used his memory to keep their hold on her. In the end she broke with them and stayed in America.

The Avengers

From 1970 she worked as a costumed adventurer in her own right, for a time in San Francisco. In 1973 she joined the Avengers. In the middle of the decade she led a short-lived team of her own in Los Angeles, the Champions.

She has served with the Avengers on and off ever since. In 1992 she became the team's chairwoman. Under her the Avengers kept to their United Nations accord through the Augment War. On 19 August 1994 the team's delegation, Captain America among it, stood with Superman before the Security Council.

Age

She was already a grown woman when she first came to America in 1964, and she has aged as everyone else has. In 1994 she is in her mid-fifties, one of the oldest of the serving Avengers after Captain America, whose years do not show.

pages.title: Blade
infobox: Deacon Frost, the vampire who fed on his mother
Sixty-five by the calendar; he looks far younger
pages.html:
Blade, born Eric Brooks in London in 1929, is a dhampir and the most famous vampire hunter of the modern age. No vampire fathered him. The vampire Deacon Frost fed on his mother while she was giving birth to him, and he came into the world with the taint of the blood in him. He has a vampire's strength and senses without its weakness to the sun. The Kindred call him the Daywalker, and he has spent his life destroying them.

Birth

His mother, Tara Brooks, went into labour in 1929 in a house in Soho, in London. A doctor was sent for, and the man who came was the vampire Deacon Frost. He fed on her as the child was born, and she died of it. The child lived. The vampire's taint passed into his blood at the moment of his birth.

The hunter

He was brought up by the women of the house where he was born. When he was nine he met Jamal Afari, an American jazz trumpeter who hunted vampires, and Afari trained him. When Afari was sired in his turn, Blade destroyed him.

He has hunted the Kindred ever since, at first with knives of teak and later with a sword. Above all he has hunted Deacon Frost.

A dhampir

By the laws of the blood, only the thin-blooded of the last generations can father children, and Blade had no vampire father at all. The Kindred count him a dhampir all the same, because he bears every mark of one. He and Alucard, the son of Dracula, are both exceptions to the rule that a dhampir is a thin-blood's child, for very different reasons.

He is far stronger and quicker than any ordinary man. He can sense the Kindred near him, no vampire can sire him, and he ages far more slowly than other men. He carries a share of the thirst as well, and has held it down all his life. He is sixty-five years old in 1994 by the calendar, and he looks very much younger.

pages.title: Blue Beetle
infobox: Mystery Men Comics #1 (August 1939); Ted Kord in Captain Atom #83 (November 1966)
pages.html:
Blue Beetle is the name of two American heroes. The first was Dan Garret, who came to public notice in 1939 and drew his powers from a scarab found in Egypt. The second is his former student, Ted Kord, an inventor with no powers at all, who has carried the name since 1966. Ted Kord helped to found the new Justice League in 1987, and in 1992 Doomsday very nearly killed him.

Dan Garret

The first Blue Beetle was Dan Garret, an archaeologist who found an ancient scarab in an Egyptian tomb. At a spoken word the scarab gave him great strength and endurance, among other powers. From 1939 he fought crime with it in a blue costume. He was killed in 1966 on Pago Island, fighting Ted Kord's uncle, Jarvis Kord, who had built an army of androids there and meant to conquer the world with it. With his last breath he passed the name to his student Ted, though not the scarab's power. Ted kept the scarab, but he never could make it answer to him.

Ted Kord

Ted Kord was a scientist, inventor and athlete who had no powers whatever. He fought as Blue Beetle with gadgets of his own design, chief among them the Bug, a flying craft shaped like a beetle, and he paid for it all with the fortune of Kord Industries. He was one of the founders of the new Justice League in 1987. In the League he became known for his jokes, and for his partnership with Booster Gold.

In the autumn of 1992 the League was the first to meet Doomsday. Blue Beetle was beaten into a coma, but he lived. Superman, who took up the fight after them, did not. Ted Kord recovered in time and went back to the League.

pages.title: Bone Gnawers
infobox: The poor quarters of every city
The poor, the homeless and the outcast
Survival, scavenging and knowing everything that happens on the streets
pages.html:
The Bone Gnawers are one of the thirteen tribes of the Garou: the tribe of the streets, living among the poor, the homeless and the outcast of the world's cities. Other tribes look down on them. There is hardly a city on earth, all the same, where the Bone Gnawers do not know exactly what is going on.

Totem and ways

The Bone Gnawers follow Rat, a spirit of survival, of cunning and of plenty in hard places. Their name comes from their habit of living off what others throw away, and they are proud of it. They make their homes in alleys, under bridges, in derelict buildings and in cardboard shelters. Their Kinfolk are the people nobody else counts: the destitute, the drifting and the forgotten.

They are scavengers, survivors and gatherers of news. A Bone Gnawer may look like a tramp on a park bench and know more about the neighbourhood than any policeman. They share what they have, and they look after their own. Their Gifts suit the life. They run to going unnoticed, finding a meal where there seems to be none, and hearing whatever the street knows.

They fight the Wyrm where it hurts the poor first: in poisoned slums, in the drug trade and in the cruelty of the powerful towards the weak.

Homelands

The tribe claims no single homeland. Bone Gnawers say they have followed people into towns ever since the first towns were built, scavenging at the edges of every settlement. They are now found in every large city in the world, wherever there are streets for people to fall through.

Place in the world

In the Garou Nation the Bone Gnawers have the lowest standing of any tribe. The proud tribes treat them as curs at the gate, the Silver Fangs above all, and the Red Talons despise them for living among men. Yet every tribe needs what they know, and few Garou who have seen them defend a city's outcasts call them cowards twice. They are on uneasy but practical terms with the Glass Walkers, the other tribe of the cities.

pages.title: Bra'tac
infobox: Well over a hundred and thirty by the 1990s
pages.html:
Bra'tac is a Jaffa master of Chulak who was once First Prime of the Goa'uld Apophis. He has spent more than a century training warriors, and the better part of it doubting the gods he serves. In 1984 he was one of those whom the Beyonder carried off to Battleworld in the Secret Wars.

Life

Bra'tac has served the Goa'uld for well over a hundred years, kept strong by the larva he carries. He is now some hundred and thirty years old. He rose to be First Prime of Apophis, the highest warrior in a System Lord's army. For generations he has trained the Jaffa of Chulak in the staff, the hand and the discipline of the warrior.

Long ago he came to believe that the Goa'uld are not gods at all, only parasites who lie to their servants. He kept the belief to himself, because to speak it would have meant death. He passed it on only to those he trusted. The best of his pupils is Teal'c, who came to him as a boy after the System Lord Cronus put Teal'c's father, Ronac, to death. Teal'c succeeded Bra'tac as First Prime of Apophis, and he shares his old master's doubt.

The Secret Wars

In 1984 the Beyonder took heroes and villains from across the world to Battleworld, the patchwork planet on which he set them to fight. Bra'tac, the Jaffa master, was among them. So it was that a servant of Apophis stood among Earth's costumed heroes and their enemies ten years before Earth opened the Stargate again. When it was over he went home to Chulak.

On Battleworld Bra'tac saw Thor for the first time, across a field of heroes. He had been brought up, like every Jaffa, on the stories of the Thunderer who killed Jaffa who surrendered. He kept his distance. Thor, who did not know who he was, never noticed him.

Later years

In 1997 Teal'c turned against Apophis and joined Earth's SG-1. From then on Bra'tac was one of Earth's closest allies, and a leader of the free Jaffa who rose against their false gods.

In 1998 he turned against Apophis aboard his mothership and helped SG-1 destroy the fleet sent against Earth. In 2003 he was a slave in Ba'al's naquadah mines on Erebus until SG-1 got him out.

In the saga

Bra'tac has not yet appeared or been named in the saga.

pages.title: Caitiff
pages.html:
Caitiff are vampires without a clan. Either their sire's blood was too thin to pass on a clan's nature, or they were Embraced and abandoned before anyone could say whose line they came from. They carry no clan's gift and no clan's curse. The name is an old word for a wretch, or a coward, and the other Kindred mean it.

Nature

A Caitiff has no Disciplines that come to it by birthright, though it may learn any it can find a teacher for. Nor does it suffer any clan's weakness. Like every vampire, it descends at the last from Cain, but it cannot say by which road.

Most Caitiff are of the later generations, far from Cain, where the blood runs too weak to carry a clan's nature. Many were Embraced carelessly, by sires who neither named nor taught them. They learnt what they were on their own, and late. Many of the thin-blooded, of the fifteenth generation and after, are Caitiff too.

Standing

The clans despise them. The Camarilla accepts Caitiff who keep the Traditions, but it treats them as lesser Kindred. Many were sired without a Prince's leave, against the Tradition of the Progeny. A Prince may destroy such a childe along with its sire, and in some cities the Prince's scourge hunts down the unsanctioned among them. A Caitiff who does answer to the Camarilla is bound by its agreement of 1900 with the wizarding world, like any other vampire of the sect: it may not hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard.

The Sabbat throws its Caitiff into its wars, though one who proves itself may win a place in a pack. In the Sabbat the clanless are called the Panders, after Joseph Pander, who won them a place in the sect almost as if they were a clan.

Many Caitiff find their way to the Anarchs, who care less about lineage. Some elders read the growing number of Caitiff in the twentieth century as a sign of the Time of Thin Blood, which the Book of Nod says will come before Gehenna.

pages.title: Camulus
infobox: Camulus, the Celtic god of war
pages.html:
Camulus is a Goa'uld System Lord who was worshipped by the Celts of Gaul and Britain as a god of war. In 2004, with his fleet destroyed and his domain overrun by Ba'al, he asked Earth for asylum. Before long Earth handed him over to Ba'al, for reasons that were largely his own doing.

The god of war

Camulus came quietly to the Celts, in defiance of Ra's ban. He kept to Gaul and the south of Britain, well away from the North. The Britons named a stronghold after him, Camulodunum, the fortress of Camulus, which the Romans later made the first capital of their province. It is now Colchester. The Romans themselves worshipped him as a form of Mars, their own god of war.

Asylum

It was Camulus who sent word to Earth in the summer of 2004, after Earth had defeated Anubis, to propose a treaty. He came to Stargate Command with Amaterasu and Lord Yu to ask for Earth's help against Ba'al. 'If you do not help us stop him,' he warned, 'millions of humans will die.' The talks broke down all the same.

His own position was worse than he had let on. His fleet had been destroyed before he came, and his domain had been among the first to fall to Ba'al. When the others went home, Camulus stayed behind and asked for asylum. Through the Stargate, he told Elizabeth Weir, nothing waited for him but shame and torture.

The other System Lords branded him a traitor and a coward. Earth locked him up in a secure facility.

The bargain

Ba'al wanted him. Soon afterwards Ba'al told Earth that he had captured SG-1, and offered to exchange them for Camulus. It was not true. SG-1 had been trapped in one of Anubis's old bases, with Ba'al's Jaffa waiting for them at the Stargate outside.

Camulus thought he knew why Ba'al wanted him. He had once boasted at a meeting of the System Lords that he had found a device of the Ancients, although he had never said where. He gave Earth the address. There SG-3 found the device, with a zero point module, one of the Ancients' power sources. It had been booby-trapped. Jack O'Neill, by then the general commanding Stargate Command, called Camulus 'Cammy'. He worked out that Camulus had never discovered what the device was for, and had made sure nobody else would. Camulus denied it, then admitted that it had been worth a try.

O'Neill then offered Camulus a chance to kill Ba'al. He would go to Ba'al with the booby-trapped power source, trade it for SG-1 and let it do the rest. Camulus found the plan amusing. What O'Neill actually sent with him was Earth's own power source, which was dead. Earth kept the other.

Camulus went through the Stargate to Ba'al with his empty gift. SG-1 fought its way home on its own. What Ba'al did with Camulus is not recorded. Some months later Daniel Jackson could say simply that Camulus was gone, beaten by Ba'al.

pages.title: Canada
infobox: Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada
pages.html:
Canada is a self-governing realm of the Crown in North America, with its capital at Ottawa. Queen Elizabeth II is its Queen. It still flies the Canadian Red Ensign: the maple-leaf designs proposed for a new flag in the 1960s were never adopted. Lester Pearson, the Liberal leader of those years, never became Prime Minister.

The flag

The Canadian Red Ensign is a red flag with the Union Flag in the upper corner by the staff, and the shield of the arms of Canada in the fly. Canadians fought under it in both world wars. Since 1945 it has flown over Parliament and the federal buildings of the country.

In the 1960s there was talk of replacing it with a new flag bearing a maple leaf, but no such flag was ever adopted. In 1994 the Red Ensign still flies over Parliament Hill. It is the flag Canadians know as their own.

Government

Canada is governed by a Parliament at Ottawa under the Crown. The Queen is represented in Canada by a Governor General. Laws are made by the House of Commons and the Senate.
